translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: It means the servant begins every act by seeking the blessing and aid of Allah alone, invoking His name as the source of all good, and placing the act under the protection of His all-encompassing mercy and His special mercy toward the believers.

translation: All praise is for Allah, Lord of all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse establishes that every form of praise, gratitude, and glorification belongs exclusively to Allah, because He alone is the Creator, Sustainer, and Sovereign Master of all created beings and realms; it directs the servant to acknowledge Allah’s lordship with heartfelt thankfulness and worship.

translation: The Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate
interpretation: These two names describe God's mercy as both all-encompassing and ever-active: Ar-Rahman signifies the vast, universal mercy that sustains all creation in this world, while Ar-Rahim signifies the special, enduring mercy by which He guides, forgives, and rewards the believers in the Hereafter. Together they teach that God's mercy is not merely an attribute but the very source of every provision, guidance, and act of grace.

translation: Master of the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse affirms that on the Day of Judgment—the Day of Recompense when every soul will be held accountable for its deeds—absolute sovereignty, authority, and ownership belong to God alone. No created being will possess any independent power, rule, or judgment on that day except by His permission. It establishes God's exclusive lordship over the final reckoning and the ultimate outcome of all creation.

translation: You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.
interpretation: This verse is the heart of pure monotheism: it directs both worship and the seeking of aid exclusively to God, meaning that no created being deserves to be worshipped or relied upon ultimately for help. It teaches that true servant-hood combines sincere devotion with humble dependence—since one cannot even worship or remain steadfast without God’s assistance—so the servant turns wholly to Him in both purpose and need.

translation: Guide us to the straight path.
interpretation: This is a supplication for divine guidance to the clear, upright, and unwavering way of truth, faith, and righteous action that leads to Allah’s pleasure and eternal success. It asks not only to be shown the right path but also to be kept firm upon it and to walk it consistently with sincerity and obedience.

translation: The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have incurred wrath, nor of those who are astray.
interpretation: This is a prayer for guidance along the way of those whom Allah favored with true faith, obedience, and right guidance, and a plea to be kept away from the way of those who knowingly rejected the truth and thereby deserved divine wrath, and from the way of those who wandered into error out of ignorance and strayed from the right path.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Alif Lam Meem.
interpretation: The Basmala is an opening invocation seeking Allah's blessing and affirming His all-encompassing and specific mercy. The disjointed letters Alif Lam Meem are among the Qur'an's miraculous openings (al-muqatta'at); their precise meaning is known only to Allah, and they serve to draw attention to the revelation's divine origin and inimitability, inviting deep reflection.

translation: This is the Book, there is no doubt in it, a guidance for the God-conscious.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the Qur’an is the Book sent by Allah, utterly free of doubt in its origin, truth, and guidance. Its guidance is received by al-muttaqin—those who guard themselves against Allah’s displeasure through faith, obedience, and a heart inclined to accept the truth.

translation: Those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend out of what We have provided them.
interpretation: These are the ones whose faith is rooted in the hidden realities that lie beyond human sight and ordinary perception, who uphold prayer as a steadfast act of worship and obedience, and who freely give from the provisions God has granted them, recognizing that all they possess is a trust from Him and a means to purify the soul and benefit others.

translation: And those who believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain.
interpretation: This verse describes true faith as embracing the unity of divine revelation: accepting the Qur’an sent to Prophet Muhammad while also affirming the earlier scriptures sent by God to previous messengers, without rejecting any part of His guidance. Their certainty in the Hereafter is not merely intellectual but existential; it makes them aware that this life is accountable to God and that ultimate success or loss lies in the next life, so their faith governs their choices, priorities, and conduct.

translation: Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the believers described are firmly established on true guidance that comes from their Lord, not from their own selves or worldly sources. Such guidance is the means by which they attain true success—flourishing, deliverance, and the ultimate good in this life and the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve—it is all the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them—they will not believe.
interpretation: This verse describes those whose hearts have become so hardened by persistent rejection of the truth that warning and admonition no longer affect them. It is not that warning is useless in itself, but that these people have closed themselves off from accepting faith. The verse consoles the Prophet and the believers that they are not responsible for forcing belief upon anyone; guidance belongs to Allah, and only hearts that are willing to receive the truth will benefit from the warning.

translation: Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and over their eyes is a veil; and for them is a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse describes the condition of those who persistently reject faith after truth has become clear to them: their hearts are sealed so that guidance does not enter, their hearing is prevented from benefiting from divine revelation, and their sight is covered from perceiving the signs of God. This sealing is a just consequence of their chosen disbelief and arrogance, not an injustice, and it leaves them deserving of a severe punishment in the Hereafter.

translation: And among the people are those who say, 'We have believed in Allah and in the Last Day,' but they are not believers.
interpretation: This verse describes the hypocrites: they verbally profess faith in God and the Last Day in order to be counted among the believers, yet their hearts do not assent to that faith. It teaches that true belief is not merely a statement of the tongue but an inward conviction and sincerity that God alone fully knows, and that a claim of faith without inner truth is false before Him.

translation: They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive none except themselves, and they do not perceive.
interpretation: The hypocrites imagine that by showing faith outwardly while hiding disbelief they can mislead Allah and the believers, but Allah knows what they conceal, and their plotting harms no one but their own souls: it corrupts their inner reality, forfeits sincerity and reward, and leaves them spiritually blind to the ruin they are bringing upon themselves.

translation: In their hearts is a disease, so Allah increased their disease; and for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie.
interpretation: This describes the hypocrites, whose hearts are afflicted with the sickness of hypocrisy, doubt, and corrupt intention. Because they chose deceit and persisted in falsehood, God increased their spiritual malady and left them further entrenched in deviation, so their recompense is a painful punishment for the lies they habitually told.

translation: And when it is said to them, “Do not cause corruption on the earth,” they say, “We are only reformers.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the self-deception of the hypocrites: when they are forbidden from spreading corruption through disbelief, hypocrisy, and sowing discord, they deny any wrongdoing and claim to be setting matters right. Their claim is false because true reform begins with submission to God and His guidance; rejecting it and opposing the believers is itself the corruption they refuse to acknowledge.

translation: Unquestionably, it is they who are the corrupters, but they do not perceive.
interpretation: Their claim to reform is exposed as self-deception: by rejecting faith and sowing discord while imagining themselves wise, they corrupt both themselves and the community, yet their heedlessness blinds them to the true nature and consequence of their deeds.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Believe as the people have believed,' they say, 'Should we believe as the foolish have believed?' Unquestionably, it is they who are the foolish, but they know it not.
interpretation: This verse exposes the stance of the hypocrites: when they are called to sincere faith like that of the Prophet’s Companions and the true believers, they mock it and dismiss the believers as foolish. Allah responds by declaring that the foolish ones are in fact they themselves, because they have rejected true guidance and chosen misguidance while wrongly imagining themselves wise. Their tragedy is that they do not know this reality due to their ignorance and spiritual blindness.

translation: And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we were only mocking."
interpretation: This verse exposes the hypocrisy of those who show faith outwardly only to deceive the believers, while privately aligning themselves with their evil leaders and companions. Their public claim of belief is not sincere; it is a pretense and a mockery of faith and the believers. The verse warns that true faith requires consistency between the outward profession and the inward reality, and that duplicity and allegiance to falsehood are condemned.

translation: Allah mocks them and extends them in their transgression, [while] they wander blindly.
interpretation: Their mockery of the believers is answered by Allah’s just mockery: He exposes their folly, lets them continue in their arrogance and disbelief, and grants them respite so that they remain bewildered, unable to find the straight path. This is not injustice but the fitting recompense for their deliberate mockery and rejection.

translation: Those are the ones who purchased error in exchange for guidance, so their transaction brought no profit, nor were they guided.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who deliberately trade the clear guidance of faith for misguidance; their bargain is utterly unprofitable because it forfeits the truth and leaves them without true direction.

translation: Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire; when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darknesses, not seeing.
interpretation: This parable describes the hypocrites: they outwardly adopt faith and enjoy its temporary light—safety, belonging, and worldly advantage—but their hearts lack sincere belief. When trial or the moment of truth comes, God removes that borrowed radiance, exposing them to spiritual blindness. They are left in layers of darkness—doubt, hypocrisy, and loss—unable to see guidance or distinguish truth from falsehood, because they relied on outward appearance rather than inward submission to God.

translation: Deaf, mute, and blind—so they will not return.
interpretation: Their spiritual senses are closed: they cannot hear the truth, speak it, or see it, and therefore they will not turn back from their misguidance to faith.

translation: Or like a heavy rain from the sky, in it are darknesses, thunder and lightning; they put their fingers into their ears because of the thunderclaps, fearing death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers.
interpretation: This parable depicts the state of the hypocrites before the Qur’an’s powerful warnings. The storm from heaven stands for the revelation that brings both illuminating truth and terrifying admonition; the darkness represents their confusion and doubt, thunder symbolizes the divine threats that shake them, and lightning is the flashes of truth they cannot fully ignore. In their terror of what the message demands and warns of, they try to shut out hearing it, as though stopping their ears can stop death and judgment. But Allah encompasses the disbelievers—His knowledge, power, and judgment surround them completely, so their evasions cannot save them.

translation: The lightning almost snatches away their sight. Whenever it flashes for them, they walk therein; and when it darkens over them, they stand still. And if Allah had willed, He could have taken away their hearing and their sight. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse portrays the unstable spiritual condition of those whose faith is not firm: they may benefit from brief flashes of guidance or signs and move forward when circumstances are favorable, but when trials, confusion, or darkness descend, they halt and remain in place. Their movement is not rooted in steadfast faith but depends on changing conditions. The statement that Allah could remove their hearing and sight warns that even the faculties by which they perceive and respond, as well as the guidance they intermittently use, are entirely under Allah’s power. He can instantly deprive them of the ability to hear or see, leaving them in spiritual blindness and deafness. Thus the verse affirms Allah’s absolute omnipotence and warns that rejecting or wavering toward divine guidance places one in grave danger.

translation: O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, so that you may attain Taqwa (God-consciousness and righteousness).
interpretation: This is a universal divine call to all humanity to direct worship exclusively to the One who created them and all previous generations. Since He alone is the originator and sustainer of every people, He alone deserves their devotion, gratitude, and obedience. The ultimate aim of this worship is not merely ritual performance but the cultivation of Taqwa—a deep, protective awareness of God that transforms the heart and conduct, leading one to obey His commands, avoid His prohibitions, and live with moral and spiritual accountability.

translation: The One who made the earth a resting place for you and the sky a structure, and sent down water from the sky and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. So do not set up equals to Allah while you know.
interpretation: This verse establishes God's exclusive right to worship by pointing to His exclusive creative and sustaining acts: He alone spread the earth as a habitable floor, built the sky as a protective canopy, and sends rain to produce food. Since you know these blessings come from Him alone, it is irrational and ungrateful to assign partners, rivals, or equals to Him in divinity, worship, or lordship. The verse thus calls to pure monotheism and warns against shirk, associating partners with God.

translation: And if you are in doubt concerning what We have sent down upon Our Servant, then produce a surah like it and call upon your witnesses besides Allah, if you are truthful.
interpretation: This verse issues a decisive challenge to those who doubt the Qur’an’s divine origin: if they think it is humanly produced, they should attempt to produce even one surah comparable to it in eloquence, truth, guidance, and wisdom, and should call upon any helpers, deities, or witnesses they rely on besides God. The inability to meet this challenge establishes that the Qur’an is from God and confirms the truthfulness of His Messenger, while also exposing the helplessness of all false objects of reliance before God.

translation: But if you do not do it—and you will never do it—then fear the Fire whose fuel is people and stones, prepared for the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse follows the Qur’an’s challenge to produce something like it and declares that its opponents will never meet that challenge. Their failure is not merely a temporary inability but a permanent proof of the Qur’an’s divine origin. Therefore, instead of persisting in rejection, they are warned to protect themselves from the Fire, which is described as fueled by human beings and stones. This imagery conveys the terrifying intensity and insatiability of Hell: even people and hard, lifeless materials become its fuel, showing that no created thing can resist or extinguish it. Some commentators understand “stones” as the idols and false objects of worship that will be cast into the Fire along with those who worshipped them, thereby exposing their helplessness. The Fire is said to be prepared specifically for the disbelievers—those who knowingly reject God’s signs and refuse to submit to the truth after it has become clear. The verse is thus a severe warning meant to awaken hearts, humble human arrogance, and call people away from disbelief before they meet the punishment prepared for it.

translation: And give glad tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds that they will have gardens beneath which rivers flow. Whenever they are provided with a provision of fruit therefrom, they will say, 'This is what we were provided with before.' And it is given to them in resemblance. And they will have therein purified spouses, and they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse promises eternal gardens to those who combine faith with righteous action. The rivers flowing beneath them symbolize continual refreshment, life, and delight. The fruits of Paradise are brought to the believers resembling what they knew before, either the fruits of the world or earlier fruits of Paradise, so that they recognize them and rejoice, yet their true taste and excellence are beyond worldly comparison. The phrase 'in resemblance' indicates that the outward forms may be similar while the inner realities are far superior and ever-renewed. The purified spouses are free from every bodily, moral, and spiritual impurity, and the final promise is permanence: they will never leave or lose that bliss.

translation: Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable—even of a mosquito or what is above it. As for those who believe, they know it is the truth from their Lord. But as for those who disbelieve, they say, 'What did Allah intend by this parable?' He misleads many by it and guides many by it. And He misleads by it only the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: Allah’s majesty is not diminished by using any created thing, however small or seemingly insignificant, as a lesson. The objection of the disbelievers to the parable of a gnat exposes their failure to grasp that the worth of an example lies in the truth it conveys, not in the status of the object used. Believers accept it as revelation from their Lord and are guided by its wisdom. Unbelievers mock and question God’s purpose, and their rejection makes the same parable a cause of further misguidance. Yet God does not mislead by it except the fasiqun—those already corrupt, rebellious, and disposed to disobedience—because their own arrogance and resistance to truth bring about that misguidance, while humble hearts receive guidance.

translation: Those who break Allah’s covenant after ratifying it, and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and spread corruption on the earth — it is they who are the losers.
interpretation: This verse describes the people of ruin as those who discard the binding covenant of faith and obedience to Allah after having firmly accepted it, who cut the ties Allah commanded to be kept—such as kinship, justice, truthfulness, and loyalty among believers—and who work corruption in the earth through disbelief, oppression, and sin. Because they betray the trust placed upon them and destroy what Allah ordered to be built, they are the ones who lose every good in this life and the Hereafter.

translation: How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life, then to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse is a rebuke of ingratitude and denial: it confronts the human being with the plain fact that he did not create himself and does not control his own life. Being “dead” before life is understood as nonexistence or lifelessness before Allah brought one into being. The One who originated life from nothing, who alone decrees death, and who will resurrect for judgment is the only true object of worship. Therefore, rejecting Him is irrational and unjust, because existence, life, death, and the final return are all in His hand. The verse establishes God’s Lordship, His power over resurrection, and human accountability before Him.

translation: He is the One who created for you all that is on the earth; then He turned to the heaven and fashioned them into seven heavens; and He is, of all things, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the earth’s resources are a deliberate gift and trust for humankind, not accidents or independent powers. After creating earthly provisions, God directed His creative command to the sky and ordered it into seven distinct heavens, showing His sovereignty over the whole cosmos. The closing affirmation of His all-encompassing knowledge means that both the material world and the unseen realms are governed with wisdom, and humans will be accountable for how they use the earth’s bounties.

translation: And when your Lord said to the angels, 'I am placing a vicegerent on the earth,' they said, 'Will You place upon it one who corrupts it and sheds blood, while we glorify You with praise and sanctify You?' He said, 'Indeed, I know what you do not know.'
interpretation: Humanity’s appointment as God’s vicegerent on earth is grounded in divine wisdom that the angels do not fully perceive: their objection about corruption and bloodshed does not overturn God’s purpose, because God alone knows the greater good, the moral testing, and the eventual guidance and righteousness that can emerge from human free will.

translation: And He taught Adam the names, all of them; then He presented them to the angels and said, 'Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful.'
interpretation: This verse establishes that God granted Adam knowledge of the names of all things—their realities, properties, and distinguishing characteristics—as the basis for his unique dignity and fitness for vicegerency. When God displayed those things before the angels and challenged them to name them if their earlier claim or objection was truthful, they could not, revealing that their knowledge was limited to what God had taught them. The verse therefore affirms that true superiority in this context comes through divinely granted knowledge, and that Adam’s comprehensive understanding distinguished him in a way the angels could not match.

translation: They said, 'Exalted are You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, it is You who are the Knowing, the Wise.'
interpretation: This verse expresses the proper posture of creatures before God: they declare His transcendence and admit that their knowledge is entirely dependent on what He grants them. It teaches that no one possesses knowledge independently of God, and that human or angelic learning is always received, limited, and subordinate to His infinite knowledge and perfect wisdom. True knowledge and wise judgment belong to God alone, so the creature's part is humility, gratitude, and reliance upon His teaching.

translation: He said, “O Adam, inform them of their names.” And when he had informed them of their names, He said, “Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you were concealing?”
interpretation: This verse establishes that true honor and fitness for God’s trust are not determined by one’s created nature—whether angel or human—but by the knowledge God grants and the capacity to comprehend realities beyond mere appearance. Adam’s ability to name the things showed that God had endowed humanity with conceptual knowledge, language, and discernment, making Adam suited for the role of vicegerent. The angels’ earlier objection was thus answered not by force but by manifesting God’s wisdom. Then God declared that He alone knows the unseen in the heavens and the earth, and He knows both what His creatures openly express and what they hide in their hearts. This exposes that any doubt, arrogance, or secret intent—such as that of Iblis—is fully known to God, and that His decree is based on complete knowledge, not on outward claims or appearances.

translation: And [mention] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate before Adam," so they prostrated, except Iblis. He refused and was arrogant and became one of the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse means that Allah commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam as an act of honor and obedience to Allah’s command, not as worship of Adam. All the angels obeyed, but Iblis refused out of arrogance and pride, considering himself superior to Adam. His refusal was not merely a lapse but a deliberate rejection of Allah’s command, and so he became among the disbelievers.

translation: And We said, 'O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from it freely wherever you wish; but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse establishes Adam and his wife in the Garden as a gift from God, granting them generous freedom to enjoy its provision, while testing them with one clear limit. The prohibition is against approaching the tree, not merely eating from it, which teaches that God's commands include safeguards against falling into sin. The warning that they would become wrongdoers means that disobedience to God is ultimately a wrong against one's own soul, and the command itself is a test of gratitude, obedience, and trust in God's wisdom.

translation: Then Satan caused them to slip from it and brought them out of what they had been in. And We said: 'Descend, some of you being enemies to others. And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and provision for a time.'
interpretation: This verse explains the consequence of yielding to Satan's deception: it leads to loss of blessing and removal from the state of ease and obedience in which Adam and his wife were. Satan's role is to entice and mislead, not to compel; the disobedience was their choice. The command to descend marks the beginning of human life on earth, a realm of trial, where people will experience conflict and enmity—both with Satan and among themselves. Yet the earth is not the final home; it is a temporary dwelling and source of provision until the appointed term. The verse thus teaches that Satan is a clear enemy, worldly life is transient, and human beings are responsible for seeking God's guidance to return to the path of safety.

translation: Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance. Indeed, He is the Acceptor of Repentance, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that after Adam’s lapse, God did not abandon him in guilt; rather, He mercifully guided him to the means of turning back. The “words” Adam received were an inspired plea for forgiveness, showing that true repentance begins with God’s grace awakening the heart to seek Him. Adam’s acceptance demonstrates that sincere remorse does not end in despair but in divine pardon. God’s names at-Tawwāb and ar-Rahīm here reveal that He continually welcomes those who return to Him and surrounds them with mercy, so no failure is final for one who turns back with humility.

translation: We said, 'Go down from it, all together. And when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance — there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.'
interpretation: This verse establishes that life on earth is a stage of testing accompanied by God’s guidance. The command to descend all together marks the beginning of the human collective experience, not a permanent abandonment; God immediately follows it with the promise of guidance. Therefore, fear and grief are removed not by worldly security but by following divine guidance. Whoever accepts God’s guidance through His prophets and revelations is granted safety regarding the future and freedom from regret over the past, because their ultimate return is to God’s mercy and pleasure.

translation: And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse means that those who reject faith and knowingly deny God's revealed signs and verses are the people of the Fire, and their punishment is everlasting; it establishes that persistent unbelief and denial of divine guidance lead to eternal separation from God's mercy in the Hereafter.

translation: O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and fulfill My covenant, and I will fulfill your covenant, and fear Me alone.
interpretation: This verse establishes that divine blessings place a binding moral obligation upon the recipient: gratitude is not mere sentiment but covenant loyalty expressed through obedience. God's promise to fulfill the covenant is conditional upon human fidelity, showing that His grace both precedes and responds to sincere commitment. The final command to fear Him alone directs all reverential awe, ultimate trust, and moral accountability exclusively to God, freeing the heart from subservience to any created power.

translation: And believe in what I have sent down, confirming that which is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it; and do not exchange My verses for a small price; and fear Me alone.
interpretation: This verse addresses the People of the Book, especially the Children of Israel, calling them to accept the revelation sent to Muhammad because it confirms the earlier scriptures they already possess. Rejecting it would not be loyalty to God but a betrayal of the very truth they were given. The warning against being “the first disbeliever in it” means they must not lead the way in rejecting it, since their example carries grave responsibility. “Do not exchange My verses for a small price” condemns using divine revelation for worldly gain—concealing, distorting, or denying it for wealth, status, approval, or power. “Fear Me alone” directs all reverence, obedience, and accountability to God, not to people or worldly interests. Thus the verse demands sincere acceptance of God’s final guidance and absolute refusal to trade His truth for any temporary benefit.

translation: And do not mix the truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth while you know [it].
interpretation: This verse forbids two related forms of dishonesty: confusing or distorting the truth by blending it with falsehood, and deliberately hiding the truth after knowing it. It condemns knowingly concealing what is right—especially divine guidance and clear evidence—and calls for truth to be stated, preserved, and distinguished from falsehood in speech, teaching, testimony, and religious matters.

translation: And establish prayer and give zakah and bow with those who bow.
interpretation: This is a directive to make worship and social responsibility inseparable: prayer trains the self in God-consciousness and obedience, zakah purifies wealth and sustains the needy, and bowing together with the worshippers signifies humble submission within a united community. It teaches that faith is not merely private belief but is expressed through regular devotion, generous giving, and joining the community in humble obedience to God.

translation: Do you order people to righteousness while forgetting yourselves, even though you recite the Book? Will you not then reason?
interpretation: This verse rebukes those who call others to virtue and obedience while neglecting the same duties in their own lives. Reciting the Scripture should produce self-accountability and sincere action, not hypocrisy or selective guidance. The closing question calls them to reason rightly: true knowledge of the Book must first reform the one who knows it, so that teaching others is joined with practicing what is taught.

translation: And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is burdensome except for the humble.
interpretation: This verse directs believers to seek God’s help in every difficulty through patience and prayer. Patience here means steadfastness, self-restraint, and trusting God’s decree even when hardship continues; prayer means turning to God with sincerity, need, and devotion. The burden and difficulty mentioned refer to prayer or to this whole command: it feels heavy to the selfish ego except for those who are truly humble before God. The humble are those whose hearts are softened by awe of God, who submit to His will, remember His presence, and trust His promise. For them, prayer is not an oppressive duty but a refuge, strength, and intimate connection with their Lord.

translation: Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that to Him they will return.
interpretation: This describes the inner conviction that makes worship and obedience light: the servant lives with the certainty that he will stand before his Lord and return to Him for reckoning, so this certainty shapes his conduct, strengthens his patience, and keeps him devoted to prayer and accountability.

translation: O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds.
interpretation: This is a divine summons to the descendants of Israel to recall the blessings, covenant, and guidance God granted them—such as deliverance from oppression, prophets, scripture, and miracles—and the distinction He gave them among the nations of their time by making them bearers of His message. The remembrance is meant to awaken gratitude, faithfulness, and acceptance of subsequent divine guidance, not to establish an inherent or everlasting superiority. Their preference was a historical trust tied to obedience, and it placed a greater responsibility upon them rather than a license for privilege.

translation: And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul in the least, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: This verse establishes that ultimate accountability before God is individual and inescapable: on the Day of Judgment, no person can bear another’s burden, no intercession will be accepted from anyone without God’s permission, no ransom or compensation will be taken, and no helper can rescue. It warns against relying on external ties, wealth, or the merits of others, and calls one to secure salvation through sincere faith, repentance, and righteous deeds.

translation: And [remember] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who were afflicting you with terrible torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women. And in that was a great trial from your Lord.
interpretation: This verse reminds the Children of Israel of God’s mercy in rescuing them from Pharaoh’s oppressive rule, which sought to weaken and humiliate them by killing their male children and keeping their women alive in servitude. Their deliverance was both a blessing and a test: it called for gratitude, obedience, and trust in God, while the persecution itself was a trial through which God refined them and demonstrated that He hears the cries of the oppressed and is able to save them from the mightiest tyrants.

translation: And [remember] when We parted the sea for you and saved you, and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were looking on.
interpretation: This verse reminds the Children of Israel of a great divine favor and miraculous deliverance: God split the sea to create a safe path for them, rescued them from Pharaoh’s oppression and pursuit, and destroyed Pharaoh’s followers by drowning them while the Israelites witnessed it. It establishes God’s absolute power over nature and tyrants, confirms His support for His messengers and believing communities, and calls the recipients to gratitude, obedience, and trust in God rather than ingratitude or arrogance after being saved.

translation: And when We appointed for Moses forty nights, then you took the calf [for worship] after him, and you were wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse condemns the Israelites’ turning to the golden calf during Moses’ absence on Mount Sinai. The forty nights were a divinely appointed period for Moses to receive revelation, but the people, left without their prophet, replaced pure monotheism with idolatry. Their act is called zulm—wrongdoing against themselves and betrayal of the covenant—because worshipping a creature instead of the Creator is the gravest injustice. It teaches that true faith must remain firm even when prophetic guidance is temporarily absent, and that divine delay is a test, not permission to invent false objects of worship.

translation: Then We forgave you after that, so that you might be grateful.
interpretation: This verse declares that Allah pardoned the Children of Israel after their grave sin of taking the calf for worship. The pardon was not because they deserved it, but as a mercy meant to awaken in them thankfulness. True gratitude here is not merely verbal; it is recognizing that forgiveness itself is a gift, and responding with sincere obedience, repentance, and devotion to Allah alone. Thus the verse teaches that divine forgiveness is granted to lead the forgiven person toward a life of thankfulness and renewed faithfulness.

translation: And [remember] when We gave Moses the Scripture and the Criterion, so that you might be guided.
interpretation: This verse reminds the Children of Israel of God’s favor in giving Moses the Scripture—the Torah—and the Criterion (al-Furqan), which distinguishes truth from falsehood, right from wrong, and guidance from misguidance. Divine revelation and discernment were granted so that they could follow the clear path and attain guidance.

translation: And [remember] when Moses said to his people, 'O my people, you have indeed wronged yourselves by taking the calf [for worship]. So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves; that is better for you in the sight of your Creator.' Then He accepted your repentance. Indeed, He is the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse presents repentance as a return to the Creator that must go beyond regret and strike at the root of the sin. Because idolatry is not merely an external offense but a corruption of the self, Moses calls it wronging one's own soul. The command to kill themselves was a severe, literal act of submission imposed on those who had taken the calf: the guilty were to be put to death by the believing members of their own community, so that the body of Israel might be purged of its betrayal. Its meaning is that the pain of obedience and self-negation is better than the lasting harm of persisting in sin, and that God's mercy is not closed even to grave disobedience. When they submitted, God turned toward them in forgiveness, showing that He is the One who repeatedly accepts repentance and extends mercy to those who return to Him.

translation: And [remember] when you said, 'O Moses, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly,' so the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.
interpretation: Their demand to see Allah openly as a precondition for believing Moses was an act of insolence and a refusal to accept the limits of human perception. It shows that faith is not to be founded on arrogant demands for direct sensory vision of God, which is impossible in this worldly existence, and that such defiance brought down a devastating punishment. The thunderbolt that overtook them while they watched was a fitting recompense for their stubbornness and a demonstration that Allah's power can seize those who test His majesty with impossible conditions.

translation: Then We raised you up after your death, so that you might be grateful.
interpretation: This means that Allah restored them to life after He had caused them to die as a consequence of their transgression, not because they deserved it, but as a mercy and a test: so that they would recognize His favor, turn to Him in thankfulness, and use their renewed life in obedience, worship, and acknowledgment of His power over life and death.

translation: And We shaded you with clouds and sent down upon you manna and quails, saying: Eat from the good things We have provided you. And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.
interpretation: This verse recounts Allah’s abundant favors upon the Children of Israel during their journey: He sheltered them from the heat with clouds and provided them with manna and quails as pure, wholesome sustenance. The command “Eat from the good things We have provided you” teaches that divine provision is meant to be received with gratitude and obedience, not greed, complaint, or rebellion. Their later disobedience did not diminish or harm Allah in any way; rather, it brought loss and harm upon their own souls. Thus the verse establishes both the generosity of Allah and the reality that human wrongdoing ultimately returns to the wrongdoer.

translation: And when We said, 'Enter this city and eat from it wherever you wish in abundance, and enter the gate in prostration and say, 'Hittah' [a plea for forgiveness]; We will forgive you your sins, and We will increase the doers of good.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's forgiveness is not earned by mere ritual but by a combination of humble submission, acknowledgment of one's sins, and a sincere plea for pardon. The command to enter with humility and to utter a word of repentance shows that the barrier to divine mercy is human arrogance and stubbornness, not God's unwillingness to forgive. The added promise of increase for the doers of good reveals that repentance does not merely restore the sinner to a neutral state; it opens the way to greater divine grace and reward for those who continue to act righteously.

translation: But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than what had been said to them, so We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the heaven because they were transgressing.
interpretation: This verse condemns the deliberate distortion and mockery of God’s command: the wrongdoers replaced the exact words of repentance and obedience they were ordered to say with a different, contemptuous wording. Their outward verbal change exposed an inner refusal to submit, so divine punishment descended upon them from above. The lesson is that altering, ridiculing, or defiantly twisting God’s revealed commands—especially after clear instruction—invites severe consequences, and that persistence in disobedience is the cause of such punishment.

translation: And [remember] when Moses sought water for his people, We said: “Strike the stone with your staff.” Then twelve springs gushed forth from it. Each group of people knew their drinking place. “Eat and drink from Allah’s provision, and do not go about the earth spreading corruption.”
interpretation: This verse presents water as a sign of Allah’s exclusive power to sustain life and to answer the call of His prophet on behalf of a whole community. The twelve springs indicate that divine provision is not only miraculous but organized and just, reaching every tribe according to its need and place. The command to eat and drink while avoiding corruption teaches that receiving Allah’s bounty is inseparable from moral responsibility: gratitude must show itself in obedience, stewardship, and social justice, not in greed, oppression, waste, or rebellion that ruins the earth. Thus the miracle is not merely a past wonder; it is a call to recognize every provision as from Allah and to use it in ways that preserve faith and order rather than corrupt them.

translation: And [remember] when you said, 'O Moses, we will never endure one kind of food; so call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions.' He said, 'Will you exchange what is lower for what is better? Go down to Egypt, for indeed you will have what you asked.' And humiliation and misery were struck upon them, and they earned wrath from Allah. That was because they used to reject the signs of Allah and kill the prophets unjustly. That was because they disobeyed and were transgressing.
interpretation: This verse diagnoses a people who, though favored with divinely provided sustenance, treated it with contempt and craved the ordinary produce of Egypt. Their complaint was not simply about food; it expressed a deeper refusal to accept God's chosen order and a preference for the familiar, base, and material over the higher, spiritual, and divinely appointed good. Moses' rebuke—'Will you exchange what is lower for what is better?'—exposes the inversion of values at work: they were willing to trade superior guidance and contentment for inferior cravings. When God says, 'Go down to Egypt, for indeed you will have what you asked,' it shows that He may let a person obtain the worldly thing he demands, but if the demand springs from ingratitude and rebellion, the gift itself becomes a path to degradation. The humiliation, misery, and divine wrath that follow are therefore not arbitrary; they are the fruit of unbelief in God's signs, unjust violence against His prophets, and a settled habit of disobedience and transgression. The passage warns that rejecting revelation and despising God's provision leads to a downward movement—from spiritual dignity to worldly servitude and ruin.

translation: Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians—whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteousness—will have their reward with their Lord, and there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse means that God's reward is not tied to a mere communal label but to the combination of true faith in God and the Last Day and righteous action. Whoever fulfills this among the mentioned groups will receive their due reward from their Lord and will be secure from fear and sorrow. It does not abolish the need for guidance and obedience to God's final revelation; rather, it states the enduring principle that sincerity of faith and good deeds are what matter before God.

translation: And [mention] when We made a covenant with you and raised the Mount above you, [saying], 'Take what We have given you with strength and remember what is in it, so that you may become righteous.'
interpretation: This is a reminder to the Children of Israel of the solemn covenant they entered into with God to obey Him and follow His revealed Book. The raising of the Mount above them was a miraculous sign instilling awe and urgency, making clear that the covenant was not to be taken lightly. The command “take what We have given you with strength” means to receive the Torah with serious resolve, firm adherence, and energetic obedience, not with half-heartedness or selective acceptance. “Remember what is in it” means to keep its teachings present in mind and practice, not merely to recite or preserve it outwardly. The purpose is “so that you may become righteous”: that this firm commitment and continual remembrance may produce taqwa, a guarding of oneself against disobedience and a life lived in reverent consciousness of God.

translation: Then you turned away after that. And if it were not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Children of Israel after they had been bound by a covenant and had witnessed clear signs, yet they turned away from obedience and broke their pledge. It declares that their preservation, forgiveness, and any opportunity for reform were not due to their own deserving, but solely to Allah’s favor and mercy. Had He not granted them that grace, they would have been utterly ruined and counted among the losers, deprived of His reward and exposed to loss in this life and the Hereafter.

translation: And you had certainly known those among you who transgressed the Sabbath, so We said to them, 'Be apes, despised.'
interpretation: This is a warning against knowingly transgressing God's sacred commands, especially by using deceitful tricks to appear obedient while violating the law's intent. The punishment of becoming 'apes, despised' signifies a severe divine humiliation: those who corrupt their covenant and mock God's limits are stripped of dignity, made examples of disgrace, and cast out of His mercy. It teaches that God cannot be deceived by legalistic loopholes, and that deliberate rebellion against clear divine prohibitions invites a degrading punishment that serves as a lesson for later generations.

translation: So We made it an exemplary punishment for those before it and those after it, and an admonition for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Allah’s punishment of the Sabbath-breakers was turned into a lasting sign and deterrent, warning the people of that generation and subsequent generations against transgressing His commands. Its benefit, however, is not automatic: it becomes a true admonition only for the muttaqun—those who are conscious of Allah and guard themselves against disobedience. Thus divine historical punishments serve to uphold moral and religious boundaries and to instruct hearts that are willing to take heed.

translation: And [mention] when Moses said to his people, 'Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow.' They said, 'Do you take us in mockery?' He said, 'I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant.'
interpretation: This exchange shows that when a divine command strikes the people as strange or inconvenient, their first impulse can be to challenge the messenger rather than examine themselves. Their question, 'Do you take us in mockery?', reveals that they measured the command by their own assumptions about what is reasonable, and so they suspected the prophet of playing with them. Moses’ response is not defensive cleverness but a turning to God for protection from the ignorance that mocks sacred instruction. The verse therefore teaches that true guidance requires humility before revelation: one may ask for clarification, but one must not treat God’s command as a joke or belittle the one who conveys it. Moses’ fear of being among the ignorant also shows that ridicule of divine matters is not merely a failure of understanding but a moral and spiritual danger from which even a prophet seeks refuge.

translation: They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is." He said, "He says: It is a cow neither old nor virgin, middle-aged between that. So do what you are commanded."
interpretation: This verse exposes the evasive questioning of the Children of Israel after they were commanded to slaughter a cow. Instead of obeying promptly, they kept asking for more details, and Moses conveyed God’s answer: the cow was to be neither aged nor young, but of middle age. The lesson is that clear divine commands should be met with submission, not endless haggling over particulars that delays obedience; hence the closing command to do what they were ordered.

translation: They said, “Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is.” He said, “He says: It is a yellow cow, intensely yellow in color, delighting those who look at it.”
interpretation: This verse shows the Israelites’ persistent evasiveness and their habit of adding conditions instead of promptly submitting to God’s command. The vivid yellow color described here is not merely an incidental detail; it signifies that the required cow would be unmistakably distinct, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, leaving no room for ambiguity. Yet their repeated questioning, rather than bringing them closer to obedience, made the matter more constrained for them, teaching that delaying compliance through excessive inquiry can turn a simple command into a burden.

translation: They said, “Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is. Indeed, the cows have become ambiguous to us, and indeed, if Allah wills, we will be guided.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the Israelites’ evasive procrastination: rather than promptly obeying God’s command to sacrifice a cow, they kept demanding further specifications, claiming that all cows seemed indistinguishable to them. Their closing words, “if Allah wills, we will be guided,” express a formal acknowledgment that guidance rests with God, yet their repeated questioning shows a reluctance to submit until every uncertainty was removed. The verse thus warns against turning sincere obedience into endless inquiry and shows that true guidance requires a willing heart, not merely verbal deference to God’s will.

translation: He said, 'He says that it is a cow neither trained to plow the earth nor to water the crop, sound, without any blemish on it.' They said, 'Now you have brought the truth.' So they slaughtered it, and they almost did not do it.
interpretation: This verse exposes the evasive, delaying attitude of the Children of Israel toward God's command. The more they questioned Moses, the more restrictive the required cow became, until it was described as one not used for labor or irrigation and completely free of defect. Their words, 'Now you have brought the truth,' show that they only conceded after every excuse was exhausted, and their slaughtering it while almost not doing so reveals reluctant, pressured obedience rather than prompt submission. The lesson is that divine commands should be fulfilled immediately and sincerely; excessive questioning and stalling can turn a simple duty into a heavy burden and expose hardness of heart.

translation: And [remember] when you killed a person and disputed about it; and Allah is the One who brings forth what you were concealing.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Children of Israel after a murder had occurred among them: they killed a person and then fell into dispute, each party shifting blame and hiding the truth. It teaches that Allah is fully aware of hidden matters and will expose whatever His servants try to conceal. Divine justice is not defeated by human deception; Allah can bring the truth to light in ways beyond human expectation, as shown by the subsequent command concerning the cow and the slain man. Thus it is a warning against concealment and a reassurance that Allah will reveal what is hidden and establish justice.

translation: Then We said, 'Strike him with part of it.' Thus Allah revives the dead and shows you His signs so that you may understand.
interpretation: This is a demonstration of Allah's absolute power over life and death: He commanded the Children of Israel to strike the slain man with a piece of the sacrificed cow, and by His will he was restored to life. The physical means had no power in itself; it was a sign establishing that resurrection is real, and that Allah can manifest His signs through whatever He chooses, so that people may use their reason and believe.

translation: Then your hearts became hardened after that, so they were like stones or even harder. And indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed, among them are those which split open so that water comes out, and indeed, among them are those which fall down from fear of Allah. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse condemns a spiritual condition in which the heart loses receptivity to divine signs and admonition. Even after witnessing clear miracles, the people’s hearts became harder than stone. The comparison is not to praise stones but to expose the hardness of hearts: stones can still respond to Allah’s power by gushing rivers, splitting with water, or falling in awe of Him, whereas a hardened heart may remain unmoved by truth. The verse warns that such hardness is not hidden from Allah, who knows every deed and will hold people accountable for what they do with the signs they receive.

translation: Do you then hope that they will believe you, while a party of them used to hear the words of Allah and then distort them after having understood them, while they knew?
interpretation: This addresses the believers’ expectation that the Jews of Medina would accept Islam. It means that some among them had heard God’s revelation, understood it, and then deliberately altered it, knowing full well what they were doing. Their rejection is therefore not due to lack of proof or mere misunderstanding, but to willful distortion and stubbornness. Hoping for mass acceptance from such people is misplaced; guidance only benefits those who approach divine truth honestly.

translation: And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe." But when they are alone with one another, they say, "Do you tell them what Allah has revealed to you, so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord? Will you not then reason?"
interpretation: This verse exposes the duplicity of those who outwardly profess faith to the believers but privately conspire among themselves, warning one another not to disclose the truths Allah had revealed in their scriptures—especially the signs and descriptions that pointed to the Prophet Muhammad—lest the believers use those very proofs as an argument against them before their Lord. It condemns this behavior as irrational: by concealing or manipulating divine truth to gain a temporary advantage, they only prove that they are not reasoning rightly, since Allah knows what they hide and what they reveal, and His truth cannot be defeated by dishonest argumentation.

translation: Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?
interpretation: This verse is a rebuke to those who hide their true intentions or deeds while presenting something else outwardly, as if God could be unaware of their secrecy. It affirms that Allah's knowledge is complete and all-encompassing: nothing hidden in the heart or done openly escapes Him. Therefore, hypocrisy, secret plotting, and concealed motives are fully known to God and subject to His judgment, so no one can deceive Him or avoid accountability.

translation: And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Book except as wishful thinking, and they are only conjecturing.
interpretation: This verse exposes a class among the People of the Book whose connection to revelation is not based on knowledge, study, or certainty, but on empty hopes, inherited assumptions, and conjecture. They do not truly know the Scripture; they merely wish, assume, or repeat claims about what they hope God will do for them. The verse warns that religious affiliation or wishful desire is no substitute for revealed knowledge, and that acting on mere speculation in matters of faith leads away from truth.

translation: So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands and then say, 'This is from Allah,' in order to exchange it for a small price. So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.
interpretation: This is a severe divine warning against knowingly fabricating or altering sacred Scripture and falsely attributing it to God for worldly gain. The double woe indicates that both the corrupt act itself and the unlawful profit it produces are condemned: it exposes the sin of exploiting religion for selfish advantage and affirms that no temporary or paltry benefit can justify distorting God's revelation.

translation: And they said, 'The Fire will not touch us except for a limited number of days.' Say, 'Have you taken a covenant with Allah? Then Allah will never break His covenant. Or do you say about Allah that which you do not know?'
interpretation: This verse rejects the claim that divine punishment is restricted to a few days merely by inherited privilege or wishful assertion. It demands proof: either they possess a binding covenant from God—and God never breaks His covenant—or they are inventing falsehood about Him. The only valid ground for hope or security is God’s revealed promise, not human speculation; to claim salvation or limited punishment without divine warrant is to speak about God without knowledge and to rely on a false hope that cannot override His justice.

translation: Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This is a decisive refutation of the notion that punishment in the Fire will be only temporary for the sinner. It means that whoever commits evil and then is wholly enclosed by his sin — persisting in it, refusing repentance, and dying in that state, so that it becomes his defining condition and cuts him off from faith and correction — such people are the rightful inhabitants of the Fire, remaining there eternally. The 'encompassing' is the key: it is not a passing slip or a sin followed by remorse and return to God, but a sin that surrounds the person from every side and seals him in rebellion.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds — those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse establishes that salvation and eternal bliss are not attained by mere profession of faith, but faith must be joined with righteous action. Calling them “companions of Paradise” signifies a settled, intimate belonging to Paradise, not a passing entry. Their abiding eternally affirms unending bliss, and this comes as the counterpart to the preceding warning about the companions of the Fire, showing that the Qur’an consistently pairs belief with deeds as the path to deliverance.

translation: And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: “You shall worship none but Allah, and be good to parents, and to relatives, orphans, and the needy; and speak to people kindly; and establish prayer and give zakah.” Then you turned away, except a few of you, and you were averse.
interpretation: This verse shows that God’s covenant is not merely a matter of affirming His oneness; it binds believers to a comprehensive moral and spiritual order. Worshiping God alone must be joined with excellence toward parents, care for relatives, orphans, and the poor, kind speech to all people, and steadfastness in both prayer and charity. The Children of Israel’s later turning away—except for a few—demonstrates that inherited identity or outward allegiance does not guarantee faithfulness. True fidelity is proven by upholding both the rights of God and the rights of His creatures, and breaking such a covenant is a grave moral failure that exposes the heart’s aversion to God’s commands.

translation: And [remember] when We took your covenant, [saying]: 'Do not shed your blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes.' Then you acknowledged it, while you were witnessing.
interpretation: This verse reminds the Children of Israel of a solemn covenant: the sanctity of life and the inviolability of homes among members of the same community. The prohibition of 'shedding your blood' means that killing a fellow member of the covenant community is like killing oneself, and 'expelling yourselves from your homes' means that driving others out is a collective self-expulsion, since the community is one body. Their affirmation while witnessing shows they accepted this obligation knowingly, so aggression against one another is a violation of that ratified covenant.

translation: Then, here you are, killing one another and expelling a group of your own from their homes, supporting one another against them in sin and aggression. And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, though it was forbidden for you to expel them. Do you then believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part? So what is the recompense for those among you who do that except disgrace in the life of this world? And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the severest punishment. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse condemns a people who claim allegiance to the Book but apply it selectively, accepting its commands when they suit them and discarding them when they do not. They honor the ransom of captives, which their Scripture required, while violating the prohibition against killing one another and expelling their own people from their homes. Their fault is therefore not a minor inconsistency but a corrupted relationship with revelation: they treat divine law as something to be divided, obeyed in part and rejected in part. Such selective belief is not true faith but manipulation of the covenant. Its consequence is humiliation in this world and the harshest punishment in the Hereafter, because Allah is fully aware of every action and no hypocrisy or injustice is hidden from Him.

translation: Those are the ones who have bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter, so the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who knowingly prefer the fleeting life of this world over the everlasting Hereafter, trading away faith, divine guidance, and eternal reward for temporary worldly gain. Their choice is a catastrophic loss: in the afterlife they will face a punishment that is never eased or reduced, and no intercessor, ally, or power will be able to rescue them. It teaches that worldly pleasures and advantages can never compensate for the loss of the Hereafter, and that those who persist in this exchange will find no help on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And We gave Moses the Scripture and sent after him messengers in succession; and We gave Jesus son of Mary clear proofs and supported him with the Holy Spirit. Is it then that whenever a messenger came to you with something your souls do not desire, you became arrogant? So some you denied, and some you kill.
interpretation: This verse exposes the root of persistent rejection of divine guidance: making one's own desires the standard for accepting or rejecting God's messengers. Arrogance is not merely intellectual doubt but a moral rebellion against any command that opposes the ego. It teaches that God's guidance has come through a connected chain of prophets, not isolated figures, and that Jesus was among those confirmed by clear signs and strengthened by the Holy Spirit, meaning the angel Gabriel. The accusation that some messengers were denied and others killed shows that claimed loyalty to God is false when it is selective. True faith requires surrender to God's message even when it contradicts personal inclination, and it requires honoring all of His messengers rather than treating revelation as something to be obeyed only when convenient.

translation: And they said, 'Our hearts are covered.' Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so little do they believe.
interpretation: This verse rejects the excuse made by those who claimed their hearts were veiled or sealed, preventing them from accepting the Prophet’s message. Allah clarifies that the real cause is not an innocent covering over their hearts but His curse upon them because of their persistent, willful disbelief. Their hearts are not excused; they have been expelled from divine mercy due to their rejection of faith. Thus their belief is paltry and profitless—they may acknowledge some truths, but they reject the decisive message, so their faith is negligible and cannot avail them.

translation: And when there came to them a Book from Allah, confirming that which was with them, although before they used to pray for victory against those who disbelieved — but when there came to them that which they recognized, they disbelieved in it; so the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse condemns the Children of Israel who had the Torah and knew its descriptions of the awaited Prophet. Before his coming, they would supplicate to God for victory over the disbelievers, expecting that the promised prophet would bring them triumph. Yet when the Qur’an came from God, confirming the Torah and the prophet they recognized, they rejected it out of envy and worldly ambition. Because they denied the truth after recognizing it, they deserved God’s curse.

translation: How evil is that for which they sold themselves: that they disbelieve in what Allah has sent down, out of resentment that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants. So they have incurred wrath upon wrath. And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who traded away their own souls by rejecting God's revelation, not because it lacked proof, but because of envy and resentment that God grants His favor and prophethood to whom He chooses among His servants. Their disbelief was rooted in arrogance and selfish grievance, so they brought upon themselves one wrath after another, and the disbelievers will receive a punishment that humiliates them.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Believe in what Allah has sent down,' they say, 'We believe in what was sent down to us,' and they disbelieve in what came after it, although it is the truth confirming what is with them. Say, 'Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you were believers?'
interpretation: This verse exposes the inconsistency of those who claim to follow what was revealed to them while rejecting the later revelation that confirms and upholds the same truth. Their claim to faith is proven false by their own history: true belief in God's prophets would never have led their predecessors to kill the prophets. Thus the verse condemns selective belief, which accepts only what suits one's inherited position and rejects the clear truth when it comes, especially when that truth confirms what they already possess.

translation: And indeed Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you took the calf [for worship] after him, while you were wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse rebukes the Children of Israel for the contradiction between the clear signs and miracles that Moses brought them and their subsequent descent into calf worship during his absence. It shows that being recipients of divine guidance does not excuse betrayal of it: their action was not merely a doctrinal mistake but a grave injustice against themselves and against God's exclusive right to worship. The verse thus condemns idolatry after manifest truth and warns that outward attachment to a prophet is meaningless if it is not joined to obedience and faithfulness.

translation: And [mention] when We took your covenant and raised above you the Mount [Sinai], [saying], 'Take what We have given you with strength, and listen.' They said, 'We hear and we disobey.' And they were made to drink [the love of] the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, 'Evil is what your faith commands you [to do], if you are believers.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the difference between outward assent and inward submission. The covenant at the Mount was meant to bind the Israelites to receive revelation with firm resolve and attentive obedience, but their response reveals a people who heard the command and inwardly refused it. The calf being 'drunk' into their hearts is a metaphor for how deeply idolatrous attachment had saturated their inner selves; disbelief made that love penetrate and dominate them. The final rebuke is that any claimed faith which produces disobedience, idolatry, and defiance cannot be true faith, for genuine iman commands adherence to God’s covenant, not rebellion against Him.

translation: Say, "If the home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you, to the exclusion of all people, then wish for death, if you are truthful."
interpretation: This verse is a decisive argument against those who claim that Allah’s final reward and Paradise are reserved only for them. It says that if such a claim were true, then death would not be a loss but the gateway to an exclusive eternal reward, so they should sincerely long for it. Their unwillingness to wish for death exposes that their claim is not based on certainty but on false presumption. The verse teaches that genuine faith in the Hereafter makes a person ready to meet Allah, while fear of death and clinging to worldly life reveal a heart that does not truly trust in what it claims to believe.

translation: And they will never wish for it, ever, because of what their hands have sent ahead. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse exposes the false claim of exclusive salvation: if they truly believed Paradise was reserved for them alone, they would eagerly seek death as the gateway to it. Their refusal, rooted in the deeds they have sent ahead, shows that they recognize their own guilt and cling to worldly life. Allah is fully aware of the unjust—nothing they conceal escapes Him, and His knowledge encompasses their rejection and deserving of punishment.

translation: And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life, and [even more eager] than those who associate others with Allah. Each one of them wishes he could be granted a life of a thousand years, but it will not remove him from the punishment that he should be granted long life. And Allah is Seeing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse exposes a spiritual disease: an excessive clinging to worldly life that surpasses even the desire of idolaters for survival. The wish for a thousand years is not merely a wish for longevity; it is a wish to postpone death, accountability, and the meeting with God. The verse declares that no extension of life can delay or avert punishment when one’s deeds deserve it. It also affirms that God sees every action, so no outward claim or hidden intention can escape His judgment. The implied remedy is to loosen the heart’s grip on dunya, repent, and prepare for the Hereafter rather than trying to outrun the inevitable.

translation: Say, 'Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel — it is he who has brought it down upon your heart by permission of Allah, confirming what was before it and as guidance and good tidings for the believers.'
interpretation: This verse rebukes those who harbor enmity toward the angel Gabriel. It clarifies that Gabriel is not an independent author of revelation but a faithful bearer of Allah’s command: he conveyed the Qur’an to the Prophet’s heart by Allah’s permission. The mention of the heart indicates that the revelation was received with full understanding, certainty, and firm conviction, not merely as external words. The Qur’an confirms the earlier revealed scriptures, provides guidance for all who seek the truth, and gives glad tidings specifically to the believers. Therefore, enmity toward Gabriel is irrational and self-defeating, because opposing him is opposition to the very revelation and guidance sent by Allah.

translation: Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael, then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse declares that enmity toward Allah, His angels, His messengers, or specifically Gabriel and Michael is disbelief, because all of them belong to one divine order and share the same mission of guiding humanity. To oppose any of God's chosen beings is to oppose God Himself, and so Allah declares Himself the enemy of those who persist in such rejection. It also teaches that true faith requires accepting all of God's messengers and angels without selectively rejecting some while claiming to believe in others.

translation: And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses, and none reject them except the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the revelation given to the Prophet consists of clear, unmistakable signs. Their clarity makes denial not an intellectual necessity but a moral and spiritual corruption: only those who have left the bounds of faith and obedience reject them. The term “fasiqun” denotes those whose disobedience has become entrenched, so their rejection is a symptom of inner rebellion rather than a lack of evidence. Thus the verse consoles the Prophet and warns that opposition to clear revelation exposes the opponents’ condition, not any deficiency in the message itself.

translation: Or is it that whenever they made a covenant, a party of them threw it away? Nay, most of them do not believe.
interpretation: This verse exposes covenant-breaking as a symptom of weak or absent faith. The rhetorical question expresses rebuke and astonishment at a repeated pattern: sacred pledges are discarded by a faction among them, yet this is not merely a moral lapse but evidence that most of them lack genuine belief. It teaches that fidelity to covenants, especially those made with God and His messengers, is inseparable from true faith, and it warns against the hypocrisy that rationalizes betrayal while claiming allegiance.

translation: And when there came to them a Messenger from Allah, confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Scripture threw the Book of Allah behind their backs, as if they did not know.
interpretation: This verse condemns the willful rejection of God’s messenger by a faction among the People of the Book. Although the Messenger came with clear confirmation of the revelation already in their possession, they cast God’s book behind their backs—meaning they abandoned, ignored, and treated it as worthless. Their action was not due to genuine ignorance but to deliberate denial, partisanship, and resistance to a messenger who did not suit their desires. “As if they did not know” exposes their feigned ignorance: they acted contrary to the very knowledge they had been given.

translation: And they followed what the devils recited concerning the kingdom of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic and that which was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. But they do not teach anyone unless they say, 'We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.' And they learn from them that by which they cause separation between a man and his wife. But they do not harm anyone by it except by permission of Allah. And they learn what harms them and does not benefit them. And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. And wretched is that for which they sold themselves, if only they knew.
interpretation: This passage dismantles the excuse that magic was a prophetic legacy. Solomon's dominion was not built on sorcery; his innocence is asserted, while the real source of sorcery is the devils' disbelief. The angels Harut and Marut appear not as patrons of magic but as a trial: their teaching came with an explicit warning that it is a test and that using it is kufr.
