translation: Then depart from where the people have departed, and seek forgiveness of Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This is a command concerning the Hajj: the pilgrims are to proceed together from the same place the mass of pilgrims proceeds from, without claiming any special privilege or separate rite. It establishes equality and unity in worship, and after fulfilling the rites they are told to seek Allah’s forgiveness for any shortcomings. Allah’s forgiveness and mercy mean He accepts the repentance of those who turn back to Him.

translation: And when you have completed your rites, remember Allah as you remember your forefathers, or with a stronger remembrance. And among the people is he who says, 'Our Lord, give us in this world,' and he has no share in the Hereafter.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the completion of Hajj should not lead back to pre-Islamic boasting and worldly preoccupation; rather, it should culminate in sincere and abundant remembrance of God. The comparison with remembering one's forefathers was meaningful to the original audience because Arab tribes took pride in ancestral lineage and used to recount it after Hajj. God elevates the standard: He deserves remembrance more intense and devoted than any inherited pride. The verse then identifies a category of people whose supplication is confined only to worldly gain—health, wealth, success, and the like—without seeking God's pleasure or the Hereafter. Such a supplication is deficient, and the one who makes it gains no reward or portion in the next life. It is a warning that ritual without God-centeredness and concern for the eternal can leave one empty, while the true believer asks for goodness in both this world and the Hereafter.

translation: And among them is he who says, "Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."
interpretation: This verse praises those who seek from God a comprehensive good: in this world, it means sound faith, beneficial knowledge, righteous deeds, lawful provision, health, safety, and contentment; in the Hereafter, it means forgiveness, Paradise, and nearness to God; and protection from the Fire is the foundation of all security. It teaches that the believer should not fixate only on worldly gain nor neglect it entirely, but should ask God for both worlds, recognizing that true success is salvation from punishment and attainment of eternal good.

translation: Those will have a share of what they earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning.
interpretation: This means that whoever turns to Allah seeking good in this world and the Hereafter will receive his due portion of reward for the deeds, supplications, and intentions he has earned; nothing of it is lost, and Allah’s accounting is swift, so His recompense is not delayed and every deed is precisely reckoned.

translation: And remember Allah during the appointed days. Then whoever hastens [to depart] in two days, there is no sin upon him; and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him—for the one who fears Allah. And fear Allah and know that to Him you will be gathered.
interpretation: This verse grants permissible latitude in the timing of leaving Mina during the Hajj while grounding that freedom in taqwa. The “appointed days” are the days of Tashriq, and remembering Allah in them means magnifying Him, thanking Him, and affirming His oneness after the completion of the rites. Hastening after two days or remaining for the third are both valid; neither choice is sinful in itself. The repeated “no sin” removes undue scrupulosity and shows that a legal concession is not moral laxity when it is joined to God-consciousness. The phrase “for him who fears Allah” ties the permission to taqwa: the value and safety of the choice depend on observing God’s limits, not merely on taking the easier option. The verse then commands taqwa and reminds the believer that all will be gathered to God, so ritual freedom must be lived under awareness of final accountability.

translation: And among the people is he whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and he calls Allah to witness to what is in his heart, yet he is the most stubborn of adversaries.
interpretation: This verse exposes a type of person whose eloquent and pleasing words about worldly affairs, along with his solemn appeals to Allah as witness of his inner sincerity, can mislead others. His true character, however, is revealed when he is opposed or challenged: he becomes a fierce, relentless, and unscrupulous opponent. The verse warns believers not to be deceived by outward charm, persuasive speech, or claims of a pure heart, since Allah alone knows what is hidden. It teaches that genuine faith and sincerity are proven not by words or oaths but by conduct, especially when truth and justice are at stake, and that a person who habitually resorts to bitter contention and deceit in disputes shows the corruption of his inner state.

translation: And when he turns away, he strives in the land to spread corruption in it and to destroy the crops and the offspring; and Allah does not love corruption.
interpretation: This verse exposes the conduct of a hypocrite whose outward appearance may seem pleasing but who, once he gains authority or turns away from guidance, exerts himself to ruin the land, wipe out its produce, and cut off its human generations. The destruction of “crops and offspring” symbolizes a comprehensive assault on the foundations of life—livelihood, stability, and continuity. Allah’s declaration that He does not love corruption is a decisive verdict: He disapproves of all such mischief, whether physical devastation or moral and social ruin, and no outward claim of religiosity can justify it. True faith must protect life, sustain the earth, and preserve generations, not destroy them.

translation: And when it is said to him, “Fear Allah,” pride seizes him in sin. So Hell is sufficient for him — and what an evil resting place.
interpretation: This verse describes a person whose arrogance prevents him from accepting admonition: when he is called to God-consciousness and to abandon wrongdoing, his sense of self-importance drives him further into sin rather than to repentance. His pride is not merely a flaw but the very means by which he persists in evil, so Hell becomes the fitting and sufficient recompense for him, and it is an utterly wretched place of rest and dwelling.

translation: And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the pleasure of Allah; and Allah is Compassionate to His servants.
interpretation: This verse praises the believer who is willing to give up his own self, life, desires, or worldly interests in exchange for Allah's good pleasure. Such a person does not act for praise, gain, or personal advantage, but out of sincere devotion and love for Allah. His sacrifice is accepted and valued by Allah, who is Ra'uf—intensely kind and compassionate—toward His servants, not unjust or harsh in His dealings with them.

translation: O you who have believed, enter into Islam completely and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: This is a command to commit wholly and sincerely to God's religion, accepting all of its teachings and obligations without selective or partial adherence, and a warning that Satan, an open enemy, tries to lead believers away through gradual and deceptive steps.

translation: So if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Almighty, Wise.
interpretation: This verse warns that turning away or deviating from the truth after clear evidence and guidance has reached a person is a serious matter. Such a fall is not overlooked, because God is All-Mighty—able to enforce His decree and exact justice—and All-Wise—perfect in His judgments, timing, and wisdom. It calls the believer to remain steadfast upon revealed truth, and reminds the one who wavers that God’s power and wisdom govern all consequences.

translation: Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, with the angels, and the matter is decided? And to Allah all matters are returned.
interpretation: This verse warns those who postpone faith until they witness the final decree. The coming of Allah here is not a physical movement like that of created beings; it refers to the arrival of His command and judgment in a manner befitting His majesty, with angels appearing in clouds. When that occurs, the matter will already be settled and no further opportunity for faith or repentance remains. It affirms that God alone controls the outcome of every affair, and that all matters—judgment, reward, and punishment—are ultimately returned to Him.

translation: Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them. And whoever changes the favor of Allah after it has come to him — then indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: This verse is a reproach and a warning. God directs His Prophet to confront the Children of Israel with the many manifest proofs and blessings He had granted them, so that they might realize that their rejection was not due to lack of evidence. The general lesson is that anyone who alters, distorts, denies, or misuses God’s favor — especially the favor of revelation, guidance, and clear signs — after it has reached him and he has recognized it, exposes himself to God’s severe punishment. The verse thus condemns deliberate ingratitude and tampering with divine guidance, and warns that such betrayal of the truth will not escape retribution.

translation: The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve, and they mock those who believe. But those who fear Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection. And Allah provides to whom He wills without account.
interpretation: This verse exposes a fundamental distortion in how people judge worth: the disbelievers take the fleeting adornments of worldly life as ultimate reality and therefore scorn the believers who prioritize faith and God-consciousness. But worldly advantage is not evidence of divine approval; on the Day of Judgment, the God-conscious will be elevated above their mockers. The phrase above them refers to rank, honor, and final success, not merely physical position. God’s provision, both in this life and the next, is not tied to disbelief or belief as a measure of worth, nor is it constrained by human expectations or accounting; He gives as He wills, abundantly and without limit. This reassures believers that present humiliation or deprivation is not their final state, and that true recompense is with God.

translation: Mankind was one community; then Allah sent the prophets as bringers of good tidings and warners and sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge between the people concerning that in which they differed. And none differed over it except those who were given it, after the clear proofs had come to them, out of envy among themselves. So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they had differed, by His permission. And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse teaches that human beings originally shared a single communal existence, but differences later arose, so God provided prophetic guidance and revealed books as the criterion of truth. The prophets both give glad tidings to the obedient and warn the disobedient, and the Scripture is sent with truth to settle disputes about belief and conduct. Yet disagreement over the revealed message did not occur because the proofs were unclear; it occurred among those who had received the Scripture, out of mutual envy and wrongful contention after clear evidence had come to them. God, by His grace and permission, guided the believers to the correct understanding of the truth in matters people disputed. Thus, true guidance is not merely a matter of inherited affiliation or argument, but a gift from God, who directs whom He wills to the straight path.

translation: Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the like of what came to those who passed away before you? They were touched by misery and hardship, and were shaken, until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, 'When will Allah's help come?' Unquestionably, Allah's help is near.
interpretation: This verse teaches that entry into Paradise is not attained by mere profession or wishful thinking; it is preceded by trials that purify the believers and distinguish true faith from mere claim. The suffering of earlier communities—poverty, illness, loss, fear, and instability—was not a sign of divine abandonment but part of the divine way of testing and refining. Even the Messenger and the believers with him reached a point of intense yearning and supplication, asking when God’s help would arrive. That question expresses profound need and trust, not disbelief or despair. God’s response, 'Unquestionably, Allah's help is near,' establishes that divine victory is certain and close by His measure, and that it comes to those who remain steadfast, patient, and hopeful throughout the trial.

translation: They ask you what they should spend. Say, 'Whatever you spend of good is for parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer. And whatever you do of good, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that charitable spending is not left to vague sentiment or display; it must be guided by a moral order of responsibility. The first claim belongs to parents, because their sacrifice and rights over the child are the strongest among creation. After them come close relatives, whose kinship creates an obligation that should not be neglected in favor of distant causes. Then the verse names those whose need is most urgent and whose vulnerability is greatest: orphans who have lost protection, the poor who lack sufficiency, and the traveler who is stranded away from home. By saying 'whatever you spend of good,' the verse widens the scope beyond a specific amount or type, showing that any sincere good offered in these directions is accepted. The closing statement that Allah knows whatever good is done corrects the hidden motive: reward is not measured by publicity, recognition, or social praise, but by the unseen intention and the real benefit given to those whom God has placed in one's path of duty.

translation: Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you do not know.
interpretation: This verse teaches that divine obligations may sometimes conflict with human inclination, especially when they involve hardship, sacrifice, or confronting aggression. The command to fight is prescribed within a framework of justice and defense, not as wanton violence, and the natural aversion to it reflects human attachment to safety, comfort, and life. Yet human perception is limited: what appears painful or undesirable may conceal protection, victory, spiritual purification, or a greater good, while what is passionately desired may lead to ruin. True faith requires trusting God’s wisdom over immediate emotional resistance, recognizing that His knowledge encompasses outcomes, consequences, and hidden realities that human beings cannot fully grasp.

translation: They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: Fighting in it is a grave matter. But preventing people from the way of Allah, disbelieving in Him, and preventing access to al-Masjid al-Haram and expelling its people from it are greater evils in the sight of Allah. And fitnah is greater than killing. And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able. And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies as a disbeliever, then those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse answers a question about fighting during a sacred month. It affirms that fighting in a sacred month is a serious sin, but it places that sin within a larger moral scale: the greater crimes are the polytheists' obstruction of God's path, their denial of Him, their blocking of the Sacred Mosque, and their expulsion of its people. Fitnah here means persecution, oppression, and faith-corrupting coercion; it is worse than killing because it attacks the very purpose of human life, which is to worship God freely and live by faith. The verse then warns that the enemies of the believers will keep fighting until they can force them away from Islam. Finally, it states that apostasy persisted in until death nullifies all deeds in this world and the Hereafter and leads to eternal punishment. Thus the passage teaches that sacred limits must be honored, yet the greater duty is to resist aggression and persecution, remain steadfast in faith, and never abandon Islam.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated and fought in the cause of Allah — those are the ones who hope for the mercy of Allah. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that genuine hope in Allah’s mercy is not passive wishful thinking; it is accompanied by faith, by sacrificing one’s home and attachments for Allah’s sake, and by striving in His path. Such actions do not earn mercy as a debt but express sincere reliance on Allah, whose forgiveness and mercy remain the ultimate ground of hope.

translation: They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In both of them is great sin and some benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit. And they ask you what they should spend. Say: The surplus. Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses so that you may reflect.
interpretation: This verse teaches that intoxicants and games of chance are not neutral acts: they carry grave moral and social harm, even if they may offer fleeting pleasure or material gain. Their evil—clouding reason, enslaving desire, causing addiction, wasting wealth, and breeding enmity—outweighs any passing benefit, so God's guidance directs people to avoid what corrupts the soul and society. It also answers the question of charitable spending by commanding generosity from one's surplus after legitimate needs are met, not from what would deprive one's family or harm oneself. The verse thus trains believers to weigh actions by their greater consequences and to reflect on God's signs as a framework for moral and economic life.

translation: ...in this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you about orphans. Say, “Setting their affairs right is best. And if you mix your affairs with theirs, then they are your brothers.” And Allah knows the corrupter from the amender. And if Allah had willed, He could have put you in difficulty. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the guiding principle in dealing with orphans is their genuine betterment—moral, material, and spiritual—not the guardian’s advantage. If a guardian shares household, wealth, or daily affairs with an orphan, that is allowed because the bond of faith makes them brothers, but God judges the inward intention: He distinguishes the one who seeks corrupt gain from the one who sincerely reforms and reconciles. The law is not meant to impose unbearable hardship; God could have made it stricter, but His command is shaped by might and wisdom, demanding justice and mercy while leaving the precise mode of care to sincere judgment.

translation: And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe. And a believing slave woman is better than a polytheistic woman, even if she pleases you. And do not marry polytheistic men until they believe. And a believing slave is better than a polytheistic man, even if he pleases you. Those invite to the Fire, but Allah invites to Paradise and forgiveness by His permission, and He makes clear His verses to the people so that they may remember.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the essential foundation of marriage in Islam is shared faith in Allah, not social status, wealth, beauty, or tribal affiliation. Unbelief is not merely a private difference; it represents a fundamental orientation of life away from God and toward the Fire. Therefore, a believer of low worldly rank is better than an unbeliever of high worldly appeal, because the believer participates in God’s invitation to Paradise and forgiveness. The verse also emphasizes God’s mercy: He does not leave people without guidance but clarifies His signs so they may reflect, remember, and choose the path that leads to eternal success.

translation: And they ask you about menstruation. Say, 'It is harm, so keep away from women during menstruation and do not approach them until they are cleansed. And when they have purified themselves, then come to them from where Allah has commanded you. Indeed, Allah loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves.'
interpretation: The verse answers a question about menstruation by declaring it a state of harm or impurity, and it prohibits sexual intercourse during that time—not ordinary social contact, kindness, or companionship. The command to keep away applies specifically to marital intimacy until the bleeding ends and the woman purifies herself, which includes the prescribed ritual bath. After purification, intimacy is permitted again in the manner Allah has made lawful, meaning through the natural place of intercourse and not in any forbidden way. The ending connects physical cleanliness with spiritual purity: Allah loves those who turn back to Him in repentance and those who seek to purify themselves outwardly and inwardly. Thus the ruling protects both bodily health and moral discipline, while reminding believers that true purity is both ritual and spiritual.

translation: Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth however you wish; and send ahead for yourselves; and fear Allah and know that you will meet Him; and give good tidings to the believers.
interpretation: This verse presents marital intimacy as a purposeful cultivation, not mere gratification: the wife is a field entrusted for nurturing offspring, chastity, and mutual good. The permission to approach 'however you wish' grants latitude in lawful manner and position within the natural place of cultivation, not license for harm or anal intercourse. The command to 'send ahead for yourselves' directs spouses to prepare righteous deeds and a sound legacy for the Hereafter, while 'fear Allah' and 'you will meet Him' make even private relations accountable. The glad tidings belong to believers who honor these limits and transform married life into worship and moral cultivation.

translation: And do not make Allah an obstacle in your oaths, preventing you from being righteous, fearing Allah, and reconciling between people. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse forbids using an oath sworn by Allah as an excuse to abandon good, avoid piety, or refuse reconciliation among people. If a person swears not to do something virtuous, they should not let that oath become a barrier to what is right; rather, they should do the good and expiate the oath, because Allah’s name must never be made a means of justifying negligence in obedience to Him or in maintaining peace among people. Allah hears every oath and knows every intention.

translation: Allah does not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He holds you accountable for what your hearts have earned. And Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing.
interpretation: This means that a mere slip of the tongue or an oath spoken without deliberate intent does not incur blame; accountability rests on the inner resolve and intention of the heart. God is forgiving of inadvertent errors and forbearing, not quick to punish His servants for what they did not seriously intend.

translation: For those who swear abstention from their wives, there is a waiting period of four months. Then if they return [to marital relations], indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse regulates the pre-Islamic practice of īlāʾ, where a husband would swear not to approach his wife, leaving her suspended indefinitely. Islam limits such an oath’s effect to a maximum of four months. During this period the husband is given the opportunity to reconsider and reconcile. If he returns to normal marital relations before or at the end of the four months, the oath is dissolved, and Allah’s forgiveness and mercy are extended to him for the oath and the period of estrangement; otherwise, the matter proceeds toward separation, as clarified in the following verse.

translation: And if they resolve upon divorce, then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This means that when the spouses firmly decide to separate after the waiting period, divorce becomes legally effective, and Allah hears the words they utter and knows the intentions and motives behind their decision. They are therefore accountable to Him for acting justly and not using divorce to wrong or harm one another.

translation: Divorced women shall wait concerning themselves for three menstrual cycles. And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they believe in Allah and the Last Day. And their husbands have more right to take them back in that period, if they desire reconciliation. And they have rights similar to those over them according to what is fair. And men have a degree over them. And Allah is Exalted in Might, Wise.
interpretation: The waiting period is a legal and moral safeguard: it protects lineage by determining whether pregnancy exists, preserves the possibility of reconciliation, and prevents hidden harm or deceit. Concealing what is in the womb or withholding the truth about the waiting period violates trust in God and accountability on the Last Day. During this period, the husband may revoke the divorce only if his aim is genuine repair, not control or injury. The verse establishes reciprocity: women have rights and obligations corresponding to those of men, to be fulfilled in recognized fairness. The degree given to men is a degree of responsibility and authority in the marital structure—such as maintenance, protection, and the prerogative of divorce—not a license to deny women their rights. God’s might and wisdom ensure that these rulings uphold justice, mercy, and the well-being of the family.

translation: Divorce is twice. Then either keep [her] in an acceptable manner or release [her] with good treatment. And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they cannot keep within the limits of Allah. But if you fear that they cannot keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame upon either of them concerning what she gives for her release. These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, it is they who are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse establishes that marital separation must be governed by justice, restraint, and mercy. The first two pronouncements of divorce are not final; they leave room for reconciliation during the waiting period, but that reconciliation must be honorable, not a means of harm or coercion. If the marriage cannot continue, the husband must release the wife kindly, without retaliation or withholding her rights. The verse forbids him from taking back what he gave her as dowry or gifts, except in the case where the wife seeks separation because the two fear they can no longer fulfill the rights and duties of marriage. In that case, she may return something as compensation to obtain her release, and neither party is blamed for agreeing to that. The closing warning defines these rules as Allah’s boundaries: they are not to be overstepped. Whoever violates them wrongs himself and others, because he replaces God’s wise limits with selfish desire and injustice.

translation: So if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him afterward until she marries another husband. Then if he divorces her, there is no blame upon them both to return to one another, if they believe they can keep within the limits of Allah. And these are the limits of Allah, which He makes clear to a people who know.
interpretation: This verse establishes the irreversible consequence of the third divorce: the former husband may not remarry his former wife unless she has entered a genuine marriage with another man and that marriage has ended. The ruling prevents divorce from being used as a means of coercion or repeated manipulation, and it protects the seriousness of marriage as a covenant governed by divine limits. If the second marriage ends and both the woman and her first husband believe they can fulfill the rights and obligations Allah has ordained, they may return to one another without sin. The verse presents these rulings not as arbitrary restrictions but as Allah’s boundaries, made clear for those who possess knowledge and take accountability seriously.

translation: And when you divorce women and they have fulfilled their term, then retain them in kindness or release them in kindness. And do not retain them to harm them, so that you transgress. And whoever does that has certainly wronged himself. And do not take the verses of Allah in mockery. And remember the favor of Allah upon you and what He has sent down to you of the Book and wisdom, by which He admonishes you. And fear Allah and know that Allah is Knower of all things.
interpretation: This verse governs the end of the waiting period after divorce: the husband must make an honorable decision either to reconcile and treat his wife justly or to release her without obstruction. Keeping her only to distress her or prevent her from moving on is oppression, and the one who does so wrongs his own soul through disobedience. It also forbids trivializing Allah’s laws or treating them as mockery, and calls believers to recall Allah’s favors, especially the revelation and wisdom He sent as guidance. The closing command to fear Allah and the reminder that He knows all things means that even hidden intentions and motives in marital dealings are fully known to Him.

translation: And when you divorce women and they have reached their term, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands, when they have mutually agreed upon what is lawful and fair. This is an admonition for whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day. That is better for you and purer. And Allah knows, while you do not know.
interpretation: This verse prohibits guardians, relatives, or others from using their authority to stop a divorced woman who has completed her waiting period from returning to her former husband, if both freely consent to a lawful and honorable marriage. It condemns coercion and unjust control over a woman’s marital choice, treating such obstruction as incompatible with sincere faith in Allah and the Last Day. The verse teaches that honoring mutual consent, upholding rights, and removing unjust barriers are better and purer for the community, and it ends by reminding people that Allah’s command contains wisdom beyond what they may perceive.

translation: Mothers shall nurse their children two complete years—for whoever desires to complete the nursing. And upon the father is their provision and clothing in a fair manner. No soul is burdened beyond its capacity. No mother shall be made to suffer because of her child, nor a father because of his child. And upon the heir is the like of that. If both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no sin upon them. And if you desire to have your children nursed by another woman, there is no sin upon you, provided you pay what you have agreed in a fair manner. And fear Allah, and know that Allah sees what you do.
interpretation: This verse establishes the child’s welfare as the governing purpose within family responsibilities: nursing is a right of the infant and a duty ordered with the father’s obligation to provide reasonably, without burdening anyone beyond capacity. It forbids parents from using the child as a means of harming or coercing one another, because the child must not become a tool of marital grievance. The permission for earlier weaning through mutual consent and consultation, and for a wet nurse when payment is made fairly, shows that the law is not rigid but seeks the child’s health, the mother’s well-being, and the father’s ability. The closing reminder of taqwa and Allah’s sight over all actions raises these domestic obligations from social custom to an act of God-consciousness and accountability.

translation: And those among you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait concerning themselves four months and ten days. Then when they have reached their term, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in a lawful manner. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse establishes the waiting period (‘iddah) for a widow: she must wait four lunar months and ten days after her husband’s death before she may remarry. This period protects lineage by making pregnancy known, honors the marital bond, and gives her time to mourn. Once the term is complete, she may lawfully decide for herself, including remarriage, without blame falling on her guardians or the Muslim community. The phrase “in a lawful manner” confines her actions to what Islamic decency and law permit. The closing words that God is fully aware of your deeds warn against pressuring, exploiting, or wronging widows and affirm that all motives and actions are known to Him.

translation: There is no blame upon you for what you allude to in proposing marriage to women or conceal within yourselves. Allah knows that you will mention them, but do not make secret appointments with them unless you speak an honorable word. And do not resolve upon the marriage contract until the prescribed term reaches its end. And know that Allah knows what is within yourselves, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse permits a man to hint indirectly at marriage to a woman who is still in her waiting period, and even to harbor that intention in his heart, without incurring blame. However, it forbids secret promises, illicit arrangements, or explicit proposals that violate the propriety of her waiting period; only honorable, modest words are allowed. It also forbids finalizing the marriage contract before the waiting period has fully ended. Since God knows the hidden thoughts and intentions, believers must guard their inner motives and avoid what He has prohibited. The ending affirms that God is Forgiving and Forbearing, meaning He pardons repentant slips and does not hasten punishment, so one should respond with restraint, sincerity, and repentance.

translation: There is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not touched them nor stipulated for them a dowry. And give them provision—the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means—a provision in a fair manner, an obligation upon the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse permits divorce before consummation and before a dower has been fixed, without sin, but it obliges the husband to give the divorced woman a parting gift (mut‘ah) suited to his financial capacity, whether he is rich or poor, in a recognized and kind way. This gift is a right and a duty upon those who seek to act with moral excellence, protecting the woman’s dignity and compensating her for the dissolution of the marriage before any marital right or agreed dower has been established.

translation: And if you divorce them before you have touched them, while you have already fixed for them an obligatory gift, then give half of what you fixed, unless they waive it, or the one in whose hand is the marriage contract waives it. And that you waive is nearer to righteousness. And do not forget graciousness among yourselves. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This passage applies when a divorce occurs before consummation but after the dower has been specified. The husband must pay half of the agreed dower as a settled right of the wife. However, the obligation can be altered by voluntary generosity: the wife may forgo her half, or the husband, who holds the marriage contract, may forgo his right to reduce the payment and pay the full dower. Such forgiveness and magnanimity are nearer to taqwa—God-consciousness and piety. The verse also reminds spouses not to erase the good and kindness that existed between them. Allah observes every intention and action, so dealings at divorce should reflect justice, mercy, and awareness of His presence.

translation: Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer, and stand before Allah devoutly obedient.
interpretation: This verse commands believers to consistently preserve and fulfill all the prescribed prayers, giving special care to the middle prayer, which is understood to be the Asr prayer. It further instructs them to stand before God in prayer with humility, stillness, and sincere obedience, directing their worship and devotion to Him alone.

translation: If you fear (danger), then (pray) on foot or riding. But when you are safe, remember Allah as He has taught you what you did not know.
interpretation: This verse establishes that prayer remains obligatory even in a state of fear, but God eases its conditions: when danger is imminent, a believer may pray while walking, riding, or in whatever manner is feasible, without the usual requirements of standing or facing the qiblah. Once security returns, one must restore the complete prescribed prayer and remember God with gratitude, because He taught believers acts of worship and guidance they would not have known by themselves. It shows that divine commands are suited to human capacity: hardship brings concession, while ease brings the full ordinance and thankfulness.

translation: And those among you who die and leave wives behind: a bequest for their wives, provision for a year, without turning them out. But if they leave, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in a lawful manner. And Allah is Almighty, Wise.
interpretation: The verse safeguards widows from being left destitute or forcibly removed from the marital home after the husband’s death. The husband’s estate is charged with a bequest that provides her maintenance and residence for a full year, and she is not to be expelled. If, however, she herself chooses to leave before the year is over, the heirs or guardians are not held responsible for any lawful decision she makes about herself, such as remarriage or moving. The ruling balances protection of the widow’s welfare with respect for her free choice, and it grounds that balance in God’s might and wisdom as the ultimate lawgiver.

translation: And for divorced women is a provision in a fair manner — a duty upon the righteous.
interpretation: This verse establishes that divorced women have a rightful claim to a parting provision or gift given according to what is recognized as fair, kind, and customary. It is not a favor left to the husband's discretion but a binding obligation upon those who are mindful of God. The verse ties the fulfillment of this right to taqwa, indicating that honoring the dignity and material needs of divorced women is an essential mark of righteousness and God-consciousness.

translation: Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses so that you may understand.
interpretation: Allah explains His signs and commands in a clear manner so that people may use their intellect, comprehend the intended guidance, and act upon it with understanding rather than ignorance or blind imitation.

translation: Have you not considered those who left their homes while they were thousands, fearing death? Then Allah said to them, 'Die,' and then He brought them back to life. Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward people, but most people are not grateful.
interpretation: This verse establishes that life and death are entirely in Allah's hands and that no human precaution can outrun His decree. The people who fled in large numbers to escape death were shown that their lives were not secured by their flight; Allah caused them to die and then restored them, proving His power to bring the dead back to life and confirming the reality of resurrection. His kindness and bounty toward people are vast, yet most people respond with ingratitude rather than acknowledging His favors and obeying Him.

translation: And fight in the way of Allah and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse commands believers to struggle in God's cause with sincere devotion, not for worldly gain, personal glory, or selfish ends, and to do so with the awareness that God hears every word and knows every intention. Since He is All-Hearing and All-Knowing, outward striving has no value without inner sincerity; the servant must align intention and action with divine command, trusting that God is fully aware of motives, circumstances, and the hidden state of the heart.

translation: Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan, so He may multiply it for him many times over? And Allah withholds and extends, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This is a divine encouragement to spend voluntarily in the way of God, described as a “loan” to God only to honor the giver, since God is free of all need. A goodly loan is one given sincerely for His sake, from lawful wealth, without boasting or harm, and with trust in His promise. God multiplies such giving far beyond its measure, in this world and the Hereafter. Because He alone withholds and extends provision, no one should fear poverty through charity; and because all will return to Him, the deed must be done seeking His acceptance alone.

translation: Have you not considered the assembly of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, 'Appoint for us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah.' He said, 'Would it be that if fighting were prescribed for you, you would not fight?' They said, 'And what is the matter with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah while we have been driven from our homes and our children?' But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away except a few of them. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse exposes the difference between loud readiness and obedient resolve. Their request seemed righteous and was justified by real loss and exile, yet it was still only a claim until God made it a duty. The prophet’s question tested whether their motive was submission to Allah or merely the recovery of what they had lost. When the command became costly, most withdrew, showing that grievance and emotion are not the same as faith. The few who remained are the truly steadfast. Allah’s knowledge of the wrongdoers means He knows those who pledge obedience and then abandon it once it demands sacrifice; such evasion is not hidden from Him.

translation: And their prophet said to them, “Indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut as king.” They said, “How can he have kingship over us while we are more entitled to kingship than he is, and he has not been given abundance of wealth?” He said, “Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature. And Allah gives His kingdom to whom He wills; and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that rightful leadership and authority are conferred by Allah according to His wisdom, not by human claims of entitlement, lineage, or wealth. The people judged by outward and material standards, but Allah selected Talut because of inward and functional qualifications: divinely granted knowledge and bodily strength. Thus, true fitness for rule includes wisdom and capacity to bear responsibility, and Allah’s sovereign choice cannot be reduced to popular preference or economic status. His giving of dominion to whom He wills reflects His all-encompassing generosity and perfect knowledge, meaning His appointment is always wise, just, and suited to His overarching purpose.

translation: And their prophet said to them, “Indeed, a sign of his kingship is that there will come to you the Ark, wherein is tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind, carried by the angels. Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.”
interpretation: This verse interprets the appointment of Talut as king as a divine matter confirmed by a supernatural sign: the return of the Ark. Its coming is not merely the recovery of an object but a manifestation of God’s sovereignty, bringing sakina—divine tranquility and reassurance—to the hearts of the Children of Israel, and containing sacred remnants from the households of Moses and Aaron that link the new leadership to the legacy of prophethood. That the angels carry it shows that this kingship is established by God’s command, not by human choice alone. The sign is therefore sufficient proof for those whose faith makes them ready to recognize and submit to God’s appointed authority.

translation: So when Talut set out with the soldiers, he said, 'Indeed, Allah will test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is indeed of me, except one who scoops a handful with his hand.' Then they drank from it except a few of them. And when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him, they said, 'We have no strength today against Jalut and his soldiers.' Those who were certain that they would meet Allah said, 'How many a small company has defeated a large company by Allah's permission? And Allah is with the patient.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine testing often comes through ordinary, small commands that reveal whether loyalty to God and His appointed leader is sincere or merely outward. The river is not merely water but a boundary between self-rule and obedient restraint; most fail because appetite and ease override commitment, while the few who restrain themselves remain truly attached to the mission. Yet passing one test does not automatically erase human fear: even after crossing, some believers feel overwhelmed by the enemy's apparent strength. The deeper meaning is that true faith does not measure victory by numbers, resources, or visible power, but by God's permission and by steadfast patience. Those certain of meeting God see beyond the imbalance of forces and trust that a small, obedient, patient group can prevail over a vast arrogant force, because divine assistance accompanies the patient.

translation: And when they went forth to face Goliath and his soldiers, they said, “Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make our feet firm, and grant us victory over the disbelieving people.”
interpretation: This is the supplication of the believers at the moment of confronting a vastly superior enemy. It teaches that true strength in struggle begins with turning to Allah, not with counting numbers or weapons. The request to “pour upon us patience” means asking for an abundant, overflowing endurance that covers the heart, steadies the nerves, and prevents despair or panic. “Make our feet firm” is a plea for steadfastness in the face of fear: not retreating, not wavering, but standing resolute on the truth. And “grant us victory over the disbelieving people” affirms that victory ultimately comes from Allah alone, not from human power. Thus the verse presents patience, firmness, and reliance on Allah as the believer’s means of triumph when facing overwhelming opposition.

translation: So they defeated them by Allah's permission, and David killed Goliath, and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom and taught him of what He willed. And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by others, the earth would have become corrupt. But Allah is possessor of bounty over the worlds.
interpretation: This verse teaches that victory is ultimately granted by God's permission, not merely by material strength. God's enabling David to slay Goliath and then granting him kingship and wisdom shows that He bestows authority, sound judgment, and knowledge according to His will, raising whom He chooses for His purposes. The statement that God repels some people by means of others expresses a divine law: He restrains corruption, oppression, and tyranny through the rise and resistance of opposing forces, preventing the earth from descending into ruin. The closing affirms that this governance is an expression of God's grace and bounty toward all creation, even when His wisdom is not fully perceived.

translation: These are the verses of Allah which We recite to you in truth, and indeed you are among the messengers.
interpretation: Allah declares that the revelations being recited to the Prophet Muhammad are His own signs and verses, conveyed with truth and certainty; they are not fabricated or doubtful. This truth-bearing recitation also serves as evidence that Muhammad is truly one of Allah's messengers, confirmed by the divine revelation given to him.

translation: Those messengers—We have favored some of them over others. Among them is he to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some of them in degrees. And We gave Jesus son of Mary clear proofs and supported him with the Holy Spirit. And if Allah had willed, those after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them, but they differed: some of them believed and some disbelieved. And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does what He intends.
interpretation: The verse establishes that Allah Himself differentiates among His messengers in rank and gifts, and that this differentiation is not injustice but wise selection: Moses was uniquely honored by direct speech, others were raised in degrees, and Jesus was given manifest miracles and strengthened by the Holy Spirit, understood as Gabriel. It then diagnoses the root of post-prophetic conflict: people split after clear signs had come, some believing and some disbelieving. Their fighting was not because divine proof was lacking, nor because Allah was unable to prevent it—had He willed, He could have made them one believing community—but He allowed their choices and disputes as part of His wise decree and test. Thus the verse combines affirmation of Allah's sovereign will over all events with the reality of human responsibility for faith and rejection, and it warns against making prophetic distinctions a cause for sectarian strife.

translation: O you who have believed, spend from that which We have provided you before a Day comes in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession. And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse commands the believers to use the wealth and blessings God has given them in ways He approves, especially by giving charity, and not to delay it until the Day of Judgment. On that Day, wealth will not be able to buy relief, close friendships will not be able to benefit anyone against God’s decree, and no intercessor will be able to intercede independently of God’s permission. The verse warns that those who reject this truth and withhold what God has commanded them to spend are the true wrongdoers, for they wrong both God’s command and their own souls.

translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what will be after them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth, and their preservation does not tire Him. And He is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute oneness of Allah and the perfection of His divine attributes. He alone is the true God, eternally living and self-subsistent, sustaining all that exists. He is free from any weakness, fatigue, or need for rest, so neither drowsiness nor sleep can affect Him. His sovereignty is total: all that is in the heavens and earth belongs to Him. No one can intercede before Him except by His permission, showing that all authority and mediation depend entirely on His will. His knowledge is all-encompassing, knowing all that has occurred and all that will occur, while creatures can access only what He grants them to know. His Kursi signifies the vastness of His dominion and authority over the heavens and earth, and preserving them is effortless for Him. He is exalted above all creation and incomparably great in His majesty.

translation: There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become clear from the wrong. So whoever rejects false deities and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which never breaks. And Allah is Hearing, Knowing.
interpretation: This verse establishes that faith is not to be imposed by force, because the truth has already been made distinct from error through clear signs and sound reason. A person is therefore responsible for choosing guidance or misguidance. True deliverance lies in rejecting every false object of worship, allegiance, or authority that is set up against Allah, and in sincerely believing in Him alone. Such a person holds fast to an unbreakable bond of security and guidance. Allah hears all claims and knows the hidden intentions of the heart, so He knows who truly believes and who merely professes.

translation: Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out from darknesses into the light. But those who disbelieve—their protectors are the false deities; they bring them out from the light into darknesses. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true guardianship and guidance belong to Allah alone. For the believers, His protecting friendship means He continually draws them out of the darkness of ignorance, shirk, doubt, and sin into the light of tawhid, faith, certainty, and obedience. In contrast, those who reject faith attach themselves to taghut—false objects of worship, tyrannical powers, or Satanic influences—and these misleaders pull them away from the light of the God-given fitrah and prophetic guidance into ever-deepening darkness. The verse therefore contrasts two paths and two destinies: divine guardianship leading to light and eternal bliss, versus submission to false guardians leading to darkness and the everlasting Fire.

translation: Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord because Allah had given him kingship? When Abraham said, “My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death,” he said, “I give life and cause death.” Abraham said, “Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east; so bring it from the west.” So the one who disbelieved was confounded. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse shows that worldly authority, however great, cannot stand as a rival to God’s absolute lordship. The king’s claim to “give life and cause death” is exposed as a confusion between human power over execution or pardon and God’s exclusive power to create, sustain, and end life. When Ibrahim moves the debate to the order of the heavens—the sun rising from the east—the king is silenced, because no human ruler can command the cosmos. His defeat is not merely intellectual but moral: arrogance joined to disbelief leaves the heart unable to receive guidance. Thus the verse teaches that unjust power is ultimately confounded before divine truth, and that God withholds guidance from those who persist in wrongdoing and oppression.

translation: Or like the one who passed by a city while it was fallen into ruins, and said: 'How will Allah bring this to life after its death?' So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him. He said: 'How long did you remain?' He said: 'I remained a day or part of a day.' He said: 'No, you remained a hundred years. So look at your food and your drink—it has not changed. And look at your donkey. And We will make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones—how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh.' So when it became clear to him, he said: 'I know that Allah is over all things competent.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the certainty of bodily resurrection and Allah's absolute power over life, death, and time. The man's question about how Allah could revive a ruined town is answered by direct divine demonstration: he himself dies for a hundred years and is raised, his food and drink remain unchanged, and his decomposed donkey is revived. The lesson is that what appears impossible to human reason—restoring life after death—is entirely subject to Allah's command. Human estimates of time and ability are limited, while Allah's knowledge and power are unlimited. The verse therefore calls the heart to firm faith in the Hereafter and to humble acknowledgment that Allah is capable of all things.

translation: And when Abraham said, “My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.” He said, “Have you not believed?” He said, “Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest.” He said, “Take four birds and draw them to yourself, then place on every mountain a portion of them; then call them—they will come to you hastening. And know that Allah is Mighty, Wise.”
interpretation: Abraham’s request was not a denial of Allah’s power or a lack of faith; it was a longing for the heart to move from assent to direct, experiential certainty. Allah’s question, “Have you not believed?” confirms that faith was already present, while Abraham’s answer, “Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest,” shows that the heart can seek a deeper tranquility through witnessing the divine act itself. The sign of the birds is a sensory demonstration of resurrection: what is scattered, lifeless, and separated over the mountains is gathered and restored at Allah’s command alone. Thus the servant is taught that life and death are not controlled by creatures or causes, but by Allah, whose power is never exhausted and whose wisdom orders every sign for the training and strengthening of faith. “Allah is Mighty, Wise” means He is fully able to revive the dead and wise in how He nurtures certainty in the hearts of His servants.

translation: The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears; in every ear is a hundred grains. And Allah multiplies for whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This parable teaches that sincere spending in God's cause is never lost or merely repaid in equal measure; it enters a divine economy where one small act can yield an immense harvest of reward. The seven ears, each containing a hundred grains, express the abundant fertility of what God accepts, while the statement that He multiplies for whom He wills shows that the increase is not a fixed human calculation but a gift apportioned by His wisdom. God's all-encompassing nature means His bounty is inexhaustible, and His knowledge means He knows the true intention, need, and circumstances behind every act of giving.

translation: Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of generosity or harm—they will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: This verse teaches that charitable spending is only truly accepted and rewarded when it is done sincerely for Allah alone and is not corrupted afterward by boasting, reminding the recipient of one’s favor, or any form of insult or injury. The giver must preserve the honor of the one helped and seek no praise or repayment from people. Such sincere givers have their reward securely with Allah, not with created beings. Because their reward is with their Lord, they are freed from fear of loss or failure and from grief over what they gave up or what they may face; their ultimate outcome is safety and joy in Allah’s pleasure.

translation: A kind word and forgiveness are better than a charity followed by injury. And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse teaches that preserving people’s dignity and speaking gently can be morally superior to giving material aid if that aid is accompanied by insult, reminder of favor, or emotional harm. Forgiveness and a gracious word reflect a pure heart, whereas charity followed by injury cancels its reward and wounds the recipient. Allah is not in need of anyone’s wealth or charity; He is Forbearing, not quick to punish those who wrong others, and He calls believers to give with humility, restraint, and respect.

translation: O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders of generosity or injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His example is that of a smooth rock with dust upon it; then a heavy rain falls upon it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse teaches that charitable giving loses its spiritual reward when it is followed by boasting, reminding the recipient of the favor, or hurting them. Such giving is compared to that of a person who gives only to be seen and praised by others rather than out of faith in Allah and the Last Day. Just as rain washes dust off a smooth rock and leaves nothing behind, insincere and harmful charity leaves no reward with Allah. True charity must be purified by sincere intention for Allah alone, without subsequent harm or display, for Allah does not guide those who persist in disbelief and hypocrisy.

translation: And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah and as a confirmation from themselves is like a garden on a high ground: heavy rain strikes it, so it brings forth its fruit twofold; and if heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This parable teaches that wealth spent with a sincere desire for Allah’s pleasure and from a heart made firm in faith is never lost; it is like a fertile elevated garden that yields abundantly. The abundance of rain represents divine blessing and acceptance, while even light rain still suffices to produce fruit, showing that Allah does not waste any sincere effort. The reward is multiplied according to the purity of intention and the firmness of the giver’s inner conviction, and Allah fully sees both the deed and the motive behind it.

translation: Would one of you wish to have a garden of date palms and grapevines, with rivers flowing beneath it, having in it every kind of fruit, while old age has struck him and he has weak children, and a whirlwind containing fire strikes it and it is burned? Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses, so that you may reflect.
interpretation: This parable warns that good deeds are like a fruitful garden that can be destroyed at the moment of greatest need. The man’s old age and weak children represent the Day of Judgment: he arrives with no strength left to earn new reward and no one able to help him. The fiery whirlwind represents the sins, showing off, reminders of generosity, or apostasy that cancel the reward of good deeds. So whoever performs righteous deeds and charity, then nullifies them by ostentation, harm, or disobedience, will find them gone when he needs them most, leaving him in loss and regret. Allah clarifies these parables so people may reflect, protect their deeds, and avoid whatever invalidates them.

translation: O you who have believed, spend from the good things which you have earned and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth. And do not aim at the bad thereof, spending from it, while you would not take it yourselves unless you close your eyes over it. And know that Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse commands believers to give charity and financial support from wholesome, lawfully acquired wealth—whether from trade, work, or the produce of the earth—rather than from worthless, corrupt, or ill-gotten property. It forbids deliberately choosing the worst of one’s possessions to give in the way of God while withholding the best for oneself, since a person would ordinarily accept such inferior goods only reluctantly, with distaste or indulgence. The verse therefore teaches that worship and charity must be offered with sincerity and excellence, using what is pure and pleasing, and it reminds believers that God has no need of their giving; He is Praiseworthy in Himself, and the benefit of charity returns to the giver.

translation: Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to immorality, while Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse exposes two opposing calls: Satan frightens people with the prospect of poverty so that they withhold good and fall into indecency, whereas Allah invites them to trust His promise of forgiveness and generous provision. The one who follows Satan is driven by fear and scarcity, but the one who follows Allah is moved by hope, mercy, and confidence in His limitless bounty; and Allah knows every intention and need, so no act of obedience or charity is lost with Him.

translation: He grants wisdom to whom He wills; and whoever is granted wisdom has certainly been given much good. And none will remember except those of understanding.
interpretation: Wisdom is a gift from God, bestowed according to His will, not merely acquired by human intellect or effort. It denotes deep understanding of divine guidance, sound judgment, and the ability to apply knowledge rightly. The one who receives it has been given an immense and enduring good, because wisdom leads to truth, righteous action, and ultimate success. However, only those with pure, sound minds and hearts—those who use their reason to reflect upon God’s signs—will take heed and benefit from this reminder.

translation: And whatever you spend of expenditure or vow of vow, indeed Allah knows it. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers.
interpretation: This verse assures that every charitable expense and every vow, whether public or hidden, is fully known to God, so He will reward it with perfect justice and nothing done sincerely for Him is lost. At the same time, it warns that those who wrongdoing—such as withholding required charity, breaking vows, or denying others their rights—will have no helpers or protectors to save them from God's judgment.

translation: If you disclose the charities, then excellent it is; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you, and He will expiate from you some of your sins. And Allah is well aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse concerns voluntary charity: giving openly is good and rewarded, but giving secretly to the poor is superior because it is farther from showing off, safeguards the recipient’s dignity, and purifies the giver’s intention. The expiation of sins mentioned here is God’s grace for sincere acts of charity; it does not replace repentance for grave sins. God’s awareness means no intention or deed, public or hidden, is hidden from Him.

translation: Not upon you is their guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills. And whatever good you spend, it is for yourselves, and you do not spend except seeking the face of Allah. And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you, and you will not be wronged.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet and every caller to faith: you are not responsible for forcing hearts to accept guidance, for God alone turns hearts and grants guidance to whom He wills. It also teaches that charitable spending is truly for the giver’s own benefit when purified by the intention of seeking God’s pleasure alone, not human praise or worldly return. Such sincere good will be repaid in full by God, and no one will suffer the least injustice or diminishment of reward.

translation: (Charity is) for the poor who are confined in the cause of Allah, unable to travel in the land. The ignorant would think them rich because of their self-restraint. You will recognize them by their mark: they do not ask people persistently. And whatever good you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.
interpretation: This verse teaches that genuine need is not always visible through begging or complaint. The truly deserving poor may be those whose circumstances—such as devotion or service in Allah’s cause—prevent them from earning a living, while their dignity and restraint make them appear self-sufficient to the unaware. Their need is known to Allah, and charity given to them is not measured by public display but by sincere response to hidden hardship. Therefore, the giver should not wait for loud appeals; Allah knows both the hidden need of the recipient and the true intention of the spender.

translation: Those who spend their wealth by night and day, privately and publicly, will have their reward with their Lord, and there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: This verse commends charity that is constant and unconditional, offered at all times and in both hidden and open ways. Spending secretly protects sincerity from ostentation, while spending openly can inspire others and strengthen communal generosity. The promise is that such expenditure is not lost but is preserved as a reward with God, and the giver is freed from anxiety about the future and sorrow over what has passed.

translation: Those who consume usury will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has struck into insanity by his touch. That is because they said, 'Trade is only like usury.' But Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury. So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, he may keep what has already passed, and his affair is with Allah. But whoever returns, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse treats riba as a corruption of wealth and soul, not merely a legal transaction. Their rising like one possessed on the Day of Judgment signifies that the one who built his life on exploitative gain will be resurrected in a disordered, degraded state, just as his worldly pursuit was a kind of spiritual insanity. Their claim that trade and riba are alike is rejected because Allah's law distinguishes them: lawful trade rests on mutual consent, exchange, risk, and productive effort, while riba is a guaranteed increase extracted unjustly from the borrower's need. The door of repentance is open for what has passed, and judgment concerning it belongs to Allah. But persisting in riba after clear warning, especially by treating it as lawful or defiantly repeating it, leads to the Fire and lasting punishment.

translation: Allah destroys riba (usury/interest) and gives increase to charities. And Allah does not love any ungrateful, sinful disbeliever.
interpretation: This verse teaches that riba may appear to increase wealth, but Allah removes its blessing and ultimately erases it, while charitable giving—though it may seem to decrease wealth—is nurtured by Allah and multiplied in reward and blessing. Allah’s disapproval is for those who persist in ingratitude, disbelief, and sin, especially those who defy His command concerning riba and charity.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, and establish prayer and give zakah—they will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: God promises that faith joined with righteous action, steadfast prayer, and obligatory charity secures a reward preserved with the Lord Himself; such a person is delivered from fear of what is to come and grief over what has passed, because their ultimate security and joy rest in God’s promise.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and give up what remains [due to you] of usury, if you are believers.
interpretation: This verse commands those who claim faith to observe taqwa—God-consciousness and obedience to Allah—and to relinquish any remaining claims or amounts connected to riba (usury/interest). It teaches that true faith requires submitting to Allah's prohibition of riba, and that continuing to take usurious gain after being warned is incompatible with sincere belief. Thus, the remaining interest owed or expected must be abandoned, not merely reduced or delayed, as a sign of obedience and trust in Allah.

translation: If you do not, then be informed of war from Allah and His Messenger. But if you repent, you shall have your principal sums; you neither wrong nor are wronged.
interpretation: This verse treats persistent usury as rebellion against God’s sovereignty and the prophetic order, because it violates the principle that wealth must circulate through just exchange rather than through a guaranteed increase extracted from the debtor’s need. The warning of war means that such conduct places a person outside the normal protection of divine law and invites direct divine and prophetic confrontation. Repentance here is not mere regret; it requires abandoning the practice and accepting only the return of the original capital. Thus the verse establishes restorative justice: the debtor is protected from exploitation, and the creditor is protected from loss of what is truly owed, so neither party may transgress against the other.

translation: And if the debtor is in hardship, then grant him respite until a time of ease. And if you remit the debt as charity, it is better for you, if you only knew.
interpretation: The verse establishes a merciful economic ethic: a creditor must not press a debtor who genuinely cannot pay, but must wait until the debtor’s circumstances improve. It then invites the creditor to go beyond strict justice by forgiving the debt entirely, because such charity is better in Allah’s measure—only those with true understanding recognize that the immediate loss is outweighed by moral purity, social solidarity, and divine reward.

translation: And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah. Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: This verse commands people to live with taqwa—God-consciousness and protective fear—by remembering the inevitable return to Allah for final reckoning. On that Day, every soul will receive the complete and exact recompense for its deeds, whether good or evil. The statement that they will not be wronged affirms Allah’s perfect justice: no good deed will be diminished, and no punishment will exceed what is deserved. Thus the verse motivates sincere obedience, repentance, and accountability before the Day when all returns to Allah.

translation: O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down. And let a scribe write between you in justice. Let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him. So let him write and let the one who has the obligation dictate. And let him fear Allah, his Lord, and not leave anything out of it. But if the one who has the obligation is of limited understanding or weak or unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate in justice. And bring to witness two witnesses from among your men. And if there are not two men, then a man and two women from those whom you accept as witnesses, so that if one of the women errs, then the other can remind her. And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called upon. And do not be too weary to write it, whether it is small or large, for its specified term. That is more just in the sight of Allah and stronger as evidence and more likely to prevent doubt between you, except when it is an immediate transaction which you conduct among yourselves. For then there is no blame upon you if you do not write it. And take witnesses when you conclude a contract. Let no scribe be harmed or any witness. For if you do so, indeed, it is grave disobedience in you. And fear Allah. And Allah teaches you. And Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: This verse makes documentation and witnessed verification a religious safeguard for justice in deferred financial obligations. It teaches that rights must not be left to memory, goodwill, or unequal power; they are to be recorded accurately and witnessed fairly so that no party can later deny or distort what was agreed. The scribe acts as a trustee of knowledge, the debtor as a trustee of truth, the guardian as a protector of the vulnerable, and witnesses as guardians of public trust. The exemptions for immediate trade and the warnings against harming scribes or witnesses show that the aim is not ritual paperwork but preventing injustice, suspicion, and exploitation. The detailed procedural measures reflect the reality of an oral society and serve to preserve testimony reliably, while the closing call to taqwa places all transactions under Allah's knowledge and accountability.

translation: And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken in hand. But if one of you trusts another, then let the one who is trusted discharge his trust and let him fear Allah, his Lord. And do not conceal testimony. And whoever conceals it, indeed his heart is sinful. And Allah knows what you do.
interpretation: This verse completes the guidance on financial dealings and debts. When a written record cannot be made, such as during travel, a pledge or security held in hand may serve as protection. Yet the deeper principle is trust: if people trust one another, the entrusted one must faithfully return what was entrusted, acting out of reverence for God. Concealing testimony is not merely a legal wrong but a corruption of the heart, because God knows all hidden intentions and actions. Thus all dealings must be governed by honesty, fulfillment of trust, and consciousness of God.

translation: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Whether you reveal what is in yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. And Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse establishes that all creation belongs to Allah and is under His absolute dominion, knowledge, and power. It teaches that human accountability is not limited to outward actions; even hidden thoughts, intentions, and inner states are known to Allah and subject to His reckoning. This awakens the conscience to sincerity and self-examination, since one cannot hide anything from God. At the same time, His response is not mechanical or owed to anyone: forgiveness and punishment proceed from His will, wisdom, mercy, and justice. His unlimited power means He is fully able to reckon, forgive, punish, and bring every matter to its proper end, so the servant should combine fear of His judgment with hope in His mercy.

translation: The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord, and so have the believers.
