But if there are women more than two, then for them two-thirds of what he left; and if there is one, then for her half. And for his parents, for each one of them a sixth of what he left, if he has a child. But if he has no child and his parents inherit from him, then for his mother a third. And if he has siblings, then for his mother a sixth — after any will he has made or debt. Your parents and your children — you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit. This is an obligation from Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes inheritance as a divinely ordained system of fixed shares, not a matter left to human custom or favoritism. It protects the rights of children and parents, especially daughters and mothers, by assigning them precise entitlements that must be honored after debts and valid bequests are settled. The rule that a son receives twice a daughter's share is part of this structure and is tied in Islamic law to the son's financial responsibilities; it is not a blanket rule for all heirs, as other shares vary. The changes in the mother's share according to whether the deceased has children or siblings show that the shares are calibrated by nearness, need, and family responsibility. The statement that you do not know which of your parents or children is nearer in benefit teaches that people cannot reliably calculate hidden benefit, so they must submit to God's all-knowing and wise apportionment. Thus the verse is an act of worship and justice, ensuring rights are not left to guesswork, greed, or social custom.

translation: And to you belongs half of what your wives leave, if they have no child. But if they have a child, then to you belongs a quarter of what they leave, after any bequest they may have bequeathed or debt. And to them belongs a quarter of what you leave, if you have no child. But if you have a child, then to them belongs an eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you may have bequeathed or debt. And if a man or a woman is inherited in kalalah and has a brother or a sister, then to each one of them belongs a sixth. But if they are more than that, then they are partners in a third, after any bequest that was bequeathed or debt, without causing harm. A commandment from Allah, and Allah is Knowing, Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse is a foundational inheritance ruling. It assigns the surviving husband half of the wife's estate if she leaves no child or descendant, and a quarter if she does; it assigns the surviving wife or wives a quarter of the husband's estate if he leaves no child or descendant, and an eighth if he does. These shares are distributed only after debts are paid and any valid bequest is fulfilled, showing that obligations to creditors and testators take precedence over inheritance. The phrase 'without causing harm' forbids using bequests or debt acknowledgments to deprive rightful heirs. The case of kalalah refers to someone who dies leaving neither parents nor children; if such a person has a maternal half-brother or half-sister, each receives one-sixth, and if there are more than two, they share one-third. The verse presents these rules as a divine ordinance, grounded in Allah's knowledge and forbearance, and as a merciful framework for justice within the family.

translation: Those are the limits set by Allah. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. And that is the great attainment.
interpretation: Allah’s laws are not arbitrary restrictions but divinely established boundaries, and true success lies in obeying Him and His Messenger; such obedience leads to eternal bliss in Paradise, which is the greatest achievement a person can attain.

translation: And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire wherein he will abide eternally, and for him is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse means that deliberately rejecting God’s command and the Messenger’s authority, and overstepping the limits God has laid down, carries the consequence of entering the Fire to remain there, along with a punishment that degrades and humiliates. It teaches that divine laws are not merely advice but boundaries set by God, and violating them with defiance is a grave matter deserving severe and lasting punishment.

translation: And those of your women who commit the immoral act — call four witnesses from among you against them. Then if they testify, confine them to the houses until death takes them or Allah makes for them a way.
interpretation: This verse lays down an initial procedure and penalty for women who are legally proven to have committed illicit sexual conduct. Because the accusation is grave, it may not be acted upon except by the testimony of four witnesses from the community. Once the offense is established by that testimony, the ruling at that stage was to keep them confined in their homes until death or until God provides another prescribed way. In classical Qur'anic commentary, the “way” is generally understood as the later, definitive legislation in Surat al-Nur (24:2) and the Prophet's Sunnah, which specify the punishments for unlawful sexual relations. The demanding four-witness requirement also functions as a strict safeguard against false accusation and slander, making conviction for such an offense exceptionally difficult and protecting people's honor.

translation: And the two who commit it among you, punish them both. But if they repent and amend, then leave them alone. Indeed, Allah is ever Accepting of repentance and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse addresses the man and woman who commit illicit sexual intercourse. It commands that they be disciplined or rebuked, but if they turn back from the sin and genuinely rectify their conduct, the punishment or censure is to cease. The verse thus teaches that the aim of such correction is reform, not revenge, and that Allah’s mercy and acceptance of repentance are vast even for those guilty of grave sexual sin.

translation: The repentance accepted by Allah is only for those who do wrong out of ignorance and then repent soon after. It is they to whom Allah turns in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing, Wise.
interpretation: This verse explains that Allah’s promise to accept repentance applies to those who fall into sin through human weakness, heedlessness, or a momentary overpowering of desire—not out of defiant rejection of Allah—and who then turn back to Him promptly, without persisting in the sin or delaying repentance until death approaches. For such people, Allah accepts their repentance and forgives them. His knowledge fully encompasses their intentions, sincerity, and circumstances, and His wisdom determines the true conditions of acceptable repentance and governs all matters with perfect justice and mercy.

translation: And repentance is not for those who commit evil deeds, until when death comes to one of them, he says, 'Indeed, I have repented now,' nor for those who die while they are disbelievers. For them We have prepared a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse clarifies that God accepts repentance only when it is offered during one's lifetime, before the moment of death and while a person still has the free choice to turn back to Him. Repentance at the point of death, when the reality of the hereafter becomes unavoidable and confession is forced by urgency, is not accepted; likewise, there is no accepted repentance for those who persist in rejection of faith until death. Such people have a painful punishment prepared for them.

translation: O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will, nor to constrain them so that you may take away part of what you have given them, unless they commit a clear immorality. And live with them in kindness. Then if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah places much good in it.
interpretation: This verse abolishes the pre-Islamic practice of treating a widow as part of an estate to be inherited and forcibly married by a male relative, and it prohibits husbands from oppressing or detaining wives in order to reclaim gifts, dower, or other property, or to pressure them into surrendering their rights. The exception for a clear, open indecency allows lawful recourse against serious marital betrayal or public immorality, but it does not license cruelty or unjust extraction of wealth. The overarching command is honorable and kind companionship. If a husband feels dislike toward his wife, he should not use that feeling as an excuse for injustice, because his aversion may conceal a matter in which God has placed abundant good—such as patience, reconciliation, offspring, or reward in the Hereafter.

translation: And if you wish to replace one wife with another and you have given one of them a great amount [of wealth], do not take anything from it. Would you take it by falsehood and manifest sin?
interpretation: This verse forbids a man from taking back the bridal gift (mahr) he gave his wife if he divorces her in order to marry another woman. Once the mahr is given, it becomes the wife’s rightful property; reclaiming it is described as a false accusation and an obvious sin, because it is unjust and violates the sanctity of the marriage contract and the wife’s rights.

translation: And how could you take it back after one of you has gone in unto the other, and they have taken from you a firm covenant?
interpretation: This is a rebuke against a husband reclaiming what he gave his wife after the marriage has been consummated, because marital intimacy has joined them and the marriage itself is a solemn, binding covenant before Allah. That covenant makes the wife’s bridal gift her rightful property and forbids treating marriage as a temporary transaction from which one may unjustly take back what was given.

translation: And do not marry women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an immorality and a hateful thing, and an evil way.
interpretation: This verse forbids a man from marrying any woman who was married to his father, making the father’s wife permanently unlawful to his son and preserving the honor and sanctity of the parental marriage. The phrase 'except what has already passed' refers to unions that took place in the pre-Islamic era before this prohibition: those past acts are not to be punished or pursued, but the ruling still closes the door to continuing or repeating such a marriage. The verse calls the practice fāḥishah, a gross and shameful sexual transgression; maqtan, an act that earns divine wrath and human hatred because it violates the father’s honor and corrupts family ties; and an evil way, because it destroys moral boundaries, respect, and lineage. Thus the prohibition protects the family structure, prevents confusion of lineage, and safeguards the dignity of parents.

translation: Forbidden to you [in marriage] are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brother’s daughters, your sister’s daughters, your milk-mothers who nursed you, your milk-sisters, your wives’ mothers, your stepdaughters under your guardianship from your wives with whom you have consummated marriage—but if you have not consummated with them, there is no blame upon you—and the wives of your sons who are from your own loins, and that you combine two sisters [in marriage], except what has already occurred. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse defines the inviolable limits of marriage, making clear that certain relationships are not merely social conventions but sacred trusts that bar marriage. It forbids union with close kin by blood, by nursing, and by marriage, thereby protecting lineage, family honor, and the dignity of vulnerable household members. The mention of stepdaughters in one’s care and mothers of wives shows that marriage creates real kinship obligations, not just a private contract. The prohibition against marrying two sisters at once guards against jealousy and divided loyalty within a family. The exception for what has already passed is a mercy for pre-Islamic communities: once the ruling is known, it must be obeyed; what is past is left to God’s forgiveness and mercy.

translation: And [forbidden to you are] married women, except those whom your right hands possess. This is the decree of Allah upon you. And lawful to you are [all] beyond these, provided you seek them with your wealth in chastity, not in fornication. And those among them whom you have enjoyed, give them their dowers as a duty. And there is no blame upon you concerning what you mutually agree to after the duty. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Wise.
interpretation: This verse concludes the list of women forbidden in marriage by declaring married women unlawful, except slave women whom one rightfully possesses under the rules of the time; it then declares all other women lawful if sought through marriage with wealth, with the intention of chastity rather than illicit sexual conduct. It obligates the husband to give the agreed dower to the woman he has enjoyed as a binding duty, and it permits the spouses to make a later mutual agreement regarding the dower after it has become due. The verse thus establishes marriage as a lawful, dignified contract grounded in financial responsibility and mutual consent, and it closes by affirming that God is all-knowing and all-wise.

translation: And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women, then [let him marry] from those whom your right hands possess among your believing slave girls. And Allah knows best about your faith. You are from one another. So marry them with the permission of their families and give them their due compensation according to what is reasonable, being chaste, not committing unlawful sexual intercourse nor taking secret lovers. Then when they are married, if they commit an immorality, upon them is half the punishment of free women. That is for whoever among you fears hardship [of falling into sin]. But patience is better for you. And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse permits a man who lacks the means to marry a free believing woman to marry a believing woman who is lawfully under another’s authority, with her family’s consent and a reasonable dowry, while insisting that the relationship be chaste and honorable rather than illicit or secretive. It teaches that faith, not social status, is the decisive bond among believers, and that God alone truly knows the sincerity of faith. It also specifies a lighter legal penalty for such a married woman if she commits adultery, compared with the penalty for a free married woman, and presents this permission as a concession for one who genuinely fears falling into sin, while stating that patient restraint is better. The closing affirmation of God’s forgiveness and mercy reassures those who struggle and repent.

translation: Allah intends to make clear to you, and to guide you to the ways of those before you, and to accept your repentance. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse shows that God’s will is directed toward human welfare through three connected gifts: clarification of truth and law, guidance along the prophetic path followed by earlier righteous communities, and merciful acceptance of repentance when people fall short. His knowledge and wisdom guarantee that His commands, guidance, and forgiveness are neither arbitrary nor excessive, but perfectly suited to purify the soul and direct it toward what is truly beneficial.

translation: And Allah wants to accept your repentance, but those who follow their lusts want you to deviate with a great deviation.
interpretation: This means that God's purpose for people is to purify them and bring them back to Him through repentance, while those enslaved by base desires seek to pull believers away from His guidance and toward unrestrained appetite. Their aim is not merely a small mistake but a profound deviation from moderation, truth, and the purpose for which humans were created.

translation: Allah intends to lighten your burden, and mankind was created weak.
interpretation: God’s desire to lighten His commands reflects His mercy and His full knowledge of human frailty. He does not burden souls beyond their capacity, and He grants concessions because humans are naturally limited in strength, endurance, and resolve. This weakness is not a condemnation but a reason for divine compassion, making His law accommodating and merciful rather than harsh and impossible.

translation: O you who have believed, do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you.
interpretation: This verse forbids acquiring wealth through unlawful means—such as theft, fraud, usury, bribery, gambling, coercion, and any exploitation that violates justice—and permits wealth to change hands only through lawful trade freely agreed upon by both parties. It also prohibits killing oneself or one another, and more broadly forbids acts that lead to self-destruction or communal ruin. The reminder that Allah is ever Merciful to you grounds these commands in divine mercy: the restrictions are not arbitrary burdens but protections for life, property, and social harmony, calling believers to uphold justice, consent, and preservation of life.

translation: And whoever does that out of transgression and injustice, We will soon cast him into a Fire; and that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: This is a stern warning that anyone who deliberately violates Allah’s limits by wronging others—such as unlawfully consuming wealth or taking life—will be made to enter the Fire. The punishment is described as “easy for Allah” to show that His justice is certain and that no sinner can escape or frustrate His will; He is fully able to carry out what He promises.

translation: If you avoid the major sins which you have been forbidden, We will remove from you your lesser evil deeds and admit you into a noble entrance.
interpretation: This verse means that Allah promises those who shun the grave sins He has prohibited that He will erase their minor sins and wrongs, and grant them an honorable entry into Paradise. Avoiding the major prohibitions is therefore a path to forgiveness of lesser faults and to a dignified, noble place of entry in the Hereafter.

translation: And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah of His bounty. Indeed, Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: This verse prohibits envy and covetousness toward the differing gifts, roles, and provisions Allah has apportioned among people. Such distinctions are not arbitrary; they are part of divine wisdom and test whether a person is content with Allah’s decree or resentful of others. It also establishes that men and women each have a real share in what they earn before Allah—responsibility, reward, and spiritual accountability are tied to one’s deeds, not to gender or worldly advantage. Rather than longing for another’s portion, the believer should turn to Allah and ask from His bounty, seeking His favor through lawful and sincere effort. Since Allah knows all things, His distribution, commands, and judgments are perfectly wise and just, even when human beings do not fully understand them.

translation: And for each We have appointed heirs for what parents and near relatives leave. And those with whom you have made a covenant, give them their share. Indeed, Allah is Witness over all things.
interpretation: This verse establishes inheritance as a divinely ordained right rather than a matter left to custom or preference: every estate has rightful heirs appointed by Allah among parents and close kin, and covenantal bonds also carry a binding claim to a share. Giving these portions is therefore an obligation of faithfulness, not a favor, and it must be fulfilled with justice because Allah witnesses every allocation, concealment, or denial.

translation: Men are the maintainers and protectors of women because Allah has favored some of them over others and because they spend from their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in the absence what Allah has guarded. As for those from whom you fear ill-conduct, admonish them, abandon them in bed, and strike them. If they obey you, do not seek a way against them. Indeed, Allah is Most High, Most Great.
interpretation: The verse establishes qiwamah as a duty of care, provision, and protection, not as a claim of essential superiority. The favor mentioned is functional and contextual: men are generally given greater physical strength and financial responsibility, and they must spend their wealth on women. Righteous women are qanitat, meaning sincerely obedient to Allah, and hafizat lil-ghayb, meaning they guard their faith, chastity, and the family's rights when the husband is absent, relying on Allah's protection. Nushuz is serious marital ill-conduct or disloyalty that threatens the family. The prescribed response is restorative and gradual: first sincere counsel, then a temporary separation in bed to awaken conscience, and finally a symbolic disciplinary strike that is not meant to injure, brutalize, or humiliate, as the Prophet's practice and teachings restrict it to the lightest measure and condemn violence. If the wife returns to obedience and harmony, the husband must not keep punishing her or seek a pretext against her. The closing declares Allah's exaltedness and greatness, warning that He sees all and will judge any oppression.

translation: And if you fear a breach between them, appoint an arbitrator from his family and an arbitrator from her family. If they desire reconciliation, Allah will reconcile them. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, All-Aware.
interpretation: This verse establishes a wise procedure for resolving marital discord: when separation is feared, trusted mediators from both spouses’ families should intervene, seeking restoration rather than victory. If the mediators sincerely aim for reconciliation, Allah will bring harmony between the spouses. Allah knows all hidden intentions and is fully aware of every circumstance, so mediation must be conducted with justice, honesty, and sincere concern for the marriage’s repair.

translation: Worship Allah and do not associate anything with Him; and do good to parents, and to relatives, and orphans, and the needy, and the near neighbor, and the distant neighbor, and the companion by your side, and the wayfarer, and those whom your right hands possess. Indeed, Allah does not love the arrogant and boastful.
interpretation: This verse makes the exclusive worship of God the foundation of all moral responsibility: because no one shares His authority, no human being may be treated with arrogance or neglect. The commands that follow are not merely social etiquette but acts of worship rooted in tawhid. The list moves outward in widening circles of duty—parents, close kin, the vulnerable, neighbors nearby and farther away, associates, travelers, and dependents—teaching that faith must express itself in concrete kindness, justice, and humility toward every category of human need and proximity. The closing warning against arrogance and boasting exposes the inner disease that corrupts these obligations: self-importance, which claims for the self a greatness that belongs to God alone and turns service to others into entitlement or display. Thus the verse presents worship as inseparable from humble, respectful, and responsible treatment of people.

translation: Those who are stingy and enjoin people to be stingy, and conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse exposes a spiritual disease that combines greed, misguidance, and ingratitude. The miser withholds what God has entrusted to him, then tries to make stinginess look normal and virtuous to others, and even hides the favors, knowledge, or blessings God gave him when they should be acknowledged and used for good. Such behavior is not merely a social flaw; it flows from a deeper denial of God’s right over His gifts. Because they sought to preserve their status or wealth by refusing God’s commands, God promises them a punishment that will humiliate them, reversing the false honor they imagined their hoarding would secure.

translation: And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people and do not believe in Allah and the Last Day. And whoever has Satan as a companion—then evil is the companion.
interpretation: This verse condemns spending wealth for show and human praise while rejecting faith in Allah and accountability in the Hereafter. Such charity is not rooted in sincere devotion, so it carries no spiritual reward; the motive is reputation, not obedience to God. The verse then warns that whoever adopts this path has taken Satan as an intimate companion, meaning the person is led by the same rebellious, self-seeking impulse that drives Satan. The phrase “evil is the companion” emphasizes that such an alliance is destructive: it corrupts intentions, wastes good deeds, and leads to ruin in this life and the next. Thus, the verse teaches that insincere generosity joined with disbelief places a person under Satan’s influence, and Satan is the worst possible associate and guide.

translation: And what harm would it be to them if they believed in Allah and the Last Day, and spent from what Allah has provided them? And Allah is ever Knowing of them.
interpretation: This is a reproachful question meant to expose the folly of withholding faith and sincere charity: their refusal does not harm God, but only deprives themselves of the good of believing in God and the Hereafter and of giving from His provision. Had they done so, it would have purified their intentions and benefited them, and God is fully aware of them—their outward deeds and inner motives—so no sincere act is lost and no hypocrisy is hidden.

translation: Indeed, Allah does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom. And if there is a good deed, He multiplies it and grants from Himself a great reward.
interpretation: Allah’s justice is absolutely precise and fair: He never wrongs anyone, even to the smallest degree, nor does He diminish or overlook any good. At the same time, His response to good is not merely equal retribution but generous multiplication; He increases the reward for a good deed and adds from His own bounty an immense reward that exceeds what the deed itself could deserve. This inspires hope in His mercy, trust in His justice, and sincerity in doing even the smallest good.

translation: So how [will it be] when We bring from every nation a witness and We bring you, [O Muhammad], against these [people] as a witness?
interpretation: This verse describes the gravity of the Day of Judgment, when God will summon a prophetic witness from every community to testify regarding how its people received and responded to divine guidance. The Prophet Muhammad will likewise be brought as a witness over his followers, confirming that he delivered the message entrusted to him. The question form is meant to inspire awe and accountability, showing how overwhelming that moment will be for those who rejected or neglected the truth.

translation: On that Day, those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them, and they will not conceal from Allah any statement.
interpretation: This verse depicts the humiliation and despair of those who rejected faith and opposed the Prophet on the Day of Judgment. Their regret will be so intense that they will wish the earth would be flattened over them or swallow them, so they might escape exposure and punishment. Yet they will not be able to hide anything from Allah: every word and deed will be brought to light, and they will be compelled to acknowledge the truth. The verse thus affirms both the severity of accountability for rejecting the Messenger and Allah’s all-encompassing knowledge, leaving no possibility of concealment.

translation: O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying, nor in a state of major impurity—except those passing through—until you have bathed. And if you are ill or on a journey, or one of you comes from the privy, or you have touched women, and you do not find water, then resort to clean earth and wipe your faces and your hands with it. Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse teaches that prayer requires both inward awareness and outward purity. Intoxication is forbidden near prayer because it destroys the faculty by which a person understands what he says before God; major impurity likewise requires full purification. But the concession of tayammum when water is unavailable due to illness, travel, or other valid circumstances shows that the Law is not designed to trap people in impurity or hardship. Its aim is to bring the servant to God with a purified body and a present heart, while God's pardon and forgiveness remain the ultimate refuge for human weakness.

translation: Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They purchase error and wish that you stray from the way.
interpretation: The verse rebukes a group among the People of the Book who were granted knowledge of earlier revelation, yet deliberately exchange it for misguidance; they barter away guidance and buy into deviation. Their corruption is not passive: they actively desire that the believers also leave the straight path. It exposes their envy and enmity toward the Muslim community and warns that outward possession of a scripture does not guarantee guidance if the heart chooses error. Allah consoles and cautions the Prophet and believers against their scheming, urging steadfastness on the revealed path rather than being swayed by those who wish to turn them away from it.

translation: And Allah is most knowing of your enemies; and sufficient is Allah as a Protector, and sufficient is Allah as a Helper.
interpretation: This verse teaches that God alone has complete and perfect knowledge of who truly opposes the believers, including hidden motives and secret plots, so His judgment and protection are fully reliable. It calls the believers to place their trust in Him, declaring that His guardianship and support are entirely sufficient against every enemy and every form of harm.

translation: Among those who are Jews are those who distort the words from their proper places and say, 'We hear and we disobey,' and 'Hear, may you not be made to hear,' and 'Ra'ina' — twisting it with their tongues and reviling the religion. And if they had said, 'We hear and we obey,' and 'Hear,' and 'Unzurna,' it would have been better for them and more upright. But Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except a few.
interpretation: This verse exposes a mode of hypocrisy that uses language itself as a weapon: altering revealed words from their intended meanings and places, then uttering phrases that sound like obedience while carrying rebellion, curses, and insults. 'We hear and disobey' is not honest submission but open defiance. 'Hear, may you not be made to hear' is a sarcastic curse, and 'Ra'ina' was twisted by them into a slur and a mockery of the faith. Allah exposes this as twisting with their tongues and smearing the religion, showing that corrupt speech about revelation is not a small matter but an attack on religion itself. Then He shows the remedy: what is better and more upright is simple, sincere speech — 'We hear and obey,' 'Hear,' and 'Unzurna' (regard us). The contrast teaches that faith is not mere verbal cleverness or outward hearing; it is humble obedience, sound words, and respect for divine revelation. Their refusal leads to the curse of disbelief, so that only a few among them turn back to truth. The verse thus warns against manipulating sacred texts and slogans to evade obedience, and calls for honesty, reverence, and submission in both tongue and heart.

translation: O you who were given the Scripture, believe in what We have sent down, confirming that which is with you, before We obliterate faces and turn them backward, or curse them as We cursed the companions of the Sabbath. And the command of Allah is ever accomplished.
interpretation: This is a stern call to the People of the Book to accept the final revelation, which confirms the earlier scriptures they already possess, before a punishment comes that may erase their very features and reduce them to a degraded, reversed state, or bring upon them a curse like that which fell upon those who broke the Sabbath. The verse teaches that rejecting clear divine guidance after it has come is perilous, and that Allah's decree, warning, and judgment are always carried out without fail.

translation: Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates partners with Allah has certainly fabricated a tremendous sin.
interpretation: This verse declares that associating partners with God—shirk—is the one sin God will not forgive for one who dies upon it without repenting, because it violates His exclusive right to divinity and worship. Sins below shirk remain subject to God's mercy and will: He may forgive them by His grace, or punish them by His justice, though repentance remains a means of forgiveness. The verse then stresses the enormity of shirk by calling it a fabricated, monstrous falsehood, since it invents rivals, equals, or intermediaries ascribed to God without truth.

translation: Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged by as much as a thread [on a date stone].
interpretation: This verse repudiates self-righteousness and the human claim to be pure or morally superior by one’s own merit. True purification belongs to Allah alone; He purifies whom He wills according to His knowledge and grace, not according to people’s self-praise. It also affirms that His judgment is perfectly just, so no one will suffer the slightest diminishment of reward or be wronged by even the most minute measure.

translation: Look how they fabricate lies against Allah; and sufficient is that as a manifest sin.
interpretation: This is a severe rebuke of those who dare to attribute to God words, laws, or promises He never revealed—especially when they do so to justify their own claims of purity, favored status, or forgiveness. Such fabrication is not a small matter: it assaults the truth about God and His exclusive authority to legislate and forgive. The verse teaches that the very act of inventing a lie about Allah is enough to establish its guilt as a clear, unmistakable sin; no further evidence of harm is needed. It warns believers to speak about God only with knowledge and reverence, never tailoring His message to human desires.

translation: Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in Jibt and Taghut and say to those who disbelieve, 'These are better guided than the believers in the way.'
interpretation: This verse exposes a profound moral and spiritual inversion: people who were entrusted with part of divine revelation nevertheless give credence to false objects of devotion and tyrannical false authorities, then openly prefer the path of disbelief over the path of faith. Their error is not merely theological but also a betrayal of the very guidance they were given. It warns that knowledge of Scripture is no safeguard if the heart is swayed by prejudice, worldly interest, or allegiance to ungodly power. True guidance is not measured by numbers, status, or political ascendancy but by fidelity to God and His revealed truth.

translation: Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed; and whoever Allah curses, you will never find for him a helper.
interpretation: This verse states that those who persist in the ways that earn divine wrath are deprived of Allah’s mercy and guidance. Allah’s curse means being cut off from His favor and protection. When Allah withdraws His support from someone, no created being can rescue or defend them, because all help and authority belong to Allah alone. It is a warning against actions that lead to divine abandonment and a call to seek Allah’s mercy through obedience and repentance.

translation: Or have they a share of sovereignty? Then they would not give the people even a speck.
interpretation: This verse censures those who grudgingly deny Allah’s favors and resent the Prophet and the believers: even if they were given any share of power or kingship, their miserliness and arrogance are so deep that they would not extend to others the smallest possible benefit, not even a speck on a date-stone. It exposes their selfishness and false sense of entitlement, and it reminds that true dominion and bounty belong to Allah alone, who bestows them upon whom He wills.

translation: Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? But We have certainly given the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom.
interpretation: This verse rebukes the envy directed at those whom Allah has favored, especially the Prophet Muhammad and the believers, for the gifts of prophethood, revelation, and guidance. It teaches that Allah’s bounty is not the exclusive right of any lineage, nation, or group; He grants it by His wisdom to whom He wills. By reminding the enviers that He had already given the family of Abraham the Scripture, wisdom, and a great kingdom, the verse shows that favoring a chosen servant with prophethood is entirely consistent with Allah’s past manner of dealing with humanity. Therefore, resentment against His favor is unjustified, because divine election is His sovereign prerogative, not something humans can rightfully claim as their own due.

translation: So among them are those who believed in him, and among them are those who turned away from him. And sufficient is Hell as a Blaze.
interpretation: The pronoun 'him' refers to the Prophet Muhammad. The verse addresses the descendants of Abraham, particularly the Jews and Christians, stating that some of them accepted his message and believed in him, while others rejected him and turned away. For those who turn away, Hell is sufficient as a punishment and a blazing fire.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our verses, We will roast them in a Fire. Every time their skins are cooked through, We will replace them with other skins, so that they may taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is ever Almighty, Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes the certainty and severity of the recompense for those who knowingly reject Allah’s revelations: their punishment in the Fire is not a passing pain but a continuously renewed suffering, since the renewal of their skins after being burned ensures they keep experiencing the torment. It also declares that this recompense proceeds from Allah’s absolute might and perfect wisdom, meaning His judgment is neither unjust nor arbitrary, but exactly measured according to His sovereignty and knowledge.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. They will have therein purified spouses, and We will admit them to a shade, ever-shading.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true faith is not merely an inward claim but is joined to righteous action; the reward of eternal gardens is promised to those whose belief produces obedience and good deeds. The flowing rivers beneath the gardens point to unceasing provision, life, and delight, while “abiding therein forever” signifies a state of security that never ends or diminishes. The “purified spouses” are companions cleansed of every physical, moral, and relational impurity, so that the relationships of Paradise are free from jealousy, harm, resentment, and defect. The “shade, ever-shading” represents complete comfort and protection from every hardship, grief, heat, and annoyance—an enduring blessedness that never fades. Thus the verse presents Paradise as both spiritual and sensory bliss, a reward from Allah that surpasses what deeds deserve and is reserved for those who combine sound belief with righteous conduct.

translation: Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their rightful owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Excellent is that which Allah instructs you. Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing.
interpretation: This verse lays down two foundational obligations: fulfilling trusts and establishing justice in judgment. Amanah includes every responsibility, right, secret, property, and position of authority entrusted to a person; it must be returned or discharged to those entitled to it. Judging with justice means deciding between people according to truth and fairness, without favoritism, bias, or personal interest. The verse connects private integrity with public justice, showing that both are essential to a God-conscious society. Allah’s instruction is excellent because it protects rights and preserves order. His being Hearing and Seeing means no act, intention, or hidden injustice escapes His knowledge, so people must fulfill trusts and judge justly with awareness of accountability before Him.

translation: O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and more suitable for final determination.
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle of obedience to God, to His Messenger, and to those entrusted with authority among the believers, while making clear that no authority is absolute or independent of divine guidance. If disagreement or conflict arises regarding any matter, the final recourse must be to God and His Messenger—that is, to the Qur’an and the Prophet’s Sunnah—for those who truly believe in God and the Last Day. This procedure is declared to be better and more excellent in its outcome, because it protects the community from partisanship, subjective opinion, and destructive division, and directs it toward the revealed standard of truth and justice.

translation: Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what was revealed to you and in what was revealed before you? They want to seek judgment from false authorities, although they were commanded to reject them. And Satan wants to lead them far astray.
interpretation: This verse exposes the contradiction of those who verbally claim faith in the revelation sent to the Prophet Muhammad and in earlier scriptures, yet willingly turn to false authorities or tyrannical systems for judgment instead of God’s revealed law. Their claim is false because true faith requires rejecting every rival authority that claims the right to legislate or judge independently of God. Such people were already commanded to disbelieve in false authority, meaning to refuse it as a source of ultimate allegiance and arbitration. Satan exploits this inclination, desiring not merely a minor error but a deep and distant deviation from the straight path. The verse therefore warns that seeking judgment from anything other than God and His Messenger is a mark of hypocrisy, a betrayal of faith, and a doorway through which Satan leads people into far-reaching misguidance.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,' you see the hypocrites turning away from you in aversion.
interpretation: This verse exposes the inner condition of the hypocrites: when called to submit to Allah’s revelation and to the Messenger’s judgment, they do not merely hesitate but actively recoil and turn aside. Their aversion shows that their professed faith is hollow and that they prefer their own desires, social loyalties, or human authorities over divine guidance. It establishes that true faith demands recourse to Allah and His Messenger, and that rejection of that authority is a mark of hypocrisy and disobedience.

translation: So how [will it be] when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have sent ahead, and then they come to you swearing by Allah, 'We intended nothing but good and reconciliation'?
interpretation: This verse rebukes the hypocrites: after their own misdeeds bring about a painful consequence, they rush to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and swear by God that they meant only goodwill and harmony. Their oath is false and self-serving; they are not truly repentant but are trying to escape blame. The verse teaches that claims of good intention cannot excuse deliberate disobedience, conspiracy, or betrayal, especially when God has exposed their true motives. It also warns that no oath can undo the consequences of what one has chosen to do.

translation: Those are the ones of whom Allah knows what is in their hearts; so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a penetrating word concerning themselves.
interpretation: This verse teaches that Allah alone knows the hidden motives, doubts, and intentions people conceal in their hearts. The Prophet is therefore directed not to become entangled in their secret scheming or waste effort in futile argument, but to disengage from their harmful conduct while still offering sincere counsel. The admonition is to be given with compassion, and the final instruction is to address them about their own inner state with words that are deeply penetrating and effective—speech that reaches the conscience, exposes self-deception, and invites repentance. Thus the verse combines divine knowledge of the hidden self with prophetic wisdom: avoid the trap of their concealed malice, yet do not abandon them to it; instead, warn them in a way that may awaken their hearts and lead them back to truth.

translation: And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by the permission of Allah. And if they, when they had wronged themselves, had come to you and asked forgiveness of Allah, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse establishes that every messenger was sent by Allah to be obeyed, and that obedience to the messenger is obedience to Allah because the messenger’s authority is granted only by Allah’s permission. It then addresses those who wronged themselves through sin, rejection, or disobedience: genuine repentance requires turning to Allah with humility and also coming to the Prophet, seeking Allah’s forgiveness and asking the Prophet to supplicate for them. Had they done so sincerely, they would have found Allah repeatedly accepting repentance and extremely merciful. Thus the verse teaches that God has appointed the messenger as the means through which His guidance and forgiveness are sought, and that He does not reject those who return to Him through the path He Himself established.

translation: But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning what has arisen between them, and then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided, and submit with full submission.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true faith is inseparable from wholehearted acceptance of the Prophet’s authoritative judgment in every dispute. It is not enough to profess belief outwardly; the believer must also be inwardly free of resistance, resentment, or doubt regarding the ruling, and must surrender to it completely. The oath sworn by Allah underscores that rejecting this submission is incompatible with genuine iman, and that divine guidance requires the human will to yield to revealed authority with sincerity, trust, and peace.

translation: And if We had prescribed for them, 'Kill yourselves,' or 'Leave your homes,' they would not have done it except a few of them. But if they had done what they were admonished to do, it would have been better for them and more strengthening.
interpretation: This exposes the gap between claim and commitment: many who profess faith would recoil from a severe divine test, while only the sincere few would obey. The actual commands and prohibitions they are urged to follow are a mercy and training, not an unbearable burden. Had they obeyed Allah and His Messenger in what they were warned about, it would have brought them greater good in this world and the Hereafter, and would have made their hearts and steps firmer in faith, because obedience to divine guidance produces certainty, steadfastness, and divine support.

translation: And then We would surely have given them from Our presence a great reward.
interpretation: If they had carried out the divine instructions and prohibitions they were admonished to follow, God would have bestowed upon them a vast reward from His own presence, as a favor and honor from Him.

translation: And We would have guided them to a straight path.
interpretation: This means that had they acted upon the divine instruction and admonition, Allah would have granted them guidance to the path of truth, sound belief, and righteous conduct, leading to His pleasure and eternal success.

translation: And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger — those will be with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.
interpretation: This verse establishes that sincere obedience to God and His Messenger is not merely a legal duty but a path to intimate fellowship in the Hereafter with the most honored servants of God. The promise is that such a person will be gathered with the prophets, the ever-truthful, those who bear witness to the truth through sacrifice, and the righteous in conduct. These four groups represent successive degrees of nearness to God, and being "with" them signifies sharing in their company, light, and honor, even if each person's rank corresponds to his or her own deeds. The ending declares that these are the best of companions, meaning that the supreme reward is not only entering Paradise but being in the presence of those whom God has specially favored and whose companionship perfects joy and dignity.

translation: That is the bounty from Allah, and Allah is sufficient as All-Knowing.
interpretation: The favor referred to—whether it is guidance, forgiveness, or the reward promised—is not something anyone can claim by right or attain by their own power; it is purely a gift and grace from God. And God is enough as the One whose knowledge encompasses all things: He knows who is worthy of His favor, who deserves His promise, and what lies in every heart, so His granting and His judgment are perfectly wise and just.

translation: O you who have believed, take your precautions and go forth in groups or go forth all together.
interpretation: This is a command to the believers to combine faith with practical prudence: before undertaking any collective struggle, they must take all necessary precautions, remain disciplined and prepared, and then march forth according to the wisdom of command—either in separate detachments for strategic flexibility or all together when unified strength is required. It teaches that reliance on God does not cancel sound planning, and that unity and organization are part of obedience.

translation: And indeed, among you is he who would surely lag behind. Then if a misfortune befalls you, he says, 'Indeed, Allah has favored me, since I was not present with them.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the mentality of the hypocrite who discourages others and holds back from struggle: when the believers face loss or hardship, he treats his own absence as a blessing from God. His words betray that he measures faith by personal safety and advantage, not by loyalty to God and the community. The verse warns that such self-serving withdrawal is a sign of weak or false faith, since a true believer does not rejoice in the community’s affliction or use religion as an excuse for cowardice.

translation: And if a bounty from Allah befalls you, he says—as if there had never been any affection between you and him—'Oh, would that I had been with them, then I would have attained a great attainment.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the hypocrite’s opportunistic and insincere allegiance. His relationship with the believers is not based on true faith or love, but on worldly advantage. When hardship strikes, he distances himself and claims he was spared; when success or spoils come, he regrets not being present and wishes he could share in the gain, speaking as though no bond of friendship ever existed. The 'great attainment' he desires is material and worldly, not the true success of faith and sincerity. The verse warns believers against such conditional loyalty and reassures them that Allah knows the hidden motives of the heart.

translation: So let those who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter fight in the way of Allah. And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or prevails—We will soon give him a great reward.
interpretation: This verse directs believers to place the eternal Hereafter above the fleeting life of this world and to strive in God’s cause with that priority. It teaches that the promised reward does not depend on outward victory alone: whether one is slain or overcomes, God grants a great recompense. The essential motive is sincerity for God and preference for the Hereafter over worldly gain; such sacrifice is never lost.

translation: And why should you not fight in the cause of Allah and for the oppressed among men, women, and children who say, 'Our Lord, bring us out of this town whose people are wrongdoers, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper'?
interpretation: This verse establishes that striving in God's cause is inseparable from defending the vulnerable and resisting tyranny. The prayer of the oppressed is not merely a plea for personal relief; it is a divine summons to the believing community to act. God censures indifference toward suffering men, women, and children, showing that faith demands solidarity with the weak and practical efforts to deliver them from unjust domination. At the same time, the verse teaches that true deliverance and protection ultimately come from God, so the believer combines reliance upon Him with the duty to be an instrument of His help and justice in the world.

translation: Those who believe fight in the cause of Allah, and those who disbelieve fight in the cause of Taghut. So fight the allies of Satan. Indeed, the scheme of Satan is weak.
interpretation: This verse reveals that the true dividing line in conflict is not merely worldly power or tribe but allegiance: either to Allah or to Taghut, the rebellious false authority that sets itself against divine guidance. The believers’ struggle is for God’s cause, while the disbelievers’ struggle serves a tyrannical, idolatrous power that ultimately belongs to Satan’s camp. Therefore, believers are told to confront the allies of Satan without intimidation, because Satan’s plotting, though deceptive and destructive, is fundamentally frail; it cannot stand against the truth and support of Allah.

translation: Have you not seen those who were told, 'Restrain your hands, establish prayer, and give zakah'? But when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a group of them feared the people as they feared Allah or with greater fear, and they said, 'Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us for a short time.' Say, 'The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for one who fears Allah; and you will not be wronged a thread.'
interpretation: This verse exposes a soul that accepts faith only while it costs little: it is willing to pray and give charity but recoils when obedience demands real sacrifice. Their fear of people exceeding or rivaling their fear of Allah shows that worldly security had become their true object of reverence. The divine reply reorders all values: worldly enjoyment is brief and deceptive, while the Hereafter is better for the mindful of Allah. What is surrendered for Allah is never lost or unjustly discounted, even to the measure of a tiny thread, so the believer should measure gain not by present safety but by eternal fidelity.

translation: Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you were in fortified towers. And if good befalls them, they say, 'This is from Allah'; but if evil befalls them, they say, 'This is from you.' Say, 'All is from Allah.' So what is wrong with these people that they hardly understand any statement?
interpretation: This verse affirms that death is inevitable and cannot be avoided by any place or fortification. It then exposes the inconsistent attitude of the hypocrites: when good comes, they attribute it to God, but when hardship comes, they blame the Prophet, as if he controls fortune. The Prophet is instructed to correct them: everything—good and misfortune—ultimately comes from God by His decree and wisdom. Their failure to grasp this truth reveals their shallow understanding.

translation: Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself. And We have sent you to the people as a Messenger, and sufficient is Allah as a Witness.
interpretation: This verse teaches that every blessing and good that reaches a person is a gift from Allah's grace, while the evil, harm, or misfortune that comes to him is the result of his own choices, sins, and shortcomings. It does not mean that anything occurs outside Allah's power or decree; rather, it directs blame away from Allah and places moral responsibility on the human being, since Allah is not unjust and does not wrong His servants. The verse then affirms that Muhammad (peace be upon him) is truly sent to all people as Allah's Messenger, and Allah Himself is enough as a witness to his truthfulness and to the message he conveys.

translation: Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah; and whoever turns away — We have not sent you as a keeper over them.
interpretation: Obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah because the Messenger conveys Allah’s commands and guidance. Those who turn away are not compelled by the Prophet; his role is to deliver the message, while guarding, compelling, or reckoning them belongs to Allah alone.

translation: And they say, “Obedience.” But when they leave you, a group of them plots by night other than what you say. And Allah records what they plot by night. So turn away from them and rely upon Allah, and sufficient is Allah as a Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: This verse exposes the hypocrisy of those who verbally profess obedience to the Prophet while secretly conspiring against his command once they are out of his presence. Their hidden nighttime plotting does not escape Allah; He records it fully and will hold them accountable. The Prophet is therefore told to turn away from their deception—not by approving it, but by not letting it consume him or seeking to match their scheming—and to place his trust in Allah. The verse teaches that when faced with betrayal, duplicity, or hidden opposition, the believer’s refuge is reliance upon Allah, who is sufficient as Guardian and Disposer of all affairs, able to protect the faithful and bring every secret plot to its proper reckoning.

translation: Do they not then reflect upon the Qur’an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction.
interpretation: This verse commands people to ponder the Qur’an deeply and to examine its meanings, not merely recite its words. It establishes that the Qur’an’s remarkable coherence and freedom from contradiction—despite being revealed over many years, addressing varied circumstances, and covering profound matters of belief, law, and guidance—is a clear sign that it comes from Allah. If it had originated from any source other than God, human or otherwise, it would inevitably contain conflicting statements, inconsistent teachings, or errors. Thus, the absence of such discrepancy is presented as evidence of its divine origin and as a rebuke to those who neglect reflection upon it.

translation: And when there comes to them a matter of security or fear, they spread it about. But if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those among them in authority, those who can investigate it would have known it from them. Were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except a few.
interpretation: This verse teaches that reports and news concerning public safety or danger must not be broadcast hastily by just anyone, because rumors can cause panic, weaken the community, and help its enemies. Such matters should be referred to the Prophet and to qualified people in authority—rulers, commanders, and knowledgeable scholars—who can verify facts, deduce the correct response, and handle the issue wisely. It establishes the principle of responsible communication, due process, and consulting those with expertise and authority. The concluding words remind believers that without Allah's favor and mercy, most people would follow Satan's promptings, including reckless speculation and rumor-mongering; divine guidance and mercy preserve only a few from that path.

translation: Fight in the way of Allah; you are not charged except with yourself, and encourage the believers. Perhaps Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve. And Allah is stronger in might and stronger in punishment.
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet Muhammad, and by extension the believers, to strive in Allah’s cause with a sense of personal responsibility, not being burdened by the failure or reluctance of others. It commands him to inspire and mobilize the believers, while placing ultimate reliance on Allah to repel the aggression of the disbelievers. The verse reassures that Allah’s power and punitive might are far greater than any worldly force, so the believer should not fear the enemy’s strength nor waver in fulfilling this duty.

translation: Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share of it; and whoever intercedes with an evil intercession will have a burden of it. And Allah is, over all things, a Keeper.
interpretation: This verse teaches that mediation and advocacy are morally consequential. When a person uses influence, speech, or position to support a good cause—such as justice, reconciliation, charity, or defending the wronged—they become a participant in that good and receive a portion of its reward. When they use the same influence to support evil, injustice, or sin, they bear a share of its guilt. The intercessor is therefore not neutral; their support aligns them with the outcome. The closing attribute, that Allah is over all things Muqit—Keeper, Maintainer, and Watcher—means no act of intercession, good or evil, escapes His knowledge, and He will sustain and recompense all things with perfect justice.

translation: And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet with one better than it or return it. Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, a Reckoner.
interpretation: This verse establishes the etiquette of greeting: when someone offers you a greeting of peace, you should respond with a better greeting—such as adding a prayer or blessing—or at least return it equally. It teaches that kindness and courtesy should be met with generosity or fairness, not ignored. The ending reminds believers that Allah is fully aware of and will reckon every deed, including how we respond to others, so our social conduct is a matter of accountability before Him.

translation: Allah—there is no deity except Him. He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. And who is more truthful than Allah in speech?
interpretation: This verse establishes that Allah alone is the true God, unique in divinity and sovereignty, and it emphasizes that His promise to gather all creation on the Day of Resurrection is absolutely certain and beyond any doubt. The rhetorical question declares that no one’s word or report is truer than Allah’s, so His revelation about the Hereafter must be accepted without hesitation. It calls the believer to live with accountability, trusting Allah’s promise and preparing for the inevitable meeting with Him, while warning those who doubt or deny the resurrection that His judgment will surely come to pass.

translation: So what is the matter with you that you are two factions regarding the hypocrites, while Allah has cast them back for what they earned? Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has led astray? And whoever Allah leads astray, you will never find for him a way.
interpretation: This verse confronts the division among the believers over how to judge the hypocrites. It states that their hypocrisy was not a neutral matter: Allah has cast them back into disbelief and ruin as a just consequence of what they themselves earned through their choices. Thus, the believers should not split into opposing camps about them, nor should they hope to guide those whom Allah has already led astray because of their persistent hypocrisy. The verse affirms that divine guidance and misguidance are governed by Allah's wisdom and justice: when He leaves someone astray, no human effort can invent a path for them unless Allah grants it. It is a warning against misplaced sympathy or partisanship toward those whose inward corruption Allah has exposed, and a call to align judgment with Allah's rather than with factional loyalty.

translation: They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so that you would become all alike. So do not take from among them allies until they migrate in the way of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them any ally or helper.
interpretation: This verse addresses a faction of hypocrites in Medina whose disbelief was not merely private but who actively desired the believers to abandon faith and join them in hostility. The prohibition against taking them as allies is tied to their ongoing enmity and their refusal to join the Muslim community through emigration in God's cause. The command to seize and fight them applies within the specific context of open warfare and betrayal, when they have aligned with the enemy and remain actively hostile; it is not a general license to kill non-Muslims or dissenters. Once they cease hostility, accept the established social and legal order, or join the Muslim body, they are no longer subject to this ruling. The verse warns believers against trusting those who actively seek to harm the community and instructs them to rely on God rather than on treacherous alliances.

translation: Except those who join a people between whom and you there is a treaty, or who come to you with hearts constrained from fighting you or fighting their own people. Had Allah willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you. So if they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you any way against them.
interpretation: This exception means that the command to fight does not apply to those who are bound by a treaty with the Muslims, nor to those who approach with restraint, unwilling to fight the Muslims or their own people. Even though God could have enabled them to harm you, He did not; therefore, if they step back, refrain from aggression, and extend peace, Muslims are given no lawful authority to attack them. The verse thus establishes that fighting is only justified against active hostility or betrayal, while neutrality, restraint, and an offer of peace remove any basis for war.

translation: You will find others who wish to be safe from you and safe from their own people. Whenever they are returned to trial, they are plunged into it. So if they do not withdraw from you, offer you peace, and restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them. And those — We have given you a clear authority over them.
interpretation: This verse describes a group of hypocrites who try to play both sides: they seek security from the Muslims and security from their own disbelieving people. Their allegiance is opportunistic and unstable. Whenever fitnah—testing, conflict, or persecution—arises, they fall back into betrayal and hostility. Therefore, if they do not withdraw from opposing the Muslims, offer a genuine peace, and stop their aggression, the Muslims are permitted to seize them and fight them wherever they encounter them. The phrase “a clear authority” means a manifest justification from God: their treacherous conduct and continued hostility remove any claim to neutrality, so fighting them is legally warranted, not arbitrary. The command is conditional; if they abstain, make peace, and restrain their hands, they are not to be fought.

translation: It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then he must free a believing slave and pay blood money to his family, unless they forgo it. If he was from a people hostile to you, while he is a believer, then he must free a believing slave. And if he was from a people between whom and you there is a treaty, then blood money must be paid to his family and a believing slave freed. Whoever cannot find [the means], then fasting two consecutive months, as repentance from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes the inviolability of a believer’s life and treats intentional killing as utterly incompatible with faith; the only situation it legislates for is unintentional homicide. For accidental killing, it imposes a twofold restitution: expiation by freeing a believing slave and compensation to the victim’s heirs, unless they forgive the killer. The expiation addresses the killer’s accountability before God, while the blood money addresses the loss to the family. If the victim was a believer living among a people at war with the Muslims, the verse drops the blood money because his heirs are in the enemy camp, but the expiation remains. If he belonged to a people bound by treaty with the Muslims, both the blood money and the expiation are required. If the killer cannot afford a slave or the payment, he fasts two consecutive months as a repentance accepted by Allah. The ending affirms that Allah knows hidden intentions and circumstances and is wise in the gradation of penalties and remedies.

translation: And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, wherein he will abide forever, and Allah is angry with him, and has cursed him, and has prepared for him a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse teaches that deliberately killing a believer is one of the gravest sins. It portrays the act as an assault on the sanctity of life and on faith itself, deserving a severe divine recompense: Hell, lasting abiding, divine wrath, curse, and a great punishment. It serves as a strong deterrent, warning that such a killer stands under Allah’s condemnation unless he repents and Allah forgives him; if he persists or treats the act as permissible, the punishment described remains his fate.

translation: O you who have believed, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully; and do not say to one who offers you peace, “You are not a believer,” seeking the fleeting goods of worldly life. For with Allah are abundant gains. Thus were you before, but Allah conferred favor upon you; so investigate carefully. Indeed, Allah is ever, with what you do, Acquainted.
interpretation: This verse commands believers to verify matters before acting, especially in situations of conflict or expedition in God’s cause. They must not hastily declare someone a nonbeliever who offers peace or a greeting, merely to pursue worldly advantage such as spoils or material gain. The verse rebukes any motive of greed and reminds them that God possesses abundant provisions and rewards. It further reminds them that they themselves were once in a similar state of ignorance or weakness before God favored them with guidance, so they should be merciful and careful. The repeated command to investigate underscores that judgments about faith and life must rest on clear evidence, not suspicion or desire. God is fully aware of all deeds, including hidden intentions.

translation: Not equal are the believers who sit [at home]—other than those who have a disability—and those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has favored those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit by a degree. And to each Allah has promised the best [reward]. And Allah has favored those who strive over those who sit with a great reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that among the believers, those who actively struggle in Allah’s cause by spending their wealth and risking their lives are not equal in rank to those who remain behind. The exception is those who have a genuine impediment such as illness, injury, disability, or a similar inability; they are not included in the blame or in the comparison. Allah has promised the best reward—Paradise and divine good pleasure—to all sincere believers, but He grants those who strive with their wealth and lives a higher degree and a great reward because their sacrifice and obedience are greater. Thus faith may be shared, but levels of reward differ according to sacrifice, sincerity, and effort in Allah’s path.

translation: Ranks from Him, and forgiveness and mercy. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse describes the reward Allah has prepared for those who struggle in His cause: He grants them ascending ranks of honor and closeness to Him, forgiveness that erases their sins, and mercy that brings them abundant good. It affirms that all of this comes from Allah alone, and that He is ever Forgiving and Merciful to those who turn to Him in obedience and repentance.

translation: Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves — they say, 'What were you engaged in?' They say, 'We were oppressed in the land.' They say, 'Was not Allah's earth spacious, so that you could migrate therein?' Those — their refuge is Hell, and evil it is as a destination.
interpretation: This verse rebukes those who remain in a land where they cannot practice or preserve their faith, using oppression or weakness as an excuse, even though they are able to migrate to a place where they can worship Allah freely. Their failure to emigrate when possible is a wrong they commit against their own souls. At death, the angels reject their claim of helplessness by pointing out that Allah’s earth is vast enough for them to move. Therefore, those who deliberately neglect this duty without a valid excuse end in Hell. The verse establishes that a believer must flee environments that endanger or corrupt faith when migration is possible; true inability is the only acceptable excuse.

translation: Except the weak among men, women, and children who are unable to devise a plan and are not guided to a way.
interpretation: This verse lifts blame from those who are truly powerless and trapped: they lack both the capacity to escape or change their situation and the guidance or means to find a path out. Their inability is genuine, so they are excused from the censure directed at those who had the ability to migrate or act but failed to do so.

translation: For those, it may be that Allah will pardon them; and Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse gives hope to those who are genuinely helpless and unable to fulfill a religious obligation, such as migration from a place of oppression, because of weakness or lack of means. Although they may fall short, God may forgive them out of His mercy. The phrase "it may be" from God does not express doubt; rather, it conveys certainty that He will pardon those He wills. He is ever Pardoning and Forgiving, covering sins and forgiving them.

translation: Whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find in the earth many a place of refuge and abundance. And whoever leaves his house emigrating to Allah and His Messenger, then death overtakes him—his reward has certainly fallen due upon Allah. And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: This is a divine assurance that hijrah for Allah’s sake is never a losing venture: God opens sources of safety, dignity, and provision beyond what the migrant can foresee. If the journey is cut short by death before reaching its goal, the intention and departure for God and His Messenger are fully credited, and the reward is guaranteed by God Himself. The closing names al-Ghafur and al-Rahim confirm that shortcomings in the migrant’s effort or preparation are met with forgiveness and mercy, so no sincere sacrifice is wasted.

translation: And when you travel throughout the earth, there is no blame upon you that you shorten the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may harm you. Indeed, the disbelievers are to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: The verse means that God, in His mercy, permits the traveling believer who fears persecution or attack from those who reject faith to shorten the obligatory prayer; this concession preserves worship under dangerous circumstances and reminds the believers that the hostility of the disbelievers is open and persistent.

translation: And when you are among them and lead them in prayer, let a group of them stand with you, and let them take their weapons. Then when they have prostrated, let them be behind you; and let another group who have not yet prayed come and pray with you, and let them take their precautions and their weapons. Those who disbelieve wish that you would neglect your weapons and your baggage, so they could swoop down upon you in one attack. But there is no blame upon you if you are troubled by rain or are ill, to lay down your weapons; but take your precautions. Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle that worship and self-defense are not mutually exclusive in times of danger. It permits the prayer to be performed in a divided formation so that one group prays while another guards, and then they alternate, ensuring both the obligation of prayer and the safety of the community are upheld. The mention of weapons and vigilance teaches that trust in Allah does not abolish the need for prudent measures; rather, taking precautions is itself part of obedience. The verse also recognizes human weakness and hardship—rain or illness—by allowing weapons to be set aside, while still commanding general alertness. It warns that the enemies of faith eagerly seek any moment of negligence to strike, and it closes with the assurance that Allah has prepared a humiliating punishment for those who persist in disbelief and aggression.
