translation: Two men from among those who feared [Allah], upon whom Allah had bestowed favor, said, “Enter upon them through the gate; for when you have entered it, you will indeed be victorious. And rely upon Allah, if you are believers.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that genuine faith combines reverent fear of Allah with confident trust in Him. The two favored men did not deny the enemy’s strength, but they directed the people to the real source of victory: obedience to Allah’s command and reliance upon His promise. Entering the gate signifies taking the step Allah commanded despite fear; once that step is taken with true tawakkul, Allah grants success. The verse thus rebukes the paralysis caused by fearing people more than Allah and shows that victory is not by numbers or power but by faith, courage, and dependence on Allah.

translation: They said, 'O Moses, indeed we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting here.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the Israelites' refusal to enter the land Allah had promised them. Their words express blatant disrespect toward Moses and, by extension, toward Allah: they tell Moses to go fight with his Lord while they remain seated. It exposes their lack of faith, obedience, and courage, and their fear of the inhabitants. As a result, they were condemned to wander in the wilderness for forty years.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, I have no authority except over myself and my brother; so separate us from the defiantly disobedient people.'
interpretation: This is Moses' plea to God when his people refused to obey the command to enter the land. He admits that his power to command obedience extends only to himself and his brother Aaron, not to the rebellious Israelites. By asking God to 'separate' between them and the defiant, he seeks divine judgment: that God distinguish the obedient from the disobedient and distance him and his faithful brother from the company of transgressors. The verse teaches that a leader cannot force faith or obedience, that true allegiance is personal, and that one must disassociate from those who persist in defiance of God's command. It also portrays prophetic humility and total reliance on God when human support fails.

translation: He said, “Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land. So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people.”
interpretation: This is a divine decree of punishment upon the Children of Israel after they refused to obey the command to enter the promised land. The land is made prohibited to them, and they are condemned to wander aimlessly for forty years. Moses is then told not to grieve over a people whose persistent defiance and disobedience brought this sentence upon themselves; their condition serves as a warning that rejecting God’s commands leads to loss and exile from His blessings.

translation: And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam in truth, when they offered an offering, and it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. He said, “I will surely kill you.” He said, “Allah only accepts from the God-conscious.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that the worth of any act of worship or sacrifice is not determined by its outward form alone but by the inward state of the one who offers it: God accepts only from those who possess taqwa, sincere God-consciousness, humility, and righteousness. The rejected brother’s threat to kill reveals how envy, arrogance, and resentment can grow when one measures himself against others instead of turning to God; the accepted brother’s reply shows that true piety does not retaliate with violence or claim superiority, but submits to God’s judgment and recognizes that acceptance depends on the heart’s fidelity to Him.

translation: If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I will not extend my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse expresses the speaker’s God-conscious restraint: even when facing deadly aggression, he refuses to answer violence with violence or to commit murder, not because he is unable, but because he fears Allah and dreads disobeying Him. His fear of the Lord of the worlds outweighs the impulse of retaliation, teaching that true piety can hold a person back from grave sin even under extreme provocation and that ultimate judgment and justice belong to God.

translation: Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and so become among the companions of the Fire. And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This is the response of Abel to his brother Cain when Cain threatened to kill him. Abel renounces retaliation and self-defense, desiring that Cain alone bear the guilt of the murder he is about to commit, along with his own prior sins and the sin of his aggression. “My sin” here means the sin of killing me—the wrong committed against me—not that Abel is transferring his personal guilt to Cain. The verse affirms that each wrongdoer bears his own responsibility before God; no soul carries the burden of another. Thus Cain, by choosing murder and injustice, earns the punishment of the Fire, which is the just recompense of the wrongdoers.

translation: So his soul permitted him to kill his brother, and he killed him, and he became among the losers.
interpretation: This verse teaches that when the lower self is allowed to dominate, it can make grave evil appear acceptable and easy, overcoming conscience and moral restraint. The killer did not gain anything by destroying his brother; rather, he brought himself into ruin, losing his moral standing, his brother, and his share of good in the sight of Allah. True loss is not merely the loss of worldly advantage, but the corruption of the soul through disobedience and injustice.

translation: So Allah sent a crow, scratching the earth, to show him how to conceal the nakedness of his brother. He said, ‘Woe to me! Have I failed to be like this crow and conceal the nakedness of my brother?’ And he became among the regretful.
interpretation: This verse conveys that even after the grave crime of murder, God in His mercy taught the killer, through the humble example of a crow, how to cover and bury his brother’s body. The crow scratches the ground and becomes an instrument of divine instruction, exposing the murderer’s ignorance and moral blindness: the one who thought himself superior is left learning a basic act of human dignity from an animal. His cry, “Woe to me!”, is a bitter self-reproach and an admission of helplessness, not a full undoing of his sin. He regrets that he could not even do what the crow did, and he becomes consumed by remorse. The verse thus underscores the sanctity of the human body, the obligation to honor the dead through burial, the seriousness of homicide, and the painful awakening of conscience that follows grave wrongdoing. It also teaches that divine guidance can come through the ordinary signs of creation, and that remorse, though it may come too late to reverse the crime, can still break the heart and expose the soul’s loss.

translation: Because of that, We decreed upon the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul—unless it be for a soul or for corruption in the land—it is as if he had killed all mankind; and whoever saves one life, it is as if he had saved all mankind. And Our messengers had certainly come to them with clear proofs. Then indeed many of them, after that, in the land were transgressors.
interpretation: This verse establishes the sanctity of human life as a universal moral principle. It teaches that the unjust killing of one person is equivalent in gravity to destroying all humanity, because it violates the God-given sacredness shared by every human being and opens the way to widespread bloodshed and social ruin. Likewise, saving or preserving one life is like saving all humanity, because it affirms that sacredness and protects the whole society. The exception—execution for a soul or for corruption in the land—shows that the prohibition targets aggression, not justice. The verse then reproaches the Children of Israel: despite clear messengers and proofs, many continued in transgression and excess on earth.

translation: Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth spreading corruption is none but that they be killed or crucified, or that their hands and feet be cut off from opposite sides, or that they be exiled from the land. That is for them a disgrace in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.
interpretation: This is the legal penalty for hirabah: armed brigandage or rebellion against the security of the community by waging war against Allah and His Messenger and spreading corruption through violence, terror, robbery, or similar crimes. It is a severe worldly deterrent meant to protect life, property, and public order, and the form of punishment is assigned according to the gravity of the offense by legitimate authority. 'Opposite sides' means, for example, the right hand and left foot or the left hand and right foot. The verse also declares that such criminals incur disgrace in this life and, if they persist without repentance, a great punishment in the Hereafter.

translation: Except those who repent before you overpower them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This exception means that if the criminals who waged war and spread corruption repent sincerely before the authorities seize them and establish power over them, the prescribed worldly punishment for that offense is waived. Allah’s forgiveness and mercy are then extended to them for the matter between them and Him, while any rights owed to people must still be restored or justly settled.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means of nearness to Him and strive in His cause, so that you may succeed.
interpretation: This verse directs believers to three connected duties: maintaining God-consciousness by avoiding what He forbids and fulfilling what He commands; seeking a valid means of drawing closer to Him through sincere worship, obedience, repentance, and good deeds; and exerting earnest effort in His path, including struggling against one’s own evil inclinations and working for justice and righteousness. The promised outcome is true success: divine pleasure, guidance, and salvation in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve — if they had all that is on the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse declares that rejecting faith leads to an inescapable punishment on the Day of Resurrection. Even if a disbeliever were to possess the entire earth and as much again, and offered all of it as a ransom to escape that punishment, it would not be accepted. The verse thus emphasizes that divine justice cannot be bought or averted by any amount of worldly wealth, and that those who persist in disbelief will inevitably face a painful torment.

translation: They will want to come out of the Fire, but they will not be coming out of it, and for them is an enduring punishment.
interpretation: This verse states that the people of Hell will desire to leave it and be saved from its torment, but their desire will not be fulfilled; they will remain in it forever. Their punishment is permanent and uninterrupted—neither ending nor being reduced—as a recompense for their rejection and persistence in disbelief and sin.

translation: And the male thief and the female thief — cut off their hands as a recompense for what they committed, a deterrent punishment from Allah. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes that theft is a grave violation of God’s order, and the fixed penalty for it is the cutting off of the thief’s hand(s), applied equally to men and women. The punishment is described as a recompense for the crime and as a nakal — an exemplary deterrent — ordained by God, not by human legislation. It reflects God’s might in upholding justice and His wisdom in prescribing a sanction that protects property, life, and social security; it is not mere retaliation, but a divinely appointed means of deterring crime and restoring justice.

translation: So whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, then indeed, Allah will accept his repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that divine forgiveness remains open even after serious wrongdoing or punishable crime, but the repentance Allah accepts is not mere regret or verbal confession; it must be joined with islah—a real correction of one’s conduct, restoration of rights, and replacement of evil with good. God’s acceptance of such repentance flows from His mercy and forgiving nature, showing that accountability for wrong does not cancel the possibility of spiritual renewal for the one who sincerely turns back and mends their ways.

translation: Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse establishes that absolute sovereignty, rule, and authority over the heavens and the earth belong exclusively to Allah. Therefore, the decision to punish or forgive any servant rests entirely with Him, according to His wisdom, justice, and mercy; no creature can compel Him, prevent Him, or question His decree. It directs the believer to live between hope in Allah’s forgiveness and fear of His punishment, while trusting that His power is unlimited over all things and that His governance is never unjust or constrained.

translation: O Messenger, do not let those who hasten into disbelief grieve you — those who say with their mouths, 'We believe,' while their hearts do not believe, and those who are Jews: eager listeners to falsehood, listeners to another people who have not come to you. They distort words from their proper places, saying, 'If you are given this, take it; but if you are not given it, then beware.' And whoever Allah intends to put to trial, you cannot avail him anything against Allah. Those are the ones whose hearts Allah did not intend to purify. For them in this world is disgrace, and in the Hereafter a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet and warns that outward profession is not true faith. The hypocrites and those who follow distorted teaching rush to reject the truth; they treat revelation selectively, listening to those who oppose the Prophet and altering scriptures or rulings to fit their desires. Their criterion is not truth but convenience: they accept only what their leaders approve and reject what challenges them. The Prophet has no power to force the hearts of those whom Allah has left in trial; purification of hearts belongs to Allah’s will and grace, and their rejection brings disgrace in this life and severe punishment in the next. The believer should not be shaken by such people’s hypocrisy or schemes, but should remain firm on the revealed truth.

translation: They are eager listeners to falsehood, devourers of unlawful gain. So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them. And if you turn away from them, they will not harm you at all. And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.
interpretation: This verse exposes a people whose approach to judgment is corrupt: they readily listen to lies and consume forbidden wealth, such as bribes. Because their motives are not the pursuit of truth, Allah gives the Prophet latitude either to judge their disputes or to decline. Their rejection cannot harm him, for his mission does not depend on their acceptance. But if he does judge, he must do so with strict equity, not favoring them or anyone else. The closing statement, that Allah loves the just, establishes justice as a divine requirement and a moral standard that must be upheld even toward hostile or dishonest people.

translation: And how do they come to you for judgment while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah? Then they turn away after that. And those are not believers.
interpretation: This verse condemns the hypocrisy of seeking a ruling only when it suits one’s desires while rejecting the clear judgment of God already present in previous scripture. Turning away after the truth has become known proves that such a claim to faith is hollow; true faith demands submission to God’s commands, not selective adherence based on convenience or preference.

translation: Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light. The prophets who submitted judged by it for the Jews, and the rabbis and scholars did likewise by what they were entrusted of the Book of Allah, and they were witnesses to it. So do not fear the people; fear Me, and do not sell My signs for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed — then those are the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the Torah was a true revelation from Allah containing guidance and light, and that the prophets, religious leaders, and scholars were obligated to judge by it and guard it faithfully. It warns those entrusted with Allah's Book not to let fear of people or desire for worldly gain lead them to conceal, alter, or abandon His rulings. The final clause declares that refusing to judge by what Allah has revealed — out of rejection, distortion, or preference for petty worldly advantage — is disbelief, because it denies Allah's authority over judgment and treats His signs as something to be exchanged for a small price.

translation: And We ordained for them therein: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth, and for wounds retaliation. But whoever gives it up as charity, it is an expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed—then it is those who are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse affirms the principle of proportional justice (qisas) for bodily harm—life for life, eye for eye, and so on—as a law prescribed by God. It teaches that justice requires equivalence, not vengeance beyond measure, and that even a wound has its due retaliation. Yet the verse immediately encourages a higher path: if the victim or rightful guardian voluntarily pardons the offender and forgoes retaliation as an act of charity, that pardon becomes an expiation for the forgiver's own sins. The final warning is severe: those who refuse to judge by God's revealed law, whether by denying it, distorting it, or preferring their own desires, are the zalimun—wrongdoers who transgress the limits set by God. Thus the passage balances strict justice with the call to mercy and ultimate submission to divine authority.

translation: And We caused Jesus, son of Mary, to follow in their footsteps, confirming what was before him of the Torah; and We gave him the Gospel, in which there was guidance and light, and confirming what was before it of the Torah, and a guidance and admonition for the righteous.
interpretation: This verse means that after the earlier prophets of the Children of Israel, God sent Jesus, son of Mary, as their successor, continuing the same prophetic mission. He did not come to abolish the Torah but to confirm its divine origin and true teachings. The Gospel revealed to him contained guidance to the truth and light by which hearts are illuminated, and it also confirmed the Torah that came before it. It is thus a direction and moral exhortation for those who are mindful of God, guarding themselves against disobedience and seeking His pleasure, showing that true piety accepts divine revelation as guidance and admonition.

translation: And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then those are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse obliges the followers of the Gospel to abide by the revelation God sent in the Injil, which originally affirmed God's oneness, the truth of His messengers, and the righteousness He commanded. It then lays down a universal principle: whoever turns away from God's revealed judgment, preferring their own desires, traditions, or laws, falls into fisq—transgression and disobedience against God. Thus the verse establishes that God's revelation is the standard for judgment, and abandoning it is a serious moral and religious deviation.

translation: And We have revealed to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Book and as a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires away from the truth that has come to you. For each of you We have made a law and a clear way. Had Allah willed, He could have made you one community, but He tests you in what He has given you. So race to good deeds. To Allah is your return, all together, and He will inform you concerning that over which you used to differ.
interpretation: This verse establishes the Qur'an as the final revealed Book, coming with truth, confirming the earlier scriptures and standing as their trustworthy guardian and criterion. It commands the Prophet, and by extension the believers, to judge according to what Allah has revealed, not according to human desires or distorted interpretations. The diversity of laws and paths among communities is not a flaw but a divine test, through which people are meant to compete in goodness rather than dispute arrogantly. All will ultimately return to Allah, and He alone will clarify the matters about which they differed.

translation: And judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you. Then if they turn away, know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins. And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This is a directive to the Prophet—and, by extension, to every Muslim judge or ruler—that authority and judgment must be based exclusively on Allah’s revelation, not on the preferences, customs, or pressures of a people. Following “their desires” means allowing human inclination to override or selectively apply divine commands. The warning “lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed” shows that partial implementation of revelation is a grave danger: one may be tricked into abandoning a single ruling while thinking the rest is intact. If they reject this judgment, their turning away is not a sign that the divine law is defective; rather, it exposes their own sin, and Allah may let them suffer some consequences of it as a just recompense. The ending notes that such defiance is characteristic of many people, so the believer should not be shaken by majority opposition to God’s law.

translation: Do they then seek the judgment of the Age of Ignorance? And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?
interpretation: This verse censures those who prefer the rulings of jahiliyyah—laws rooted in ignorance, caprice, and human desire—over God's revealed law. It declares that no one's judgment is better, more just, or more wise than Allah's, and that this truth is recognized by those who possess firm certainty in His knowledge, justice, and authority. In its context, it establishes that true faith requires accepting God's ruling as the standard, rather than following inherited customs or corrupt desires.

translation: O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed, he is one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse forbids believers from adopting Jews and Christians as awliyā’ in the sense of loyal patrons, protectors, or confidants to whom one turns for allegiance, support, and guidance in opposition to God and the Muslim community. It does not forbid ordinary kindness, fair dealing, or peaceful coexistence with non-Muslims who are not fighting Muslims; other Qur’anic verses permit justice and kindness toward those who do not fight or expel Muslims. The phrase “some of them are allies of one another” indicates that the Jewish and Christian groups in that context were united in opposing the believers, so taking them as confidants or protectors would mean joining their camp. “Whoever takes them as allies among you is one of them” means that such a person’s loyalty places him in their category in terms of allegiance and enmity, not necessarily that he becomes Jewish or Christian by faith. “Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people” means this misplaced loyalty is an act of injustice against God, oneself, and the community, and God withholds guidance from those who persist in it.

translation: So you see those in whose hearts is a disease, racing to them, saying: 'We fear that a turn of fortune may strike us.' But perhaps Allah will bring about victory, or a command from Him, and then they will become regretful over what they concealed within themselves.
interpretation: This verse condemns opportunism and concealed hypocrisy: people whose loyalty is not grounded in faith rush to side with those opposing Allah’s cause, justifying it by fear of political shifts. Their real motive is self-preservation and hidden doubt. The verse teaches that divine decree can suddenly change circumstances—victory for the believers or an order from God—exposing hidden agendas and turning their secrecy into shame and regret. It warns believers against making fear the basis of allegiance and assures them that God will vindicate truth, so no one should compromise principle for imagined security.

translation: And those who believe will say, 'Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their strongest oaths that they were with you?' Their deeds have become worthless, and they have become losers.
interpretation: This verse exposes the hypocrisy of those who made solemn oaths of loyalty to the believers while secretly supporting their enemies. When Allah grants the believers victory, the believers will marvel at these hypocrites and ask whether these are the same people who swore their strongest oaths that they were on their side. Because their oaths and deeds lacked sincere faith and were motivated by opportunism and betrayal, all their works are nullified; they gain no reward and end up in utter loss in this life and the Hereafter.

translation: O you who have believed, whoever of you turns back from his religion, then Allah will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers, striving in the way of Allah and not fearing the blame of a blamer. That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills. And Allah is all-Encompassing, all-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse teaches that allegiance to God is not secured by human numbers or inheritance; if any abandon faith, God can raise another people whose bond with Him is reciprocal love. Their love for God expresses itself as mercy and humility toward the faithful, but as firmness and dignity against unbelief, without fear of human disapproval in matters of religion. Such devotion and courage are not a human achievement but a divine gift granted by God’s all-encompassing wisdom and knowledge, showing that He is never in need of any particular group and that true honor belongs to those whom He chooses and who remain steadfast for His sake.

translation: Your guardian is only Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe—those who establish prayer and give zakat while bowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that ultimate protection, authority, and allegiance belong to God alone, and that He entrusts this guardianship to His Messenger and to those believers whose faith is lived out through constant prayer, charitable giving, and humble submission. It means that true leadership and loyalty in the community are not based on lineage, wealth, or power, but on sincere devotion to God and active compassion for others.

translation: And whoever takes Allah and His Messenger and those who have believed as allies — then indeed, the party of Allah are the victorious.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true loyalty to God, His Messenger, and the community of believers constitutes membership in God's party, and God's party is the one that ultimately prevails. It teaches that alignment with divine guidance and the believing community is not a mere affiliation but a commitment that brings divine support and final success. The victory is assured in the overarching divine order, even if circumstances appear otherwise, because God's cause cannot be defeated.

translation: O you who have believed, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion in ridicule and amusement among those who were given the Scripture before you and the disbelievers. And fear Allah, if you are believers.
interpretation: This verse forbids believers from entering into a relationship of loyal allegiance and protective friendship with those who mock Islam, whether they are from among the People of the Book or from the disbelievers. It does not forbid ordinary kindness, justice, or fair dealing; rather, it prohibits allowing the mockery of faith to be embraced through close alliance and patronage. The command to fear Allah is a reminder that true faith requires placing loyalty to Allah and His religion above every social, political, or communal tie. A believer’s identity and allegiance must be shaped by iman, and one who truly believes will not consent to a bond that legitimizes or protects the ridicule of Allah’s religion.

translation: And when you call to prayer, they take it in ridicule and play. That is because they are a people who do not reason.
interpretation: This verse exposes the condition of those who mock the call to prayer: their ridicule is not a reasoned objection to worship but a sign of a heart and mind devoid of sound understanding. The call to prayer is an invitation to God’s remembrance, to prayer, and to true success, so mocking it amounts to mocking the very means of guidance. Because they do not grasp its purpose or the truth it conveys, they treat it as amusement. Their contempt therefore arises from a failure of reason and insight, not from evidence, and it warns believers that rejection of sacred rites can descend into mockery when understanding is abandoned.

translation: Say, "O People of the Book, do you resent us except because we have believed in Allah and in what was revealed to us and in what was revealed before, while most of you are defiantly disobedient?"
interpretation: This verse addresses the People of the Book through the Prophet, exposing that their hostility toward the Muslims has no just cause. The only reason they object is that the Muslims have believed in Allah, in the Qur’an revealed to them, and in the earlier scriptures revealed before them. Their resentment is therefore not against wrongdoing or injustice, but against faith itself and against the consistent prophetic message. By affirming belief in earlier revelations, the verse also shows that Islam does not reject the former prophets or books; rather, it confirms them. The concluding charge that most of them are fasiqun means they have departed from obedience to God and His covenant, opposing the truth after recognizing it. Thus the verse rebukes an unreasonable enmity rooted in rejection of divine guidance.

translation: Say, 'Shall I inform you of what is worse than that as recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and upon whom He has become angry, and of whom He made apes and pigs, and who worshipped false deities. Those are worse in position and further astray from the straight path.'
interpretation: The rhetorical question is a rebuke to those who mock the believers: it exposes that the truly wretched recompense is not the faith of the Muslims but the state of those who have drawn Allah's curse and anger, who suffered the humiliation of transformation into apes and pigs, and who enslaved themselves to Taghut, meaning any false god, idol, Satanic path, or tyrannical authority obeyed against Allah. Their superiority in worldly terms is worthless; before Allah they are worse in destination and farther from the balanced straight path. The verse thus measures honor by divine favor and guidance, not by status, lineage, or mockery, and it warns against following desires or false authorities that lead away from tawhid and obedience to Allah.

translation: And when they come to you, they say, 'We believe,' but they entered with disbelief and they departed with it. And Allah is most knowing of what they used to conceal.
interpretation: This verse exposes the hypocrisy of those who approach the Prophet and the believers with a false profession of faith: their coming and going brings no change of heart, for they entered as disbelievers and left as disbelievers. Their words 'we believe' are merely outward dissimulation, while Allah fully knows the disbelief and malice they hide, so He will hold them accountable for their secret intentions.

translation: And you see many of them hastening into sin and transgression and their devouring unlawful gain. Evil indeed is what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse condemns the eagerness of many among those addressed to plunge into wrongdoing without restraint. 'الإثم' is any sin that corrupts the soul; 'العدوان' is aggression against people's rights and dignity; and 'السحت' is wealth acquired through forbidden means—such as bribery, usury, extortion, and unlawful consumption. Their rushing into these together shows how sin, oppression, and illicit gain reinforce one another. The closing censure declares that such conduct is not a minor lapse but an evil course persistently chosen, deserving divine condemnation.

translation: Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them from their sinful speech and their consuming of unlawful gain? Evil indeed is what they have been doing.
interpretation: This verse condemns the religious leaders and learned scholars among the Children of Israel for failing to use their authority to stop the people’s sins, especially sinful speech and devouring unlawful wealth such as bribes, usury, and stolen property. Their silence and failure to forbid wrong is not neutral; it is itself an evil act. The verse teaches that religious scholars and leaders have a duty to enjoin good and forbid evil, particularly when corruption becomes public and widespread. When they remain silent for fear, social pressure, or worldly benefit, they become complicit in the wrongdoing and help it spread. It also warns that knowledge and religious status increase responsibility, so failing to act upon them deserves divine blame.

translation: And the Jews said, 'Allah's hand is shackled.' Their hands are shackled, and they were cursed for what they said. Rather, His two hands are outstretched; He gives as He wills. And what has been sent down to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. And We have cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. Whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it. And they strive upon the earth spreading corruption. And Allah does not love the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse rejects the claim that God is withholding provision or is miserly. The image of a shackled hand is a slander against God, so the verse declares that the hands of those who said it are restrained from good, and they incurred divine curse. God is not stingy: both His hands are open, meaning His giving is abundant and continuous, and He provides however He wills. The revelation sent to the Prophet increases many of them in arrogance and denial because of their resistance to truth. God also placed hostility and hatred among them until the end of time, so their unity is broken. Their plans for war are thwarted; whenever they ignite the flame of conflict, God extinguishes it. Their effort on earth is to spread corruption, and God does not love those who corrupt.

translation: And if the People of the Book had believed and feared Allah, We would have removed from them their misdeeds and admitted them to Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true faith in Allah and His final Messenger, together with taqwa—God-consciousness expressed by avoiding disbelief, sins, and disobedience—are the means by which a person attains forgiveness and eternal bliss. It addresses the People of the Book specifically to show that their claim to scriptural lineage does not by itself save them; had they accepted the truth brought to them and lived with reverent restraint, Allah would have erased their previous sins, not holding them to account for them, and would have entered them into the Gardens of Delight. The wording conveys God's immense mercy: He does not merely pardon but covers and removes evil deeds, and He grants the reward of Paradise as a favor from Him. Thus the verse teaches that salvation is conditional upon sincere belief and righteous conduct, and that divine forgiveness and the bliss of the Hereafter are open to all who respond to Allah with faith and piety.

translation: And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet. Among them is a moderate community, but many of them do evil.
interpretation: This verse means that had the People of the Book truly established the Torah and the Gospel—believing in them, preserving their original teachings, and acting upon what God revealed, including the Qur’an sent to Muhammad—God would have opened for them abundant blessings from every direction. “Eating from above them and from beneath their feet” signifies provision coming down from the sky and growing up from the earth: rain, crops, fruits, and comprehensive worldly and spiritual goodness. The verse also notes that not all are alike: among them are those who are balanced and upright, holding to truth and justice, while many others persist in disbelief, corruption, and evil deeds, and their conduct is wretched.

translation: O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people. Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse places the duty of complete and faithful proclamation upon the Messenger: the revelation entrusted to him must be delivered in its entirety, without concealment, distortion, or selective omission. The warning that failing to convey would mean not having conveyed the message shows that the prophetic office is inseparable from full delivery of what God reveals. The promise of divine protection assures him that the opposition, plots, or threats of people cannot prevent the fulfillment of that mission unless God permits it; therefore fear of human harm must not lead to withholding any part of the revelation. At the same time, the final statement declares that ultimate guidance belongs to God alone: those who persist in rejection and disbelief will not be guided, so the Messenger’s responsibility is to convey clearly, while hearts are turned to faith only by God’s will.

translation: Say, "O People of the Scripture, you are not on anything until you establish the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to you from your Lord." And what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Jews and Christians, declaring that their claim to be upon true religion is empty unless they truly uphold the Torah and the Gospel—meaning they accept their original divine teachings, act upon them, and recognize the Prophet Muhammad, whom those scriptures foretold. The phrase “and what was revealed to you from your Lord” confirms the Qur’an as the final revelation that validates and completes the earlier scriptures. Yet for many of them, this very revelation only intensifies their arrogance and rejection, because it exposes the gap between their claims and their actual fidelity to God’s commands. The Prophet is therefore consoled not to grieve over those who deliberately persist in disbelief after the truth has come to them.

translation: Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians—whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds—then no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.
interpretation: This verse establishes that salvation and security before God are not granted by communal or religious labels alone, but by the combination of sincere faith in God and the Hereafter with righteous action. The mention of Jews, Sabians, and Christians shows that anyone among them who meets this criterion is included in God’s promise of freedom from fear concerning what lies ahead and grief over what is past. It is a call to inward monotheism, moral responsibility, and deeds that accord with divine guidance, rather than reliance on inherited identity.

translation: We certainly took a covenant from the Children of Israel and sent messengers to them. Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a party they denied and a party they kill.
interpretation: This verse condemns the attitude of those who claim loyalty to God’s covenant while measuring revelation by their own inclinations. Their repeated pattern—rejecting some messengers and murdering others—shows that the problem was not a lack of divine communication but a refusal to submit when the truth opposed their desires. It warns that a covenant with God demands receiving His messengers and commands with humility, not selective acceptance based on convenience; rejecting or harming the bearers of truth is a grave violation that invites divine judgment.

translation: And they thought there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf. Then Allah turned to them in forgiveness; then many of them became blind and deaf. And Allah is Seeing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse exposes the self-deception of those who assume that violating God’s covenant will bring no test or consequence. Their spiritual blindness and deafness are not merely physical but describe a hardened incapacity to perceive truth or heed warning. When God grants them a chance to repent, it is pure mercy, yet many relapse into the same blindness and deafness, showing that repeated disregard for divine guidance deepens ruin. God’s sight encompasses every deed, so no action is hidden from His judgment and no one escapes accountability.

translation: They have certainly disbelieved who say, “Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary.” But the Messiah said, “O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.” Indeed, whoever associates partners with Allah, Allah has forbidden Paradise for him, and his refuge is the Fire. And there are no helpers for the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse declares that equating God with Jesus, the Messiah son of Mary, is disbelief. Jesus himself never claimed divinity; rather, he called his people to worship Allah alone, acknowledging Allah as his Lord and their Lord. The verse therefore establishes the absolute oneness of God and rejects any association of partners with Him. Whoever dies in a state of shirk—assigning divine status or worship to anyone besides Allah—is deprived of Paradise and destined for the Fire, and no created being can rescue or intercede for such a person against Allah’s judgment. The “wrongdoers” here are specifically those who commit the grave injustice of polytheism, and they will find no supporters to avert their punishment.

translation: They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Allah is the third of three." And there is no god except one God. And if they do not desist from what they are saying, a painful punishment will surely strike those who disbelieved among them.
interpretation: This verse is a decisive rejection of any plurality or division within the divine essence. It declares that claiming God is one of three—whether understood as a trinity of persons or as multiple gods—is unbelief, because the truth is that there is no deity except the One God, absolutely unique and without partner, equal, or son. The warning that a painful punishment will strike those who persist shows that this belief is not a minor matter; if they do not abandon it, they will face severe consequences. The verse therefore calls to pure monotheism and warns against any doctrine that compromises God's oneness.

translation: Will they not then repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse is a divine reproach and invitation: it calls the sinner to turn back from disobedience to God with sincere regret and to ask for His pardon, showing that repentance is not merely a way to escape punishment but a return to the right relationship with the Creator. The rhetorical question implies that they should hasten to do so, since God’s forgiveness and mercy are vast and His door of pardon remains open. The ending affirms that He is غفور, abundantly forgiving, and رحيم, merciful, so no one who sincerely turns to Him should despair of His mercy.

translation: The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; messengers have already passed away before him. And his mother was a truthful woman. They both used to eat food. Look how We make clear to them the signs, then look how they are deluded.
interpretation: This verse affirms the true status of Jesus: he is a human messenger of God, not God or a son of God. His mother Mary is described as truthful and righteous, not divine. The statement that both ate food is decisive proof of their created, human nature, because eating demonstrates need, dependence, bodily limitation, and mortality. Whatever requires food cannot be the self-sufficient Creator or a partner in divinity. The verse therefore exposes the contradiction of those who raise Jesus above his prophetic station, and it shows that God’s signs are clear, but such people turn away from them through their own falsehood and delusion.

translation: Say, "Do you worship besides Allah that which does not possess for you [the power of] harm or benefit? And Allah is the Hearing, the Knowing."
interpretation: This verse is a rebuke to those who direct worship to anything other than Allah—such as idols, saints, or created beings—even though those objects have no power to harm or benefit anyone independently. The rhetorical question exposes the irrationality of worshipping what cannot answer prayers, avert harm, or grant any good. Only Allah possesses full authority over benefit and harm, and He is the Hearer of every supplication and the Knower of every hidden intention. Therefore, worship and reliance belong exclusively to Him, for He alone is able to help and He is fully aware of all that His servants do and say.

translation: Say, O People of the Book, do not exceed the limits in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who went astray before, and who misled many, and who strayed from the right way.
interpretation: This verse commands the People of the Book to avoid exaggeration and extremism in religion by not overstepping the bounds of the truth God revealed. It warns them against following the whims and inherited deviations of earlier groups who first went astray themselves, then led many others away from guidance, and finally deviated from the balanced, straight path. The intended meaning is that true religious commitment must be measured by revealed truth, not by excess, innovation, or the desires of those who corrupted the way before.

translation: Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed by the tongue of David and Jesus, son of Mary. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.
interpretation: This verse declares that God’s curse—meaning expulsion from His mercy and deserved punishment—was pronounced upon the disbelieving Israelites through the prophetic words of David and Jesus. The curse was not arbitrary; it was the consequence of their persistent disobedience to God and their habit of transgressing His limits and the rights of others. Mentioning David and Jesus together shows that the same judgment against unbelief and wrongdoing was conveyed across successive revelations, and that their rejection of faith was tied to a deeper moral corruption: they knowingly rebelled and repeatedly violated divinely set boundaries.

translation: They did not forbid one another from the wrong they committed. Evil indeed is what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse condemns a people who not only committed a munkar but also failed to forbid one another from it. It teaches that guilt is not limited to the direct doer; a community shares responsibility when it remains silent and does not deter evil. Such silence allows sin to become habitual and widespread, and it earns God's severe censure: the evil is not merely the act itself but also the collective failure to oppose it.

translation: You see many of them taking as allies those who disbelieved. Evil indeed is what their own selves have sent ahead for them: that Allah is angry with them, and in the punishment they will abide forever.
interpretation: This verse rebukes a people whose claim or association with faith is contradicted by their loyalty to those who reject God. Their alliance with disbelief is not merely a social or political tie; it is a moral choice that reveals what they truly love and trust. The phrase 'what their own selves have sent ahead' means that their deeds have already been stored for the Day of Judgment, and the worst deed is that they earned God's wrath instead of His pleasure. The verse therefore teaches that loyalty and support must be given to God and His faithful servants, not to those who oppose Him. Chosen out of hypocrisy, fear, or worldly advantage, such an alliance brings no lasting benefit; it ends in divine anger and an eternal punishment that the verse presents as the inevitable consequence of persisting in that betrayal.

translation: And if they had believed in Allah and the Prophet and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies. But many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse exposes the inconsistency between claimed faith and misplaced loyalty. True belief in God, His Prophet, and the revelation sent to him would prevent a person from taking God’s opponents as intimate allies, protectors, or partisans. The fact that many persist in such alliances proves that their profession is not sincere faith but fisq—willful disobedience and departure from God’s command. Thus loyalty and friendship are a test of faith: one cannot genuinely believe in God and His message while aligning with those who reject and oppose it.

translation: You will surely find the most hostile of people toward the believers to be the Jews and the polytheists, and you will surely find the closest of them in affection toward the believers to be those who say, 'We are Christians.' That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant.
interpretation: This verse describes a historical and spiritual pattern: in the Prophet’s era, the factions among the Jews and the Arab polytheists who had rejected the truth were the most entrenched in enmity toward the believers, while many Christians—especially the devout monks and priests—were nearer in affection and more inclined to listen to the message. The reason given is their humility and religious devotion, not a blanket endorsement of every Christian doctrine; the Qur’an elsewhere corrects theological errors such as the Trinity. Thus closeness or hostility to the believers is ultimately measured by how one responds to the truth and whether one is freed from arrogance, for arrogance is what hardens the heart against guidance.

translation: And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they have recognized of the truth. They say, 'Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses.'
interpretation: This verse portrays the response of hearts attuned to divine truth: on hearing the Qur'an, they do not resist or turn away but recognize in it the truth they already know, and that recognition moves them to tears. Their weeping is not mere sentimentality but the fruit of clear perception of God's revelation and humility before it. They then confirm that recognition with faith and ask to be recorded among the witnesses—those who testify to the truth, stand with the messengers, and will bear witness on the Day of Judgment. It teaches that genuine knowledge of God leads to submission, and that the sign of true faith is a heart softened by truth, not a heart hardened by arrogance.

translation: And why should we not believe in Allah and in what has come to us of the truth, while we hope that our Lord will admit us among the righteous people?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical affirmation of faith: the speakers see no valid reason to reject Allah after the truth has reached them. Their belief is not merely intellectual; it is joined to a longing for God's grace—that He will place them with the righteous, meaning those whose faith and conduct are sound and who are honored by God. The verse thus presents faith as a reasonable response to revealed truth and as a hope-filled movement toward God's mercy and the company of the virtuous.

translation: So Allah rewarded them for what they said with gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they abide eternally. And that is the reward of the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse teaches that God recompenses people according to the truthfulness and sincerity of their words when those words arise from genuine faith. Their confession of belief and their longing to be counted among the righteous are not empty speech; God accepts them and grants the eternal bliss of gardens with flowing rivers. The reward is described as the portion of the muhsinin—those who excel in faith, sincerity, and righteous conduct—showing that God’s recompense is generous, permanent, and reserved for those who respond to divine truth with humble hearts and good deeds.

translation: And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of Hell.
interpretation: This verse establishes that those who reject faith in Allah and knowingly reject His revealed signs as false are the people of Jahim, the blazing Hell; their denial makes Hell their fitting abode in the Hereafter.

translation: O you who have believed, do not prohibit the good things which Allah has made lawful to you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not like transgressors.
interpretation: This verse forbids inventing religious restrictions that God never ordained, especially declaring wholesome and lawful blessings to be forbidden. It teaches that piety is not measured by self-imposed deprivation or harshness, but by gratefully accepting what God has made lawful while respecting His limits. The warning against transgression includes both exceeding God's commands through excess and exceeding them through undue prohibition; God's love is not for those who overstep His boundaries.

translation: And eat of what Allah has provided you as lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you are believers.
interpretation: This verse commands the believers to partake of God's provisions that are both halal and tayyib: halal in that they are not forbidden by divine law and are acquired through permissible means, and tayyib in that they are pure, wholesome, and beneficial. It rejects the extreme of forbidding what God has made lawful, as some do out of misplaced asceticism or man-made restrictions, while also rejecting the opposite extreme of consuming what He has prohibited or what is corrupt. The command to fear Allah, in whom they believe, ties lawful eating to God-consciousness: gratitude for His provision is expressed by obeying His limits, and true faith entails seeking His pleasure in even the most ordinary acts, such as eating and drinking. Thus the verse establishes that the believer's life is governed by divine guidance, not by arbitrary prohibitions or unrestrained desire.

translation: Allah does not take you to task for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He takes you to task for oaths you have deliberately bound. The expiation for that is feeding ten poor people with food of the average quality you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. But whoever cannot afford it, then fasting for three days. That is the expiation for your oaths when you have sworn. And guard your oaths. Thus Allah makes clear to you His signs so that you may be grateful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that Allah is merciful regarding oaths that are spoken unintentionally or without the serious intent to bind oneself; such slips are not grounds for blame or expiation. However, when a person deliberately swears an oath and then breaks it, the oath carries accountability and requires expiation. The prescribed expiation—feeding ten needy people from the average food one feeds one’s family, clothing them, or freeing a slave—shows that oaths are not trivial matters and that their violation has social and moral consequences. If one lacks the means, fasting three days replaces the material expiation, demonstrating that divine law considers intention, ability, and circumstance. Guarding one’s oaths means avoiding careless swearing, not making oaths except when necessary, and honoring or expiating them when broken. The verse concludes by reminding believers that these clear rulings are signs from Allah meant to evoke gratitude for guidance, mercy, and a law that rectifies both individual conduct and communal responsibility.

translation: O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, sacrificing on stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.
interpretation: This verse decisively prohibits intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars of sacrifice, and divination arrows, classifying them all as rijs—spiritual filth and moral pollution—originating from Satan’s deception. The command to avoid them entirely is a condition for true success, meaning that the believer’s welfare, purity, and ultimate salvation depend on shunning these Satanic works and the disobedience and corruption they bring.

translation: Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred between you through intoxicants and gambling, and to divert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. Will you not then refrain?
interpretation: This verse identifies intoxicants and gambling as instruments of Satan, whose aim is to corrupt both human relationships and worship. They stir up enmity and hatred among people and turn the heart away from remembering God and establishing prayer. The closing question is a firm call to abandon them completely, since whatever produces such harm cannot be compatible with faith and obedience to God.

translation: And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance.
interpretation: This verse obliges believers to obey Allah and His Messenger, and to guard against disobedience. If they turn away, the Prophet's role is solely to deliver the message clearly; he is not responsible for compelling them to accept it. Thus, obedience is a duty, and the Messenger's accountability is limited to conveying the divine message.

translation: There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have tasted [in the past], when they fear Allah and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good. And Allah loves the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse removes liability from believers for intoxicants or other things they consumed before God prohibited them, provided their lives are characterized by taqwa, faith, and righteous action. The repeated sequence—fear of Allah, faith, righteous deeds, then deeper fear and faith, then fear and excellence—shows that the standard is not merely past behavior but an ongoing state of God-consciousness and spiritual growth. It is not permission to continue what God has forbidden; rather, it distinguishes between what occurred before the command and what must be abandoned after it. The closing statement that Allah loves the doers of good (muhsinin) indicates that the goal is not only avoiding sin but striving for excellence in worship, character, and conduct.

translation: O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and spears can reach, so that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen. Then whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse presents a divine test through permissible-looking game made easily accessible, so that people’s inward obedience becomes evident. The test is not for Allah to gain new knowledge, since He knows all things; rather, it exposes and distinguishes those who restrain themselves out of sincere fear of Allah even when no human authority sees them. The mention of hands and spears indicates how close and attainable the temptation is, removing excuses based on difficulty. Thus, whoever violates the prohibition after this clear warning transgresses against God’s command and deserves painful punishment.

translation: O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram. And whoever among you kills it deliberately, the compensation is the like of what he killed from livestock, judged by two just men among you, as an offering reaching the Ka'bah, or expiation by feeding the poor, or the equivalent of that in fasting, so that he may taste the consequence of his deed. Allah has forgiven what is past; but whoever repeats, Allah will take retribution from him. And Allah is Mighty, Owner of Retribution.
interpretation: This verse establishes the inviolability of hunted game during the sacred state of ihram, treating hunting as a breach of the holiness and discipline that pilgrimage imposes. The compensation is not merely punitive but restorative and penitential: it must correspond to the harm done, be determined by two upright judges, and be offered at the Ka'bah; where that is not possible, feeding the poor or an equivalent fast serves as a substitute according to one's capacity. The aim is to make the offender inwardly taste the seriousness of disobedience. Allah's pardon for what has already passed expresses mercy for prior ignorance or weakness, but deliberate persistence after knowing the ruling places one under divine retribution, for Allah is Almighty and fully capable of exacting punishment.

translation: Lawful for you is the catch of the sea and its food, as provision for you and for travelers; but forbidden for you is the catch of the land as long as you are in a state of ritual consecration. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.
interpretation: This verse establishes that during the sacred state of ihram, hunting land animals is forbidden, while taking from the sea and eating its food remains lawful. The permission is a mercy and provision for those resident and those traveling, showing that Allah does not burden His servants beyond capacity in matters of sustenance. The prohibition of land hunting applies specifically while one is in ihram; once that sacred state ends, the restriction is lifted. The command to fear Allah and the reminder of being gathered to Him urges obedience to these limits and mindfulness that all actions will be judged by the One who ordained them.

translation: Allah has made the Ka‘bah, the Sacred House, a means of support for the people, and the sacred month, and the sacrificial animals, and the garlands. That is so you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: This verse explains that Allah established the Sacred House, the sacred months, the sacrificial animals, and the garlands as pillars of order, security, and religious life for people. The Ka‘bah is the center of worship, pilgrimage, and unity; the sacred months preserve safety and restraint from violence; the offerings and garlands mark devotion and serve as recognizable signs that protect pilgrims and sacrifices. All these institutions are not merely social customs but divine arrangements grounded in Allah’s perfect knowledge of what is in the heavens and the earth. Their purpose is to make people aware that Allah knows all hidden and visible realities, and that His laws and sanctities are wisely ordered for human benefit. Recognizing this should deepen trust in Allah, reverence for His commands, and certainty that nothing escapes His knowledge or care.

translation: Know that Allah is severe in punishment and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse calls believers to hold together two fundamental truths about God: His justice is uncompromising toward those who knowingly persist in sin and oppression, so no one should feel safe in disobedience; and His mercy is vast for those who turn back to Him, so no one should despair of His forgiveness. It cultivates a heart that neither dismisses divine accountability nor doubts divine compassion.

translation: The Messenger is not bound to anything except delivering [the message]. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.
interpretation: The Prophet’s duty is solely to transmit the revelation faithfully; he cannot compel hearts or bear responsibility for those who reject it. Allah alone knows all that people make public and all that they hide, so He will hold them accountable for both outward actions and inner intentions. This absolves the Messenger of blame for his audience’s response and warns them that no secret motive or hidden denial escapes God’s knowledge.

translation: Say: The impure and the pure are not equal, even though the abundance of the impure may impress you. So fear Allah, O people of understanding, so that you may succeed.
interpretation: This verse teaches that moral and spiritual impurity can never be equal to purity and goodness, no matter how widespread or impressive the impure may appear. The majority, popularity, or abundance of something corrupt does not make it true, beneficial, or acceptable before God. People of sound understanding are therefore called to God-consciousness, avoiding what He has forbidden and choosing what He has made pure, so that they may attain true success in this life and the Hereafter.

translation: O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if disclosed to you, would distress you. But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you. Allah has pardoned [you for] it. And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse teaches believers to avoid prying into matters Allah has left unspecified or concealed, especially hypothetical or unnecessary questions whose answers could impose hardship, expose shortcomings, or create confusion. It does not forbid seeking necessary religious knowledge; rather it forbids obstinate questioning, testing the Prophet, or demanding details beyond revelation. During the period of revelation, such questions could receive direct divine answers, sometimes resulting in stricter obligations. Allah's silence on certain matters is a mercy, and He has pardoned what was asked before or left unlegislated. His names Forgiving and Forbearing show He does not punish immediately, overlooks faults, and tolerates His servants with patience, inviting them to repentance and restraint.

translation: A people before you asked about them, then they became disbelievers therein.
interpretation: This verse warns that pressing for details about matters Allah has left unspecified, or demanding signs and rulings out of curiosity or testing, can lead a person toward disbelief. Earlier communities asked their prophets about such things; when the answers came and obligations were imposed, they rejected them and fell into denial. So the verse teaches submission and restraint: believers should not probe what Allah has left unlegislated, lest questioning turn into refusal of the truth.

translation: Allah has not ordained any Bahirah, nor Sa'ibah, nor Wasilah, nor Ham. But those who disbelieve invent falsehood about Allah, and most of them do not reason.
interpretation: This verse rejects the pre-Islamic customs in which certain camels, sheep, or livestock were dedicated, left to roam, or exempted from use based on superstitious classifications, while people claimed these were divinely appointed laws. Allah declares that He never legislated such things; they are human inventions falsely attributed to Him. Those who do so fabricate lies against Allah, and most of them do not use their reason to distinguish between God’s true law and inherited falsehood. Thus the verse affirms that the authority to declare things lawful or unlawful belongs to Allah alone, not to custom, clergy, or ancestral tradition.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,' they say, 'Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon.' Even if their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?
interpretation: This verse condemns blind adherence to ancestral customs and inherited beliefs when they are set up against Allah’s revelation and the guidance of His Messenger. It shows that the mere fact of following one’s forefathers is not a valid proof of truth, especially if those forefathers lacked true knowledge and were not rightly guided. True guidance is not measured by what a community inherited, but by conformity to what Allah revealed and to the Messenger who conveys it.

translation: O you who have believed, take care of yourselves. Those who have gone astray will not harm you if you are guided. To Allah is your return, all together, and He will inform you about what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse establishes that ultimate accountability before Allah is individual: each person is primarily responsible for guarding their own faith, obedience, and moral integrity. It does not mean believers may be indifferent to others or abandon enjoining good; rather, it means that once they have sincerely upheld guidance and fulfilled their duty of warning and counsel, the misguidance or rejection of others cannot harm them spiritually. Guidance benefits the one who accepts it, and misguidance harms the one who chooses it. Since all people will return to Allah together, every deed will be disclosed and judged with perfect justice and knowledge.

translation: O you who have believed, the witnessing between you, when death approaches one of you at the time of the bequest, is two just men from among you, or two others from outside you, if you are traveling in the land and the affliction of death strikes you. You shall detain them after the prayer, and they shall swear by Allah, if you doubt, “We will not sell it for a price, even if he be a near relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed, we would then be among the sinners.”
interpretation: This verse establishes the procedure for validating a bequest when death approaches, especially during travel. Ordinarily, two upright witnesses from the Muslim community are required; but in the exigency of travel, when such witnesses are unavailable, two witnesses from outside that community are permitted as a concession. If the heirs suspect dishonesty or alteration of the will, the witnesses are to be held after prayer and made to swear by Allah that they will not trade His testimony for any worldly gain, even to favor a relative, nor hide it. The oath serves as a solemn safeguard for the rights of heirs and the integrity of the bequest, and it warns that concealing God’s testimony is a grave sin. Thus the verse combines practical legal protection with a strong moral and religious deterrent against false testimony.

translation: But if it is discovered that the two witnesses have incurred guilt, then two others shall stand in their place from among those who have a rightful claim against them, and they shall swear by Allah: “Our testimony is more true than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers.”
interpretation: This verse establishes a legal safeguard for cases in which a bequest or will is disputed and the original witnesses are suspected or proven to have acted falsely or unjustly. When their wrongdoing becomes evident, their testimony is not allowed to stand unchallenged. Two others from among the injured heirs or rightful claimants take their place and swear that their claim and testimony are more credible than the accused witnesses’ testimony, and that they are not demanding more than what is rightfully theirs. The oath serves both as evidence and as a moral restraint: it protects the estate and the rights of the heirs from false testimony, and it warns the swearer that if he lies he would be counted among the wrongdoers before God. Thus the verse upholds justice in inheritance and bequest matters by preventing false witnesses from defeating the rights of those who are entitled to them.

translation: That is more likely that they will give testimony in its proper form, or fear that oaths will be turned back after their oaths. And fear Allah and listen; and Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the prescribed legal procedure—administering oaths and allowing a later counter-oath—serves as a strong deterrent against false testimony. It makes witnesses more likely to testify truthfully, because they fear that their oaths may be rejected or superseded by later oaths and their dishonesty exposed. The command to fear Allah and listen means that justice and truth must be upheld out of consciousness of God and obedience to His rulings, not merely through legal pressure. Finally, Allah’s refusal to guide the fasiqun means that those who persistently reject His commands and corrupt the truth are deprived of divine guidance; guidance is granted to those who heed God and submit to His law.

translation: On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, 'What response were you given?' They will say, 'We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that on the Day of Judgment, the messengers will defer all final knowledge of how their communities truly responded to God. Their statement, 'We have no knowledge,' expresses that the inward reality of people's faith, rejection, sincerity, and hypocrisy, as well as what happened after the messengers' lifetimes, is beyond their limited awareness. They therefore return the matter to God, who alone knows the unseen and will judge with complete and perfect knowledge. It establishes that ultimate accountability belongs to God, not to His messengers.

translation: When Allah will say: O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favor upon you and upon your mother, when I supported you with the Holy Spirit, so you spoke to the people in the cradle and in maturity; and when I taught you the Scripture and wisdom, and the Torah and the Gospel; and when you made from clay the form of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission; and you healed the blind and the leper by My permission; and when you brought forth the dead by My permission; and when I restrained the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear signs, and those who disbelieved among them said: ‘This is nothing but clear magic.’
interpretation: This verse is a divine address to Jesus on the Day of Judgment, enumerating the favors and miracles granted to him and his mother. It establishes his true station as a servant of Allah and a prophet, not a god or son of God. Every miraculous act is tied to Allah’s permission—speaking in the cradle, being taught the Scripture, wisdom, Torah, and Gospel, forming a bird from clay, healing the blind and the leper, and raising the dead—to show that Jesus possessed no independent divine power. The support of the Holy Spirit refers to Gabriel, who strengthened him. The refusal of the disbelievers to accept his clear signs, calling them magic, illustrates how rejection of truth can persist despite undeniable proofs. Thus the verse reinforces pure monotheism, honors Mary, vindicates Jesus against his enemies, and warns against exaggerating him beyond his human and prophetic limits.

translation: And when I inspired the disciples, 'Believe in Me and in My Messenger.' They said, 'We have believed, and bear witness that we are Muslims.'
interpretation: This verse recounts Allah’s grace in guiding the disciples by an inward inspiration to faith. It shows that true faith is not merely inherited or outward; it is placed in the heart by divine guidance and answered by willing submission. Their response, 'We have believed,' joins inner conviction with outward confession, and their request, 'bear witness that we are Muslims,' expresses that faith in Allah and His Messenger is inseparable from islam—humble obedience and surrender to Allah alone. It also honors the disciples as sincere believers who submitted to Allah’s command through His Messenger.

translation: When the disciples said, 'O Jesus, son of Mary, is your Lord able to send down to us a table from heaven?' He said, 'Fear Allah, if you are believers.'
interpretation: The disciples' question was not necessarily a denial of God's power, but a request for a heavenly sign; Jesus responds by calling them to taqwa, because a believer's proper stance is trust in God's unlimited power rather than challenging it or demanding miracles as proof. The verse teaches that faith should not depend on spectacular signs and that reverence for God protects the heart from doubt and presumption, while Jesus is shown as a prophet directing his followers to God-consciousness.

translation: They said, “We wish to eat from it, so that our hearts may be reassured, and we may know that you have spoken the truth to us, and that we may be witnesses to it.”
interpretation: This verse reports the disciples’ request to Jesus for a heavenly table as a sign. Its meaning is that they sought a direct, experiential confirmation of God’s power and Jesus’ truthfulness: eating from it would satisfy a real need, calm their hearts with certainty, verify that Jesus had conveyed God’s message truthfully, and enable them to testify to that sign before others. Their request is presented as a desire for deeper assurance and witness, not simply as idle curiosity or outright denial.
