translation: A group He has guided, and a group has justly deserved misguidance. Indeed, they took the devils as allies instead of Allah, and they think that they are guided.
interpretation: This verse explains that humanity is divided into two groups: those whom Allah has guided by His grace, and those for whom misguidance became due because they deliberately chose the devils as protectors and patrons instead of Allah. Their misguidance is not arbitrary; it is the consequence of their own preference for false guardians over divine guidance. The verse warns that a person can fall into grave error while sincerely imagining himself to be rightly guided, so self-confidence in one’s own guidance is not proof of it—true guidance comes from Allah and is confirmed by taking Him alone as Lord and Protector.

translation: O children of Adam, take your adornment at every mosque, and eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like those who are excessive.
interpretation: This verse establishes that worship requires dignified covering and adornment; it refutes the pre-Islamic practice of circumambulating the Kaaba naked and the ascetic prohibition of good, lawful food and drink. It teaches that the body's needs and lawful pleasures are not inherently opposed to piety, but must be enjoyed within God's limits, without waste, vanity, or excess. The verse connects outward decency in prayer with gratitude for provision, and it identifies israf—exceeding bounds in consumption or conduct—as something God dislikes.

translation: Say, 'Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?' Say, 'They are for those who believe during the life of this world, exclusively theirs on the Day of Resurrection.' Thus do We detail the verses for a people who know.
interpretation: This verse is a divine rebuke to those who invent prohibitions and declare unlawful what God has made lawful, whether outward adornments or wholesome sustenance. God's created goods and pure provisions are not inherently unholy; they are meant to be received with gratitude and used within His limits. In this worldly life, believers and disbelievers may both benefit from them outwardly, but on the Day of Resurrection these blessings will be purely and exclusively for the believers, who used them in obedience and faith. So true piety is not rejecting God's permissible good things, but acknowledging them as His gifts and living thankfully before Him. The verse is thus an invitation to understand that legislation of halal and haram belongs to God alone, and that detailed revelation guides those who possess knowledge.

translation: Say, 'My Lord has only forbidden immoralities—what is apparent of them and what is concealed—and sin, and oppression without right, and that you associate with Allah that for which He has not sent down authority, and that you say about Allah what you do not know.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that Allah's prohibitions are rooted in His lordship and wisdom and are meant to protect both the inner and outer life of the human being. He forbids shameful acts whether done openly or secretly, because corruption of the heart and corruption of public conduct are equally destructive. He forbids sin itself, meaning disobedience that burdens the soul, and He forbids unjust aggression, meaning transgression against others without valid right. He also forbids associating partners with Him without any authority He has revealed, since worship must be based on His command alone, not on human invention. Finally, He forbids speaking about Him without knowledge—whether about His essence, attributes, laws, or promises—because such speech replaces divine guidance with conjecture and can lead people into falsehood while claiming to represent God.

translation: And for every nation is a [fixed] term. So when their term comes, they will not delay it by a moment, nor will they advance it.
interpretation: This verse declares that every community, nation, or generation has an appointed time decreed by God for its collective existence, judgment, or end. When that divinely fixed term arrives, it cannot be postponed or hastened by even the smallest unit of time; human effort, power, or pleading cannot alter God's decree. It teaches that history and the rise and fall of peoples unfold under God's precise command, and that all should live responsibly before the inevitable meeting with their appointed end.

translation: O children of Adam, if there come to you messengers from among you relating to you My verses, then whoever fears Allah and reforms — no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.
interpretation: This address is to all humankind, the descendants of Adam: God will send messengers from their own kind, reciting His revealed signs. The promise is for those who combine taqwa—guarding against disbelief, disobedience, and His displeasure—with islah, setting right their beliefs, worship, and conduct. Such people are secure from the terror and punishment of the Hereafter and from the sorrow of losing any worldly good, because God's pleasure and eternal reward are theirs. The verse thus establishes that guidance comes through God's messengers, and that salvation depends on responding with God-consciousness and righteous reform.

translation: And those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse declares that the Fire is the destined abode of those who combine rejection of God’s revealed signs with arrogance toward them. Their denial is not merely a failure of knowledge but a willful pride that refuses to submit to the truth and regards divine guidance as beneath them. Such people are the rightful inhabitants of the Fire, and their punishment is everlasting; the verse warns that persistent arrogance toward God’s signs seals a person in the ruin they have chosen.

translation: Who then is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or rejects His signs? Those will receive their share from the Book [as decreed]. Until, when Our messengers [angels] come to them to take them in death, they say, “Where are those you used to invoke besides Allah?” They will say, “They have vanished from us.” And they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse is a severe reproach against two attitudes that ultimately converge: inventing lies about God—whether by false attribution, distorting revelation, or claiming authority to speak in His name—and rejecting His clear signs. It teaches that such people are not outside God’s decree; they receive their allotted share of worldly life, sustenance, and lifespan exactly as written, which may be a test and a respite, not an endorsement. When the angel of death arrives, the false supports they relied on vanish, and they are forced to admit their own disbelief. Thus the verse emphasizes that no false object of worship can save a person at death, that denial is self-condemning, and that true success is not measured by temporary worldly portion but by fidelity to God and His signs.

translation: He will say: Enter among the communities that have passed away before you, of jinn and mankind, into the Fire. Every time a community enters, it curses its sister-community. Until, when they have all followed one another into it, the last of them will say about the first of them: Our Lord, these led us astray, so give them a double punishment of the Fire. He will say: For each is double, but you do not know.
interpretation: This verse portrays Hell as a gathering of communities united by shared disbelief and misguidance. The damned enter in groups, and each group curses its counterpart or predecessor, showing that the solidarity they had in sin turns into mutual blame and hatred. When the followers among them see the leaders, they accuse them of leading them astray and ask God to double the leaders' punishment. God's reply establishes that the doubled torment is not only for the leaders: it applies to each group according to its responsibility. The leaders are doubly punished for their own disbelief and for misleading others, while the followers are also doubly punished for their disbelief and for following false guidance. Their request to shift the greater blame is thus corrected, and the phrase 'but you do not know' indicates that the exact justice and measure of that doubled punishment are known only to God.

translation: And the first of them will say to the last of them: 'You have no advantage over us, so taste the punishment for what you used to earn.'
interpretation: This exchange takes place among those who followed one another into punishment. The earlier leaders reject the later followers’ attempt to blame them exclusively, declaring that the followers had no special merit, immunity, or excuse that placed them above accountability. They were not forced into disbelief or sin; they chose their path and earned its consequence. Thus the verse establishes that guilt cannot be shifted onto others, and no rank, following, or claim of being misled can shield a person from the just recompense of their own deeds. Each soul tastes the punishment for what it itself committed.

translation: Indeed, those who deny Our signs and are arrogant toward them—the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle. And thus do We recompense the criminals.
interpretation: This verse declares that those who knowingly reject God’s revealed signs and, worse, disdain them with arrogance are barred from divine acceptance and mercy. Their rejection is not mere doubt but prideful defiance, so the gates of heaven remain closed to their deeds and supplications, and Paradise is made utterly inaccessible to them. The image of a camel passing through the eye of a needle expresses an absolute impossibility, showing that while they persist in arrogance, their entrance into Paradise can never occur. God’s recompense for such criminals is perfectly just: the same pride that led them to turn away from His signs becomes the cause of their eternal exclusion.

translation: For them is a bed of Hell, and over them are coverings. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This describes the punishment of the unjust as total and inescapable: they are enveloped by Hell from beneath and from above, so there is no relief, shelter, or way out. The phrase “thus do We recompense the wrongdoers” affirms that this is God’s exact justice—those who knowingly covered over the truth and persisted in transgression receive a recompense matching their deeds, not an arbitrary penalty.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds—We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity—those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse joins true faith with righteous action as the condition for entering Paradise, and it places between them the assurance that God never imposes on a soul more than it can bear. The parenthetical statement “We do not burden any soul except within its capacity” means that divine commands are mercifully proportionate to human ability; God does not require the impossible, nor does He hold anyone responsible beyond what He has enabled them to do. Thus, the verse both encourages believers to persist in faith and good works and reassures them that the path of obligation is within their God-given capacity. Those who meet this condition are not merely promised Paradise but are described as its “companions” or rightful inhabitants, and their dwelling there is eternal, never to be cut off or ended.

translation: And We will remove whatever resentment is within their breasts; rivers will flow beneath them. And they will say, “All praise is due to Allah, who has guided us to this; and we would never have been guided had Allah not guided us. Indeed, the messengers of our Lord came with the truth.” And it will be proclaimed to them, “This is Paradise, which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do.”
interpretation: This verse depicts the purification of the believers’ hearts in Paradise: God removes all traces of rancor, envy, hatred, and ill will, so they dwell together in perfect harmony and peace. The rivers flowing beneath them symbolize continuous, abundant bliss and divine favor. Their words show that they recognize guidance as purely God’s grace, not their own achievement, and they affirm the truth of the prophets’ message. Being “made to inherit” Paradise indicates that it is granted by God’s mercy and generosity as a permanent home, while their deeds are the means by which God enables them to attain it—not a price that earns it independently of His grace.

translation: And the companions of Paradise will call out to the companions of the Fire: “We have indeed found what our Lord promised us to be true. Have you also found what your Lord promised you to be true?” They will say, “Yes.” Then a caller will announce between them that the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse portrays the moment after judgment when the reality of God’s promises and warnings becomes unmistakably clear. The people of Paradise address the people of the Fire not to mock them, but to confirm that what God had promised the righteous—reward and fulfillment—has proven true. When they ask whether the people of the Fire also found their Lord’s warning true, the answer “Yes” admits that divine justice and punishment are equally real. The announcement of God’s curse upon the wrongdoers means they are deprived of His mercy and excluded from His grace because they knowingly persisted in injustice, denial, and transgression. The verse thus affirms that divine promises are certain, that human choices have eternal consequences, and that wrongdoing ultimately leads to separation from God’s mercy.

translation: Those who turn others away from the path of Allah and seek to make it crooked, and who disbelieve in the Hereafter.
interpretation: This verse describes people who combine three evils: they block others from Allah’s straight path, they try to distort that path and make it appear deviant, and they reject the Hereafter. Their denial of final accountability is the root that enables them to mislead and corrupt without fear of judgment, so the verse exposes them as enemies of guidance and warns against accepting their distortion of Allah’s way.

translation: And between them is a barrier, and on the Heights are men who recognize all by their marks. And they call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you." They have not entered it, but they hope.
interpretation: Al-A'raf is an elevated partition between Paradise and Hell. The men standing upon it are those whose good and bad deeds are equal; they are delayed there until God admits them to Paradise by His mercy. They recognize the people of both abodes by their distinguishing signs. Their greeting of peace to the people of Paradise expresses their longing for the same end; though they have not yet entered Paradise, they hope in God’s mercy and do not despair. The passage thus teaches that final admission to Paradise is through divine grace and that hope in God remains obligatory even for those who are held back for a time.

translation: And when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say, “Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people.”
interpretation: This verse expresses the humility and God-consciousness of the people on the Heights: even while witnessing the fate of the people of the Fire, they do not gloat or feel secure in their own deeds. They turn to God in supplication, seeking refuge from being joined with the unjust. It teaches that seeing the punishment of others should move a believer to fear, self-examination, and reliance on God’s mercy, not to arrogance. Their plea is not merely to avoid the Fire but to avoid the company and path of the wrongdoing people, showing that one’s ultimate association—in belief, character, and conduct—determines one’s final destination. The verse also warns that injustice, in all its forms, leads to ruin, and that only God can place a person among the saved.

translation: And the companions of al-A'raf called out to men whom they recognized by their marks, saying, 'What did your gathering avail you, and what you used to be arrogant about?'
interpretation: The verse conveys that worldly resources, followers, status, and arrogance cannot avert divine judgment. Those who took pride in their strength, wealth, or numbers will find all of it worthless when Allah’s decree comes, and the very signs by which they are known will expose them rather than honor them. True deliverance lies in faith, humility, and righteous deeds, not in self-exaltation or the multitude of one’s supporters.

translation: Are these the ones whom you swore that Allah would not bestow mercy upon them? Enter Paradise; you shall have no fear, nor shall you grieve.
interpretation: This is a divine rebuke to those who arrogantly claimed that the weak or lowly believers could never receive Allah’s mercy. On the Day of Judgment, their false oath is overturned: the very people they despised are admitted into Paradise, secure from all fear and grief. The verse affirms that Allah’s mercy is His sovereign gift, not something earned or blocked by worldly status, wealth, or power, and that those mocked for their faith are ultimately vindicated and honored.

translation: And the companions of the Fire will call to the companions of Paradise, “Pour upon us some water or from whatever Allah has provided you.” They will say, “Indeed, Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers.”
interpretation: This verse depicts the anguish and utter deprivation of the inhabitants of Hell on the Day of Judgment: they beg the people of Paradise for even a drop of water or a morsel of sustenance, but their plea is refused because the bounties of Paradise are reserved exclusively for those who believed and obeyed Allah. The response declares that Allah has made those blessings forbidden to the disbelievers, meaning their rejection of faith in this life has permanently cut them off from divine mercy and reward. It conveys the irreversible justice of that Day: no relief, no sharing of bliss, and no escape for those who knowingly denied the truth.

translation: Those who took their religion as amusement and play, and were deceived by the life of this world. So today We will forget them just as they forgot the meeting of this Day of theirs, and as they used to reject Our verses.
interpretation: This means that those who reduced religion to entertainment, mockery, and play, and were deluded by worldly life, will on the Day of Judgment be abandoned by God—left out of His mercy and consigned to punishment—as a just recompense for having disregarded and denied the meeting of that Day and persistently rejecting His signs. God's 'forgetting' them here is not a lapse in divine knowledge but His leaving them in the Fire, ignoring their plea, just as they ignored the accountability He had set before them.

translation: And indeed We have brought them a Book which We have expounded in detail with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Qur'an is a divine Book given to humanity, meticulously explained and clarified by Allah's all-encompassing knowledge. Its detailed laws, teachings, promises, and warnings are not haphazard but are based on perfect wisdom. It serves as guidance to the straight path and as mercy bringing worldly and eternal good, but this benefit is realized by those who believe—those who accept it, follow it, and shape their lives according to its message. For them it removes doubt, directs to truth, and brings Allah's compassion and reward.

translation: Do they wait except for its fulfillment? On the Day its fulfillment comes, those who had forgotten it before will say, 'Indeed the messengers of our Lord came with the truth. So are there any intercessors for us who could intercede for us, or could we be returned so that we might do other than what we used to do?' They have lost their souls, and what they used to invent has strayed away from them.
interpretation: This verse describes the regret of those who denied the revelation once the promised reality arrives: the Resurrection, judgment, and requital. It means their waiting was not sincere inquiry but evasion, and when the truth is finally unveiled, confession and pleading come too late. No intercessor can help them, and no return to worldly life will be granted so they can amend their deeds. Their loss is self-inflicted, and the false deities, excuses, and fabrications they relied upon vanish and lead them to ruin.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days and then established Himself above the Throne. He covers the night with the day, which chases it rapidly; and the sun, the moon, and the stars are subjected by His command. Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse teaches that lordship belongs exclusively to Allah: He alone originated all things, governs them, and issues the command that orders the cosmos. The orderly succession of night and day and the subjugation of the sun, moon, and stars are not accidents or independent powers; they are signs of His continuous control and mercy. Creation and command are His together, so worship, reliance, and obedience are due to Him alone. His being above the Throne affirms His exalted sovereignty over all existence in the manner that befits His majesty, without reducing His transcendence or likening Him to creatures. Thus true blessedness and peace are found in recognizing Him as the Lord, Nourisher, and Sovereign of all worlds.

translation: Call upon your Lord in humility and privately. Indeed, He does not like the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse commands believers to supplicate God with sincere humility, brokenness, and neediness, and to do so quietly and discreetly rather than with ostentation or excessive loudness. Such supplication reflects true submission and recognition of God’s majesty. The verse then warns that God does not love those who overstep His limits, which includes transgressing in supplication—such as showing off, being arrogant, making demands improperly, or asking for what is unlawful—and transgressing in any other matter by disobeying His commands.

translation: And do not cause corruption upon the earth after it has been set right, and call upon Him in fear and hope. Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse forbids spreading corruption in the earth after Allah has set it right through His guidance, natural order, and the mission of His prophets. Corruption here includes sins, injustice, oppression, exploitation, and destruction of what Allah entrusted to humanity. It also commands supplication to Allah with a heart balanced between fear of His punishment and hope for His mercy, so that the believer neither despairs nor feels falsely secure. The verse concludes by affirming that Allah’s mercy is near to the doers of good—those who worship Him sincerely, obey His commands, and treat His creation with justice, compassion, and excellence.

translation: And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy, until, when they have carried heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land and send down water thereby, and bring forth thereby from all fruits. Thus We will bring forth the dead, so that you may remember.
interpretation: This verse uses the cycle of rain and plant growth as a clear sign of God's power to resurrect. The winds are sent as heralds of His mercy, meaning the rain that gives life. He directs heavy clouds to barren, lifeless land, sends down water, and causes every kind of fruit to emerge. In the same way, God will bring the dead out of their graves. The verse calls people to reflect on how easily God revives dead earth, so they may remember and believe in the reality of the Hereafter and His authority over life and death.

translation: The good land brings forth its vegetation by the permission of its Lord, while the bad land brings forth nothing but with hardship. Thus We explain the verses in various ways for a people who are grateful.
interpretation: This is a parable of human hearts before revelation: a pure, receptive heart accepts God's guidance and yields faith and good deeds by His enabling, while a corrupt, unreceptive heart responds to the same message only with resistance and barrenness. God diversifies His signs so that those who are thankful—whose gratitude disposes them to receive the truth—may understand and benefit.

translation: Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, so he said: “O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a great Day.”
interpretation: This verse establishes that Noah was a true messenger sent by Allah to call his people to the foundational message of all prophets: the exclusive worship of Allah alone, since no being besides Him deserves divinity or worship. Noah’s fear for them is not doubt in Allah’s power but a compassionate warning that persisting in shirk—associating others with Allah—will bring them to the punishment of the Great Day, the Day of Resurrection, whose severity, accountability, and consequences are immense. The verse therefore teaches that authentic guidance begins with pure monotheism, and that rejecting it exposes a person to grave and eternal loss.

translation: The chiefs of his people said, “Indeed, we surely see you in clear error.”
interpretation: This is the response of the arrogant leaders among Prophet Nuh’s people to his call to worship Allah alone. They did not answer his message with proof; instead, they dismissed him as plainly misguided because he opposed their inherited idolatry and because those who followed him were often the weak and lowly. Their accusation shows that they judged truth by social rank, ancestral custom, and the interests of power, not by revelation. It also exposes a recurring pattern: when prophets confront corrupt elites, those elites brand the truth as error to protect their authority, while in reality it is their own rejection of Allah that is manifest misguidance.

translation: He said: O my people, there is no misguidance in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds.
interpretation: Noah addresses his people after they accused him of being astray. He denies any deviation in himself and declares that his true station is that of a messenger sent by Allah, the Lord of all creation. His call is therefore not a personal opinion or an invented path, but a message grounded in divine revelation and commission. The verse shows that the prophets are protected from misguidance in what they convey, and that rejecting their message is ultimately rejecting the Lord who sent them.

translation: I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I advise you sincerely, and I know from Allah what you do not know.
interpretation: The speaker, Prophet Noah, is establishing the credibility and sincerity of his prophetic mission: he faithfully delivers God’s commands and warnings without distortion, he counsels his people purely for their benefit and out of compassion, and his knowledge is received from God’s revelation rather than from human speculation. This means his warnings about accountability, divine judgment, and the consequences of obedience or rejection carry certainty beyond what his people can perceive by their own limited understanding, so they should respond to his call with trust and heedfulness.

translation: Do you wonder that there has come to you a reminder from your Lord through a man from among you, so that he may warn you, and that you may fear God, and that you may receive mercy?
interpretation: This verse addresses the people's astonishment that God's reminder and revelation should come through a human being from their own community rather than through an angel or someone extraordinary. It teaches that the messenger's humanity is part of divine wisdom: he is one of them, accessible to them, and able to convey the warning clearly. The purpose of the reminder is to call them to taqwa—guarding themselves against disobedience and seeking protection from God's punishment—so that they may become worthy of God's mercy. Thus the verse rejects the objection to a human prophet and presents warning, God-consciousness, and mercy as the intended path of revelation.

translation: So they denied him, but We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a people blind.
interpretation: This verse teaches that rejecting Allah’s messengers and signs brings destruction, while faith and obedience bring deliverance. Noah’s ark represents divine mercy and protection for those who follow the truth, even when the surrounding world is drowned in its own denial. The punishment of the deniers is just because it comes after clear warning, and their being “blind” is not physical blindness but a spiritual blindness: they saw the signs yet refused to understand or accept them. Thus the verse warns that persistent denial darkens the heart, until a person can no longer perceive the guidance that was plainly set before them.

translation: And to 'Aad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then fear [Him]?'
interpretation: This verse establishes the core prophetic call: Hud, a member of the 'Aad people, is sent to them as a warner, not to claim divinity or lordship. His message directs them away from false gods to the exclusive worship of Allah, the only true deity. The final rhetorical question presses them to recognize that refusing this worship is not merely an intellectual error but a moral and spiritual danger; 'taqwa' here means to guard themselves against Allah's displeasure and punishment by sincerely turning to Him. Thus the verse emphasizes both the unity of God and the accountability of the people to whom the messenger was sent.

translation: The disbelieving chiefs of his people said, “Indeed, we see you in foolishness, and indeed, we think you are among the liars.”
interpretation: This verse exposes how arrogant worldly leaders often respond to prophetic truth: instead of weighing the message, they attack the messenger’s character, calling him foolish and deceitful. Their accusation reflects not evidence but the offense caused by a call that challenges their inherited authority and corrupt status. It teaches that rejection of divine guidance can make people invert reality—labeling the wise as foolish and the truthful as liars—because accepting the prophet would require humbling themselves before Allah.

translation: He said, "O my people, there is no foolishness in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: The prophet rejects the people's charge that he is foolish or deceived. His mission is not a product of ignorance or self-delusion; it is a serious, truthful call rooted in divine authority. By identifying himself as a messenger from the Lord of all worlds, he clarifies that his message is not his own invention but comes from the sovereign Creator who sustains and governs all creation. Therefore, their accusation is not merely an insult against him but a rejection of the One who sent him.

translation: I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am to you a sincere and trustworthy adviser.
interpretation: The speaker affirms that his sole duty is to deliver the revelations of God faithfully and without alteration, and that his counsel toward his people is motivated by genuine concern, honesty, and trustworthiness. He is not seeking authority, gain, or praise; rather, he combines faithful transmission of the divine message with sincere well-wishing, so his warnings and guidance deserve to be received as truthful advice from one who can be trusted.

translation: Do you wonder that a reminder has come to you from your Lord through a man from among you, to warn you? And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah and increased you in creation extensively. So remember the favors of Allah, so that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse reproaches those who find it strange that divine warning should come through a human messenger rather than something extraordinary. It teaches that God’s guidance is conveyed through chosen men so that the warning is clear, accessible, and suited to human understanding, and that rejecting it out of pride is a failure to recognize God’s wisdom. It then calls them to remember that their position, strength, and ample form are not inherent rights but gifts: God made them inheritors after a destroyed nation and expanded their capacity in creation. Therefore, true success comes from recalling God’s favors with gratitude, humility, and obedience, not from arrogance toward His messengers.

translation: They said, “Have you come to us so that we may worship Allah alone and abandon what our forefathers used to worship? Then bring us what you promise us, if you are truthful.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the disbelievers’ defiant refusal of pure monotheism. They did not deny the prophet’s message on the basis of clear proof; rather, they clung to inherited idolatry and treated ancestral practice as a sufficient reason to reject Allah’s exclusive right to worship. Their demand to be brought the threatened punishment was not sincere seeking of truth but a mocking challenge, born of arrogance and hardness of heart. It shows how blind conformity to forefathers and resistance to divine authority can lead people to demand signs or punishment rather than humbly submit to the truth.

translation: He said, “There has already fallen upon you defilement and wrath from your Lord. Do you dispute with me concerning names which you and your forefathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority? So wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait.”
interpretation: This verse conveys that the people addressed had already incurred divine disgrace and anger because they persisted in worshipping invented names and false objects of devotion that had no sanction from God. Their dispute was not based on any revealed proof but on inherited custom and human invention. The prophet therefore disowns their authority and warns them to await the outcome, while he too awaits the judgment of God, confident that the promised punishment will come upon the deniers and that God’s word will prevail.

translation: So We saved him and those with him by mercy from Us, and We cut off the root of those who denied Our signs, and they were not believers.
interpretation: Allah delivered His messenger and the believers who followed him through His pure grace, while utterly eradicating the rejecters of His signs; their destruction was because they remained entrenched in disbelief and never accepted the truth.

translation: And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said, “O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has come to you a clear proof from your Lord. This she-camel of Allah is a sign for you. So leave her to eat in the land of Allah, and do not touch her with evil, lest a painful punishment seize you.”
interpretation: This verse presents the prophetic mission of Salih as a call to pure monotheism and as a test of obedience to a clear divine sign. Salih does not begin with the miraculous she-camel but with the foundational truth: worship belongs to Allah alone, and no other being shares His divinity. The she-camel is then identified as “Allah’s she-camel” and as a “sign,” meaning she is not merely a creature among creatures but a proof bearing divine authority. The command to let her eat in Allah’s land teaches that the earth and its provisions are not the absolute possession of any people; they are trusts from Allah, and His creatures have a right to benefit from them without human cruelty or arrogance. The prohibition against harming her is a test of whether the people will submit to Allah’s command even when it limits their sense of control, pride, or convenience. The warning of painful punishment shows that rejecting or abusing a divine sign after clear proof is not a small matter; it is a direct rebellion against Allah and His messenger. Thus the verse interprets true faith as worship of Allah alone, gratitude for His provision, reverence for His signs, and readiness to obey His commands rather than follow tribal arrogance or self-interest.

translation: And remember when He made you successors after 'Aad and settled you in the land — you take for yourselves palaces from its plains and carve out homes from the mountains. So remember the blessings of Allah and do not go about in the land spreading corruption.
interpretation: This verse is a reminder to the people of Thamud that their power, architecture, and settled life were blessings granted by Allah after He destroyed 'Aad. It teaches that succession to a previous nation is a test: those who inherit land and authority must use it in gratitude and obedience, not in arrogance, exploitation, or moral and social corruption. 'Remembering Allah's blessings' means acknowledging Him as the source of every provision and responding with worship, justice, and humility; 'not spreading corruption' forbids sins that damage faith, society, and the earth, including oppression, extravagance, and rejection of divine guidance. Thus the verse interprets worldly civilization as a trust whose value depends on gratitude to God and righteous conduct.

translation: The arrogant chiefs of his people said to those who were oppressed, to those who believed among them, 'Do you know that Salih is sent from his Lord?' They said, 'Indeed, we are believers in what he has been sent with.'
interpretation: This verse contrasts the arrogant elite's attempt to undermine the faith of the weak and oppressed believers with the believers' firm and unwavering response. The leaders' question is not a sincere inquiry but a rhetorical, mocking challenge meant to sow doubt about Salih's prophethood and to pressure the vulnerable into abandoning him. The believers answer with a clear declaration: they believe in the message sent by God through Salih. The verse thus teaches that true faith is not dependent on social standing, power, or the approval of the arrogant; the oppressed can possess certainty and sincerity, while the arrogant reject the truth out of pride. It also shows that the prophet's authority comes from God alone, and the response of the faithful is to accept what God has revealed.

translation: Those who were arrogant said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you have believed."
interpretation: This verse exposes the root of the arrogant elite’s rejection: it was not a lack of evidence or understanding, but pride and self-exaltation. They openly declare their disbelief in the very faith embraced by the weak and oppressed among their people, showing that their haughtiness made them refuse to submit to a truth that would place them on equal footing with those they considered inferior. Their statement is a deliberate, defiant rejection of God’s message, and it fixes upon them the guilt of knowingly denying the truth after it had become clear. It is a warning that kibr—arrogance—can harden the heart until one openly chooses disbelief, even when the message has reached him.

translation: So they hamstrung the she-camel and rebelled against the command of their Lord, and said, “O Salih, bring us what you promise us, if you are indeed among the messengers.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the arrogance and hardened disbelief of the Thamud. The she-camel was a clear divine sign and a test for them; by killing it, they openly defied God’s command and showed that their rejection was not due to lack of evidence but to wilful rebellion. Their demand that Salih bring the promised punishment at once was not a sincere request for guidance; it was a mocking challenge, as if to say that if he were truly a messenger, he should prove it by invoking the judgment he warned them about. This reveals how sin, when persisted in, breeds contempt for sacred signs and for the messengers who call people back to God. It also warns that demanding God’s signs or punishment on one’s own terms, while refusing to submit, invites destruction rather than guidance.

translation: Then the earthquake seized them, and they became within their homes fallen prone, lifeless.
interpretation: This verse depicts a people overwhelmed by divine punishment after they rejected their messenger and persisted in defiance. The violent shaking or quake struck them suddenly, and their own homes—places they thought offered safety and permanence—became the site of their ruin. They were left “jāthimīn”: fallen upon their knees or faces, motionless and humiliated, unable to stand, flee, or resist. It conveys that human strength, wealth, and fortified dwellings cannot shield anyone from God’s judgment when it comes, and that the punishment of the Hereafter is greater still for those who deny the truth.

translation: So he turned away from them and said, “O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you sincerely, but you do not like sincere advisers.”
interpretation: This verse conveys that the messenger has fully discharged his prophetic duty: he delivered God’s message faithfully and offered sincere counsel aimed at his people’s good. Their rejection is attributed not to any shortcoming in the message or the messenger, but to their own dislike of those who advise them truthfully. It teaches that a caller to God is responsible for faithful conveyance and sincere advice, while guidance and acceptance rest with God; and it exposes the tragedy of a people who resent sincere counsel because it confronts their desires and wrongs.

translation: And Lot, when he said to his people, "Do you commit such immorality as no one in all the worlds has ever committed before you?"
interpretation: This verse is a rebuke delivered through Prophet Lot to his people: they had normalized a sexual transgression so grave and unprecedented that no earlier community had practiced it in that form. The rhetorical question conveys astonishment and condemnation, showing that their act was not merely a private sin but a public moral corruption that violated the natural order God had established. It serves as a warning that inventing and spreading such indecency invites divine punishment, and it marks the crime as an extreme departure from both prophetic guidance and human decency.

translation: Indeed, you approach men with desire instead of women. Rather, you are a people transgressing all bounds.
interpretation: In this verse, Prophet Lut confronts his people’s sexual misconduct as a deliberate pursuit of lust outside the lawful and natural order God established. The emphasis on “with desire” shows that the act was driven by carnal appetite, and “instead of women” highlights their abandonment of the natural means of conjugal relations. By calling them “a people transgressing all bounds,” the Qur’an characterizes their sin as part of a larger pattern of excess and defiance: they exceeded God’s limits, corrupted their society, and persisted in it despite prophetic warning. Thus the verse condemns the act as immoral and identifies its root in unrestrained desire and communal transgression.

translation: And the answer of his people was nothing except that they said, “Expel them from your city. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the moral inversion of Lot’s people: when he called them to abandon their indecency, their only response was to demand the expulsion of the believers, branding them as people who purify themselves. Their words were not a sincere compliment but a hostile and mocking rejection: the purity and chastity of Lot’s followers reproached their corrupt practices, so instead of repenting they sought to remove the righteous from their midst. It shows how a society steeped in sin may treat the call to moral purity as an offense and resort to exclusion and persecution when it cannot justify its own conduct.

translation: So We saved him and his family, except his wife; she was among those who remained behind.
interpretation: This verse establishes that deliverance from divine punishment is linked to faith and righteousness, not merely to family ties. Lut’s wife was excluded from salvation because she chose to remain aligned with the corrupt people and their ways, so she was left behind to share in the fate that overtook them.

translation: And We rained upon them a rain, so see how was the end of the criminals.
interpretation: This verse refers to the punishment inflicted upon the people of Lot: after they persisted in their grave sins and rejected the warnings sent to them, Allah destroyed them with a rain of stones. The command to observe their fate is a lesson that those who knowingly reject divine guidance and persist in criminal disobedience ultimately meet a dreadful and ruinous end.

translation: And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has come to you a clear proof from your Lord. So give full measure and weight, and do not deprive people of their things, and do not cause corruption in the earth after its reformation. That is better for you, if you are believers.'
interpretation: This verse presents Shu'ayb’s call as rooted first in tawhid: the one God alone deserves worship, and from this follows justice in human dealings. The “clear proof” makes the message authoritative and leaves the people accountable, not merely invited. Honest measure and weight, and not withholding people’s rights, are not separate from faith but are its practical expression; exploiting others in trade is a violation of both divine command and human dignity. “Do not cause corruption in the earth after its reformation” means do not undo the moral and social order that God’s guidance and earlier prophets have set right through greed, fraud, or injustice. The statement “that is better for you, if you are believers” teaches that God’s commands are for human benefit, and that genuine iman must show itself in economic honesty, fairness, and resistance to corruption.

translation: And do not sit on every road, threatening and preventing from the way of Allah those who believe in Him, seeking to make it crooked. And remember when you were few and He increased you. And observe how was the end of the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse condemns the oppressive practice of controlling roads and public pathways in order to intimidate people, block them from the way of Allah, and make His straight path appear deviant or crooked. It exposes a combined injustice: using power and position to threaten others, to stop them from faith or obedience to God, and to corrupt the guidance itself by misrepresenting or obstructing it. The command to remember their former weakness and God’s subsequent multiplication of them is a call to gratitude, humility, and accountability: strength and numbers are not grounds for arrogance but trusts from God. Finally, it directs them to reflect on the fate of previous corrupters, warning that those who spread oppression, religious obstruction, and moral corruption will meet a destructive end.

translation: And if there is a group among you who have believed in what I have been sent with, and another group who have not believed, then be patient until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges.
interpretation: This verse teaches that when people divide over the message sent by God, the final decision is not left to human power, argument, or force, but to God alone. The believer’s duty is patient steadfastness upon the truth, trusting that God will judge with perfect justice and ultimately distinguish the sincere from the rejecters. The command to wait is not despair or inactivity; it is confidence that God’s judgment will settle the dispute and vindicate what is right.

translation: The arrogant chiefs of his people said, 'We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who have believed with you from our town, or you must return to our religion.' He said, 'Even if we are averse?'
interpretation: This verse exposes how arrogant power responds when it cannot refute the truth: it resorts to expulsion or forced conformity. Shu'ayb's response is a rhetorical rejection of compulsion in religion. It teaches that faith is valid only when freely chosen; to compel someone back to a creed they detest is unjust and tyrannical. The leaders were not merely disagreeing but using their dominance to silence and displace the believers, showing that their opposition was rooted in pride and worldly authority rather than sincere inquiry. For believers, the verse affirms that staying faithful may cost them their home or social standing, but they must not trade conviction for convenience or safety. It also portrays the prophetic stance: to call with clear proof, to refuse coercion, and to entrust the outcome to God.

translation: We would have fabricated a lie against Allah if we returned to your creed after Allah had saved us from it. It is not for us to return to it unless Allah, our Lord, wills. Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. In Allah we put our trust. Our Lord, judge between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of judges.
interpretation: This verse expresses the steadfastness of true faith and the impossibility of reverting to falsehood after being delivered by Allah. To go back to the creed of disbelief would not be a neutral change; it would be inventing a lie against Allah, because it would deny the truth He has already made clear and attribute to Him what is untrue. The speaker affirms that returning to error is not within human power to will independently: even such a return could only occur if Allah, the Lord, willed it, showing that all guidance and misguidance are encompassed by His sovereign will. Since His knowledge embraces all things, He knows the sincerity of the believers and the hidden motives of their opponents. Therefore the believer places complete trust in Allah alone and asks Him to judge decisively between the two parties with truth. The request “افتح بيننا” is a plea for Allah’s verdict, separation of truth from falsehood, and vindication of the truthful, because He is the best of judges and the best to open a way to justice and victory.

translation: And the leaders who disbelieved among his people said, 'If you follow Shu'ayb, indeed, you will then be the losers.'
interpretation: The disbelieving elite of Shu'ayb's people warned the community that accepting his call would bring ruin and loss. They meant loss of worldly wealth, status, and familiar economic advantage, because Shu'ayb condemned their dishonest trade and false worship. Their claim inverted reality: they thought following prophetic truth would destroy them, while in fact rejecting it was the real and lasting loss.

translation: So the convulsion seized them, and they lay motionless in their dwellings.
interpretation: This signifies the sudden and irresistible nature of divine punishment upon a people who persisted in denial: the violent tremor overwhelmed them, leaving them prostrate and lifeless in their own homes, unable to flee or resist. Their dwellings, strength, and numbers offered no protection once God’s decree came.

translation: Those who denied Shu'ayb—as if they had never dwelled therein. Those who denied Shu'ayb were themselves the losers.
interpretation: This verse declares that the people who rejected Prophet Shu'ayb and persisted in disbelief were destroyed so completely that it was as though they had never lived in their towns, and their wealth, power, and traces were cut off. The true loss fell upon them, because they forfeited both worldly standing and eternal success, while the Prophet and the believers were not harmed by their denial.

translation: So he turned away from them and said, “O my people, I have conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you sincerely; so how could I grieve over a disbelieving people?”
interpretation: This verse shows the prophet Shu‘ayb after his people were overtaken by punishment. He turns away from them in submission to God’s decree, not in bitterness or neglect of his duty. He testifies that he delivered the divine messages fully and gave them sincere counsel, so their ruin was due to their own persistent disbelief. His rhetorical question, “how could I grieve,” expresses that his sorrow cannot change their fate or be counted as a failure on his part; he is consoled by having fulfilled his prophetic responsibility and by trusting in God’s justice. It teaches that a caller to truth must do his part with sincerity, then leave the outcome to God, not let grief over those who reject faith overwhelm him.

translation: And We did not send a prophet into any town except that We seized its people with misery and hardship, so that they might humble themselves.
interpretation: This verse describes God’s consistent way of dealing with communities that receive a prophet: before any final punishment, He tests them with poverty, illness, loss, and other afflictions. The purpose is not mere suffering but corrective mercy—to break their arrogance, awaken their conscience, and lead them to humble themselves before God in repentance and supplication. If they respond with humility, they are spared; if they persist in rejection, the affliction serves as a warning before a greater judgment.

translation: Then We replaced the bad condition with good, until they increased and said, "Our forefathers were touched by hardship and ease." So We seized them suddenly while they were unaware.
interpretation: This verse portrays a recurring divine pattern: hardship is sent to soften hearts and prompt humility, but when relief and prosperity follow, people often mistake it for proof that life is simply an alternating cycle inherited from their ancestors rather than a test from God. Their heedlessness grows, gratitude fades, and they feel secure in their comforts. At that point, divine punishment overtakes them unexpectedly, when they least anticipate it. The meaning is that ease after affliction can be more spiritually dangerous than the affliction itself, because it breeds complacency and blinds people to the suddenness of judgment.

translation: And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth, but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn.
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine principle that faith in Allah and God-consciousness are the keys to receiving both heavenly and earthly blessings. When a people believe and guard themselves against disobedience, Allah opens for them sources of mercy, provision, security, and goodness from above and below. But when they reject the truth and persist in wrongdoing, they cut themselves off from those blessings and are held accountable by the very deeds they have earned.

translation: Did the people of the towns then feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them at night while they were asleep?
interpretation: This is a rebuke of false security: those who reject divine warnings should not assume they are safe from God's judgment simply because they enjoy peace and routine. God's punishment can arrive suddenly, even at night during sleep, when people are most unaware and defenseless. The verse teaches that no earthly settlement, power, or moment of comfort guarantees protection from God's decree, and that heedlessness toward His messengers is a dangerous delusion.

translation: Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the morning while they are playing?
interpretation: This verse rebukes heedlessness and false security. It asks, rhetorically, whether the inhabitants of towns believed they were safe from God's punishment simply because it had not yet struck them, and whether they imagined it could only come at night while they slept. The verse reveals that divine punishment can seize a people at any time—even in broad daylight, while they are distracted by play and worldly amusement. Their "playing" symbolizes negligence, arrogance, and immersion in trivial pursuits rather than preparing for accountability. The warning is against complacency: no one should consider themselves immune to God's decree or presume that ease and delay mean safety. It calls for vigilance, repentance, and awareness that God's plan cannot be thwarted or predicted by human confidence.

translation: Did they then feel secure against the plan of Allah? But none feels secure against the plan of Allah except the people who are losers.
interpretation: This verse rebukes those who presume they are safe from Allah’s hidden plan and His gradual punishment. It teaches that security from Allah’s plotting—meaning His wise and just handling of those who persist in rebellion—is itself a mark of those already heading toward loss. True faith requires humility, vigilance, and fear of Allah’s judgment, never arrogance or complacency in His mercy.

translation: Is it not a guidance for those who inherit the earth after its former people that, if We willed, We could have punished them for their sins? And We seal up their hearts, so they do not hear.
interpretation: This verse warns those who come to possess the earth after earlier nations were destroyed: their inheritance of the land is not a sign that they are safe from God’s judgment. If God willed, He could seize them for their own sins just as He did those before them. When people persist in heedlessness and sin, their hearts become sealed, so they no longer hear or accept divine guidance and warning. Thus the verse calls later generations to learn from history, repent, and not repeat the ways that led earlier peoples to ruin.

translation: These are the towns whose stories We relate to you. Their messengers had certainly come to them with clear proofs, but they were not to believe in what they had denied before. Thus does Allah seal the hearts of the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the destroyed nations were not denied divine evidence; their messengers brought manifest signs. Yet their persistent, prior rejection had so hardened them that when the truth came, they were no longer disposed to accept it. Their unbelief was therefore a just consequence of their own repeated denial, expressed as Allah sealing their hearts—meaning He withholds faith from hearts that have wilfully and persistently refused it. This is a warning that sustained rejection of clear guidance leads to spiritual hardening and divine abandonment.

translation: And We did not find for most of them any [fidelity to] covenant, and indeed We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: God declares that most of the communities addressed failed to honor the covenant placed upon them; they did not prove faithful to any pledge with Him. Having tested and known them, He found the majority to be fāsiqūn—those who depart from obedience, violate His limits, and persist in transgression. The verse thus exposes the widespread human tendency to betray sacred commitments and confirms that such defiance merits divine punishment.

translation: Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his establishment, but they were unjust to them. So observe how was the outcome of the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse marks a transition in prophetic history: after earlier messengers, God commissioned Moses with clear miraculous signs to Pharaoh and his ruling elite. Their response was not honest inquiry but unjust rejection—they knowingly denied and opposed the signs because accepting them threatened their power, privilege, and corrupt order. The command “so observe” invites reflection on the inevitable end of those who persist in corruption: Pharaoh’s tyranny, his oppression of the Israelites, and his defiance of God led to his and his followers’ destruction. Thus the verse establishes a divine law: corrupt leaders who reject truth and spread oppression may enjoy temporary power, but their outcome is ruin and disgrace, while God’s message and the oppressed are ultimately vindicated.

translation: And Moses said, "O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: Moses confronts Pharaoh by declaring that his authority comes not from any earthly power or from Pharaoh himself, but from the Lord of all creation. This statement directly challenges Pharaoh’s claim to divinity and absolute rule, asserting that there is a higher sovereign over all worlds to whom Pharaoh is accountable. It also establishes Moses’ prophetic mission as universal in scope and rooted in God’s lordship over everything.

translation: It is incumbent upon me that I say nothing about Allah except the truth. I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord, so send the Children of Israel with me.
interpretation: This is Moses addressing Pharaoh, declaring that as a prophet he is bound to speak only the truth about God and never invent or distort divine revelation. He then establishes the authenticity of his mission by pointing to a clear sign or miracle from his Lord. His demand, “so send the Children of Israel with me,” means Pharaoh must release the Israelites from bondage and let them depart with Moses so they can worship and serve God freely.

translation: He said, "If you have come with a sign, then bring it, if you are of the truthful."
interpretation: This is Pharaoh’s arrogant challenge to Moses: he demands a miracle as proof, making acceptance conditional on Moses satisfying his terms. It exposes a heart that does not sincerely seek truth but seeks to dominate and dismiss the divine message. The sign is not produced to gratify Pharaoh’s challenge, but as God’s decisive proof; yet obstinate denial can persist even when the miracle appears.

translation: So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent.
interpretation: This was one of the miracles granted to Moses: when he cast down his wooden staff before Pharaoh, Allah transformed it into a real, visible serpent, clear and undeniable, so that the sign would be witnessed as a divine proof rather than mere magic or illusion.

translation: And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the beholders.
interpretation: This is the second miraculous sign granted to Moses: when he drew his hand out from his garment or bosom, it appeared intensely white and radiant to all who looked on, not as a symptom of leprosy or disease, but as a clear divine sign confirming his prophethood before Pharaoh and his people.

translation: The chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said, 'Indeed, this is a learned magician.'
interpretation: Pharaoh’s influential leaders and courtiers, after witnessing Moses’ miracles, rejected them as divine signs and instead accused Moses of being a highly skilled sorcerer. They portrayed his extraordinary acts as the product of advanced magic rather than God’s power, aiming to discredit him before the people and justify their continued opposition to his call. This reflects the way obstinate deniers often reinterpret clear divine signs as trickery or sorcery in order to avoid submitting to the truth.

translation: He wants to expel you from your land, so what do you command?
interpretation: This statement reflects how entrenched power responds to prophetic truth by turning it into a political and territorial threat, then seeking a unified decree to suppress it. It exposes a mindset that values control over land and authority more than recognizing the truth, and it warns against allowing fear of losing worldly position to drive collective opposition to God’s messengers.

translation: They said, "Postpone him and his brother, and send among the cities gatherers."
interpretation: This is the counsel of Pharaoh’s court after Moses showed his signs: instead of deciding immediately, they advised Pharaoh to hold Moses and Aaron back temporarily and dispatch mobilizers throughout the cities to assemble the kingdom’s skilled magicians. Their aim was to muster a powerful counter-display of magic, calm public opinion, and shore up Pharaoh’s authority. It exposes their reliance on cunning, spectacle, and worldly power to resist the truth, and their fear that Moses’ message would spread if left unchallenged.

translation: They will bring to you every learned magician.
interpretation: This statement expresses the confidence of Pharaoh's advisers that by mobilizing all the most skilled sorcerers of the land they can confront and defeat the sign brought by Moses. It reflects a worldview that treats divine revelation as something to be matched by human craft and illusion, and it prepares for the Qur'anic lesson that no amount of expertise, power, or deception can prevail against God's command.

translation: And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh; they said, “Indeed, for us there is surely a reward if we are the victors.”
interpretation: Their demand for a reward before the contest shows that they approached the confrontation as a professional bargain, trusting in their magical skill and assuming they would win. It reveals a worldly, transactional mindset: they measured success by payment and their own expertise, not yet recognizing that the outcome belongs to God alone.

translation: He said, “Yes, and indeed you are among those brought near.”
interpretation: This is Pharaoh’s reply to the magicians, promising them not only a reward but also a privileged rank in his court. Their request for reward is met with a worldly incentive: nearness to the tyrant. The verse exposes how corrupt power buys loyalty by offering status and access, while true honor belongs only to those brought near to Allah. The magicians later chose faith in Moses over Pharaoh’s promised closeness, showing that nearness to a false master is worthless compared with nearness to the Almighty.

translation: They said, "O Moses, either you throw, or we will be the ones who throw."
interpretation: The sorcerers give Moses the choice of beginning the contest, intending to display their magical power and confident that their sorcery will prevail; but their challenge sets the stage for the divine miracle by which Moses’ staff will overcome their illusion and expose their falsehood.

translation: He said, "Throw." So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people and terrified them, and produced a great magic.
interpretation: This verse shows that the sorcerers’ power was only a deceptive manipulation of perception and fear, not a real change in God’s creation; it magnifies the contrast between human magic and the divine sign that follows, proving that falsehood may appear overwhelming but cannot withstand prophetic truth.

translation: And We inspired to Moses, "Throw your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they were falsifying.
interpretation: This verse signifies that God directly aided Moses by turning his staff into a serpent that consumed the magicians' deceptive illusions. Their sorcery was only a false appearance, unable to produce real change, while Moses' miracle was a divine act establishing the truth. It teaches that God's command and power override all human artifice, and that falsehood, however impressive, is ultimately swallowed up and rendered void when confronted by divine truth.

translation: So the truth came to pass, and what they had been doing became null and void.
interpretation: This is the decisive vindication of God’s truth over every false claim and fabricated power. The sorcerers’ magic, though impressive to the eye, had no reality before the divine miracle; it was exposed as illusion and its effect collapsed. The verse establishes that falsehood may appear dominant for a time, but when God’s command arrives it is uprooted, and all efforts to oppose His signs are rendered fruitless. It also teaches that only what is grounded in truth endures, while works built on deception, arrogance, or resistance to God inevitably come to nothing.

translation: So they were defeated there and returned humiliated.
interpretation: This means that Pharaoh’s sorcerers were utterly overcome by the sign God gave Moses: their magic was exposed as false, their power collapsed, and they were left disgraced and subdued, unable to stand against the truth.

translation: And the magicians fell down in prostration.
interpretation: This describes the instant the sorcerers recognized the miracle of Moses as divine truth and were overwhelmed by it, so they cast themselves down before God in submission. Their prostration marks their turning away from magic, from Pharaoh’s power, and from their former role, acknowledging the lordship of God alone after clear proof had come to them.

translation: They said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: This is the magicians’ declaration of faith after witnessing the clear sign given to Moses: they affirm that Allah alone is the Rabb of all creation—their Creator, Sustainer, and Sovereign—and thereby reject Pharaoh’s false claim to lordship, choosing obedience to God over the tyrant’s threats.

translation: Lord of Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: It declares that the true Lord, Creator, and Sovereign is the One who sent Moses and Aaron, affirming that He alone deserves worship and obedience; Pharaoh’s claim to lordship is therefore false, and the miracle witnessed by the magicians confirmed the authority of Moses and Aaron as messengers of that same Lord.

translation: Pharaoh said, "Did you believe in him before I gave you permission? Indeed, this is a plot you have plotted in the city to drive out its people from it. So you will come to know."
interpretation: Pharaoh does not engage the truth of the sign that has just overwhelmed the magicians; instead, he attacks the challenge to his own absolute authority. By calling their faith a secret conspiracy “plotted in the city,” he reframes sincere belief as political sedition aimed at expelling the established order. This exposes the tyrant’s logic: he cannot tolerate allegiance to any authority higher than himself, so he treats obedience to God as a crime requiring his permission. His closing threat, “So you will come to know,” is meant to terrorize them into submission, but it also turns back on him, for the real reckoning belongs to God. The verse shows how oppressive power often criminalizes faith, invents plots to justify persecution, and uses fear to preserve control, while true conviction remains unmoved by such threats.

translation: I will surely cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides, then I will crucify you all together.
interpretation: This is Pharaoh’s tyrannical threat against those who believed in Moses after witnessing the truth. It expresses the rage of a despot who uses extreme torture and public execution to suppress faith and terrify others into submission. The verse exposes Pharaoh’s arrogance, cruelty, and abuse of power, while highlighting the moral contrast between his worldly coercion and the believers’ resolve to remain faithful to God despite threatened suffering and death.

translation: They said, “Indeed, we are returning to our Lord.”
interpretation: This is a declaration of certainty in the final return to God and a refusal to let any worldly power, threat, or punishment override that truth. It means the speaker’s ultimate loyalty, hope, and destination are with the Lord alone; therefore, death or hardship in His cause is not loss but a passage to His presence. Such conviction frees the soul from servitude to tyrants and from fear of created beings, because it measures all things by the eternal meeting with God rather than by temporary gain or harm.

translation: And you do not resent us except because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord, pour upon us patience and cause us to die as Muslims.
interpretation: This is the believers’ reply to Pharaoh’s tyranny: his only grievance against them is their acceptance of the truth after clear signs came. They do not beg Pharaoh for mercy or recant; instead they turn to God, asking Him to flood them with steadfastness so they can endure persecution and remain faithful until death. It teaches that when faith is tested by power and threat, the believer’s refuge is patience from God and a firm end upon submission to Him, not the approval of tyrants.

translation: And the chiefs of Pharaoh's people said, “Will you leave Moses and his people to cause corruption in the land and to abandon you and your gods?” He said, “We will kill their sons and spare their women, and indeed we are dominant over them.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the logic of tyrannical power when confronted by a liberating call: the ruling elite recast resistance to oppression as “corruption in the land” because it threatens their political control and official religion. Pharaoh’s response—killing the male children while keeping the women alive—is a policy of terror and enslavement aimed at breaking the oppressed community’s strength and will. His boast that “we are dominant over them” reveals that his authority rests not on justice but on coercion, violence, and dehumanization. The verse thus condemns the use of state power and religious pretexts to crush dissent and portrays Pharaoh as the archetype of arrogant, oppressive rule.

translation: And Moses said to his people, “Seek help from Allah and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as inheritance to whom He wills among His servants. And the final outcome is for the righteous.”
interpretation: This verse directs the believer, when oppressed or constrained, to begin with reliance upon God and steadfast patience rather than despair or self-reliant defiance. It teaches that dominion over the earth is never absolute for any tyrant; God alone owns and disposes of it, raising and replacing whoever He wills. Therefore, apparent power is not the criterion of success. The favorable end belongs to those who live with taqwa—God-consciousness, moral restraint, and loyal obedience—so patience is not surrender but a disciplined trust that God’s judgment and succession will ultimately vindicate the upright.

translation: They said, “We were persecuted before you came to us and after you came to us.” He said, “Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and then He will see how you behave.”
interpretation: The complaint reflects a common human expectation that the arrival of divine guidance should immediately end hardship. Moses does not deny their suffering; he redirects them from despair to hope in God’s power and promise. The destruction of the oppressor and the transfer of authority to the oppressed are not mere rewards or ethnic privileges; they are a test. When God grants succession, dominion, or freedom, the question is not only whether oppression has ended but how the new possessors of power will act: with gratitude, justice, obedience, and mercy, or with the same arrogance and corruption they once suffered under. Thus the verse teaches that deliverance and authority are themselves arenas of moral examination.

translation: And indeed We seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and scarcity of fruits, so that they might remember.
interpretation: This verse describes a warning and punishment sent upon Pharaoh and his followers: prolonged famine and crop failure. The hardship was intended to make them reflect, humble themselves, and remember God and the truth brought by Moses. It shows that worldly deprivation can be a divine means of awakening people to repentance and turning back to their Lord, though Pharaoh’s people continued in arrogance and disbelief.

translation: So when good came to them, they said, ‘This is ours.’ But if evil befell them, they took it as a bad omen from Moses and those with him. Unquestionably, their omen is only with Allah, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse condemns a double standard rooted in arrogance and superstition: blessings are claimed as personal entitlement, while misfortunes are blamed on Allah’s messenger and the righteous. Its core teaching is that good and harm, blessing and trial, all proceed from Allah’s decree and wisdom; no person or group is an independent source of evil luck. Therefore a believer should receive good with gratitude to Allah and meet hardship with patience and trust, not with omens or hostility toward the righteous. Their true omen—their fate, record, and recompense—is with Allah, and most people remain ignorant of this reality.

translation: And they said, 'Whatever sign you bring us to bewitch us with it, we will never believe in you.'
interpretation: This is the speech of Pharaoh’s people to Moses: they had already resolved not to accept his message, so every miracle was reinterpreted as sorcery. The verse exposes a hardened disbelief that does not await proof but hides behind accusations; it teaches that signs and arguments only benefit a heart willing to submit, while arrogance and attachment to power can make one reject the clearest truth.

translation: So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood—distinct signs—yet they were arrogant and were a criminal people.
interpretation: These were not random disasters but clear, successive divine signs sent to Pharaoh and his people as proofs against their denial. Their refusal was not due to lack of evidence; it came from pride and a hardened criminal disposition that resisted submission to God even when His power was manifest. The verse shows that arrogance can blind a people to unmistakable signs, and that persisting in rejection after clear guidance turns them into criminals deserving of judgment.

translation: And when the plague fell upon them, they said, 'O Moses, call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. If you remove the plague from us, we will surely believe you, and we will surely send with you the Children of Israel.'
interpretation: This verse exposes a faith that is reactive and transactional: Pharaoh’s people turn to Moses only when suffering becomes unbearable, invoking the special covenant God gave him not out of sincere submission but as a means of securing relief. They promise belief and the release of the Children of Israel only on the condition that the punishment is lifted, showing that their acknowledgment of God’s power does not amount to repentance or true faith. They treat Moses as an intermediary for worldly deliverance while still resisting the divine command itself, and their later reneging confirms that their vow was opportunistic. The verse thus condemns bargaining with God under duress and shows that signs and plagues do not soften hearts that are resolved to remain in defiance.

translation: But when We removed from them the punishment until a term they were to reach, behold, they broke their word.
