translation: But when He saved them, behold, they transgress in the land without right. O mankind, your transgression is only against yourselves—[it is but] an enjoyment of worldly life. Then to Us is your return, and We will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse exposes the human tendency to turn away from God after being rescued from hardship. The same people who cry out to Him in danger often become arrogant, unjust, and corrupt once they feel safe. Their wrongdoing does not harm God or escape His knowledge; its harm falls back upon their own souls. What they pursue—power, pleasure, and worldly gain—is only a fleeting provision of this temporary life, not the true purpose of existence. All people will ultimately return to God, and He will make clear the reality of every deed, exposing what was done and bringing about just accountability. Thus the verse warns against ingratitude, oppression, and being deceived by the brief enjoyment of the world, and it calls attention to the certainty of the Hereafter and divine judgment.

translation: Indeed, the example of worldly life is like water We send down from the sky, then the plants of the earth mix with it, from which people and livestock eat, until when the earth takes its adornment and is beautified and its inhabitants think they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or day, and We make it harvested as if it had not flourished yesterday. Thus do We detail the verses for a people who reflect.
interpretation: This parable teaches that the worldly life is a fleeting and deceptive adornment: it may flourish, please, and create a false sense of security and control, but Allah’s decree can suddenly strip it away so that it is as though it never existed. Therefore, one should not be deceived by worldly prosperity or place ultimate reliance upon it; rather, one should recognize Allah’s absolute sovereignty and use this transient life for what endures, reflecting on the signs He sets forth.

translation: And Allah invites to the Home of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse means that God calls all people to the Abode of Peace—Paradise, the realm of perfect security, harmony, and freedom from every harm—and that guidance to the straight path, the path of truth, right belief, and righteous conduct, is granted by His will and wisdom to whom He chooses.

translation: For those who do good is the best [reward] and more; neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces. Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse promises that those who perfect their faith and conduct will receive al-Husna—the best reward, Paradise—and ziyadah, an added bounty beyond what they deserve. That increase is understood as the vision of God and His good pleasure, which surpasses every delight of Paradise. Their faces will remain radiant and untouched by grief, sin, or disgrace, because God will safeguard their honor and remove every cause of shame. They are the people of Paradise, established there eternally, never to be removed.

translation: And those who have earned evil deeds — the recompense of an evil deed is the like thereof, and humiliation will overwhelm them. They will have no protector from Allah. It will be as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night. Those are the inhabitants of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse establishes God's justice: the punishment for an evil act is exactly its like, not greater, while the preceding verse shows that good is rewarded manifold. The humiliation mentioned is a profound disgrace that overtakes them on the Day of Judgment, and no created being can shield them from God's decree. The covering of their faces with strips of dark night is a vivid image of the gloom, shame, and punishment that envelop them, both metaphorically in this life and literally on that Day. The final sentence identifies them as the people of Hell, consigned to remain there eternally, which the scholars apply to those who die in persistent disbelief and rejection of God's guidance.

translation: And on the Day when We gather them all together, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah, “Stay in your places, you and your associates.” Then We will separate them, and their associates will say, “It was not us that you worshipped.”
interpretation: This verse depicts the exposure and collapse of shirk in the Hereafter. Those who set up partners with Allah are made to stand with their claimed partners—idols, false deities, jinn, or human leaders—but then Allah separates them so that falsehood becomes manifest and each party is cut off from the other. The so-called partners deny being the true object of worship, meaning the polytheists did not actually worship a real divine being; rather they followed invented names, desires, and satanic suggestions. On that Day, the false objects of worship disown their worshippers, no partnership with Allah remains, and the polytheists find that their supposed intercessors possess no power or share in divinity. The verse thus affirms Allah’s exclusive oneness and shows the utter failure of every form of shirk.

translation: So sufficient is Allah as a witness between us and you; indeed we were unaware of your worship.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the false partners whom the polytheists associated with Allah will disown their worshipers and call Allah to witness that they had no awareness of the worship directed to them, never commanded it, and never approved of it. This exposes the emptiness of idolatrous devotion: the alleged gods neither knew of it nor could they benefit or harm, while Allah alone is the all-knowing witness and the only true object of worship.

translation: There, every soul will be put to trial for what it did before, and they will be returned to Allah, their true Protector, and lost from them will be what they used to invent.
interpretation: This verse describes the moment of reckoning when each soul is confronted with the full reality of what it sent ahead in life. Its deeds are no longer hidden or deniable; they are tasted, tested, and reaped as either comfort or regret. The return to Allah, the true Master and Protector, means that all false claims of independence, all imagined intermediaries, and every invented object of trust collapse. Only God’s guardianship remains real. What people fabricated—false gods, empty hopes, distorted beliefs, and excuses—will abandon them, proving that accountability is inescapable and that ultimate authority belongs to Allah alone.

translation: Say, "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Or who possesses hearing and sight? And who brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living? And who directs the affair?" They will say, "Allah." Say, "Then will you not fear Him?"
interpretation: This verse forces the idolaters to confront the contradiction in their own beliefs. They acknowledge that Allah alone sends provision from the sky and earth, controls hearing and sight, gives life and death, and manages every affair, yet they associate others with Him in worship. The questions are not seeking new information but drawing out their admission so that it becomes a proof against them. Since all provision, perception, life, death, and governance belong exclusively to Allah, He alone deserves worship, gratitude, obedience, and reliance. The final question, "Will you not fear Him?", summons them to taqwa: to guard themselves against His punishment and displeasure by abandoning false gods, repenting from disobedience, and living in conscious awareness of His sovereignty and accountability.

translation: That is Allah, your Lord, the Truth. So what is there after the truth except misguidance? So how are you turned away?
interpretation: This verse declares that Allah is the only true Lord and that truth is not merely an abstract idea but is embodied in Him and His guidance. Once the truth has come, any path that departs from it is misguidance, because there is no sound middle ground between truth and error. The question “how are you turned away?” is a rebuke to those who, despite the clarity of the truth, allow themselves to be diverted by desire, custom, or falsehood away from the worship and obedience of Allah.

translation: Thus the word of your Lord has been fulfilled against those who defiantly disobeyed, that they will not believe.
interpretation: This means that Allah’s decree and warning have been justly established against those who persist in rebellion and transgression. Because they knowingly reject the truth and continue in disobedience, their hearts become fixed in disbelief, and they are left among those who will not believe. The verse affirms divine justice: the judgment is not arbitrary but is the consequence of their own defiant rejection of faith after clear signs have come to them.

translation: Say, 'Is there any of your partners who originates creation and then repeats it?' Say, 'Allah originates creation and then repeats it; so how are you deluded?'
interpretation: The verse exposes the helplessness of every claimed partner or intercessor: none can create from nothing, nor restore creation after death. Since only Allah begins and repeats creation, any devotion, fear, or hope directed to others is founded on delusion. The rhetorical question “how are you deluded?” indicts a mind that sees the evidence yet still turns away, because acknowledging Allah as sole Creator necessarily entails His sole right to be worshiped and His power to resurrect.

translation: Say, 'Is there any of your partners [with Allah] who guides to the truth?' Say, 'Allah guides to the truth. Then is He who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or he who cannot guide unless he is guided? So what is [wrong] with you? How do you judge?'
interpretation: This verse confronts the worshippers of false deities with a rational argument: none of the beings they associate with Allah can bring anyone to the truth, because they themselves stand in need of guidance. Only Allah is the true Guide. Therefore Allah alone deserves to be followed and obeyed. The verse exposes the inconsistency of their judgment: they follow powerless created beings while refusing the One who guides all to truth. It establishes tawhid in the domain of guidance and lordship.

translation: And most of them follow nothing but conjecture. Indeed, conjecture does not avail against the truth at all. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse warns that a majority may persist in beliefs and practices based on inherited assumptions, speculation, and unverified opinion rather than revealed truth. Such conjecture cannot stand in place of certainty or shield anyone from the reality God has established. Since God is fully aware of every action, He will judge people according to what they actually did, not according to what they imagined or claimed.

translation: And this Qur’an could not have been fabricated by anyone besides Allah, but it is a confirmation of what came before it and a detailed explanation of the Scripture, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The Qur’an’s origin, inimitability, and perfect coherence make it impossible for any created being to invent or falsely attribute it to God. Its role is to authenticate the earlier revealed books and to clarify, specify, and expound the divine Book and its rulings, wisdom, and guidance. It is entirely certain, free of doubt, and sent down by the Lord and Sustainer of all creation.

translation: Or do they say, 'He has invented it'? Say, 'Then bring a surah like it and call upon whoever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.'
interpretation: This verse confronts the Meccan polytheists' accusation that Muhammad fabricated the Qur'an. Allah issues a public challenge: if the Qur'an were human invention, they should be able to produce even one surah matching its eloquence, guidance, and coherence, and they may summon any helpers or false deities besides Allah to assist them. The conditional 'if you are truthful' exposes that their claim is not based on truth but on stubborn denial. The verse thus establishes the Qur'an's inimitability as a sign of its divine origin and vindicates the Prophet: human and jinn together cannot meet this challenge. It also teaches that false allegations must be substantiated, and the inability to do so proves the accusers' falsehood.

translation: Rather, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge, and whose interpretation had not yet come to them. Thus did those before them deny. So observe how was the end of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse reproaches those who rush to reject divine revelation merely because they cannot fully comprehend it or because its promised outcome has not yet unfolded. It teaches that lack of complete knowledge is not a valid basis for denial; rather, it calls for humility, patience, and readiness to accept the truth once its meaning and fulfillment become clear. The same pattern existed among earlier nations, who rejected their messengers before seeing the consequences of their rejection. The verse therefore warns that unjust denial, rooted in arrogance and impatience, inevitably leads to a disastrous end, and it urges reflection on the fate of those who persist in opposing revealed truth.

translation: And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it. And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse declares that people are divided regarding the revelation: some accept it with faith, while others reject it. It consoles the Messenger and the believers by stating that rejection is not hidden from God. The closing phrase, “And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters,” means that God fully knows those who persist in denial, oppose the truth, and spread corruption; He will hold them accountable for their choices, and His knowledge encompasses both the believers and the corrupters.

translation: And if they deny you, say, “For me is my deed, and for you is your deed. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do.”
interpretation: This verse establishes a principle of prophetic conduct when facing rejection: the messenger is not to compel belief or bear responsibility for the choices of those who deny him. By declaring that each party owns its own deeds, it affirms individual moral accountability and separates the believer’s conduct from the opponents’ conduct. The disavowal here is of deeds, not of the obligation to convey the truth or to treat people justly; it means the Prophet is not accountable for their denial, and they are not accountable for his obedience and worship. It consoles the faithful that rejection does not diminish the mission or make them answerable for others’ disbelief, and it entrusts final judgment to God.

translation: And among them are those who listen to you. But can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not reason?
interpretation: This refers to people who outwardly lend an ear to the Prophet’s message but do not truly understand or accept it. Their listening is like the listening of the deaf, because they have closed their hearts and refuse to reflect. The rhetorical question means that just as one cannot make a physically deaf person hear, the Prophet cannot force guidance into those who have made themselves spiritually deaf and unwilling to reason. It consoles him and shows that true guidance depends on Allah opening the heart.

translation: And among them are those who look at you. But can you guide the blind even though they do not see?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical address to the Prophet. Some disbelievers would gaze at him and observe his person and conduct, yet their hearts remained blind to the truth he brought. The verse teaches that merely seeing the Prophet or witnessing outward signs does not benefit one who lacks inner sight; the Prophet’s duty is to convey the message and invite, not to force faith into hearts. True guidance belongs to Allah, who grants it to those willing to perceive. Thus the verse consoles the Prophet and shows that spiritual blindness, not any deficiency in his message, is what prevents them from believing.

translation: Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people in anything, but the people wrong themselves.
interpretation: Allah is absolutely just and never unjustly diminishes anyone’s rights, rewards, or due; whatever suffering, loss, or punishment people experience is the consequence of their own choices, sins, and rejection of guidance. Human beings wrong themselves by misuse of free will, disobedience, and turning away from the truth, so divine justice remains perfect while moral responsibility rests upon them.

translation: And on the Day when He gathers them, it will be as if they had not remained [in the world] except an hour of the day, recognizing one another. Those who denied the meeting with Allah have certainly lost, and they were not guided.
interpretation: The verse confronts people with the reality of resurrection: the whole span of worldly life, with its pleasures, disputes, and attachments, will seem no longer than a single hour. The mutual recognition among those gathered shows that they are the same conscious, accountable persons, not annihilated; yet that reunion cannot restore lost opportunity. True loss belongs to those who rejected the meeting with their Lord—His judgment, reward, and punishment—because such denial kept them from living under divine guidance. Their failure was not merely intellectual but spiritual: they refused the path that would have made that meeting a success, so on that Day they find themselves among the losers.

translation: And if We show you some of what We promise them, or We cause you to die, to Us is their return; then Allah is Witness over what they do.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet and establishes the certainty of divine recompense. Whether he is shown a portion of the promised punishment in his lifetime or dies before it, the disbelievers' final return is to Allah, who is fully aware of all their deeds. It teaches that the fulfillment of God's warnings is not tied to the Prophet's lifespan; accountability and judgment rest entirely with God, whose witnessing encompasses every action, hidden or open.

translation: And for every nation is a messenger. So when their messenger comes, judgment will be passed between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: This verse establishes that God has sent a messenger to every community, so no people are left without divine guidance and accountability. When each community’s messenger is brought forward as a witness on the Day of Judgment, God will judge them with perfect equity, and no one will suffer the slightest injustice. The verse affirms God’s justice, the universality of prophethood, and the certainty that every nation’s response to its messenger will be fairly weighed.

translation: And they say, "When will this promise [come to pass], if you are truthful?"
interpretation: This is the voice of denial and mockery: the rejecters do not ask in order to submit to the truth, but to taunt the believers and measure God's promise by their own impatient expectations. The "promise" is the resurrection, judgment, and the warning of punishment, which God has fixed for an appointed time that no one can advance or delay. Their demand for immediate fulfillment is itself a symptom of unbelief, because faith in the truthfulness of the Messenger entails trusting that God's promise is certain even when its timing remains hidden.

translation: Say, 'I have no power over any harm or benefit for myself except as Allah wills. For every nation is an appointed term. When their term comes, they will not delay it by an hour, nor will they advance it.'
interpretation: In this verse, Allah commands the Prophet to declare that he, as a human messenger, possesses no independent power to avert harm or secure benefit for himself or others; all such power belongs solely to Allah and occurs only by His will. The verse then establishes that every community or nation has a fixed, divinely appointed term. When that decreed time arrives, no one can postpone it or hasten it, even by a single moment. This teaches absolute reliance on Allah, submission to His timing, and the urgency of turning to Him before the appointed deadline, while also refuting demands for miracles or punishment to be brought on human whims rather than by Allah's decree.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered: if His punishment should come to you by night or by day, what [part] of it are the criminals seeking to hasten?'
interpretation: This verse confronts those who mockingly demand that God's punishment be brought on quickly. It reminds them that punishment can strike at any moment—by night or by day—when they least expect it, and that hastening it brings no advantage. The criminals are those who persist in denial and wrongdoing; their challenge is foolish because once the torment arrives, it will not be something they welcome but something overwhelming and inescapable. The question exposes their heedlessness and calls them to reflect before the decree comes, rather than arrogantly testing God's timing.

translation: Is it then that when it befalls, you will believe in it? Now—while you were [already] seeking to hasten it?
interpretation: This is a rebuke to those who mocked the warning and demanded that the punishment be brought quickly. When it finally comes upon them, their belated profession of faith is rejected as too late: they are told, in effect, that the time for believing was before the punishment arrived, not when it has already struck and there is no longer any merit or choice in accepting it.

translation: Then it will be said to those who did wrong: 'Taste the punishment of eternity. Are you recompensed except for what you used to earn?'
interpretation: This verse declares that on the Day of Judgment the wrongdoers—those who denied God’s signs and persisted in injustice—will be addressed with a command that exposes their punishment as both everlasting and perfectly just. The rhetorical question affirms that their recompense is not arbitrary but is exactly the fruit of their own deeds, so they have no plea against God’s justice.

translation: And they ask you to inform them, “Is it true?” Say, “Yes, by my Lord, it is surely true, and you cannot escape.”
interpretation: This verse affirms the certainty of the divine warning of judgment and punishment. The disbelievers ask the Prophet to confirm whether it is real, and God commands him to swear by His Lordship that it is absolutely true. The closing phrase means that no one can escape God’s decree, overpower Him, or prevent the promised judgment from occurring.

translation: And if every soul that has wronged had all that is on the earth, it would offer it as ransom. And they will conceal regret when they see the punishment, and it will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: This verse depicts the utter helplessness of the wrongdoer on the Day of Judgment: even if such a person possessed the entire wealth of the earth, he would eagerly give it all to escape the punishment, but no ransom will be accepted. Their regret will be concealed—hidden out of shame, humiliation, and despair—when they witness the torment, yet this hidden remorse cannot avert the consequences of their deeds. Then God will judge among His creation with perfect justice, giving each exactly what is due, neither wronging anyone by punishing an innocent person nor by increasing a sinner’s punishment beyond what his deeds deserve. Thus the verse affirms that on that Day, wealth, worldly status, and outward excuses are worthless, and only God’s absolute justice prevails.

translation: Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Unquestionably, the promise of Allah is true, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse establishes that Allah alone owns and governs all that exists in the heavens and the earth, so every matter ultimately returns to His authority and decree. Because His dominion is absolute, His promise is inevitably true and cannot fail; whatever He has pledged—whether resurrection, judgment, reward, punishment, or aid—will certainly come to pass. The statement that most people do not know means that many remain unaware of this reality through ignorance, heedlessness, or denial, not because the truth itself is doubtful. The verse therefore calls for firm conviction in Allah’s promise and reliance upon Him, while warning against being among those who fail to recognize His sovereignty and truthfulness.

translation: He gives life and causes death, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse establishes that absolute authority over life and death belongs to God alone: He originates life, decrees its end, and after death every soul returns to Him for judgment and accountability. It calls people to recognize His sovereignty, live in awareness of resurrection, and place their ultimate hope and fear in Him rather than in created beings.

translation: O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord, and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.
interpretation: This verse declares that the revelation sent by God is addressed to all people as a warning and reminder that turns them away from heedlessness and error. It is also a cure for the inner diseases of the heart—such as doubt, hypocrisy, arrogance, envy, and disordered desires—by removing them and restoring spiritual soundness. Furthermore, it is a light of guidance leading to the straight path and a mercy that brings good in this life and the Hereafter, but its guidance and mercy are fully received and benefited from by those who believe.

translation: Say, 'In the bounty of Allah and His mercy—in that let them rejoice. It is better than what they accumulate.'
interpretation: True joy and worth are to be found in Allah’s favor and mercy—above all in guidance, faith, forgiveness, and the revelation that leads to eternal good—rather than in worldly wealth, status, or possessions. These divine gifts are better than anything people gather, because worldly gains are temporary and uncertain, while Allah’s bounty and mercy endure and bring true success.

translation: Say, “Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you as provision, then you have made some of it unlawful and some lawful?” Say, “Has Allah permitted you, or are you fabricating lies against Allah?”
interpretation: This verse decisively rejects any human authority to legislate religious laws of halal and haram according to desire, custom, or inherited falsehood. Allah alone is the Lawgiver, and His revelation alone defines what is lawful and unlawful. If people declare His provision forbidden or permitted without His command, they are not simply expressing personal preference; they are attributing to Allah a ruling He never authorized. The rhetorical question exposes the matter: either they possess divine permission—which they do not—or they are inventing falsehood against Allah. Therefore, matters of lawful and unlawful must be referred to Allah’s command, and religion may not be reshaped by human invention.

translation: And what do those who fabricate lies against Allah think [will happen] on the Day of Resurrection? Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward people, but most of them do not give thanks.
interpretation: This verse rebukes those who invent falsehoods about God—such as denying His signs, attributing partners to Him, or distorting His commands—by asking what they expect on the Day of Judgment. Do they imagine their lies will save them or that God will not call them to account? God is gracious and forbearing, granting people countless favors, including respite to repent, yet most fail to show gratitude through faith and obedience.

translation: And whatever state you may be in, and whatever you recite from it of the Qur’an, and whatever deed you [people] do, We are witnesses over you when you are engrossed in it. And not absent from your Lord is an atom’s weight in the earth or in the heaven, nor smaller than that nor greater, except that it is in a clear Book.
interpretation: This verse affirms God’s absolute, all-encompassing knowledge and witnessing presence over every condition, word, and action. It teaches that no human state—whether the Prophet’s circumstances, the recitation of the Qur’an, or the deeds of people—is hidden from God; He witnesses it at the very moment it occurs. The mention of the atom’s weight and what is smaller or greater in earth and heaven declares that nothing, however subtle or vast, escapes divine awareness. The “clear Book” signifies the encompassing divine record in which all realities are preserved and from which ultimate justice and accountability follow. Thus the verse calls for God-consciousness, sincerity, and awareness that every intention and action is observed and recorded, and it assures that no good or evil, however small, is overlooked.

translation: Unquestionably, the allies of Allah — no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.
interpretation: This verse declares that those who are truly devoted to Allah, by faith and consciousness of Him, are under His protection and care. They need not fear the future or any coming hardship, nor grieve over the past or any loss, because their loyalty is to Allah and their ultimate end is security, mercy, and good pleasure with Him.

translation: Those who believed and were mindful of Allah, fearing Him.
interpretation: This verse defines Allah’s true faithful servants by two inseparable qualities: sincere belief in Him and enduring taqwa—God-consciousness that leads a person to obey His commands, avoid His prohibitions, and guard themselves from His displeasure. Faith alone is not the full picture; it must be paired with a life of reverence, obedience, and moral vigilance. Such people are the ones who attain Allah’s protection and the peace that comes with it.

translation: For them are glad tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. There is no changing the words of Allah. That is the great triumph.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God’s believing and God-conscious servants receive good news both in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. In this world, that good news is realized through guidance, inner peace, divine support, acceptance, and the fulfillment of God’s promises; in the Hereafter, it is realized through forgiveness, Paradise, and nearness to God. The declaration that there is no change in God’s words means His promises and decrees are absolutely reliable and can never be altered, revoked, or broken. Therefore, the true and supreme success is attaining what God has guaranteed for the righteous: eternal security and His pleasure in the Hereafter.

translation: And do not let their speech grieve you. Indeed, all honor and power belong to Allah entirely. He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet and the believers against the pain caused by the disbelievers’ mockery, false accusations, and rejection. It teaches that people’s words cannot diminish the servant of God, because true honor, strength, dignity, and victory belong solely to God. Since He is All-Hearing, He hears every word they utter; since He is All-Knowing, He knows their hidden motives and plots. Therefore, the believer should not let their speech break his heart or turn him away from his mission; he should rely on God, who will vindicate His cause and grant honor to whom He wills.

translation: Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth. And those who invoke besides Allah [false] partners follow nothing [real]. They follow nothing but conjecture, and they are not but falsifying.
interpretation: This verse affirms that all beings in the heavens and the earth belong to Allah alone, so any so-called partners invoked besides Him have no real authority or existence. The idolaters are not following true divine beings; they are only following inherited conjecture, guesswork, and baseless assumptions. Their attribution of partners to Allah is therefore a lie against Him, not a matter of knowledge or truth.

translation: He is the One who made for you the night so that you may rest in it, and the day giving sight. Indeed in that are signs for a people who hear.
interpretation: God points to His purposeful ordering of night and day as a mercy and evidence of His power: the night is made for repose and stillness, while the day is made bright and visible for activity, work, and seeking provision. These alternations are not random but are signs for those who truly listen—who hear divine revelation with attentive hearts and allow it to awaken reflection, gratitude, and obedience.

translation: They said, 'Allah has taken a son.' Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. You have no authority for this. Do you say about Allah what you do not know?
interpretation: The claim that God has taken a son is a false and grave assertion. 'Glory be to Him' negates any defect or need, and 'He is the Self-Sufficient' means He needs nothing and cannot be subject to offspring, which implies dependence, likeness, and need. Since all that is in the heavens and earth belongs to Him, He is the sole owner, creator, and sustainer; no created being can be His child or partner. The verse then challenges the claimants: they have no proof, no revealed warrant, and no rational authority for such a belief. It warns that speaking about God without knowledge is forbidden and dangerous. Thus it establishes God's absolute transcendence and self-sufficiency, and it obliges people to affirm only what God has revealed.

translation: Say, "Indeed, those who invent falsehood about Allah will not succeed."
interpretation: This verse declares that anyone who fabricates lies against God—by falsely attributing to Him partners, rulings, or promises He never made—will never attain true and lasting success; any temporary gain in this world is ultimately overtaken by loss and ruin.

translation: [It is but] a provision in the worldly life; then to Us is their return, and then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve.
interpretation: This means that whatever enjoyment, wealth, or ease the disbelievers are given in this world is only a temporary provision that soon ends and is not a sign of divine approval. Their ultimate destination is return to Allah alone, where they will face the consequence of their rejection: a severe punishment in the Hereafter, corresponding to their persistent denial of the truth and their refusal to believe.

translation: And recite to them the news of Noah, when he said to his people, 'O my people, if my stay and my reminding you of the signs of Allah has become burdensome to you, then upon Allah I rely. So resolve upon your plan and call upon your associates. Then let not your plan be obscure to you. Then carry it out against me and give me no respite.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that true prophetic commitment rests on complete trust in Allah, not on people's acceptance or rejection. Noah declares that if his presence and preaching have become unbearable to his people, he will not compromise or retreat, for his reliance is upon Allah alone. His challenge for them to gather their schemes and false supports and carry them out without delay is an expression of certainty that no plot can harm him except by Allah's decree. It also establishes the decisive nature of prophetic warning: after the message is delivered, the oppressors are left with their own choice and full responsibility, while the believer remains steadfast, free of fear, and dependent solely on his Lord.

translation: If you turn away, then I have not asked you for any reward. My reward is only with Allah, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.
interpretation: These are the words of Prophet Nuh to his people after calling them to Allah. He declares that he seeks no material payment or worldly gain from them for delivering the message, so their rejection does not place him under obligation to them. His sole reward is with Allah, meaning his recompense, honor, and acceptance rest entirely with his Lord. He was commanded to be among the Muslims—that is, among those who submit themselves wholly to Allah, worship Him alone, and obey His command. The verse teaches that the true caller to Allah acts with sincerity, free of selfish motive, and remains firm in submission whether people accept or turn away.

translation: So they denied him, and We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We made them successors, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. So observe how was the outcome of those who were warned.
interpretation: This verse teaches that rejecting a prophet after receiving warning does not harm God but brings ruin upon the rejecters. God rescues His messenger and the faithful with him, establishes them as inheritors of the earth after the destruction of the deniers, and makes the end of the warned a lesson for all who reflect. It is a call to consider history, where divine aid follows patient belief and divine punishment follows persistent denial.

translation: Then, after him, We sent messengers to their peoples; they came to them with clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before. Thus We seal the hearts of the transgressors.
interpretation: This means that after Noah, God sent messengers to their own communities with clear signs, yet those people refused to believe in the same truth they had already rejected earlier. Their rejection was not because the evidence was lacking, but because of their prior denial and stubbornness. So, as a just consequence, God seals their hearts—meaning He blocks guidance from entering them—because they persistently overstepped His limits and chose transgression.

translation: Then after them We sent Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his chiefs with Our signs, but they were arrogant and were a criminal people.
interpretation: This verse marks the transition from earlier prophetic missions to the mission of Moses and Aaron. The 'signs' are the miracles that authenticated their prophethood. Pharaoh and his court did not reject them for lack of evidence; their rejection sprang from istikbar—wilful arrogance and refusal to submit to a power above their own. That arrogance is not merely a character flaw but the root of their criminality: they suppressed truth, enslaved and oppressed the Children of Israel, and defied God's command. Thus 'a criminal people' describes a collective whose social and political order was built on denial of God and injustice. The verse teaches that confronting tyrants with truth may be met by elite arrogance, and that persistent rejection of clear divine signs hardens a people into criminality.

translation: So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, “Indeed, this is clear magic.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the response of Pharaoh and his people to the signs brought by Moses: they did not deny the truth because it was unclear, but because it came from God and demanded submission, humility, and the abandonment of their inherited authority and false beliefs. By labeling the divine signs as “clear magic,” they attempted to discredit them as mere human trickery, thereby avoiding the moral obligation the truth imposed. The verse thus illustrates how arrogance, vested interests, and attachment to power can cause people to reject evident revelation and reinterpret it as falsehood, showing that such denial is often rooted in spiritual and moral resistance rather than genuine lack of evidence.

translation: Moses said, "Do you say about the truth when it has come to you, 'Is this magic?' But magicians do not succeed."
interpretation: This verse rebukes those who meet divine truth with mockery and mislabel it as sorcery. Moses confronts their false accusation: magic is deception whose practitioners ultimately fail, whereas the truth sent by God is not sorcery and cannot be defeated. The verse teaches that rejecting revelation by calling it magic or illusion is a sign of stubborn disbelief, and that such opposition is doomed, while the truth ultimately prevails.

translation: They said, “Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon, and so that you two may have grandeur in the land? But we are not believers in you.”
interpretation: This is the response of Pharaoh and his people to Moses and Aaron. They reject the call not because they have examined its truth, but because it challenges the inherited religion of their ancestors and threatens their social and political dominance. Their appeal to “what we found our fathers upon” shows how blind traditionalism can be used to resist divine guidance, while their accusation that the prophets seek “grandeur in the land” reveals their own worldly mindset: they assume the messengers are only after power and prestige. In reality, Moses and Aaron call them to worship God alone and to release the Children of Israel from oppression. Their final statement, “we are not believers in you,” expresses a stubborn refusal to submit to the truth, rooted in arrogance, vested interests, and loyalty to inherited falsehood rather than evidence.

translation: And Pharaoh said, 'Bring me every learned magician.'
interpretation: Pharaoh responded to the signs brought by Moses with arrogance and denial: instead of recognizing them as divine proofs, he dismissed them as sorcery and summoned every skilled magician to oppose the truth. This reveals his spiritual blindness, his rejection of prophetic authority, and his reliance on worldly power and deception to preserve his false claim to lordship.

translation: So when the magicians came, Moses said to them, 'Throw what you are going to throw.'
interpretation: Moses deliberately let the sorcerers act first so that their magic would be fully displayed and then completely overwhelmed by the divine sign he would bring. This was not hesitation but confidence in God: it removed any excuse that the contest was unfair or that he had prevented them from showing their power, and it made the coming victory unmistakably a triumph of truth over falsehood.

translation: So when they threw [their ropes and staffs], Moses said, “What you have brought is magic. Indeed, Allah will nullify it. Indeed, Allah does not set right the work of corrupters.”
interpretation: This verse expresses the certainty that falsehood, however impressive or powerful it may appear, cannot ultimately prevail against divine truth. Moses identifies the magicians’ display as sorcery, not a real alteration of reality, and declares that God will expose and abolish its effect. The statement “Allah does not set right the work of corrupters” means that God does not bless, validate, or grant lasting success to deeds rooted in corruption, deception, or opposition to His messengers. Such works may dazzle temporarily, but they are spiritually barren and destined to collapse. The verse teaches reliance on God when confronting falsehood and affirms that true reform and enduring good come only through truth and righteousness.

translation: And Allah will establish the truth by His words, even if the criminals dislike it.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God’s decree and promise are irresistible: the truth He establishes through His words—His commands, revelations, and promises—will prevail over falsehood, no matter how much the guilty or corrupt oppose it. Their aversion cannot frustrate God’s purpose; it only reveals their enmity. The verse is therefore a declaration of divine sovereignty and justice, assuring the faithful that Allah will vindicate His truth and that no power can ultimately suppress or defeat it.

translation: So none believed in Moses except a few offspring of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs, lest they be persecuted. And indeed, Pharaoh was haughty in the land, and indeed, he was of the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse reveals that the main barrier to accepting Moses’ message was not lack of evidence but the coercive atmosphere created by Pharaoh and his elite. Faith became a risk because Pharaoh and his court could inflict ‘fitnah’—persecution aimed at testing, torturing, or turning believers away from their religion. That only a small ‘dhurriyyah’—an offspring or remnant of his people—believed suggests that truth often first finds acceptance among the weaker or younger generation, while the powerful and the broader society hold back through fear. Pharaoh’s ‘uluww’ is not merely political superiority; it is self-exaltation and a claim to absolute authority, and his ‘israf’ is excess in tyranny and denial of God. The verse thus teaches that oppressive regimes can suppress public allegiance but cannot annihilate inward faith, and that God will ultimately judge the arrogant transgressor.

translation: And Moses said, "O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims [submitting to Him]."
interpretation: Moses is teaching his people that true faith in Allah is not merely an inward claim; it must produce reliance upon Him alone. If they truly believe and have submitted themselves to Allah, then they should entrust their affair to Him, especially when facing Pharaoh’s oppression. Trusting in Allah is therefore both the proof of sincere faith and the practical expression of Islam, meaning wholehearted submission to His will.

translation: So they said, "Upon Allah we rely; our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people."
interpretation: They entrust their affairs to God and ask Him not to let the unjust gain dominance over them in a way that becomes a trial and temptation for the oppressors—leading them to persist in their wrongdoing, to imagine that their false way is vindicated, or to use the believers’ suffering as a means of persecution. It is a plea for divine protection, steadfastness, and deliverance from being made an instrument of testing for the wrongdoers.

translation: And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This is a supplication taught to the believers: true deliverance from the hostility, oppression, and harmful influence of those who reject faith is not achieved by human strength but by God’s mercy. It asks God to rescue the faithful from being subjected to the disbelievers, from their plots, and from the trial of living under or alongside disbelief in a way that harms one’s faith, while affirming complete reliance on God’s compassion as the source of safety and salvation.

translation: And We inspired Moses and his brother, “Settle your people in Egypt in houses, and make your houses a place of worship, and establish prayer; and give good tidings to the believers.”
interpretation: Allah directed Moses and Aaron to arrange the Children of Israel in Egypt as a worshipping community under persecution. Their homes were to be made places of prayer and devotion, oriented toward God, so that faith would continue even when public worship was impossible. The command to establish prayer means they were to uphold it regularly and steadfastly as the core of their spiritual life. The glad tidings to the believers is the promise of deliverance, victory, and divine help for those who remain faithful and patient.

translation: And Moses said, 'Our Lord, You have indeed given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the worldly life. Our Lord, [it is] so that they may lead [people] astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment.'
interpretation: Moses, peace be upon him, after confronting Pharaoh's tyranny, acknowledges that God had granted Pharaoh and his nobles worldly splendor and riches, which they then used to deceive people and turn them away from God's path. He prays for divine justice: that their wealth be erased and their hearts hardened as a fitting consequence of their arrogance and persistent denial. The request that they not believe until they see the painful punishment means that their chosen disbelief will continue until the torment overtakes them, at which point belief will be too late and of no avail. It is not a plea for unjust coercion but an appeal that their punishment match their crimes: their material power stripped away and their hearts sealed in the state they themselves chose.

translation: He said, 'Your supplication has been answered. So remain steadfast, and do not follow the way of those who do not know.'
interpretation: Allah informs Moses and Aaron that He has accepted their supplication, and He commands them to remain firm and upright in His religion and in conveying His message, and He prohibits them from following the path of the ignorant—those who lack knowledge of Allah and His promise and who rely on their own opinions and desires. This confirms that after the acceptance of prayer, steadfastness and avoidance of the ignorant's ways are required.

translation: And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh and his troops pursued them in oppression and aggression, until, when drowning overtook him, he said, “I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am one of the Muslims.”
interpretation: This verse describes God’s deliverance of the Children of Israel through the sea and Pharaoh’s arrogant pursuit, driven by injustice and hostility. When Pharaoh is overtaken by drowning and certain death, he declares belief in the God of Israel and claims to be among those who submit. His confession, however, comes only at the point of no escape and after a lifetime of defiance; it is therefore not a sincere, freely chosen faith but a compelled acknowledgment under the pressure of impending punishment. The verse teaches that God’s decree cannot be resisted by worldly power, that He saves the oppressed and destroys the oppressive, and that faith or repentance extracted only when destruction has already arrived is not the faith that benefits a person.

translation: Now? But you disobeyed before and were among the corrupters.
interpretation: This is a divine rebuke of Pharaoh at the moment he declares faith while drowning. It means his confession is too late: it is not sincere repentance offered during the time of free choice, but a desperate plea when punishment has already come. His previous life of defiance, oppression, and corruption invalidates that last-minute profession. The verse teaches that faith and repentance are accepted when they occur before the decisive decree and before punishment overtakes a person; once the unseen reality is forced upon someone, a coerced or escapist declaration does not benefit. It also affirms God's justice in holding people accountable for the conduct they freely chose, and it warns against delaying submission to God and moral reform until the moment of no return.

translation: So today We will save you in your body, that you may be a sign for those who come after you. And indeed, many of the people are heedless of Our signs.
interpretation: This is a divine address to Pharaoh at the moment of his drowning: God will preserve and bring forth his lifeless body as a visible lesson for later generations, so that his fate becomes an enduring sign of the truth of Moses’ message and the reality of divine punishment. Despite such clear signs, most people remain inattentive and unmindful of God’s revelations.

translation: And We settled the Children of Israel in a goodly settlement and provided them with good things, and they did not differ until knowledge came to them. Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which they used to differ.
interpretation: This verse reminds that Allah granted the Children of Israel a secure, honorable dwelling and wholesome provisions. Their later divisions over religious truth were not caused by ignorance or lack of evidence; they differed only after clear knowledge and revelation had come to them, driven by envy, partisanship, or worldly motives. Therefore their dispute is blameworthy because it occurred after the truth had been made known. The verse also consoles the Prophet and the believers: Allah alone will settle all such disputes on the Day of Resurrection, so final judgment belongs to Him, and knowledge increases one’s responsibility before God.

translation: So if you are in doubt concerning what We have sent down to you, then ask those who have been reading the Book before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.
interpretation: This is a rhetorical address meant to establish certainty, not to suggest that the Prophet actually doubted. It directs attention to the people of the earlier scriptures—those who read the Torah and the Gospel—because they possess knowledge that confirms the same essential truth and recognize the Qur’an’s agreement with what was revealed before. Since the truth has come from the Lord with clear evidence, the only fitting response is firm faith; therefore doubt is to be rejected entirely.

translation: And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.
interpretation: This verse is a firm warning to the Prophet, and through him to every believer, not to take the path of those who reject or bely Allah’s revelations. It teaches that deliberately denying Allah’s signs leads to ruin and loss, both in this life and in the Hereafter, so one must hold firmly to faith, affirm the truth, and avoid any attitude or action that resembles the deniers.

translation: Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe.
interpretation: This verse means that those whom God has already decreed to be people of rejection, because of their persistent denial and refusal of the truth, will not come to faith. God’s word has become binding upon them in His perfect justice, since they knowingly choose disbelief and turn away from clear signs, so their unbelief is not a matter of God wronging them but of their own settled rebellion and the decree that follows it.

translation: And even if every sign came to them, until they see the painful punishment.
interpretation: This conveys that obstinate denial is not caused by a lack of evidence; it is a settled spiritual condition in which a person refuses willing faith regardless of how many divine signs appear. Such people may only yield when the painful punishment becomes directly visible, but that recognition is not the faith that saves—it is compelled certainty after the time of testing has ended. The verse thus warns that faith must be embraced in response to revelation while it is still a matter of choice, before witnessing the consequence makes belief too late to benefit.

translation: So why was there not a city that believed and its belief benefited it, except the people of Jonah? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world, and We granted them enjoyment for a while.
interpretation: This verse establishes that, as a rule, communities that persisted in denial until the punishment became imminent did not benefit from a late faith; the people of Jonah are the sole exception. When they turned to God in sincere collective repentance before destruction fell, God in His mercy lifted from them the degrading punishment threatened in this worldly life and allowed them to live out their appointed term. Their faith therefore benefited them in this world, but the respite was only until the decreed time, not an exemption from ultimate accountability. The verse highlights God’s readiness to accept genuine repentance and His power to avert worldly chastisement, while warning that such acceptance is tied to turning back before punishment becomes inevitable.

translation: And if your Lord had willed, all those on the earth would have believed, all of them together. So would you compel the people until they become believers?
interpretation: This verse teaches that faith and guidance are ultimately by God’s will and decree, not by human force. Had God willed, He could have made every person on earth believe without exception; therefore, the Prophet and the believers are not tasked with coercing people into faith. True belief is a matter of the heart, which only God can open and guide. The duty of the messenger is to convey the message clearly and invite with wisdom, while the outcome of who accepts faith is left to God.

translation: And no soul can believe except by the permission of Allah. And He places impurity and punishment upon those who do not use reason.
interpretation: Faith is not something a person can produce by sheer will or personal merit; it comes only by Allah’s enabling permission and grace. Those who stubbornly refuse to use the reason and insight Allah has given them, rejecting clear guidance, are left in spiritual defilement and liable to His displeasure, because their disbelief is rooted in willful ignorance rather than in a lack of evidence.

translation: Say, 'Observe what is in the heavens and the earth.' But signs and warnings do not benefit a people who do not believe.
interpretation: The verse directs people to reflect deeply on the created order—the heavens and the earth and all they contain—because these are not random phenomena but signs pointing to God's power, wisdom, and oneness. Yet it also states that no amount of evidence or warning will profit those who are resolved to reject faith. The problem is not a lack of proofs; it is a hardened will and a refusal to receive guidance. Thus the verse teaches that signs benefit only those who approach them with openness and readiness to believe, while persistent disbelief renders even the clearest evidences ineffective.

translation: So do they wait except for the like of the days of those who passed away before them? Say, 'Then wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait.'
interpretation: This verse confronts the obstinate rejecters with the unchangeable divine practice: the punishments and judgments that overtook earlier nations for their denial will likewise overtake those who persist in the same course. The command 'then wait' is not a neutral invitation but a solemn warning that the decree of God will certainly come, and the Prophet’s statement that he too waits signifies his certainty that God’s promise of help for the believers and justice against the deniers will be fulfilled in its appointed time, even if the exact timing remains with God alone.

translation: Then We will save Our messengers and those who believed. Thus it is incumbent upon Us to save the believers.
interpretation: God declares that His established way never changes: when judgment falls upon a people who reject the truth, He delivers His chosen messengers and everyone who followed them in faith. This deliverance is not merely a kindness but a binding promise He has taken upon Himself, because His perfect justice and mercy require that faith in Him and His messengers not end in ruin or disgrace. The believer may suffer trials, opposition, or seem overwhelmed by the enemies of truth, but God's commitment to rescue the faithful remains certain—both from the specific punishments that overtake the deniers and, ultimately, from eternal loss. The verse reassures the Prophet and the believers that their safety and victory are guaranteed by God's own decree, so they should remain steadfast and not fear the apparent power of disbelief.

translation: Say, O mankind, if you are in doubt concerning my religion, then [know that] I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah, but I worship Allah, who causes you to die, and I have been commanded to be among the believers.
interpretation: This verse establishes pure monotheism and the Prophet’s complete disavowal of every false object of worship. It declares that the only One worthy of worship is the One who has absolute authority over life and death, for the One who causes all souls to pass from this world is alone the true Lord and Sovereign. The command to be "among the believers" shows that faith is not a passive label but an active, divinely ordained commitment of the heart and will to God alone. Those who doubt the religion are confronted with the clarity and firmness of the prophetic stance: no compromise in worship, no associating created beings with the Creator, and total reliance upon the One to whom every soul ultimately returns.

translation: And [I have been commanded]: Set your face toward the religion, as one upright by nature, and do not be among the polytheists.
interpretation: This verse commands complete devotion of one’s whole self—face, intention, and purpose—to the religion of Allah alone, with pure and exclusive monotheism. “Upright by nature” (ḥanīf) means turning away from all false ways and inclining solely toward the truth of Allah’s exclusive lordship and worship. The prohibition “do not be among the polytheists” forbids any association of partners with Allah, whether in belief, worship, obedience, or ultimate loyalty. Though addressed to the Prophet, it establishes the enduring obligation for every believer to purify worship for Allah alone and to renounce all forms of shirk.

translation: And do not invoke besides Allah that which neither benefits you nor harms you; for if you did, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse forbids directing worship or supplication to any being other than Allah, since no created thing has the power to bring benefit or cause harm independently. Turning to such powerless objects or beings is not merely futile; it is an act of injustice and transgression, because it assigns to creation what belongs exclusively to the Creator. The one who does so joins those who wrong themselves and violate the fundamental right of Allah to be worshipped alone.

translation: And if Allah should touch you with harm, there is none to remove it except Him; and if He intends good for you, there is none to repel His bounty. He causes it to reach whom He wills of His servants. And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse establishes that all harm and benefit are ultimately under Allah’s exclusive authority. No created being can independently remove suffering or block the good He decrees. Therefore, the servant’s reliance, fear, and hope should be directed to Allah alone, trusting that whatever He sends is by His wisdom and will, and that His forgiveness and mercy remain the refuge of those who turn to Him.

translation: Say, "O mankind, the truth has come to you from your Lord. So whoever is guided is only guided for the benefit of his own soul, and whoever goes astray only goes astray against it. And I am not a guardian over you."
interpretation: This verse declares that the divine message is not a private possession of one tribe or people but a universal truth sent from the Lord of all. It places responsibility for accepting or rejecting guidance squarely on each person: guidance benefits the one who accepts it, while straying harms only the one who chooses it. The Prophet’s duty is to convey the truth clearly, not to force belief or control hearts; therefore, he is not a guarantor or disposer of their affairs. The verse affirms human accountability, the mercy of guidance, the consequence of misguidance, and the principle that faith must be embraced willingly rather than coerced.

translation: And follow what is revealed to you, and be patient until Allah judges, and He is the best of judges.
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet, and through him every believer, to submit wholly to the guidance revealed by Allah, making it the standard for belief, speech, and action, and to persevere patiently when truth is opposed or delayed in prevailing. Patience here is not passive resignation but steadfast obedience and trust while refraining from impatience, retaliation, or attempting to force an outcome. The command to wait “until Allah judges” affirms that ultimate decision, vindication, and justice belong to Allah alone; His ruling is neither premature nor unjust, and His wisdom governs what people cannot see. The closing declaration, “He is the best of judges,” is both reassurance and a call to rely on His perfect justice and mercy, especially when human judgments fail or oppressors appear secure.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been firmly established and then explained in detail, from One who is Wise and All-Aware.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Qur’an is a divinely revealed Book whose foundations, rulings, and truths are made precise, unshakable, and free from contradiction or deficiency, and then its meanings, commands, promises, warnings, and stories are expounded and clarified in detail. This perfect firmness and detailed clarification come from Allah alone, who is Wise in all that He ordains and All-Aware of every condition, need, and reality of His creation, so His Book guides with perfect knowledge and wisdom.

translation: That you worship none but Allah. Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bearer of glad tidings.
interpretation: This verse establishes the core of the prophetic message: absolute monotheism, meaning that all worship, devotion, and obedience must be directed exclusively to Allah, with no partner associated with Him. The messenger is sent by Allah in two complementary roles: as a warner who cautions those who persist in idolatry, disbelief, and disobedience about the grave consequences of their path, and as a bearer of glad tidings who announces Allah's mercy, forgiveness, and reward to those who accept His oneness and follow His guidance. The phrase “from Him” clarifies that both the warning and the glad tidings are not the messenger's own invention but originate from Allah, reinforcing the authority and sincerity of the call and the accountability of those who hear it.

translation: And seek forgiveness from your Lord; then turn to Him in repentance. He will grant you good enjoyment until an appointed term, and give every possessor of merit his merit. But if you turn away, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great Day.
interpretation: This verse calls for two connected acts: seeking God’s forgiveness for past sins and then sincere repentance, which means turning away from disobedience and returning to God with obedience and devotion. The promise attached is that such repentance brings a good, wholesome life in this world—security, provision, and blessing—until the appointed term decreed by God, and that God will not neglect the reward of anyone who possesses virtue or does good. If people instead reject the call and turn away, the warning is of severe punishment on the great Day, the Day of Judgment, when all deeds will be recompensed.

translation: To Allah is your return, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse affirms that every person’s ultimate destination is God alone: after death and resurrection, all will be brought back before Him for judgment. His absolute power over all things means nothing can prevent Him from raising the dead, gathering creation, and exacting justice or granting mercy, so the return to Him is certain and inescapable.

translation: Unquestionably, they fold their breasts to hide from Him. Unquestionably, when they wrap themselves in their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts.
interpretation: This is a declaration that no inward concealment or outward disguise can escape God's knowledge. The folding or bending of the breasts points to hiding intentions, doubts, or hostility within the heart, while wrapping oneself in garments points to trying to conceal one's true state behind a physical or figurative covering. God knows both the secret and the open because His knowledge penetrates the innermost self—what the hearts hide, intend, and deliberate—so inward sincerity and surrender are as necessary as outward compliance.

translation: And there is no moving creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah, and He knows its dwelling place and its resting place. All is in a clear Book.
interpretation: The verse signifies that God has taken upon Himself the guarantee of sustenance for every animate being on earth; no creature lies outside His providential care. His knowledge encompasses each one’s temporary abode in life and its final repository after death, or its place of settlement and place of storage, all inscribed in the Clear Book (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Thus it calls for reliance upon God, assurance of provision, and awareness that divine knowledge and decree encompass all existence.

translation: And He is the One Who created the heavens and the earth in six days—and His Throne was upon the water—so that He might test you as to which of you is best in deeds. And if you say, 'You will indeed be raised after death,' those who disbelieve will surely say, 'This is nothing but clear magic.'
interpretation: This verse establishes that creation is not accidental or purposeless: God's creative authority over the heavens, the earth, and the water beneath His Throne is directed toward testing human conduct. The test is not merely how much one does but how well—sincerity, righteousness, and conformity to divine guidance determine who is 'best in deeds.' The mention of the Throne upon the water before creation signifies God's absolute sovereignty prior to and over all created order, and the six days indicate a measured, ordered act of creation under divine will, not exhaustion or need. The second part shows that denial of resurrection is often rooted not in lack of evidence but in a hardened will that dismisses prophetic truth as sorcery; such rejection is a moral and spiritual disease, not a reasoned conclusion.

translation: And if We delay the punishment for them until a limited term, they will surely say, 'What detains it?' Unquestionably, on the Day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them, and they will be enveloped by what they used to ridicule.
interpretation: The delay of punishment is a respite decreed by God, not a sign that it will never come. The mockers demand to know what holds it back, treating the delay as proof against the warning, but when the appointed time arrives, nothing can repel it, and the very chastisement they derided will surround and overwhelm them.

translation: And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing and ungrateful.
interpretation: This verse describes a weakness in human nature when a person is given a blessing and then has it taken away: he tends to lose hope entirely and becomes ungrateful for what he once received. It calls the believer to resist this tendency by recognizing that all blessings are from God, that their removal is a test, and that one should respond with patience, gratitude, and continued trust in God rather than despair or denial of His favors.

translation: And if We let him taste a blessing after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, 'The evils have departed from me.' Indeed, he is exultant and boastful.
interpretation: This verse exposes a common human failing: when distress is removed and ease returns, a person may credit himself for the relief, assume the misfortune is gone forever, and become arrogant and boastful. It teaches that ease after hardship is also a test from God, just as hardship is, and the proper response is gratitude, humility, and awareness that both favor and trial come from God. The person described here is intoxicated by comfort, forgetful of God's grace, and boastful before others, rather than recognizing that his previous affliction and present relief are under God's decree.

translation: Except those who are patient and do righteous deeds—those will have forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: This verse singles out the believers who remain steadfast in hardship and obedient to God, doing good works, from the general human tendency toward despair or arrogance when circumstances change. Their patience and righteous conduct earn them God's forgiveness for their shortcomings and a vast reward in the Hereafter.

translation: Then perhaps you would leave aside some of what is revealed to you, and your breast would be constrained thereby, because they say, 'Why has a treasure not been sent down to him, or an angel come with him?' You are only a warner, and Allah is Disposer of all things.
interpretation: This verse consoles and strengthens the Prophet: it warns him against allowing the disbelievers’ mockery and their demands for extraordinary signs—such as a treasure being sent down or an angel accompanying him—to make him feel pressure to abandon or conceal any part of the revelation. His duty is not to satisfy their arbitrary conditions or produce miracles according to their whims, but only to deliver the warning faithfully. The reminder that Allah is the Guardian and Disposer of all affairs means the outcome is in God’s hands, so the Prophet should not grieve over their rejection nor alter the message to appease them.

translation: Or do they say, “He has fabricated it”? Say, “Then bring ten sūrahs like it, fabricated, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.”
interpretation: This verse confronts the accusation that the Prophet Muhammad fabricated the Qur’an. It turns that claim into a public challenge: if the Qur’an were merely human invention, then those accusing him—people skilled in Arabic eloquence and rhetoric—should be able to produce ten sūrahs comparable to it, even fabricated ones, and may seek help from anyone besides God. The phrase “if you are truthful” exposes that the accusation is not rooted in honesty but in stubborn rejection. The inability of the Arabs, despite their linguistic mastery and hostility, to meet this challenge demonstrates the Qur’an’s inimitability and confirms that it is divinely revealed, not the work of Muhammad. Thus the verse establishes the truthfulness of the Prophet and the obligation to respond to the Qur’an with faith rather than denial.

translation: So if they do not respond to you, then know that it has been sent down only by the knowledge of Allah, and that there is no deity except Him. So will you be Muslims?
interpretation: This verse follows the challenge to the rejecters to produce something comparable to the Qur’an. Their failure to respond is itself a proof that the Qur’an is not a human invention but is revealed by the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah. It then proclaims the core truth of tawhid—that there is no god worthy of worship except Him—and concludes with a direct appeal: since the evidence has become clear, will you surrender yourselves to Allah in Islam, submitting to Him alone with sincere faith and obedience?

translation: Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornments, We will fully repay them for their deeds therein, and they will not be deprived therein.
interpretation: This means that God’s justice is exact: if a person’s ultimate aim is only the life of this world and its ornaments, then whatever good or effort he expends is repaid to him in this world through worldly benefit, reputation, comfort, or success, without any reduction. The verse warns that such a person has confined his intention and hope to the transient world; therefore, his works are not directed toward the eternal reward of the Hereafter, and his share of the Hereafter is determined by that worldly-oriented intention.

translation: Those are the ones who have nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire; and whatever they did therein is wasted, and worthless is what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse describes the end of those whose ultimate concern is worldly life and its enjoyments. Even if their actions appear good or beneficial in the world, they are rendered null and void in the Hereafter because they were not grounded in faith in God, sincerity, and preparation for the final accounting. Their works are described as wasted and false, meaning they carry no lasting reward and cannot benefit them after death; their only recompense in the Hereafter is the Fire. The verse teaches that deeds derive their true value from correct belief and sincere intention, not from worldly success or outward appearance.

translation: Is he who is upon a clear proof from his Lord, and a witness from Him recites it, and before it is the Book of Moses as a guide and mercy, [like those who are not]? Those believe in it. But whoever disbelieves in it among the factions, the Fire is his promised place. So do not be in doubt about it. Indeed, it is the truth from your Lord, but most people do not believe.
interpretation: The verse establishes that true faith rests on divine evidence, not conjecture. The Prophet Muhammad is the one grounded in clear proof from his Lord, and the witness from God who recites the revelation to him is Gabriel, confirming his mission. The earlier Book of Moses, the Torah, also came as guidance and mercy, so the Qur'an does not contradict but completes the same prophetic line. Therefore, those who recognize this evidence believe in the Qur'an, while any faction that rejects it faces the Fire. The Prophet is reassured that the Qur'an is the absolute truth from his Lord, and the widespread disbelief of people cannot alter that reality.

translation: And who is more unjust than he who fabricates a lie against Allah? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, 'These are the ones who lied against their Lord.' Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse declares that no wrongdoing is graver than inventing falsehood about God—such as attributing partners, offspring, or false commandments to Him, or denying His messengers. It warns that such people will be made to stand before their Lord on the Day of Judgment, publicly disgraced, while the witnesses—the angels who recorded deeds, and the prophets and believers—testify that they lied against their Lord. Then God pronounces His curse, meaning exclusion from His mercy, upon all such wrongdoers. It is therefore a severe condemnation of lying about God and a call to speak of Him only with revealed truth.

translation: Those who prevent [people] from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked, and they are disbelievers in the Hereafter.
interpretation: This verse exposes the mindset of those who oppose divine guidance: they not only refuse it themselves but actively repel others from it, and they attempt to depict Allah's straight path as deviant or flawed. Their denial of the Hereafter is the root of this conduct, since it frees them from any sense of ultimate accountability and makes them persist in disbelief.
