translation: Those were not causing failure [i.e., escaping Allah] on earth, nor did they have besides Allah any protectors. For them the punishment will be doubled. They were not able to hear, nor did they see.
interpretation: This refers to those who persist in rejecting the truth: their strength, numbers, and worldly means cannot frustrate God's decree or protect them from His judgment, since they have no true guardian besides Him. Their punishment is multiplied because they combined their own disbelief with misleading others and hardening themselves against guidance; by refusing to listen to revelation and refusing to see its signs, they lost the ability to perceive and accept the truth.

translation: Those are the ones who have lost their souls, and what they used to invent has strayed away from them.
interpretation: This verse means that the people described before it have suffered the ultimate loss: they ruined themselves by choosing disbelief, idolatry, and falsehood over faith and guidance, so they enter the Hereafter empty of any true benefit. Whatever they fabricated against Allah—false deities, intercessors, claims, or religious innovations—will vanish and abandon them. Nothing they invented will rescue them or remain for them; it goes astray from them, leaving them with only the consequences of their deeds.

translation: No doubt, they are in the Hereafter the greatest losers.
interpretation: This verse emphatically declares that those who barter away the Hereafter for worldly gain, and who follow falsehood and fabricated hopes, will in the final accounting be the most complete and irreparable losers. Their loss is not a temporary setback but an eternal ruin: they forfeit their own souls, their deeds come to nothing, and whatever they relied upon besides God will abandon them. The emphatic construction “no doubt” removes any uncertainty about this outcome, and the definite intensive form “the greatest losers” indicates that no one can be more profoundly deprived than those who lose the everlasting reward for something passing and worthless.

translation: Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds and humbled themselves before their Lord—those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse teaches that eternal Paradise is not earned by faith alone or by outward deeds alone, but by the union of sincere belief, righteous action, and a heart humbled and submissive before its Lord. The word "akhbatu" indicates a deep inward surrender, repentance, and turning to God with humility, which purifies intention and makes deeds acceptable. Such people are truly the people of Paradise, and their abiding there is everlasting because their orientation was wholly toward God.

translation: The example of the two parties is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in example? Will you not then remember?
interpretation: This verse compares two groups: those who reject God’s guidance and those who accept it. The rejecters are likened to a person who is both blind and deaf—blind to the signs of God and deaf to His revelation—so they cannot perceive the truth or benefit from warning. The believers are likened to a person who sees and hears—aware of God’s signs and attentive to His message—so they respond with faith and obedience. The rhetorical question declares that the two are not equal; their inward condition is utterly different. The closing call, “Will you not then remember?” urges people to reflect, take heed, and choose spiritual sight and hearing over heedlessness.

translation: And We had certainly sent Noah to his people, [saying], 'Indeed, I am to you a clear warner.'
interpretation: This verse establishes that Noah was divinely commissioned to his people with a warning that was unmistakable and fully communicated. His declaration, “I am to you a clear warner,” means his message left no room for confusion or excuse: he called them to worship God alone, to heed His commands, and to understand the serious consequence of persisting in denial. It also reflects the consistent divine pattern that God sends messengers before punishment so that people are warned with clarity and given the opportunity to repent.

translation: That you worship none but Allah. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a painful Day.
interpretation: This is the core of Noah’s call to his people: to devote all worship exclusively to Allah alone and to abandon every false object of worship. He warns them out of deep concern that if they persist in rejecting this truth, they will face the torment of a Day whose punishment is intensely painful. The verse establishes that pure monotheism is the foundation of the prophetic message, and that the messenger’s warning is motivated by compassion for his people and fear of the consequences they will suffer in the Hereafter if they do not heed the call.

translation: And the chiefs of his people who disbelieved said: “We see you only as a human being like ourselves, and we see that none have followed you except the lowest among us, acting on first impulse. And we do not see that you have any superiority over us; rather, we think you are liars.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the mindset of arrogant rejection: the disbelieving elite dismiss the messenger not because of any proof against him, but because he is a human being like them, because his followers are the weak and socially despised, and because he has no worldly rank or privilege they recognize. They measure truth by status, power, and majority, then declare him a liar on that basis. The verse thus condemns judging divine guidance by the social class of its bearer or followers, and warns that pride and inherited privilege can blind people to moral and prophetic truth. It also shows that the oppressed and humble often accept truth first, while those invested in unjust superiority resist it because the message threatens their self-image and interests.

translation: He said, 'O my people, have you considered: if I should be on clear evidence from my Lord, and He has given me mercy from Himself, but it has become obscured to you, could we compel you to accept it while you are averse to it?'
interpretation: This verse teaches that the prophet’s message rests on clear evidence from God and on a mercy granted by Him—namely revelation and guidance—but that such guidance cannot be imposed on hearts that deliberately reject it. Noah’s rhetorical question exposes the futility and wrongness of forcing faith on unwilling people: true faith must be accepted freely, not by compulsion. The obscuring is not a failure of the evidence itself but a consequence of the people’s aversion, and the messenger is only a warner and conveyer, not one who coerces belief.

translation: And O my people, I do not ask you for wealth concerning it. My reward is only with Allah. And I am not one to drive away those who have believed. Indeed, they will meet their Lord, but I see you are a people acting ignorantly.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the true caller to God must be free of material self-interest: his reward is with God alone, so he cannot alter the message to please the wealthy or powerful. The refusal to expel the believers shows that worth before God is based on faith, not social rank or worldly influence. The demand to remove the weak believers was rooted in ignorance of God's justice and the coming meeting with Him, when every believer will receive his or her due. Therefore, no human being has the right to reject those whom God has accepted, and religious arrogance that despises the poor or lowly believers places one under divine accountability.

translation: And O my people, who would protect me from Allah if I drove them away? Then will you not remember?
interpretation: This is a warning from Prophet Nuh to his people, especially those who demanded that he expel the poor and weak believers from his company. He is saying: if I were to drive them away just to please you, no one could shield me from Allah’s punishment, because I would be committing an injustice against sincere believers. The verse teaches that a prophet—and by extension anyone calling to God—cannot abandon or reject people of faith because of pressure from the arrogant or influential. True protection comes only from Allah, and the final question urges them to reflect: God does not judge by social rank or wealth, but by sincerity and faith. Therefore, rejecting believers to satisfy worldly elites is not a path to safety, but to divine accountability.

translation: And I do not say to you that I possess the treasures of Allah, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I say that I am an angel, nor do I say concerning those whom your eyes despise that Allah will not give them any good. Allah knows best what is in their souls. Indeed, I would then be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: In this verse, Prophet Nuh addresses his people with humility and truthfulness, clarifying that he is only a human messenger and not a possessor of divine treasures, unseen knowledge, or angelic nature. He refuses to accept the arrogant judgment of his people who despised the poor and weak believers, and he warns that no one has the right to declare who will or will not receive Allah’s good. True worth and faith are known only to Allah, who sees the innermost intentions and states of the heart. If Nuh were to condemn those whom the elites looked down upon, he would be acting unjustly and would join the wrongdoers. Thus the verse teaches that divine knowledge belongs to Allah alone, that outward social status is not a measure of spiritual worth, and that a prophet or believer must never belittle sincere people based on worldly standards.

translation: They said, "O Noah, you have disputed with us and been lengthy in dispute with us, so bring us what you promise us, if you should be of the truthful."
interpretation: This verse depicts the obstinate response of Noah's people to his persistent call: rather than considering the truth of his warning, they treat his preaching as mere quarreling and demand that the threatened punishment be brought immediately as proof of his sincerity. Their demand reveals arrogance, impatience, and a refusal to accept prophetic authority, since they wrongly assume that a messenger controls the timing of God's judgment; in reality, the decree and timing belong to God alone, and the demand for signs or punishment on their own terms is not true seeking of guidance but a pretext for rejection.

translation: He said, “It is only Allah who will bring it upon you, if He wills, and you cannot escape [His decree].”
interpretation: This verse shows that the sending of punishment or relief is entirely in Allah’s hand; the prophet has no power to produce it by his own will. It also declares that no people can overpower Allah, evade His decree, or frustrate His purpose. They may demand proofs or challenge the messenger, but ultimate authority belongs solely to Allah, who acts when and how He wills, and no one can render Him powerless.

translation: And my advice will not benefit you, if I intended to advise you, if Allah intends to leave you astray. He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: Noah is telling his people that his sincere counsel cannot change their state if God, in His wisdom and justice, has willed to leave them in error because of their persistent rejection of truth. This affirms God's absolute sovereignty over guidance and misguidance, while their return to Him means they remain fully accountable for their choices before their Lord.

translation: Or do they say, 'He has fabricated it'? Say, 'If I have fabricated it, then upon me is my crime, and I am free of what you commit.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers’ accusation that the Prophet Muhammad fabricated the Qur’an. God instructs him to respond that if he had invented it, the guilt and consequence of that crime would fall upon him alone, but he is innocent of and disassociated from the crimes they commit—namely, their lies, rejection, and false charges against him. It is a decisive denial of their accusation and a declaration of his integrity and complete freedom from their wrongdoing.

translation: And it was revealed to Noah, "Never will any of your people believe except those who have already believed, so do not grieve over what they have been doing."
interpretation: This verse informs Noah that the period of his people's testing has reached its end: no one else among them will accept faith, and only those who have already believed will remain. His sorrow over their rejection is therefore not warranted, because their disbelief is a settled divine decree and their harmful deeds will be recompensed by God, not borne by Noah as a personal failure.

translation: And construct the ship under Our eyes and Our inspiration, and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned.
interpretation: This verse directs Noah to build the ark under God’s watchful care and revealed guidance, assuring him that the work is divinely protected and ordered. It also instructs him not to plead or speak to God on behalf of the wrongdoers who persisted in denial and corruption, because their punishment has been decreed: they will be drowned. The verse thus teaches reliance on God’s command, confidence in His protection for the faithful, and the finality of judgment upon those who knowingly persist in injustice and reject divine warning.

translation: And he was constructing the ship, and whenever a group of his people passed by him, they ridiculed him. He said, 'If you ridicule us, then indeed we will ridicule you just as you ridicule.'
interpretation: This verse depicts Noah patiently carrying out God's command to build the Ark while his people mocked him. His response is not petty retaliation but a warning that their mockery will be turned back upon them: when God's judgment comes, they will be the ones disgraced and mocked, just as they now mock the believers. It affirms steadfastness in obeying God despite ridicule and assures that divine decree will reverse the apparent triumph of the scoffers.

translation: So you will soon know who it is to whom comes a punishment that disgraces him, and upon whom a lasting punishment will descend.
interpretation: This is a decisive warning that mockery and rejection cannot avert Allah’s decree. The coming punishment will expose the truth and assign disgrace to those who persisted in arrogance, while the abiding punishment upon them will be neither temporary nor escapable. It affirms that divine justice is certain, that the messengers are ultimately vindicated, and that the fate of the deniers is lasting humiliation and ruin.

translation: Until, when Our command came and the oven overflowed, We said: 'Carry in it two of every kind, and your family—except those against whom the word has already gone forth—and those who believed.' And none believed with him except a few.
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of the flood in the story of Noah: God’s decree arrived, and the appointed sign—the overflowing of the oven—occurred, signaling the eruption of water and the end of the respite. Noah is commanded to load the ark with pairs of living creatures to preserve their kinds, and with his household, except those whom God had already decreed would perish because of persistent disbelief, even if they were close relatives. Only a small number of his people had accepted his message. This shows that deliverance comes through faith and obedience to God’s command, not through family lineage or the approval of the majority, and that the truth is not measured by how many accept it.

translation: And he said, 'Embark in it. In the name of Allah is its course and its mooring. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.'
interpretation: This verse reports Noah’s instruction to those with him to board the ark, beginning the journey with Allah’s name. It teaches that both the ship’s movement and its safe arrival are decreed and sustained by Allah alone, so the believer should entrust every undertaking to Him. By calling Allah “Forgiving and Merciful” at this moment, Noah acknowledges that divine mercy remains open to those who obey Him, even as the flood executes judgment upon the corrupt. Thus the verse combines reliance on God, remembrance of His name at the start and end of a matter, and hope in His forgiveness and compassion.

translation: And it sailed with them amid waves like mountains, and Noah called out to his son, who had stood apart: “O my son, embark with us and do not be with the disbelievers.”
interpretation: This scene shows that deliverance comes through responding to God’s call, not through kinship or proximity to a prophet. Noah’s plea expresses a believer’s deep compassion even amid overwhelming judgment, while his son’s separation signifies a spiritual isolation caused by refusing faith. The invitation “embark with us” is a call to join the community of salvation, and the warning “do not be with the disbelievers” teaches that remaining aloof from truth or allied with denial places one under the same peril. Thus the verse emphasizes personal responsibility: being near the righteous is not enough; one must answer the call and separate from disbelief.

translation: He said, 'I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water.' He said, 'There is no protector today from the command of Allah except the one He has mercy on.' And the wave came between them, so he was among the drowned.
interpretation: The verse means that when Allah’s decree comes, no created refuge—such as a mountain or any material means—can shield a person from it; true safety lies only in Allah’s mercy and in submitting to His command. The son’s trust in a physical height despite Noah’s warning shows that disbelief and reliance on worldly causes cannot avert divine judgment, and so he was overtaken by the flood.

translation: And it was said, 'O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, cease.' And the water was made to abate, and the decree was fulfilled, and it came to rest on al-Judi. And it was said, 'Away with the wrongdoing people.'
interpretation: The verse expresses the absolute sovereignty of God over creation at the climax of the flood: He commands the earth and sky directly, and the destructive waters recede not by chance but by His decree. The resting of the ark on al-Judi marks the completion of God's judgment and the preservation of Noah and those with him, while the pronouncement of ruin upon the wrongdoing people shows that divine justice ultimately removes the oppressors from mercy and leaves their fate as a warning. It teaches that when God's command comes, no force can resist it, and that salvation belongs to those whom God protects, whereas persistent wrongdoing ends in irreversible loss.

translation: And Noah called to his Lord and said, 'My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges.'
interpretation: This verse captures Noah's heartfelt appeal to God after the flood, when he believed his son should have been included among those saved as part of his family. Its meaning is that divine promises are fulfilled according to God's perfect wisdom and justice, not according to human assumptions about lineage or natural attachment. Noah submits to God as the most just of judges, and the verse teaches that true belonging to God's saved community is determined by faith and righteousness, not merely by blood relation.

translation: He said, “O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose work was other than righteous. So do not ask Me that of which you have no knowledge. I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant.”
interpretation: God is teaching Noah—and through him all believers—that the kinship that matters before Him is not biological descent but faith and righteous action. Noah’s son had separated himself from Noah’s spiritual household by disbelief and unrighteous conduct, so Noah’s plea for him was based on natural fatherly attachment and on a limit of his own knowledge, not on God’s judgment. Therefore God forbids him to ask for what he cannot truly know or what contradicts divine justice. The warning against being among the ignorant means that a believer must not let blood ties or emotional longing override revealed truth; nearness to God is attained by faith and righteous deeds, and God’s decree remains wise and just even when it wounds the heart.

translation: He said: My Lord, I seek refuge with You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that a believer must not petition God for matters beyond his knowledge or for what may be contrary to divine wisdom; true servitude includes admitting ignorance and seeking refuge from presumptuous requests. It also shows that even a prophet cannot rely on his own righteousness—forgiveness and mercy are necessary for salvation—and that without them, a person is ruined, not merely disadvantaged.

translation: It was said: O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon communities from those with you. And there are communities whom We will grant enjoyment, then there will touch them from Us a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse marks the end of the flood and the beginning of life after the ark. Allah addresses Nuh with safety, mercy, and blessings, and extends those blessings to believing generations that would come from those who were with him in the ark. At the same time, it foretells that other communities from among his descendants will choose disbelief; they may be given worldly enjoyment for a time, but afterward they will meet a painful punishment from Allah. Thus the verse combines divine favor and promise for the faithful with a warning of accountability for those who reject the truth.

translation: That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you; you did not know it, nor did your people, before this. So be patient; indeed, the outcome is for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the accounts of the past prophets and nations are part of the hidden knowledge that only Allah can disclose. Their revelation to the Prophet Muhammad, who had no prior access to such detailed history, is evidence of the Qur’an’s divine origin. It also strengthens the Prophet and the believers: when facing denial, hardship, or opposition in conveying the truth, they must remain patient and steadfast. The final success, victory, and good end belong to those who are conscious of Allah and persevere in obedience to Him.

translation: And to 'Aad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. You are only fabricators."
interpretation: Allah sent the prophet Hud to the people of 'Aad as one of their own kinsmen, so they could not claim he was a stranger unfamiliar with them. Hud's message was the same call of all prophets: to worship Allah alone, because He is the only true God and has no partner. Any so-called gods they worshipped besides Him were false, invented by their own hands and imaginations. Their claim that those idols deserved worship was not based on truth but was a fabrication against Allah.

translation: O my people, I do not ask you for any reward for it. My reward is only from the One who created me. Then will you not reason?
interpretation: The prophet is declaring that his call to God is utterly free of selfish motive: he seeks no wealth, status, or payment from the people. His only hoped-for reward is from the Creator who brought him into existence and fashioned him. The rhetorical question rebukes them: if the caller gains nothing from them, then rejecting him out of suspicion of ulterior motives is unreasonable. They are being urged to use their intellect to recognize his sincerity and, more importantly, to acknowledge that the One who created them alone deserves their worship, obedience, and ultimate accountability.

translation: And O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. He will send the sky upon you in abundant showers and increase you in strength added to your strength. And do not turn away as criminals.
interpretation: This verse teaches that sincere repentance is the key to both spiritual and worldly well-being: asking God's forgiveness and turning back to Him with obedience brings divine mercy, symbolized by abundant rain and fertility, and grants an increase in power, dignity, and communal strength. The final warning tells them not to turn away from this call or persist in wrongdoing, for rejection would make them guilty before God.

translation: They said, "O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods merely because of your word, nor will we believe in you."
interpretation: This verse depicts the arrogant rejection of the people of ‘Ad toward their prophet Hud. They dismiss his message as lacking a clear sign, though their demand is not sincere; they are determined to remain loyal to their inherited idols. Their refusal to leave their gods “because of your word” shows that they are not judging by reason or evidence but by stubborn attachment to tradition and power. By saying they will not believe in him, they openly declare their unbelief, not because the truth is unclear, but because they do not want to submit. The verse illustrates how falsehood often masks itself as a demand for proof while remaining unmoved by any proof, and how prophetic preaching cannot benefit hearts that have resolved to reject guidance.

translation: They said, “We only say that one of our gods has afflicted you with evil.” He said, “Indeed, I call Allah to witness, and you be witnesses, that I am free from what you associate.”
interpretation: This verse shows that the polytheists, unable to meet Hud’s clear call to monotheism, resorted to the claim that his rejection of their idols had caused him to be touched by madness or harm from those idols. Hud’s reply is a decisive declaration of tawhid: he calls Allah as witness and calls them to witness that he completely disavows their shirk. The meaning is that the idols have no independent power to benefit or harm; any harm can only occur by Allah’s permission, and the true servant of Allah does not fear false gods. His public disavowal is not merely a rejection of their worship but a declaration of total reliance upon Allah and freedom from every form of associating partners with Him. It teaches that faith in Allah requires clear separation from shirk, courage in the face of threats, and confidence that Allah alone is the Disposer of all affairs.

translation: besides Him. So plot against me, all together, then give me no respite.
interpretation: This is the declaration of Hud, peace be upon him, to his people: he completely disavows every object of worship they associate with Allah. He boldly challenges them and their false gods to gather all their forces and contrive whatever harm they can against him, without granting him even a moment's delay. The deeper meaning is that false deities have no power to benefit or harm, and that the true servant of Allah relies on Him alone. When one's trust is firmly placed in Allah, the schemes of created beings cannot ultimately prevail except by Allah's permission, so the believer remains fearless and steadfast in pure monotheism.

translation: Indeed, I have placed my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no moving creature but that He holds it by its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path.
interpretation: This verse teaches that true reliance upon God is grounded in the realization that He alone has absolute control over every living being, so nothing can escape His grasp or act outside His will. Because His governance and decrees are perfectly just, wise, and upright, the believer entrusts all affairs to Him with confidence that His path is straight and His judgment is never unjust.

translation: But if they turn away, then I have conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you. And my Lord will replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is over all things a Guardian.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the messenger’s duty is only to deliver the divine message clearly, not to force people into faith. If a community rejects the truth, it does not weaken or harm God in any way; rather, it loses its own standing and may be replaced by another people who will inherit its role and blessings. God’s guardianship over all things means He preserves His revelation, records every deed, and will bring all matters to their just conclusion.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.
interpretation: This verse relates that when God’s decree of destruction came upon the disbelieving people of ‘Ad, He rescued Prophet Hud and the believers who were with him. Their salvation was not earned by their own strength or merit but was granted by God’s mercy, and He delivered them from the harsh, overwhelming torment that struck the deniers. It shows that divine punishment is severe for those who reject the truth, while deliverance for the faithful is a pure favor and compassion from God.

translation: And that was 'Ad: they denied the signs of their Lord and disobeyed His messengers and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.
interpretation: This verse identifies the ruin of 'Ad as the consequence of a triple spiritual corruption: rejecting God's clear signs, rebelling against the prophetic call, and surrendering their will to arrogant, stubborn leaders. Their denial of Hud was not treated as a minor disagreement but as rejection of the divine messengers as a whole, because the message is one. Their obedience to every 'jabbar 'anid'—a tyrant hardened in defiance—shows how disbelief in God is often paired with blind loyalty to oppressive human authority. The verse thus warns that those who dismiss divine guidance and follow the loudest, most obstinate power rather than truth will meet the same pattern of destruction.

translation: And they were pursued by a curse in this worldly life and on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, 'Aad disbelieved in their Lord. So away with 'Aad, the people of Hud!
interpretation: This verse declares that the nation of 'Aad was overtaken by a lasting curse in this world and will also be cursed on the Day of Resurrection because they rejected their Lord. Their punishment is presented as the direct consequence of denying the truth brought by Prophet Hud: they are cut off from divine mercy and consigned to ruin, both in worldly disgrace and in the Hereafter.

translation: And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. He created you from the earth and settled you therein, so seek His forgiveness and then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive.'
interpretation: This verse sets forth the core of Salih's prophetic call to Thamud: absolute monotheism. Worship is due to Allah alone because He is the sole Creator and Sustainer, who brought humankind into existence from the earth and made them dwellers and builders upon it. The command to seek forgiveness and then repent shows that pardon must be sought for past failure, and that this must be followed by a decisive turning back to God with sincerity. The closing declaration that God is near and responsive assures believers that He is not distant from His servants; He hears supplication, accepts repentance, and answers those who call upon Him. Thus the verse combines tawhid, gratitude for God's creative and civilizing favors, hope in divine mercy, and the obligation of sincere repentance.

translation: They said, “O Salih, you were a hope among us before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? And indeed we are in grave doubt about that to which you call us.”
interpretation: The people of Thamud are addressing Prophet Salih with astonishment and objection. They acknowledge that before his call they had regarded him as a respected figure in whom they placed hope, perhaps as a leader or guide. But now they resent that he calls them away from the idols inherited from their ancestors. Their question is not a sincere request for understanding but a rhetorical protest against abandoning ancestral tradition. Their claim of being in “grave doubt” expresses deep unease and suspicion toward his message, revealing that their real barrier is not lack of evidence but attachment to inherited worship and unwillingness to accept prophetic guidance.

translation: He said, "O my people, have you considered: if I should be upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself, then who would protect me from Allah if I disobeyed Him? So you would not increase me except in loss."
interpretation: The prophet Salih is telling his people that he stands on clear proof and guidance from God, and that God has granted him mercy—namely prophethood, revelation, and guidance. If he were to disobey God by abandoning that message or yielding to their demands, no one could shield him from God’s punishment. Their pressure and opposition, therefore, do not help him at all; they only add to his loss if he were to follow them. The verse teaches that divine proof and mercy demand firm obedience, and that no human support can protect a person from God if he turns away from Him.

translation: And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah as a sign for you. So leave her to eat in the land of Allah, and do not touch her with harm, lest a near punishment seize you.
interpretation: The she-camel is a miraculous sign and a test from God, and their treatment of it reveals whether they submit to His command. Letting her graze freely acknowledges that the earth belongs to God and that His creatures are under His care; harming her is an act of defiance against the sign and will bring a swift, inevitable punishment.

translation: So they hamstrung her. He said, 'Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied.'
interpretation: This verse marks the final warning given to the people of Thamud after they slaughtered the she-camel. They are granted three days of respite in their dwellings, but it is not a reprieve from accountability; it is a fixed decree. The statement that this is a promise not to be belied affirms that God's warning is certain and will inevitably come to pass, and no one can avert or falsify it.

translation: So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him, by a mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that Day. Indeed, your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty.
interpretation: This verse teaches that when God's decree of punishment arrives, His mercy is the only true means of deliverance. He rescues His prophets and the believers not by their own power but by His grace, and He saves them from both worldly destruction and the humiliation of the Day of Judgment. It also establishes that God's strength and might are absolute, so His protection of the faithful and His retribution against the guilty are certain.

translation: And the wrongdoers were seized by the Cry, so they became in their dwellings lifeless, fallen on their knees.
interpretation: This verse declares that God’s punishment overtook the unjust people with a sudden, overwhelming cry, leaving them prostrate and motionless in their own homes. It signifies that persistent wrongdoing and rejection of divine warning lead to inevitable destruction, and neither strength nor shelter can save those whom God seizes in justice.

translation: As if they had never lived there. Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. So away with Thamud!
interpretation: This verse seals the fate of Thamud: their destruction was so complete that their dwellings seemed never to have been inhabited, and their former strength and prosperity were erased as though they had never existed. Their crime was rejecting their Lord and denying His messengers. The phrase “away with Thamud” is a pronouncement of ruin, curse, and expulsion from God’s mercy. The repeated emphasis (“Unquestionably… So away…”) conveys the certainty and severity of divine judgment: no worldly power, wealth, or civilization can protect a people once they persistently turn away from their Creator and reject His guidance.

translation: And certainly Our messengers came to Abraham with good tidings. They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace." And he did not delay before bringing a roasted calf.
interpretation: This verse teaches that true faith is expressed through gracious hospitality and prompt generosity. Abraham receives the angels’ greeting with a peace that is both a response and a prayer for their safety, then hastens to serve them a roasted calf, showing that the righteous honor guests with dignity, humility, and eagerness, treating hospitality as an act of worship and a mark of prophetic character.

translation: But when he saw their hands not reaching for it, he felt unfamiliar with them and conceived fear of them. They said, 'Do not fear; indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot.'
interpretation: This verse describes Abraham’s natural human reaction when his guests—angels appearing in human form—did not eat the food he had offered. In his culture, refusing a host’s food could signal hostility or ill intent, so he became uneasy and fearful. The angels immediately reassured him, revealing that they were not enemies but messengers sent by God with a specific mission: to bring judgment upon the people of Lot for their grave sins. The verse thus shows that God’s messengers can come in human form, that divine reassurance removes fear for those who trust God, and that God’s justice is executed upon communities that persist in corruption.

translation: And his wife was standing, and she laughed, so We gave her glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob.
interpretation: This verse refers to Abraham’s wife Sarah. Her laughter expressed astonishment or joy at the angels’ visit and at the seemingly impossible news that she, an aged and barren woman, would bear a child. The glad tidings of Isaac, and then of Jacob after Isaac, signify that God’s power surpasses natural causes and that His blessing upon Abraham’s household would continue across generations. It affirms that the prophetic line would remain among Abraham’s descendants, and that what is beyond human hope is easily accomplished by God’s decree.

translation: She said, "Oh, woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman, and this my husband is an old man? Indeed, this is an amazing thing!"
interpretation: This is the astonished exclamation of Sarah, the wife of Ibrahim, when she received the glad tidings of a child. Her words express utter amazement at the natural impossibility of bearing a child in old age, especially when her husband is also advanced in years. The phrase “Oh, woe to me!” is not a rejection of God's decree but an idiom of shock and wonder at something extraordinary. The verse thus highlights that divine power is not constrained by ordinary causes: what is impossible by human standards is entirely possible for Allah. Her amazement is the natural human reaction to a miracle, and it serves to magnify the miraculous nature of the gift and the limitless power of God.

translation: They said, "Are you amazed at the command of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings are upon you, O people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious."
interpretation: The angels are addressing Sarah’s astonishment at the news of a child in her old age, teaching that God’s decree is not bound by ordinary causes; His mercy and blessings are specially upon the household of Abraham, and He is praiseworthy in all His acts and majestic in His essence and command.

translation: And when the fear had gone away from Abraham and the good tidings came to him, he began to plead with Us concerning the people of Lot.
interpretation: This verse portrays Abraham’s deep compassion and moral concern: once his initial fear subsided and he received the glad tidings of a son, he turned to intercede and argue with God’s messengers on behalf of Lot’s people, hoping that their punishment might be averted. It shows that a true believer may sincerely plead for mercy even for a sinful people, while ultimately submitting to God’s wisdom and justice. His debate was not out of rebellion but out of mercy, reflecting the Qur’anic ideal of combining firm faith with profound human empathy.

translation: Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, tender-hearted, and ever returning [to Allah].
interpretation: This verse praises Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) with three qualities: forbearance, meaning he was gentle and slow to anger; a tender, compassionate heart that sighed in humble supplication and cared for others; and a constant turning back to Allah in repentance, obedience, and reliance. It presents him as a model of moral strength joined with deep sensitivity and unwavering devotion to God.

translation: O Abraham, turn away from this. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed, there will come to them a punishment that cannot be repelled.
interpretation: This verse conveys that Abraham’s compassionate pleading on behalf of Lot’s people must cease because the divine decree has already been issued. It teaches that when God’s command for judgment becomes final, intercession or debate cannot alter it, and the punishment appointed for a persistently corrupt people is irrevocable. The verse highlights both Abraham’s merciful nature and the firmness of divine justice: mercy does not override the settled consequence of defiant wrongdoing once God’s decree has come.

translation: And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed because of them and felt constrained by them, and he said, 'This is a trying day.'
interpretation: Lot was deeply grieved and anxious when the angels arrived in human form, not because of any fault in them, but because he feared for their safety at the hands of his corrupt people. He felt powerless to protect his guests, and his words 'this is a trying day' express his dread of the evil and conflict he expected. The verse highlights Lot's righteous concern, his compassion for others, and the severity of the moral corruption surrounding him, which made hospitality and protection nearly impossible.

translation: And his people came rushing to him, and previously they had been committing evil deeds. He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a right-minded man?"
interpretation: Lot’s people, already steeped in habitual sexual transgression and public indecency, rushed to his house intending to assault his guests. Lot did not excuse their craving or negotiate over the sin; he redirected them to what was lawful—marriage with women—declaring that path purer and more honorable. He appealed to their fear of God and to the shame of violating hospitality toward his guests, then exposed their corruption by asking whether even one sound-minded man among them would restrain the crowd. The verse condemns sexual deviance, the violation of a guest’s safety, and the loss of moral reason that makes a people persist in evil despite clear correction.

translation: They said: “You certainly know that we have no claim/right to your daughters, and indeed you know what we want.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the brazen defiance and moral corruption of Lot’s people: they openly admit that lawful marriage to his daughters is not what they seek, and that he fully knows their intention is to commit indecency with his male guests. Their words are not a denial of knowledge but a confession of deliberate sin—they reject the lawful path and insist on pursuing their illicit desire, showing that their corruption is rooted in willful rebellion rather than ignorance.

translation: He said, "If only I had against you some power, or could take refuge in a strong support."
interpretation: This expresses Prophet Lut's deep distress and helplessness before his people's collective aggression: he wishes he had either personal strength to repel them or a powerful clan, fortress, or ally to protect him and his guests. It reflects the limits of human capability when confronting widespread corruption and the need for divine aid, not a lack of trust in God.

translation: They said, 'O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So set out with your family in a portion of the night, and let no one among you look back, except your wife. Indeed, what strikes them will strike her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?'
interpretation: The angels' words assure Lot that divine protection shields him from the mob's power, but rescue requires immediate, obedient departure without lingering attachment to the doomed city. The prohibition against looking back symbolizes total severance from the corrupt society and trust in God's command. Lot's wife is singled out because her inward allegiance remained with the wicked; sharing their fate, she illustrates that familial ties cannot save one who persists in disbelief. The appointment at dawn declares that God's judgment is neither forgotten nor delayed beyond its fixed time, and the rhetorical question presses the hearer to recognize how close that reckoning is.

translation: So when Our command came, We turned its uppermost part into its lowermost, and We rained upon it stones of baked clay, layered one upon another.
interpretation: This verse depicts the execution of God's decree against the people of Lot: their settlements were overturned and pelted with stones of hardened clay, a punishment combining total upheaval with a deadly shower from above. It conveys that when God's command arrives, no people can resist it, and that persistent corruption and defiance invite a precise, overwhelming judgment arranged by divine will.

translation: Marked by your Lord, and it is not far from the wrongdoers.
interpretation: These stones were divinely marked and appointed by your Lord for the destruction of the wrongdoing people; the verse warns that God's punishment is never distant from those who persist in injustice and transgression, so every wrongdoer should fear that divine judgment may reach them.

translation: And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said, “O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. And do not diminish the measure and the scale. Indeed, I see you in prosperity, but I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing Day.”
interpretation: This verse establishes that the prophetic call to Madyan began with tawhid: sole worship of Allah, because all moral and social reform derives its authority and accountability from the Creator. Shu‘ayb then addresses the specific corruption of his people: cheating in trade by giving less than due in measure and weight. The prohibition is not merely against a minor commercial irregularity but against a whole economic culture that treats other people’s rights as negotiable for profit. Shu‘ayb acknowledges that they possess outward prosperity and abundance, yet he does not bless their wealth as proof of divine approval; rather, he fears that the same system of injustice will bring a punishment that surrounds them completely, leaving no avenue of escape. The “encompassing Day” signifies a calamity, whether in this world or in the Hereafter, that will overtake every dimension of their lives because their wrongdoing has become collective and entrenched. Thus the verse teaches that worship of Allah alone must express itself in honesty, fairness, and protection of others’ rights, and that material comfort built on exploitation is a warning, not a security.

translation: And O my people, give full measure and weight in justice, and do not deprive the people of their due, and do not commit evil in the land, spreading corruption.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true faith demands justice in all dealings, especially in economic transactions. It obligates honesty and fairness in measuring and weighing, prohibits taking away or diminishing the rights and property of others, and forbids spreading corruption, disorder, or exploitation in society. The command joins commercial integrity with moral and social responsibility: cheating people of their due is not merely a business fault but a violation of justice and a form of corruption on earth.

translation: What remains with Allah is better for you, if you are believers. And I am not a keeper over you.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the lawful gains, rewards, and blessings that Allah preserves for a person are far better than any illicit profit or worldly advantage gained through wrongdoing. If someone truly believes, they should trust that obedience to Allah and contentment with His provision bring greater good than cheating, hoarding, or exploiting others. The speaker also declares that he is not a guardian appointed to force people’s obedience or compel their hearts; his role is only to convey the truth and give sincere counsel, while ultimate reckoning and protection belong to Allah alone.

translation: They said, “O Shu‘ayb, does your prayer command you that we should abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we should not do with our wealth whatever we wish? Indeed, you are surely the forbearing, the right-minded!”
interpretation: This verse exposes the mockery and resistance of Shu‘ayb’s people, who measure truth by inherited custom and personal desire rather than by divine guidance. By reducing his prophetic call to “your prayer,” they imply that his devotion has no right to challenge their ancestral worship or their unrestricted control over wealth. Their sarcastic praise of him as “forbearing” and “right-minded” shows that they dismiss his moral authority: they cannot accept that a gentle, prudent man would forbid what their forefathers practiced or interfere with how they use their property. The verse thus warns against letting blind tradition and greed make one ridicule revelation, especially when it calls for accountability in both worship and economic conduct.

translation: He said, “O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has provided me with a good provision from Himself? And I do not intend to act contrary to you by doing what I forbid you. I only intend reform as far as I am able. And my success is only through Allah. Upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn.”
interpretation: This is Prophet Shu‘ayb’s declaration to his people: his call is not based on personal whim, greed, or desire for authority, but on clear proof from his Lord and the good, lawful provision God granted him. Therefore his prohibition of corruption, injustice, and false worship is not hypocrisy—he refuses to command them to avoid something while doing it himself. His sole aim is sincere reform and restoration of what is right, to the extent he is able, not domination or self-interest. He then confesses that no human effort succeeds by itself: all enabling success comes only from Allah. So he places his trust in Allah alone and constantly turns back to Him in obedience and repentance. The verse thus presents the model of a truthful caller: consistency between word and deed, sincerity of purpose, humble dependence on God, and perpetual return to Him.

translation: And O my people, let not your dissension with me cause you to suffer the like of what befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih. And the people of Lot are not far from you.
interpretation: This is a warning that stubborn opposition to God’s prophet and division from his message can bring upon a people the same kind of punishment that destroyed earlier nations who rejected their prophets; and the nearness of Lot’s people—whether in time, place, or resemblance in sin—means the warning is immediate, so they must turn back before the same fate reaches them.

translation: And seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving.
interpretation: This verse directs people to seek God's forgiveness for their sins and then to return to Him with sincere repentance, turning away from disobedience and toward obedience. It assures them that God is Rahim—intensely merciful—and Wadud—loving and compassionate toward His servants—so He accepts those who repent and draws them near with kindness rather than rejecting them.

translation: They said, 'O Shu'ayb, we do not comprehend much of what you say, and indeed we see you weak among us. Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you, and you are not mighty over us.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the mindset of Shu'ayb's people: their rejection was rooted in arrogance and worldly calculation. They could not grasp the substance of his message because they measured truth by social strength and status. Calling him weak and admitting that only his clan restrained them from killing him shows that their loyalty was to tribal power, not to God or justice. They denied him any honor or authority over them, meaning they did not fear him personally and would not submit to his call. Thus the verse portrays how a prophet may be despised by his own people when he lacks worldly backing, yet their threat cannot harm him beyond God's decree.

translation: He said, "O my people, is my clan more honored by you than Allah? And you have taken Him behind your backs. Indeed, my Lord encompasses whatever you do."
interpretation: This verse rebukes a people who let tribal loyalty and social status outweigh their obligation to God: they spare the speaker only because of his family, while treating God’s authority as something neglected and cast behind them. It declares that such misplaced reverence and disregard cannot escape God’s knowledge or judgment, for He fully encompasses and records all their deeds.

translation: And O my people, work according to your position; indeed, I am working. You will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him and who is a liar. And wait; indeed, I am with you, watching.
interpretation: This is a decisive warning from Shu'ayb to his people: let each continue in his chosen course. The truth will be made manifest by the outcome—who is visited by the humiliating punishment and who is the liar. The command to wait is not passive resignation but an assured awaiting of God's judgment. God is the watcher over all, so His promise of justice cannot fail.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and the blast seized those who did wrong, so they became fallen lifeless in their homes.
interpretation: This verse teaches that when Allah’s decree of judgment arrives, deliverance comes only through His mercy, not through worldly strength or alliances. Shu‘ayb and the believers were saved because Allah favored them with mercy, while the wrongdoers were overtaken by a sudden, overwhelming punishment. The blast seizing them signifies that divine chastisement can come instantly and irresistibly, and their becoming motionless in their own dwellings shows that no place of apparent security can protect those who persist in injustice and rejection of truth. Thus the verse contrasts the fruit of faith and obedience—mercy and rescue—with the end of wrongdoing—sudden ruin and humiliation.

translation: As if they had never lived there in comfort. Unquestionably, away with Madyan, just as Thamud were done away with.
interpretation: This is a declaration of total erasure: their dwellings and traces were so completely wiped out that it was as though they had never enjoyed habitation and prosperity there. The phrase “away with Madyan” is a curse of banishment from God’s mercy and every good, pronounced upon them because they rejected Shu‘ayb and persisted in corruption. By linking them to Thamud, the Qur’an places them in the same pattern: a community given clear warning, then destroyed when it chose denial and injustice. The verse warns that divine judgment can annihilate a people so thoroughly that only a lesson remains, and that being far from God’s mercy is the true ruin.

translation: And indeed We sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority.
interpretation: Allah affirms that He sent Moses equipped with His miraculous signs and an unmistakable, divinely granted proof and authority, so that his message would be established by clear evidence and not merely by human claim. The verse emphasizes that Moses’s prophethood carried both visible miracles and an irrefutable warrant from God, making the truth he brought evident to those he was sent to.

translation: To Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided.
interpretation: This verse teaches that when God sends clear guidance, people may still choose to follow a human authority instead. Pharaoh’s court obeyed his orders rather than God’s message, and the verse declares that Pharaoh’s command was not based on sound judgment or righteousness. It is a warning against blind obedience to corrupt or arrogant leaders, showing that any command which opposes divine guidance cannot lead to what is right and will only lead its followers to ruin.

translation: He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them to the Fire; and wretched is the place to which they are brought.
interpretation: This verse exposes the end of Pharaoh as the archetypal tyrant who led his people into disbelief. On the Day of Resurrection he will walk ahead of them, not to honor or salvation, but to drive them into the Fire. The wording uses the image of arriving at a watering place, but here the “water” is Hell and the arrival is misery. It teaches that those who follow corrupt leaders in falsehood will find their leader at the front of their punishment, and that the worst destination is the one reached through obedience to evil. The verse warns against blindly following any path or authority that leads away from God, because such leadership ends in the Fire for both the followed and the followers.

translation: And they were followed by a curse in this world and on the Day of Resurrection. Evil is the gift that is given.
interpretation: This verse refers to Pharaoh and his followers: they are pursued by a curse in this worldly life and will also be pursued by one on the Day of Resurrection. The curse is expulsion from God's mercy and enduring punishment. The phrase "evil is the gift that is given" means that what they receive as their recompense is not a blessing but an evil portion—curse compounded upon curse, and aid that is in reality ruin. It emphasizes that the oppressive leaders and their followers are granted the worst of gifts: continuous disgrace and punishment in both this life and the Hereafter.

translation: That is from the news of the cities which We relate to you; among them are some standing and some mown down.
interpretation: This verse informs the Prophet that the accounts of earlier towns are revealed by God as a warning and lesson. Some of those ruined settlements still have traces standing, while others have been completely cut down and erased, because their people rejected the messengers and persisted in disbelief. It shows that divine punishment is real, and that nations are not protected from destruction when they turn away from God.

translation: And We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. So their gods which they called upon besides Allah did not avail them at all when the command of your Lord came, and they increased them in nothing but ruin.
interpretation: The verse declares Allah’s absolute justice: the destruction that befell those nations was not arbitrary or unjust, but the inevitable consequence of their own choices—associating partners with Allah and rejecting His messengers. The false deities they invoked could not avert the divine decree when it came; instead of helping them, those objects of worship only increased them in loss and perdition. Thus, shirk leaves a person utterly helpless at the moment of judgment, and the only true refuge is sincere worship of Allah alone.

translation: And thus is the taking of your Lord when He takes the towns while they are unjust. Indeed, His taking is painful and severe.
interpretation: This verse means that Allah’s punishment of communities that persist in wrongdoing is a settled divine pattern, not an isolated event. When He seizes them while they remain unjust—after warnings and opportunities to reform—His grasp is agonizing and crushing. It is a warning that oppression and denial do not escape divine justice, and that the severity of His punishment is proportionate to the persistence of the wrongdoers.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day that will be witnessed.
interpretation: This is a lesson drawn from God’s destruction of the unjust nations and His rescue of the believers: His judgment is certain, and the warning benefits those who truly fear the punishment of the Hereafter. The Day of Resurrection is a universal gathering in which all people are assembled before God for reckoning, and it is a witnessed Day—seen and experienced by all creatures—so no deed, hidden or open, will be left unaccounted. Fear of that Day should therefore lead a person to heed God’s signs, repent, and live in obedience before the unavoidable meeting with Him.

translation: And We do not delay it except for a specified term.
interpretation: This means that the postponement of the Day of Judgment is only until a precise, already-fixed time in God's knowledge. The delay is not indefinite or arbitrary; the term is counted and limited, so that Day will certainly come when its appointed measure is complete. It shows that God's forbearance is not negligence, and it calls people to prepare for the inevitable reckoning.

translation: On the Day when it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission; then among them will be wretched and blessed.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, when God’s decree for judgment arrives, no person will be able to speak, plead, or intercede except by His leave. God will then divide humanity into two ultimate groups: the wretched, who by their rejection of truth and evil deeds are consigned to punishment, and the blessed, who by faith and righteous deeds attain God’s mercy and eternal happiness. The verse thus affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over the final accounting and the two destinies of every soul.

translation: As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire; for them therein is sighing and wailing.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of the people of misery and ruin, whose disbelief and evil deeds have made them deserving of the Fire. Their punishment is portrayed through the sounds of profound anguish: “زفير” is the painful exhaling of a heart crushed by sorrow, and “شهيق” is the drawn-out inhaling or wailing of one in torment. It signifies that Hell is not merely an external punishment but an all-encompassing state of regret, despair, and humiliation. The phrase “لهم فيها” emphasizes that this suffering is specifically theirs and remains their condition, underscoring divine justice: they chose a path that led to wretchedness, so they are placed in an abode whose misery corresponds to their deeds, with no escape or relief.

translation: Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is doer of what He intends.
interpretation: This verse declares that the people of the Fire will remain in it as long as the heavens and the earth remain—an expression of unending duration—while making their permanence wholly subject to God's will. The exception “except what your Lord wills” does not negate the reality of the punishment; it affirms that nothing, including the duration of the Hereafter, occurs independently of God's decree. The closing statement, “Indeed, your Lord is doer of what He intends,” establishes His absolute sovereignty: He is not questioned about what He does, and His will is always carried out. Thus the verse teaches that the eternal abode is eternal only because God, who does whatever He wills, has willed it so.

translation: And as for those who are blessed, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills—an unceasing gift.
interpretation: This means that the people of felicity remain in Paradise forever. The phrase “as long as the heavens and the earth endure” is an Arabic expression for endless duration, and the exception “except what your Lord wills” does not imply that their bliss will be cut off; rather, it shows that their eternal abiding depends on God’s will and grace, not on any independent right or inherent necessity. This is confirmed by “an unceasing gift”: it is a bestowal that is never severed, revoked, or diminished. Thus the exception may refer to the period before they enter Paradise, or it may simply affirm that God’s will is the source of their everlasting stay, while the gift itself remains without end.

translation: So do not be in doubt, [O Prophet], about what these people worship. They worship only as their forefathers worshipped before. And indeed, We will surely give them their share in full, without any decrease.
interpretation: This addresses the Prophet so that he should not waver concerning the falsehood of the polytheists’ worship. Their rites are not founded on any revealed proof or truth; they are merely imitating the ancestral practices of their forefathers. Their persistence, numbers, or inherited tradition does not make their worship valid. God then declares that He will repay them their allotted portion—their recompense and punishment—completely and exactly, withholding nothing. The verse thus establishes that the disbelievers’ way is baseless ancestral imitation, and that divine justice will reach them in full, so the Prophet should remain firm and certain.

translation: And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture, but they differed concerning it. And were it not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been judged between them. And indeed they are in disquieting doubt about it.
interpretation: This means that difference and rejection did not begin with Muhammad’s people: Allah gave Moses the Torah, but his people split over it, some accepting it and others denying or altering it. Had Allah not already decreed that final judgment would be deferred to an appointed time, He would have settled their dispute at once, exposing the truth and requiting falsehood. Their continuing doubt about the Scripture is therefore not honest uncertainty but a suspicious, unsettling wavering caused by resistance to the clear message. The verse consoles the Prophet and warns all who dispute revelation that Allah alone will judge their disagreements.

translation: And indeed, all of them—your Lord will surely repay them in full for their deeds. Indeed, He is Aware of what they do.
interpretation: This is a decisive assurance of universal accountability: no person or group, whatever their claims or divisions, will escape the exact requital of their actions. God's exhaustive knowledge of every deed—its motive, circumstance, and consequence—guarantees that His repayment will be perfectly just, neither increased nor diminished. Thus the verse grounds reward and punishment in God's all-encompassing awareness, prompting sincerity, repentance, and reliance on His justice and mercy.

translation: So remain steadfast on the right course as you have been commanded, you and those who have turned to Allah with you, and do not transgress. Indeed, He is fully aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet Muhammad and the believers who repent and turn to Allah to uphold steadfastness in faith and obedience exactly as Allah has commanded, without deviation. It warns against transgression—exceeding the limits set by Allah or falling short in His commands—and reminds them that Allah sees all their deeds, so their steadfastness must be sincere and according to His guidance, not based on personal desire or extremism.

translation: And do not incline toward those who do wrong, lest the Fire touch you; and you have no protectors besides Allah, and then you will not be helped.
interpretation: This verse warns that any leaning of the heart, loyalty, approval, or practical cooperation toward wrongdoing and its perpetrators drags a person into their moral and spiritual ruin and exposes them to the Fire. Since no ally, authority, or power can shield anyone from God's judgment, the only safety is to disown injustice, refuse to legitimize it, and align oneself with God's command; if one instead relies on the unjust or seeks their protection, there will be no helper when punishment comes.

translation: And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and at the approach of the night. Indeed, good deeds do away with misdeeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.
interpretation: This verse commands the establishment of ritual prayer at both ends of the day—meaning the morning and the later part of the day—and during the early hours of the night. It teaches that righteous deeds, especially prayer performed sincerely, erase sins and failings. This command and promise serve as an admonition and reminder for those who are mindful of God, so they may persist in worship, seek forgiveness, and remain conscious of their accountability to Him.

translation: And be patient, for indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse commands steadfast patience in obeying God, avoiding sin, and enduring trials, and it grounds that command in God's perfect justice: He never lets the reward of those who act with sincere goodness and excellence (ihsan) be lost or diminished. Every righteous effort, even if unnoticed or unrewarded by people, is preserved with God and will be fully compensated.

translation: So why were there not, among the generations before you, people of remaining virtue who forbade corruption on the earth, except a few of those whom We saved among them? And those who did wrong followed what they had been given to enjoy in luxury, and they were criminals.
interpretation: This verse teaches that past communities were not left without an opportunity to reform: they should have produced a righteous remnant that actively opposed moral and social corruption. The only ones who fulfilled this duty were a small group whom Allah saved. The wrongdoers, however, made the luxurious comforts and pleasures they were given their central pursuit, following them instead of God’s guidance, and so they became confirmed criminals. The lesson is that a community’s survival depends on the presence of people who enjoin good and forbid evil, and that material indulgence, when it turns people away from truth and responsibility, leads to ruin.

translation: And your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reformers.
interpretation: God’s punishment of a people is never arbitrary or unjust; He does not destroy a community while it remains in a state of righteousness and reform. Destruction comes only after corruption, wrongdoing, and the abandonment of reform become widespread. Therefore, a society’s commitment to justice, uprightness, and reform is a means of safety from divine punishment, and the verse establishes both God’s justice and the collective responsibility of people to maintain moral and social reform.

translation: And if your Lord had willed, He could have made mankind one community; but they will not cease to differ.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God could have compelled all people to follow a single religion or way of life, but by His wisdom He did not. Human disagreement and diversity persist because people are given the capacity to choose, and many deviate from the truth. The statement is a consolation to the Prophet: the fact that people continue to differ in belief is not a sign that God is unable to unite them, but rather it reflects His will and the reality of human freedom and responsibility.

translation: Except those on whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind together.
interpretation: God’s mercy is the sole exception to humanity’s recurring disagreement and deviation; He created people so that His mercy might reach them, guiding whom He wills to truth and unity. Yet His decree is irrevocable: Hell will be filled with all those among jinn and humans who knowingly reject that mercy and persist in disobedience.

translation: And all that We relate to you of the news of the messengers is that by which We make firm your heart. And there has come to you in this the truth, and an admonition and a reminder for the believers.
interpretation: God tells the Prophet that recounting the trials, patience, and outcomes of earlier messengers is meant to strengthen his heart and steady him against hardship and opposition. The revelation that has come to him contains the truth itself, along with warning and counsel, and it is a reminder that benefits those who believe, calling them to firm faith, patience, and trust in God’s promise.

translation: And say to those who do not believe: 'Work according to your position; indeed, we are working.'
interpretation: This is a decisive warning and a declaration of disavowal: the disbelievers are left to their chosen way and false standing, while the Prophet and the believers remain firm on the path God has assigned them. Both sides are acting, but the final outcome and judgment belong to Allah, who will make clear who was truly guided and who was misguided.

translation: And wait; indeed, we are waiting.
interpretation: This verse is a decisive declaration that the believers, having delivered the divine message, leave the outcome to God. It tells the deniers to continue awaiting whatever end they expect, while the Prophet and believers await God’s promised help and judgment. The verse affirms that God’s decree is certain, and the final result will expose who stood on truth and who stood on falsehood.

translation: And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him all matters are returned. So worship Him and rely upon Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the knowledge of all that is hidden—whether in the heavens or the earth—belongs exclusively to Allah, and that every affair, decree, and final outcome ultimately returns to Him. Therefore, the only proper response is sincere worship of Him alone and complete reliance upon Him in all matters, since He alone disposes of all things and no one else shares in His unseen knowledge or sovereign authority. The closing statement affirms that Allah is fully aware of every deed His servants perform, so nothing is hidden from Him and none will be neglected in His judgment.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the clear Book.
interpretation: The disjointed letters at the beginning of the surah are among the signs whose full meaning is known to Allah and which point to the miraculous nature of the Qur'an. The verses that follow belong to a Book that is manifestly clear: it presents truth, guidance, and divine instruction with such clarity that it removes doubt and distinguishes right from wrong.

translation: Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the Qur'an was revealed in Arabic, the language of its first audience, so that its message could be grasped, reasoned upon, and applied. The Arabic form is not an end in itself but serves comprehension and accountability, showing that revelation addresses human intellect and responsibility: it is made clear in a precise linguistic context so people may move from hearing to understanding, and from understanding to conscious submission.

translation: We relate to you the best of stories through what We have revealed to you, this Qur’an, although before it you were among the unaware.
interpretation: Allah addresses the Prophet Muhammad, informing him that He Himself narrates to him the most excellent of accounts by means of the Qur’an He has revealed. The “best of stories” means the most truthful, beneficial, and beautifully ordered narratives—those that purify the heart, clarify guidance, and lead to faith and right action. The phrase “although before it you were among the unaware” establishes that the Prophet had no prior knowledge of these revealed accounts, so their precise arrival through revelation is a sign that the Qur’an is from Allah alone, not from human learning. Thus the verse affirms the divine origin of the Qur’an, its superiority over all other narratives in truth and guidance, and the Prophet’s being taught directly by revelation.

translation: When Joseph said to his father, 'O my father, I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me.'
interpretation: The dream is a divine sign of Joseph’s future exaltation: the eleven stars represent his eleven brothers, and the sun and moon represent his father and mother. Their prostrating to him is not worship of Joseph, but a symbolic acknowledgment of the high rank and authority God would grant him, as later fulfilled when his family came before him in Egypt and submitted to God’s decree concerning him.

translation: He said, "O my son, do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they contrive a plot against you. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy."
interpretation: This is Jacob’s wise warning to Joseph: the dream foretold a high station, and revealing it prematurely could stir envy in his brothers and move them to scheme against him. The verse teaches discretion about blessings and favors, because not every listener will receive them with good will. It also identifies Satan as the open enemy of humanity, who exploits jealousy, rivalry, and ambition to incite people toward wrongdoing and division.

translation: Thus your Lord will choose you and teach you from the interpretation of dreams and events, and He will complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, just as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This is a divine reassurance that God, by His perfect knowledge and wisdom, selects whom He wills for prophethood and grants deep insight into the hidden meanings of dreams, events, and revelation. The favor promised to Joseph is not merely worldly distinction but spiritual election, guidance, and a prophetic legacy that continues through the family of Jacob, just as it was granted to Abraham and Isaac.
