The completion of favor means that God brings His chosen servants to the fullness of His blessing in faith, understanding, and nearness to Him, and this unfolds according to His all-encompassing knowledge and wise governance of all affairs.

translation: Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers there were signs for those who ask.
interpretation: The verse declares that the account of Joseph and his brothers is not mere history but a treasury of divine signs for every seeker of truth. It teaches that God’s wisdom governs all events, even apparent injustice and suffering, and that He ultimately brings about protection, elevation, and reconciliation for those who remain patient, chaste, and conscious of Him. What appears as loss or betrayal can become the very means by which God fulfills His promise and turns sorrow into mercy.

translation: When they said, “Joseph and his brother are more beloved to our father than we, while we are a strong group. Indeed, our father is clearly mistaken.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the envy and resentment Joseph’s half-brothers felt because their father Jacob loved Joseph and Benjamin more than them. Their claim that their father was in clear error was itself a grave mistake: they judged his divinely guided affection as partiality, while in reality Jacob’s love for Joseph was tied to God’s chosen purpose for him. Their sense of strength as a group did not justify their accusation or their later plot against Joseph.

translation: Kill Joseph or cast him out to some land; your father’s face will be free for you, and after that you will be a righteous people.
interpretation: This is the proposal of Joseph’s brothers: they conspire to remove him—either by murder or exile—so that their father’s exclusive affection and attention will turn to them. Their words “and after that you will be a righteous people” expose their self-deception and moral corruption: they imagine they can commit a grave crime against their brother and father, then simply repent later and become righteous. It shows how sin is made to appear manageable when desire and jealousy dominate, and it warns against rationalizing evil by promising future reform.

translation: One of them said, "Do not kill Joseph, but cast him into the bottom of the well; some caravan will pick him up, if you are going to do anything."
interpretation: This is the counsel of one among Joseph’s brothers who refused to consent to murder. He proposes casting Joseph into the hidden depth of a well instead, so that a passing caravan may rescue and take him away. The verse shows that even within a collective plot driven by envy, a voice of restraint can remain, and it also indicates how God’s providential plan advances through human scheming: their attempt to remove Joseph becomes the very means by which he is carried toward Egypt and later raised to honor. The closing condition, “if you are going to act,” is a rebuke of their resolve and a plea to choose the lesser evil rather than bloodshed.

translation: They said, “O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph, when indeed we are sincere well-wishers to him?”
interpretation: This verse reports the brothers of Joseph addressing their father Jacob, questioning why he does not entrust Joseph to their care despite their claim to be sincere. Their words were a deceptive prelude to their plot against Joseph; they outwardly professed concern and loyalty while inwardly intending harm, illustrating how false sincerity can be used to manipulate trust.

translation: Send him with us tomorrow, that he may enjoy himself and play; and indeed, we will surely be his guardians.
interpretation: The brothers present their request as concern for Benjamin’s refreshment and youthful recreation, and they seal it with an emphatic promise of protection. The verse exposes how a self-serving aim can be dressed in kindly counsel: they speak to reassure their father and lower his guard, while their guarantee of safety rests only on human ability. In the larger story, their confident “we will surely guard him” cannot withstand God’s decree, showing that no pledge of security, however strong, can override what Allah has planned, and that true protection belongs to Him alone.

translation: He said, "It truly grieves me that you should take him away, and I fear that the wolf may eat him while you are unaware of him."
interpretation: This verse expresses Jacob’s deep paternal love and anxiety for Joseph: the thought of being separated from him causes him real sorrow, and he worries that harm may befall him when the brothers are inattentive. His mention of the wolf reflects a natural fear for a young son’s safety, while also exposing the emotional vulnerability that the brothers later exploit when they claim a wolf devoured Joseph.

translation: They said, “If the wolf devours him while we are a strong group, then we would indeed be losers.”
interpretation: This is a rhetorical assurance by Yusuf’s brothers: they argue that with their number and strength, it would be an unbearable disgrace and clear loss if they failed to protect him from a wolf. Their words reveal false confidence in collective power and conceal their true intention, showing that outward strength is no guarantee of safety and that security belongs to Allah alone.

translation: So when they took him away and agreed to cast him into the bottom of the well, We revealed to him: 'You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive.'
interpretation: This verse marks the point at which Joseph’s brothers’ jealousy turns into action: they take him away and unanimously resolve to throw him into the dark depths of a well, intending to remove him from their father’s favor and perhaps from life itself. Yet at that very moment of apparent abandonment, God inspires Joseph with a promise that he will one day confront them with this very deed, though they will not recognize him or realize that their plot is unfolding within God’s decree. The well, meant as a place of disappearance, becomes the first stage in Joseph’s rise toward prophethood and authority. The verse thus teaches that human schemes cannot defeat divine providence: what seems like a fatal end can be the hidden beginning of God’s plan, and God may grant His servant reassurance and future vindication even in the darkest moment.

translation: And they came to their father in the evening, weeping.
interpretation: Their weeping was a deceptive performance, not genuine sorrow: they used false grief to make their lie about Joseph seem credible and to manipulate their father’s trust. The verse thus exposes how outward displays of emotion can be used to conceal wrongdoing, and it warns against accepting tears as proof of truth when they serve a self-serving story.

translation: They said, “O our father, indeed we went racing with one another and left Joseph with our belongings, so the wolf ate him. But you will not believe us, even if we were truthful.”
interpretation: This is the brothers’ fabricated excuse to their father Jacob, designed to make their betrayal sound like a tragic accident. They dress the lie in ordinary details—racing, leaving Joseph with their goods, a wolf attacking—so that it appears plausible and beyond their control. Their closing words are especially revealing: by saying that Jacob will not believe them even if they are truthful, they try to make his distrust seem unreasonable and to cast themselves as victims of suspicion. The verse thus exposes how falsehood often seeks credibility through vivid storytelling and self-pitying rhetoric, while the guilty conscience anticipates disbelief and resents it. It also reflects the painful position of a father hearing a story that sounds possible but contradicts his deep hope and trust in God’s protection.

translation: And they brought upon his shirt false blood. He said, 'Rather, your own selves have enticed you into a matter. So patience is most fitting. And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe.'
interpretation: The brothers attempted to make their false claim believable by producing a visible sign—Joseph’s shirt stained with blood—as if it proved he had been devoured. Jacob, however, perceived that the matter was not as they described, and he attributed it to their own souls having made the deed seem fair and easy for them. His words express a firm resolve not to trade trust in God for agitation, accusation, or despair. Beautiful patience here means a patience unmarred by complaint against God, resentment that denies His wisdom, or hasty retaliation against people. He seeks God’s help against the false narrative they keep repeating, meaning that only God can expose the truth, aid the wronged, and bring about relief. Thus the verse guides the wronged person to patient reliance on God, to discernment beyond outward appearances, and to entrust the outcome to the One who knows and controls all affairs.

translation: And there came a caravan, so they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said, 'Good news! This is a boy.' And they concealed him as merchandise; and Allah is Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse marks a pivotal turning point in Yusuf’s story: after being cast into the well, he is discovered by a passing caravan and drawn out through ordinary human means, showing that Allah’s decree unfolds even through seemingly chance events. The water-drawer’s joyful cry recognizes the boy as a valuable find, but the caravan people conceal him and treat him as merchandise, likely hiding the truth of his situation in order to profit from selling him. Their action exposes human greed and injustice, yet Allah is fully aware of what they do. The verse thus teaches that no scheme, concealment, or exploitation escapes Allah’s knowledge, and that He can use even the wrongdoing of others to move His chosen servant toward the next stage of His plan.

translation: And they sold him for a paltry price—a few dirhams—and they were of those who were indifferent toward him.
interpretation: This verse exposes the brothers' contempt for Joseph: they traded him away for a trifling sum, treating him as worthless and wanting only to be rid of him. Their indifference was not a true measure of his worth but evidence of their jealousy and hardness of heart. In God's decree, however, what they sold cheaply was the very one He would raise to honor and use to save many, showing that human valuation can be utterly opposed to divine purpose.

translation: And the one who bought him in Egypt said to his wife, "Make his stay honorable; perhaps he may benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son." And thus We established Joseph in the land, and that We might teach him from the interpretation of events. And Allah is predominant over His affair, but most people do not know.
interpretation: This verse teaches that Allah’s decree unfolds through ordinary human decisions and apparent hardships. The Egyptian official’s kindness toward Yusuf was not merely personal goodwill; it was the outward means by which Allah prepared Yusuf for prophethood, authority, and the ability to interpret dreams and events. What people intended for worldly benefit or adoption, Allah directed toward a greater purpose. The verse affirms that Allah’s command and plan always prevail, even when most people cannot perceive how He is arranging matters.

translation: And when he reached his full maturity, We gave him wisdom and knowledge. And thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse speaks of Joseph (Yusuf), peace be upon him: when he attained complete physical, mental, and moral maturity, Allah granted him sound judgment and beneficial knowledge as a reward for his righteousness, chastity, and patient reliance upon Allah. The statement “thus do We reward the doers of good” establishes a general divine principle: those who perfect their faith and conduct, and persevere in obedience and restraint, are granted by Allah clarity of understanding, right judgment, and knowledge of matters of religion and life. Thus wisdom and knowledge are not merely acquired by age, but are gifts from Allah bestowed upon the sincere and virtuous.

translation: And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him against his will. She closed the doors and said, 'Come to me.' He said, 'I seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, he is my master who has made good my residence. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.'
interpretation: The verse presents the decisive power of God-consciousness: when desire and opportunity are combined, Yusuf refuses not merely out of social shame but because he seeks refuge in God and recognizes that betraying the trust of the one who sheltered and honored him would be an act of injustice. It teaches that moral restraint and fidelity to trust are the true path to success, while wrongdoing, however tempting or concealed, cannot ultimately prosper.

translation: And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus it was, so that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our sincere servants.
interpretation: This verse conveys that the woman’s intent was sinful, while Joseph’s natural human inclination was immediately restrained and overruled by the divine proof and inner light granted to him by God. His protection from wrongdoing was not merely the result of his own strength but of God’s special care, averting from him evil and indecency because he was among the sincerely devoted and chosen servants. Thus the verse exonerates Joseph from any actual sin and highlights God’s guardianship over His faithful servants, steering them away from moral corruption.

translation: And they both raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from the back. And they found her master at the door. She said, 'What is the recompense for one who intended evil toward your family except imprisonment or a painful punishment?'
interpretation: This verse exposes the false accusation leveled against Yusuf after he resisted seduction and fled. The torn shirt from the back is the physical sign that he was moving away from her, not toward her, so her claim that he intended evil against her master's family is proven to be a slander. Her demand for imprisonment or painful punishment shows how sin, once exposed, often turns to blame and vengeance rather than repentance. It also teaches that God defends the innocent and that chastity may be tested by both desire and false accusation.

translation: He said, "It was she who sought to seduce me." And a witness from her family testified, "If his shirt has been torn from the front, then she has told the truth, and he is among the liars."
interpretation: This verse recounts Prophet Yusuf’s defense when he was accused by the wife of the Aziz. He states that she, not he, initiated the seduction. A member of her own household then proposes a just way to determine the truth: examining Yusuf’s shirt. If it is torn from the front, that would indicate he was the aggressor and she was resisting him, making her claim true and his denial false. The verse thus emphasizes the importance of evidence and impartial investigation before accepting an accusation, and it exposes the falsehood of the charge against Yusuf while leaving the decisive outcome to be confirmed by the shirt’s condition.

translation: But if his shirt has been torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful.
interpretation: This conditional sign establishes physical evidence as the criterion for judging the dispute: a tear from the back would indicate that he was moving away from her and she was pulling him from behind, which vindicates his account and proves her accusation false. It teaches that truth and falsehood in such matters should be determined by objective evidence, not mere claims.

translation: So when he saw his shirt torn from the back, he said, 'Indeed, this is of your guile. Indeed, your guile is great.'
interpretation: The torn shirt from behind is decisive proof that Joseph was fleeing, not attacking, and that the charge against him was a fabricated scheme. The speaker’s words expose the plot as an expression of womanly cunning and warn of how powerful and destructive such deceit can be, while vindicating Joseph.

translation: Joseph, turn away from this; and you [O woman], seek forgiveness for your sin. Indeed, you were among the sinful.
interpretation: This verse places blame squarely on the woman who attempted to seduce Joseph, while protecting Joseph’s innocence and dignity. Joseph is told to disregard the matter and not dwell on it or publicize it, which preserves his moral standing and avoids scandal. The woman is commanded to repent and seek forgiveness, because her desire and scheming were a serious wrong. The phrase “you were among the sinful” confirms that the fault was hers, not Joseph’s, and calls her to acknowledge her transgression, turn back to God, and reform. Thus the verse distinguishes between the one who is wrongly tempted and the one who actively pursues sin, and it emphasizes repentance as the proper response to guilt.

translation: And women in the city said, 'The wife of the chief minister is seeking to seduce her young servant; he has deeply pierced her with love. Indeed, we see her in clear error.'
interpretation: This verse depicts how the scandal became public gossip among the women of the city, who condemned the wife of al-Aziz for pursuing Yusuf and described her as consumed by passion and clearly misguided. Their words reveal the social disapproval and moral judgment she faced, while also setting the stage for their own encounter with Yusuf, which will expose the weakness of their own hearts and vindicate Yusuf's chastity and righteousness.

translation: Then when she heard of their scheming, she sent for them and prepared for them a banquet, and gave each one of them a knife, and said, 'Come out before them.' And when they saw him, they exalted him, and cut their hands, and said, 'God forbid! This is not a human being. This is none but a noble angel.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the power of God-given beauty as a trial that can overwhelm human composure. The women had been secretly scheming and mocking Zuleikha, so she arranged a scene that would make them experience the very thing they blamed her for. Giving them knives while presenting Joseph was a calculated test: when they saw him, their awe was so intense that they cut their own hands instead of the fruit, revealing that their earlier criticism was hollow. Their exclamation, 'God forbid! This is not a human being; this is none but a noble angel,' is a hyperbolic expression of astonishment at his extraordinary beauty and purity, not a literal denial of his humanity. The verse thus warns against self-righteous judgment of others’ desires, shows how sudden fitna can seize even those who mock it, and highlights Joseph’s exceptional status without divinizing him.

translation: She said, 'That is the one about whom you blamed me. And I did seek to seduce him, but he protected himself. And if he does not do what I command him, he will surely be imprisoned and will be among the humiliated.'
interpretation: The verse exposes how illicit desire, once exposed, may harden into coercion: the woman confesses her pursuit not in repentance but to justify herself, and when Yusuf refuses, she threatens prison and humiliation. 'He protected himself' indicates that chastity is not mere willpower but a refuge sought in God; Yusuf's refusal is faithfulness to divine limits, not weakness. The threat of imprisonment and degradation shows corrupt power trying to punish righteousness when it cannot seduce it. True humiliation (الصغار) belongs to those who surrender to sin or use authority to force it, while God-given honor belongs to those who remain steadfast, even if outwardly jailed or degraded.

translation: He said, "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than that to which they invite me. And if You do not avert from me their plot, I may incline toward them and be among the ignorant."
interpretation: This is the supplication of Prophet Yusuf after enduring the pressure of seduction and temptation. He declares that imprisonment, though painful, is preferable to falling into the sin they call him toward, because preserving faith and chastity is dearer than comfort and freedom. Yet he does not rely on his own strength; he openly admits that if God does not turn their scheming away from him, he could be drawn toward them and become one of the ignorant—those who act foolishly and disobey God. It teaches that true moral strength comes from God’s protection, that one should flee from sin even at great cost, and that the believer should combine resolve with humble dependence on God.

translation: So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their scheming. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: God answered the supplication of His servant and averted from him the women's plotted seduction and conspiracy, because He hears every prayer and knows every hidden intention and secret. The verse thus teaches that God's hearing and knowledge are the basis of His perfect protection: He is fully aware of what His servants face and of what their enemies plot, and He is able to turn their harm away. Refuge and deliverance therefore come through sincere reliance on Him, who never fails to answer and never overlooks any hidden design.

translation: Then it appeared to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time.
interpretation: This verse exposes the moral inconsistency of the Egyptian authorities: despite the clear proofs of Yusuf’s innocence—the torn shirt, the witness’s testimony, and other signs that exposed the false accusation—they chose to jail him anyway, not out of justice but to suppress scandal and manage public perception. Their decision shows how worldly power can knowingly trade truth for convenience, imprisoning an innocent man “for a time” to protect reputations and avoid confronting the wrongdoing among them.

translation: And there entered with him into the prison two young men. One of them said, “I saw myself pressing wine.” And the other said, “I saw myself carrying bread on my head, from which the birds were eating. Tell us its interpretation; indeed, we see you among the doers of good.”
interpretation: These dreams are symbolic signs whose meanings will unfold through Joseph’s interpretation. Pressing wine points to restoration and return to service, while carrying bread on the head that birds eat points to execution and exposure. The prisoners seek Joseph’s help because his righteousness is evident even in confinement, showing that God’s chosen servants may be recognized by their character and that hardship does not remove a believer’s dignity, wisdom, or ability to serve as an instrument of God’s guidance. The verse also teaches that outcomes of ease or ruin belong to God’s decree, and that true goodness is a trust that draws others to seek truth.

translation: He said, "No food will come to you as your provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is from what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah, and they are disbelievers in the Hereafter."
interpretation: This statement of Joseph reveals that his knowledge of dream interpretation is not magic, guesswork, or human learning, but a prophetic understanding taught directly by God. He presents it as certain evidence of divine favor, telling the prisoners that he can explain the meaning of their dreams even before their provisions arrive. His humility is central: he does not attribute this knowledge to himself, but to his Lord. At the same time, he distances himself from the false religion of those who reject God and deny the Hereafter, showing that true guidance and inspired knowledge are connected to pure monotheistic faith and turning away from disbelief. The verse also shows Joseph using his God-given gift as an opportunity to call others toward belief in Allah alone and accountability in the afterlife.

translation: And I have followed the religion of my forefathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It was not for us to associate anything with Allah. That is from the favor of Allah upon us and upon the people, but most people do not give thanks.
interpretation: This verse declares that Prophet Joseph’s faith is the same pure monotheism taught by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: worshiping Allah alone and rejecting any partner associated with Him. Such pure belief is not achieved by human power or inherited privilege; it is a favor and mercy from Allah granted to the prophets and offered to all people through divine guidance. Yet most people fail to recognize this blessing and respond with gratitude, obedience, and acknowledgment of Allah’s oneness, remaining instead in ingratitude and shirk.

translation: O my two companions of the prison! Are many different lords better, or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?
interpretation: This verse is a rational and spiritual invitation to reject the worship of numerous false gods and to recognize the exclusive oneness and supreme power of Allah. Joseph addresses his fellow prisoners by asking whether a multiplicity of separate, competing, and dependent lords is preferable to the single, unique God who alone possesses absolute authority and subdues all things. The implied answer is that only Allah, the One, deserves worship, because false gods are fragmented, impotent, and incapable of creation, benefit, or harm, whereas Allah is indivisibly one and all-powerful over every affair.

translation: You worship not besides Him except [mere] names you have named—you and your forefathers—for which Allah has sent down no authority. Judgment is only for Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.
interpretation: This verse establishes pure monotheism by exposing every object of worship besides Allah as nothing more than an invented name or label, lacking any divine authorization. It affirms that ultimate authority, legislation, and judgment belong exclusively to God, and that His fundamental command is to worship Him alone. This exclusive worship is the straight and established religion, yet most people remain ignorant of this truth and instead assign divine authority to false deities or man-made claims.

translation: O my two companions of the prison, as for one of you, he will give his master wine to drink; and as for the other, he will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head. The matter has been decided about which you inquire.
interpretation: This verse conveys Joseph’s authoritative interpretation of the two prisoners’ dreams: the first will be restored to his service and again give wine to his master, while the second will be executed and crucified in disgrace, his body left exposed until birds consume from his head. But the deeper meaning is that these outcomes are not mere forecasts; they are already decreed by God. Their inquiry cannot alter what God has settled. Thus the verse teaches that God’s command is decisive and infallible, that He alone controls elevation and humiliation, life and death, and that His prophets speak with certainty because what they convey is from divine knowledge, not human speculation.

translation: And he said to the one of the two whom he thought would be saved, “Mention me before your master.” But Satan made him forget to mention him to his master, so he remained in prison for a few years.
interpretation: This verse conveys that Yusuf (Joseph) sought a lawful means of release by asking the cupbearer to intercede, but the cupbearer forgot due to Satan’s influence. The delay of several years was not merely a result of human forgetfulness; it was within Allah’s wise decree. It teaches that while one may take permissible means, the heart should not rely on them instead of Allah, for placing undue reliance on people can lead to delay or disappointment. Allah allowed the forgetfulness so that Yusuf’s vindication would come through the king’s dream, making his release clear, his innocence established, and his elevation to authority manifest. Thus the verse underscores Allah’s sovereignty, the reality of Satan’s whisperings, and the need for patience and trust in Allah’s timing.

translation: And the king said, 'Indeed, I see seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and other dry ones. O chiefs, advise me concerning my vision, if you are able to interpret visions.'
interpretation: This dream is a divine sign of a coming cycle of seven years of abundant harvests followed by seven years of severe famine. The seven fat cows and seven green ears symbolize the years of plenty, while the seven lean cows and seven dry ears symbolize the years of scarcity that will consume the stored surplus of the fruitful years. The king’s address to his nobles shows that such matters require true insight and interpretation, which they lack, setting the stage for Joseph’s God-given ability to explain it and advise accordingly.

translation: They said, "These are confused dreams, and we are not knowledgeable in the interpretation of dreams."
interpretation: The verse conveys the courtiers' dismissal of the dream as a meaningless jumble and their admission that dream interpretation is beyond their expertise. It highlights the limits of human knowledge and sets up the contrast with prophetic insight granted by God.

translation: And the one who was saved of the two remembered after a period and said, 'I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me.'
interpretation: This verse indicates that Allah may delay relief until an appointed time and then bring it about through a person who had been forgotten or overlooked, so no believer should despair at delay. The speaker does not claim interpretation for himself but offers to convey it from the one who possesses knowledge of it, showing that lawful means and intermediaries may be used while true knowledge and outcomes belong ultimately to Allah. It also teaches the value of remembering the righteous and connecting others to them when a need arises.

translation: Joseph, O truthful one, explain to us [the meaning of] seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and [seven] others dry, so that I may return to the people, that they may know.
interpretation: This verse marks the point at which the knowledge granted to Yusuf becomes a means of public guidance and deliverance. The dream’s symbols point to an economic and social cycle: years of fertility and abundance followed by years of severe scarcity that devour the surplus of the good years, while the green and dry ears reinforce the same lesson of plenty overtaken by drought. The address “O truthful one” acknowledges that Yusuf’s earlier interpretation proved true, and the request is made so the messenger can carry the answer back to Pharaoh and the people, enabling them to understand what is coming and prepare wisely. Thus the verse shows that God’s gift of interpretation is not for private prestige but for preserving life and directing a nation through coming hardship.

translation: He said, 'You will sow for seven consecutive years; and whatever you harvest, leave it in its ears except a little of which you eat.'
interpretation: This is Joseph’s interpretation of the dream: Egypt will enjoy seven years of good harvests, then face seven years of severe famine. He advises them to plant continuously during the fertile years, store the surplus grain without threshing it, and keep it in its ears, because that preserves it better from spoilage and pests. Only a small amount should be taken for immediate eating. The verse teaches wise planning, careful management of resources, and taking practical means while trusting God’s decree for the coming hardship.

translation: Then after that will come seven severe years which will consume what you have stored for them, except a little of what you keep guarded.
interpretation: This verse conveys that the coming famine years will exhaust nearly all the surplus food saved during the years of plenty, leaving only the small portion deliberately preserved as seed or essential reserve. Its lesson is that survival through hardship depends on prudent planning, rationing, and protecting the means to begin again after the trial has passed.

translation: Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given relief and rain, and in which they will press [grapes and olives].
interpretation: This is part of Joseph’s interpretation of the king’s dream: after the seven years of severe famine, God will bring a year of relief when rain returns, the land becomes fertile again, and people will press fruits such as grapes and olives, restoring abundance after hardship.

translation: And the king said, 'Bring him to me.' So when the messenger came to him, he said, 'Return to your master and ask him: What about the women who cut their hands? Indeed, my Lord is fully aware of their scheming.'
interpretation: This verse highlights Prophet Yusuf’s moral integrity, patience, and trust in God. Although release from prison was offered, he did not accept it until his innocence was publicly established and the truth about the women’s plot was made clear. By asking the king to investigate the matter, he sought vindication rather than revenge, protecting his reputation and the honor of the office he might soon hold. His words “my Lord is fully aware of their scheming” express complete reliance on God’s knowledge and justice, affirming that no hidden motive or false accusation is beyond God’s awareness. It teaches that one may rightly seek clearing of false charges before assuming responsibility, and that ultimate judgment belongs to God, who knows all hidden plots.

translation: He said, 'What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph?' They said, 'Exalted is Allah! We know no evil of him.' The wife of the Aziz said, 'Now the truth has become clear. I sought to seduce him, and indeed he is among the truthful.'
interpretation: This verse marks the moment when hidden truth is divinely uncovered: the women's denial of any wrongdoing by Yusuf and the Aziz's wife's confession together establish Yusuf's innocence and chastity. Its deeper meaning is that no conspiracy, however prolonged or socially powerful, can ultimately conceal the truth from Allah; He vindicates the wronged and brings the guilty to admit what they denied. The wife's words, 'Now the truth has become clear,' show that genuine acknowledgment of sin is the beginning of moral repair, while her admission that Yusuf is 'among the truthful' confirms that his steadfastness was real and not a mere appearance. Thus the verse teaches trust in God's justice, the honor of chastity and truthfulness, and the inevitability of divine exposure for those who scheme in secret.

translation: That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in secret, and that Allah does not guide the plot of the betrayers.
interpretation: The speaker, the wife of al-Aziz, clarifies that her confession is meant to establish that she did not commit adultery with Yusuf behind her husband’s back. She also affirms that God does not grant success to the schemes of those who betray; treachery ultimately fails and cannot achieve its intended end.

translation: And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the self is a persistent commander of evil, except that upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This is a confession of human weakness and dependence on God: no person can honestly claim complete moral purity or self-sufficiency, because the lower self tends to incline toward evil, justify it, and command it. Only God's mercy can restrain, purify, and protect a person from that inclination. Therefore one should not boast of innocence or rely on one's own strength, but should humbly seek God's forgiveness and mercy, since He is forgiving and merciful to those who turn to Him.

translation: And the king said, “Bring him to me; I will appoint him exclusively for myself.” And when he spoke to him, he said, “Indeed, you are today, in our presence, firmly established and trustworthy.”
interpretation: This verse marks the moment the Egyptian king, convinced by Joseph’s interpretation of the dream, seeks to draw him close as a trusted confidant. After speaking with him directly, the king recognizes two qualities essential for leadership: Joseph is firmly established, capable, and worthy of authority, and he is trustworthy and faithful. The verse thus teaches that honor and responsibility should be given to those who combine competence with integrity, and that Allah can raise a person from imprisonment to a position of trust and influence when their character is sound.

translation: He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land. Indeed, I am a trustworthy guardian, knowledgeable."
interpretation: Yusuf’s request is not a bid for power or personal enrichment, but an offer of service based on two essential qualifications: integrity in guarding what is entrusted and expertise in managing resources wisely. He presents himself as capable of preserving Egypt’s stores and planning against coming famine, combining moral trustworthiness with practical knowledge. The verse thus teaches that it is legitimate for a qualified person to seek responsibility when the public good requires it, and that sound leadership must join faithfulness in trust with competence in administration.

translation: And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not waste the reward of the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse marks Joseph’s elevation from imprisonment and obscurity to authority and security in Egypt. God’s establishment of him in the land was not merely political empowerment; it was the fulfillment of a divine promise after long trials. His ability to settle where he wished signifies sovereignty, freedom, and honor after slavery and prison. The verse teaches that God grants His mercy by His wise will, not by human entitlement, yet He never overlooks the reward of those who act righteously. The righteous may endure hardship, but their good deeds are never lost; God compensates them in this world through vindication and honor, and in the Hereafter with greater reward. It calls believers to patience, trust in God’s timing, and perseverance in goodness, knowing that true success comes from God alone.

translation: And indeed the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and used to fear Allah.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the reward Allah has prepared in the Hereafter is far better and more enduring than any worldly gain, and it is reserved for those who combine true faith with taqwa—ongoing God-consciousness that produces obedience, sincerity, and avoidance of sin. It directs the believer’s hope beyond temporary worldly returns toward the eternal recompense granted to the people of faith and piety.

translation: And Joseph's brothers came and entered upon him, so he recognized them, while they did not recognize him.
interpretation: Although years had passed and Joseph’s status had changed from an enslaved youth to a high official in Egypt, God allowed him to know them immediately, while they remained unaware of his identity. This reveals that God’s decree can bring people face to face with their past without their realizing it, and it gave Joseph the opportunity to act with restraint, wisdom, and eventual mercy rather than immediate revenge.

translation: And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he said, 'Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure, and that I am the best of hosts?'
interpretation: In this verse, Yusuf is gently setting in motion the next stage of Allah’s plan to reunite his family. He does not use his power to punish his brothers for their past wrong against him; instead, he shows generosity and fairness, then asks them to bring their younger brother, Benjamin. The request tests whether they will now act justly toward their father and sibling, and his reminder that he gives full measure and is the best of hosts assures them that returning with Benjamin will bring them honorable treatment and provision. Thus the verse highlights Yusuf’s wisdom, restraint, and benevolence, and shows that divine providence advances through mercy and moral testing rather than revenge.

translation: But if you do not bring him to me, then you will have no measure from me, nor shall you come near me.
interpretation: This is a conditional warning from Joseph: he makes the continued grant of grain and access to his presence dependent on their bringing Benjamin. It signifies that the favor and provision he extends are not unconditional; rejecting his stated requirement forfeits both material benefit and relational closeness. It also serves as a test of their truthfulness and of whether they will honor the trust placed in them.

translation: They said, “We will try to persuade his father away from him, and indeed we will do it.”
interpretation: This statement conveys the speakers’ firm resolve and confident commitment to carry out a difficult request. The emphatic wording shows that they intended to use persuasion and persistence, presenting themselves as capable of achieving what was asked. Yet the verse also subtly points to the limits of human planning: their certainty about what they would do does not place the outcome beyond Allah’s will, for decrees unfold according to His wisdom, not merely according to human promises.

translation: And he said to his servants, “Place their goods in their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they return to their family, so that they may return.”
interpretation: Joseph secretly returned the payment for the grain to his brothers’ luggage. His purpose was that when they reached home and opened their bags, they would see that their goods or money had been given back, recognize his generosity and fairness, and therefore be moved to come back to him again, rather than staying away because they had taken provisions without payment or because they feared hardship. Thus the restoration was a wise invitation for them to return.

translation: So when they returned to their father, they said: O our father, the measure has been denied to us, so send with us our brother that we may measure, and indeed we will surely guard him.
interpretation: This verse reports the brothers returning to Jacob and telling him that they will not be given further grain unless they bring their younger brother Benjamin. They ask Jacob to send Benjamin with them so they can obtain the needed provisions, and they pledge to protect him. Their words reflect both their need for food and their attempt to reassure their father after the earlier loss of Joseph, though the pledge is framed as a firm promise of guardianship.

translation: He said, 'Should I entrust him to you except as I entrusted his brother to you before? But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.'
interpretation: This verse expresses that ultimate safety and protection belong to Allah alone. Yaqub does not let past betrayal make him despair of God's mercy; rather, he combines prudent caution with complete reliance on Allah, acknowledging that no human promise can guarantee what only God can guard. It teaches that when loved ones are beyond our control, we should place them in God's care, trusting His guardianship and mercy above all human arrangements.

translation: And when they opened their baggage, they found their merchandise returned to them. They said, “O our father, what more could we desire? This is our merchandise returned to us. And we will provision our family, and we will protect our brother, and we will add a camel’s load. That is an easy measure.”
interpretation: This verse shows that Allah’s provision can come through hidden and unexpected means: what the brothers thought they had paid away was restored to them, turning apparent loss into a sign of divine care. Yet their words also expose a subtle test: they treated the returned goods and their own resolve to “protect” Benjamin as sufficient security, while true protection and provision belong to Allah alone. The verse thus invites trust in Allah’s unseen arrangement rather than confidence in material calculations or human strength.

translation: He said: I will not send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge by Allah that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are overwhelmed. Then when they gave him their solemn pledge, he said: Allah is Guardian over what we say.
interpretation: This verse teaches that in matters of trust, especially regarding those under one’s care, it is prudent and permissible to seek the strongest covenant and to invoke Allah as witness, because human promises are fragile. Ya‘qub’s demand is not a lack of trust in Allah but a wise precaution after prior grief; his final words place the outcome in Allah’s hands: Allah is Wakil—He witnesses the agreement and is the disposer of affairs, so the brothers are responsible before Him, and the father entrusts the result to Him. The exception acknowledges that no human pledge can override Allah’s decree or human inability when circumstances become overwhelming.

translation: And he said, 'O my sons, do not enter from one gate, but enter from separate gates. And I cannot avail you against Allah at all. Judgment is only for Allah. Upon Him I rely, and upon Him let all those who rely put their trust.'
interpretation: Jacob’s advice to his sons was a lawful precaution: entering Egypt separately would shield them from undue attention, envy, or collective harm, but he made clear that such measures cannot override Allah’s decree. The verse teaches that using means is not contrary to trust in Allah; rather, the believer acts prudently while acknowledging that all judgment and authority belong to Allah alone. True reliance is therefore placed solely in Him, for no created thing can benefit or harm except by His will.

translation: And when they entered from where their father had commanded them, it did not avail them against Allah in anything, except a need within Jacob's soul which he fulfilled. And indeed, he was possessed of knowledge because of what We had taught him, but most people do not know.
interpretation: This verse clarifies that Jacob’s instruction to his sons was a precautionary measure born of paternal concern, not a means of altering God’s decree. Whatever God had ordained would occur regardless; the only effect was the satisfaction of Jacob’s inner need—his protective anxiety or fatherly solicitude—which he fulfilled by giving the instruction. His knowledge was not mere human guesswork but was granted by God, who taught him. Yet most people fail to recognize that true knowledge comes from God and that prudential means do not override His will.

translation: And when they entered upon Joseph, he took his brother to himself and said, “Indeed, I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do.”
interpretation: The verse conveys that when God grants relief after long trial, the believer should not remain captive to sorrow over past wrongs. Joseph’s private reassurance to his brother teaches that divine providence can turn suffering and separation into a means of reunion, elevation, and vindication. True brotherhood in faith consoles and protects; it does not leave one crushed by the injustice of others when God has already begun to reverse it.

translation: So when he had furnished them with their provisions, he placed the drinking cup in his brother's saddlebag; then a caller cried out, 'O caravan, you are surely thieves!'
interpretation: This was Joseph’s deliberate arrangement to keep Benjamin with him. Since he could not seize his brother under the king’s law without a charge, he hid the royal cup in Benjamin’s baggage and caused the caravan to be accused, so that the search would expose the cup and provide the legal grounds for detaining Benjamin. In the wider meaning of the passage, it shows how God’s plan unfolds through Joseph’s wise, concealed measures, and it tests the brothers’ response after their earlier wrongdoing against Joseph.

translation: They said, turning toward them, “What is it that you are missing?”
interpretation: Their question expresses genuine surprise and a clear conscience: by asking what item was lost, they show they have no knowledge of the alleged theft and are ready to clarify the matter. Turning toward the accusers signals earnest engagement rather than guilt or evasion.

translation: They said, 'We are missing the king's cup, and whoever brings it will have a camel's load, and I am its guarantor.'
interpretation: This is the announcement made by the Egyptian officials after Joseph secretly placed the royal measuring cup in Benjamin's baggage. The reward of a camel-load was meant to motivate the caravan to surrender what was sought. The speaker's pledge that he was personally responsible for the reward shows it was a firm and reliable promise. In the wider Qur'anic narrative, this event is part of Joseph's God-guided arrangement to keep Benjamin with him under Egyptian law, since he could not lawfully detain his brother otherwise. It thus illustrates how divine providence operates through ordinary human customs and legal measures, while also testing Joseph's brothers at a moment when their earlier jealousy and remorse had begun to be transformed.

translation: They said, 'By Allah, you have certainly known that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we are not thieves.'
interpretation: The brothers swear a solemn oath by Allah, appealing to the Egyptians' own knowledge of their past conduct: they had come only to obtain provisions and had never intended to spread mischief or commit theft in the land. Their statement is a strong protest of innocence against the accusation of stealing the king's measuring cup, asserting that their character and prior dealings with Egypt should testify to their honesty. It also reflects their confidence that the Egyptians could verify they were not corruptors or thieves, even though the cup was later found in Benjamin's bag as part of a divinely arranged test.

translation: They said, 'Then what is its recompense, if you are liars?'
interpretation: This verse captures a moment of self-judgment by procedure: rather than imposing a penalty immediately, the questioners ask the accused to state what the law demands if their denial proves false. The conditional phrase 'if you are liars' does not presume guilt; it sets the terms by which the coming search will be judged. Spiritually, it teaches that divine wisdom often works through the very words and standards of the people involved, so that when the truth is exposed, no one can plead ignorance or unfairness. It also warns that false oaths are not hidden from Allah: the same criterion a person pronounces can become the means by which he is measured.

translation: They said, "Its recompense is that he in whose saddlebag it is found—he himself shall be its recompense. Thus do we punish the wrongdoers."
interpretation: The verse means that, according to the law the brothers followed, the thief found with the stolen item must forfeit his own person as restitution: he is taken as a servant/slave by the owner instead of merely paying a fine or receiving another punishment. Their statement “Thus do we punish the wrongdoers” expresses their own legal norm: theft is an injustice, and its penalty in their tradition is the enslavement of the thief. This is a report of their custom, not a universal divine ruling for all peoples.

translation: So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother, then he extracted it from his brother's bag. Thus did We devise a plan for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother by the king's law except that Allah willed. We raise in ranks whom We will. And above every possessor of knowledge is One more knowing.
interpretation: This verse reveals that the apparent discovery of the cup was Allah's subtle arrangement to fulfill Joseph's purpose of keeping his brother Benjamin with him, beyond what Egypt's legal system would normally allow. Allah alone controls the means and outcomes; human law, strategy, and power cannot achieve His decree unless He wills it. The raising of ranks teaches that knowledge, wisdom, and honor are gifts Allah bestows on whom He chooses, and the final phrase declares that every human possessor of knowledge is surpassed by another, ultimately by Allah, whose knowledge encompasses all. Thus the verse calls for trust in Allah's plan, humility in knowledge, and recognition that His wisdom prevails over all human arrangements.

translation: They said, “If he steals, then a brother of his stole before.” So Joseph kept it within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said, “You are in a worse position, and Allah knows best what you describe.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the brothers’ readiness to slander Joseph and Benjamin rather than submit to God’s decree: when Benjamin is accused, they revive an old accusation against Joseph to justify their contempt. Joseph’s response is inward restraint, not public retaliation; he does not expose their lie or defend himself before them. His words “you are in a worse position” mean their moral standing is worse because of envy, false accusation, and willingness to wrong others, while “Allah knows best what you describe” means the truth of their claims is fully known to God, who will judge with perfect justice. The verse teaches that when falsely accused, one may restrain anger, avoid quarreling, and entrust the matter to God’s all-encompassing knowledge and justice.

translation: They said, "O Aziz, indeed he has a father, an old man, great in years. So take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you among the doers of good."
interpretation: The verse shows that appealing to a person’s known moral character—"we see you among the doers of good"—is a valid and dignified way to seek mercy, and that true moral excellence (ihsan) is tested precisely when one has the power to enforce a claim but is asked to show compassion. The brothers’ offer to substitute themselves reflects a deep sense of responsibility and self-sacrifice for the sake of their father’s fragile state, indicating that preserving a parent from devastating grief can be a weighty obligation. At the same time, the verse does not condemn the official for maintaining the law; it presents a moment of moral tension where human mercy and divine decree intersect. The believer learns to combine justice with kindness, to recognize the humanity in others’ pleas, and to trust that even when compassionate requests are not granted as hoped, Allah’s wisdom may be working a greater good.

translation: He said, “May Allah forbid that we take except him with whom we found our property. Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers.”
interpretation: The speaker refuses to detain or punish anyone other than the person in whose possession the missing property was found. He invokes God’s protection against such an act because substituting one person for another would violate justice: the one actually found with the item is the one liable, and taking an innocent substitute would make them unjust oppressors. The verse therefore upholds strict justice over family loyalty or emotional appeals, insisting that guilt and punishment must fall only on the one justly shown to be responsible.

translation: So when they despaired of him, they withdrew to consult in private. The eldest of them said, 'Did you not know that your father took from you a solemn covenant by Allah, and before that you failed concerning Joseph? Therefore I will not leave this land until my father gives me permission or Allah judges for me; and He is the best of judges.'
interpretation: This verse marks a moment of moral reckoning among Yusuf’s brothers after they lose hope of securing Benjamin’s release. Their private counsel is not mere strategizing; it exposes the weight of the binding oath they had made to their father Ya‘qub in God’s name. The eldest brother’s refusal to leave Egypt expresses that a believer’s covenant and word are sacred, especially when God is invoked as witness. He acknowledges their earlier wrongdoing against Yusuf and refuses to repeat that betrayal by returning without Benjamin. His waiting for his father’s permission or God’s decree reflects tawakkul—trust in God’s judgment even when all human avenues seem closed—and adab toward parental authority. The declaration that God is “the best of judges” affirms that apparent dead ends remain under divine wisdom and governance; true resolution comes through patience, loyalty, and submission to God’s decree, not through force or deception.

translation: Return to your father and say, 'O our father, indeed your son has stolen, and we did not testify except to what we knew, and we were not guardians of the unseen.'
interpretation: This verse records the brothers’ instructed words to Jacob after Benjamin was detained in Egypt. They confess only to what appeared to them—that the king’s cup was found in Benjamin’s possession—and disclaim any knowledge of the hidden truth, such as whether he was innocent, framed, or what God had decreed. It teaches that human testimony is limited to observed facts and that no one can guard or fathom the unseen except God; therefore, they cannot absolve themselves of responsibility before their father nor claim certainty about matters beyond their perception.

translation: And ask the town where we were and the caravan in which we came, and indeed we are truthful.
interpretation: This verse conveys the brothers' plea to their father Yaqub to verify their report by asking the people of Egypt and the caravan they traveled with, insisting that their account of Benjamin's detention is true and that they bear no blame. It underscores the principle of seeking corroboration for news and shows their attempt to clear themselves, while the full reality of the event was known to Allah and formed part of His plan for Yusuf.

translation: He said, “Rather, your own selves have made this matter seem fair to you. So patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.”
interpretation: Ya‘qub does not accept his sons’ account at face value. He discerns that their inner selves made their action appear justified and easy to them, so he refuses to build his response on their narrative alone. His “beautiful patience” is not despair or bitterness; it is patient endurance that does not complain against Allah and keeps trust in Him. His words “Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me” express hopeful reliance on Allah’s hidden plan—that He may reunite him with Yusuf, Benjamin, and the son who remained behind. By ending with “He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise,” the verse grounds this patience in certainty that Allah knows the full truth and that His wisdom governs every delay and every reunion.

translation: And he turned away from them and said, "Alas, my grief over Joseph!" And his eyes turned white from grief, and he was suppressing [his sorrow].
interpretation: This verse expresses the profound, patient sorrow of Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob). He withdraws from his sons to pour out his grief over Yusuf, not in despair or protest against Allah, but as a heartfelt lament before his Lord. His eyes lose their sight from continuous weeping, yet he remains kazeem—one who swallows his anguish, restraining complaint and preserving trust in Allah's decree. It teaches that intense human grief and true patience can coexist: the believer may feel overwhelming pain while still refusing to object to God's wisdom or abandon hope in His mercy.

translation: They said, 'By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become gravely ill or you are among those who perish.'
interpretation: This verse expresses the exasperation of Jacob's sons/people at his unrelenting grief over Joseph. Their oath means that his constant remembrance would either waste him away into illness or bring him to death. It reveals the intensity of Jacob's paternal love and sorrow, and contrasts their limited, impatient view with his steadfast hope in Allah's mercy and his refusal to abandon trust in God even amid overwhelming grief.

translation: He said: I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know.
interpretation: This verse teaches that a believer may bring the deepest pain and sorrow to God alone, seeking relief and mercy from Him rather than complaining to people or despairing of His decree. Jacob’s complaint is not a protest against God but an intimate supplication and an expression of trust. His words that he knows from God what they do not know indicate his certainty in God’s promise, revelation, and hidden wisdom—that Joseph is alive and that God will bring about relief and reunion—so he combines human grief with prophetic hope.

translation: O my sons, go and search for Joseph and his brother, and do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse teaches that even after long hardship and apparent hopelessness, believers must continue to seek Allah’s mercy and relief and must never give up hope in Him. Despairing of Allah’s mercy is condemned as a characteristic of disbelief, because it implies doubt in His power and compassion, whereas faith requires trusting that He can bring about deliverance from any situation.

translation: So when they entered upon him, they said, 'O Aziz, hardship has afflicted us and our family, and we have brought poor merchandise. So give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable.'
interpretation: This verse conveys that true need should be acknowledged before God and before those He has placed in authority, without pride, and that asking for help with humility is a recognized part of faith. The brothers confess their weakness and the worthlessness of what they bring, then appeal not merely to the ruler's generosity but to God's reward for charity. The deeper lesson is that charity is not a loss; it is a transaction with Allah, who never lets the sincere giver's kindness go unrewarded. It also teaches that those in power should respond to the needy with full justice and extra mercy, and that the best appeal for help is one joined to the recognition that Allah is the ultimate Recompenser.

translation: He said, "Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother, when you were ignorant?"
interpretation: Joseph, now in a position of power, is addressing his brothers not to take revenge but to bring them to awareness. He asks whether they now realize the wrong they committed against Joseph and his full brother Benjamin—the envy and cruelty that led them to cast Joseph into the well and later to separate Benjamin from their father—actions they carried out in a state of ignorance: ignorance of God's decree, of the true nature of their oppression, and of the eventual outcome. The question is a gentle but piercing rebuke that prepares them to recognize their sin and seek forgiveness.

translation: They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said, "I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has surely bestowed favor upon us. Indeed, whoever is conscious of Allah and is patient — then indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good."
interpretation: This verse teaches that divine honor and relief come after trials to those who combine taqwa, a reverent awareness of God, with sabr, patient perseverance. Joseph does not claim personal greatness; he attributes the reunion and elevation to God’s grace and identifies his brother as part of that favor. The enduring principle is that God’s promise is reliable: He preserves and multiplies the reward of those who do good, especially those who remain faithful and patient when tested.

translation: They said, 'By Allah, Allah has indeed preferred you over us, and we were indeed sinners.'
interpretation: This verse expresses the brothers' acknowledgment of Joseph's divinely granted superiority and their own moral failure. Their oath by Allah signals a deep, unreserved confession: they recognize that God had chosen Joseph, endowed him with favor, wisdom, and honor, while they had acted wrongly against him. Their words 'we were indeed sinners' admit not merely a mistake but a culpable offense, showing remorse and the reversal of their earlier arrogance. The verse thus marks a moment of repentance and recognition that God's favor rests on whom He wills, and that human envy and wrongdoing cannot overturn His decree.

translation: He said, "No blame will be upon you today. May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."
interpretation: These are the words of Joseph to his brothers after they had wronged him and later recognized him. He declares that he will not reproach, shame, or punish them for what they did: “No blame will be upon you today.” Having the power to retaliate, he instead pardons them and even prays for God’s forgiveness for them, showing that true forgiveness rises above revenge and seeks the wrongdoer’s good. By saying “May Allah forgive you,” he directs them and himself to the ultimate source of mercy, and by ending with “He is the Most Merciful of the merciful,” he acknowledges that divine mercy is boundless and surpasses all human mercy. The verse thus teaches magnanimity, reconciliation, and trusting in God’s all-encompassing compassion.

translation: Take this shirt of mine and cast it upon my father’s face; he will regain sight, and bring me all your family.
interpretation: This verse marks the turning point from separation to reunion: the shirt is a divinely appointed means through which Jacob’s lost sight is restored, showing that God can bring relief and healing through something ordinary when He wills. The command to bring the whole family to Joseph signifies the completion of God’s promise to reunite them, vindicate Joseph, and fulfill the dream he had seen in his youth.

translation: And when the caravan had set out, their father said, 'I do indeed sense the scent of Joseph, were it not that you would call me senile.'
interpretation: This verse portrays Prophet Ya'qub's God-given intuition and unshakable hope: though separated from Yusuf for years and far from Egypt, he detects a sign of Yusuf's nearness that ordinary senses and reason could not account for. His declaration also confronts the cynicism of those around him; he knows they may accuse him of senility, yet he refuses to surrender his trust in Allah's promise. The lesson is that divine mercy can arrive through means beyond human calculation, and that the faithful should not let the mockery or limited perception of others extinguish their hope and spiritual insight.

translation: They said, “By Allah, indeed you are in your old error.”
interpretation: They swore by Allah that Ya‘qub was still caught in what they considered his old delusion—his persistent hope that Yusuf was alive and his claim to sense his scent—because they could not understand his deep trust in Allah and his grief-driven certainty. In truth, their accusation was mistaken: what they called misguidance was a steadfast hope later vindicated by Allah.

translation: Then when the bearer of glad tidings came, he cast it over his face, and he regained his sight. He said, 'Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?'
interpretation: This verse marks the moment God restored Jacob’s sight through Joseph’s shirt, showing that relief and restoration come from God alone after long sorrow. Jacob’s words remind his sons that his earlier confidence was not mere optimism: he knew, through faith in God’s promise and wisdom, that Joseph was alive and that God would bring about what they could not foresee. The verse teaches that divine knowledge and decree often unfold beyond human expectations, and that patient trust in God is vindicated even when circumstances seem hopeless.

translation: They said, “O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins. Indeed, we have been sinners.”
interpretation: This verse expresses the brothers’ remorse and their plea to their father Jacob to intercede for them by praying to God for forgiveness. Their admission that they were “sinners” is a confession of guilt and a turning back to God, showing that true repentance includes acknowledging one’s wrong, seeking forgiveness, and relying on the supplication of a righteous servant while recognizing that forgiveness ultimately comes from God.

translation: He said, "I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful."
interpretation: This is Ya'qub’s response to his sons’ request that he seek forgiveness for them. He promises to turn to God in supplication on their behalf, showing that he does not rely on himself or on any created power to forgive, but directs the matter to his Lord alone. By saying “my Lord,” he expresses humble servitude, dependence, and nearness to God. The words “Indeed, He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful” ground his hope in God’s own attributes: His forgiveness is abundant and repeated, and His mercy is vast and enduring. Thus the verse teaches that a believer may seek forgiveness for others through prayer, that no one should despair of God’s mercy, and that ultimate forgiveness and mercy belong exclusively to God.

translation: And when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his parents to himself and said, "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, safe and secure."
interpretation: This verse depicts the joyful reunion of Joseph with his family in Egypt. Joseph honors his parents by embracing them and bringing them close to himself, showing filial devotion and the softening of hearts after years of separation and hardship. His statement, "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, safe and secure," is both a gracious invitation and a reassurance: he invites them to settle in Egypt under his care, but he attributes their safety to Allah’s will, acknowledging that security and peace come only by divine decree. It also signals the fulfillment of Joseph’s earlier dream and the transformation of his family’s suffering into a state of dignity, protection, and reunion. Thus the verse teaches gratitude, reliance on Allah, honoring parents, and the merciful outcome of patience and trust in God.

translation: And he raised his parents onto the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration. And he said, 'O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before. My Lord has made it true. And He was certainly good to me when He brought me out of prison and brought you from the desert after Satan had sown enmity between me and my brothers. Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what He wills. Indeed, it is He who is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.'
interpretation: This verse records the fulfillment of Joseph's childhood dream: his parents and brothers prostrating before him. Their prostration was a gesture of honor, respect, and joy, not divine worship, for worship belongs to God alone; it was a customary salutation in that earlier law, later forbidden in the final law. Joseph acknowledges that God alone made the dream come true, and he speaks with humility and gratitude, recalling God's favor in freeing him from prison and reuniting his family after Satan had caused division between him and his brothers. He attributes everything to God's subtle wisdom, knowledge, and wise decree, showing that God's promises may unfold over long trials and that His kindness works quietly through them.

translation: My Lord, You have given me some sovereignty and taught me some interpretation of dreams. Originator of the heavens and the earth, You are my protector in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous.
interpretation: This supplication teaches that every station of honor, authority, and knowledge is a gift from God, not a claim of personal merit. True protection and allegiance belong to God alone, the Creator and Sustainer of all existence. The highest request is not worldly success but a good end: to die in submission to God and to be gathered with the righteous, meaning that one's ultimate concern should be fidelity to God until death and companionship with those whom He has favored.

translation: That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you, and you were not with them when they agreed upon their plan and were plotting.
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine origin of the Qur’anic narrative: the detailed account of Yusuf’s story could not have been known by the Prophet Muhammad through ordinary means, since he was not present with Yusuf’s brothers when they conspired against him. Its precise knowledge is therefore proof of revelation from God, who alone knows the unseen and informs whom He wills.

translation: And most of the people, even if you eagerly desire it, will not believe.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad, consoling him and clarifying the limits of his mission: although he intensely longed for all people to accept the truth, most of them would not believe. Faith is not something a prophet can force into hearts by his own anxiety or effort; it comes through God's guidance and a person's willing response. The verse therefore teaches that the Messenger's duty is to convey the message clearly, not to compel belief, and that the majority's rejection does not invalidate the truth he brought. It also warns believers that numbers and popular acceptance are not the measure of truth; divine guidance is the real criterion.

translation: And you do not ask them for any reward for it. It is only a reminder to all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Prophet conveys the Qur’an purely for God’s sake, seeking no payment or worldly gain from his audience. The message is not a personal enterprise but a universal reminder and admonition for all creation, calling them to remember God and heed divine guidance. Its worth lies in being God’s remembrance, not in any material return.

translation: And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth do they pass by while they are turning away from it.
interpretation: This verse reproaches those who live amid countless created signs—the heavens and earth with their luminaries, seasons, creatures, and ordered phenomena—that testify to Allah's existence, oneness, power, knowledge, and will, yet they move past them without reflection, gratitude, or obedience. Their problem is not a scarcity of evidence but aversion: they deliberately disregard the signs and refuse to let them lead to faith, so the verse establishes that unbelief is a moral and spiritual turning away rather than a consequence of insufficient proof.

translation: And most of them do not believe in Allah except while they are polytheists.
interpretation: This verse means that many people may acknowledge Allah as Creator, Provider, or Lord, yet their belief is not pure monotheism because they still associate others with Him in worship, obedience, love, or reliance. Such a faith is incomplete and contradictory: it affirms God in one respect while denying His exclusive right to be worshipped alone. The verse condemns any form of shirk mixed with belief and calls for sincere, unmixed tawhid.

translation: Do they then feel secure that an overwhelming punishment from Allah will not come upon them, or that the Hour will not come upon them suddenly while they are unaware?
interpretation: This verse is a warning and rebuke to those who remain heedless and persist in sin: their feeling of safety is an illusion. Allah may overtake them with a sweeping punishment in this world, or the Hour may come upon them suddenly before they repent, when they least expect it and while they are unaware. It calls them not to mistake Allah’s delay as acceptance, but to repent and prepare for the meeting with Him.

translation: Say, 'This is my way: I call to Allah upon clear insight—I and whoever follows me. And glory be to Allah, and I am not of those who associate others with Him.'
interpretation: This verse means that the Prophet’s path is to invite people to the worship and obedience of Allah alone, and that this invitation is based on clear knowledge, certainty, and inner sight, not on blind imitation or conjecture. Those who truly follow him share in this same insight and method. It also declares Allah free from every defect and far above any partner or rival, and it affirms that the Prophet is completely innocent of polytheism and has nothing to do with those who associate others with Allah.

translation: And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed, from among the people of the towns. Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them? And the home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah. Will you not then understand?
interpretation: This verse establishes that divine guidance has consistently come through human messengers chosen from settled communities, not through angels or beings removed from human experience. It therefore refutes the objection that Muhammad’s humanity disqualifies him from prophethood; his likeness to earlier messengers is evidence of the constancy of God’s way. The call to travel and observe is not merely sightseeing but a summons to historical and moral reflection: those who rejected messengers before them were eventually overtaken by the consequences of their denial, showing that God’s judgment operates according to a fixed pattern. The verse then corrects the disbelievers’ scale of values: worldly dominance and resistance to truth are temporary, while the Hereafter is genuinely better for those who guard themselves against sin and disbelief. The final rhetorical question rebukes them for failing to use reason, since sound reasoning would lead them to recognize the coherence of prophethood, the lesson of history, and the superiority of the path of taqwa.

translation: Until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they were denied, Our help came to them, and whoever We willed was saved. And Our punishment cannot be averted from the criminal people.
interpretation: This verse teaches that divine victory often comes after the severest trial, when the messengers have lost visible hope and feel utterly rejected. At Allah’s appointed time, He sends His help, saves whom He wills from among His faithful servants, and His punishment inevitably seizes those who persist in sin and denial; nothing can repel it.

translation: Indeed, in their stories there is a lesson for people of understanding. It is not a fabricated statement, but a confirmation of what came before it, and a detailed explanation of all things, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the narratives of the prophets and their communities are not recounted for mere entertainment or historical curiosity, but as profound moral and spiritual instruction for those who possess sound reason and discernment.
