It declares Allah far above and pure from any such attribution, for He is perfect, self-sufficient, and has no offspring or equal. Their claim is especially contradictory because they reserved for themselves what they desired—such as sons and other preferences—while assigning to Allah what they themselves disliked or deemed inferior. The verse exposes their unjust and arbitrary reasoning: they did not apply to Allah the honor and perfection due to Him, but spoke about Him according to their own false desires and social prejudices.

translation: And when one of them is given good tidings of a female, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief.
interpretation: This verse condemns the pre-Islamic Arab mindset that regarded the birth of a daughter as a disgrace and a cause for sorrow, exposing its injustice and inconsistency: they would attribute daughters to Allah while feeling ashamed and grieved if a daughter was born to themselves. It teaches that such aversion is a wrongful human prejudice, not a divine judgment, and that a female child is no less a blessing or a sign of Allah’s wisdom than a male child.

translation: He hides himself from the people because of the evil of that with which he has been given good tidings. Will he keep it in humiliation, or bury it in the dust? Unquestionably, evil is what they judge.
interpretation: This verse depicts the pre-Islamic Arab who receives news of a daughter and is so ashamed that he withdraws from people, then weighs whether to keep her alive despite social disgrace or bury her alive. It condemns that mindset: the “evil tidings” is only evil according to their corrupt valuation of females, and the choice to bury her is an appalling crime. The final phrase rebukes the very standard by which they judge—preferring sons, despising daughters, and treating such false judgments as acceptable—declaring it evil.

translation: For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is an evil description, and to Allah belongs the highest description. And He is the Almighty, the Wise.
interpretation: This means that those who reject the Hereafter ascribe to Allah defective, false, or created attributes, while Allah is absolutely exalted above every imperfection. The “highest description” belongs to Him alone: His names and attributes are perfect, limitless, and free from any resemblance to creation. He is al-Aziz, prevailing over all, none able to resist or overpower Him, and al-Hakim, perfectly wise in His creation, commands, decrees, and in the resurrection and judgment that the disbelievers deny.

translation: And if Allah were to take people to account for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single moving creature. But He delays them to an appointed term. Then when their term comes, they can neither delay it by an hour nor advance it.
interpretation: This verse shows that Allah’s forbearance is not negligence: if He were to punish every human injustice immediately and fully, no living creature would remain on earth, because His judgment would engulf creation. His delay is wisdom and mercy, granting time for repentance before a fixed decree. When that appointed term arrives, no one can postpone it or hasten it by even a moment, so people should not mistake divine patience for permission or escape; accountability is certain at the precise time Allah has set.

translation: And they assign to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues assert the falsehood that they will have the best [reward]. No doubt, for them is the Fire, and they will be abandoned.
interpretation: This verse condemns the inconsistency and deception of those who reject the truth: they themselves detest certain things, yet they falsely attribute them to Allah, and they let their tongues claim that they will receive the best outcome. Their claim is a lie, for their end is the Fire, and they will be left abandoned and neglected, without any helper or escape.

translation: By Allah, We indeed sent [messengers] to communities before you, but Satan made their deeds appear attractive to them; so he is their protector today, and they will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: This oath stresses that God’s sending of messengers to previous nations was an established reality, leaving those nations without excuse. Their ruin came not from a lack of divine guidance but from their choice to let Satan beautify their falsehoods and sins. When they preferred his deception, Satan became their intimate ally and authority in this life, while in the Hereafter their loyalty to him yields only severe, painful chastisement. The verse warns the Prophet’s addressees—and every reader—that the same pattern repeats: whoever lets Satan make evil seem good will find in him a guardian instead of God, and will bear the consequence of that allegiance on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And We have not sent down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them that over which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur’an as God’s decisive criterion sent through the Prophet: its primary function is to resolve the disagreements people fell into regarding divine revelation—who God is, what He requires, the truth about the prophets and the Hereafter—by setting forth the correct understanding with clarity and authority. Yet this clarification is not a neutral announcement; for those who assent to it, it becomes both guidance that directs the intellect and will toward truth and mercy that rescues them from confusion, error, and the consequences of sin. Thus the benefit of the Book is conditional upon faith: it adjudicates disputes for all who hear, but only believers receive it as guidance and mercy.

translation: And Allah sends down water from the sky and revives the earth after its death. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who hear.
interpretation: This verse directs attention to Allah’s exclusive power to give life after death: just as He sends down rain and brings forth life from the barren, dead earth, He is able to resurrect the dead. The revival of the earth is a clear proof of the resurrection and of His oneness, but only those who truly listen—accepting the message, reflecting on it, and letting it reach their hearts—will take heed from it.

translation: And indeed, for you in the cattle is a lesson: We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, from between excretion and blood, pure milk, palatable to those who drink.
interpretation: This verse is a call to recognize God's wise and subtle power in His creation and provision. The livestock are a sign because milk is produced inside the animal from substances that pass between digested matter and blood, yet it emerges pure, wholesome, and easy for people to drink. This shows that God arranges hidden natural processes with perfect precision, brings clean and beneficial sustenance out of what would otherwise be impure, and provides for His creatures in a way that should inspire gratitude, reflection, and acknowledgment of His lordship.

translation: And from the fruits of the date palm and the grapevine you take an intoxicant and a good provision. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason.
interpretation: This verse directs attention to God's bounty in creating the date palm and grapevine and in enabling humans to process their fruits into different products. The "intoxicant" (sakar) represents the misuse of that divine gift when it is turned into something that clouds reason and harms the soul, while the "good provision" (rizq hasan) represents the lawful and wholesome use of the same bounty for nourishment, gratitude, and well-being. The sign is that God provides the raw material and the human intellect to transform it, and true understanding lies in recognizing the Creator's favor, choosing the pure and beneficial over the harmful, and allowing reason to guide one toward thankfulness and obedience.

translation: And your Lord inspired the bee, [saying], 'Take for yourself among the mountains, houses, and among the trees, and in that which they construct.'
interpretation: The 'inspiration' here is God's innate guidance implanted in the bee's nature, not a verbal revelation. It means that the bee's skill in building its dwelling and its choice of habitats—mountains, trees, and human-made structures—are directed by divine wisdom. This shows that even the smallest creatures act under God's providence, and that human construction can serve as part of the natural order God has arranged for their sustenance and function.

translation: Then eat from all the fruits and follow the ways of your Lord, made easy. There comes forth from their bellies a drink of varying colors, wherein there is healing for people. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reflect.
interpretation: This verse points to the bee as a creature guided by God's subtle inspiration: it ranges over fruits and follows paths God has made subservient to it, and from its body issues honey, varying in color and quality, carrying healing for humanity. The sign is not merely honey's usefulness but the hidden order, wisdom, and mercy behind it: a small creature fulfills its role with precision, and its product benefits people in ways they could not devise. For those who reflect, this calls them to recognize the Creator's power and providence, to see His signs in nature, and to respond with gratitude, contemplation, and faith rather than passing over such everyday wonders.

translation: And Allah created you, then He causes you to die. And among you is he who is returned to the most decrepit age, so that he knows nothing after having known. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah alone originates human life and decrees its end, and that the stages of life—creation, death, and for some, decline into extreme old age and loss of mental faculties—are signs of His absolute authority and knowledge. The return to “the most abject age” is not a flaw in divine creation but a manifestation of human weakness and dependency, reminding people that knowledge, strength, and faculties are gifts from Allah that can be withdrawn. Since Allah is All-Knowing, He encompasses every condition and stage of His creation; since He is All-Powerful, He is able to create, cause death, diminish human capacities, and resurrect. The verse calls for humility, reliance upon Allah, and preparation for the hereafter rather than arrogant confidence in one’s own intellect or worldly lifespan.

translation: And Allah has favored some of you over others in provision. But those who have been favored would not give their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they would be equal in it. Then do they deny the favor of Allah?
interpretation: This verse uses a human social reality to expose the folly of shirk. If people who have been given greater wealth and status would never accept their servants or slaves as equal partners in their property, then how can they assign partners to Allah in His dominion, Lordship, and blessings? Allah alone apportions provision by His wisdom, and differences in wealth are a test, not proof of independent divine powers. To deny Allah’s favor means to reject His exclusive right to gratitude, worship, and obedience, especially by associating others with Him.

translation: And Allah has made for you spouses from among yourselves, and has made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren, and has provided you with good things. Do they then believe in falsehood and deny the blessings of Allah?
interpretation: The verse presents marriage, family, and lawful provision as signs of Allah's creative power and kindness, not merely natural accidents. Because He alone originates these blessings, the fitting response is gratitude and worship of Him alone. To turn instead to falsehood—any claimed source of benefit, guidance, or divinity apart from Allah—and to deny His favors by attributing them to others or using them in disobedience is a contradiction of both reason and gratitude.

translation: And they worship besides Allah that which does not possess for them any provision from the heavens and the earth, and they are unable to do anything.
interpretation: This verse exposes the futility of worshipping anything other than Allah: such false objects of worship have no power whatsoever to provide sustenance, whether from the heavens or the earth, nor can they bring any benefit or harm. It establishes that worship is due only to Allah, the sole Creator and Sustainer, and that turning to created beings or imaginary deities for provision or aid is utterly irrational and powerless.

translation: So do not set forth parables for Allah. Indeed, Allah knows, and you do not know.
interpretation: This is a prohibition against likening Allah to anything else, whether by setting up rivals, equals, or false comparisons to Him, or by describing Him according to human limitations and created things. Such analogies arise from ignorance of His true nature. Allah alone knows His essence, names, attributes, and the realities of all things, while human beings do not know; therefore, they must not invent comparisons for Him but must affirm Him as He has described Himself, without resemblance or equal.

translation: Allah sets forth a parable: a slave owned by another, having no power over anything, and one whom We have provided with a good provision from Us, so he spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal? All praise is due to Allah. But most of them do not know.
interpretation: This parable exposes the absurdity of equating false deities with Allah. The owned slave who controls nothing represents the idol, which has no power to create, provide, benefit, or harm. The one whom Allah has provided with good and enabled to spend freely, secretly and openly, represents the servant who receives Allah’s bounty and uses it in obedience. They are not equal. Therefore all praise, provision, and authority belong to Allah alone, and He alone is worthy of worship; yet most people remain ignorant of this truth and persist in associating others with Him.

translation: And Allah presents an example of two men: one of them is mute, unable to do anything, and he is a burden on his master; wherever he directs him, he brings no good. Is he equal to one who commands justice, and he is on a straight path?
interpretation: This parable contrasts the utter helplessness of false deities with the perfection and guidance of Allah. The mute man who can do nothing and brings no good represents the idols, which are powerless to benefit or harm, and are a burden upon those who rely on them. The one who commands justice and is on a straight path represents Allah, the Just, who guides to the truth and commands all that is right. The rhetorical question establishes that they are not equal, proving the folly of worshipping powerless idols instead of the One who is perfectly just and rightly guides.

translation: And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. And the matter of the Hour is only like the twinkling of an eye, or it is nearer. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse establishes that all hidden realities in the heavens and the earth are exclusively known and governed by Allah. It then states that bringing about the Hour is effortless for Him: it will come in an instant, like a glance or even faster, because His power is absolute and nothing can delay or obstruct His decree. The verse thus calls the servant to live with awareness that the Final Hour is near and sudden, to entrust the unseen to Allah alone, and to rely on His all-encompassing knowledge and perfect capability.

translation: And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, not knowing anything, and He made for you hearing, sight, and hearts, so that you may be grateful.
interpretation: This verse reminds people that their existence and knowledge are gifts from Allah: they entered the world in complete ignorance, and He endowed them with the faculties of hearing, seeing, and inner understanding so they could learn, perceive, and reason. These faculties are not merely biological functions but means by which humans come to know their Lord and recognize His favors. The purpose of these blessings is gratitude—using one's senses and intellect in obedience and thankfulness to the One who granted them.

translation: Do they not see the birds made subject in the sky? None holds them up except Allah. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: This verse calls attention to the birds suspended and moving in the open air as a visible sign of Allah’s power and ongoing control. Their flight, balance, and preservation from falling are not due to their own independent power, but because Allah has subjected them to His command and holds them up by laws He created and sustains. For people who believe, such an ordinary yet wondrous sight is not merely a natural event; it is evidence of the Creator’s wisdom, mercy, and constant providence. It invites the believer to see Allah’s hand in creation, to acknowledge that no creature sustains itself, and to deepen trust in the One who governs all things.

translation: And Allah has made for you from your homes a place of rest, and has made for you from the hides of livestock tents which you find light on the day of your departure and the day of your stay; and from their wool, fur, and hair, furnishings and provision for a time.
interpretation: This verse presents divine provision as encompassing both permanence and mobility: the home is a gift of tranquility, security, and settled rest, while animal hides become portable shelters that ease travel and temporary residence. The wool, fur, and hair of livestock are likewise signs of God's care, supplying materials for comfort and household use. The phrase “for a time” teaches that these blessings are temporary and appointed, so they should be received with gratitude to God, used responsibly, and not treated as ultimate ends. The verse thus points to God's wisdom in creating resources and inspiring human skill to use them, and to the believer's need for contentment, thankfulness, and awareness of life's transience.

translation: And Allah has made for you shade from what He created, and has made for you from the mountains places of refuge, and has made for you garments protecting you from heat, and garments protecting you from your mutual violence. Thus He completes His favor upon you, so that you may submit [to Him].
interpretation: This verse draws attention to Allah’s exclusive role as the Provider of both physical and protective blessings: natural shade, mountain refuges, clothing that shields from heat, and protective gear that guards against the harm people inflict on one another in conflict. These are not autonomous human achievements but created means Allah has subjected to human use. The concluding clause reveals the aim of all such favors: God perfects His outward and inward blessing upon people so that they may submit themselves sincerely to Him. Thus the verse links material providence with the call to Islam—wholehearted surrender and obedience—so that gratitude is expressed not only by using the blessings but by acknowledging and worshiping the One who bestowed them.

translation: So if they turn away, then your duty is only the clear conveyance.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Messenger and defines the limit of his responsibility: he is not required to force belief or produce faith in hearts. His task is to deliver God's message plainly and completely; accountability for accepting or rejecting it belongs to God, who alone guides or leaves astray.

translation: They recognize the blessing of Allah, then they deny it, and most of them are disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse exposes the hypocrisy and willful ingratitude of those who inwardly acknowledge Allah’s favors—especially the greatest favor of the Prophet and the Qur’an—yet outwardly reject them, refusing gratitude, obedience, and submission. Their denial is not born of ignorance but of arrogance and stubbornness, and the majority among them persist in disbelief.

translation: And [mention] the Day when We will raise up from every nation a witness; then permission will not be given to those who disbelieved, nor will they be asked to make amends.
interpretation: This refers to the Day of Judgment, when every community will be brought forth with a witness—its prophet or messenger—who will testify about how they responded to the divine message. After that testimony is established, the disbelievers will not be granted permission to speak, offer excuses, or plead their case, nor will they be asked to repent or seek God's pleasure, because the time for faith and repentance has ended. The verse affirms the finality and justice of the reckoning: once the truth has been made clear and the witnesses have testified, there is no further opportunity for apology, negotiation, or correction.

translation: And when those who wronged see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be granted respite.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the unjust on the Day of Judgment: when they finally witness the punishment they were warned about, it will not be reduced or eased for them in any way, and they will not be given any delay or postponement. It emphasizes the absolute certainty and severity of divine justice, showing that once the punishment comes into view, the time for repentance, amendment, or appeal has ended, and no relief or respite remains.

translation: And when those who associated others with Allah see their partners, they will say, "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to invoke besides You." But they will cast back to them the word, "Indeed, you are liars."
interpretation: This verse depicts the humiliation and self-exposure of the polytheists on the Day of Judgment. They will present the beings they had taken as partners with Allah, hoping perhaps to justify themselves, but those very partners will reject them and declare that their claim of partnership and worship was false. The idols, false deities, or objects of devotion will not confirm the polytheists’ assertion; instead, they will disown them. The verse establishes that associating partners with Allah is a lie against Him and against reality, and that on the Day of Judgment every false claim will be exposed and denied by the very things that were falsely invoked.

translation: And they will surrender to Allah on that Day, and lost from them will be what they used to fabricate.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, when Allah’s absolute authority and the truth of His oneness become undeniably manifest, those who had associated partners with Him will submit and yield to His decree, unable to resist or escape. The false gods, intercessors, and invented claims they relied upon in worldly life will vanish and fail them, bringing no benefit and exposing their falsehood.

translation: Those who disbelieved and obstructed others from the way of Allah—We will increase them in punishment over punishment because they used to spread corruption.
interpretation: This verse warns that those who combine denial of God with actively preventing others from following His path receive a punishment greater than that of ordinary disbelievers. Their torment is multiplied because their crime has two dimensions: they rejected the truth themselves and then worked to corrupt and misguide others. The phrase 'punishment over punishment' shows that the additional penalty is directly tied to the harm they caused by spreading corruption and blocking access to divine guidance. It teaches that those who use their influence, power, or words to turn people away from God bear an extra burden of responsibility for the consequences of their misdeeds.

translation: And [mention] the Day when We will raise up in every nation a witness against them from among themselves, and We will bring you as a witness against these. And We have sent down to you the Book as clarification for all things and as guidance and mercy and good tidings for the Muslims.
interpretation: This verse establishes that accountability on the Day of Resurrection is both universal and personal: every community will be confronted by a witness taken from within it, namely its prophet or messenger, who will testify to how they received and responded to the divine message. The Prophet Muhammad is then specifically addressed as the witness over his own people, meaning his testimony will confirm the truth he conveyed and expose the responses of those addressed by the final revelation. The Book given to him is described as clarification for all things in the sense that it provides the decisive exposition of what human beings need regarding belief, worship, morality, law, and the path to God. It is guidance that directs away from error, mercy that alleviates ignorance and sin through divine instruction, and glad tidings for the Muslims—those who submit themselves to God—promising them success and reward for accepting the truth.

translation: Indeed, Allah commands justice, goodness, and giving to relatives, and He forbids shameful deeds, evil, and aggression. He admonishes you so that you may remember.
interpretation: This verse establishes the foundations of God-conscious conduct: that God obligates fairness in dealings and rights, excellence in word and deed beyond mere justice, and maintaining ties and support for kin. It prohibits all that corrupts the self and society—sexual indecency and shamelessness, any recognized evil or wrong, and transgression against others' lives, property, honor, or rights. By presenting these commands and prohibitions as admonition, it calls people to internalize them, reflect, and let remembrance of God guide their choices, since true remembrance produces obedience and moral restraint.

translation: And fulfill the covenant of Allah when you have made a covenant, and do not break oaths after confirming them, while you have made Allah a guarantor over you. Indeed, Allah knows what you do.
interpretation: This verse commands faithfulness to every covenant, pledge, and oath, especially those made in Allah’s name. Once a promise or agreement is confirmed, it becomes a solemn trust that must not be betrayed. Breaking it is not merely a social failure but a religious violation, because Allah has been invoked as witness and guarantor. His knowledge covers both outward actions and hidden intentions, so no deception or excuse escapes Him. The verse therefore establishes truthfulness, contract-keeping, and loyalty as essential duties of faith, and warns that Allah will hold people accountable for how they honor or violate their commitments.

translation: And do not be like her who unraveled her spun thread after it had become strong, breaking it into fibers. You take your oaths as a means of deceit among yourselves, merely because one community is more numerous than another community. Allah only tests you by this, and He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that over which you used to differ.
interpretation: This verse condemns breaking pledges and covenants for worldly gain. It compares those who cancel agreements to a foolish woman who spins yarn and then undoes it after it has become strong. The immediate context is tribal alliances: do not betray a pact or use your oaths as tools of treachery just because another group is larger, richer, or more powerful. Such shifting loyalty for advantage is a test from God. Numerical or material superiority is not a valid reason to abandon faithfulness. God tests people through these inequalities and disputes, and on the Day of Resurrection He will expose and judge the truth of all their disagreements. Thus the verse establishes that covenant, oath, and trust must be kept for God’s sake, not according to changing worldly balance.

translation: And if Allah had willed, He could have made you one community, but He causes whom He wills to go astray and guides whom He wills. And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God’s will is supreme: if He had willed, all people would have been a single believing community, but He, in His wisdom, allows some to go astray and guides others. Guidance and misguidance are ultimately tied to His will, yet this does not cancel human responsibility, for the verse concludes by warning that every person will be questioned about their deeds. Thus belief and disbelief unfold within God’s overarching will, while humans remain accountable for the choices they make.

translation: And do not take your oaths as a means of deception among yourselves, lest a foot should slip after being firmly planted, and you taste the evil because you hindered from the way of Allah; and for you is a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse forbids using oaths, pledges, or covenants as tools of deceit, betrayal, and manipulation. Such conduct undermines trust and stability, causing a person or community to fall from faith, honor, and security after having been firmly established. The “evil” they taste is the worldly and spiritual ruin that follows when their treachery turns others away from Allah’s path. The “great punishment” is the ultimate divine recompense for corrupting trust and obstructing people from obedience to God.

translation: And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price. Indeed, what is with Allah is better for you, if you only knew.
interpretation: This verse forbids betraying any covenant, pledge, oath, or trust made with Allah or in His name for the sake of some petty worldly gain. It teaches that no temporary profit, advantage, or approval is worth violating one's commitment to Allah, because the reward, protection, and recompense that Allah has stored up are far better and more enduring than anything one might gain by breaking faith. The phrase 'if you only knew' calls people to weigh matters with true understanding: worldly goods are little and passing, while what is with Allah is great and everlasting, so the believer should remain faithful even when keeping the covenant seems costly.

translation: Whatever you have will run out, but what is with Allah is everlasting. And We will surely reward those who patiently persevere with their reward according to the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse contrasts the temporary, perishable nature of all worldly possessions and gains with the eternal, unfailing reward that is with Allah. It assures believers that whatever they give up or endure for His sake will never be lost; rather, Allah will recompense those who remain patient in faith, obedience, and adversity by giving them the best reward for the best of their righteous deeds. It calls for detachment from fleeting material things and steadfast perseverance in seeking what is with God.

translation: Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely give them a good life, and We will surely reward them with their reward according to the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse teaches that Allah’s promise of a good life and generous reward is tied to faith and righteous action, not to gender. A male or female believer who performs righteous deeds is promised a good life—understood as contentment, peace, sufficiency, and divine guidance in this world—and in the Hereafter they will be rewarded according to the best of their deeds, meaning their sincere and most excellent actions will be the basis of their recompense.

translation: So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from Satan, the accursed.
interpretation: This verse instructs the reciter to begin recitation by seeking God's protection from Satan, who is expelled from His mercy. It means that since Satan tries to whisper doubts, distractions, and corrupt intentions into the heart, the one reciting the Qur'an must turn to Allah for refuge so that the recitation is protected, sincere, and beneficial, and so that Satan's influence is repelled.

translation: Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and upon their Lord they rely.
interpretation: This means that Satan has no compelling power or dominion over true believers; his influence cannot overpower hearts that are grounded in faith and that place their trust entirely in God. Their reliance on their Lord is their protection, so his whisperings may tempt them but cannot command or rule them, because they have entrusted their affairs to God and seek His safeguarding.

translation: His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him.
interpretation: This means that Satan’s influence and dominion are not forced upon everyone; they become effective only over those who willingly choose allegiance to him by obeying him, and over those who commit shirk by associating partners with Allah. His power is thus connected to a person’s own choice to turn away from God and submit to his whispering, while those who sincerely believe and rely upon Allah are outside his authority.

translation: And when We replace a verse with another verse — and Allah is most knowing of what He sends down — they say, "You are only a fabricator." Rather, most of them do not know.
interpretation: God may replace one revealed verse or ruling with another according to His wisdom, and He knows best what He sends down and why. The disbelievers seize on such replacement to accuse the Prophet of inventing lies against God. But their accusation is false: it stems from ignorance of God's sovereign method of revealing, abrogating, and substituting verses as He wills.

translation: Say, "The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth, to make firm those who believe, and as guidance and good tidings for the Muslims."
interpretation: The Holy Spirit is Jibril (Gabriel), whom Allah sent with the Qur'an; it is revealed from your Lord with truth, not falsehood. Its purpose is to strengthen the faith of believers so they remain steadfast, and it serves as guidance and glad tidings for those who submit themselves to Allah.

translation: And We certainly know that they say, "It is only a human being who teaches him." The tongue of the one they refer to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic.
interpretation: This verse refutes the disbelievers’ claim that Muhammad (peace be upon him) was taught the Qur’an by another human being. God exposes the falsity of their accusation by pointing to the language of the person they name: he is a non-Arab whose speech is foreign, whereas the Qur’an is in clear, eloquent Arabic. Therefore, the Qur’an could not have come from such a human instructor; its Arabic clarity and eloquence are themselves evidence that it is from God, and God is fully aware of what they say in secret and in public.

translation: Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah — Allah will not guide them, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This means that persistent, willful rejection of Allah’s revealed signs and guidance brings about a just withholding of divine guidance: because they refuse the means of guidance, Allah leaves them in their chosen misguidance, and their denial leads inevitably to a painful punishment in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, those who invent falsehood are only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah, and it is they who are the liars.
interpretation: This verse clarifies that fabricating lies against Allah, His revelation, or His Messenger is the practice of those whose hearts reject faith in Allah’s signs. Such people are the real liars, because their denial leads them to distort the truth, falsely claim divine authority for their inventions, and accuse the truthful of lying. Thus, the verse exposes the moral root of falsehood: unbelief in Allah’s verses, and it identifies those who persist in it as liars in reality, even if they present themselves as truthful.

translation: Whoever disbelieves in Allah after having believed—except one who is coerced while his heart is at rest with faith—but whoever expands his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith is determined by the heart’s inner consent, not merely by outward words or actions. If a believer is forced to utter or display disbelief under coercion while his heart remains firmly settled in faith, he is not truly a disbeliever and is not subject to Allah’s wrath or punishment. In contrast, those who willingly and deliberately open their hearts to disbelief, accepting it by their own choice, incur Allah’s wrath and a great punishment. Thus the decisive factor is the heart’s voluntary allegiance: compulsion does not negate faith, but inward consent to kufr does.

translation: That is because they preferred the life of this world over the Hereafter, and Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse explains that their ruin was rooted in a deliberate reversal of values: they loved and chose the fleeting life of this world above the eternal Hereafter, allowing worldly desire to dominate their judgment. Because they persisted in rejecting faith and turned away from the truth, Allah, in His justice, withheld His guidance from them; such guidance is not given to those who knowingly choose disbelief and prefer it to the path He has made clear.

translation: Those are the ones whose hearts, hearing, and sight Allah has sealed, and those are the heedless.
interpretation: This verse means that those who persist in denying and rejecting divine guidance are left by Allah with their inner faculties closed: their hearts no longer accept faith, their ears no longer benefit from the truth, and their eyes no longer perceive the signs that should lead them to God. As a result, they become entirely unmindful of God's remembrance, accountability, and the Hereafter.

translation: No doubt, they are the losers in the Hereafter.
interpretation: This is an emphatic declaration that such people—those who disbelieve and prefer the fleeting life of this world—will suffer true, irreversible loss in the Hereafter. Their loss is complete and exclusive: they forfeit eternal bliss and face punishment, and the emphasis indicates that the reality of loss belongs to them in the fullest sense.

translation: Then, indeed, your Lord — for those who emigrated after they had been persecuted, then strove and were patient — indeed, your Lord, after that, is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse consoles and reassures believers who had been oppressed or coerced into abandoning faith before they migrated for God’s sake. Their previous weakness under persecution does not permanently disqualify them from divine mercy: once they undertake emigration, exert themselves in God’s cause, and endure with patience, God’s forgiveness and compassion embrace them. The phrase “after that” shows that even a prior failure under torment is not beyond God’s pardon when it is followed by sincere repentance, sacrifice, and steadfastness. It teaches that God’s mercy is not withheld from those who return to Him after having faltered; rather, it is granted to those whose later faith, action, and patience prove their sincerity.

translation: On the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself, and every soul will be paid in full for what it did, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: This verse describes the absolute individual accountability of the Hereafter: on that Day, each soul will be concerned only with its own fate and will argue or plead on its own behalf, unable to depend on anyone else. God will then repay every person exactly according to their deeds, and because His judgment is perfectly just, no one will suffer any injustice—neither loss of reward for good nor punishment for what they did not do.

translation: And Allah has set forth an example: a town which was safe and secure, its provision coming to it in abundance from every place, but it denied the favors of Allah. So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear because of what they used to do.
interpretation: This parable teaches that security, tranquility, and abundant provision are gifts from Allah, not entitlements earned by a people's own power. When a community receives these blessings but responds with ingratitude, denial, and disobedience, it forfeits the protection those blessings carried. Allah then makes it taste the opposite: hunger and fear become like a garment covering it completely, a just consequence of its own deeds. The verse warns every nation and individual that gratitude to Allah preserves blessings, while ungratefulness and rejection of His favors lead to their removal and to a life of anxiety and scarcity.

translation: And there had certainly come to them a Messenger from among themselves, but they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse condemns the Meccan rejecters for denying Muhammad, a messenger sent from their own people, known to them and speaking their language. Their rejection was not due to ignorance but to willful defiance, so divine punishment overtook them—chastisement in this world and the greater punishment in the Hereafter—because they were wrongdoers who had unjustly rejected God's messenger and oppressed the believers.

translation: So eat of what Allah has provided you, lawful and good, and be grateful for the favor of Allah, if it is Him you worship.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s lawful, wholesome provisions are meant to be received with gratitude and used in obedience to Him. It ties thankfulness directly to sincere worship: one who truly worships God alone will acknowledge His gifts, avoid the unlawful, and respond to His blessings with praise and obedience, not with denial or misuse.

translation: He has only forbidden to you dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah. But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor transgressing its limit, then indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse establishes that these four things are forbidden because they are impure or because their slaughter has been dedicated to other than Allah. Yet the prohibition is lifted for one who is forced by genuine need and does not eat out of craving or exceed what is necessary to survive. In that case, Allah's mercy allows the exception, and His forgiveness covers the one who takes only what necessity demands.

translation: And do not say, concerning what your tongues falsely describe, “This is lawful and this is unlawful,” in order to invent falsehood about Allah. Indeed, those who invent falsehood about Allah will not succeed.
interpretation: This verse forbids people from assigning legal rulings of halal and haram according to their own desires, cultural customs, or baseless claims, as if they were speaking on Allah’s behalf. It warns that declaring something permitted or forbidden without divine authority is a grave form of inventing lies about Allah, because it usurps His exclusive right to legislate. Such people will not attain true success; their false claims cannot change Allah’s law or ultimately benefit them, and they will be held accountable for attributing to Him what He did not command.

translation: A fleeting enjoyment, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse warns that the worldly gains, pleasures, and advantages obtained through falsehood—especially by inventing lies about Allah and claiming His authority for one’s own rulings—are only a small, passing enjoyment. They are temporary and deceptive, while the recompense awaiting such people is an agonizing punishment. It teaches that trading divine truth for a brief worldly benefit leads to lasting loss.

translation: And to those who are Jews We forbade what We have already related to you. And We did not wrong them, but it was they who wronged themselves.
interpretation: This verse clarifies that the dietary restrictions imposed on the Jews were not an unjust burden from God; they were a consequence of their own disobedience and wrongdoing. God had already informed the Prophet about some of these prohibitions, and He affirms that His rulings are just. The people wronged themselves by their sins and rejection of guidance, so the restrictions were a fitting consequence of their own choices, not an act of divine injustice.

translation: Then, indeed, your Lord—for those who committed evil out of ignorance and then repented after that and reformed—indeed, your Lord after that is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse is an assurance that God does not close the door of forgiveness to those who fall into sin through ignorance—meaning heedlessness, weakness, or failure to consider the gravity of the act—if they afterwards sincerely repent and repair their conduct. Sincere repentance means regret, abandoning the sin, and turning back to God; “reform” means mending what was broken and replacing evil with good. The verse stresses that after such repentance and reform, God’s forgiveness and mercy are certain, so no one should despair of His mercy or continue in wrongdoing under a false sense of security.

translation: Indeed, Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, inclining toward truth, and he was not of those who associate others with Allah.
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham as a complete model of faith: he is called an ummah because he embodied, by himself, the virtues and guidance of a whole believing community. His qunut means constant, humble obedience and worship directed to Allah alone. His being hanif means he was firmly turned toward pure monotheism, away from every false creed. The final statement declares him free of shirk, showing that true Abrahamic faith is exclusive devotion to Allah, not the associational worship into which his people had fallen.

translation: Grateful for His blessings. He chose him and guided him to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse praises Prophet Ibrahim as one who constantly acknowledged and thanked Allah for His favors. In return, Allah selected him for a special closeness and prophethood, and guided him to the straight path of pure monotheism, truth, and obedience. It teaches that true gratitude is expressed by recognizing Allah’s blessings and using them in His service, and that Allah’s choosing and guiding are favors from Him that lead a person to the upright way.

translation: And We gave him good in this world, and indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous.
interpretation: This is a declaration of God’s favor upon Abraham: He granted him a virtuous, blessed, and honored state in the present life—guidance, prophethood, acceptance, and good repute—and in the next life he is among those whose righteousness is complete and whose final destination is God’s pleasure and the company of the righteous.

translation: Then We revealed to you, [O Muhammad], to follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth, and he was not of the polytheists.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet and, through him, the believers to adhere to the way of Abraham, which is pure, exclusive monotheism and sincere devotion to God alone. Abraham’s “millah” is not a set of ethnic or later sectarian laws, but the original faith of turning wholly away from falsehood and idolatry toward the one Creator. The word “hanif” means upright and inclined to truth, rejecting every form of shirk. The declaration that Abraham was not among the polytheists refutes any claim that associates him with idol worship or with religious paths that compromise God’s oneness, and it establishes that the true Abrahamic legacy is precisely the worship of God without partners.

translation: The Sabbath was only enjoined upon those who differed concerning it. And indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which they used to differ.
interpretation: This verse clarifies that the Sabbath was not a universal ordinance of Abrahamic monotheism, nor is it part of the law given to Muhammad. It was imposed specifically on the Children of Israel after they disputed about it, becoming a binding test and a distinguishing obligation for them. Their differences over its observance, its day, and its implications are known to God alone, and He will settle those disputes on the Day of Resurrection with perfect justice. The verse thus directs the Prophet and the believers away from getting entangled in the religious quarrels of previous communities and entrusts final judgment of such disagreements to God.

translation: Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in the best manner. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of who are guided.
interpretation: This verse establishes the method of calling people to God: it must begin with wisdom—speaking truth with knowledge, clarity, and appropriateness to the listener—and with beautiful exhortation that softens hearts without harshness or coercion. If disagreement arises, it should be met with the best kind of argument: reasoned, respectful, and aimed at clarification rather than humiliation or force. The ending reminds the caller that guidance and misguidance are ultimately known to God alone, so one should focus on sincere invitation and good conduct, not on controlling outcomes or judging hidden hearts.

translation: And if you retaliate, retaliate with the like of what you were made to suffer. But if you are patient, that is better for the patient ones.
interpretation: This verse establishes that retribution is permitted only to the exact extent of the harm suffered, without excess or transgression; yet it directs the believer to the higher path of patient restraint and forgiveness, which is better in reward and character.

translation: And be patient, and your patience is only through Allah. And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress because of what they plot.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet and the believers to remain steadfast in the face of opposition, recognizing that true patience and perseverance come from Allah’s help, not from human strength alone. It also forbids allowing the rejection, hostility, or scheming of enemies to produce sorrow or inward distress, because reliance upon Allah frees the heart from being overwhelmed by their plots and places the matter in God’s care.

translation: Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good.
interpretation: God’s help, protection, and guidance are with those who are consciously mindful of Him, avoid disobedience, and perfect their conduct by doing good toward Him and His creation.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Exalted is He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed, in order to show him some of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.
interpretation: This verse is the clearest Qur'anic affirmation of the Night Journey (al-Isra). Allah declares Himself far above any imperfection by announcing that He transported His chosen servant Muhammad (peace be upon him) at night from Masjid al-Haram in Makkah to Masjid al-Aqsa in Jerusalem, a place He has surrounded with both outward and inward blessings. The purpose was not merely travel but to display to the Prophet some of Allah's greatest signs, confirming divine lordship, the truth of revelation, and the Prophet's honored station. By ending with 'He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing,' Allah assures that He heard the Prophet's supplications, saw his hardships, and arranged this miraculous journey with perfect knowledge and wisdom.

translation: And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, [saying], 'Do not take besides Me any guardian.'
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Torah was granted to Moses as divine guidance for the Children of Israel, and its central directive is pure monotheism: they must not adopt any protector, trustee, or object of reliance besides God. It warns against entrusting one's ultimate affairs to anyone other than Him, whether in worship, dependence, or authority.

translation: O descendants of those We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.
interpretation: This addresses the Children of Israel as the offspring of those whom God saved in the ark with Noah, reminding them that their ancestral deliverance should inspire gratitude and faithful obedience to God alone. Noah is singled out as a model of perfect servitude because he constantly acknowledged God's favors with thankfulness, so the verse invites them—and all people—to inherit not merely lineage but the grateful, devoted character of Noah.

translation: And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture: 'You will surely cause corruption on the earth twice, and you will surely rise to great arrogance.'
interpretation: This verse is a divine decree and prophecy concerning the Children of Israel: Allah informed them in their Book that they would commit two major episodes of corruption in the land and would exalt themselves with great haughtiness and transgression. It means they would repeatedly violate God's commands, spread mischief, and oppress others through arrogance and unjust domination. The statement is not merely a prediction but a binding decree that exposes their moral decline and warns that such corruption and haughtiness inevitably bring about divine accountability and punishment.

translation: So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours possessing great might, and they penetrated through the inner parts of the dwellings, and it was a promise fulfilled.
interpretation: This verse conveys that the first major corruption of the Children of Israel triggered an appointed divine punishment through a formidable human power described as God’s servants, meaning that all strength and dominion ultimately serve His decree. Their penetration into the very midst of the dwellings signifies a complete collapse of security, exposing the community’s private and sacred spaces to defeat. The closing phrase affirms that God’s promise of requital is not a mere threat but an inevitable reality: when its time comes, it is carried out without fail, teaching that collective transgression invites overwhelming worldly consequences as part of God’s wise and unchallengeable governance.

translation: Then We gave you back the upper hand over them, and We aided you with wealth and children, and We made you more numerous in manpower.
interpretation: This verse reminds the Children of Israel that after their first defeat, Allah restored their strength and allowed them to prevail over their enemy, enriching them with property, offspring, and increased numbers. It shows that Allah alone controls the rise and fall of nations: He can turn humiliation into dominance and weakness into abundance. These blessings were both a mercy and a test, calling them to gratitude and obedience rather than arrogance, for if they returned to corruption, punishment could return as well.

translation: If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is against yourselves. Then when the promise of the Hereafter comes, they will sadden your faces and enter the mosque as they entered it the first time, and they will destroy whatever they have overcome with utter destruction.
interpretation: This verse establishes that moral acts return upon the doer: goodness benefits one’s own soul, while evil harms it, since God is in no need of either. It then warns the Children of Israel that the second appointed punishment will come as a historical consequence of their corruption: their enemies will humiliate them, enter the sanctuary as conquerors, and demolish their power completely. The verse thus teaches both personal accountability and the certainty of divine justice in history, where wrongdoing ultimately brings ruin upon those who persist in it.

translation: It may be that your Lord will have mercy on you; but if you return [to disobedience], We will return [to punishment]. And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse holds together hope and warning: God’s mercy remains open to those who repent and turn back to Him, but if they revert to their previous corruption and rejection, He will likewise return to punishing them. Hell is called a حصير—an enclosure or prison—meaning that for the disbelievers it becomes an inescapable confinement, holding them within its punishment.

translation: Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward.
interpretation: The Qur'an directs people to the straightest, most just, and most balanced way in belief, worship, and conduct, and it announces glad tidings to those who combine faith with righteous action: that God has prepared for them an immense reward.

translation: And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter — We have prepared for them a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse declares that those who reject belief in the Hereafter, denying resurrection, judgment, and accountability before God, are met with a severe and agonizing punishment that God has already prepared for them. Their disbelief is not merely an intellectual mistake; it reflects a refusal to live in light of ultimate truth, and thus it carries grave consequences in the next life.

translation: And man supplicates for evil as he supplicates for good, and man is ever hasty.
interpretation: This verse points to a deep flaw in human nature: impatience and impulsiveness. In moments of anger, frustration, or despair, a person may rashly ask for punishment, harm, or misfortune to fall upon himself or others, just as earnestly as he asks for good and blessings. If God were to answer every such reckless prayer immediately, people would destroy themselves. The verse therefore highlights God’s forbearance and mercy in not always granting what a person asks in haste, and it warns people to guard their tongues and desires, to pause before demanding outcomes, and to recognize that human beings are naturally inclined to want things at once without considering consequences.

translation: And We made the night and the day two signs, then We erased the sign of the night and made the sign of the day giving sight, so that you may seek bounty from your Lord and so that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. And We have explained everything with clear detail.
interpretation: This verse presents the alternation of night and day as deliberate divine signs, not merely natural occurrences. The darkening of the night’s sign and the illuminating of the day’s sign reflect God’s purposeful ordering of creation: the day is made visible and usable so that human beings can move about, work, and seek His provision, while the night serves rest and repose. Embedded within this cycle is a mercy and a means of knowledge: by observing the regular recurrence of night and day, people can measure time, count years, and calculate dates, which is essential for worship, transactions, history, and social life. The closing statement that God has explained everything in detail affirms that this order is neither accidental nor obscure; it is part of a precisely arranged divine guidance in which even the rhythms of the cosmos point to the Creator’s wisdom, power, and care.

translation: And We have bound every human being’s fate to his neck, and on the Day of Resurrection We will bring out for him a book which he will find spread open.
interpretation: The “bird” bound to the neck symbolizes each person’s deeds and their consequences: every choice, intention, and action is inseparably attached to the individual, so no one can flee from his own record or deny it. On the Day of Resurrection, that record is brought out and laid open before him, exposing the full reality of what he did. Thus the verse teaches that accountability is personal and inescapable; the open book is the clearest witness for or against the soul, and it compels each person to confront the truth of his life.

translation: Read your book! Sufficient is your own self against you this day as a reckoner.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, every person will be confronted with the record of their deeds and commanded to read it. Their own self will be enough as a witness and reckoner against them, because they will recognize and acknowledge what they did. No external proof or accuser is needed; the record and the soul’s own awareness establish perfect justice and personal accountability.

translation: Whoever is guided is only guided for his own soul, and whoever goes astray only goes astray against it. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And We never punish until We have sent a messenger.
interpretation: This verse establishes individual moral responsibility: the benefit of guidance returns to the person who accepts it, and the harm of misguidance falls upon the person who chooses it. It rejects the idea that anyone can bear another’s sin or be punished for another’s guilt. It also affirms God’s justice: punishment is not meted out until He has sent a messenger to convey the truth and establish the proof, so accountability follows the delivery of divine revelation.

translation: And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, so they transgress therein, then the word [of punishment] becomes justified against it, and We destroy it utterly.
interpretation: This verse describes a divine pattern: before a community is destroyed, God sends commands and warnings to its affluent and powerful elite, since they are the most responsible for shaping society. Instead of reforming, they persist in fisq—moral corruption and defiance—so the decree of punishment becomes deserved, and the town is completely annihilated. The verse teaches that privilege and wealth increase accountability, and that collective ruin follows when those with influence use it for corruption rather than reform. God’s destruction is therefore not arbitrary; it comes after clear moral responsibility has been betrayed.

translation: And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah! And sufficient is your Lord, of the sins of His servants, All-Aware and All-Seeing.
interpretation: This verse is a warning and a consolation: God has destroyed many generations after Noah because of their sins and rejection of His messengers, showing that His punishment is real and that no nation is exempt from accountability. It also declares that God's knowledge of His servants' deeds is perfect and His sight of them is complete, so His judgment is never unjust, mistaken, or based on ignorance. The verse therefore calls every person to take heed, repent, and live with awareness that nothing—whether open or hidden—is beyond God's knowledge and sight.

translation: Whoever desires the fleeting life, We hasten for him therein whatever We will for whom We intend; then We have made for him Hell, which he will enter, blamed and rejected.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the pursuit of worldly gain as one’s ultimate goal is governed by God’s will, not by human entitlement. God may grant the worldly seeker some of what he craves, but such attainment is neither proof of divine pleasure nor true success; it is a temporary allotment subject to God’s decree. The one whose heart is fixed on the immediate rather than the Hereafter is ultimately led to Hell, disgraced and cast away from mercy. The verse thus warns against making the transient world the final object of desire and shows that true honor lies in seeking what is eternal and pleasing to God.

translation: And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it, while he is a believer — then those, their striving will be gratefully acknowledged.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the desire for the Hereafter is not enough by itself; it must be joined with earnest, rightly directed effort and with faith. The “striving due to it” means using one’s life, faculties, and deeds in obedience to God and in preparation for the next life, not merely wishing for reward. The condition “while he is a believer” shows that correct belief is the foundation that makes such effort acceptable to God. For those who combine faith, sincere intention, and action, God promises that their labor will not be lost; He will receive it with gratitude and reward it generously. Thus the verse teaches that the Hereafter is attained through believing commitment expressed in action, and that God is not unjust to those who strive for His sake.

translation: Each [of them] We extend—these and those—from the gift of your Lord. And the gift of your Lord is not withheld.
interpretation: God’s worldly provision and favors are not confined to one group; He grants them to the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever, according to His wisdom. This unrestricted giving in the present life is not evidence of His approval, nor does it remove accountability; it is a test and an opportunity, while the true distinction between people is in the Hereafter according to faith and deeds.

translation: Look how We have favored some of them over others. And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in favor.
interpretation: This verse calls attention to Allah’s wisdom in distributing worldly advantages unequally—wealth, status, strength, and opportunities differ among people. These differences are neither ultimate proof of honor nor a reason for arrogance; they are a test and a means by which people may serve and depend upon one another. The true and lasting distinction is in the Hereafter, where ranks, rewards, and divine favor are far greater and more excellent. Therefore, one should not be deceived by worldly superiority or envy it, but should strive for the higher and everlasting favor of the next life through faith and righteous action.

translation: Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit down blameworthy and forsaken.
interpretation: This verse is a decisive prohibition of shirk—associating any partner with Allah in worship, lordship, or devotion. It warns that whoever takes another god alongside Allah will end up blameworthy, disgraced, and abandoned, deprived of divine support and left without any true helper or protector. True dignity and support come only through pure monotheism and sincere devotion to Allah alone.

translation: And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be kind to parents. If one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them 'Uff,' nor repel them, but speak to them a noble word.
interpretation: This verse joins the absolute command to worship God alone with the command to treat parents with excellence. It teaches that honoring parents is not merely social courtesy but a sacred duty rooted in obedience to God. The mention of old age highlights when parents are most vulnerable, weak, and in need of patience; at that stage, even a slight expression of annoyance or contempt is forbidden. The believer is instead to respond with dignified, gentle, and generous speech, showing gratitude, humility, and compassion.

translation: And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say, “My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small.”
interpretation: This verse commands children to show their parents profound humility, gentleness, and compassionate care, not as demeaning servitude but as an expression of mercy. The “wing of humility” is a metaphor for tender lowering of oneself before them, protecting and honoring them. It also directs the child to pray for God’s mercy upon the parents, remembering their sacrificial upbringing in childhood and seeking ongoing divine compassion for them, especially as they age or after their death.

translation: Your Lord is most knowing of what is within yourselves. If you should be righteous, then indeed, He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back [to Him].
interpretation: This verse teaches that Allah alone knows the hidden intentions, thoughts, and motives of the heart. A person is not judged merely by outward appearances, but by the sincerity and righteousness within. If someone sincerely strives to be righteous, then even if they fall short or make mistakes, Allah is forgiving toward those who repeatedly turn back to Him in repentance. The term "awwabin" refers to those who return to Allah again and again, seeking His pardon and correcting their course. Thus the verse combines divine knowledge of the inner self with hope: God is not unaware of your struggles, and He does not abandon the one who keeps turning toward Him with a sincere heart.

translation: And give to the relative his right, and to the needy and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully.
interpretation: This verse establishes a binding order of social and financial responsibility: one must first fulfill the legitimate rights of close relatives, then extend support to the poor and the stranded traveler, and in doing so avoid wasteful, reckless spending. It teaches that wealth is a trust to be directed toward those who have a rightful claim upon it, not scattered beyond measure or spent on excess, and that true generosity is guided by justice, balance, and concern for the needy rather than by impulse or display.

translation: Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils, and the Devil is ever ungrateful to his Lord.
interpretation: This verse condemns wasteful and extravagant spending as a moral and spiritual disease. Calling spendthrifts “brothers of the devils” does not mean literal kinship but likeness in conduct: just as Satan rebelled against God and refused to acknowledge His authority, the wasteful person mishandles God’s blessings by squandering them instead of using them responsibly and gratefully. The verse teaches that wealth is a trust from God, so it should be spent in moderation, on what is good and permissible, and in ways that reflect thankfulness to the Lord rather than ingratitude and defiance.

translation: And if you turn away from them seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then say to them a gentle word.
interpretation: This verse teaches that when one is unable to give material help to relatives, the poor, or the wayfarer because of one's own lack while awaiting God's provision, one must not turn away harshly or dismissively. The turn away is permitted only as seeking God's mercy, not as rejection of the needy. In such a situation, the believer should speak a kind, easy, and comforting word—such as a gentle apology, a prayer for them, or a promise of help when able—thereby preserving their dignity, maintaining compassion, and keeping social bonds intact even when material generosity is not possible.

translation: And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely, lest you sit blameworthy and regretful.
interpretation: This verse commands moderation in spending and generosity. It forbids two extremes: miserliness that withholds wealth as though one’s hand were tied to the neck, and reckless extravagance that gives away everything without prudence. The balanced path is to give generously while preserving enough to fulfill one’s responsibilities. Whoever falls into either extreme ends up blameworthy and regretful—either censured for failing to meet obligations through hoarding, or left destitute and remorseful through exhausting all resources. Wealth is therefore to be handled as a trust, with wisdom, dignity, and moderation.

translation: Indeed, your Lord extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is ever, concerning His servants, Acquainted and Seeing.
interpretation: Allah alone governs the distribution of provision; He enlarges it for some and narrows it for others according to His perfect wisdom, not out of neglect or favoritism. Since He is fully aware of His servants’ inward and outward states and sees what is best for them, His apportioning of wealth and sustenance is a test and a mercy, calling them to trust Him, be content, and use whatever they receive in obedience to Him.

translation: And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Indeed, their killing is a great sin.
interpretation: This prohibition addresses infanticide motivated by economic fear, particularly the pre-Islamic practice of killing infant daughters. It teaches that fear of want cannot justify taking a child’s life, because God’s provision extends to both the child and the parents; the child is not merely a burden but a life whose sustenance is already guaranteed by God. Thus the verse establishes the child’s inviolable right to life and declares killing them a grave transgression against divine law.

translation: And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse. Indeed, it is ever an immorality and is evil as a way.
interpretation: This prohibition forbids not merely the act of zina but every step, inclination, and means that leads toward it, guarding the heart, gaze, speech, and conduct. It is called fahishah because it is a gross indecency that transgresses God's limits and corrupts individual honor, family lineage, and social trust; and it is an evil path because it opens the door to further sins, remorse, and ruin in this life and the Hereafter.

translation: And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right. And whoever is killed unjustly, We have given his heir authority, so let him not exceed in killing. Indeed, he is supported.
interpretation: This verse establishes the sanctity of human life: a person may not be killed except through a legitimate, divinely sanctioned legal cause, such as just retribution for murder. If someone is wrongfully killed, God grants the victim’s rightful heir or guardian the authority to seek justice—normally through proportional retribution or lawful compensation—but that authority is strictly limited. The heir must not overstep by killing beyond the perpetrator, mutilating, or taking innocent life in revenge. The closing assurance means that the one who pursues justice within God’s limits is aided and supported by God.

translation: And do not approach the orphan's property except in the best manner, until he reaches his maturity. And fulfill the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be questioned about.
interpretation: This verse commands guarding the orphan's wealth as a trust: no one may draw near it for personal gain or misuse, but only in the way that benefits and protects the orphan, such as preserving, managing, or increasing it honestly, until the orphan reaches full maturity and sound judgment. At that point the wealth is to be handed over. It also binds every person to honor covenants—promises, contracts, oaths, and trusts—because every covenant is a responsibility for which one will be held accountable before Allah.

translation: And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with the straight balance. That is better and best in outcome.
interpretation: This is a command to uphold honesty and justice in all dealings of measure and weight. It forbids cheating, shortchanging, and using inaccurate scales, and it requires that people be given exactly what is due to them. The “straight balance” means fairness and exactness, not tilting the scale in one’s own favor. Allah declares that such integrity is better and has the best final outcome, both in this world through trust and good reputation, and in the Hereafter through divine reward.

translation: And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart—all of those will be questioned about it.
interpretation: This verse establishes that knowledge and verification are a precondition for belief, speech, and action. It prohibits following conjecture, rumor, suspicion, hearsay, or inherited custom when no real knowledge or evidence exists. Then it declares that hearing, sight, and the inner faculty of understanding and intention are not merely tools one may use irresponsibly; they are trusts and means of accountability. On the Day of Judgment, a person will be questioned about how these faculties were employed: what was listened to, what was looked at, and what was believed, intended, or resolved in the heart. Therefore the verse obliges one to guard the senses and mind, to seek sound evidence, and to avoid passing on or acting upon unverified claims.

translation: And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear the earth open, and you will never reach the mountains in height.
interpretation: This verse forbids arrogant, self-important behavior, especially walking with haughty pride and vanity. It reminds the human being that no matter how strong or mighty he imagines himself to be, he cannot split or pierce the earth by his steps, nor can he attain the towering grandeur of the mountains. Arrogance is therefore exposed as foolish and baseless: a person’s pride cannot change his limited reality or raise him above what God has created. The verse calls for humility, modest conduct, and awareness that all power and elevation belong to God alone.

translation: All of that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the moral wrongness of the prohibited acts mentioned is measured by God’s own judgment, not by human custom or preference. Their evil is not incidental but intrinsic, and God detests it. Therefore, the believer is called to abandon not merely the outward act but the corrupt disposition and harm within it, seeking what is pleasing to the Lord rather than what people may tolerate or approve.

translation: That is from what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom. And do not set up with Allah another god, lest you be cast into Hell, blameworthy and rejected.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the moral, ethical, and devotional teachings revealed to the Prophet are not mere human philosophy but divine wisdom whose foundation is pure monotheism. The prohibition against making any other god alongside Allah is not merely a rejection of idols; it is a warning against allowing any created thing—desire, wealth, power, ego, or another being—to receive the absolute loyalty, fear, love, and obedience that belong to Allah alone. Such association corrupts the root of all wisdom and leads to a state of disgrace: the person is blameworthy because they knowingly diverted worship from their Creator, and rejected because they are driven away from divine mercy and every good outcome. Thus the verse teaches that true wisdom begins and ends with exclusive devotion to Allah, and that abandoning it results in eternal loss.

translation: Has your Lord chosen you for sons and taken from the angels females? Indeed, you are saying a monstrous thing.
interpretation: This verse condemns the polytheists’ claim that the angels are Allah’s daughters while they themselves prided themselves on having sons and disdained daughters.
