It exposes their contradiction: they assigned to Allah what they disliked for themselves and spoke about Him without knowledge. Such an attribution is a grave and monstrous statement because it falsely imputes to Allah a deficient likeness and is rooted in ignorance and whimsical falsehood.

translation: And We have certainly elaborated and varied [the message] in this Qur'an so that they may remember and take heed, but it only increases them in aversion.
interpretation: Allah has set forth the Qur’an in diverse ways—repeating admonitions, parables, proofs, promises, and warnings, and turning its meanings in various forms—so that people might be reminded and turn back to the truth. However, those who are obstinate in disbelief and whose hearts are closed do not benefit from this clarification; rather, the very repetition and variety of the divine message drives them further away, increasing their rejection and distaste for it. Thus the Qur’an is a means of guidance and remembrance for the receptive, while for the heedless it becomes a cause of greater estrangement because of their own arrogance and unwillingness to submit.

translation: Say, "If there were with Him gods, as they say, then they would surely have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne."
interpretation: This verse presents a decisive argument against polytheism. If other gods existed alongside Allah, as the polytheists claim, those gods would not remain passive or subordinate; they would seek a path or means to the Owner of the Throne—whether to approach Him, compete with Him, or claim a share in His dominion. The fact that no such rival can attain or challenge His sovereignty proves that there is no deity besides Him. Allah alone owns the Throne and absolute authority; every other being is His creation and servant, unable to possess divine power or independent access to His rule.

translation: Exalted is He and high above what they say by great sublimity.
interpretation: This declares that Allah is absolutely free from every imperfection and infinitely exalted above all false descriptions, especially the polytheistic claims that He has partners, equals, or offspring. It affirms that His transcendence is essential and absolute, beyond any resemblance to creation, beyond human speech, imagination, and conjecture. No false statement can diminish or reach His majesty; He is far above all that they attribute to Him.

translation: The seven heavens and the earth and all who are in them glorify Him. And there is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing, Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse teaches that glorification of God is not limited to human words or rituals; the whole creation—the seven heavens, the earth, and every being within them—declares His transcendence and praise. Every creature’s existence, order, and submission to the divine will is itself a mode of tasbih, even if humans cannot perceive or comprehend it. The verse humbles human beings by showing that their awareness is limited, while God is fully aware of all praise. The closing names al-Halim and al-Ghafur indicate that God bears patiently with human ignorance, heedlessness, and sin, and forgives those who repent, despite His absolute right to be worshipped and glorified.

translation: And when you recite the Qur’an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier.
interpretation: This means that when the Prophet recites the Qur’an, God sets an unseen veil between him and those who deny the Hereafter, preventing them from understanding its guidance and from being able to harm him. The veil is a barrier of separation brought about by their own disbelief and rejection of accountability, so the message is recited but they are screened from its light.

translation: And We have placed coverings over their hearts so that they do not understand it, and in their ears a deafness. And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn on their backs in aversion.
interpretation: This verse describes the condition of those who persistently reject the truth: their failure to grasp the Qur'an is not due to a lack of evidence but because God has placed a barrier on their hearts and deafness in their ears as a consequence of their defiance. When the Prophet calls to the pure worship of God alone, they recoil and flee because it exposes the falsehood of their idolatry and their ego refuses exclusive submission to Him.

translation: We know best that which they listen for when they listen to you, and when they hold secret talks, when the wrongdoers say, 'You follow none but a man bewitched.'
interpretation: Allah tells His Prophet that He fully knows the hidden motives of the disbelievers: they did not listen to the Qur’an seeking guidance, but to mock, distort, and find pretexts against it; and in their private gatherings they conspired and slandered him as one bewitched—meaning deluded or controlled by magic—so as to turn people away from his message. This verse consoles the Prophet, exposes their secret councils, and declares that their rejection came from arrogance and malicious distortion, not from any deficiency in the message or the Messenger.

translation: Look how they strike parables for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.
interpretation: Allah directs the Prophet to observe the contradictory false analogies the rejecters invent about him—calling him a poet, a sorcerer, a madman, and the like—which reveal their confusion and cause them to stray from the straight path. Because their rejection rests on caprice rather than evidence, they are unable to find any sound way to the truth or any convincing means to discredit the Messenger.

translation: And they say, 'When we are bones and crumbled dust, will we indeed be raised as a new creation?'
interpretation: This verse reports the disbelievers' incredulous denial of resurrection: they consider it impossible that after their bodies have decomposed into bones and scattered fragments, they could be brought back to life. Their question is rhetorical, expressing mockery and rejection rather than seeking an answer. It shows they measure God's power by human limitations, forgetting that the One who created them from nothing can easily recreate them as a new creation. The phrase 'a new creation' stresses a fresh bringing-into-existence, not merely reassembling decayed matter, which is wholly within God's power.

translation: Say, "Be stones or iron."
interpretation: This is a divine challenge to those who deny resurrection: even if you were to become the hardest and most lifeless of materials—stone or iron—God is fully able to restore you to life and bring you forth for judgment. The verse emphasizes that no condition, however far removed from living flesh, can frustrate God's power to resurrect His creation.

translation: Or some created being of whatever your hearts deem great. Then they will say, 'Who will bring us back?' Say, 'The One who created you the first time.' Then they will shake their heads at you and say, 'When will it be?' Say, 'Perhaps it is near.'
interpretation: This verse confronts the deniers’ assumption that resurrection is impossible. Even if they were turned into stone, iron, or any created thing their minds consider greater and harder to bring to life, God’s power is not limited by material hardness or human estimation. Their question, “Who will restore us?”, is answered by pointing to the first creation: the One who originated them from nothing can surely recreate them. Their shaking of heads and asking “When?” express mockery and impatience, but the response teaches that the promised resurrection and reckoning are near in God’s decree, and certainty of its occurrence should concern them more than knowing its exact time.

translation: On the Day when He will call you, and you will respond with praise of Him, and you will think that you had remained only a little.
interpretation: This verse describes the certainty and ease of the resurrection: when God summons all creatures from their graves, they will rise and answer His call, acknowledging His praise and power, and their prior life—whether in this world or in the grave—will seem to them only a brief moment. It emphasizes that the passage of time before the Hereafter is fleeting, and that no one can resist God’s summons when it comes.

translation: And tell My servants to say that which is best. Indeed, Satan stirs up discord among them. Indeed, Satan is to man a manifest enemy.
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet to instruct believers to always choose the best and kindest words when speaking to others. Satan uses harsh, provocative, or evil speech to incite quarrels and enmity between people; therefore, good speech is a protection against his scheming. It also reminds that Satan is an open enemy of humanity, so people must resist his attempts to corrupt their relationships through words.

translation: Your Lord knows best about you. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you; or if He wills, He will punish you. And We have not sent you over them as a guardian.
interpretation: This verse establishes that God alone has full knowledge of His servants’ inner states and what they deserve, and that mercy and punishment are entirely subject to His sovereign will and wisdom. It also defines the Prophet’s role: he is not a guardian or controller appointed to compel people’s faith or manage their final outcome. His duty is to convey the message, while ultimate guidance, judgment, and accountability belong to God alone.

translation: And your Lord is most knowing of whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And indeed, We have preferred some prophets over others, and We gave David the Zabur (Psalms).
interpretation: This verse establishes that God’s knowledge encompasses all beings in the heavens and the earth, so His selection of messengers and His apportioning of ranks among them is based on perfect wisdom. The varying degrees among prophets do not negate their truthfulness; they reflect God’s sovereign choice and the different missions and revelations He entrusted to them. Giving Dawud the Zabur is a concrete example of that divine bestowal, confirming that revelation comes from God and that He knows best whom to favor and with what.

translation: Say, "Call upon those whom you claimed besides Him; they have no power to remove harm from you or to avert it."
interpretation: This verse addresses those who invoke beings other than Allah, claiming they have divine power or influence. It declares that such invoked beings cannot remove any harm, suffering, or difficulty from anyone, nor can they transfer or avert it. Since they possess no authority over harm or benefit, invoking them is futile; all power to relieve distress and change any condition belongs exclusively to Allah.

translation: Those whom they call upon seek the means of access to their Lord—[each] seeking which of them is nearer—and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is [something] to be avoided.
interpretation: This verse refutes the practice of invoking created beings—such as angels, prophets, or righteous people—as if they could answer prayers. The very beings that are called upon are themselves servants of Allah: they seek a way to draw nearer to Him, compete in nearness, hope for His mercy, and fear His punishment. Therefore, they are not lords or gods, and directing worship or supplication to them is false. Worship and reliance belong to Allah alone, and even the highest creatures live in hope and awe of Him. His punishment is a serious reality that every aware servant must dread and avoid.

translation: And there is no city but We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection, or We will punish it with a severe punishment. That has been written in the Book.
interpretation: This verse declares that God has decreed for every settlement or community, without exception, that it will face either destruction or severe punishment in this worldly life before the Day of Resurrection because of its sins and rejection of divine guidance. This decree is fixed and recorded in the Preserved Book, meaning it is already written and unavoidable, serving as a warning that no nation can escape God's judgment for persistent wrongdoing.

translation: And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a clear sign, but they wronged her. And We do not send the signs except as a warning.
interpretation: This verse clarifies that God’s withholding of demanded miracles from the disbelievers is not due to any inability or deficiency, but because the pattern of earlier nations shows that such signs often only increase obstinate rejection and bring down punishment. The she-camel given to Thamud was a manifest, undeniable miracle, yet they wrongfully opposed and harmed it, proving that external wonders do not benefit hearts that are determined to deny. Therefore, signs are sent primarily as a warning and awakening: to make people fear God, reflect on their accountability, and repent, not to force faith or satisfy arrogant demands for proof.

translation: And [mention] when We said to you, 'Indeed, your Lord has encompassed the people.' And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people, and [also] the accursed tree in the Qur'an. And We warn them, but it only increases them in great transgression.
interpretation: This verse reassures the Prophet that Allah's authority and knowledge encompass all people, so He will protect him from their plots. The vision he was shown—the night journey and ascension—was made a test for the people: it distinguished those firm in faith from those who would turn away. The cursed tree mentioned in the Qur'an was similarly a test, because the disbelievers used it as an occasion for mockery and doubt. Though Allah warns them through signs and revelations, their response is only greater arrogance, rejection, and disobedience.

translation: And [mention] when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,' so they prostrated, except Iblees. He said, 'Should I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?'
interpretation: The prostration commanded here was not worship of Adam but a divine ordinance honoring him and acknowledging the station God had granted him. Iblees’s refusal was rooted in arrogance: by fixing on Adam’s creation from clay, he sought to justify his disobedience with a claim of superior origin. The verse thus exposes how pride and self-importance can corrupt a creature’s reasoning and lead it to reject God’s command while imagining itself justified.

translation: He said, 'Do You see this one whom You have honored above me? If You reprieve me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely destroy his descendants except a few.'
interpretation: This is Iblis's defiant protest after being commanded to prostrate to Adam. He acknowledges that God has favored Adam over him, but rather than submit, he resents it and vows, if given time until the Day of Resurrection, to overwhelm and mislead Adam's descendants, leading them to ruin except for a small remnant. It exposes Satan's arrogance, envy, and determination to corrupt humanity, while also showing that God's grace will preserve a few from his destructive influence.

translation: He said: Go, then whoever follows you among them — indeed, Hell is your recompense, an ample recompense.
interpretation: This is a decisive divine decree addressed to Iblis after his refusal and arrogance: he is granted freedom to invite and mislead, but he has no authority over anyone except those who choose to follow him. The verse establishes that Hell is the just and complete repayment for both the deceiver and those who imitate him in disbelief and disobedience. The phrase "an ample recompense" indicates that the punishment will be full, fitting, and neither reduced nor unjust, corresponding to the gravity of freely chosen rebellion against God. It also teaches that Satan's misguidance does not compel anyone; his followers bear responsibility for their own acceptance of his path, and the final recompense belongs to God alone.

translation: And incite whoever you can among them with your voice, and rally against them your cavalry and your infantry, and share with them in wealth and children, and promise them. But Satan does not promise them except delusion.
interpretation: This is part of Allah's address to Iblis after his vow to mislead Adam's descendants. It grants him a period of testing, not independent power. His “voice” is every whispering, call, and enticement toward disobedience; his “cavalry and infantry” are his hosts from jinn and humans who advance his seduction; “sharing in wealth and children” means people obeying him in unlawful earning, spending, and in how they rear and direct their offspring, including shirk and sin; and his “promises” are false assurances of gain, safety, delay of judgment, or cheap forgiveness. Yet all his promises are empty deception, for he cannot force the heart. He only invites, and those who follow him do so by their own choice. The verse therefore exposes Satan's methods and warns people to resist them through faith, remembrance of Allah, and obedience.

translation: Indeed, over My servants you have no authority. And sufficient is your Lord as a Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: This verse declares that Satan has no compelling dominion or coercive control over Allah’s devoted servants. His influence is limited to whispering, beautifying evil, and inviting toward misguidance; he cannot force the hearts of those who sincerely rely on Allah. Therefore, the believer’s protection lies in turning to Allah, for He alone is sufficient as guardian, trustee, and disposer of all affairs, guarding His servants from the enemy’s domination.

translation: Your Lord is the One who drives for you the ships upon the sea, so that you may seek of His bounty. Indeed, He has ever been Merciful to you.
interpretation: This verse points to God’s mercy as the hidden foundation of human movement, provision, and trade. The sailing of ships is presented not merely as a natural event but as an act of divine facilitation: God orders the winds, water, and human capacity so that people can travel and seek lawful provision. Therefore, worldly effort is not independent of God; it is a response to His enabling grace. The verse teaches that material pursuit should be joined with gratitude, trust, and recognition that every benefit ultimately comes from His mercy.

translation: And when harm touches you at sea, lost are those you call upon except Him. But when He saves you to land, you turn away. And man is ever ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that in extreme peril, human beings instinctively recognize that no created power can save them and that only Allah has real authority over life and rescue. The false objects of reliance then vanish from the heart, even if people normally invoke them. Yet when Allah grants safety and ease, many turn away from Him and forget the One who delivered them. This exposes the human tendency toward ingratitude: remembering God in distress but neglecting Him in comfort.

translation: Do you then feel secure that He will not cause a side of the land to swallow you up, or send against you a storm of stones? Then you will find no guardian for yourselves.
interpretation: This is a warning that safety from one danger is not evidence of security from all divine punishment. Allah, who has power over sea and land, can cause the earth to sink beneath them or send a punishing wind carrying stones or hail, and no one can rescue or protect them. The verse calls people to humility, repentance, and reliance on Allah, not presumption, because absolute security belongs only to Him, and any presumed protector besides Him is powerless.

translation: Or do you feel secure that He will not return you to it another time and send against you a violent wind and drown you because of your disbelief? Then you will not find for yourselves against Us any avenger.
interpretation: This is a warning to those who were saved from the sea and then turned away in ingratitude: do not assume that safety from Allah’s power is permanent. He can return you to the sea and send a destructive wind that drowns you because of your denial. On that Day, no one can rescue you, defend you, or hold Allah accountable. The verse teaches that deliverance is by Allah’s mercy, not by human strength, and that persistent disbelief can bring punishment in this very world with no helper or avenger against Allah.

translation: And We have certainly honored the children of Adam, and carried them on land and sea, and provided them with good things, and preferred them over many of those We created with a clear preference.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God has bestowed an intrinsic dignity upon every human being as a child of Adam, not because of their own merit, but by His generous decree. He has subjected the means of travel on land and sea to them, granted them pure and wholesome sustenance, and favored them over many of His creatures. This honor is both a gift and a trust: it calls humans to gratitude, humility, and moral responsibility, recognizing that their superiority over many created beings is not absolute and does not dispense them from accountability before God.

translation: On the Day We will call every people with their leader: then whoever is given his record in his right hand — those will read their record, and they will not be wronged even a thread.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, God will summon each community together with the one it followed and took as its guide in the world, making clear that people are judged in relation to the path and leadership they chose. Whoever receives the record of his deeds in his right hand has attained acceptance and success; he reads his record with joy and relief, and God’s judgment is perfectly just, so no one is wronged by even the smallest amount — not even the fine thread on a date pit. The right hand signifies honor, safety, and a favorable reckoning.

translation: And whoever is blind in this [life] will be blind in the Hereafter, and more astray in way.
interpretation: This means that one who refuses to see and follow God's guidance in this worldly life, remaining blind to the truth, will likewise be blind in the Hereafter to the path of deliverance and even farther removed from the right way.

translation: And indeed, they were about to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you, so that you might invent against Us something other than it; and then they would have taken you as a friend.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), stating that the unbelievers nearly succeeded in luring him away from the revelation God had sent him, urging him to fabricate a different message in God's name to suit their desires. Had he yielded to them, they would have accepted him as a close ally. It thus highlights the pressure to compromise divine truth for worldly acceptance and affirms that the Prophet remained steadfast, protected by God from such deviation.

translation: And had We not made you firm, you would have almost inclined toward them a little.
interpretation: This is a divine address to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, declaring that his unwavering steadfastness upon the truth was due to God’s direct strengthening and protection. Without that divine support, the pressure of the disbelievers’ persistent proposals, compromises, and attempts to draw him toward their ways could have caused a slight inclination. The verse therefore affirms God’s guardianship over His Prophet, his protection from falling into even a minor deviation in conveying the message, and the profound lesson that firmness in faith is ultimately a gift from God that believers must seek and depend upon.

translation: Then We would have made you taste double [punishment in] life and double [after] death; then you would not find for yourself against Us any helper.
interpretation: This is a warning that the station of prophethood carries the strictest accountability: any compromise with falsehood by the one entrusted with revelation would incur doubled suffering in this world and the next, and no power could shield him from God's judgment. It teaches that nearness to God increases responsibility, not immunity, and that divine support is conditional upon fidelity to His command.

translation: And indeed, they were about to provoke you out of the land to expel you from it, and then they would not remain after you except a little.
interpretation: This verse exposes the Quraysh’s plot to harass and drive the Prophet Muhammad out of Mecca. God informs him that their scheme would not give them lasting security: had they succeeded in expelling him, their own stay in the land would have been very short before divine punishment overtook them for their rejection and persecution. It is both a warning that opposing God’s Messenger brings swift ruin and a consolation that God will protect and establish him.

translation: A precedent set by those We sent before you among Our messengers; and you will never find in Our precedent any change.
interpretation: This means that Allah’s manner of dealing with earlier messengers and their peoples is a fixed, unchanging law: whenever a people conspire to expel, harm, or kill the messenger sent to them, Allah supports His messenger and brings His judgment upon the conspirators. Their schemes may seem to prevail briefly, but they cannot overturn God’s established practice. The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad and warns his opponents that their plot to drive him out will not escape this divine pattern; the same fate decreed for previous rejecters will reach them, and Allah’s decision cannot be altered or diverted.

translation: Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation at dawn. Indeed, the recitation at dawn is ever witnessed.
interpretation: This verse sets the times of the prescribed prayers: beginning when the sun passes its zenith and continuing until the night's darkness, covering the obligatory prayers of Zuhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isha; then it singles out the dawn prayer and recitation as a time especially attended and witnessed by the angels. It presents prayer as a fixed, God-ordained discipline tied to the sun's movement through the day, and it honors the Fajr prayer with the testimony of the angels.

translation: And in part of the night, offer tahajjud as an extra devotion for you; perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet to devote part of the night to voluntary prayer beyond the obligatory prayers, showing that nearness to God is attained through extra worship and sincere night devotion. The promised “praiseworthy station” is the exalted rank of intercession granted to him on the Day of Judgment, where his Lord will raise him to a position that all creation will acknowledge and praise.

translation: And say: My Lord, admit me with an entrance of truth and bring me out with an exit of truth, and grant me from Yourself a helping authority.
interpretation: This is a supplication taught to the Prophet, especially at the time of the Hijrah, asking God to make his departure from Mecca and his entry into Medina both be grounded in truth, sincerity, and divine acceptance, and to grant him a supporting power that would aid and defend the message. In a broader sense, it teaches the believer to ask God that every coming and going, every beginning and ending, be undertaken truthfully and righteously, and that God provide from His own presence a firm support and victory that upholds what is right.

translation: And say, “The truth has come, and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish.”
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet to proclaim that the truth—God’s revelation, pure monotheism, and the prophetic message—has arrived, while falsehood—idolatry, disbelief, and every way opposed to divine guidance—is defeated and destined to pass away. Its enduring lesson is that falsehood has no permanence: it may appear powerful for a time, but by its very nature it is bound to vanish, whereas truth ultimately prevails.

translation: And We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers, but it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss.
interpretation: The Qur'an is a remedy for spiritual sickness—doubt, hypocrisy, and heedlessness—and a mercy for those who believe in it and act upon it; yet the same revelation only deepens the ruin of the unjust because they reject it, mock it, and persist in their wrongdoing.

translation: And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and withdraws to his side; and when evil touches him, he is ever despairing.
interpretation: This verse describes a blameworthy human tendency: when given blessings, ease, or wealth, a person may become arrogant, turn away from God, and avoid gratitude and obedience; but when hardship, illness, or loss afflicts him, he loses hope and falls into despair. The verse contrasts ungrateful heedlessness in prosperity with hopelessness in adversity, urging the believer to remain humble, thankful, and hopeful in both states.

translation: Say, 'Each works according to his own disposition; but your Lord is most knowing of who is best guided in the way.'
interpretation: This verse declares that every person acts according to his own inner nature, character, inclination, and chosen path, so outward deeds alone cannot reveal the full reality of guidance. Ultimate knowledge of who is truly better guided belongs to God alone, for He knows the hidden motives, capacities, and sincerity behind every action. Thus people should not arrogantly claim superiority or pass final judgment on others’ guidance; rather, they should act sincerely according to the truth they know and leave the final assessment to their Lord, who alone knows the straightest path.

translation: And they ask you about the spirit. Say, "The spirit is from the command of my Lord, and you have not been given of knowledge except a little."
interpretation: This verse teaches that the spirit or soul is a reality brought into being by God’s command, and its true essence belongs to the realm of divine knowledge that is not fully accessible to human beings. Even with all the knowledge humans may accumulate, they possess only a small portion of it, so they cannot fully comprehend the spirit’s nature. It calls for humility before God and recognition of the limits of human understanding.

translation: And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We have revealed to you; then you would not find for yourself any guardian against Us.
interpretation: This verse declares Allah's absolute sovereignty over revelation and His complete freedom to give or withdraw it. If He willed, He could remove the Qur'an from the Prophet's heart and memory, and no one could prevent Him or protect the Prophet from that decree. It teaches that the Qur'an is not preserved by any human power, nor is Allah bound by anyone's claim over it; its preservation is purely by Allah's will and mercy. It also instills humility, dependence, and gratitude, reminding the recipient that every divine gift remains entirely in Allah's hand.

translation: Except as a mercy from your Lord. Indeed, His favor upon you has ever been great.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the preservation of revelation, guidance, and prophethood with the Prophet Muhammad is not owed to any human power or merit, but is purely a mercy from Allah. If Allah willed, He could remove the Qur’an and its guidance, and no one could restore it. Its continued presence is therefore a divine gift, and Allah’s favor upon the Prophet is immense, encompassing revelation, prophethood, protection, and the safeguarding of the message.

translation: Say, 'If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce the like of it, even if they were to one another assistants.'
interpretation: The Qur'an's inimitability is absolute: no created being, not even all humans and jinn combined and helping one another, can match its eloquence, guidance, and perfect coherence. This impossibility is not due to insufficient effort or cooperation but because the Qur'an is divine revelation, beyond the capacity of any created speech, and thus it stands as conclusive proof of its origin from God and of the prophethood of Muhammad.

translation: And indeed We have set forth for mankind in this Qur'an every kind of example, but most people refuse to accept anything but disbelief.
interpretation: The verse declares that the Qur'an contains ample, varied, and repeated lessons and parables sufficient to guide anyone, yet most people meet them not with faith or gratitude but with denial and rejection. Their refusal is not due to a lack of clarification, but due to their own stubborn rejection of the truth.

translation: And they said, "We will never believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth."
interpretation: This verse reports the obstinate demand of the disbelievers: they made faith contingent on the Prophet Muhammad producing a miracle of their own choosing—making water burst forth from dry ground. It exposes their arrogance, for they were not seeking truth sincerely but imposing conditions on prophethood. It also teaches that miraculous signs do not compel faith; hearts that insist on disbelief will keep demanding extraordinary proofs unless they humble themselves and submit to God’s guidance.

translation: Or you have a garden of date palms and grapes, and cause rivers to gush forth within it abundantly.
interpretation: This is one of the demands made by the obstinate disbelievers: they will not believe unless the Prophet Muhammad is given a private garden of date palms and grapevines with rivers made to burst forth through it. It exposes their insistence on extraordinary sensory miracles and their refusal to accept prophetic guidance on its own clear evidence.

translation: Or you make the sky fall upon us in pieces, as you have claimed, or you bring Allah and the angels before us face to face.
interpretation: This verse exposes the disbelievers’ arrogant insistence on sensory miracles and their mockery of the Prophet’s warning. They demanded that he force God’s punishment to descend immediately or that he summon God and the angels visibly before them as proof. Such a demand is not a sincere search for truth but a challenge born of pride and a refusal to submit to prophetic authority. It also reflects a grave misunderstanding of God’s transcendence: the Creator is not subject to human whims, nor is He summoned by creatures. The messenger’s role is only to convey the clear revelation, not to command God or manipulate divine signs. Therefore, the verse underscores that faith should rest on the truth of the message and the evidence already given, not on presumptuous demands for supernatural displays.

translation: Or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky. But we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book we can read. Say, "Glory to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?"
interpretation: This verse exposes the disbelievers’ escalating and insincere demands: they make faith contingent on the Prophet producing a gilded house or climbing into heaven and delivering a readable heavenly book. Their challenge is not a sincere search for truth but a refusal to submit unless the Prophet conforms to their arbitrary terms. The command to say “Glory to my Lord” affirms God’s transcendence and freedom from human conditions, while “Am I anything but a human messenger?” clarifies that the Prophet’s role is to convey revelation, not to control miracles or satisfy every demand. True faith responds to the message and to God’s will, not to coercive signs.

translation: And nothing prevented people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said, "Has Allah sent a human being as a messenger?"
interpretation: This verse exposes the real reason for the disbelievers’ rejection: it was not a lack of clear guidance or proof, but their arrogant objection that a messenger should be a human being like themselves. They assumed that divine messengers must be angels or some other-than-human beings, using this expectation as a pretext to refuse faith. The verse shows that such an excuse is hollow, because God’s wisdom in sending human messengers is precisely so that people can recognize, understand, and follow them. Their rejection therefore stems from pride and a false standard, not from genuine inability to believe.

translation: Say, "If there were upon the earth angels walking about securely, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger."
interpretation: This verse answers the disbelievers’ demand that an angel be sent as a prophet by explaining that messengers are sent in the nature of those addressed: if the earth were inhabited by angels who walked and settled in it, God would have sent an angel to them from heaven. Since humankind inhabits the earth, the messenger sent to them is a human being, so that they can receive, understand, and follow the message. The verse also affirms God’s wisdom in matching the messenger to the kind of creation being addressed, and it implies that rejecting a human messenger merely because he is not an angel is not a valid objection.

translation: Say, “Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you. Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing.”
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet to answer those who dispute or deny him by appealing to Allah’s testimony alone, for no witness is more authoritative or complete. Allah’s witnessing is sufficient because His knowledge is all-encompassing: He is fully aware of the outward and inward realities of His servants, their words, deeds, intentions, and hidden secrets. Therefore, the truth of the Prophet’s message and the falsehood of its rejecters are not left unknown or unrecorded; Allah observes all and will judge with perfect knowledge and justice. The verse also affirms two divine attributes: al-Khabīr, meaning the One fully acquainted with all things, and al-Baṣīr, meaning the One who sees all things.

translation: And whoever Allah guides, he is the rightly guided; and whoever He sends astray, you will never find for them any protectors besides Him. And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection on their faces, blind, dumb, and deaf. Their refuge is Hell; every time it subsides, We increase for them a blaze.
interpretation: This verse teaches that guidance and misguidance are ultimately by Allah's decree, yet human responsibility remains: the one whom Allah guides is truly guided, while the one He leaves astray has no guardian or ally besides Him. The gathering on their faces signifies extreme humiliation and the inversion of their worldly pride. Blind, dumb, and deaf in the Hereafter means they will be deprived of the very faculties they refused to use for truth—unable to see the way, speak a defense, or hear any relief. Hell is their final abode, and its punishment is unceasing: whenever its flame calms or seems to abate, Allah increases its blazing intensity, indicating that the torment is perpetual and escalating. The verse thus warns that rejecting divine guidance leads to a state of utter loss, where the faculties that could have saved one become instruments of regret, and the punishment never reaches an end.

translation: That is their recompense because they disbelieved in Our verses and said, 'Is it that when we are bones and crumbled remains, we will indeed be raised as a new creation?'
interpretation: Their punishment is the just consequence of two connected sins: rejecting Allah’s revealed signs and denying the resurrection. Their question is not an honest inquiry but a scornful expression of disbelief, as they regard it impossible that Allah could bring them back after their bodies have decayed into bones and scattered dust. The verse thus exposes their materialistic doubt and affirms Allah’s absolute power to recreate and the certainty that every person will be raised for judgment.

translation: Have they not seen that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the like of them? And He has appointed for them a term, about which there is no doubt. But the wrongdoers refuse except disbelief.
interpretation: This verse establishes the reality of resurrection by pointing to God’s power shown in the creation of the heavens and the earth. The One who originated such vast creation is fully capable of recreating human beings after death. The fixed term God has appointed is the time of their death and raising, and it is certain beyond doubt. Yet the wrongdoers respond to this clear proof not with reflection or acceptance but with persistent denial and ingratitude toward God’s power and promise.

translation: Say, 'If you possessed the treasuries of my Lord's mercy, you would surely withhold them out of fear of spending. And man is ever stingy.'
interpretation: The verse diagnoses a deep human tendency: people often treat even God's limitless mercy as though it were a scarce resource, and so they hoard and refuse to spend generously. It teaches that miserliness is not merely a practical response to limited means but a moral and spiritual sickness in the human self. If humans had control over divine treasures, they would still fear depletion and withhold, showing that true generosity requires trust in God's inexhaustible provision and a heart freed from possessive fear.

translation: And We had certainly given Moses nine clear signs. So ask the Children of Israel when he came to them, and Pharaoh said to him, 'Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched.'
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah granted Moses nine manifest miracles as proof of his prophethood, and directs the Children of Israel—who witnessed them—to be asked about their truth. Yet when Moses presented these signs to Pharaoh, Pharaoh did not reject them on rational grounds; he responded with arrogant dismissal, accusing Moses of being under a spell or mentally altered. The verse thus shows that clear evidence does not compel a heart hardened by pride and denial, and that opposition to a prophet often resorts to slander rather than confronting the signs themselves.

translation: He said, "You have certainly known that none has sent down these [signs] except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear proofs. And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed."
interpretation: The verse means that the miracles shown to Pharaoh were not magic or human invention but divine signs from the Lord of the heavens and the earth, serving as enlightening proofs. Pharaoh inwardly recognized this truth, yet his arrogance and tyrannical power led him to deny it. Moses then declares that Pharaoh is "مثبورا"—ruined, cursed, deprived of good, and destined for destruction—warning that his stubborn rejection of the truth will bring utter loss in this world and the Hereafter. Thus the verse exposes how a tyrant can know the truth while persisting in denial, and how such defiance inevitably leads to perdition.

translation: So he intended to drive them out of the land, but We drowned him and all those who were with him.
interpretation: This verse exposes Pharaoh’s plan to uproot and expel the believers from the land through intimidation and persecution. Allah declares that His response was not to allow the tyrant’s scheme to succeed, but to destroy him and his followers together by drowning. The meaning is that oppressive power, when it plots to remove or annihilate the faithful, ultimately falls under divine judgment; God protects His chosen servants and turns the oppressor’s designs back upon him.

translation: And We said after him to the Children of Israel, 'Dwell in the land; then when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you as a mixed multitude.'
interpretation: This verse follows the destruction of Pharaoh and tells the Children of Israel that, after his drowning, God settled them in the land as a deliverance and respite. Yet settlement in any land is not ultimate security; the 'promise of the Hereafter' is the sure appointment of resurrection and judgment. On that day God will gather them 'lafifan'—all together, a mixed crowd drawn from every direction and joined with the rest of humanity, none omitted or hidden. The verse thus affirms God's power to ingather all people after death, reminds the Israelites that worldly dwelling is temporary, and warns that final destiny belongs to God alone.

translation: And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended. And We did not send you except as a bearer of good tidings and a warner.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Qur’an is entirely founded upon truth: God revealed it in truth, it came down in truth, and everything it contains—its reports, commands, promises, and warnings—is true and free from falsehood. It also defines the Prophet’s mission: he is not sent to force people into faith, but to convey to them the good news of God’s mercy and reward for those who believe and obey, and to warn them of the consequences of denial and disobedience.

translation: And it is a Qur’an which We have separated [into parts] that you may recite it to the people over a prolonged period, and We have sent it down progressively.
interpretation: The Qur’an was not revealed all at once but was sent down in measured, successive portions over time. God did so that the Prophet could convey it to people gradually, allowing them to understand, memorize, and act upon its guidance with deliberation and steadfastness. Its gradual descent also demonstrates that it is a true, divinely ordered revelation, sent down by God’s wisdom and not composed by any human being.

translation: Say, "Believe in it or do not believe. Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it – when it is recited to them, they fall upon their faces, prostrating."
interpretation: This verse establishes that the Qur'an's truth is not dependent on the acceptance of any particular audience. Those who possess genuine knowledge from earlier revelations recognize the Qur'an as confirming what they already know, so they respond with deep humility and worship. Their falling upon their faces in prostration signifies complete submission, reverence, and gratitude when they hear the truth recited.

translation: And they say, 'Exalted is our Lord! Indeed, the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled.'
interpretation: These are the people of knowledge who, upon hearing the Qur'an, prostrate and glorify God, acknowledging that He is free of any deficiency and that His promise to send the final Messenger—or every promise He makes—is inevitably carried out. Their words combine reverence, submission, and certainty in God's truthfulness; they do not doubt or resist the revelation but humble themselves before it.

translation: And they fall upon their faces, weeping, and it increases them in humility.
interpretation: This verse describes the profound effect of the Qur’an upon those whose hearts are open to truth: when they hear it, they are overwhelmed with reverence and fall in prostration, weeping out of awe, repentance, and longing for God. Their weeping is not grief without hope, but a sign of softened hearts and sincere submission. The phrase “it increases them in humility” means that every encounter with divine revelation deepens their khushū‘—their reverent humility, lowliness before Allah, and readiness to obey Him. Thus the verse teaches that true knowledge of God and His message does not lead to pride, but to greater brokenness before Him, increased worship, and a humbler heart.

translation: Say, 'Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.' And do not be loud in your prayer, nor silent therein, but seek a way between that.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the One being invoked is the same whether He is called Allah or al-Rahman; the diversity of His beautiful names does not indicate separate deities, but directs the servant to the one God through whatever name is most fitting. It also establishes moderation in prayer: vocal worship should neither become ostentatious and disturbing nor so hidden that it loses its purpose. The believer is to seek a balanced path in calling upon God and in worship—sincere, humble, attentive, and considerate of others—so that devotion remains pure and neither excess nor neglect corrupts it.

translation: And say, 'All praise is due to Allah, who has not taken a son and has no partner in dominion and has no protector out of weakness. And magnify Him with great magnification.'
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet and every believer to declare God's exclusive praise and absolute transcendence. God is not in need of a son, because He is self-sufficient and beyond all likeness; He has no partner in sovereignty, because His dominion is indivisible; and He has no ally or protector, because He is never overcome or humiliated. Any claim that He has offspring, a rival, or a helper necessitated by weakness is false. Therefore, He alone deserves to be glorified and acknowledged as greater than all descriptions and needs, with the utmost magnification in speech, belief, and worship.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. All praise is due to Allah, Who sent down the Book upon His servant and did not make in it any crookedness.
interpretation: This verse opens Surah al-Kahf by praising Allah for revealing the Qur’an to His servant Muhammad. It emphasizes that the revelation is perfectly straight, free from any deviation, inconsistency, or distortion; its guidance is upright, coherent, and preserved from error so that it may lead creation to the truth.

translation: [It is] upright, to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward.
interpretation: The Qur’an is straight and free of deviation, established as a warning against the severe punishment that comes from God alone, and as glad tidings for those who combine sincere faith with righteous action: their reward with God is good, pleasing, and lasting.

translation: Abiding therein forever.
interpretation: This describes the eternal permanence of the reward promised to the believers who do righteous deeds: they will remain in it forever, never leaving it and never being deprived of it.

translation: And to warn those who say, 'Allah has taken a son.'
interpretation: This verse warns those who claim that God has taken a son. Such a claim is false and incompatible with God's absolute oneness and self-sufficiency, for He is far above having offspring or needing anyone. The warning is meant to make them realize the gravity of this belief and turn away from it before they meet its consequences.

translation: They have no knowledge of it, nor did their forefathers. Dreadful is the word that comes out of their mouths. They say nothing but a lie.
interpretation: This verse condemns the claim that Allah has taken a son, stating that neither the claimants nor their ancestors possessed any true knowledge or revealed evidence for it. Such a statement is described as enormously grave because it speaks about God without knowledge and falsely attributes to Him something that contradicts His unique divinity and transcendence. It is not merely an innocent mistake but an utter falsehood, since it is asserted without proof and against the truth of God's oneness.

translation: Then perhaps you would kill yourself with grief, following their footsteps, if they do not believe in this discourse.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and, by extension, every caller to truth: the deep sorrow and anxiety he feels over people turning away from the Qur’an should not drive him to destroy himself. Guidance is not in the Messenger’s power to force into hearts; his duty is to convey the message clearly and sincerely, while ultimate acceptance or rejection belongs to Allah. The verse teaches that love and concern for others must be balanced with trust in God, patience, and submission to His wisdom, and that the truth of the revelation is not diminished by people’s disbelief.

translation: Indeed, We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it, so that We may test them as to which of them is best in deeds.
interpretation: The verse means that all worldly possessions, beauties, and enjoyments are only a temporary ornament and a means of trial, not the ultimate goal of human existence. God tests people through them to reveal who uses them in the most excellent, God-conscious way, seeking His pleasure rather than being deceived or consumed by them.

translation: And indeed, We will surely make whatever is on it a barren, level expanse.
interpretation: This verse declares that all the adornments, resources, structures, and living beings upon the earth are temporary and subject to God’s decree of annihilation. The earth, after serving as a place of testing, will be stripped of every trace of life and beauty and left as a lifeless, desolate plain. Therefore, worldly attractions are not the true purpose of existence; they are a trial to reveal whose deeds are best, and only what is done for God’s pleasure endures beyond this fleeting world.

translation: Or did you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were, among Our signs, a wonder?
interpretation: This is a gentle correction of the assumption that the story of the People of the Cave and ar-Raqim is the most astonishing of God’s signs. It does not deny that they were a sign, but it situates them within the far greater scope of divine signs—such as creation, revelation, providence, and resurrection—and prepares the listener to receive the story as a lesson in faith, patience, and God’s power rather than as an isolated marvel.

translation: When the youths sought refuge in the cave and said, 'Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and prepare for us a right course in our affair.'
interpretation: This is a supplication of faithful young people under pressure: they did not demand a specific worldly outcome but asked God for mercy from His own presence and for sound guidance in their uncertain situation, showing that true deliverance begins by turning to God, seeking His special care, and asking Him to make one's steps and decisions rightly directed.

translation: So We struck upon their ears in the cave for a number of years.
interpretation: This means that Allah caused the youths to fall into a deep, prolonged sleep inside the cave, sealing their hearing from the sounds around them so that they remained unaware and undisturbed for many years, as a sign of His protection and power.

translation: Then We raised them up so that We might know which of the two parties would best calculate how long they had remained.
interpretation: Allah awakened the people of the Cave after their long sleep to make manifest—not because He lacked knowledge—which of the two groups would most accurately reckon the duration they had tarried. This was a sign of His absolute power over life, death, and time, and a proof of the resurrection, distinguishing truthful reckoning from mere conjecture and showing that knowledge of the unseen belongs ultimately to Allah alone.

translation: We relate to you their story in truth. Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the account of the People of the Cave is being revealed by God Himself with absolute truth, free from the distortions and conjectures of earlier narrators. It identifies them as young believers who, despite living in a milieu of disbelief and corruption, anchored their faith exclusively in their Lord. Their youth suggests sincerity, courage, and a willingness to sacrifice for conviction. The statement that God increased them in guidance teaches that guidance is not static: when a person sincerely turns to God and holds fast to faith, God grants them greater clarity, steadfastness, and direction. Thus their initial belief became the cause of further divine favor, and their story stands as a lesson that God protects and elevates those who prioritize loyalty to Him over the pressures of their surroundings.

translation: And We strengthened their hearts when they stood up and said, 'Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never call upon any god besides Him; indeed, we would then have uttered an outrageous deviation.'
interpretation: God granted these believers inward firmness and resolve, enabling them to stand openly and proclaim the exclusive lordship and worship of the Creator. Their declaration affirms tawhid: the heavens and the earth have one Lord, and no created being deserves to be invoked or worshipped alongside Him. The statement that they would otherwise have spoken an enormity means that if they were to call upon another deity after recognizing the truth, their claim would be a grave falsehood and a serious departure from right belief. The verse therefore teaches that true faith requires courage in professing God's oneness, that steadfastness of heart is a gift from God, and that associating partners with Him is not a small matter but an extreme transgression against the truth.

translation: These, our people, have taken besides Him gods. Why do they not bring for them a clear authority? And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?
interpretation: This is the righteous youths’ rebuke of their people’s idolatry: they adopted gods besides Allah without any clear proof. The rhetorical challenge exposes that such worship has no divine warrant. The verse then declares that no injustice is greater than inventing a falsehood about Allah, which includes attributing partners, laws, or claims to Him without His authority. It establishes that true worship must rest on clear divine evidence, and that fabricating lies against Allah is the gravest wrong.

translation: And [remember] when you withdrew from them and from what they worship except Allah, then seek refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will prepare for you a means of comfort from your affair.
interpretation: This verse teaches that separating from a corrupt environment and its false objects of worship should be joined with turning wholly to Allah for protection. The cave symbolizes any refuge taken to preserve faith and flee religious harm. Allah’s promise to spread His mercy and prepare a beneficial, comfortable way shows that He will not abandon those who sacrifice worldly ties for His sake; He grants them relief, guidance, and ease in their affairs. It is a call to trust in Allah when circumstances become narrow, and to let Him arrange a path of safety and benefit.

translation: And you would see the sun, when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it set, passing them by on the left, while they were in a hollow of it. That is among the signs of Allah. Whoever Allah guides is rightly guided; and whoever He sends astray — you will never find for him a protecting guide.
interpretation: This verse describes how Allah protected the youths of the cave by a subtle miracle: although they were exposed within a cave, the sun’s rising and setting rays were turned away from them, so they were preserved from its direct heat and harm. This was not by human design but by divine arrangement, and therefore it is one of Allah’s signs. The verse then establishes the principle that guidance belongs to Allah alone: whom He guides is truly guided, and whom He leaves astray cannot find any guardian or guide who can bring him to the right path.

translation: And you would think them awake, while they were asleep. And We turned them to the right and to the left, while their dog stretched out its forelegs at the threshold. If you had looked at them, you would have turned away from them in flight and would have been filled with dread of them.
interpretation: This verse presents the companions of the cave as a sign of Allah’s absolute power over time, bodily preservation, and the unseen. Their outward appearance suggested wakefulness, but in reality they were held in a deep divinely appointed sleep; Allah Himself turned them from side to side so that their bodies would not be harmed or decay during their long slumber. The dog at the threshold, with its forelegs outstretched, marks the boundary of this protected place and shows that even the animal shared in the outwardly strange scene. The terror that would overcome any onlooker was not merely natural fear but awe before an uncanny sight: bodies that seemed alert yet remained motionless under an invisible divine guardianship. Thus the verse points to Allah’s intimate care for His righteous servants, His mastery over the laws of nature, and the ease with which He can restore life and preserve identity on the Day of Resurrection.

translation: And thus We awakened them so that they might question one another. One of them said, 'How long have you remained?' They said, 'We have remained a day or part of a day.' They said, 'Your Lord is most knowing of how long you remained. So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city, and let him look for which food is purest, and let him bring you provision from it; and let him be subtle, and let no one make you known.'
interpretation: This scene teaches that God's miraculous care for the sleepers did not remove their need to deliberate and act. Their uncertainty about how long they stayed is resolved by referring absolute knowledge to God, showing that when matters exceed human perception, the believer submits to God's knowledge rather than insisting on conjecture. Sending one of them with the silver coin to the city directs them to use available means, to seek the purest and most lawful sustenance, and to act with discretion and gentleness in a hostile setting. It joins reliance on God's power with prudent planning, lawful provision, and protective caution.

translation: Indeed, if they gain dominance over you, they will stone you or return you to their religion; and then you will never succeed.
interpretation: This verse expresses the severe pressure and threat faced by the believing youths if their opponents discovered and overpowered them: they would either be executed by stoning or forced back into the religion of unbelief. It warns that yielding to such coercion might secure temporary safety, but it would bring eternal failure. Therefore, the verse teaches that true success is not found in escaping persecution by abandoning faith, but in remaining firm upon true belief even when the worldly consequences are severe.

translation: And similarly, We caused them to be discovered, so that they might know that the promise of Allah is true and that the Hour is beyond doubt. When they disputed among themselves concerning their affair, they said, 'Build over them a structure. Their Lord knows best about them.' Those who prevailed in their affair said, 'We will surely take over them a place of worship.'
interpretation: The verse recounts how God unveiled the Sleepers of the Cave to their people as a decisive proof of resurrection and the certainty of the Hour. Their discovery was not random; it served to confirm God's promise and remove doubt about the Hereafter. Yet instead of simply accepting the sign, the people quarreled over how to memorialize the sleepers. Some wanted to seal or cover the cave with a building, while the dominant faction resolved to erect a mosque at the site. The Qur'an presents this as a lesson: people often divert a sign of God's power into dispute and exaggerated veneration of the righteous. Islam therefore directs worship exclusively to Allah and warns against turning graves into places of worship, even if the intent begins as honor. The true response to such signs is belief in God's promise and preparation for the Hour, not quarreling over monuments.

translation: They will say, 'Three, and the fourth of them was their dog.' And they say, 'Five, and the sixth of them was their dog,' guessing at the unseen. And they say, 'Seven, and the eighth of them was their dog.' Say, 'My Lord is most knowing of their number. None knows them except a few.' So do not argue about them except with an obvious argument, and do not seek a verdict about them from any of them.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disputes that arose among later people concerning the number of the People of the Cave. It exposes the first two claims as mere conjecture about hidden matters, while the third report is stated without the censure of guessing. The decisive teaching is that God alone has certain knowledge of their true number, though He may inform a few of His servants. Therefore the believer should not engage in futile argument over details God has not made binding, nor seek answers from those who speculate; discussion should be limited to what is clearly established by revelation.

translation: And do not say of anything, 'I will do that tomorrow.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that a person must not make an unconditional assertion about future actions, because the future is not under human control; all matters depend on God’s will and decree. It calls for humility and reliance upon God, so that one acknowledges that any planned action can occur only if God wills it.

translation: Except if Allah wills. And remember your Lord when you forget, and say, 'Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer than this in right guidance.'
interpretation: This teaches that human resolves concerning the future remain subject to God's will, so a believer should always attach intention to divine permission. If one forgets or neglects this remembrance, the remedy is to return to God in awareness and hope, asking that He guide to a path even closer to truth, correctness, and righteousness than what one had intended.

translation: And they remained in their cave for three hundred years, and added nine.
interpretation: This verse states that the People of the Cave stayed in their cave for a period of three hundred years plus nine more, making a total of three hundred and nine years. It is a precise declaration of the length of their miraculous sleep.

translation: Say, Allah is most knowing of how long they stayed. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How Seeing is He and how Hearing! They have no protector besides Him, and He shares not in His judgment with anyone.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the exact knowledge of hidden affairs—including the duration of the People of the Cave—belongs exclusively to Allah. Since He alone possesses the unseen of the heavens and earth, His sight and hearing encompass every secret and every consequence, so He is the most reliable authority and no creature can rival His knowledge or perception. It further teaches that no one besides Allah can be a guardian who independently benefits, harms, or manages human affairs, and that His rule, decree, and judgment admit no partner. Thus all supplication, reliance, and submission concerning both the seen and unseen must be directed to Him alone, and any claim to share in His authority or hidden knowledge is false.

translation: And recite what has been revealed to you from the Book of your Lord. None can alter His words, and you will never find besides Him any refuge.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet, and through him every believer, to persist in reciting and conveying Allah’s revealed Book as the sole source of guidance. It declares that Allah’s words—His commands, promises, warnings, and decrees—are unalterable and cannot be changed, substituted, or nullified by any created being. No power can corrupt their truth or prevent their fulfillment. Since no refuge, protector, or escape from Allah exists except with Him, the servant must turn wholly to Him, hold fast to His revelation, and seek safety and direction only through Him, not through any other authority or path.

translation: And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face. And let not your eyes overlook them, seeking the adornment of the worldly life. And do not obey the one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his own desire, and whose affair has been excess/transgression.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet—and by extension every believer—to remain steadfastly in the company of sincere worshippers who invoke God at all times, not for social advantage but solely for His pleasure. It warns against letting one's attention or affection be drawn away from such believers toward worldly wealth and status. It also forbids compliance with those whose hearts have become unmindful of God, who are led by their whims, and whose conduct has transgressed the proper limits. Thus, the criterion of worth is God-consciousness and sincerity, not worldly adornment or the approval of the heedless.

translation: And say: The truth is from your Lord. So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve. Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose walls surround them. And if they cry for relief, they will be given water like molten brass that scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the truth comes from God alone, not from human desire, and that people are free to accept or reject it. That freedom is not without consequence: choosing disbelief and wrongdoing is what makes one a wrongdoer liable to the Fire, which will encompass them so that there is no escape. Their plea for relief will only bring a boiling, filth-like liquid that burns the face, showing that the punishment is both physically agonizing and humiliating. The final words describe the drink as wretched and the resting place as evil, stressing the utter ruin and regret of those who knowingly turn away from the truth after it has come to them.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—We will not let the reward of any who does good deeds go to waste.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true faith is inseparable from righteous action, and it contains a divine guarantee that God never disregards or diminishes the recompense of those who sincerely strive to do good. The phrase "who does good deeds" points not merely to the quantity of actions but to their quality—performing them with excellence, sincerity, and conformity to God's guidance. It affirms God's perfect justice and generosity: no effort made in faith is lost, and those who combine belief with beautiful conduct will find their reward preserved and fully given by their Lord.

translation: Those—for them are the Gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade, reclining therein on couches. Excellent is the reward, and good is it as a resting place.
interpretation: This verse portrays the ultimate reward of the believers: eternal gardens of Eden where divine provision flows perpetually beneath them. The gold bracelets and green garments of fine silk and brocade signify honor, purity, dignity, and the joy of a perfected existence, while reclining on couches conveys perfect security, rest, and freedom from all hardship. The closing praise—that this is an excellent reward and a beautiful resting place—declares that God's promise is true and that the bliss of His pleasure and nearness is the highest attainment, far beyond any temporary pleasure of this world.

translation: And set forth for them a parable of two men: We made for one of them two gardens of grapevines, and We surrounded them both with palm trees, and We placed crops between them.
interpretation: This verse opens a parable contrasting two attitudes toward worldly blessing. The two vineyards, the encircling palms, and the crops in between represent abundant, ordered, self-renewing prosperity. Its lesson is that such wealth is not proof of spiritual favor or personal superiority; it is a trust and a test. The man given these gardens can be lulled into crediting himself, relying on his possessions, and forgetting the Giver and the Hereafter. The verse therefore directs the heart beyond the garden itself to the God who creates, sustains, and can remove it at will. True success is not measured by the extent of one’s estate but by faith, gratitude, and accountability to God.

translation: Both gardens yielded their fruit, and did not withhold anything of it; and We caused a river to flow between them.
interpretation: This verse describes the two gardens as giving their produce fully and without deficiency, while Allah caused a river to flow through them. It signifies that the blessing was complete and divinely sustained: the orchards were not only fertile but irrigated by a river running amid them, showing Allah’s power, generosity, and care. In the context of the parable, it teaches that such abundant provision should inspire gratitude and humility, not arrogance, since it is Allah alone who grants and preserves all blessings.

translation: And he had fruit, so he said to his companion while conversing with him, 'I am more than you in wealth and mightier in men.'
interpretation: This verse exposes how the owner of the two gardens let his prosperity deceive him. His words are not a fair comparison but a boast born of arrogance: he measures worth by wealth and the number of supporters, claiming superiority over his companion. It warns that material abundance can become a trial, leading a person to forget the Giver, belittle others, and rely on worldly means instead of God. True honor lies not in riches or followers but in faith and righteousness.

translation: And he entered his garden while he was unjust to himself. He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish."
interpretation: This verse portrays the wealthy owner of the two gardens in Surah al-Kahf. His entering the garden 'while unjust to himself' means he had ruined his soul through arrogance, ingratitude, and disbelief in the resurrection. By saying that his garden would never perish, he expressed an excessive attachment to worldly possessions and a denial of God's power to destroy them and to raise the dead. His self-confidence in his wealth made him forget his Creator, so his wrong was not against others but against his own eternal interest.

translation: And I do not think the Hour will ever come. And if I am indeed returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a final return.
interpretation: This verse exposes a delusion rooted in worldly prosperity: the speaker denies the coming Hour, yet even when he imagines a return to his Lord, he assumes he will receive something better than his present garden. His error is that he treats material blessing as proof of divine approval and as a guarantee of a good outcome, whereas wealth can be a trial and does not indicate righteousness or safety in the Hereafter. The verse warns against letting worldly success breed arrogance, heedlessness of accountability, and false confidence before God.

translation: His companion said to him, while he was conversing with him, “Have you disbelieved in the One who created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then fashioned you into a man?”
interpretation: This is a rebuke against arrogance and disbelief. The companion confronts the man’s denial of God by pointing to the very stages of his own creation: God originated him from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then shaped and completed him as a man. The meaning is that the One able to create man in successive stages from such humble beginnings is fully able to resurrect him after death. Disbelief here is not merely a theoretical denial but a failure to acknowledge the Creator’s power and one’s total dependence upon Him. The verse teaches that worldly wealth, strength, or status should never lead a person to reject the Creator, and that recognizing God’s creative power naturally leads to faith in resurrection and accountability.

translation: But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with my Lord.
interpretation: This is the believer’s declaration of unshakable faith in the story of the two men in Surah al-Kahf. He contrasts his arrogant companion’s disbelief with his own resolve: whatever the other says, he affirms that Allah alone is his Lord. He refuses to associate any partner with Him—no idol, person, power, or worldly attachment—in lordship, worship, or obedience. The phrase “but as for me” signals personal commitment: even if others reject Allah and the Hereafter, he will remain steadfast upon pure monotheism.

translation: And why did you not, when you entered your garden, say: 'What Allah has willed [is what comes to pass]; there is no power except with Allah'? If you see me less than you in wealth and children...
interpretation: This verse is a rebuke and a reminder: the blessing of a garden, wealth, or children is not the result of one's own power, but comes by Allah's will alone. A believer should meet any blessing with the confession that it is what Allah willed and that no strength or ability exists except through Him. Boasting over someone poorer in wealth or offspring is therefore foolish, since outward abundance is not proof of divine favor; the one who seems lesser may be greater with Allah, and all provisions can be altered by Him. The true measure is humble recognition of Allah's sovereignty and reliance on Him, not comparison with others.

translation: Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden, and send upon it a calamity from the sky, so that it becomes a barren, slippery ground.
interpretation: The speaker, though poorer in worldly wealth, trusts that God can grant him better than the rich man’s garden, while warning that the same garden could be destroyed by a divine punishment from the heavens and left utterly barren and useless. The verse teaches that material possessions and cultivated wealth are temporary and can be withdrawn at any moment, so one should not boast or rely on them; true security lies in faith, humility, and reliance upon God.

translation: Or its water becomes sunken deep, so you will never be able to find it.
interpretation: This verse expresses the absolute dependence of all life and provision upon God’s sustaining power. The water that gives the garden its life can be caused to disappear into the depths of the earth, beyond any human reach or effort, and no amount of wealth, planning, or technology can bring it back. It is a confession that blessings are not secured by human ownership or ability but by God’s will, and that He can withdraw them at any moment.
