It warns against arrogance, self-reliance, and attachment to worldly wealth, and it calls the believer to recognize that every favor is a trust from God, to be used in obedience and with gratitude, while seeking what is eternal rather than relying on what is perishable.

translation: And its fruit was encompassed by ruin, so he began to wring his hands over what he had spent on it, while it lay in ruins upon its trellises, and he said, 'Oh, I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the crushing regret of the wealthy garden owner after his property is destroyed. His wringing hands show helpless grief over the wealth and effort he had poured into it, now that it lies utterly ruined. His lament—wishing he had never associated partners with his Lord—reveals that the real loss is not merely material but spiritual: his arrogant reliance on wealth and his shirk could not avert Allah’s decree, and in the end he recognizes too late that true security lies only in exclusive faith in Allah.

translation: And he had no group to help him against Allah, nor could he defend himself.
interpretation: This verse describes the regretful end of the man who had boasted of his wealth and denied the resurrection. When Allah’s punishment came upon him, his possessions, followers, and allies were utterly useless: none could rescue him from Allah’s decree, and he could not rescue himself. The verse teaches that created things have no power to avert divine judgment, and that relying on wealth, status, or human support instead of Allah is a delusion. True help comes only from Allah, and every soul stands before Him in need and helplessness.

translation: There, the authority belongs to Allah, the True God. He is best in reward and best in outcome.
interpretation: This verse affirms that true protection, guardianship, and authority belong exclusively to Allah, the Absolutely True, especially when all worldly supports and false claims fail. He alone gives the finest reward to those who rely on Him and the finest final destination, so the servant should place trust, loyalty, and hope in Him alone.

translation: And present to them the example of the life of this world: it is like water which We send down from the sky, so the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, then it becomes dry debris scattered by the winds. And Allah is ever, over all things, competent.
interpretation: This parable teaches that worldly life is fleeting and deceptive: whatever grows from it flourishes only briefly, like plants nourished by rain, then quickly withers and is blown away as worthless chaff. Its beauty and prosperity are not lasting, so one should not cling to them as if they were ultimate. Allah’s absolute power over all things means He alone controls giving, taking, flourishing, and decay, and He is fully able to bring creation to an end and resurrect it.

translation: Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world. But the enduring righteous deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope.
interpretation: This verse teaches that wealth and offspring are temporary ornaments and blessings of worldly life, not its ultimate purpose. The lasting good deeds—faith, righteous conduct, and remembrance of God—are far superior because their reward with God is eternal and they give a more reliable hope for the future. Believers are thus directed to prioritize enduring righteousness over fleeting worldly attachments.

translation: And [mention] the Day when We will set the mountains in motion, and you will see the earth exposed, and We will gather them and not leave behind any one of them.
interpretation: This verse describes the overwhelming reality of the Day of Resurrection: the mountains, which seem so firmly fixed, will be moved and reduced to shifting dust, and the earth will appear laid bare, with all its hidden places exposed and leveled. Every human being will then be gathered before Allah for judgment, without exception or omission. It emphasizes Allah's absolute power over creation, the certainty of resurrection, and the complete accountability of every soul.

translation: And they will be presented before your Lord in rows: 'Indeed, you have come to Us just as We created you the first time. But you claimed that We would never appoint for you a meeting.'
interpretation: This is the resurrection scene: every soul is brought before God in ranks, with no worldly rank, wealth, or intercessor able to shield it. Humanity returns to the state of its first creation—bare, individual, and dependent—demonstrating that the One who originated creation can restore it. The disbelievers’ denial of resurrection and judgment is exposed as false: the promised meeting with God, which they assumed would never be appointed, has occurred. The verse affirms God’s absolute power, the certainty of accountability, and the folly of treating the hereafter as an empty claim.

translation: And the Book will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, and they will say, 'Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves out neither small nor great except that it has counted it?' And they will find what they did present. And your Lord does not wrong anyone.
interpretation: This verse portrays the moment of divine accountability, when the record of every person’s deeds is laid open. The criminals are overcome with dread and remorse because the Book exposes everything—no deed, whether seemingly insignificant or grave, is omitted. Their outcry expresses despair at the completeness of the record and the inescapability of what they had done. Their deeds are then found present before them, not lost or forgotten. The closing statement affirms God’s perfect justice: He does not wrong anyone, for the record is exact and the recompense is strictly according to what was actually committed. Thus the verse instills both awe of God’s all-encompassing knowledge and confidence in His fairness.

translation: And [mention] when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate before Adam,' and they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn, and he departed from the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his descendants as allies besides Me, while they are enemies to you? How evil for the wrongdoers is that exchange!
interpretation: This verse clarifies that Iblis was not an angel but one of the jinn, so his refusal was a willful transgression rather than a natural angelic incapacity. The prostration commanded to the angels was an act of honor for Adam, not worship of him, and Iblis’s disobedience was a deliberate departure from God’s command. The rhetorical question then warns humans against taking Iblis and his progeny as patrons and allies instead of God, even though they are open enemies. It exposes the folly of the wrongdoers who exchange God’s guidance and guardianship for the enmity and deception of Satan, and it establishes that true faith requires rejecting allegiance to Iblis and all that follows his path.

translation: I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of their own selves, nor would I take the misleaders as helpers.
interpretation: In this verse, God declares that Iblis and the forces of misguidance were neither present at nor participants in the creation of the heavens, the earth, or even their own selves. They have no creative power, no independent authority, and no share in God’s dominion. Therefore, taking them as allies, helpers, intercessors, or objects of worship is false and futile. God is utterly self-sufficient and does not seek aid from those who lead others astray; He alone creates, sustains, and governs all things. The verse refutes polytheism and warns that Satan and his followers cannot benefit anyone, since they had no role in creation and cannot assist God in any way.

translation: And [mention] the Day when He will say, 'Call upon My partners whom you claimed.' So they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and We will place between them a barrier of ruin.
interpretation: This verse rebukes the false claim of associating partners with Allah. On the Day of Judgment, those who worshipped false deities will be commanded to call upon those they claimed shared in divinity. Their calls will go unanswered, proving that the alleged partners have no power, knowledge, or ability to help. The “mawbiq” is a barrier of destruction, separation, or ruin placed between the worshippers and the false objects of worship, cutting off any hoped-for connection, rescue, or intercession. The verse establishes that absolute authority and response belong to Allah alone, and that every false object of reliance will fail its followers in the Hereafter.

translation: And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain that they are to fall into it, and they will not find any way of escape from it.
interpretation: This verse depicts the state of the guilty on the Day of Judgment after they are confronted with Hell. Their seeing the Fire eliminates doubt; they become certain that they are about to enter it. Despite their former denial or procrastination, at that moment there is no route of escape, no detour, no refuge, and no way to bargain or substitute. It conveys the terrifying finality of divine judgment: the evildoer’s regret is too late, and the reality of accountability cannot be evaded.

translation: And We have certainly set forth for people in this Qur’an every kind of example, but man is, in most things, disputatious.
interpretation: God has varied, repeated, and clarified every kind of parable, sign, and proof in the Qur’an so that people may be guided and reflect; yet the human being is often consumed by argumentation and contention, disputing the truth rather than submitting to it. This rebukes the tendency to debate merely for the sake of dispute and calls for humility, reflection, and acceptance of clear guidance.

translation: And nothing prevents people from believing when guidance has come to them, and from seeking forgiveness of their Lord, except that there comes to them the way of the former peoples, or that the punishment comes to them face to face.
interpretation: This verse exposes the excuse of the deniers: it is not that the truth is unclear or that guidance is absent. What holds them back from faith and repentance is their stubborn demand to see the same fate Allah decreed for earlier rejecting nations—destruction in this world—or to have the punishment brought before their very eyes. In other words, they effectively condition belief on the arrival of coercion, doom, or a visible sign of wrath, which is not true faith but a challenge to God's judgment. The verse is a warning that such an attitude only hastens the very punishment they mockingly demand, and that faith after punishment is no longer the free response God calls for.

translation: And We do not send the messengers except as bringers of good tidings and warners. But those who disbelieve dispute with falsehood to invalidate thereby the truth, and they take My verses and that of which they were warned in ridicule.
interpretation: This verse establishes that Allah's messengers are sent solely to convey glad tidings to the obedient and warnings to the disobedient; they are not sent to compel hearts or force belief. It then exposes the disbelievers' tactic: instead of responding to the truth with sincere reflection, they argue using falsehood in order to erase or defeat the truth. Their mockery of Allah's signs and of the warnings delivered by the prophets reveals arrogance and heedlessness, not genuine doubt. Such attempts are ultimately futile, because falsehood cannot stand against the truth, and those who ridicule divine revelation only bring ruin upon themselves.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the verses of his Lord, then turns away from them and forgets what his hands have sent forth? Indeed, We have placed coverings over their hearts lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness. And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, then, ever.
interpretation: This verse describes the gravest form of wrongdoing as knowingly turning away from God’s revelations after being reminded of them while neglecting the consequences of one’s own deeds. Its deeper meaning is that persistent rejection of truth brings about a spiritual hardening: the heart is veiled from understanding and the ear is made dull to hearing, not as an arbitrary punishment but as a just consequence of repeatedly choosing heedlessness. Such a person does not merely lack guidance; he loses the receptivity by which guidance could reach him. Therefore, even sincere invitations to the right path will not benefit him unless God Himself removes the barrier. The verse teaches that guidance is ultimately from God and that continual refusal of it can lead to a condition in which one can no longer perceive or accept the truth.

translation: And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of Mercy. If He were to take them to task for what they have earned, He would hasten for them the punishment. But they have an appointed time, and they will not find besides Him any refuge.
interpretation: The verse affirms that Allah's forgiveness and mercy are the reason He does not immediately punish people for their sins. If He were to hold them accountable instantly for every deed, punishment would come upon them without delay. Yet He grants them respite until a fixed, appointed term. This delay is not neglect or weakness; it is mercy and an opportunity for repentance. When that appointed time comes, no one will find any escape or refuge apart from Allah, and no power can avert His judgment. Thus divine mercy should lead to sincere turning back to Him, not to false security.

translation: And those towns, We destroyed them when they did wrong, and We appointed a fixed time for their destruction.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the destruction of earlier communities was not arbitrary but was the just consequence of their persistent wrongdoing, especially their rejection of divine guidance and their corruption. God granted them respite until a decreed term, so their punishment came only when the appointed time arrived. It warns that sin and denial, if unrepented, lead to ruin, and that God’s judgment is certain and fixed, neither hastened nor delayed beyond His knowledge and wisdom.

translation: And when Moses said to his servant, “I will not cease until I reach the junction of the two seas, or I will continue for a very long time.”
interpretation: This verse expresses Moses’s firm resolve and patient perseverance in seeking the appointed meeting at the junction of the two seas, even if the journey requires an exceedingly long time. It teaches that the seeker of knowledge and guidance must endure hardship, remain steadfast, and not abandon the quest until reaching the goal, and that spiritual knowledge may require humility, travel, and following a righteous guide.

translation: So when they reached the junction between them, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, as a passage.
interpretation: This event is a divinely arranged sign at the meeting point of the two seas. The fish’s return to life and its escape into the sea by an unusual passage—described as a sarb, a tunnel or burrow—marked the exact spot Moses was seeking, and their forgetting it was part of Allah’s plan to lead him to al-Khidr. It teaches that Allah’s decrees often unfold through matters that appear ordinary or forgotten, and that the seeker of knowledge must remain attentive to the signs placed in his path.

translation: So when they had passed beyond, he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal. We have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey of ours."
interpretation: This verse portrays the human weakness and need of even the greatest of God's messengers. Moses, peace be upon him, having traveled a long distance in search of knowledge and guidance, turns to his young companion for food and openly admits his exhaustion. The lesson is that striving in the way of God does not exempt one from physical limitations, and acknowledging them is not a lack of trust or piety. Moreover, this moment of fatigue precedes the recollection of the miraculous fish, showing that divine openings often come after effort and apparent depletion, and that the seeker of truth must persevere, remain humble, and attend to the signs around him.

translation: He said, "Did you see when we sheltered by the rock? I forgot the fish, and none made me forget it except Satan, so that I would not mention it. And it took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner."
interpretation: The speaker admits that at the stopping place he failed to recall the sign of the fish, which had miraculously come back to life and escaped into the sea. He attributes his lapse of remembrance to Satan’s distracting influence. The fish’s strange path through the sea is the extraordinary marker of the meeting place appointed by God, showing that divine signs may appear through unlikely means and that human forgetfulness cannot prevent God’s plan from being fulfilled.

translation: He said, “That is what we were seeking.” So they returned, retracing their footsteps.
interpretation: The speaker recognizes in the strange incident of the fish the very sign he had been made to seek, not merely a lost provision. His words express that the true objective lay behind them, at the point where the sign occurred. Their turning back “upon their traces” signifies a deliberate return to the exact place appointed by God for the meeting, showing that divine guidance may appear through an event one initially overlooks, and that once the sign is recognized, one should retrace one’s steps to it without delay.

translation: And they found a servant from among Our servants, whom We had granted mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Our presence.
interpretation: This servant, traditionally identified as al-Khidr, is shown to be chosen by God and endowed with two gifts: mercy directly from Him and knowledge taught by Him. His knowledge is not merely acquired learning but a special understanding granted by God, and his mercy is a divine favor that qualifies him for a role beyond ordinary human judgment. The verse therefore teaches that God bestows His grace and knowledge on whom He wills, that divine wisdom may transcend what even a prophet like Moses can grasp by his own knowledge, and that true guidance and understanding must be sought from God with humility.

translation: Moses said to him, "May I follow you so that you teach me of what you have been taught of right guidance?"
interpretation: This verse expresses Moses’s humility and his earnest desire to learn from the knowledge God had granted to al-Khidr. Although Moses was himself a prophet, he asks permission to accompany him as a student, recognizing that divine knowledge is not possessed equally by all and that true guidance may be learned from those whom God has specially taught. It teaches that seeking beneficial knowledge is a virtue, that one should approach teachers with respect and willingness to follow, and that the goal of such learning is not mere information but 'rushd'—right guidance, moral discernment, and closeness to God.

translation: He said, "Indeed, you will never be able to have patience with me."
interpretation: This means that the companion possessed of divinely taught knowledge is telling Moses that he will not be able to patiently endure what he is about to witness, because those actions will outwardly appear to contradict the sacred law and ordinary judgment. True patience here requires restraining objection and trusting that every act has a hidden wisdom, even if its justification is not immediately apparent. Thus the statement points to the limits of outward knowledge when confronted with the unseen purposes of God.

translation: And how can you be patient with that which you have not encompassed in knowledge?
interpretation: This verse teaches that patience becomes especially difficult when the wisdom behind events is hidden from human sight. It points to the limits of human knowledge: one may judge an outward action as wrong or harmful because its inward purpose and final outcome are unknown. True patience, therefore, requires trust in God’s wisdom even when His decree or the actions of His servants cannot be fully understood, and it cautions against letting incomplete knowledge produce hasty objection or impatience.

translation: You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any command.
interpretation: This is a statement of humble resolve: the speaker does not rely on his own strength to remain patient or obedient, but conditions his promise on God’s will, acknowledging that steadfastness and compliance are gifts from God. It teaches that even one seeking knowledge must approach a teacher with patience, submission to guidance, and awareness of personal weakness.

translation: He said: "So if you follow me, do not ask me about anything until I mention it to you myself."
interpretation: The verse teaches that accompanying a teacher or spiritual guide requires patience and trust: the follower should not hasten to question or object to actions whose inner wisdom he cannot yet grasp, but should wait until the guide himself explains them.

translation: So they set out, until when they had boarded the ship, he made a hole in it. He said, 'Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a grave thing.'
interpretation: This verse shows that human judgment based on outward appearances cannot grasp the hidden wisdom of God's decree. Moses, zealous for justice and the sanctity of life, condemns what looks like deliberate destruction and a threat to innocent passengers. Yet the act was done by divine command and was later revealed as a means of protecting the boat from a tyrannical king. The verse thus teaches that an apparent evil may conceal a greater mercy, and that true knowledge requires patience, trust, and waiting for God's purpose to unfold.

translation: He said: Did I not say that you would not be able to bear with me patiently?
interpretation: Al-Khidr is reminding Moses of the condition set before they began: Moses would not be able to remain patient with actions whose hidden wisdom he did not yet know. The question is a gentle reproach, showing that Moses’ objection came from judging by outward appearance, while al-Khidr was acting by divine command toward a greater purpose. The verse teaches that limited human knowledge cannot bear the deeds of divine wisdom until their explanation is made clear, and that true patience here means withholding judgment until the hidden meaning is disclosed.

translation: He said, "Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot, and do not burden me with hardship in my affair."
interpretation: This is Moses’s plea for leniency after he unintentionally broke the condition of silence he had accepted. It teaches that a sincere seeker may slip through forgetfulness or human weakness, and that a teacher or guide should respond with patience and mercy rather than harshness. Moses asks not to be taken to task for an honest lapse and not to be made to bear difficulty in his effort to follow and learn. The verse thus highlights humility, acknowledgment of one’s shortcomings, and the importance of gentleness in correcting and guiding others.

translation: So they set out, until when they met a boy, he killed him. He said, 'Have you killed a pure soul without [it being for] a soul? You have certainly done a dreadful thing.'
interpretation: This verse condemns the unjust taking of human life as a grave and abominable wrong, and it shows Moses’s moral outrage at what appeared to be the killing of an innocent child. It teaches that life is sacred and must not be destroyed without just cause, while also indicating that acts that seem evil to human eyes may carry a hidden divine wisdom beyond ordinary judgment.

translation: He said, "Did I not tell you that you would never be able to have patience with me?"
interpretation: This is a reminder and gentle reproach from the divinely taught servant: true patience in his company required Musa to withhold judgment concerning acts whose inward wisdom he could not yet see. It points to the limit of judging by outward appearances alone, since God’s hidden decree may place mercy, justice, or protection within what initially looks harmful or wrong. The verse therefore teaches that accompanying divine knowledge demands surrender of superficial judgment, and it exposes the human inability to endure what the outward intellect cannot yet justify.

translation: He said, "If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep company with me. You have already reached from me an excuse."
interpretation: This is Moses speaking to al-Khidr after Moses has twice objected to al-Khidr’s actions, despite having promised patience. Moses now admits that if he questions al-Khidr again, al-Khidr is fully justified in ending their companionship. The phrase "you have already reached from me an excuse" means that Moses himself acknowledges al-Khidr has a valid reason to separate from him, since Moses has repeatedly failed the condition of patience. It expresses Moses’s honesty, self-accountability, and recognition of the limits of human patience before the hidden wisdom of God.

translation: So they set out, until when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food, but they refused to offer them hospitality. Then they found in it a wall that was about to collapse, so he set it upright. He said, 'If you had wished, you could have taken a payment for it.'
interpretation: This scene conveys that the servant of God acts purely for God's sake, not for worldly gain or human reciprocity. Even when people are ungenerous, the righteous may still bring benefit to them, because the ultimate reward is with God. Moses' objection reflects the human calculus of justice and compensation, while Khidr's conduct points to a higher, divinely guided wisdom that transcends immediate reward and social expectation.

translation: He said, “This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not have patience.”
interpretation: This statement marks the end of the companionship: the repeated failure to remain patient and refrain from questioning has severed the condition of the journey. Yet it also carries a promise of disclosure—what appeared troubling or unjust in the events will now be explained according to its true purpose and divine wisdom, so that the outward acts are understood in light of their hidden ends.

translation: As for the ship, it belonged to poor people who worked at sea, so I intended to make it defective, for behind them was a king who was seizing every ship by force.
interpretation: This verse shows that God’s wisdom can be hidden behind apparent harm. The deliberate damaging of the boat was not cruelty but a protective mercy: the poor owners would have lost their livelihood entirely if the tyrant king had taken their seaworthy vessel by force. By allowing a lesser outward defect, Khidr preserved their means of survival from a greater injustice. The verse teaches that events may seem destructive while concealing divine protection, that God’s knowledge encompasses outcomes unseen by human judgment, and that safeguarding the weak and their livelihood may require accepting a temporary or apparent loss. It also warns against judging an act solely by its surface, because the deeper purpose may be known only to God.

translation: And as for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with transgression and disbelief.
interpretation: This verse explains that the boy whom al-Khidr killed would, had he grown up, have become a cause of grave harm to his believing parents—either by dragging them into sin and disbelief through their love for him, or by oppressing them with his own rebellion and unbelief. His death was thus an act of divine mercy: God removed an impending trial from them and, as later stated, replaced him with a child better in purity and dutifulness. The phrase “we feared” conveys the certainty of the harm from the perspective of al-Khidr and the divine wisdom behind the deed, not that God experiences fear.

translation: So we intended that their Lord should replace him for them with one better than him in purity and nearer in mercy.
interpretation: This verse conveys that the loss of the boy was not an arbitrary tragedy but part of a divine plan to give the believing parents a child who would be superior in spiritual purity and more dutiful, compassionate, and supportive toward them. It teaches that God's wisdom may remove what seems good in order to replace it with a greater good, and that apparent affliction can conceal mercy for the righteous.

translation: And as for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them; and their father was righteous. So your Lord willed that they should reach their maturity and bring forth their treasure—as a mercy from your Lord. And I did not do it of my own bidding. That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience.
interpretation: This verse teaches that God’s hidden mercy can operate through events that appear destructive or unjust. The wall was repaired to safeguard the rightful inheritance of two orphans, and God honored the righteousness of their father by preserving their future. It shows that divine wisdom governs all things, that a person’s righteousness can benefit their descendants, and that apparent misfortunes may be means of mercy. It also underscores that humans cannot judge God’s decrees by surface appearances; patience is required to perceive the deeper purpose.

translation: And they ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn. Say, 'I will recite to you about him a report.'
interpretation: This verse presents the divine answer to a question posed to the Prophet: knowledge of Dhul-Qarnayn is not left to human speculation but is communicated through revelation. The command “Say” shows that the Prophet’s response is authorized by God, and “I will recite to you” indicates that the following account is a revealed remembrance carrying lessons about power, justice, and accountability before God. Thus the verse establishes revelation as the criterion for knowing the affairs of earlier peoples and prepares the listener to receive the story as guidance, not mere legend.

translation: Indeed, We established him in the earth and gave him from every thing a means.
interpretation: God is the true source of all authority and provision: He grants whom He wills dominance and stability in the land, and He supplies him with the means, causes, resources, and pathways by which he can attain every intended objective. Human power and capability are therefore not independent achievements but divine gifts and trusts, and success depends on the ways God provides.

translation: So he followed a way.
interpretation: Dhul-Qarnayn set out again, using the means and resources God had granted him, and traveled along an accessible route toward another region.

translation: Until, when he reached the setting place of the sun, he found it setting in a murky spring, and he found near it a people. We said: 'O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish [them] or treat them with kindness.'
interpretation: This verse describes Dhul-Qarnayn’s westward journey and what appeared to him at the farthest western horizon: the sun seemed to set into a dark, muddy spring. It was not a literal astronomical setting into water, but a description from his human vantage point. There he encountered a people, and God granted him authority over them, testing how he would exercise power. The divine address—“either you punish or treat them with kindness”—shows that rulers are accountable to God and must govern with justice and moral responsibility. The verse thus teaches that political power and conquest are not ends in themselves; they are a trust from God, to be used with justice, restraint, and benevolence toward those who are receptive to good.

translation: He said, 'As for one who does wrong, we will punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment.'
interpretation: This verse lays out Dhul-Qarnayn’s principle of justice: wrongdoing and oppression may be restrained by worldly authority, but earthly punishment is not the final accountability. The wrongdoer must still return to his Lord, who alone knows the full reality of his deeds and will subject him to a severe, unprecedented chastisement. Thus the verse distinguishes between corrective justice in this life and ultimate divine justice in the Hereafter, emphasizing that no human penalty can substitute for the judgment of God or exhaust the gravity of persistent wrongdoing.

translation: But as for one who believes and does righteous deeds, he will have the best reward, and We will speak to him from Our command with ease.
interpretation: True success combines faith in God with righteous action. Such a person is promised al-husna—the best and most excellent recompense, namely God's pleasure and eternal bliss. The statement that God will speak to him from His command with ease means that God will address him gently and make his affair light, not burdensome; He will deal with him through kindness, facilitation, and mercy in this life and the Hereafter. So the believer's sincere effort is met with God's generous ease and gracious reward.

translation: Then he followed a way.
interpretation: This indicates that after reaching one stage of his journey, Dhul-Qarnayn proceeded by another route or means. It emphasizes that God grants capability and access to means, while the servant must actively use them to continue fulfilling the mission entrusted to him, moving from one task to the next with resolve and obedience rather than stopping at partial success.

translation: Until, when he reached the rising place of the sun, he found it rising upon a people for whom We had not made any shelter from it.
interpretation: This verse describes a stage in Dhul-Qarnayn’s journey: he reached the easternmost point where the sun appears to rise and found a people living fully exposed to its rays. Allah had not provided them any covering, shade, or structure to shield them from the sun. Their condition demonstrates the vastness of the earth, the diversity of human circumstances, and the absolute power and knowledge of Allah over all peoples and places. It also shows that Dhul-Qarnayn’s dominion and travel were under Allah’s authority, and that every community, however remote or exposed, remains within Allah’s knowledge and decree.

translation: Thus [it was], and We encompassed in knowledge what was with him.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God’s knowledge fully encompasses Dhul-Qarnayn—his power, his journeys, his armies, and all his affairs—so nothing about him or his accomplishments was hidden from God; his success and dominion were under God’s knowledge and will.

translation: Then he followed [another] way.
interpretation: This phrase marks the beginning of a further journey after a previous undertaking. “Way” (sabab) here means the means, route, or practical access that Allah had granted him. “Then he followed” indicates that he did not stop after one mission; he resumed striving, using the resources and capabilities placed at his disposal to reach another destination and fulfill further responsibilities. It teaches that divine help is sought through taking the available means, and that one should move from one beneficial task to another with resolve and reliance upon Allah.

translation: Until, when he reached between the two barriers, he found before them a people who could scarcely understand a word.
interpretation: This verse marks a stage in Dhul-Qarnayn’s journey: he arrived at a narrow passage between two barriers and encountered a people so isolated and linguistically unfamiliar that they could hardly comprehend spoken communication. Their inability to understand speech indicates their remoteness from other nations and sets the context for their need to communicate through others or by signs.

translation: They said, “O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the land, so may we pay you a tribute on condition that you make between us and them a barrier?”
interpretation: This verse conveys that corruption and aggression in the land are grave evils that a community may rightly seek to repel through just leadership and defensive means. It also teaches that a righteous ruler does not exploit people’s fear for personal gain; Dhul-Qarnayn’s refusal of payment in the following verses shows that authority and resources are to be used for protection, reform, and the relief of the oppressed, relying ultimately on God’s help.

translation: He said, 'What my Lord has established me in is better; so assist me with strength, and I will make between you and them a barrier.'
interpretation: This verse shows that true authority and provision come from God, and what He grants is better than any wealth or tribute people may offer. Dhul-Qarnayn refuses to take personal gain from the people and instead calls them to cooperate through effort and strength in building a protective barrier. It teaches that leadership should be used for the welfare and security of others, that collective work is needed to repel harm, and that reliance should be placed on God’s enablement rather than on material payment.

translation: “Bring me pieces of iron.” Then when he had leveled [them] between the two cliffs, he said, “Blow.” Then when he made it fire, he said, “Bring me, that I may pour over it molten copper.”
interpretation: This verse conveys the final stage of Dhul-Qarnayn’s defensive barrier: he gathers iron, arranges it to fill the pass between two natural mountain supports, then has it heated until it becomes like fire, and finally pours molten copper over it to bind and seal it into a massive, durable wall. Its meaning is that God-given authority must combine sincere reliance upon God with the fullest use of practical means, skill, and cooperation to establish security and restrain corruption. The iron symbolizes strength, the fire symbolizes refinement and transformation, and the molten copper symbolizes cohesion and sealing; the resulting barrier is not magic but a divinely guided use of created causes, and its effectiveness ultimately rests in God’s will.

translation: So they were unable to surmount it, nor were they able to pierce it.
interpretation: This verse declares that the barrier made by Dhul-Qarnayn was completely impassable to Gog and Magog: they could neither climb over it because of its height and smoothness, nor breach it by digging or piercing through because of its firmness and strength. Their failure in both directions shows that the barrier was not merely a physical obstacle but a divinely secured restraint, preventing their corruption from spreading beyond it until the appointed time.

translation: He said, 'This is a mercy from my Lord; but when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level with the ground. And the promise of my Lord is ever true.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that the barrier built by Dhul-Qarnayn was not a product of human power or permanence, but a mercy granted by Allah to protect people from corruption. Yet even this great sign will not last forever: when Allah’s appointed promise arrives, He will reduce it to dust and level ground. The verse affirms that Allah’s promises are inevitably fulfilled, and that every worldly means of protection, no matter how strong, is subject to Allah’s decree and will pass away, while His word remains true and unchanging.

translation: And We will leave them that day surging over one another, and the Horn will be blown, and We will gather them all together.
interpretation: On that day, after the barrier is breached, Gog and Magog will be left to surge like waves, flowing over one another in chaos. Then the Horn will be blown, and Allah will gather all of humanity and jinn together for the reckoning—a complete and comprehensive gathering from every generation.

translation: And We will present Hell that Day to the disbelievers, a clear presentation.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, God will make Hell openly visible and manifest to those who rejected faith, bringing them face to face with the punishment they denied, so that they witness its terrifying reality as the just consequence of their disbelief.

translation: Those whose eyes had been under a covering from My remembrance, and they were unable to hear.
interpretation: This verse describes those who rejected divine guidance: their inner sight was blocked from perceiving and remembering God, and their hearing was closed to receiving His revelation. It is not merely physical blindness or deafness, but a moral and spiritual incapacity caused by their persistent denial, so they neither reflect on God's signs nor accept the truth when it is conveyed to them.

translation: Do those who disbelieve think that they can take My servants as allies besides Me? Indeed, We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as a lodging.
interpretation: This verse condemns the false presumption of the disbelievers that they may take Allah’s created servants—such as angels, prophets, or righteous beings—as guardians, patrons, or objects of worship besides Allah. Those servants have no independent power to protect or benefit anyone, for they are themselves wholly subject to Allah. Therefore, those who persist in denying Him and rely on others besides Him are only preparing themselves for the destiny Allah has readied: Hell, described ironically as a “lodging” or place of reception, which will be their inevitable abode.

translation: Say, "Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in deeds?"
interpretation: This verse teaches that true loss is measured by the outcome of one's deeds before God, not by worldly success or visible effort. The "greatest losers" are those whose works are ultimately void because they are not grounded in faith and sincere submission to God, even if they may regard themselves as successful or virtuous. It warns that exhausting oneself in action without the right orientation to the Creator leads to ruin in the Hereafter, since deeds derive their value from being directed toward the truth and accepted by God.

translation: Those whose striving has gone astray in the life of this world, while they think that they are doing well.
interpretation: This verse describes people whose deeds are wasted because their efforts are directed away from the truth and from what God has prescribed, even though they sincerely believe they are on the right path and doing good. Their loss is not due to lack of effort or conviction, but because their effort is built on misguidance and false assumptions. It warns that sincerity alone is not enough; it must be joined with true faith and correct guidance. On the Day of Judgment, such people will find that their supposed good works carry no weight, and their self-confidence will not excuse their error.

translation: Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in the meeting with Him, so their deeds became worthless, and We will not give them any weight on the Day of Resurrection.
interpretation: This verse means that rejecting God's revealed signs and denying the encounter with Him in the Hereafter strips human actions of all true worth. Deeds that might outwardly appear good are rendered fruitless because they are not rooted in faith in the Creator and in accountability to Him. On the Day of Judgment, such people will have no weight or honorable standing before God; their claims, accomplishments, and very selves will carry no value in the divine measure. It establishes that eternal success depends not merely on outward works but on faith in God's revelations and in the meeting with Him.

translation: That is their recompense: Hell, because they disbelieved and took My verses and My messengers in mockery.
interpretation: This verse means that Hell is the just and fitting recompense for those who persist in disbelief and treat God's revealed signs and His messengers with contempt. Their punishment is not arbitrary; it corresponds to their willful rejection of guidance and their mockery of the very means by which God calls humanity to truth. It warns that ridiculing divine revelation and the messengers who convey it is a grave sin that leads to eternal loss, and it affirms that God's judgment is perfectly just.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds—they will have the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging.
interpretation: This verse means that those who combine true faith in Allah with righteous actions will be honored with the Gardens of Firdaws, the highest and most excellent part of Paradise, as their eternal home and welcoming gift. The word “nuzul” conveys the sense of prepared hospitality and generous reception, showing that their reward is not merely a place to stay but an honor bestowed by Allah, lasting forever.

translation: They will abide therein forever, never desiring any change from it.
interpretation: This means the people of Paradise will remain in eternal bliss without interruption or end, and their contentment will be so complete that they will never wish to leave it, exchange it for something else, or seek any alternative state or dwelling.

translation: Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as further supply.
interpretation: This verse declares the infinitude of Allah’s knowledge and words: no created means—even all the oceans turned into ink, and then another ocean like it added—can encompass or exhaust them. It teaches that divine knowledge, wisdom, commands, and decrees are boundless, while creation is finite and limited; human beings can never fully comprehend or record them. Thus it calls for humility before Allah and trust that His knowledge encompasses all things, and whatever He reveals is only a small portion of His unlimited wisdom.

translation: Say, "I am only a human being like you. It has been revealed to me that your god is one God. So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord."
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Messenger is a human being, not a divine figure; his true distinction is that revelation comes to him from God. The core message he conveys is absolute monotheism: there is only one God worthy of worship. Therefore, anyone who sincerely hopes to meet his Lord must combine correct belief with righteous action, and that action must be devoted purely to God alone, without directing any act of worship, devotion, or ultimate reliance to any created being alongside Him.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Kaf, Ha, Ya, Ain, Sad.
interpretation: The basmala begins with God's name and invokes His all-encompassing mercy; the following disjointed letters are among the mysterious openings of certain surahs, and their precise meaning is known only to Allah, serving as a sign of the Qur'an's divine origin and inimitability.

translation: A mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zechariah.
interpretation: This verse introduces the ensuing account as a remembrance and exposition of God's mercy, directing attention to how divine compassion and favor are manifested toward a devoted servant. It establishes that God's mercy is the governing reality in the event being recounted, and that Zechariah's servitude is the relational context in which that mercy is granted and made known.

translation: When he called upon his Lord with a hidden call.
interpretation: This teaches that supplication made in secret, with complete sincerity and concentration, is among the most intimate forms of worship; it is free from ostentation and closer to humility, and Allah hears the quiet call just as He hears the loud one.

translation: He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me, and my head has flared with white hair, and I have never been wretched in my supplication to You, my Lord."
interpretation: This is Zakariya’s supplication, in which he humbly acknowledges the frailty and decline of old age—his bones weakened and his head overtaken by gray hair—not as a complaint, but as a confession of need before God. He then appealsto God’s past goodness: never had he called upon his Lord and been left wretched, denied, or disappointed. The verse teaches that sincere prayer joins awareness of one’s helplessness with trust in God’s generosity, and that remembering previous answers to prayer strengthens hope for what is still sought.

translation: And indeed I fear the kinsmen after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir.
interpretation: This is Zakariyya’s supplication: he fears that after his death his relatives will not preserve the prophetic legacy, faith, and spiritual leadership of his house, and since his wife is barren, he asks God for a righteous successor from His special favor—not as something earned by natural means, but as a pure divine gift to continue the mission and uphold the religion.

translation: Who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Jacob. And make him, my Lord, pleasing [to You].
interpretation: This is Zakariyya’s supplication that the heir granted to him be a successor in the prophetic mission and religious legacy of the house of Jacob, carrying on faith, knowledge, and guidance after him, and that Allah make him righteous, accepted, and well-pleasing to his Lord.

translation: O Zechariah, indeed We give you good tidings of a boy whose name is John. We have not made anyone before him bearing that name.
interpretation: This verse conveys that God answers Zechariah's supplication with the glad tiding of a son named John (Yahya). The statement that no one before him was given this name highlights that John was specially chosen and divinely named, not merely following a prior namesake or familiar pattern. It points to the miraculous nature of his birth, the fulfillment of God's promise, and the honor granted to him as a prophet, while affirming God's power to bring about what is beyond ordinary causes.

translation: He said, "My Lord, how will I have a boy when my wife has been barren and I have reached extreme old age?"
interpretation: This is not a denial of God's promise but an expression of astonishment and a desire to understand how the divine decree will come to pass. It teaches that God's power is not limited by natural causes: He can grant a child despite barrenness and advanced age, and His command is fulfilled whenever He wills.

translation: He said, "Thus [it will be]. Your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and I created you before, when you were nothing.'"
interpretation: This verse is part of the exchange between Zakariyya and the angel. Zakariyya had expressed astonishment at how he could have a son given his old age and his wife's barrenness. The angel replies that Allah's decree is not limited by natural causes: what is impossible by human standards is easy for Allah. The final clause reminds Zakariyya that his very existence was brought about from nothing, so the creation of a child from a barren womb and an aged father is no greater miracle. It affirms Allah's absolute power and the fact that He creates as He wills, whenever He wills, without needing ordinary means.

translation: He said, "My Lord, make for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights, while being sound."
interpretation: This verse reports Zakariyya’s request for a confirming sign after being given the glad tidings of a son. The sign given to him was a miraculous withholding of ordinary speech toward people for three consecutive nights, even though he remained physically sound and free of disease or muteness. His inability to address people was not a natural ailment but a divine sign, while his tongue could still be used in remembrance and praise of God. Thus the sign served as both confirmation of the promise and a means of directing him toward devoted worship and gratitude.

translation: So he came out to his people from the prayer chamber and signaled to them: “Glorify [Allah] morning and evening.”
interpretation: This refers to Zakariyya (Zechariah): after Allah gave him the sign of being unable to speak to people, he came out from his private place of worship and, because he could not address them normally, conveyed by gesture or sign that they should glorify and praise Allah at dawn and at dusk. The “revelation” here means a signal or gestural communication, not prophetic revelation. The verse shows that his enforced silence was itself the sign, yet it did not stop him from directing his people to regular worship and remembrance of God, morning and evening.

translation: O Yahya, take the Scripture with strength. And We gave him judgment while a child.
interpretation: This means God commanded Yahya (John) to receive and uphold the revealed Book with serious resolve, obedience, and unwavering commitment, not casually or weakly. Then God mentions His favor upon him: He granted him al-hukm—sound judgment, deep understanding, and prophethood—while he was still young. Thus true wisdom and divine selection are gifts from God, and He can prepare and entrust someone with revelation even in childhood, while the human duty is to hold the Scripture firmly.

translation: And tenderness from Us, and purity; and he was devoutly righteous.
interpretation: God granted John a compassionate, merciful heart as a gift from His own presence, along with inward purity and spiritual purification. He was also deeply God-conscious, guarding himself from sin and living in reverent obedience to God.

translation: And dutiful to his parents, and he was neither arrogant nor disobedient.
interpretation: This verse describes true righteousness as inseparable from humble, loving devotion to one’s parents and from refusing the twin evils of domineering pride and rebellious disobedience. The word “birr” denotes far more than outward compliance: it is an ongoing, tender goodness that honors parents and seeks their welfare. To be free of “jabbār” means not using strength, status, or speech to coerce or belittle others; to be free of “ʿaṣiyy” means not breaking faith with God or those owed obedience and kindness. Thus the praised servant is one whose character is both gentle toward parents and submissive to God, never arrogant toward people nor defiant toward divine guidance.

translation: And peace be upon him the day he was born, and the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.
interpretation: This verse conveys God’s special greeting of security, mercy, and protection upon John (Yahya) at the three decisive moments of every human being’s existence: birth, death, and resurrection. It means he was kept safe from harm and divine displeasure when entering this world, will be kept safe at the time of his death from the terror and punishment that may accompany it, and will be kept safe on the Day of Resurrection from the fear and disgrace of that great gathering. Thus it affirms God’s guardianship over His faithful servant across all stages of life and after death, and it establishes the reality of the resurrection and accountability before God.

translation: And mention in the Book, Mary, when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place.
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet and every reader to commemorate Maryam in the revealed Book as a chosen and truthful servant. Her withdrawal to an eastern place was a deliberate seclusion for worship, purity, and devotion, not a rejection of family, but a turning away from worldly distractions toward God. The eastward location may refer to a chamber east of the Temple or her family’s home, and spiritually it signifies orientation toward light, chastity, and intimate service to the Lord. In that solitude, God prepared the miraculous conception of Jesus, showing that His power works beyond ordinary causes and that sincere seclusion can become the setting for His command.

translation: And she took, besides them, a screen. Then We sent to her Our Spirit, and he appeared to her as a well-proportioned man.
interpretation: This verse describes Mary’s seclusion and modesty: she withdrew behind a curtain to devote herself to worship and protect her chastity. God then sent Gabriel, called “Our Spirit” because he is a pure created spirit honored by God, and he appeared to her in the form of a sound, complete human being. He took this human form so that she would not be terrified by an angelic appearance and so that the encounter would be bearable for her as he conveyed God’s decree.

translation: She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you should be fearing Allah."
interpretation: This is Maryam’s immediate response when a man suddenly appeared before her: she turns at once to Allah, seeking His protection through His name “the Most Merciful,” and appeals to the visitor’s conscience by saying, in effect, that if he truly fears Allah he will not harm her. It expresses her chastity, her deep trust in Allah’s refuge, and her recognition that reverence for the Most Merciful is the strongest restraint against violating another’s honor.

translation: He said, "I am only a messenger of your Lord, to grant you a pure boy."
interpretation: This is the angel Gabriel speaking to Mary, clarifying that he is not acting on his own but is sent by her Lord. The promised child is Jesus, described as pure: created by God’s command without a father, righteous, blessed, and kept from the defilement of sin.

translation: She said, "How can I have a boy when no man has touched me, nor have I ever been unchaste?"
interpretation: This expresses Mary’s profound astonishment before a birth that cannot occur through any ordinary human cause. Her words affirm her purity and her complete lack of any natural means of conceiving, so the answer she receives will not be a explanation of biology but a declaration of God’s creative power: the child will come into being by divine command, as a sign for humanity, not through a father.

translation: He said, "Thus [it will be]; your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and [We will do so] that We may make him a sign for mankind and a mercy from Us. And it is a matter already decreed.'"
interpretation: This verse conveys that Allah’s creative command is not limited by ordinary causes: the birth of Jesus without a father is effortless for Him. The child is appointed as a clear sign of Allah’s power and as a mercy from Him, so people may recognize the Creator’s ability to bring life into being as He wills. The decree is already settled and inevitable; it is not a possibility but a determined matter that will certainly come to pass.

translation: So she conceived him, and she withdrew with him to a distant place.
interpretation: This verse refers to Maryam (Mary) after she received the glad tidings of Jesus. It means she became pregnant with him by Allah's command without a human father, then left her people and secluded herself in a far-off location. This withdrawal was to escape their accusations, to find solitude for the approaching birth, and to devote herself to Allah. It shows the miraculous nature of Jesus's conception and Allah's protection and provision for Maryam in her hardship.

translation: Then the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of the palm tree. She said, “Oh, would that I had died before this and had been a forgotten thing, utterly forgotten.”
interpretation: This verse portrays Maryam’s human vulnerability under the crushing pain of childbirth and her dread of the accusation and shame she expected. Her wish to have died beforehand is not a complaint against Allah’s decree or a loss of trust in Him, but an expression of extreme distress and a desire for obscurity rather than becoming a trial or scandal for her people. It shows that even the most righteous can feel overwhelmed, and that Allah, who later comforts and provides for her, does not reproach her for this cry.

translation: So he called to her from beneath her: "Do not grieve; your Lord has made beneath you a stream."
interpretation: This is a moment of divine reassurance to Maryam in her pain and fear. The call comes from beneath her—understood here as the newborn Jesus speaking by God’s power—comforting her and telling her not to sorrow, because her Lord has already placed a flowing stream beneath her. It means that God’s mercy and provision can be present precisely where His servant feels most helpless. The stream is a literal relief and a sign of God’s care, preparing her for the further provision of fresh dates from the palm tree and showing that her difficult trial is surrounded by divine help.

translation: And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates.
interpretation: This is a divine command and gracious provision to Maryam at the moment of her childbirth: Allah directs her to shake the palm trunk, and He causes fresh, ripe dates to fall for her. It teaches that even when a servant is in pain, weakness, and apparent isolation, Allah can bring forth sustenance through a small action He enables. The dates are both nourishment and healing for the mother after delivery, a sign of Allah’s mercy, care, and power to provide in a barren place, and a comfort that she is not abandoned but supported by her Lord.

translation: So eat and drink and be content. Then if you see any human being, say, 'Indeed, I have vowed a fast to the Most Merciful, so I will not speak today to any human being.'
interpretation: This verse expresses Allah's direct care and reassurance to Maryam after the miraculous birth: He provides her with sustenance and inner peace, and He instructs her to meet any human questioning with a vow of silence dedicated to the Most Merciful. The silence is not mere refusal to speak but an act of worship and trust, guarding her from dispute and allowing the miraculous event to speak for itself. It highlights Allah's mercy in comforting the distressed, His power to provide in impossible circumstances, and the dignity of Maryam's devotion through a fast of speech.

translation: Then she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said, “O Mary, you have certainly done a monstrous thing!”
interpretation: Their words are an accusation of unchastity, since they judged only by outward appearances and did not know of the miraculous birth. The term fariyya conveys something monstrous, unheard-of, and shocking, showing the intensity of their condemnation and the severe trial Mary faced. The verse sets the stage for Jesus’ defense of his mother, showing that God vindicates the innocent and that His acts may appear impossible to those who judge only by ordinary causes.

translation: O sister of Aaron, your father was not an evil man, nor was your mother unchaste.
interpretation: This is the reproach of Mary’s people when she returned with Jesus. By calling her “sister of Aaron,” they linked her to a righteous, priestly lineage—or to Aaron’s devout character—and then pointed to her father’s uprightness and her mother’s chastity to imply that her pregnancy could only have come from wrongdoing. The verse therefore records their false accusation and their failure to understand that Jesus’ birth was a miraculous act of God, not a violation of Mary’s purity.

translation: So she pointed to him. They said, 'How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?'
interpretation: This verse marks the moment when Mary, rather than answering her accusers directly, directs them to the child, and their astonished question exposes their assumption that a cradle-bound infant cannot speak. Its meaning is that God is about to manifest a clear miracle: the infant Jesus will speak in defense of his mother's honor and as a sign of his prophethood, showing that divine power is not limited by ordinary human expectations.

translation: He said, "Indeed, I am a servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet."
interpretation: This verse declares Jesus's true station: he is a worshipping servant of Allah, not God or a son of God, and Allah honored him with revelation and prophethood. His speaking as an infant was itself a miracle, and his words establish that his prophethood and the Scripture given to him were purely by Allah's decree, not by any divine nature of his own.

translation: And He has made me blessed wherever I may be, and He has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah as long as I live.
interpretation: This means that God made Jesus a source of blessing, benefit, and guidance wherever he was, not limited to one place or nation, and He bound him to the continual duties of prayer and zakah for his whole life. True blessedness therefore comes through worship of God and social responsibility toward others, and Jesus is shown as a devoted servant of God who remained under divine command throughout his life, not as a divine being or as one exempt from religious obligation.

translation: And dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me a tyrant, wretched.
interpretation: This means that God made Jesus deeply devoted, kind, and obedient to his mother, and did not make him arrogant, domineering, oppressive, or miserable. It affirms his humility as a servant of God and his honoring of Mary, and it denies any claim that he was a tyrant or wretched.

translation: And peace be upon me the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.
interpretation: This is Jesus declaring that God's peace, protection, and blessing accompany him at his birth, his death, and his resurrection, confirming that he is a servant of God who will die and be raised, and that God's favor is with him throughout these stages.

translation: That is Jesus, son of Mary—the word of truth about which they dispute.
interpretation: This verse concludes the account of Jesus’ birth by affirming that he is truly the son of Mary, a human prophet and servant of God, brought into being by God’s command without a father. It declares the Qur’anic account to be the true statement from God, while those who argue about Jesus’ nature—claiming divinity or sonship for him or rejecting him altogether—are disputing on the basis of doubt and conjecture. The truth is that Jesus is not God or the son of God; he is the Messiah, a messenger, and the miraculous birth does not change his created, human servanthood.

translation: It is not for Allah to take a son; glory be to Him! When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, “Be,” and it is.
interpretation: This verse declares that Allah is far above having a son, because His essence is absolutely one and self-sufficient, and offspring would imply need, likeness, or partnership. His power is not limited by ordinary causes: whenever He wills something, His command “Be” brings it into existence. Thus the miraculous birth of Jesus without a father does not make him a son of God; it only shows Allah’s unrestricted creative power, and Jesus remains a created servant brought into being by Allah’s decree.

translation: And indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.
interpretation: The verse presents Jesus as affirming his own servitude to Allah and calling all people to the worship of the One Lord. It excludes Jesus himself from divinity and directs worship exclusively to Allah. The “straight path” is the way of pure monotheism, prophethood, and obedient worship, which is the only path that leads to Allah’s acceptance and salvation.

translation: Then the factions differed among themselves; so woe to those who disbelieved from the witnessing of a great Day.
interpretation: This condemns the splintering of the People of the Book and others into conflicting parties concerning Jesus after the clear signs came to them—some deifying him, some denying his prophethood, some distorting his message. Their disagreement was not an excuse but a mark of disbelief. The 'great Day' is the Day of Resurrection, when every faction will be brought to the scene of judgment and will see the truth it rejected; woe, ruin, and punishment await those who persisted in unbelief at that awesome witnessing.

translation: How clearly they will hear and see on the Day they come to Us! But the wrongdoers today are in manifest error.
interpretation: On the Day they return to Us, the disbelievers’ hearing and sight will be intensely sharp, and they will plainly perceive the truth they had denied. Yet in this present life, the unjust remain in clear, obvious misguidance, heedless of the warnings and blinded by their own wrongdoing.

translation: And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter has been decided, while they are in heedlessness and they do not believe.
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet to warn people of the Day of Judgment, which is called the Day of Regret because the disbelievers and the negligent will then see the truth clearly and bitterly regret their rejection and wasted opportunities, though that regret will not benefit them. “When the matter has been decided” means the final decree has been carried out: judgment is over, people are separated into their eternal destinations, and no further action or repentance can change anything. Their present condition is described as heedlessness—being absorbed in worldly life and unaware of the coming reckoning—and as disbelief, meaning they refuse to accept the truth. The warning is therefore given while belief and righteous action are still possible, before the moment when only sorrow remains.

translation: Indeed, it is We who will inherit the earth and whoever is upon it, and to Us they will be returned.
interpretation: This verse declares that all worldly dominion, ownership, and existence are temporary; after every created being and possession passes away, Allah alone remains as the eternal Owner and Inheritor of the earth and all that is on it. Every soul will ultimately return to Him for judgment and accountability, so ultimate reliance, hope, and fear belong to Him alone.

translation: And mention in the Book Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet.
interpretation: Allah directs the Prophet Muhammad to recount and preserve the account of Abraham in the Qur’an, and He praises Abraham with two lofty qualities: he was a siddiq—utterly truthful, sincere, and firmly confirming the truth in belief, word, and deed—and a nabi, chosen by Allah to receive revelation and convey guidance. The verse thus establishes Abraham’s exalted rank and presents him as a model of truthfulness and prophethood, whose life and message are to be remembered, honored, and followed.

translation: When he said to his father, 'O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees nor can avail you in anything?'
interpretation: This verse presents Prophet Ibrahim’s gentle but firm call to his father to abandon the worship of idols. The idols are described as utterly powerless: they cannot hear those who call upon them, cannot see those who need them, and cannot bring any benefit or remove any harm. Therefore, worship should be directed solely to Allah, who alone hears, sees, and controls all affairs. Ibrahim’s use of the tender address “O my father” shows that his rejection of idolatry was rooted in compassion and sincere concern, not disrespect.

translation: O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to an even path.
interpretation: This verse teaches that true guidance is not inherited or based on seniority but comes from God through revelation. Ibrahim’s tender address to his father shows that inviting others to truth must be done with respect, humility, and compassion, even when correcting deeply held beliefs. The “even path” is the balanced way of pure monotheism and obedience to God, free from the extremes of idolatry and blind adherence to ancestral tradition.

translation: O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed Satan has ever been, to the Most Merciful, disobedient.
interpretation: This verse records Prophet Abraham’s loving warning to his father: do not submit to Satan or follow his command, for Satan has continually refused obedience to the Most Merciful. To worship Satan means to yield to his deception and obey him in disbelief, idolatry, or sin; and since Satan is persistently rebellious against God, taking him as a guide leads away from the mercy and obedience owed to the Compassionate Lord.

translation: O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would become an ally of Satan.
interpretation: This is Ibrahim’s compassionate warning to his father: he dreads that if his father continues in rejection of God, a chastisement from the Most Merciful—whose mercy he is refusing—may reach him, and he will thereby be joined to Satan as one of his followers and companions in ruin. The verse teaches that unrepented disbelief aligns a person with Satan, and that sincere concern for others should be expressed through gentle warning while leaving guidance to God.

translation: He said, 'Are you turning away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so abandon me for a long while.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the violent defensiveness of idolatrous tradition when confronted by pure monotheism. The father equates Abraham’s rejection of idols with a personal betrayal, threatens him with death, and demands separation, showing that false worship can harden the heart against both truth and family. Abraham’s calm persistence teaches that calling to God may provoke hostility even from those closest to him, yet the believer must remain steadfast, entrust the outcome to God, and separate from evil without abandoning hope for the other’s guidance.

translation: He said, 'Peace be upon you. I will seek forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has been ever gracious to me.'
interpretation: This is Prophet Ibrahim's response to his father's rejection and threat. It reveals that true faith produces gentleness, forgiveness, and patience: he does not answer harshness with harshness but gives a greeting of peace, continues to show compassion by promising to pray for him, and rests in the knowledge that his Lord has always been kind and attentive to him. The verse thus teaches that the call to God should be carried out with mercy and good character, and that a believer should remain hopeful in God's grace even when people turn away.

translation: And I will withdraw from you and from what you invoke besides Allah, and I will call upon my Lord. Perhaps I will not be, in calling upon my Lord, wretched.
interpretation: This is Abraham’s declaration of dissociation from his people and their false objects of worship. He turns away from all that is invoked besides Allah and directs his worship and supplication exclusively to his Lord alone. His words express hope and trust that his prayer to Allah will not leave him deprived, disappointed, or miserable; rather, he hopes for Allah’s response, blessing, and guidance. It teaches sincere monotheism, separation from false worship, and hopeful reliance on Allah in supplication.

translation: So when he withdrew from them and from what they worshipped besides Allah, We granted him Isaac and Jacob, and each We made a prophet.
interpretation: This verse describes how Abraham, upon abandoning his people and the idols they worshipped instead of Allah, was compensated by Allah with righteous offspring: Isaac and Jacob, both of whom were made prophets. It teaches that true sacrifice and separation from falsehood for the sake of Allah are never left unrewarded; rather, Allah may grant a person blessings that extend through generations, and He alone bestows prophethood as a favor upon whom He wills.

translation: And We bestowed upon them from Our mercy, and We made for them a truthful, exalted reputation.
interpretation: This means Allah favored Abraham and his descendants Isaac and Jacob with His mercy and granted them a high, enduring good name: they are remembered with truth and honor among later generations. Their “tongue of truth” is a metaphorical expression for truthful, exalted renown, not a physical tongue.

translation: And mention in the Book Moses. Indeed, he was chosen, and he was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet Muhammad to recount Moses’s story in the Qur’an as a lesson and reminder. It praises Moses as one whom Allah purified and selected for His service, combining in him the ranks of messenger and prophet. This signifies his elevated station, his sincerity and trustworthiness in delivering revelation, and that Allah’s choice of him was due to his devotedness and readiness to bear the message.

translation: And We called him from the right side of Mount Tur, and brought him near for intimate conversation.
interpretation: This refers to Moses, whom Allah honored by calling him from the blessed right side of the mountain and drawing him close in direct, private speech—an elevated station of nearness and divine favor.

translation: And We granted him, out of Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet.
interpretation: This verse means that God answered Moses’ supplication by giving him his brother Aaron as a prophet, not as something Moses earned or achieved, but as a pure act of divine mercy. Aaron’s prophethood served as a support and strength for Moses in delivering the message, sharing the burden of prophethood, and standing with him before Pharaoh and the Children of Israel. It shows that God’s mercy can manifest through companionship, brotherhood, and shared responsibility in calling people to truth.

translation: And mention in the Book Ishmael. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: Allah directs the Prophet Muhammad to commemorate Ishmael in the Qur’an as an honored figure. The verse praises Ishmael specifically for being faithful to his word and fulfilling his promises, a quality that reflects profound sincerity, patience, and righteousness. It also states that he held the rank of both messenger and prophet, meaning he was entrusted with conveying divine guidance to his people and receiving revelation from Allah, indicating his high station and steadfastness in God’s service.

translation: And he used to enjoin upon his family the prayer and the zakah, and he was, in the sight of his Lord, pleasing.
interpretation: This verse presents a model of prophetic household leadership: true righteousness is not confined to private devotion but extends to guiding one’s family toward the two foundational duties of prayer, which maintains the servant’s bond with God, and zakah, which purifies wealth and cultivates concern for others. The phrase “he was, in the sight of his Lord, pleasing” indicates that such consistent worship, moral instruction, and charitable responsibility earn God’s acceptance and good pleasure.
