It teaches that the most honored state before God is a life of obedience that also seeks to bring one’s nearest relations closer to Him.

translation: And mention in the Book, Idrees. Indeed, he was a truthful prophet.
interpretation: Allah directs the Prophet to commemorate Idris in the revealed Book and praises him as one who was profoundly truthful and sincere, whose words and conduct conformed to truth and divine guidance, and who was honored with prophethood. The verse establishes Idris’s lofty rank and presents truthfulness and prophethood as qualities worthy of remembrance and emulation.

translation: And We raised him to a high station.
interpretation: This means God elevated Idris in honor, proximity, and spiritual rank, granting him a lofty status and a place of nearness to Him.

translation: Those are the ones whom Allah has favored among the prophets, from the descendants of Adam, and from those We carried with Noah, and from the descendants of Abraham and Israel, and from those We guided and chose. When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell down prostrating and weeping.
interpretation: This verse describes the true nature of divine favor upon the prophets: it is not mere lineage or inherited status, but a reality of guidance, selection, and profound surrender to God. Although they came through noble prophetic lines—Adam, Noah, Abraham, and Israel (Jacob)—God singles out those whom He guided and chose, showing that honor with Him rests on His grace and their responsive faith, not ancestry alone. Their defining sign is their reaction to revelation: when the signs of the Most Merciful are recited, they do not turn away or remain hard-hearted; they fall in prostration and tears. That prostration and weeping express humility, awe, gratitude, and hearts softened by the knowledge of God. They are the model of those drawn near by divine mercy, and the verse teaches that authentic nearness to God produces lowliness before Him and tenderness before His revelation.

translation: Then there came after them successors who neglected the prayer and followed desires; so they will encounter ruin.
interpretation: This verse warns that a generation may inherit outward guidance yet lose the reality of prayer—by abandoning it, delaying it, or stripping it of sincerity and its due rights—and instead submit to their appetites. Such people will meet ruin: the loss of right guidance and a destructive end, because when prayer is lost, desire takes command of the soul and leads it away from God.

translation: Except those who repent and believe and do righteous deeds; those will enter Paradise, and they will not be wronged in the least.
interpretation: This verse means that God’s door of repentance remains open: a person is not doomed by past disbelief or sin if he turns back to God, affirms faith in Him, and confirms that faith with righteous conduct. Such people are given the promise of Paradise, and God’s judgment is perfectly just—their reward will not be reduced or denied, nor will they suffer any undeserved loss.

translation: Gardens of Eden which the Most Merciful has promised His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever to be fulfilled.
interpretation: This verse establishes that Allah’s promise of eternal gardens is a reality beyond human sight, believed in by faith in the unseen, and that His promise is absolutely certain—it will inevitably come to pass and be delivered without fail or hindrance, for Allah never breaks His word.

translation: They will not hear therein any idle talk, but only greetings of peace; and they will have their provision therein morning and evening.
interpretation: This verse describes the perfect condition of the people of Paradise: their hearing is protected from vain, false, or harmful speech, and the only words they hear are peaceful greetings and expressions of safety. Their sustenance is also guaranteed and continuously available, described as coming morning and evening to convey unending comfort, abundance, and honor, not any limitation or interruption.

translation: That is Paradise which We give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who were God-fearing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the eternal Garden is granted by God as an enduring inheritance to those among His servants who adopt taqwa—a vigilant God-consciousness that leads to obeying His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Thus, the decisive criterion for inheriting Paradise is not worldly lineage, wealth, or status, but being a God-fearing servant. The phrase “Our servants” shows that this honor belongs to those who submit to God, and taqwa is the spiritual condition by which one receives that promised inheritance through God’s favor and mercy.

translation: And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that. And your Lord is never forgetful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the angels are entirely under Allah's command and never act independently; their descent, delay, or arrival occurs only by His decree. All times and affairs—past, future, and present—belong to Him, so nothing is outside His knowledge or control. Allah is never forgetful, meaning He does not neglect His creation, forget His promises, or fail to send what is needed at the appointed time; any delay in revelation or help is according to His wisdom, not oversight.

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them; so worship Him and be constant and patient in His worship. Do you know any equivalent or namesake for Him?
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah alone is the Lord, Creator, Owner, and Sustainer of the heavens, the earth, and everything between them. Because He alone has absolute lordship and no partner in creation or governance, He alone deserves worship. The command to worship Him is therefore a call to sincere, exclusive devotion, and the command to be patient and constant in His worship means to persevere in obedience, prayer, remembrance, and monotheism despite hardship, opposition, or personal weakness. The rhetorical question, “Do you know any equivalent or namesake for Him?” means that no being is like Him, shares His divine names and attributes, or can be compared to Him in essence, lordship, or right to be worshipped. Thus the verse establishes pure monotheism and steadfast worship of the One who has no equal or rival.

translation: And man says, 'When I die, will I be brought out alive?'
interpretation: This is a rhetorical expression of disbelief and astonishment by one who rejects resurrection, doubting that life can be restored after death. It reflects the human tendency to judge divine power by worldly limitations, forgetting that the One who created him in the first place is fully able to bring him back to life.

translation: Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?
interpretation: This verse is a rebuke to those who deny the resurrection and a proof of God's power to recreate. It reminds the human being that his very existence began from nothing: God brought him into being when he was not anything. Therefore, the One who originated his creation is fully able to restore him after death and hold him accountable. It also calls for reflection, humility, and acknowledgment of the Creator's favor and might.

translation: So by your Lord, We will surely gather them together with the devils; then We will surely bring them around Hell on their knees.
interpretation: Allah swears by His own Lordship that He will certainly resurrect and gather all people, along with the devils, and then bring them encircling Hell, kneeling in humiliation and terror. This underscores the certainty of the Hereafter, Allah's absolute power over every created being, and the utter helplessness of those who denied Him when they are summoned for judgment.

translation: Then We will surely extract from every faction those among them who were most insolent toward the Most Merciful.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, Allah will sort out every group, sect, or band of followers and single out from it the ones who were most extreme and stubborn in their defiance of the Most Merciful. The verse declares that the leaders and worst offenders in disbelief and rebellion will be the first to be seized for punishment, because their guilt is greater and their example led others astray. It affirms that no faction can shelter its most guilty members from God's justice, and that He alone knows the varying degrees of defiance in every heart and will repay each according to the severity of the offense.

translation: Then We are surely most knowing of those who are most deserving of it [the Fire] to be burned therein.
interpretation: Allah affirms that He alone has complete knowledge of every soul’s inward and outward state. After declaring that He will separate out from every faction the most rebellious, He states that He knows best which particular individuals are most deserving to enter and suffer the Fire. The verse establishes that divine punishment is perfectly just: it is not based on outward labels or group affiliation, but on His exact knowledge of each person’s defiance, disbelief, and sins, and no one is assigned to it wrongly or beyond what they deserve.

translation: And there is none of you but will come to it. That is, upon your Lord, an inevitable decree.
interpretation: This verse means that every human being must be brought to the Fire on the Day of Judgment; this is an unavoidable event decreed by Allah. The righteous who feared Him will be saved and pass safely, while the wrongdoers will be left in it. So the arrival is certain for all, but its outcome differs according to faith and deeds.

translation: Then We will save those who feared Allah and leave the wrongdoers therein kneeling.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, after all creation passes over or is brought near the Fire, Allah will rescue the people of taqwa—those who were mindful of Him and avoided His prohibitions—while the wrongdoers who persisted in injustice and disbelief will be left in Hell, fallen on their knees in humiliation, unable to rise or escape. The verse distinguishes the outcome of the God-fearing from that of the unjust, showing that deliverance belongs to those who guarded themselves against sin, whereas the wrongdoers remain in punishment, subdued and despairing.

translation: And when Our verses are recited to them as clear proofs, those who disbelieve say to those who believe, “Which of the two parties is better in standing and better in assembly?”
interpretation: This verse exposes the disbelievers’ evasion of clear divine signs by shifting the discussion from truth to worldly status. Instead of answering the revelation’s call, they compare the social position, influence, and gatherings of the believing and unbelieving groups, implying that worldly honor and communal strength prove who is rightly guided. The Qur’an presents this as a false criterion: material rank, prestige, and impressive company are not evidence of spiritual truth or divine acceptance. True honor is not measured by one’s standing among people or the size and splendor of one’s assembly, but by faith, righteousness, and obedience to God. The verse also consoles believers, teaching them not to be shaken when the arrogant mock them or boast of their worldly advantages, because such boasting only reveals the emptiness of their argument before God.

translation: And how many a generation have We destroyed before them, who were better in possessions and appearance!
interpretation: This verse warns that worldly wealth, property, and outward splendor are not signs of divine favor or security. Earlier generations surpassed the disbelievers in material goods and physical appearance, yet God destroyed them for their rejection of the truth. So their riches and impressive forms did not protect them from punishment, nor did they make them superior before God.

translation: Say, 'Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension, until, when they see what they are promised—either the punishment or the Hour—then they will know who is worse in position and weaker in forces.'
interpretation: This verse addresses those who judge truth by worldly power, numbers, and enjoyment. It says that a person persisting in misguidance is not thereby proven right; rather, God may continue to extend him respite, wealth, and time as a test and gradual entrapment, not as a sign of honor. When the promised punishment or the Hour comes, the deception ends: such people will realize that their place is the worst and their supporters and forces are the weakest. So outward prosperity is no proof of divine acceptance, and apparent weakness in the believers is no proof of abandonment; true standing is decided by God in the end.

translation: And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance. And the enduring righteous deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in return.
interpretation: Whoever responds to Allah’s guidance and acts upon it is granted an increase of light, certainty, and steadfastness, so guidance becomes a growing reality in the heart rather than a static claim. The deeds that remain and are done sincerely for Allah—faith, worship, remembrance, and righteous conduct—are the most valuable before Him in reward and the best thing to which one can return in the Hereafter.

translation: Have you then seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said, “I will surely be given wealth and children”?
interpretation: This verse condemns the arrogant disbeliever who rejects God’s signs yet boldly claims that, even if resurrected, he will be favored with wealth and offspring. His claim is not based on faith or divine promise but on worldly prosperity and self-delusion. The question “Have you seen?” expresses astonishment at his audacity and warns that material blessings are not proof of God’s acceptance; they can be a test or temporary enjoyment. Such a person’s false confidence in wealth and children will not save him, and he will eventually stand before God alone, stripped of the very things he relied upon.

translation: Has he looked into the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?
interpretation: This is a rebuke to the one who claims certainty about his future reward despite his disbelief. It asks: Does he have access to the hidden knowledge of the Hereafter, or does he possess a binding pledge from Allah? He has neither. His assertion is therefore baseless, because no one can know the unseen or the final outcome except through revelation from Allah or a covenant He has granted—and His promise of salvation is not for those who persist in denial.

translation: No! We will record what he says, and We will extend for him a punishment extensively.
interpretation: This is a decisive divine warning: the boastful rejecter’s words are not overlooked but are precisely recorded, and his punishment will be stretched out, prolonged, and increased without relief. The verse establishes that Allah’s knowledge and justice are complete, that arrogant denial does not escape accountability, and that any seeming delay or worldly respite is not approval but only adds to the burden of responsibility. The punishment is described as “maddan” to convey extension, amplification, and continuity, matching the offender’s persistent falsehood and rebellion.

translation: And We will inherit from him what he says, and he will come to Us alone.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbeliever who boastfully claimed he would be given wealth and children. God declares that all he says and possesses will be taken from him and returned to God, and he will not retain any of it. On the Day of Judgment he will come before his Lord utterly alone—without wealth, offspring, helpers, or supporters—stripped of every worldly claim and resource, to face his reckoning individually and dependently. Thus the verse exposes the emptiness of worldly boasting and affirms that every soul ultimately returns to God alone.

translation: And they have taken besides Allah [other] gods, so that they may be for them a source of honor.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who adopt false deities besides God, hoping such beings will bring them honor, power, or protection. It exposes the futility of their reliance: what they imagine as a source of dignity will ultimately fail them, and on the Day of Judgment those supposed gods will disown their worshippers and become their adversaries.

translation: No indeed! They will disbelieve in their worship of them and will be adversaries against them.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the false deities and objects of worship that people associated with Allah will disown those who worshipped them. They will reject the worship offered to them and become enemies of their worshippers, not helpers, intercessors, or sources of honor. Thus the idolaters’ reliance on them will prove utterly false, and the very worship they expected to bring them nearness and benefit will return upon them as loss, regret, and punishment.

translation: Do you not see that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with constant incitement?
interpretation: This means that because the disbelievers have chosen rejection and persisted in it, Allah lets the devils be set upon them to provoke, lure, and urge them further into disbelief, sin, and hostility toward the truth. Their restlessness and agitation in falsehood are not a sign of strength or divine favor, but a consequence of their own corrupt choice and a step toward their punishment.

translation: So do not hasten against them; We are only counting for them a count.
interpretation: This verse reassures the Prophet and the believers that God’s punishment of the persistent disbelievers is neither delayed out of neglect nor to be demanded hastily. Their appointed time is fixed, and every moment of their respite is precisely counted by God. The delay is part of divine wisdom: it gives opportunity for repentance, establishes the proof against them, and ensures that when judgment comes it will be perfectly measured and just. Thus, believers should not be impatient for their destruction, because God is fully aware and has already set a precise term for reckoning.

translation: On the Day We will gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as honored delegates.
interpretation: This verse describes the honor and dignity of the God-conscious on the Day of Judgment: they will not be driven harshly, but gathered as noble guests and delegations proceeding toward the Most Merciful, moving toward His mercy, reward, and nearness. It contrasts the honorable arrival of the righteous with the humiliating treatment of the guilty.

translation: And We will drive the criminals to Hell, as a thirsty herd.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, those who persisted in sin and denied the truth will be forcibly herded toward Hell like livestock driven to a watering place. They will arrive exhausted and parched, expecting drink or relief, but what awaits them is the Fire. This shows the severity of divine justice: God’s power compels them, and their own deeds have made them deserving of that destination.

translation: They do not possess intercession, except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, no created being has any independent power or right to intercede for another. Intercession occurs only by Allah’s permission and only for those who have bound themselves to Him through a true covenant—namely, sincere faith in His oneness, acceptance of His messengers, and fulfillment of their pledge to Him. Such people are granted intercession by His mercy and authorization, while any claim of intercession based on false gods, idols, or human presumption is utterly void.

translation: And they say, 'The Most Merciful has taken a son.'
interpretation: This verse reports the false and grave claim made by some disbelievers that Allah, the Most Merciful, has a child. It is a denial of His absolute oneness and transcendence, for Allah is eternal and self-sufficient, far above having offspring, a consort, or any equal.

translation: You have indeed brought forth a monstrous thing.
interpretation: This is a severe divine rebuke declaring that the utterance just made is an enormity and a grave falsehood, utterly repugnant to God's majesty and transcendence. It marks the claim as a monstrous transgression, not a small mistake, because it attributes to God something wholly incompatible with His oneness and perfection.

translation: The heavens are almost torn asunder by it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains fall down in ruins.
interpretation: This verse conveys the immense gravity of ascribing a child to Allah: creation itself is depicted as recoiling in near-cataclysmic horror, because such a claim violates the absolute oneness, majesty, and transcendence of God. It teaches that falsehood about God is not a light matter but a reality-shattering affront, and it underscores tawhid—that God is utterly beyond any partner, offspring, or likeness.

translation: That they have attributed to the Most Merciful a son.
interpretation: This verse condemns the claim that Allah has a son as a monstrous falsehood against divine oneness. Attributing offspring to the Most Merciful implies need, likeness, or partnership, all of which are impossible for Allah, who is absolutely self-sufficient and incomparable. The verse identifies this false assertion as the reason for the cosmic horror described just before it, showing that such a claim is not a minor theological error but a violation of God's transcendent majesty and mercy.

translation: And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.
interpretation: This verse declares that attributing a son to Allah is utterly incompatible with His divine majesty and perfection. The name “the Most Merciful” emphasizes that His mercy is not derived from or dependent upon anyone, nor does His lordship require an offspring to sustain, inherit, or complete it. Taking a son would imply need, likeness to created beings, or a deficiency in His self-sufficiency, all of which are impossible for Allah. Thus the verse firmly negates any claim that Allah has a child and affirms His absolute oneness, transcendence, and freedom from all such attributions.

translation: There is no one in the heavens and the earth except that he will come to the Most Merciful as a servant.
interpretation: This verse declares that every created being—whether in the heavens or on the earth, including angels, prophets, and all whom people may wrongly associate with divinity or sonship—is entirely subject to Allah’s lordship and will be brought before Him on the Day of Resurrection as a servant, utterly dependent and submissive. None possesses independent authority, kinship with God, or equality with Him; all are His created servants under His dominion.

translation: He has certainly enumerated them and counted them with precise counting.
interpretation: This means that Allah’s knowledge fully encompasses every created being in the heavens and the earth; none is hidden from Him, and He has recorded and numbered each one exactly, without omission or error. The emphasis on counting affirms that resurrection, presentation before Him, and reckoning will be perfectly precise: every servant will be brought before Allah individually, and no one will be forgotten or left out.

translation: And all of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, every individual will be brought before God in a state of complete solitude, without any of the worldly attachments, supporters, or possessions that once gave them a sense of security or superiority. No one will be able to rely on lineage, wealth, or the advocacy of others; each person will stand accountable solely for their own deeds. This verse emphasizes that God’s judgment is entirely individual and just, and it calls every soul to prepare for that meeting through sincere faith and righteous action.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds — the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection.
interpretation: God will place a special love for them in the hearts of His creation and will honor them with His own love, so that sincere faith joined with righteous action becomes a cause of being beloved and accepted.

translation: So We have made it easy in your tongue only that you may give good tidings thereby to the righteous and warn thereby a people obstinately disputatious.
interpretation: God made the Qur’an easy by revealing it in the Prophet’s own language so that he could clearly convey it: bringing glad tidings to those who are mindful of God and obedient to Him, and warning a people who are stubbornly contentious, clinging to falsehood and disputing the truth. The ease of the tongue is both a mercy for conveying the message and a proof against those who reject it, while the God-conscious receive the good news and the obstinate are warned of the consequences of their defiance.

translation: And how many generations have We destroyed before them! Can you perceive from them any one, or hear from them any sound?
interpretation: This verse warns that many past peoples were utterly destroyed for their denial and rebellion. They left behind no visible remnant and no audible voice—neither a person to be seen nor even a faint sound to be heard. It consoles the Prophet and admonishes the disbelievers: the same fate can overtake them, and Allah alone remains ever-living and able to resurrect and judge all generations.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ta-Ha.
interpretation: Ta-Ha is one of the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) that begin certain surahs. Its precise meaning is known only to Allah; it serves to draw attention to the revelation, affirms the miraculous nature of the Qur'an, and challenges the Arabs—who used these same letters—to produce anything like it.

translation: We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to cause you distress.
interpretation: This verse declares that the revelation of the Qur'an is not meant to impose unbearable hardship, anxiety, or misery upon the Prophet Muhammad, nor upon those who follow it. It corrects any mistaken notion that receiving and conveying divine guidance requires self-destructive exhaustion, constant sorrow, or a joyless life. The Qur'an was sent as guidance, healing, mercy, and reminder; whatever difficulty the Prophet faced came from the resistance and hostility of his people, not from the Qur'an itself. Thus the verse establishes that true religion is not intended to oppress or crush the human soul, but to direct it toward what is right and beneficial, with ease and purpose.

translation: But only as a reminder for those who fear [Allah].
interpretation: The verse clarifies that the Qur’an’s purpose is to serve as an admonition and reminder that awakens hearts to God’s presence, accountability, and guidance. Its benefit is realized by those who possess reverent fear of Allah and are willing to heed the warning, reflect on its message, and align their lives with divine guidance.

translation: A revelation from the One who created the earth and the lofty heavens.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the Qur’an is sent down by the Creator of the earth and the exalted heavens, the One whose power and wisdom encompass all creation. It affirms that revelation comes from the same Lord who originated the vast universe, and therefore it is neither human invention nor vain speech; rather, it is authoritative guidance from the Sovereign Creator, whose majesty in creation testifies to His absolute right to command, guide, and be obeyed.

translation: The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah, the Most Merciful, is exalted and firmly established upon the Throne in a manner that befits His majesty alone, signifying His sovereign rule, supreme authority, and merciful governance over all creation, without resembling His creation or being confined by space.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.
interpretation: This verse establishes that absolute ownership, sovereignty, and authority belong exclusively to Allah over all realms of existence: the heavens, the earth, everything between them, and everything hidden beneath the ground. Nothing in creation—whether seen or unseen, above or below—is outside His dominion, knowledge, or control.

translation: And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is most hidden.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah’s knowledge is absolute and all-encompassing. Whether a person speaks openly or keeps something concealed in the heart, He knows it completely; indeed, He knows even the innermost thoughts, unspoken intentions, and hidden realities that are more concealed than ordinary secrets. Nothing can be hidden from Him, so worship and awareness of Him should not depend merely on outward speech or public appearance.

translation: Allah—there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute oneness of God: He alone is the sole object of worship, and no being, power, or concept shares in His divinity. The phrase “to Him belong the most beautiful names” means that all names and attributes of perfection, majesty, mercy, and beauty are exclusively His. They describe His essential perfection and are not merely titles but realities of His nature. Believers are therefore to know Him through these names, worship Him alone, and avoid attributing any divine name or attribute to any created thing.

translation: And has there come to you the story of Moses?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical question addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, meant to capture attention and affirm that the account of Moses is being revealed to him by God. It serves as reassurance and strengthening: just as God aided Moses against a tyrannical ruler and delivered the oppressed, He will aid His Prophet and the believers, and the outcome belongs to the God-conscious.

translation: When he saw a fire, he said to his family, “Stay here; indeed, I have perceived a fire; perhaps I can bring you a burning brand from it, or find at the fire guidance.”
interpretation: This scene shows Moses seeking a source of light and warmth for his family, but his words also reveal a deeper openness: he hopes either to bring back a burning ember or to find true guidance at the fire. God uses this ordinary human need and search to draw Moses toward the sacred encounter at the burning bush, where apparent fire becomes a means of divine address and where real guidance is found not in the fire itself but in the Lord who speaks from it.

translation: So when he came to it, he was called, “O Moses!”
interpretation: This is the moment when the seeking of a fire becomes a direct encounter with the Divine: the passive “he was called” veils the Speaker to magnify the awe of the event, while the intimate address “O Moses” signals election, nearness, and the beginning of prophethood. It teaches that revelation is not ultimately a human achievement but God’s initiative, turning an ordinary journey into a chosen meeting that commissions Moses and inaugurates his mission.

translation: Indeed, I am your Lord, so remove your sandals. Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.
interpretation: These are God's words to Moses at the burning bush. He establishes His lordship over Moses, commands him to take off his sandals as an act of humility and reverence, and declares that the place where he stands is the sacred valley of Tuwa, made holy by God's presence and the revelation being granted there.

translation: And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed.
interpretation: God is informing Moses that He has selected him for a special mission and honored him with direct revelation. Therefore, he must listen attentively and obediently to what is being revealed to him, receiving it with full acceptance, focus, and readiness to act upon it and convey it as commanded.

translation: Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.
interpretation: This verse is God's direct address to Moses, affirming His exclusive divinity and oneness. It commands that worship be directed to Him alone, and it defines prayer as a means of keeping His remembrance alive in the heart and life of the believer. The verse thus grounds true religion in tawhid and continuous conscious devotion to God.

translation: Indeed, the Hour is coming—I almost conceal it—so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the final Hour is absolutely certain, while its precise timing is hidden within God's exclusive knowledge so that no one can claim to know or control it. This concealment serves a moral purpose: every person is held in a state of accountability, and on that day each soul will be repaid exactly for what it intentionally pursued, whether good or evil. Thus the verse calls for vigilance, sincerity, and steadfast striving, since nothing done for good or ill will be overlooked in the final recompense.

translation: So let not those who disbelieve in it and follow their own desires divert you from it, lest you perish.
interpretation: This verse warns the believer that conviction about the Hour and accountability before Allah must not be weakened by those who deny it and are controlled by their appetites. Such people invite others to share their heedlessness, but following them away from revealed truth leads to spiritual ruin. The verse therefore calls for steadfast faith, discipline, and guarding one’s heart against the influence of those who live only for immediate desire.

translation: And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?
interpretation: This is a divine question not asked out of ignorance, but to focus Moses’s attention on the staff he already possesses, so that he may recognize that the ordinary object in his hand is entirely under Allah’s command and is about to become a clear sign of divine power. It teaches that Allah can turn humble, familiar means into great miracles, and it prepares Moses to receive revelation with attentiveness and awe.

translation: He said, 'It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I beat down leaves with it for my sheep, and I have other uses for it.'
interpretation: This verse shows Moses answering God with humble, practical honesty: he values the staff not as a mere object but as a means of support, provision for his flock, and service in his daily labor. His detailed reply reflects a shepherd’s intimacy with his livelihood and his reliance on ordinary means, even as God is about to turn that same staff into a great sign. It teaches that acknowledging lawful, everyday benefits is not contrary to trust in God, and that the believer should remain ready to surrender even familiar tools when God commands.

translation: He said, "Throw it down, O Moses."
interpretation: This is God's command to Moses to cast down the staff he was holding, so that the miracle of its transformation into a serpent could occur. It serves as a divine sign confirming Moses' prophethood and demonstrating that true power belongs to God, not to created instruments or worldly means.

translation: So he threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent, moving.
interpretation: This is a demonstration of Allah’s absolute creative power: the inanimate staff was instantly transformed into a living, moving creature, not merely an illusion or trick. The sign confirms Moses’ prophethood and serves as a decisive miracle before Pharaoh, showing that divine command operates beyond natural laws and cannot be matched by human magic.

translation: He said, "Take it and do not fear. We will restore it to its former state."
interpretation: This verse signifies that true courage in the prophetic mission comes from God's direct assurance: the frightening, miraculous transformation is not an independent threat but a sign wholly governed by God's will. Moses is commanded to take up what he fears, and the promise to return it to its original form shows that God can suspend and restore the natural order at will. The deeper meaning is that fear of created appearances must give way to trust in the Creator's sovereign control, and that divine reassurance prepares the prophet to carry out his mission before Pharaoh.

translation: And press your hand to your side; it will come out white without blemish, as another sign.
interpretation: This is a command from God to Moses to place his hand under his arm or against his side, and it will emerge shining white, free from any disease or defect such as leprosy. It is called “another sign” because it accompanies the miracle of the staff. Its meaning is that God can suspend the ordinary properties of the body and produce a luminous, harmless miracle as clear proof of Moses’ prophethood and of God’s power over all things.

translation: That We may show you [some] of Our greatest signs.
interpretation: Allah is addressing Moses, explaining that the miracles just granted—the staff turning into a serpent and the hand becoming white—are not ends in themselves but means of giving Moses direct, sensory proof of God's absolute power and of his own selection as a prophet. It teaches that divine signs are bestowed to establish certainty in the recipient and to prepare him for the heavy task of confronting Pharaoh, so that his resolve rests not on his own ability but on the overwhelming evidence of God's Lordship.

translation: Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.
interpretation: God commands Moses to confront Pharaoh because Pharaoh has overstepped the limits set by God through arrogance, tyranny, and self-deification. The verse establishes that the divine call must be delivered even to the most powerful tyrant, and that Pharaoh’s transgression is the very reason he must be warned and summoned back to submission to God.

translation: He said, "My Lord, expand for me my breast."
interpretation: This is Moses asking God to grant him inner spaciousness, calm, and strength of heart. It means: remove the tightness, anxiety, and inadequacy I feel, and fill my heart with confidence, patience, and readiness so I can bear the burden of the mission and speak with clarity and courage.

translation: And make my affair easy for me.
interpretation: This is Moses’ supplication to God to remove hardship from his mission and to facilitate every aspect of the task entrusted to him, so that he may fulfill the heavy responsibility of conveying God’s message with ease and success.

translation: And untie the knot from my tongue.
interpretation: This is a supplication by Moses asking God to remove the impediment or tightness in his tongue, so that his speech may become clear, fluent, and effective in conveying the divine message.

translation: so that they may understand my speech
interpretation: This is Moses’s supplication that God grant him clear, effective speech so that his hearers—Pharaoh and his people—may grasp the divine message; it teaches that prophetic communication aims at understanding and that removing impediments to comprehension is part of the messenger’s preparation.

translation: And appoint for me a helper from my family.
interpretation: This is a supplication by Moses asking Allah to grant him a trusted assistant from his own kin. The request shows that carrying a divine mission requires not only personal resolve but also loyal support; seeking such help through prayer is an act of humility and reliance upon Allah. A "wazir" here is one who shares the burden, strengthens the caller, and helps fulfill the responsibility, and choosing him from family points to the value of kinship in providing sincere, dependable support for matters of faith.

translation: Aaron, my brother.
interpretation: Moses names Aaron as his brother and asks God to make him a companion and support in his prophetic mission, highlighting the closeness of their kinship and the need for shared strength in delivering the divine message.

translation: Strengthen my back through him.
interpretation: This is Moses asking Allah to make Aaron a means of firmness, support, and resolve for him in bearing the prophetic mission. It teaches that reliance on Allah does not negate the need for righteous companionship; rather, Allah often strengthens His servants through those who share their faith and purpose, and seeking such support for obedience to Allah is an act of humility and wisdom.

translation: And make him share in my affair.
interpretation: This is Moses’s request that God join Aaron with him in the prophetic mission, so that Aaron would assist him, share the burden of delivering the message, and strengthen him in confronting Pharaoh and bearing the responsibilities of prophethood.

translation: So that we may glorify You much.
interpretation: This expresses that the purpose of the requested support and companionship is devoted, abundant worship: continually declaring God’s transcendence and praise, and making His glorification the enduring aim of speech, action, and mission rather than a passing or minimal act.

translation: and we remember You much
interpretation: It signifies a commitment to constant, abundant remembrance of God—mentioning Him with the heart and tongue in every state—as an act of worship, a means of seeking His aid, and a way of keeping one’s purpose sincerely devoted to Him.

translation: Indeed, You are ever Seeing of us.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah’s sight and knowledge encompass His servants at every moment: He sees their outward actions and inward intentions, knows their needs and weaknesses, and nothing about them is hidden from Him. It is therefore a declaration of complete reliance upon Allah’s watchful care and a recognition that He will guide and assist those who sincerely seek His help.

translation: He said, "You have been granted your request, O Moses."
interpretation: This signifies that God responds to the sincere supplication of His chosen servant with immediate acceptance, granting not only the outward means needed for the mission but also the inner strength, reassurance, and support that make obedience and steadfastness possible.

translation: And indeed We conferred a favor upon you another time.
interpretation: God is reminding Moses of an earlier act of grace and protection shown to him before the present moment. This favor was His saving and nurturing care over Moses in his infancy—when He inspired his mother to entrust him to the river, then returned him to her, and later delivered him from Pharaoh’s oppression—so that Moses would recognize that the God now speaking to him had always been guiding and caring for him.

translation: When We inspired to your mother what was inspired.
interpretation: This verse recalls God’s hidden guidance placed directly into the heart of Moses’ mother at a moment of extreme danger. The “inspiration” here is not prophethood or a new scripture, but a saving instruction and reassurance from God: she was moved to entrust her infant to the river and was promised that he would be returned to her and made one of God’s messengers. It shows that God’s care for His chosen servants begins before they are aware, and that He can inspire whom He wills, even a grieving mother, to become an instrument of His plan.

translation: Place him in the chest, then cast him into the river, and let the river cast him to the shore; an enemy to Me and an enemy to him will take him. And I cast upon you love from Me, and so that you may be brought up under My eye.
interpretation: This verse reveals that God's providence uses even hostile forces to accomplish His purpose. The mother's act of surrender is met with divine assurance: the child will not be lost but will be taken by Pharaoh, the very enemy of God and of the child, yet God will cast love upon him so that he is received with affection and nurtured under God's direct care. Thus the verse teaches that true protection is not the absence of danger but being under God's watchful eye, and that God can turn an enemy's grasp into the means of preserving and preparing His chosen servant.

translation: When your sister walked along and said, 'Shall I show you someone who will nurse him and take care of him?' So We returned you to your mother, that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, so We saved you from the distress, and We tried you with trials. Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan. Then you came at the appointed time, O Moses.
interpretation: This verse is a divine reminder to Moses of God's uninterrupted providence from infancy to the moment of his commissioning. The sister's initiative and the return to his mother show that God arranges means and protects the bond of mercy; the mother's joy is explicitly honored. The killing and subsequent escape from grief, followed by trials upon trials and years in Madyan, indicate that even painful and confusing episodes were not accidents but stages of formation under God's decree. Moses' arrival at an appointed measure means his prophethood came precisely when God willed, after a lifetime of preparation. The passage teaches that God's care may work through hardship, that He can turn danger into deliverance, and that He prepares chosen servants through experience before entrusting them with revelation and mission.

translation: And I have chosen you for Myself.
interpretation: In this verse, God addresses Moses, declaring that He has specially selected, cultivated, and dedicated him exclusively to His service and nearness. It signifies that Moses was chosen to carry out God’s purpose, to receive His revelation, and to stand before Him with a mission directed solely to God’s will, not to any human agenda.

translation: Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not slacken in My remembrance.
interpretation: This is a divine command to Moses and Aaron to go together to Pharaoh armed with God’s miraculous signs, coupled with an instruction not to grow weary or negligent in remembering God. Its meaning is that the success of their mission depended on continual awareness of God, reliance upon Him, and steadfastness in calling to Him; they were not to let fear, delay, or hardship weaken their devotion, courage, or perseverance in conveying His message.

translation: Go, both of you, to Pharaoh. Indeed, he has transgressed.
interpretation: This is a divine command to Moses and Aaron to confront Pharaoh, identifying the cause of the mission as Pharaoh’s tyrannical self-exaltation and transgression against God’s limits. It teaches that oppressive power must be addressed with prophetic truth, and that God’s messengers are sent with clarity and resolve because the tyrant’s condition is known to God and his oppression cannot be left unchallenged.

translation: So speak to him with gentle speech, so that he may remember or fear.
interpretation: This verse instructs Moses and Aaron to address Pharaoh with mildness, kindness, and respect rather than harshness or provocation, even though he was a tyrant. The purpose of gentle speech is to appeal to his conscience and reason, hoping he might take heed of the reminder, repent, or at least fear God's punishment. It teaches that conveying truth should be done with wisdom and softness, since harshness often hardens hearts, while gentleness may open them. At the same time, the phrase “perhaps he may remember or fear” shows that guidance belongs ultimately to God; the speaker’s duty is to deliver the message in the best manner, while the result rests with Allah.

translation: They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will act excessively against us or that he will transgress."
interpretation: This verse expresses the natural human fear felt by Moses and Aaron as they prepare to confront Pharaoh. They do not fear disobeying God’s command; rather, they fear Pharaoh’s response—either that he will hastily punish or harm them before they can deliver the message, or that he will grow even more arrogant and tyrannical. Their words teach that fear is not itself a lack of faith when it is brought honestly before God; true reliance on Him means turning such fear into prayer and continuing to fulfill the duty entrusted to them, trusting that God’s protection and command take precedence over the power of any earthly ruler.

translation: He said, "Do not fear. Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see."
interpretation: God reassures Moses and Aaron that they should not be afraid of Pharaoh or his threat, because He is with them through His support, protection, and aid. His statement that He hears and sees means He is fully aware of their situation, hears their words and prayers, sees their actions and the actions of their enemy, and will not abandon them or let them be overcome.

translation: So go to him and say, 'Indeed, we are messengers of your Lord, so send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord, and peace be upon whoever follows guidance.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the pattern of divine advocacy: God's messengers confront oppressive authority not with violence but with a clear declaration of their commission, a demand for justice and freedom for the oppressed, and the offer of a sign. The final phrase indicates that true peace is not a political concession but a fruit of following guidance; Pharaoh's rejection places him outside that peace.

translation: Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment will be upon whoever denies and turns away.
interpretation: This is a warning from Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh: God has informed them by revelation that His punishment falls upon the one who rejects the truth after it has reached him and turns away from accepting it and obeying God. Denial and turning away are the two causes of ruin; whoever denies the messenger and refuses to submit deserves the chastisement. The verse thus teaches that divine punishment is not arbitrary but is the consequence of willful rejection of guidance and withdrawal from faith and obedience.

translation: [Pharaoh] said, "Then who is the Lord of you two, O Moses?"
interpretation: This is Pharaoh’s challenge to Moses and Aaron, asking who this Lord is whom they call to worship. By addressing Moses specifically, he singles him out as the main speaker and tries to undermine his authority, while implying that no lord should be recognized besides Pharaoh himself. It expresses arrogant denial of God’s lordship and a rhetorical attempt to intimidate them.

translation: He said: Our Lord is the One who gave every thing its creation, then guided.
interpretation: This means that God is the sole Lord who originated and formed every created thing, giving each its particular nature, form, and capacities, and then guided it toward the fulfillment of its purpose: He directed every creature to what is suited to it, to the means of its sustenance and survival, and—for those endowed with reason and moral responsibility—to the path of right guidance and knowledge of Him.

translation: He said, "Then what is the case of the former generations?"
interpretation: This is Pharaoh's challenge to Moses: he asks what will happen to the peoples who lived and died before this new message, implying that if they were not held accountable, then neither should his own generation be, or that God's guidance cannot be newly revealed. The verse thus raises the question of how past nations relate to divine judgment, and Moses' answer—that their knowledge is with God, who neither errs nor forgets—affirms that God alone knows their state and will judge all generations with perfect justice.

translation: He said: “Its knowledge is with my Lord, in a Book. My Lord does not err, nor does He forget.”
interpretation: This means that the full account of every generation—its deeds, circumstances, and final destiny—is preserved with God in a guarded Record. His knowledge is perfect and active: He neither overlooks any matter nor lets it slip from His memory. Therefore, no soul’s history is hidden from Him, and His judgment of all people will be exact and just.

translation: [It is He] who has made for you the earth as a bed and threaded for you therein roads and sent down water from the sky; and We have brought forth thereby diverse pairs of plants.
interpretation: This verse directs attention to God’s exclusive creative power and ongoing provision: He alone subdued the earth as a place of rest and habitation, made it traversable through pathways for human movement and livelihood, and sends down rain from the sky to produce every kind of paired vegetation. The shift from speaking about Him in the third person to “We” in the final clause underscores His majesty and direct involvement in bringing life out of the earth. Thus the verse presents these visible blessings as signs that should lead people to recognize their Creator, depend upon Him alone, and reflect on His ability to bring forth life and diverse forms from the earth, which also attests to His power over resurrection.

translation: Eat and pasture your livestock. Indeed, in that are signs for people of understanding.
interpretation: This verse directs people to benefit from God’s provision and to care for their livestock, then calls them to reflect on the order, sustenance, and interdependence in creation. Such provision and balance are clear evidence of God’s power, mercy, and wisdom, but only those who use their intellect rightly—those who look beyond mere consumption and see the Creator’s hand—will truly understand and benefit from these signs.

translation: From it [the earth] We created you, and into it We return you, and from it We will bring you forth once again.
interpretation: This verse declares that the earth is the material origin of human creation, the place to which every person returns through death and burial, and the source from which God will bring humanity out again for resurrection. Its meaning is that human beings are not self-created or self-sustaining: their beginning is from lowly dust, their end is a return to it, and their final emergence from it depends entirely on God’s power. Thus it combines a call to humility with a certainty of death and a firm affirmation of bodily resurrection and accountability before God.

translation: And We certainly showed him all Our signs, but he denied and refused.
interpretation: This verse condemns the willful rejection of clear divine proofs: despite being shown every sign of Allah’s power and truth, the addressee did not merely doubt or fail to understand, but deliberately pronounced them false and arrogantly refused to submit. It exposes the moral corruption of denying what is manifestly true when it demands humility, repentance, and obedience.

translation: He said, "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land by your magic, O Moses?"
interpretation: This is Pharaoh's rejection of Moses' prophetic mission: he recasts God's signs as sorcery and portrays Moses as a subversive outsider who wants to dispossess the Egyptians. It reveals the oppressor's arrogance, his fear of losing dominance, and his attempt to discredit the truth by calling it magic, while showing that those entrenched in power often resist a call to faith and justice by accusing the messenger of corrupting the land.

translation: So we will surely bring you magic like it; so appoint between us and you a meeting place which we will not fail to keep—neither we nor you—at a place equally suitable.
interpretation: This is Pharaoh's defiant response to Moses after witnessing the signs: instead of recognizing them as divine proofs, he dismisses them as sorcery and challenges Moses to a public contest. His insistence on a fixed appointment and a neutral location reveals his arrogant confidence in falsehood and his attempt to publicly defeat the truth. Yet the verse also exposes how those who reject God's messengers often reduce clear signs to mere magic or trickery, opposing revelation with fabricated power and treating the truth as a matter of rivalry rather than submission.

translation: He said, 'Your appointment is the Day of the Festival, and that the people be gathered at forenoon.'
interpretation: This appointment was deliberately set for a day of public festivity and a morning hour so that the confrontation would be witnessed by the greatest number of people, making the divine sign manifest openly and cutting off any excuse of concealment or private trickery.

translation: So Pharaoh turned away, gathered his scheme, then came.
interpretation: This verse describes Pharaoh turning his back on the truth after witnessing clear signs, choosing instead to muster all his sorcery, supporters, and deceptive devices against Moses. It highlights his arrogance and reliance on fabricated power, and that he then proceeded to the appointed contest, only to be defeated by the truth.

translation: Moses said to them, "Woe to you! Do not invent a lie against Allah, lest He destroy you with a punishment. And whoever invents a lie has indeed failed."
interpretation: Moses warned his opponents—those who were rejecting God’s signs and opposing His message—not to fabricate falsehoods about God, such as denying His revelation, calling His truth magic, or claiming divine authority for their own inventions. If they did so, God would destroy them with a punishment, and any person who invents lies against God ultimately ends in utter loss and disappointment. The verse teaches that falsely attributing anything to God is a serious sin whose consequence is ruin, and it calls people to truthfulness, reverence, and acceptance of divine revelation.

translation: Then they disputed their affair among themselves and concealed the private conversation.
interpretation: This describes the magicians and Pharaoh’s people when Moses warned them: they fell into disagreement over how to confront him, then whispered secretly among themselves so that Moses would not hear their plotting. Their secret counsel reveals their confusion and fear, and that their scheme against Moses was not based on truth or unity.

translation: They said, 'Indeed, these two are surely magicians who want to drive you out of your land by their magic and do away with your exemplary way.'
interpretation: The verse exposes how tyrannical power defends itself: it brands the truth as sorcery and subversion, accuses the messengers of plotting to destroy the people’s noble order, and uses fear of losing status and tradition to turn hearts against divine guidance. In reality, it is Pharaoh’s system that suppresses and exploits; the accusation is a projection meant to preserve its own privilege and prevent liberation.

translation: So gather your plot, then come in a row; and whoever prevails today will indeed succeed.
interpretation: These are the words of Pharaoh’s magicians urging one another to unite their magic and confront Moses in a single rank. They measure success purely by worldly victory and dominance: whoever overcomes his opponent is deemed successful. The verse exposes a limited, power-centered view of success and sets the stage for its reversal, since Allah’s truth prevails through Moses and the magicians are ultimately defeated. True success is not merely rising above others by force or cunning; it is standing with divine truth.

translation: They said, "O Moses, either you throw [your staff], or we will be the first to throw."
interpretation: The sorcerers address Moses with a challenge, offering him the choice to begin the contest or else letting them set the precedent. This reveals their confidence in their magic and their attempt to dictate the terms, yet it also sets the stage for the divine miracle that will expose their arts as false.

translation: He said, "Rather, you throw." Then suddenly their ropes and staffs seemed to him, by their magic, to be moving.
interpretation: This verse exposes the nature of the sorcerers’ craft: it was not a real transformation of ropes and staffs into living serpents, but an illusion cast upon the sight. Their magic could deceive perception and make the inanimate appear to move, yet it could not change creation or produce true life. Moses’ invitation for them to throw first reflects his certainty in God’s power and sets the stage for the true miracle that follows, where his staff becomes a real serpent by divine command and swallows their false wonders. Thus, the verse distinguishes between counterfeit magic, which only tricks the eyes, and prophetic miracles, which are real acts of God.

translation: So Moses conceived a fear within himself.
interpretation: This indicates that prophetic closeness to God does not abolish natural human emotion. Moses’ fear was not disbelief or distrust in God, but a passing human apprehension caused by the alarming display of the sorcerers’ illusion. It teaches that inward fear may arise even in the righteous, yet it becomes blameworthy only if it leads to despair or disobedience; God therefore immediately reassured Moses of His help and supremacy.

translation: We said, 'Do not fear. Indeed, you are the superior.'
interpretation: This is God's reassurance to Moses at the moment of confrontation with Pharaoh's magicians: the apparent power of sorcery and tyranny must not cause him to fear, because divine support places him above them. It teaches that true superiority belongs to God's cause, and whoever stands with God will prevail over falsehood, no matter how overwhelming it may seem.

translation: And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have made. What they have made is only the trick of a magician, and the magician will not succeed wherever he goes.
interpretation: This verse conveys that the power given to Moses is a divine miracle, not magic. When he throws his staff, it consumes the sorcerers’ fabricated illusions, exposing their works as mere deception. The verse teaches that sorcery, however impressive, has no lasting power or divine blessing and cannot achieve true success. In the end, falsehood is defeated by God’s command, and those who rely on deception for gain or authority will fail, regardless of their skill or position.

translation: Then the magicians fell down in prostration, saying, 'We believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa.'
interpretation: This verse marks the moment when the Egyptian magicians, summoned to challenge Moses, recognized that what they witnessed was not human magic but a divine sign. Overwhelmed by the truth, they prostrated themselves and declared faith in the Lord of Aaron and Moses. Their words deliberately identify God as the Lord of Moses and Aaron, rejecting Pharaoh’s claim to lordship and showing that true submission belongs to Allah alone. Their prostration signifies a profound transformation: those who came as opponents of Moses became believers, demonstrating that divine signs can penetrate even hardened hearts and that faith can arise suddenly when the truth becomes unmistakable.

translation: He said, "You believed him before I gave you permission. Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees, and you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more lasting."
interpretation: This is Pharaoh's tyrannical response to the magicians' faith: unable to refute the truth, he calls it a conspiracy and claims Moses was their master in magic, then uses mutilation and crucifixion as instruments of terror to restore his dominance. The verse exposes how oppressive power resorts to cruelty and intimidation when it loses the argument, and it sets Pharaoh's threatened punishment against the punishment of God; though he boasts that his retribution is harsher and more enduring, his power is only worldly and temporary, while God's punishment and reward are truly more severe and everlasting.

translation: They said, “We will never prefer you over what has come to us of clear proofs, and over He who created us. So decree whatever you are to decree. You only decree concerning this worldly life.”
interpretation: This verse expresses the believers’ unwavering commitment to God over any earthly tyrant: the clear evidences they have received and the awareness of God as their Creator outweigh Pharaoh’s threats and promises. They tell him that his power to command, punish, or judge is confined to this temporary worldly life; it cannot reach the eternal realm or determine their final outcome. Therefore they entrust the ultimate judgment to God and refuse to abandon faith for the sake of escaping worldly harm.

translation: Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, so that He may forgive us our sins and what you compelled us to do of magic. And Allah is better and more enduring.
interpretation: The sorcerers, after witnessing Moses' sign, declare faith in God and seek His forgiveness for their past sins and for the magic they practiced under Pharaoh's coercion. They recognize that Pharaoh's power and threats are temporary, while God's forgiveness, reward, and justice are superior and everlasting.

translation: Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, then indeed for him is Hell, wherein he neither dies nor lives.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of those who meet their Lord persisting in disbelief and grave sin: they are condemned to Hell, where they neither die completely so as to find rest from torment, nor live a true, beneficial life. Their state is an unending punishment between death and life, emphasizing the severity and eternity of the loss suffered by those who reject God and persist in wrongdoing.

translation: And whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds — then those will have the highest ranks.
interpretation: This verse teaches that ultimate success before God depends on coming to Him with sincere faith accompanied by righteous deeds; such people are granted the loftiest levels of Paradise, which are ranks of honor, reward, and nearness to God that surpass all others.

translation: Gardens of perpetual residence, beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide forever. And that is the reward of whoever purifies himself.
interpretation: This reward belongs to the one who purifies his inner self from disbelief, sin, and moral corruption, and turns to God with sincere faith and righteous action. The rivers flowing beneath these gardens symbolize unending provision, freshness, and delight that never diminishes, while the promise of eternal abiding confirms that this reward is neither temporary nor interrupted. The phrase “whoever purifies himself” shows that ultimate success is tied to spiritual cleansing—repentance, obedience, and devotion—not to worldly status, lineage, or possessions.

translation: And We certainly revealed to Moses: “Set out by night with My servants, and strike for them a dry path through the sea. You will not fear being overtaken, nor will you be afraid.”
interpretation: This verse conveys God’s direct instruction and reassurance to Moses at the moment of deliverance: he was to lead the oppressed Children of Israel out under cover of night, and when the sea stood as an impassable barrier, he was to strike it so that a dry passage would open. The assurance “you will not fear being overtaken, nor will you be afraid” means that Pharaoh and his forces would not catch them, and no harm from the sea or any other source would overtake them. It is a declaration that God’s command carries with it protection, that divine power overrides natural limits, and that those whom God chooses to save need not dread the pursuer behind them or the unknown ahead.

translation: So Pharaoh pursued them with his soldiers, and there covered them from the sea that which covered them.
interpretation: This describes the final drowning of Pharaoh and his army after they pursued Moses and the Children of Israel into the sea. The waters closed over them and engulfed them completely. The phrase “what covered them” is intentionally awe-inspiring and indefinite, conveying the overwhelming, inescapable nature of their destruction. It signifies that Pharaoh’s arrogant power was utterly crushed by Allah’s command, and that divine punishment overtakes tyrants when they persist in oppression and in chasing the faithful.

translation: And Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide [them].
interpretation: This verse declares that Pharaoh's leadership was not guidance but misguidance: he drew his people away from the truth and toward their own destruction, deceiving them with claims of lordship and false promises. It warns that those who follow corrupt leaders blindly share in the loss, and that Pharaoh neither possessed nor offered true guidance, despite his arrogant pretense of guiding and reforming.

translation: O Children of Israel, We saved you from your enemy, and We appointed for you the right side of Mount Sinai, and We sent down to you manna and quails.
interpretation: This verse reminds the Children of Israel of three great divine favors: deliverance from their enemy, the appointment at the right side of Mount Sinai for receiving revelation, and the provision of manna and quails. Its meaning is that Allah alone is the true Savior, Guide, and Provider; therefore, those favored must respond with gratitude, obedience, and faithfulness to His commands rather than ingratitude and rebellion.

translation: Eat of the good things We have provided you, and do not transgress in them, lest My wrath come upon you; and whoever My wrath comes upon, he has indeed fallen.
interpretation: This is a directive to enjoy God’s pure and lawful provisions with gratitude while remaining within His limits; the blessing itself must not become a means of disobedience, arrogance, extravagance, or injustice. To transgress regarding it is to invite divine wrath, and divine wrath, once it settles upon a person, casts him down from guidance and well-being into loss and ruin.

translation: And indeed, I am surely Oft-Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then is guided.
interpretation: This is a divine promise that God's forgiveness is vast and repeated for the one who joins repentance from sin, sincere faith, righteous action, and then steadfastness in guidance. The word 'then' shows that forgiveness is not granted for a mere claim or a single moment, but for a life that moves from turning back to God, to belief, to good deeds, and then remains upon the right path; such a person God receives with forgiveness and does not let their striving go to waste.

translation: And what made you hasten ahead of your people, O Moses?
interpretation: Allah is gently questioning Musa about why he came to the appointed meeting before his people, showing that Musa’s haste sprang from eager longing for his Lord’s revelation; it also hints that his people needed his presence and guidance, and prepares for the account of their trial in his absence.

translation: He said, 'They are these [people] following my tracks, and I hastened to You, my Lord, so that You may be pleased.'
interpretation: Moses explains that his people are close behind him, following the path he has taken, while he hurried ahead to the appointed meeting with his Lord. His haste was not neglect of his responsibility but an expression of intense longing for God's good pleasure and acceptance, showing that a servant may eagerly rush toward God's call while trusting that those under his care remain guided along the way.

translation: [Allah] said, "Indeed, We have tried your people after you [departed], and al-Samiri has led them astray."
interpretation: This means that the deviation of Musa’s people after his departure was a trial decreed by Allah, while the direct cause of their misguidance was al-Samiri, who exploited their weakness and turned them toward worshipping the calf. It warns that trials may come through the absence of a guiding leader and through deceitful figures who corrupt religious loyalty, and it holds people responsible for following such misguidance even as it affirms that every trial unfolds under Allah’s decree.

translation: So Moses returned to his people, angry and sorrowful. He said, 'O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise? Did the time of the covenant seem long to you, or did you intend that wrath from your Lord should fall upon you, so you broke your promise to me?'
interpretation: This verse expresses Moses’s righteous anger and deep grief at his people’s lapse into calf worship. His questions expose the irrationality of their betrayal: God’s promise was good and certain, so the delay in Moses’s return was no valid excuse. Either they grew impatient and let the covenant seem too long, or they deliberately chose a path that invited divine wrath. By breaking their pledge to Moses, they did not merely offend him; they violated their covenant with God and betrayed the guidance they had received. The verse thus warns that spiritual impatience and the craving for tangible substitutes can lead a community to exchange divine truth for false worship, bringing God’s anger and the prophet’s sorrow.

translation: They said: 'We did not break our promise to you by our own will, but we were made to carry burdens of the people's ornaments, so we threw them [into the fire], and likewise did the Samiri throw.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the calf-worshippers' attempt to justify their breach of the covenant by denying deliberate intent. They claim they were merely weighed down by the ornaments they had carried and cast them away, and that the Samiri did the same, thereby shifting blame onto circumstances and onto a deceiver. The deeper meaning is that idolatry and betrayal of faith often arise from attachment to worldly wealth and from blindly following a charismatic leader, yet such excuses do not remove moral responsibility, for they willingly surrendered the gold and cooperated with the Samiri's initiative to fashion the calf.

translation: Then he brought out for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and they said, 'This is your god and the god of Moses, but he has forgotten.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the emptiness of the idolatry into which the Israelites were led during Moses’ absence. The calf was merely a fashioned body that produced a sound like lowing; it had no life, power, knowledge, or ability to create, sustain, guide, or answer prayer. Calling it “your god and the god of Moses” was a false and blasphemous claim, and saying that Moses “forgot” was a slander against a prophet, implying that he had been mistaken about the true God or had forgotten his Lord. The passage teaches that divinity belongs to Allah alone, and no created image or object—however impressive or miraculous it may appear—can share in His lordship or deserve worship.

translation: Do they not then see that it does not return any speech to them, and that it possesses neither harm nor benefit for them?
interpretation: This is a decisive rebuke of idolatry: the object of worship is exposed as utterly powerless and non-responsive. Since it cannot hear, answer, or control any good or harm, it cannot be a god; therefore, devotion, fear, and hope must be directed only to Allah, who alone hears, responds, and disposes all benefit and harm.

translation: And Aaron had already said to them before: "O my people, you have only been tested by it. And indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command."
interpretation: This verse declares Aaron’s innocence and clarifies that he had warned the Israelites before Moses returned. The golden calf was not a god but a trial (fitnah) designed to expose whether they would cling to prophetic guidance or be seduced by a fabricated object of worship. By calling them to the Most Merciful (al-Rahman), Aaron directs them away from the calf to the true Lord, whose mercy should inspire repentance and sincere worship. His command to follow and obey him is not an assertion of personal authority; it is the obligation to obey God’s appointed prophet, through whom divine guidance is conveyed. Their sin was therefore not due to ignorance or lack of warning, but to their refusal to submit to prophetic authority and worship the one true God alone.

translation: They said, "We will not cease being devoted to it until Moses returns to us."
interpretation: This statement expresses stubborn persistence in idolatry and a refusal to accept Aaron’s guidance during Moses’ absence. Their claim to wait for Moses was not a sincere search for truth but a pretext to continue worshiping the calf, showing that their hearts were firmly attached to a false object of devotion. It warns that outward patience or waiting can become a tool for delaying obedience, and that devotion, when directed wrongly, hardens the heart against clear prophetic correction.

translation: He said, “O Aaron, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray?”
interpretation: This is Moses rebuking his brother Aaron for not taking a firm stand when he witnessed the Israelites deviating into calf-worship. It does not mean Aaron caused their misguidance; rather, it charges him with failing to confront or clearly oppose the error as the one left in authority, teaching that witnessing misguidance while remaining passive is itself a serious matter for those entrusted with guiding others.

translation: Why did you not follow me? Did you then disobey my command?
interpretation: This is Moses’ rebuke to his brother Aaron when he returned to find the Israelites had fallen into calf worship. Moses reproaches Aaron for not upholding his directive and for failing to take a firm stand against their deviation, asking whether that failure amounted to disobedience to his order.

translation: He said, "O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard nor by my head. I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel, and you did not wait for my word.'"
interpretation: This is Harun’s plea to Musa when Musa returned in anger and seized him by the beard and head. Harun clarifies that he did not approve of the Israelites’ worship of the calf, nor did he abandon his duty out of negligence. Rather, he feared that if he confronted them forcefully alone, it would split the Children of Israel into factions and lead to conflict before Musa returned. So he chose restraint and waited for Musa’s instruction, preferring the preservation of unity and obedience to his brother’s leadership over acting independently. The verse thus emphasizes the value of maintaining communal unity, avoiding schism, and acting with patience and wisdom in matters of leadership and reform.

translation: He said: 'Then what is your case, O Samiri?'
interpretation: This is Moses’s rebuke and demand for accountability from the Samiri after he led the people into worshipping the golden calf. It asks: What drove you to this?
