What was your aim, and what excuse do you have? It exposes that his action was a deliberate affair for which he must answer, not an unavoidable mistake, and it prepares the way for his punishment.

translation: He said, “I perceived what they did not perceive, so I took a handful from the trace of the messenger and threw it; and thus my soul made it seem fair to me.”
interpretation: This is the confession of al-Samiri: he claims to have noticed something the Israelites did not—the trace/passage of the divine messenger (interpreted as the angel Gabriel)—and he took a handful of dust from that trace and cast it into the golden calf, producing a misleading effect. His words show that his sin was not merely ignorance but a self-deceiving misuse of a perceived secret: his own soul made the scheme appear clever and justified. The verse thus warns against trusting private intuitions or hidden “insights” that lead one to disobey prophetic guidance, for self-desire can dress up misguidance as something good.

translation: He said, "Then go! Indeed, for you in this life is that you say, 'Do not touch [me].' And indeed, for you is an appointment you will not fail to keep. And look at your god to which you remained devoted. We will surely burn it and then scatter it into the sea, scattering [it]."
interpretation: This is Musa’s judgment upon al-Samiri, the maker of the calf. His worldly punishment is lifelong social isolation: he must proclaim “no touching,” meaning people must avoid contact with him, and he has an inescapable appointed time of reckoning with Allah. Musa then destroys the idol itself, burning it and scattering its ashes into the sea, to expose the utter powerlessness of a fabricated god. The verse teaches that idolatry ends in humiliation, loss, and exclusion; that false deities can neither benefit nor harm and are utterly destructible; and that divine justice will never be evaded.

translation: Your god is only Allah, there is no deity except Him. He has encompassed all things in knowledge.
interpretation: This verse establishes pure monotheism: the only true deity worthy of worship is Allah alone, and every claim of divinity besides Him is false. It also affirms that His knowledge is all-encompassing—nothing in creation, whether hidden or manifest, escapes His awareness—so He alone is deserving of worship, obedience, and reliance.

translation: Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has gone before, and We have certainly given you from Us a Reminder.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the histories of earlier peoples and prophets are revealed to Muhammad by God Himself, not as mere stories but as authoritative reminders that confirm the continuity of divine guidance and warn against repeating past disobedience. The "Reminder" given from God's presence is the Qur'an, which serves as the enduring source of counsel, honor, and guidance for the Prophet and for all who heed it.

translation: Whoever turns away from it — indeed, he will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden.
interpretation: The pronoun “it” refers to the Reminder, the Qur’an sent down to Muhammad. Turning away means rejecting, neglecting, or refusing to heed its guidance and warnings. The verse declares that such rejection does not escape accountability: on the Day of Resurrection the person will carry a wazr, a heavy load of sin and guilt, which will weigh him down and bring him to ruin. It teaches that divine guidance is a trust and that the consequence of willful disregard is borne personally in the Hereafter.

translation: Abiding therein forever, and evil will be their burden on the Day of Resurrection.
interpretation: This is a warning that those who turn away from God’s revelation carry a spiritual and moral burden that becomes their permanent state. “Abiding therein” signifies that the consequence is not temporary: the burden of heedlessness and sin hardens into an everlasting punishment. “Evil is their load” means that what they have accumulated—denial, wrongdoing, and rejection of guidance—will be a wretched thing to carry on the Day of Judgment, exposing their loss and bringing them ruin rather than relief.

translation: On the Day when the Trumpet is blown, and We will gather the criminals on that Day, blue-eyed.
interpretation: This verse depicts the terror and humiliation of the guilty at the resurrection: the trumpet blast signals the end of worldly life and the beginning of judgment, and the criminals are gathered in a visibly altered, frightful state. Their eyes turning blue symbolizes extreme fear, anguish, and loss of dignity or clarity, showing that they are powerless before God and fully exposed for their deeds. It affirms the certainty of accountability and the severity of the fate awaiting those who persist in wrongdoing.

translation: They will whisper among themselves, “You stayed only ten.”
interpretation: This verse portrays the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection murmuring to one another, judging that their stay in the world or in the grave was no more than a very short period—ten days or nights. Their altered sense of time shows how fleeting and insignificant worldly life will appear once they face eternity, and it deepens their regret over how they wasted that brief span.

translation: We are most knowing of what they say, when the most moderate of them in manner says, “You stayed only a day.”
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah alone encompasses every whispered debate and every claim people make, even when they argue about how long they remained in the world or in the grave. On the Day of Resurrection, their sense of time will be so overwhelmed by the reality of the Hereafter that the most balanced and reasonable among them will estimate their stay as merely a single day. The point is not the exact number but the collapse of worldly time before eternity: the life they disputed over, built upon, and measured so carefully will seem almost nothing. Thus the verse warns against being deceived by the fleeting nature of this world and calls hearts to prepare for the meeting with Allah, whose knowledge and reckoning are exact. In the end, every estimate belongs to Him, and all human calculations fade before His omniscience.

translation: And they ask you about the mountains, so say, 'My Lord will scatter them utterly.'
interpretation: This verse declares that on the Day of Resurrection, the immense, seemingly permanent mountains will be entirely uprooted and reduced to scattered dust by God’s command. Their destruction demonstrates that no created thing, however solid or enduring it appears, can withstand the divine will when the appointed time comes. The answer given to the questioners is not merely about the mountains’ physical fate but about the certainty of the Hereafter: the One who made the mountains can just as surely erase them, bringing all creation before Him for reckoning.

translation: Then He will leave it a barren, level plain.
interpretation: This means that on the Day of Resurrection God will utterly crush and scatter the mountains, reducing the earth to a completely flat and featureless surface. No hill, valley, ridge, or unevenness will remain; all landmarks and distinctions of terrain will be erased, leaving one exposed, level ground upon which every creature will stand before God for judgment.

translation: You will not see therein any crookedness or unevenness.
interpretation: This refers to the earth after the mountains have been uprooted and leveled on the Day of Judgment: it is made completely flat, with no deviation, depression, or elevation. The negation of both 'عوج' (crookedness/deviation) and 'أمت' (unevenness/curvature) emphasizes absolute levelness and smoothness, leaving no irregularity whatsoever.

translation: On that Day they will follow the caller, with no deviation from him; and voices will be subdued before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a faint whisper.
interpretation: This verse depicts the absolute submission and stillness of all creation on the Day of Resurrection. The call to the gathering is irresistible and straight, leaving no room for refusal, turning aside, or avoidance; every soul proceeds exactly as summoned. Human voices, which in worldly life often rise in dispute, pride, or protest, become hushed and humbled before God’s majesty and power. The only sound left is a faint whisper, signifying that awe, fear, and utter helplessness have silenced all claims and arguments before the Most Merciful.

translation: On that Day, intercession will not benefit except one to whom the Most Merciful has granted permission and with whose word He is pleased.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, no one can intercede by their own authority or standing. Intercession is entirely subject to God’s permission. Only the intercessor whom the Most Merciful allows and whose speech He accepts—namely, one whose words are founded on truth and sincere affirmation of God’s oneness—may intercede. This affirms that all judgment, mercy, and mediation belong ultimately to God alone, and it nullifies any claim that any created being can intercede independently of His will.

translation: He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not encompass Him in knowledge.
interpretation: Allah’s knowledge encompasses all creatures and all times—what lies ahead of them and what lies behind them—while no creature can fully encompass Him with knowledge. He is beyond their complete comprehension, and any knowledge they have of Him is only what He grants and reveals.

translation: And all faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence. And he will have failed who carries wrongdoing.
interpretation: This verse describes the total submission and humiliation of every creature before Allah on the Day of Judgment. Every face—every soul—will be lowered and subdued before the Ever-Living, whose life is eternal and who alone sustains and governs all things. No one will be able to stand on pride, power, or self-sufficiency. The second part declares that true loss and ruin belong to the one who comes carrying zulm—wrongdoing, injustice, or the grave wrong of associating partners with Allah—for such a burden destroys the bearer and prevents salvation.

translation: And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer, he will not fear injustice nor deprivation.
interpretation: This verse establishes that faith and righteous action together secure a person from ultimate loss: God will not wrong such a person by punishing him for what he did not do, nor will He diminish or withhold any part of the reward due for his good deeds. His effort is accepted and fully recompensed, so he has no fear of being treated unjustly or of having his good works reduced.

translation: And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur’an, and We have varied within it the warnings, so that they may become righteous or it may produce for them a remembrance.
interpretation: The verse explains that the Qur’an was revealed in Arabic, a clear and eloquent language suited to its first addressees, and that God has repeated and diversified His warnings in it—through promises, threats, parables, and reminders—to move the human heart. Its purpose is either that people may adopt taqwa, guarding themselves against His displeasure and punishment, or that the revelation may generate in them a new awareness and remembrance of God, truth, and responsibility. Thus the variety of warnings is a mercy and a means of awakening, not mere repetition.

translation: Exalted is Allah, the True King. And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you, and say, 'My Lord, increase me in knowledge.'
interpretation: This verse declares Allah’s supreme transcendence, absolute sovereignty, and truth. It instructs the Prophet, and by extension every believer, not to rush ahead of divine revelation—specifically, not to recite, judge, or act upon the Qur’an before its revelation is fully delivered and clarified by Allah. Instead, one should wait upon Allah’s timing and turn to Him with the supplication, “My Lord, increase me in knowledge.” Thus it teaches patience in receiving divine guidance, submission to Allah’s command, and humble dependence on Him for all true knowledge.

translation: And We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no firm resolve.
interpretation: This verse teaches that Adam was entrusted with a covenant and a command, but human nature is prone to forgetfulness and weakness of resolve when faced with temptation. Adam’s lapse was not due to a hardened rejection of God, but to forgetting and a lack of steadfast determination. It shows that humans need God’s guidance and forgiveness, and that sincere return to God after failure is the path of repentance.

translation: And when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate before Adam,' so they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused.
interpretation: This command was a test of obedience and a directive from God to honor Adam, not to worship him, since worship belongs to God alone. The angels submitted immediately, but Iblis refused out of arrogance and self-exaltation, allowing his pride to override the divine command. His refusal was not an honest inability or misunderstanding; it was a deliberate disobedience rooted in contempt for Adam and rebellion against God's authority. The verse thus teaches that true faith requires humble submission to God's commands, and that arrogance can lead even a created being with knowledge to fall into defiance.

translation: Then We said, 'O Adam, indeed this [Satan] is an enemy to you and to your wife. So let him not drive you both out of Paradise, lest you fall into misery.'
interpretation: This verse establishes that Satan’s enmity toward humankind is fundamental and deliberate: he seeks to deprive people of the state of ease, honor, and nearness to God that Paradise represents. God’s warning to Adam and his wife is an act of mercy, teaching them to recognize the enemy and guard against his deception. It shows that yielding to Satan’s whisperings leads to expulsion from bliss and to the hardship, toil, and discontent of worldly life. At the same time, the verse affirms human free will and moral responsibility: God does not compel disobedience but clearly warns against the path that produces misery. Thus true felicity lies in heeding divine guidance and refusing to let the enemy become the cause of one’s downfall.

translation: Indeed, for you [is the assurance] that you will not be hungry therein, nor will you be naked.
interpretation: This is Allah’s assurance to Adam concerning the Garden: within it he would be free from the hardship of hunger and the disgrace of nakedness, meaning that his sustenance and covering were guaranteed, and he would not suffer deprivation or exposure there.

translation: And that you will not be thirsty therein, nor will you suffer from the heat of the sun.
interpretation: This is a divine assurance of complete physical comfort in Paradise: no thirst, no dehydration, and no exposure to scorching heat or sunburn. It signifies that the inhabitants of Paradise will enjoy perpetual refreshment and shade, free from the bodily harms and hardships that afflict people in the worldly life.

translation: Then Satan whispered to him, saying, 'O Adam, shall I guide you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not wear out?'
interpretation: The devil approaches Adam not with a command but with a seductive question, offering what appears to be immortality and endless kingship. The lesson is that temptation often disguises itself as a path to permanence, honor, and self-fulfillment, while in reality it leads to loss. Adam is addressed personally to make the proposal feel intimate and tailored, and the 'tree of eternity' and 'kingdom that does not decay' represent the human desire to escape mortality and hold onto power without God's grant. This verse reveals Satan's method: he cannot force, so he whispers, embellishes, and proposes; and it marks the moment when Adam's obedience is tested through an appeal to his deepest aspirations.

translation: So they both ate of it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves of Paradise. And Adam disobeyed his Lord and erred.
interpretation: This verse describes the immediate consequence of the forbidden act: shame became exposed, and the first humans tried to conceal themselves with Paradise’s leaves. It teaches that disobedience brings a loss of dignity and inner peace, and that human beings are prone to error. Yet Adam’s disobedience was a lapse, not a defiant rejection of God; the following context shows his repentance and God’s forgiveness. Thus it conveys both the seriousness of sin and the hope of divine mercy for those who turn back.

translation: Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.
interpretation: This verse means that after Adam’s mistake, God favored him by selecting him for His grace, accepting his repentance, and guiding him back to the path of obedience and right conduct. It shows that sincere repentance is met with divine forgiveness and that God’s guidance is a mercy granted to those who turn to Him.

translation: He said: 'Descend, both of you, from it, all together. Some of you are enemies of others. If there comes to you guidance from Me, then whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be wretched.'
interpretation: This is God's address after Adam and Eve's disobedience and their descent to earthly life. It teaches that worldly existence includes conflict and enmity, but God does not leave humanity without a way back: He promises to send guidance. The one who follows that guidance is saved from the two fundamental losses—going astray from truth in this life and suffering misery in the Hereafter. Thus the criterion of success is not remaining in the original state but adhering to divine guidance when it comes.

translation: And whoever turns away from My remembrance — indeed, for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.
interpretation: This is a warning that whoever rejects God’s revelation, guidance, and remembrance, and turns away from faith and obedience, will live a narrow, distressed, and joyless existence even if outwardly wealthy, because the heart is severed from the contentment and light that come from God; and on the Day of Resurrection such a person will be raised blind, unable to see the way to salvation or to present any valid excuse, as a just recompense for choosing blindness toward God’s signs in this world.

translation: He will say: “My Lord, why have You raised me blind while I was [once] seeing?”
interpretation: This is the protest of the one who turned away from God’s remembrance. His blindness in the Hereafter is the outward manifestation of an inner condition he chose in worldly life: he had sight and faculties but failed to use them to perceive and follow divine guidance. The verse teaches that worldly sight is a trust; if it is not directed toward truth and obedience to God, it becomes spiritual blindness, and the resurrection exposes that hidden state as a reality.

translation: He will say, “Thus did Our signs come to you, and you forgot them; and thus today you will be forgotten.”
interpretation: This is the address of God to the one who neglected His revealed guidance: because when the clear signs and verses of God came to him in the world, he abandoned them, ignored them, and did not take them as a way of life, so on the Day of Judgment he is abandoned and left in punishment, cut off from mercy and care. The recompense is fitting: whoever forgets God’s guidance by refusing to live by it will himself be forgotten by God in the sense of being left to his own ruin and chastisement.

translation: And thus do We recompense he who transgressed and did not believe in the signs of his Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting.
interpretation: This verse declares that God justly recompenses those who exceed the limits by persisting in disbelief and rejecting the revelations of their Lord. Their ultimate punishment in the Hereafter is far more intense and enduring than any suffering or consequence in this worldly life, warning that turning away from divine guidance leads to lasting loss.

translation: Has it not guided them how many generations We destroyed before them, in whose dwellings they walk? Indeed in that are signs for those of understanding.
interpretation: This verse confronts the heedless with a living lesson from history: the ruined homes they pass through are not mere ruins but traces of nations destroyed for denying God and His messengers. If God could annihilate those generations and leave their dwellings as testimony, He can also raise the dead and hold all accountable. The signs are not profitable to everyone; they instruct only “ulu al-nuha”—those who use their God-given reason to infer from outward ruins the inner reality of divine justice, power, and the inevitability of returning to Him.

translation: And were it not for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord, and an appointed term, it would have been inevitable.
interpretation: The verse means that the punishment deserved by the deniers was not sent immediately only because of Allah’s prior decree to delay it and the fixed time He has set for it; had that decree and appointed term not existed, the punishment would have become binding and unavoidable at once.

translation: So be patient over what they say, and glorify with the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day, so that you may be pleased.
interpretation: It directs the Prophet, and every believer, to meet the harm and falsehood of opponents not with despair or retaliation but with steadfast patience and continuous remembrance of God. The appointed times—before sunrise, before sunset, at night, and at the edges of the day—train the soul to keep divine awareness throughout the day, so that the heart is detached from people's words and attached to God's praise. The promise “so that you may be pleased” means that this patient worship will lead to a state of contentment and divine good pleasure, as God grants victory, reward, and spiritual satisfaction.

translation: And do not extend your eyes toward that which We have given to categories of them to enjoy — the adornment of worldly life — so that We may test them in it. And the provision of your Lord is better and more enduring.
interpretation: This is a divine instruction to the Prophet, and by extension to the believers, not to gaze longingly at the fleeting wealth, status, and pleasures granted to some worldly people. Such enjoyment is only a temporary splendor and a trial by which God tests them. The reward, sustenance, and nearness granted by your Lord are superior in quality and everlasting, so the believer's aspiration should be fixed on the hereafter rather than envious attachment to worldly luxuries.

translation: And enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you. And the final outcome belongs to Taqwa (piety and righteousness).
interpretation: This verse teaches that prayer is not merely a private individual act but a responsibility that begins within one’s household: one should call one’s family to prayer and remain patient and consistent in establishing it. It also removes a major excuse, namely anxiety over livelihood. God clarifies that He is not asking people to provide for Him or to carry the burden of their own sustenance independently; rather, He is the Provider. Therefore, devotion to prayer should not be abandoned out of fear of losing worldly provisions. The verse ends by declaring that the ultimate good end, success, and reward belong to Taqwa—God-consciousness, piety, and righteous conduct—so the true measure of a blessed outcome is not wealth or worldly gain but faithfulness and obedience to God.

translation: And they say, 'Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?' Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?
interpretation: Their demand for a new miraculous sign is answered by the evidence already available: the Qur'an itself, whose truth is confirmed by and consistent with the earlier revealed scriptures. The objection is not caused by a lack of proof, but by their refusal to accept the messenger and the revelation, so the verse directs them to the greater sign they are overlooking.

translation: And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before him, they would have said, 'Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so we could follow Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced?'
interpretation: This verse establishes that God’s punishment is not arbitrary: it comes only after a messenger has been sent and the truth made clear. If the disbelievers had been destroyed before the coming of the Messenger, they would have used that as an excuse, claiming they were never given guidance. Therefore, sending the Messenger is a mercy and a proof against them. After the message has reached them, rejecting it leaves no plea of ignorance; their refusal will lead to humiliation and disgrace. The verse thus combines divine justice—no punishment without warning—with a warning that following God’s signs must not be delayed until the moment of ruin and shame.

translation: Say, 'Each [of us] is waiting; so wait. Then you will know who are the companions of the straight path and who is rightly guided.'
interpretation: This verse is a final address in which the Prophet is told to declare that everyone is waiting for the outcome: the believers await God's promise, while their opponents await what they expect. The passage leaves the matter to time and divine judgment, asserting that events will soon make clear who truly follows the upright, balanced path and who has actually received guidance. It is a call to patient confidence in the truth rather than to haste or argument.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The reckoning of the people has drawn near, while they are in heedlessness, turning away.
interpretation: This verse warns that the time of accountability before Allah has come close, yet many people remain oblivious to it and continue to turn away from the signs and reminders that call them to prepare. It describes a dangerous condition: the event that demands readiness is near, but heedlessness and avoidance keep them from taking it seriously.

translation: No fresh reminder comes to them from their Lord except that they listen to it while they are playing.
interpretation: This verse condemns the heedless attitude of those who encounter divine revelation as though it were mere amusement: they hear it outwardly, but their hearts do not receive it with seriousness, obedience, or seeking guidance. Their listening is accompanied by mockery and distraction, showing that the revelation does not move them to reflect or reform.

translation: Their hearts are distracted. And they conceal the secret conversation—those who do wrong—[saying], 'Is this but a human being like you? Will you then come to magic while you see?'
interpretation: Their hearts are diverted from the reminder by idle amusement and heedlessness. The wrongdoers secretly conspire, objecting that the Prophet is only a human like them, as if prophethood could not come through a human being. They dismiss the revelation as magic even while seeing its evident truth and the Prophet’s honesty. The verse exposes their rejection as arrogant, self-contradictory, and rooted in desire rather than proof; it warns that hearts preoccupied with play and secret plotting cannot recognize divine guidance.

translation: He said: My Lord knows the speech in the heaven and the earth, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that every word spoken in the heavens and the earth—whether uttered openly or kept hidden—is fully within Allah’s knowledge. He is not absent from the sayings of His creation, nor unaware of their intentions; His hearing and knowledge are perfect and all-encompassing, so He will judge every utterance and deed with perfect justice.

translation: Nay, they say: 'Confused dreams! Nay, he has fabricated it! Nay, he is a poet! So let him bring us a sign like those sent to the former peoples.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the disbelievers’ contradictory and evasive response to the Qur’an. Unable to refute it, they shift between labels: sometimes calling it jumbled dreams, sometimes claiming the Prophet fabricated it, and sometimes dismissing him as a poet. These accusations cannot all be true at once; they reveal not sincere inquiry but obstinate rejection. Their demand for a sign “like those sent to the former peoples” is likewise a pretext, since earlier communities often received miracles and still disbelieved. The verse shows that denial of revelation is often driven by pride and unwillingness to submit, not by lack of evidence, and that the Qur’an itself stands as the enduring sign and criterion of truth.

translation: No city before them that We destroyed ever believed. Will they then believe?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical rebuke and warning: earlier communities that demanded signs and persisted in denial did not attain true faith even when signs came; instead, they were destroyed. So the verse warns the rejecters that merely witnessing a miracle will not force them into faith, and if they continue in stubborn disbelief, they will meet the same fate. True faith comes through Allah’s guidance and willing submission, not through coercion by signs, and belief at the point of punishment is too late.

translation: And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the Reminder, if you do not know.
interpretation: This verse refutes the objection that a messenger must be an angel rather than a human being: God’s established way is to send human men as recipients of His revelation. The command to ask the people of the Reminder—those who possess knowledge of earlier revealed scriptures—confirms that the previous prophets were also men, and it establishes that one who lacks knowledge should turn to those who are qualified to teach it.

translation: And We did not make them bodies that do not eat food, nor were they immortal.
interpretation: Allah is declaring that the messengers He sent were not angels or disembodied beings exempt from human needs; they were human beings who ate food and were subject to death. Their need for sustenance and their mortality do not diminish their prophethood or the truth of their message. The verse refutes the demand that a messenger be a supernatural being who neither eats nor dies, and establishes that God's chosen messengers are fully human, sustained by God like other people, and not everlasting in this world.

translation: Then We fulfilled for them the promise, and We saved them and whom We willed, and We destroyed the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah’s promise to His messengers and the believers is true and inevitably fulfilled: He rescues His faithful servants, along with whoever He wills, from the punishment that overtakes the people of corruption. At the same time, those who persist in excess, denial, and rebellion against divine guidance are brought to ruin. It presents a divine law: deliverance follows faithfulness, while arrogant transgression against Allah’s limits leads to destruction.

translation: We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which there is your mention/reminder. Will you not then reason?
interpretation: This verse declares that the Qur'an is a divine Book revealed for humanity, containing what truly reminds them of God, their purpose, and their moral responsibility. It is also a source of honor and elevation for those who accept and live by it. The closing question rebukes heedlessness: if people reflected with sound reason, they would recognize that this Book addresses their deepest need and would not ignore it.

translation: And how many a city that was unjust have We shattered, and We raised up after it another people.
interpretation: This verse warns that Allah's destruction of unjust towns is not an isolated event but a recurring pattern: He can utterly break the power of a wrongdoing society and replace it with a new people, showing that divine justice is certain and that no community has permanence if it persists in oppression.

translation: And when they sensed Our punishment, behold, they were running away from it.
interpretation: This depicts the guilty at the moment Allah’s judgment becomes undeniably present: the very punishment they denied and mocked is suddenly felt, and their instinct is to flee. Yet their running exposes that there is no refuge and no escape from Allah’s decree. The verse thus teaches that when divine punishment arrives, human power collapses, and attempts to escape only reveal helplessness and the futility of rejecting the truth.

translation: Do not run away; return to what you were made to luxuriate in and to your dwellings, so that you may be questioned.
interpretation: This is a rebuke to those who try to escape the consequences of their deeds once divine punishment overtakes them. They are ordered back to the very comfort, wealth, and homes in which they had been spoiled and heedless—not to enjoy them again, but to be held accountable for how they lived and what they denied. It teaches that no one can outrun God’s decree, and that material ease and familiar dwellings cannot shield anyone from questioning and reckoning.

translation: They said, "O woe to us! Indeed, we were wrongdoers."
interpretation: This is the remorseful confession of those whom God’s punishment overtook: they recognize too late that they had been unjust, primarily by rejecting His messengers and persisting in disbelief and corruption. Their cry expresses despair and self-condemnation, not repentance that can still avert judgment, showing that arrogance and heedlessness collapse when divine punishment arrives and that true remorse must come before the decree of chastisement.

translation: So that cry of theirs did not cease until We made them mown down, lifeless.
interpretation: This means their repeated lamentation and admission of guilt continued only as long as they were being destroyed, and it did not save them. God compares them to a field cut down and a fire extinguished—completely finished, with no life, movement, or hope of recovery left. It underscores that once divine punishment arrives, belated remorse cannot reverse it.

translation: And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.
interpretation: Allah affirms that the creation of the heavens, the earth, and all that lies between them is not an act of idle amusement, sport, or purposelessness. It is founded on truth, wisdom, and a serious divine purpose: to manifest His lordship, oneness, power, and perfect wisdom, and to serve as a realm of moral testing and accountability for human beings. The verse therefore rejects any view that the universe is meaningless or created for mere play, and calls people to reflect on its order and live responsibly before their Creator.

translation: Had We willed to take a diversion, We would have taken it from Our own presence, if We were to do so.
interpretation: This verse is a decisive negation of any notion that Allah engages in idle play, takes amusement, or needs a consort or child. The conditional form does not affirm the act; it emphasizes that such a thing is beneath His perfection and wisdom. If He had ever willed any such diversion, He would have originated it from His own presence and self-sufficiency, not from His creation. Since He does not do so, the heavens, earth, and all that lies between them are created with truth and serious purpose, and God is utterly transcendent above any partner, offspring, or purposeless sport.

translation: Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, so that it vanishes. And woe to you for what you describe.
interpretation: Allah actively establishes the truth against every fabricated falsehood, breaking its power and exposing it as fleeting and unable to endure. The truth here is His revelation and true reality, while falsehood is every invented claim that misrepresents Him—especially ascribing to Him partners, offspring, or attributes that do not befit His majesty. When the truth strikes falsehood, falsehood is not merely weakened but demolished and shown to be perishing. The declaration of woe is a severe warning to those who persist in describing Allah with lies: their descriptions cannot change the truth, and the harm of such falsehood returns upon them.

translation: And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And those who are near Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they tire.
interpretation: This verse establishes that every being in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, is created by Him, and remains under His absolute dominion. The phrase “those who are near Him” refers especially to the angels, who are honored with nearness to Allah; yet they never consider themselves above worshipping Him out of pride, nor do they become exhausted or weary in worship. Their condition shows that true nearness to Allah produces deeper humility and constant devotion, not arrogance or neglect. It also implicitly rebukes anyone who refuses to worship Allah out of pride or laziness, since even the noblest and closest creatures never tire of His worship.

translation: They glorify [Him] night and day; they do not slacken.
interpretation: The verse expresses that the angels’ glorification of God is continual, unwavering, and free from any fatigue, boredom, or lapse; their worship is pure, constant devotion, never interrupted or diminished.

translation: Or have they taken gods from the earth who raise the dead?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical rebuke of those who worship beings or idols that originate from the earth—created, material, and powerless—and yet ascribe to them the divine act of giving life and raising the dead. The question implies that such earthly gods cannot create or revive anything; they are themselves dependent and lifeless. Resurrection and the bringing forth of life from death belong exclusively to Allah, so taking any earthly object or being as a god is shown to be futile and contradictory to the truth of His sole lordship and power over life and death.

translation: Had there been within the heavens and earth gods besides Allah, they would both have fallen into ruin. So glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.
interpretation: The existence of more than one deity governing the heavens and earth would necessarily produce conflicting wills, competing decrees, and mutual resistance, so the ordered universe would collapse into corruption. The coherence, interdependence, and regularity of creation therefore point to a single, all-powerful Lord. Allah is then declared free of every false claim, especially the attribution of partners, peers, or offspring, and He is the Lord of the Throne, the supreme sovereign over all existence.

translation: He is not questioned about what He does, but they are questioned.
interpretation: This affirms God’s absolute sovereignty and perfect wisdom: His actions are not subject to human scrutiny, objection, or accountability, because His knowledge, justice, and will are complete and unerring. Creatures, however, are accountable and will be questioned about their deeds, since they act within limits and stand under divine judgment. The verse thus establishes the fundamental distinction between the Creator, whose authority is unrestricted, and creation, which bears moral responsibility before Him.

translation: Or have they taken gods besides Him? Say, 'Bring your proof. This is the Reminder of those with me and the Reminder of those before me.' But most of them do not know the truth, so they are turning away.
interpretation: The verse establishes that any claim of other deities besides Allah is a baseless assertion requiring decisive evidence. Since no proof can be produced, the call to bring proof exposes the emptiness of polytheism. The Qur'an and the earlier revealed scriptures all agree in bearing witness to Allah's exclusive divinity and to the truth brought by His messengers. Therefore, the majority of the rejecters do not deny it out of certain knowledge, but out of ignorance of the truth and a willful turning away from its clear signs.

translation: And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me.
interpretation: This verse establishes the unity of God as the shared foundation of every prophetic message. Every messenger sent before Muhammad was given the same essential revelation: that no being, power, or object deserves worship except God alone. Therefore, the only proper response to this truth is sincere worship of Him alone—directing one’s devotion, obedience, supplication, fear, hope, and love exclusively to God, without associating any partner with Him. It also confirms that the Prophet Muhammad did not bring a new or different deity-concept, but reaffirmed the timeless message of all previous messengers.

translation: And they said, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Exalted is He! Rather, they are honored servants.
interpretation: This verse rejects the claim that Allah has offspring. Allah is far exalted above having a son or any partner; those whom the disbelievers wrongly imagined as His children are in truth only honored servants of Allah, not divine offspring.

translation: They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.
interpretation: This describes the angels: they never utter a word before Allah has decreed or permitted it, and they carry out whatever He orders them to do with perfect obedience.

translation: He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not intercede except for whom He approves, and they are apprehensive out of fear of Him.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's all-encompassing knowledge of the seen and unseen, including the affairs of the angels. It clarifies that no one, not even the angels, can intercede independently; intercession is only by God's permission and for those He is pleased with. The angels' fear and reverence of God demonstrate their complete servitude, refuting any claim that they are divine or partners with God. It teaches that true closeness to God is accompanied by awe and humility.

translation: And whoever among them says, 'Indeed, I am a god besides Him' — that one We will recompense with Hell. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse establishes that no created being, however exalted—including angels—may claim divinity or lordship besides God. Such a claim is the ultimate injustice, since it usurps the exclusive right of the Creator and seeks to place a creature on the level of the One who alone deserves worship. God therefore declares that He will repay the claimant with Hell, and He makes this the just recompense for all wrongdoers who transgress His exclusive divinity. The verse closes every path to shirk and every pretext for associating partners with God, whether through worship of angels, prophets, righteous servants, or any other creature.

translation: Have those who disbelieved not seen that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, then We separated them and made from water every living thing? Will they not then believe?
interpretation: This verse is a call to reflect on two great signs of God's creative power: the origin of the cosmos as a single joined creation that He split into the heavens and the earth, and the dependence of all living things on water. It addresses the disbelievers who deny resurrection and divine authority, urging them to see that the One able to originate and separate such vast creations and to give life through water is surely able to bring the dead to life. Thus the verse invites them to faith and acknowledges God as the sole Creator and Giver of life.

translation: And We have placed in the earth firm mountains, lest it should shake with them, and We have made therein broad pathways as roads, so that they may be guided.
interpretation: This verse reminds people of Allah’s power and mercy in ordering the earth for human life: He fixed mountains as stabilizing anchors so the ground would not shift and convulse beneath them, and He opened wide passes and traversable routes through the land so they could travel, find their way, and reach their destinations. The deeper meaning is that the same Lord who arranged the physical earth with signs of stability and guidance also calls people to recognize His oneness and follow the path that leads to true guidance.

translation: And We made the sky a protected ceiling, yet they turn away from its signs.
interpretation: This verse declares that God fashioned the heaven as a secure canopy over the earth—preserved from collapse and guarded against forces that would disrupt the order of life—so that it stands as a clear evidence of His power, wisdom, and mercy. The tragedy is that despite these visible signs, many people remain heedless, refusing to reflect on them or acknowledge the Creator to whom they point.

translation: And He is the One Who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon; each is floating in an orbit.
interpretation: This verse establishes that Allah alone is the Creator and Controller of time and the heavenly bodies. The night, day, sun, and moon are not independent powers or deities; they are created servants moving with precision in the orbits He has ordained. Their ordered, continuous motion points to His oneness, power, and wisdom, and it calls people away from worshipping created signs to worshipping the One who created and directs them.

translation: And We did not make for any human before you immortality. So if you die, will they be immortal?
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad, clarifying that no human being before him was granted eternal life on earth, and he is no exception. The rhetorical question denies the false expectation that if he dies, his opponents or any people will remain forever. It affirms that death is the universal lot of all human beings, while absolute permanence belongs to God alone. The verse thus corrects any attitude that treats a prophet as more than human or that fears his death as though it would secure others from their own mortality, and it reminds listeners that every soul will perish and return to God.

translation: Every soul will taste death. And We test you with evil and good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse affirms that death is inevitable for every living soul, and that both hardship and ease are tests from God to reveal who remains patient and grateful; ultimately, all people return to God for judgment and recompense.

translation: And when those who disbelieve see you, they take you only in mockery: “Is this the one who mentions your gods?” And they are, at the mention of the Most Merciful, disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse exposes the disbelievers’ hypocrisy and mockery: they ridicule the Prophet for criticizing their false idols, yet they themselves reject and deny the Most Merciful—Allah—when He is mentioned. They are quick to defend lifeless gods but refuse to acknowledge the One who is the source of all mercy, showing that their objection is not sincere but rooted in arrogance and disbelief in the truth.

translation: Man was created of haste. I will show you My signs, so do not ask Me to hasten.
interpretation: Human beings are naturally impatient and quick to demand immediate results, especially when warned or challenged. God assures that He will manifest His signs and bring His decrees to pass at the time He has appointed, so people must not try to rush Him or mockingly demand that punishment or proof come at once. The verse calls for patience, trust in divine timing, and submission to God's wisdom rather than yielding to human impulsiveness.

translation: And they say, “When will this promise come to pass, if you are truthful?”
interpretation: This is a mocking challenge from those who reject the message: they demand to know when the promised resurrection and divine judgment—or the warned punishment—will occur, using its delay as a pretext to doubt the Prophet’s truthfulness. It exposes their arrogance and impatience, since the appointed time of Allah’s promise is known only to Him, and no one can hasten or delay it. The verse thus rebukes those who treat the unseen decree as something subject to their demands and who mistake delay as evidence against the truth.

translation: If only those who disbelieved knew the time when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces or their backs, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: This verse is a severe warning and a rebuke of the disbelievers’ heedlessness. The conditional “if only they knew” points to the moment of punishment in the Hereafter; had they truly known it, they would not have persisted in denial and mockery. The Fire will surround them from every side—they cannot shield their faces, the noblest part, nor their backs—and there is no helper, intercessor, or power that can rescue them. Thus the verse establishes their utter helplessness and the certainty of divine judgment.

translation: Nay, it will come upon them suddenly and bewilder them, so they will not be able to repel it, nor will they be given respite.
interpretation: This verse warns that the promised Hour or punishment will not arrive according to the disbelievers’ timing or after giving them the chance to prepare once it is due; it will strike unexpectedly and overwhelm them, leaving them utterly stunned and powerless. They will have no means to turn it away, delay it, or escape it, and no further time will be granted to them. The verse thus emphasizes the certainty, suddenness, and inescapability of God’s judgment, and it calls people to take heed before that moment comes, rather than mocking or demanding it.

translation: And certainly, messengers before you were ridiculed, so those who ridiculed them were encompassed by that which they used to ridicule.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet and warns the mockers: ridiculing Allah’s messengers does not damage the truth or the messenger ultimately; rather, the very punishment or reality that was mocked recoils upon those who mock it. It establishes that hostility to divine guidance is an old pattern, and that divine judgment will inevitably overtake those who persist in derision.

translation: Say, 'Who protects you by night and day from the Most Merciful?' Rather, they are, from the remembrance of their Lord, turning away.
interpretation: This verse is a rebuke to those who ignore God's constant care and protection. It poses a rhetorical question: who else can guard you at every moment, night and day, from the punishment or harm that only the Most Merciful controls? No one can shield you from Him if He wills to test or punish you. The very safety and provision you enjoy are signs of His mercy, yet you turn away from remembering Him. The verse exposes human ingratitude and heedlessness: instead of reflecting on the continuous protection they receive, they are negligent of their Lord's remembrance. It calls them to recognize that only Allah is the true Guardian and to turn back to Him.

translation: Or have they gods that can protect them from Us? They cannot help themselves, nor can they be protected from Us.
interpretation: This is a rhetorical rebuke to those who associate partners with Allah: their supposed deities are utterly powerless. They cannot avert Allah’s will from anyone, cannot rescue even themselves, and cannot be shielded from Allah’s judgment by any ally or intercessor. The verse thus exposes the falsehood of relying on created beings for protection and establishes that all authority, aid, and safety belong to Allah alone.

translation: Nay, We gave enjoyment to these and their forefathers until life grew long for them. Do they not see that We are coming to the land, reducing it from its borders? Then are they the victors?
interpretation: This verse rejects the assumption that long life, inherited prosperity, and worldly power are proof that God is pleased with a people or that they are secure from His decree. God’s granting them and their ancestors enjoyment over many generations was a respite and a test, not a guarantee of salvation. The gradual reduction of the land from its edges is a sign of God’s sovereign control: territories, dominions, and nations are diminished and transferred by His will. Therefore, their apparent strength does not make them the ultimate victors; God is the true Overcomer, and the final authority and outcome belong to Him alone.

translation: Say, 'I only warn you by revelation.' But the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned.
interpretation: This verse declares that the Prophet's warning is based solely on divine revelation, not on personal reasoning or desire. It then illustrates that those who reject the message are like the deaf: the warning is given, but it does not enter their hearts because they have closed themselves off from accepting guidance.

translation: And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord should touch them, they would surely say, "O woe to us! Indeed, we were wrongdoers."
interpretation: This verse shows how the slightest contact with divine punishment would instantly shatter human defiance and bring about a confession of guilt. The use of "a breath" indicates that even the faintest trace of the Lord's chastisement is enough to make those who denied and persisted in wrongdoing cry out in remorse, admitting that they had wronged themselves. It underscores both the severity of the coming punishment and the blindness of those who remain heedless until the moment of affliction, when regret can no longer avail them.

translation: And We will set up the scales of justice on the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in the least. And if it be the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it. And sufficient are We as reckoners.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute justice of God on the Day of Judgment. The “scales” signify that every deed, intention, and consequence will be weighed with perfect equity, and no person will suffer the slightest injustice. Even the smallest possible thing—a mustard seed’s weight—will be brought forward and accounted for, showing that nothing is overlooked or forgotten. God’s sufficiency as Reckoner means He alone fully knows every hidden and open matter and is perfectly able to judge and requite without need of any record, witness, or helper. The verse therefore calls the human being to live with deep accountability, sincerity, and awareness that no good or evil is insignificant before God.

translation: And We had certainly given Moses and Aaron the Criterion, and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing.
interpretation: Allah reminds that He granted Moses and Aaron the Scripture that distinguishes truth from falsehood, and made it an illuminating guidance and an admonition that benefits those who are mindful of Him and guard themselves against His displeasure. The verse teaches that revelation is both discernment and light: it separates right from wrong in belief and conduct, and it awakens the conscience of the pious, who alone truly take heed and live by it.

translation: Those who fear their Lord in the unseen, and they are apprehensive of the Hour.
interpretation: This describes the God-conscious whose reverence for Allah is sincere and inward, not dependent on being seen by others, because they know He sees them; and because they are anxiously aware of the coming Hour, they live in a state of preparation, accountability, and obedience rather than heedlessness.

translation: And this is a blessed Reminder which We have sent down. So are you, to it, deniers?
interpretation: This verse declares the Qur’an to be a blessed Reminder sent down by Allah. Its blessing lies in its guidance, mercy, healing, and ability to bring people to truth and righteousness. The rhetorical question rebukes those who reject it, expressing astonishment that after such clear divine favor and evidence they would still deny it. It calls them to accept, honor, and follow this revelation rather than meet it with disbelief.

translation: And We had certainly given Abraham his guidance beforehand, and We were knowing of him.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Abraham’s right guidance was not something he achieved independently, but a gift from God granted by His prior knowledge and choice. God knew Abraham’s sincere receptiveness and worthiness, so He guided him to recognize His oneness and reject idolatry even before his prophetic mission and before later revealed scriptures. It teaches that true guidance comes from God, and that He selects and prepares those whom He knows to be fit for His message.

translation: When he said to his father and his people, 'What are these statues to which you are devoted?'
interpretation: This verse recounts Prophet Ibrahim’s confrontation with his father and his people regarding their idolatry. His question is one of rebuke and astonishment, not mere inquiry: he exposes the irrationality of devoting themselves to carved statues that are lifeless, powerless, and unable to benefit or harm. The phrase “devoted” indicates persistent attachment, standing before them in worship, reverence, and service. By asking this, Ibrahim challenges their inherited blind following and prepares them to recognize that worship belongs only to Allah, the Creator and Sustainer, not to man-made images. This is a foundational prophetic call to pure monotheism and a rejection of all false objects of worship.

translation: They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them."
interpretation: This verse exposes blind imitation of ancestors as an invalid basis for religious worship. The idolaters offered no rational or revealed proof for their idolatry; they merely appealed to inherited custom. It thus condemns uncritical conformity in matters of belief and worship, teaching that truth and divine guidance must be followed even if they contradict the practices of one’s forefathers. Worship belongs to God alone, and ancestral tradition cannot justify associating partners with Him.

translation: He said, "Indeed, you and your fathers have been in clear error."
interpretation: This is Prophet Ibrahim’s direct rebuke of his father and his people: their devotion to idols, passed down from their ancestors, is not true guidance but a manifest deviation. Their appeal to inherited tradition does not make false worship valid; it only shows that the error is deeply rooted and plainly recognizable, since they worship created things instead of the One God.

translation: They said, “Have you come to us with the truth, or are you among those who jest?”
interpretation: This verse reports the response of Abraham’s people when he called them away from idol worship. Instead of seriously weighing his argument, they ask whether he is bringing them a true message or merely playing and mocking them. Their question exposes their unwillingness to accept the truth and their attempt to dismiss his call as frivolity, while the verse implies that Abraham’s message is indeed serious truth, not idle play.

translation: He said, "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them, and I am, concerning that, among the witnesses."
interpretation: This is Ibrahim’s declaration of tawhid and his disavowal of the idolatry of his people. By pointing to the One who brought the heavens and the earth into existence without any prior model, he establishes that lordship belongs exclusively to their Creator and Sustainer. His statement that he is among the witnesses means he bears firm testimony to this truth with knowledge and conviction, and he stands as a witness against the false worship they directed to created beings instead of the One who originated all things.

translation: And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned away and gone back.
interpretation: Prophet Ibrahim swears a solemn oath that he will carry out a deliberate plan against the idols once the people leave them unattended. His aim is to expose the idols’ complete inability to defend themselves or benefit anyone, thereby proving the futility of worshipping them instead of Allah.

translation: So he made them into fragments, except for a large one of theirs, so that they might return to it.
interpretation: Abraham deliberately shattered the idols and left the largest one standing so that his people would return to it, question it, and discover its complete helplessness—thus exposing the falsehood of idol worship and turning them back toward the truth of God alone.

translation: They said, "Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is surely among the wrongdoers."
interpretation: This is the reaction of the idolaters when they discovered their idols broken. They regarded the act as an injustice against their false deities, showing how deeply attached they were to idol worship. Their claim that the one who did it was among the wrongdoers is itself misguided, because the true wrongdoers are those who set up false gods besides Allah and worship created things instead of the Creator. The verse exposes their inverted moral judgment: they condemned the destruction of lifeless idols while ignoring the greater crime of shirk.

translation: They said, "We heard a young man mentioning them; he is called Abraham."
interpretation: This statement shows that the opponents themselves identified Ibrahim as the one who had spoken against their idols, unintentionally confirming his steadfast monotheism. It teaches that even in a hostile society, a believer’s clear denunciation of false gods becomes known and cannot be hidden; Ibrahim’s youth did not prevent him from being recognized as the one who rejected idolatry. Their words also show that truth may be acknowledged by those who oppose it, and they set the stage for Ibrahim’s confrontation with his people, in which he would rely upon God alone.

translation: They said, "Then bring him before the eyes of the people, so that they may witness."
interpretation: They wanted Abraham brought out publicly so that the people could see him and bear witness to his trial and punishment. This demand reflects their aim to make his case a public spectacle, to establish his condemnation before the community, and to deter others from following him or challenging their idols.

translation: They said, "Have you done this to our gods, O Abraham?"
interpretation: The idolaters confront Abraham in anger and shock, accusing him of smashing their idols. Their question shows how devoted they were to false deities that could neither speak nor defend themselves, and it sets the stage for Abraham to expose the futility of worshipping powerless objects instead of the one true God.

translation: He said, "Rather, this—the largest of them—did it, so ask them, if they should be able to speak."
interpretation: Abraham uses this as a decisive argument against his people's idolatry: by attributing the act to their largest idol and daring them to question it, he exposes that their gods can neither act nor speak nor answer. The point is to make them realize that beings incapable of speech or response cannot be deities, and that worshipping them is therefore false and irrational.

translation: So they returned to themselves and said, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers."
interpretation: The verse conveys a moment of inward self-accusation: the idolaters’ own conscience momentarily testified that they had wronged themselves by worshipping lifeless idols that could neither speak nor benefit them. Their acknowledgment of guilt shows that truth can be recognized even by those who deny it, though such recognition does not necessarily lead to sincere repentance or lasting change.

translation: Then they were turned upside down on their heads: 'You already know that these do not speak.'
interpretation: This verse critiques the disbelievers' relapse into stubborn irrationality. Having briefly acknowledged their own wrong in worshiping idols, they reversed and confronted Ibrahim with the idols' inability to speak, as if that excused idolatry. But the fact that the idols cannot speak and cannot respond is itself proof of their helplessness and falsehood. They were not seeking truth; they were defending inherited falsehood. The verse shows that when truth exposes falsehood, its followers may become more entrenched, using even the obvious deficiencies of their false objects of worship as a pretext, rather than accepting the logical conclusion that speechless, powerless beings cannot be gods.

translation: He said, "Then do you worship besides Allah that which neither benefits you in any way nor harms you?"
interpretation: This is a rebuke against worshiping created things or false deities that possess no independent power to bring good or avert harm. It exposes the irrationality of directing devotion to what is utterly powerless and affirms that worship belongs solely to God, who alone controls benefit and harm.

translation: Fie upon you and upon what you worship besides Allah! Will you not then reason?
interpretation: This is a sharp rebuke from Prophet Abraham to his idolatrous people. He expresses disgust at them and at the false objects of their worship, because they have turned away from Allah—the only One who truly deserves worship—to things that have no power to benefit or harm. The rhetorical question “Will you not then reason?” exposes the irrationality of their position: if they used the intellect Allah gave them, they would recognize that helpless created things cannot be gods, and that worship must be directed to the Creator alone. It is a call to abandon blind imitation and inherited falsehood, and to submit to Allah with clear reasoning and sincere faith.

translation: They said, “Burn him and support your gods, if you are to do anything.”
interpretation: This verse reports the idolaters’ response to Abraham after he exposed the futility of their idols: since they had no proof, they turned to violence, ordering him burned to avenge and defend their supposed deities. It shows that false gods are helpless and must be defended by their worshippers, whereas the true God needs no defense. Their command is also an incitement: if you are serious about defending your gods, then carry out this act. It reveals the pattern of falsehood—when arguments fail, it seeks to suppress the truth by force—and it sets the stage for Allah’s intervention to save Abraham and disgrace their plot.

translation: We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham."
interpretation: God commanded the fire to cease its burning nature and become cool and safe for Abraham, so that it could not harm him; this was a direct miraculous protection of His prophet.

translation: And they intended against him a plan, but We made them the greatest losers.
interpretation: They plotted to destroy Abraham by fire, seeking to defeat Allah’s prophet and extinguish his call. But Allah turned their scheme against them: He made the fire cool and safe for Abraham, frustrated their design, and left them in utter loss—deprived of success in this world and of any share in the Hereafter. Their cleverness became the very cause of their ruin, and their hostility toward the truth only increased their perdition.

translation: And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We have blessed for the worlds.
interpretation: This verse recounts Allah’s deliverance of Ibrahim (Abraham) and Lut (Lot) from the persecution of Ibrahim’s people, guiding them to the blessed land—identified in Islamic tradition as the Levant (al-Sham), including Jerusalem and its surroundings. Allah describes this land as blessed for all peoples because He placed in it prophethood, revelation, guidance, and abundant good. The verse thus affirms that Allah protects and rescues those who remain steadfast in faith, that migration may be required to preserve one’s religion, and that divine blessing upon a place or people is ultimately intended to serve humanity and advance the truth.

translation: And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift, and We made each of them righteous.
interpretation: This verse means that God blessed Abraham with Isaac and Jacob as a gracious extra favor, beyond what was requested, and He made both of them righteous—meaning He purified them, guided them, and chose them for prophethood and moral integrity.

translation: And We made them leaders guiding by Our command, and We inspired to them the doing of good deeds, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakah; and they were worshippers of Us.
interpretation: This verse shows that true religious leadership is a station granted by God, not acquired by human claim or inheritance alone. Such leaders guide others according to God’s command, meaning their guidance is rooted in divine authority and not in personal desire or mere worldly authority. God’s inspiring them to good deeds, prayer, and zakah indicates that prophetic leadership is first inward and moral: it is built on righteousness, constant remembrance and worship of God, and social responsibility through charity. Prayer represents the servant’s direct duty toward God, while zakah represents duty toward His creation; together they form the practical expression of guided leadership. Their being described as “worshippers of Us” is the foundation of their rank: they lead others only because they themselves are wholly devoted servants of God.

translation: And Lot, We gave him judgment and knowledge, and We saved him from the city that was committing evil deeds. Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse highlights Allah's favor upon Prophet Lot: He granted him sound judgment and prophetic knowledge, and He rescued him from the corrupt city whose inhabitants practiced abominable acts. Their persistent immorality and defiance of divine commands made them a wicked and transgressing people. The verse thus teaches that wisdom and knowledge are divine gifts, that Allah protects the righteous from environments of sin, and that societies which institutionalize moral corruption invite divine punishment.

translation: And We admitted him into Our mercy. Indeed, he was among the righteous.
interpretation: God granted Lot entry into His mercy, meaning He saved him from the punishment that destroyed his people and encompassed him in divine protection and favor. This was because he was among the righteous—those upright in faith and action whom God selects for His mercy.

translation: And Noah, when he called out before, so We answered him and saved him and his household from the great distress.
interpretation: Noah's supplication was a sincere turning to God after long suffering and rejection; God's response shows that He hears the oppressed and delivers those who rely on Him, rescuing Noah and his believing family from the overwhelming calamity that destroyed the deniers.

translation: And We supported him against the people who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were an evil people, so We drowned them all.
interpretation: God granted His prophet Noah victory and protection against the people who stubbornly rejected the divine signs. Their denial was not merely a rejection of evidence but a settled moral corruption, described as being an evil people. Therefore, divine justice overtook them completely: they were all drowned, showing that God aids His messengers and that persistent rejection of His signs leads to total ruin.

translation: And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field, when the sheep of the people pastured in it at night; and We were witness to their judgment.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah fully knows and witnesses every judgment, and it highlights the wisdom He granted to David and Solomon. The dispute concerned damage done to a cultivated field by a flock grazing at night, requiring a ruling that would compensate the field’s owner without unjustly ruining the livestock owner’s livelihood. Solomon’s discernment lay in a restorative solution: the flock’s benefits would be used to repair the field while its ownership remained intact, showing that divinely guided judgment seeks both restitution and equity. Thus it teaches that true justice weighs harm and mercy together under Allah’s watchful knowledge.

translation: So We gave Solomon understanding of it; and to each We gave judgment and knowledge. And We subjected the mountains with David, glorifying, and the birds; and We were the Doers.
interpretation: The verse means that Allah alone grants true comprehension of rulings and matters, and He may give one servant deeper insight than another while both remain recipients of His wisdom and knowledge. Solomon’s understanding did not cancel David’s prophetic rank; rather, it shows that Allah distributes His gifts according to His sovereign will. The submission of the mountains and birds to David in glorifying Allah signifies that all creation is under Allah’s command and can be made to join His chosen servants in worship and miraculous signs. The closing words “and We were the Doers” affirm that every such favor, miracle, and act of guidance occurs by Allah’s effective power, not by any independent power of the prophets. Thus the verse teaches humility in knowledge, recognition that understanding is a divine grant, and awe at Allah’s absolute control over creation.

translation: And We taught him the craft of making armor for you, to protect you from your violence. So will you then be grateful?
interpretation: This verse teaches that the skill of making protective armor was a blessing taught by God to Prophet David, not something arising independently of divine guidance. Its purpose is to shield people from the harm and destruction they cause one another in conflict. The closing question is a call to gratitude: people should acknowledge God's provision of means for their safety and respond with thankful obedience, using such gifts for protection and good rather than for aggression or ingratitude.

translation: And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, blowing violently, running by his command to the land which We blessed. And We are ever, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: God granted Solomon authority over the wind as a sign of his prophethood and kingship: it would blow fiercely yet serve him, carrying him or his forces swiftly wherever he commanded, especially toward the blessed land (the Levant). This demonstrates that all natural forces are under God’s command, and that His knowledge encompasses everything, so He knows perfectly what He grants and to whom.

translation: And among the devils were those who dived for him and did other work besides that; and We were their guardians.
interpretation: This verse describes how God subjected the rebellious jinn to Solomon, forcing some of them to dive into the sea to extract pearls and treasures and to perform other arduous tasks. God’s guardianship means He watched over and controlled them, preventing them from overstepping His command, escaping their service, or harming Solomon, so that His decree and order remained fully enforced.

translation: And [mention] Job, when he called to his Lord, 'Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.'
interpretation: This is the supplication of Prophet Ayyub (Job), peace be upon him, who turns to God in a state of severe affliction. He does not complain against God or question His wisdom; rather, he acknowledges that harm has befallen him and immediately calls upon God's mercy, saying that God is the Most Merciful of the merciful. The verse teaches the proper manner of supplication: presenting one's need with humility, praising God's mercy, and placing complete hope in Him. It shows that suffering does not diminish a servant's closeness to God when met with patience and sincere reliance, and that true relief comes only from God, whose mercy is limitless and surpasses all other mercy.

translation: So We answered him, and We removed the harm that was upon him, and We gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.
interpretation: Allah answered Ayyub’s supplication, relieved him of the affliction and distress he suffered, and restored to him his family along with others like them, as a sign of His mercy and as an admonition for those who worship Him, so they may learn that patience and sincere reliance on Allah lead to relief and reward.

translation: And [mention] Ishmael, Idris, and Dhul-Kifl; all were among the patient.
interpretation: God praises these prophets by affirming that they were characterized by patience: they remained steadfast in worship, endured hardship for His sake, and persevered in faith and obedience. Their mention together teaches that true patience is a mark of prophetic virtue and a quality believers should imitate.

translation: And We admitted them into Our mercy. Indeed, they were among the righteous.
interpretation: God’s admission of them into His mercy means He granted them His special grace, forgiveness, and the eternal reward of Paradise, a favor bestowed upon them because they were truly righteous—firm in faith, obedient, and steadfast in doing good.

translation: And [mention] Dhun-Nun (Jonah), when he went away in anger and thought that We would not have power over him. Then he called out in the darknesses: “There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that a servant’s deliverance from distress is not secured by anger, impatience, or self-justification, but by returning to Allah with pure tawhid, glorifying Him, and admitting one’s own fault. The “darknesses” represent the layered confinements of outward crisis and inward remorse, where every created support fails and only sincere recognition of Allah’s exclusive divinity remains effective. Jonah’s prayer shows that repentance begins with affirming Allah’s oneness, exalting Him above any deficiency, and then acknowledging one’s own injustice; even from the deepest point of failure, Allah’s mercy is accessible to the one who turns back in humility.

translation: So We answered him and saved him from the distress. And thus do We save the believers.
interpretation: This verse teaches that Allah responds to the sincere call of the one in hardship and removes the grief that overwhelms him. His deliverance of the Prophet Yunus is not an isolated event but a demonstration of His unchanging way: whenever believers turn to Him with faith, humility, and reliance, He rescues them from their distress and grants them relief.

translation: And [remember] Zechariah, when he called out to his Lord: “My Lord, do not leave me alone [childless], and You are the best of inheritors.”
