interpretation: This verse refers to the believers who endured hardship, remained steadfast in faith, and persisted in obedience to Allah despite trials; their reward is the elevated dwelling place in Paradise, and therein they will be received with salutations of safety, honor, and peace from angels and from one another.

translation: They will abide therein forever. Excellent is it as a dwelling place and residence.
interpretation: This verse describes the eternal reward of the righteous in Paradise: they will remain there forever, never removed or expelled. God praises that abode as the best place of settlement and the finest place of residence, meaning it combines perfect permanence with perfect honor, comfort, and security—unlike worldly homes, which are temporary and imperfect.

translation: Say, "My Lord would not care for you at all were it not for your supplication. But you have denied, so it will be inevitable."
interpretation: This verse shows that human beings have no value or claim before God except through their turning to Him in worship and supplication. Since the rejecters denied the truth and abandoned that connection, the punishment they were warned about will become an inescapable reality that clings to them; it cannot be turned away or avoided.

translation: Ta-Seen-Meem.
interpretation: These are among the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'at) that open certain surahs of the Qur'an; their exact meaning is known to Allah, and they serve as a sign of the Qur'an's inimitability and a challenge to those who deny it to produce anything like it.

translation: These are the verses of the clear Book.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Qur’anic revelations are signs of a Scripture that is manifestly clear: clear in its wording, guidance, and proofs, and clarifying the truth so that it is distinguished from falsehood.

translation: Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers.
interpretation: This is a tender reproach from Allah to Prophet Muhammad: his sorrow over the people’s rejection was so intense that he was nearly consuming himself. Allah tells him that their refusal of faith is not his burden to bear; he cannot compel hearts, and his responsibility is only to convey the message. The verse consoles him and teaches that one who calls to truth should not destroy himself over those who choose disbelief.

translation: If We will, We can send down upon them from the sky a sign, so their necks would remain bowed before it in humility.
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah’s absolute power over the hearts and wills of people: if He wished, He could send a miraculous sign from the sky so overwhelming that they would all yield to it, their necks lowered in submission. It shows that their continued denial is not because Allah is unable to compel them, but because He does not force faith upon them. He grants them the opportunity to choose, so that belief may be sincere and accountable, rather than an outward submission produced only by an irresistible display of power.

translation: And no fresh reminder comes to them from the Most Merciful except that they turn away from it.
interpretation: This verse reproaches those who meet every newly revealed divine reminder with rejection and indifference. The reminder is described as coming from the Most Merciful to show that revelation is an act of mercy, yet they respond by turning aside. Their failure is not due to any lack of guidance, but to a willful aversion that refuses to receive what God sends for their correction and benefit.

translation: They have indeed denied, so there will come to them the tidings of what they used to mock.
interpretation: This is a severe warning to those who reject divine revelation: their mockery does not nullify the truth, and the realities they ridiculed—such as punishment, resurrection, and accountability—will soon become manifest to them as unavoidable news, bringing them regret and consequences.

translation: Do they not look at the earth, how many of every noble kind We have caused to grow therein?
interpretation: This verse directs human attention to the earth as a sign of God's creative power and generosity. The diverse, beneficial, and honorable kinds of vegetation He brings forth from the soil demonstrate that He is able to give life after death. It is a call to reflect on His wisdom, providence, and ability to resurrect, and a rebuke to those who deny or ignore His signs.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: The verse conveys that the events and punishments of past nations are a clear lesson and proof of Allah's power, justice, and truthfulness of His messengers. It also states that despite these manifest signs, the majority of those nations did not accept faith, showing that signs alone do not compel belief; hearts need divine guidance and humble receptivity. Thus, the scarcity of believers is not evidence against the message, and the believer should not measure truth by majority acceptance but should take heed from history and submit to God.

translation: And indeed, your Lord—He is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse declares that the Lord who nurtures and governs you is, with emphatic certainty, al-‘Azīz—the Almighty whose power is absolute, invincible, and never diminished—and al-Raḥīm—the Most Merciful, whose mercy is vast and repeated, especially toward those who turn to Him. The pairing teaches that His might does not negate His mercy, nor does His mercy imply weakness; He can decisively punish the arrogant and still respond to the repentant with compassion. Thus the believer should stand in awe of His power and live in hope of His mercy.

translation: And [mention] when your Lord called out to Moses, [saying], “Go to the wrongdoing people.”
interpretation: This verse recounts God’s command to Moses to confront the unjust people—Pharaoh and his followers—who persisted in oppression and denial. It establishes that God directly commissions His messengers to warn tyrants, and it consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that opposition to divine guidance is an old pattern, while the duty remains to deliver God’s message to the wrongdoers.

translation: The people of Pharaoh—will they not fear Allah?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical rebuke and summons to taqwa: Pharaoh’s people are called to awaken to God-consciousness, which would restrain them from tyranny, arrogance, and rejection of Moses’ message. Their refusal to fear Allah is presented as the root of their injustice and the reason they stand warned.

translation: He said, "My Lord, indeed I fear that they will deny me."
interpretation: This expresses Moses' concern that his audience will reject his message and accuse him of lying, making it difficult for him to deliver God's command; it reflects a human awareness of opposition, not a lack of trust in God.

translation: And my breast tightens, and my tongue does not loosen, so send for Aaron.
interpretation: Moses asks God to send Aaron as a helper and partner in the mission because his own heart is constricted by anxiety and his tongue cannot speak with fluency and ease before Pharaoh; his request expresses reliance on God to supply through his brother the strength and eloquence he lacks.

translation: And they have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me.
interpretation: Moses acknowledges that the Egyptians hold a grievance against him—referring to his killing of an Egyptian man—and therefore fears that if he returns to Pharaoh, they will execute him in retaliation. This expresses his human apprehension and his need for God's protection as he undertakes the mission.

translation: He said, "No! Go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed, We are with you, listening."
interpretation: The divine response rejects Moses’ fear of being killed and replaces it with a firm assurance of protection and aid. The command to go “both” includes Aaron as the requested helper, and “with Our signs” means carrying the miraculous proofs that establish God’s authority and the truth of the message. “Indeed, We are with you, listening” signifies God’s encompassing support and awareness: He hears every word, threat, and scheme of Pharaoh and his people, and He will not abandon or fail His messengers.

translation: So go, both of you, to Pharaoh and say, 'Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This means Moses and Aaron are commanded to confront Pharaoh with a declaration that their authority is not from any human source but from God, the Lord and Sustainer of all creation. Although two men are sent, they carry one unified message and represent one divine commission, so their claim is not merely personal but a summons to Pharaoh to recognize the universal lordship of God over every realm, including his own kingdom.

translation: That you let the Children of Israel go with us.
interpretation: This is a decisive demand to Pharaoh to release the Children of Israel from slavery and allow them to depart with Moses and Aaron. It shows that their prophetic mission to Pharaoh was not merely to convey a creed but also to confront tyrannical oppression and secure the freedom of an enslaved people. Pharaoh’s refusal would therefore be a rejection of God’s authority and a continuation of unjust domination.

translation: He said: Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life?
interpretation: This is Pharaoh’s rhetorical reproach to Moses: he reminds him that he was brought up in Pharaoh’s household from infancy and lived among them for many years, aiming to shame him for opposing Pharaoh and to frame Moses’ prophetic mission as ingratitude and betrayal of favor. In the Qur’anic context, it exposes how Pharaoh judges truth by personal favors and loyalty to his own power rather than by God’s signs.

translation: And you did your deed which you did, and you are among the ungrateful.
interpretation: This is Pharaoh’s accusing taunt to Moses: he dredges up the killing Moses committed before prophethood and brands him ungrateful—or, in a broader sense, a denier—in order to discredit him and make his call to truth seem hypocritical. The verse exposes how tyrants use a person’s past errors as a weapon, while the Qur’anic context clarifies that a sin committed before guidance, followed by repentance, does not negate later faith or divine commissioning.

translation: He said, "I did it then, while I was among those who were misguided."
interpretation: This is Moses acknowledging that the act he committed—striking the Egyptian who then died—occurred before Allah granted him prophethood and its direct guidance. By saying he was then "among the misguided," he means he acted without the revealed guidance and prophetic knowledge he later received, not that he was a disbeliever after having been guided. It expresses his recognition of a past error committed in ignorance or before his mission, and it contrasts that former state with the guidance Allah subsequently bestowed upon him.

translation: So I fled from you when I feared you, but my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers.
interpretation: This is Prophet Moses recalling how he left Egypt out of fear of Pharaoh and his people after the accidental killing of an Egyptian. He does not present his flight as disobedience, but as part of the circumstances through which Allah later showed him mercy. The verse teaches that Allah can turn a person’s fear, weakness, or difficult past into the path of honor and guidance: He granted Moses “hukm,” meaning sound judgment, knowledge, prophethood, or revealed understanding, and then included him among His messengers. Thus the verse is an acknowledgment of Allah’s favor and a declaration that prophethood and messengership come solely by Allah’s choosing and grace, not by human power or status.

translation: And is that a favor you remind me of, that you have enslaved the Children of Israel?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical rebuke by Moses: Pharaoh’s claim of having raised him is not a true favor but a hypocritical boast, because Pharaoh had enslaved Moses’ people, the Children of Israel. The verse exposes that Pharaoh’s supposed benevolence was built upon oppression, so his reminder is not grounds for gratitude but a mark of his tyranny and guilt.

translation: Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?"
interpretation: This is a question of denial and mockery, not a sincere inquiry. Pharaoh, who claimed lordship over his people, asks this to reject Moses' call and to belittle the idea of a Lord and Sustainer of all creation, disclosing his arrogance and his refusal to submit to the One who truly governs every world.

translation: He said, "The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you are to be certain."
interpretation: This is Moses’ answer to Pharaoh’s question about the Lord of the worlds. He declares that the true Lord is not a local or national deity but the sovereign Creator and Sustainer of the heavens, the earth, and all that exists between them. The phrase “if you are to be certain” appeals to sincere reasoning: if Pharaoh and his people would reflect on the order, unity, and dependent nature of the whole universe, they would arrive at the certainty that such universal lordship belongs to God alone. Thus the verse calls them beyond inherited denial to the conviction that follows from contemplating creation.

translation: He said to those around him, 'Will you not listen?'
interpretation: This is Pharaoh addressing his courtiers in astonishment and disdain at Moses’ answer. He is not seeking information but is inciting them to reject and mock Moses, as if saying: Do you not hear this strange and unacceptable claim? It expresses his attempt to rally those around him into shared denial of the truth.

translation: He said: Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the former ones.
interpretation: Moses confronts Pharaoh by declaring that the God he speaks of is not a distant or unknown deity but the very Lord who governs Pharaoh himself and all the generations before him. Pharaoh is therefore not a lord over his people; he and his ancestors are created servants under the one true God. The verse affirms God's eternal lordship across every generation and dismantles any claim to divinity or inherited authority that sets itself against Him.

translation: He said, 'Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman.'
interpretation: Pharaoh resorts to labeling Moses insane because he cannot refute the truth Moses has brought. It is a smear intended to discredit the prophetic message before his court and people, showing that his authority relies on ridicule and coercion rather than evidence. The charge also exposes the spiritual blindness of those who reject divine guidance: they dismiss the messenger as irrational because they judge reality only by their own corrupt norms, while the verse vindicates the prophet against the slander of arrogant power.

translation: He said: Lord of the east and the west and whatever is between them, if you were to reason.
interpretation: This verse identifies the true Lord as the One who owns, creates, and governs all directions and everything that lies between them—meaning the entire universe in its vastness and order. The mention of east and west encompasses all horizons and all that exists within creation. The call “if you were to reason” is a challenge to Pharaoh and his people: if they used their intellect rightly, they would recognize that such absolute sovereignty over all existence cannot belong to a finite human ruler, but only to the Creator and Sustainer of all things. It also indicates that rejecting God is not a conclusion of sound reasoning but a failure to reason correctly.

translation: [Pharaoh] said: If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned.
interpretation: This verse exposes Pharaoh’s tyrannical arrogance: he claims exclusive lordship and responds to Moses’ call to worship God alone with a threat of imprisonment. It shows that corrupt power, when unable to answer the truth, resorts to coercion and punishment to silence faith, while also highlighting the believer’s trial in standing firm against an unjust ruler who sets himself up as a false god.

translation: He said, 'Even if I brought you something clear?'
interpretation: This is Moses’ reply to Pharaoh’s threat of imprisonment: he asks whether Pharaoh would still reject and punish him even if he came with an unmistakable sign from God. The rhetorical question exposes Pharaoh’s arrogance and injustice—he is not seeking truth but clinging to power—and it shows that a clear divine proof is enough for anyone sincerely willing to accept it.

translation: He said, "Then bring it, if you are of the truthful."
interpretation: Pharaoh's demand is a challenge born of arrogance and unbelief: he does not seek guidance but wants a pretext to reject Moses. The verse shows that when truth is met with hardened denial, even the request for a sign is not sincere; it is a refusal to submit unless the messenger conforms to the disbeliever's terms. It also teaches that truthfulness is ultimately proven by God's power, not by human approval—yet those who demand miracles to avoid faith will not be convinced by them if their hearts remain closed.

translation: So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clear serpent.
interpretation: This is a sign granted to Moses before Pharaoh: when he cast down his staff in obedience to God’s command, it instantly became a real, visible serpent. It was a manifest miracle, not illusion or magic, demonstrating God’s power to transform created things and confirming Moses as a true prophet. The miracle was unmistakable and served as clear evidence against Pharaoh’s denial and as a warning to those who rejected God’s signs.

translation: And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the beholders.
interpretation: This is a miraculous sign granted to Moses: when he withdrew his hand from his garment, it emerged radiantly white, shining with a light that was plainly visible to all who looked. It was not a defect such as leprosy, but a divine wonder confirming his prophethood. The phrase “to the beholders” stresses that the miracle was public and perceptible, not a private illusion, and that it demonstrated God’s absolute power to override natural properties in support of His messenger.

translation: He said to the chiefs around him, 'Indeed, this is a learned magician.'
interpretation: Pharaoh addresses his inner circle of nobles and officials, dismissing Moses’ miraculous signs as nothing more than expert sorcery. By calling him a skilled magician, Pharaoh seeks to deny the divine origin of the signs and rally his court against Moses, framing him as a dangerous illusionist rather than a prophet.

translation: He wants to drive you out of your land by his magic, so what do you command?
interpretation: Pharaoh is addressing his court and presenting Moses’ God-given signs as sorcery, thereby turning a call to truth into a supposed plot to seize their land and displace them. He then invites his chiefs to advise him on how to respond. The verse exposes how tyrannical power defends itself: it discredits divine guidance by mislabeling it as magic, converts a moral and spiritual challenge into a national-security threat, and seeks collective approval for suppressing the truth.

translation: They said, 'Delay him and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers.'
interpretation: This is the counsel of Pharaoh’s chiefs after Musa’s sign: instead of submitting to the truth, they advised Pharaoh to postpone the matter of Musa and Harun and to dispatch recruiters throughout Egypt’s cities to assemble the magicians. Their plan was to buy time, mobilize the regime’s resources, and stage a contest of sorcery against the prophetic miracle, revealing their confidence in human craft and state power rather than in God.

translation: They will bring you every learned magician.
interpretation: This is Pharaoh’s command to summon the most skilled sorcerers to confront Moses, showing his confidence that expert magic and human cunning could overpower the divine sign and silence the prophetic message.

translation: So the magicians were gathered for the appointment of a known day.
interpretation: This verse indicates that the confrontation between Moses and the sorcerers was deliberately arranged by Pharaoh at a fixed, preappointed time and day. The sorcerers were assembled and prepared so that the contest would be public and witnessed, reflecting Pharaoh’s reliance on their magic as an established power. Yet the precise appointment also sets the stage for the divine miracle that would expose and nullify their sorcery.

translation: And it was said to the people, 'Are you gathered?'
interpretation: It signifies a public summons: the people were asked to assemble so that the coming confrontation would be witnessed by the masses, turning it into a demonstration intended to uphold the ruling authority's prestige and to discredit the divine message brought by Moses.

translation: Perhaps we will follow the magicians if they are the victorious.
interpretation: This statement exposes a corrupt criterion for allegiance: the people were not asking what is true or right, but who would win. Their willingness to follow the magicians was conditioned purely on victory, showing blind partisanship to Pharaoh’s order and a mindset that treats power and spectacle as the measure of legitimacy. It warns against following a path merely because its adherents appear dominant, rather than judging by truth, evidence, and divine guidance.

translation: So when the magicians came, they said to Pharaoh, 'Will there indeed be a reward for us if we are the victors?'
interpretation: This verse exposes the magicians' worldly motivation: before confronting Moses, they seek Pharaoh's assurance of payment, showing that they served his false claim for material gain and status. It teaches that allegiance to falsehood is often transactional, yet divine truth can transform even such self-interested hearts, as these same magicians later submitted to God after witnessing the miracle.

translation: He said: Yes, and indeed you will then be among those brought near.
interpretation: This is Pharaoh’s affirmative response to the magicians’ request for a reward: he confirms that they will be paid and adds that, if they prevail, they will also receive a privileged status of closeness and favor with him, making the offer more enticing and securing their loyalty.

translation: Moses said to them, "Throw what you are going to throw."
interpretation: Moses deliberately let Pharaoh’s magicians cast first so that their sorcery would be fully displayed, after which God’s sign would openly overpower it, proving that divine truth prevails over human falsehood and illusion.

translation: So they threw their ropes and their staffs and said, 'By the might of Pharaoh, indeed we will surely be the victors.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the sorcerers’ arrogant confidence as they display their magic before Pharaoh, swearing by his power and glory that they will overcome Moses. Their boast reveals that their trust is placed entirely in a human ruler’s might rather than in God, and it sets up the coming humiliation of their false power when Moses’ miracle swallows up their illusions.

translation: So Moses threw his staff, and behold, it swallowed up what they were falsifying.
interpretation: This verse depicts the decisive triumph of Moses’ God-given miracle over the magicians’ deceptive arts. Their sorcery was only an illusion and fabrication, whereas Moses’ staff was a real sign from God; it consumed and nullified their false displays. The meaning is that divine truth cannot be overcome by human trickery or falsehood, however impressive it may appear, and that God’s power exposes and erases deception.

translation: Then the magicians fell down prostrate.
interpretation: This describes the magicians’ instantaneous surrender to the truth after witnessing Moses’ miracle. Their prostration was not merely physical but a profound act of faith: they recognized that what Moses brought was not sorcery but a sign from God, and so they abandoned their craft, their position, and Pharaoh’s favor to worship the Lord of Moses and Aaron.

translation: They said, “We believe in the Lord of the worlds.”
interpretation: This statement means that they acknowledged Allah alone as the true Lord, Sovereign, and Nurturer of all creation, rejecting every false claim to lordship and committing themselves to Him with sincere faith, even in the face of worldly power and persecution.

translation: Lord of Moses and Aaron
interpretation: This verse declares that the Lord in whom the magicians believed is the same Lord who sent Moses and Aaron, namely Allah, the sole Creator and Sovereign. It affirms that true lordship belongs exclusively to Him, and it repudiates Pharaoh’s false claim to divinity. Their faith thus acknowledges that the God of the prophets is the only true God, worthy of worship and obedience, even when confessing Him brings worldly danger.

translation: He said, 'Did you believe him before I gave you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. So you shall soon know. I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all.'
interpretation: Pharaoh reacts with fury to the magicians' faith, revealing his tyrannical claim to absolute authority: he treats their belief as a crime because it occurred without his permission. By calling Moses their 'chief' who taught them magic, he tries to dismiss the miracle as a prearranged trick and to discredit the truth rather than face it. His threats of mutilation and mass crucifixion are instruments of terror meant to coerce them back into submission and deter others from believing. The verse exposes how corrupt power responds to undeniable signs with slander, intimidation, and cruelty. It also highlights the magicians' moral courage: having recognized the truth, they endure persecution rather than obey an unjust ruler, showing that faith cannot be legitimately controlled by political permission and that divine truth is worth suffering for.

translation: They said, "No harm. Indeed, to our Lord we will return."
interpretation: This expresses the believers' firm resolve before threat and punishment: worldly suffering cannot truly harm them, because their ultimate return is to Allah. Their loss of life or property is not the final measure of success; their Lord is their destination, and with Him is the true recompense. They therefore reject Pharaoh's intimidation and place their hope in Allah's justice and mercy, knowing that every soul returns to its Lord for judgment and reward.

translation: Indeed, we hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, since we were the first of the believers.
interpretation: This verse expresses the hope of those who turned to God after having been deeply involved in falsehood: they do not rely on their own merit, but on God’s mercy, and they plead that their sincere acceptance of the truth as the first among their people may be accepted as a reason for pardon. It teaches that no past sin is beyond forgiveness when a person genuinely repents and believes, and that God’s mercy embraces those who respond to guidance even after grave error.

translation: And We inspired Moses, [saying], “Set out with My servants by night; indeed, you will be pursued.”
interpretation: This verse conveys that Allah directly guided Moses to lead the oppressed Children of Israel out of Pharaoh’s dominion under the cover of night, while informing him that pursuit would follow. It teaches that divine deliverance often begins with a commanded step of action and trust: Allah knows the danger ahead, prepares His chosen servant for it, and uses the ensuing pursuit to manifest His power and rescue the faithful from tyranny.

translation: Then Pharaoh sent among the cities gatherers [of troops].
interpretation: Pharaoh dispatched recruiters throughout his towns and provinces to muster an army and mobilize forces to pursue Moses and the Children of Israel.

translation: Indeed, these are a small band.
interpretation: This is a statement of contempt and underestimation: Pharaoh dismisses the believers as a weak, insignificant few, trying to make them appear harmless and to justify his oppressive pursuit of them. It conveys that worldly power often belittles the faithful because it measures strength only by numbers and might, while God’s help can overturn such arrogant calculations.

translation: And indeed, they are surely enraging us.
interpretation: Pharaoh and his people admit that the Children of Israel have become a cause of intense anger to them. This anger is not a response to any crime or injustice committed by the Israelites; it arises because the oppressed have believed in God, followed Moses, and are escaping Pharaoh’s domination. The verse exposes the psychology of tyrannical power: it regards the liberation and faith of the weak as an insult to its own supremacy. Such rage is therefore a sign of arrogance, not moral outrage, and it drives Pharaoh to pursue them, while God’s plan for the oppressed moves forward.

translation: And indeed, we are all vigilant.
interpretation: This is Pharaoh’s warning to the Egyptians: he presents himself and his people as a united force, fully alert, armed with caution, and prepared to confront Moses and the Children of Israel. The word “حاذرون” conveys a state of fearful watchfulness and military readiness, revealing Pharaoh’s anxiety that the Israelites might escape or grow influential, and his resolve to suppress them through collective intimidation and force.

translation: So We expelled them from gardens and springs.
interpretation: This refers to Allah driving Pharaoh and his people out of the fertile gardens and water sources of Egypt as a punishment. After they pursued Moses and the Children of Israel in arrogance, Allah removed them from those blessings and destroyed them, showing that worldly luxuries cannot protect the unjust from divine judgment.

translation: And treasures and a noble station.
interpretation: This refers to the hoarded wealth and the elevated, honored status, dignity, and rank that Pharaoh and his people possessed in Egypt—worldly blessings and worldly honor that were taken from them and left behind.

translation: Thus. And We made the Children of Israel inherit them.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah, by His decree, transfers worldly blessings, resources, and authority from one people to another, and that He fulfills His promise to the oppressed by making them heirs of what their oppressors once possessed.

translation: So they pursued them at sunrise.
interpretation: This verse depicts Pharaoh and his forces setting out after the Children of Israel in the early morning, when the sun had risen. It highlights their persistent arrogance and hostility: despite having been warned and having witnessed clear signs, they continued their pursuit to destroy the believers. The timing also emphasizes the dramatic nature of the deliverance that follows, as the pursuit takes place at the start of the day, yet ends in the pursuers’ destruction, showing that worldly power cannot overcome divine decree.

translation: So when the two hosts saw each other, the companions of Moses said, “Indeed, we are surely to be overtaken.”
interpretation: This is a moment of severe testing: the Israelites, seeing Pharaoh’s forces behind them and the sea before them, judge by outward circumstances and fear annihilation. Their cry reveals how terror can eclipse trust in God’s promise. It also highlights the contrast between ordinary human apprehension and prophetic certainty; the scene teaches that when means seem exhausted, divine deliverance is near, and that apparent pursuit does not negate God’s command or covenant.

translation: He said, "No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me."
interpretation: This is Moses’ firm reply to his companions when they feared being overtaken: he rejects their despair and affirms that God’s help, protection, and guidance are with him. “My Lord is with me” means by His support and care, not in a physical localized sense, and “He will guide me” means God will direct him to the means of deliverance and safety, so they should not fear.

translation: So We inspired Moses: 'Strike the sea with your staff.' Then it split, and each part was like a great mountain.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the miraculous parting of the sea came about solely by Allah’s command, with Moses’ staff serving only as an outward instrument. It teaches that divine power transcends all natural laws, that Allah alone controls the forces of creation, and that He makes a way of deliverance for His chosen servants even when every worldly path is closed. The towering walls of water also signify the coming judgment upon Pharaoh’s tyranny, as the same miracle that saved the believers became the means of drowning the oppressors.

translation: And We brought the others near there.
interpretation: Allah caused Pharaoh and his hosts to draw near to the sea after the Children of Israel had crossed, so that they would follow them into the opened path and be overtaken by the water as punishment for their disbelief and pursuit.

translation: And We saved Moses and all those who were with him.
interpretation: This verse signifies that Allah alone grants deliverance to His messengers and those who follow them, showing that His promise of rescue is fulfilled completely for the faithful and that divine aid encompasses the whole community of believers who stand with the prophetic mission.

translation: Then We drowned the others.
interpretation: After delivering Moses and the believers with him, Allah caused Pharaoh and his pursuing forces to be drowned in the sea, showing that deliverance for the faithful is accompanied by the destruction of oppressive pursuers.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse highlights that the preceding narrative contains a clear divine sign and lesson, yet the majority of those addressed did not accept faith. It teaches that signs alone do not force belief, since hearts can still refuse the truth. It also emphasizes that the truth is not determined by majority acceptance, and it serves as both a consolation to the Messenger and a warning to those who persist in denial.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God's absolute power and His mercy are both perfect and inseparable. His might does not make Him unjust or distant, and His mercy does not diminish His majesty; rather, He governs all things with complete authority while showing compassion to His creation, so the heart should fear His power and hope in His forgiveness.

translation: And recite to them the news of Abraham.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet Muhammad to present the account of Abraham to his people as a lesson and warning. Abraham is invoked as the model of pure monotheism: he rejected the idolatry of his people, challenged the worship of created things, and devoted himself solely to Allah. By recalling his story, the verse confronts the disbelievers with the contradiction between their claim to follow Abraham’s way and their actual practice of shirk, urging them to abandon false worship and heed the truth of revelation.

translation: When he said to his father and his people, “What do you worship?”
interpretation: This is Ibrahim’s opening challenge to the inherited idolatry of his father and his people. His question is not asked for information but as a rhetorical and prophetic confrontation: he makes them state plainly what they worship so that the futility and falsehood of their gods may become evident. It affirms that worship must be directed to the true God alone and rejects blind conformity to ancestral religion, calling them to reflect on whether the objects of their devotion truly deserve to be worshipped.

translation: They said, "We worship idols and remain devoted to them."
interpretation: This verse reports the answer of Ibrahim's people: they openly confess that their worship is directed to idols and that they persist in clinging to them with constant devotion. The word "عاكفين" conveys staying, attending, and being firmly bound to something; so their response shows not a reasoned faith but an inherited, stubborn attachment to false objects of worship. It exposes the emptiness of their position: they devote themselves to lifeless idols and remain fixed in that devotion even when called to reflect.

translation: He said, 'Do they hear you when you call?'
interpretation: This is Abraham’s rebuke of idol worship: the false gods they invoke cannot even hear their calls, so they are utterly powerless to answer, benefit, or harm. The verse exposes the futility of supplicating created things and points to the exclusive right of the One who truly hears every call.

translation: Or do they benefit you, or harm you?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical question from Prophet Ibrahim to his people concerning their idols. He is not asking for information but exposing the idols’ total inability: they cannot benefit anyone, nor can they cause harm. Since they possess no power to help or hurt, they are unworthy of worship. True divinity belongs only to Allah, who alone hears, benefits, and harms. Thus the verse establishes that anything unable to bring benefit or avert harm cannot be an object of worship.

translation: They said, "No, but we found our fathers doing likewise."
interpretation: This response shows that they had no rational or revealed proof for their idolatry; they justified it only by blindly following the inherited practices of their ancestors. It exposes how ancestral custom can become a barrier to accepting prophetic truth when people cling to tradition instead of examining whether their worship is truly right.

translation: He said, "Have you considered what you have been worshipping?"
interpretation: This is a rhetorical challenge from Prophet Ibrahim to his people: he calls them to reflect seriously on the idols they and their ancestors devoted themselves to, showing that such worship is blind and baseless. The question exposes that these objects of worship have no power to hear, benefit, or harm, and therefore are unworthy of the devotion due to Allah alone.

translation: You and your forefathers of old.
interpretation: This phrase confronts the worshipers and their ancient ancestors together, exposing that inherited tradition and ancestral custom cannot make a false object of worship divine or worthy of devotion. It rejects the authority of mere antiquity and communal practice in matters of worship, preparing the way for exclusive devotion to Allah alone.

translation: Indeed, they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This is the declaration of Abraham that all false objects of worship are, in effect, enemies to him: he disowns them, rejects any allegiance to them, and opposes them because they cannot benefit or harm and are not worthy of worship. The only exception is the Lord of all worlds, Allah, whom he affirms as his true Lord, to whom alone he is devoted, and from whom he seeks guidance and salvation.

translation: Who created me, and He guides me.
interpretation: This is Abraham’s affirmation that the One who brought him into existence from nothing is the same One who continually directs him to the truth, right belief, and the path of righteousness. Creation and guidance are both exclusively from Allah, so no created thing or idol deserves to be associated with Him in either.

translation: And it is He Who feeds me and gives me drink.
interpretation: This is a declaration that all provision and sustenance—food, drink, and every means of nourishment—come ultimately from God alone. He is the One who creates, provides, and sustains; no created being can feed or give drink except by His will and grant. Therefore, reliance, gratitude, and worship belong to Him alone.

translation: And when I am ill, it is He who heals me.
interpretation: This verse expresses pure reliance on Allah in the matter of healing: ultimate cure belongs to Allah alone, even when medical means are used. It also reflects prophetic etiquette in speech, as Ibrahim attributed illness to himself while attributing healing directly to Allah, though all things occur by Allah’s decree. The believer should seek permissible treatment but place trust in Allah as the One who truly grants recovery.

translation: And [it is He] who will cause me to die and then bring me to life.
interpretation: This is a declaration that Allah alone has full authority over death and resurrection. After death, He will restore life for the Hereafter, when every soul will stand before Him for judgment. It expresses complete trust in Allah’s power over the final transition and certainty in the life to come.

translation: And He who, I hope, will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: Forgiveness is to be sought from God alone, and even a righteous servant must hope in His mercy rather than rely on his own deeds. The Day of Judgment is the Day of Recompense, when every soul is held accountable, and only God’s pardon can remove the consequence of sin. Saying “I hope” shows that forgiveness is not owed to anyone but is a matter of divine grace, so the believer should live with humble hope, not presumption, concerning sins and shortcomings.

translation: My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous.
interpretation: This is a supplication by Prophet Ibrahim asking God for sound judgment, religious understanding, and prophetic wisdom, and for him to be joined with the righteous in faith, conduct, and final destiny—both in this world and in the Hereafter.

translation: And grant me a tongue of truth among later generations.
interpretation: Ibrahim asks God to place his name and message in the mouths of future peoples with truthfulness, so that he is remembered not for worldly fame but as a sincere servant and caller to pure monotheism, and so that later generations may follow the faith he preached.

translation: And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss.
interpretation: This is a supplication to Allah to be included among those who will inherit the Garden of Bliss in the Hereafter—that is, to be granted permanent entry into Paradise and its eternal delights. It expresses the believer’s hope for Allah’s mercy and reward, acknowledging that Paradise is inherited by Allah’s grace and granted to His righteous servants.

translation: And forgive my father; indeed, he was among the misguided.
interpretation: This is part of Prophet Ibrahim's supplication to Allah. He asks forgiveness for his father, who was an idolater, while acknowledging that his father was among those who deviated from the truth. The prayer reflects Ibrahim's compassion and his hope for his father's well-being, but it does not imply that Allah forgives unrepentant disbelievers. It was made before Ibrahim became certain that his father was an enemy of Allah; afterward he disassociated himself from him. The verse teaches that believers may desire guidance and forgiveness for misguided relatives, but ultimate forgiveness belongs to Allah and is granted to those who repent and believe.

translation: And do not disgrace me on the Day when they are resurrected.
interpretation: This is a supplication to Allah asking to be spared from shame, humiliation, and exposure on the Day of Resurrection, when all people will be raised for judgment. It expresses the worshipper’s deep need for Allah’s mercy, forgiveness, and protection from public disgrace before all creation on that decisive day.

translation: The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the things people usually rely on in this world—money, possessions, and offspring—will be of no avail to save a person from Allah’s reckoning. This verse teaches that worldly advantage and family ties cannot substitute for faith and a sound heart before God; only what is directed sincerely to Him will matter.

translation: Except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.
interpretation: This means that on the Day when people meet their Lord, nothing of worldly wealth, status, or descendants will avail them; only a heart that is spiritually intact will benefit. A sound heart is one purified of disbelief, hypocrisy, doubt, arrogance, and corrupt intentions, and firmly grounded in sincere faith, love of Allah, and submission to Him alone. Such a heart is not merely free of spiritual disease; it is alive with remembrance of Allah, humble before Him, and oriented toward His pleasure. Thus the verse places ultimate success not in what a person accumulates or leaves behind, but in the inward state with which he returns to his Creator.

translation: And Paradise will be brought near to the righteous.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, Allah will draw the Garden close to those who guarded themselves against His displeasure by faith and obedience, honoring them with the sight of its bliss and granting them entry into it as the reward of their taqwa.

translation: And Hellfire will be brought into view for those who went astray.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the Fire will be unveiled and made plainly visible to those who deviated from truth and divine guidance, so that they witness the reality they denied and recognize it as the place prepared for their willful straying.

translation: And it will be said to them, "Where is that which you used to worship?"
interpretation: This is a divine rebuke and challenge addressed to the idolaters on the Day of Judgment. It is not a genuine request for information, but a rhetorical question meant to expose the utter worthlessness of the false deities they devoted themselves to. By asking where those objects of worship have gone, it forces them to confront that their gods can neither benefit, harm, nor intercede for them. The verse thus declares the nullity of associating partners with Allah and establishes that worship belongs to Allah alone, the only one who can rescue or punish.

translation: So they will be hurled into it, they and the erring ones.
interpretation: This describes the fate of the idolaters and all who followed them in deviation: on the Day of Judgment, they will be cast headlong into the Fire together with the false objects of worship and the leaders of misguidance. It emphasizes that those who led others astray and those who willingly followed them share the same punishment, and that the false deities they invoked can neither rescue them nor themselves. The verse serves as a warning that choosing a path of disbelief and spiritual deviation leads to humiliation and ruin in the Hereafter.

translation: And the hosts of Iblis, all together.
interpretation: They are the followers, allies, and troops of Iblis among jinn and humankind who obeyed him in disbelief and misguidance; on the Day of Judgment they will all be gathered together and driven into the Fire, with none of them left out.

translation: They will say, while they are quarreling therein.
interpretation: This verse depicts the people of Hell arguing among themselves in the Fire, each blaming the other for the misguidance that brought them there. Their dispute is not a sincere search for truth but the bitter recrimination of those who now see the truth too late and are powerless to escape. It shows that following false leaders, false gods, or one’s own desires ends in futile accusation and regret in the Hereafter, where no argument can alter the punishment or bring relief.

translation: By Allah, indeed we were in manifest error.
interpretation: Their oath expresses the certainty and intensity of their remorse: they now see that the path they followed was not a slight misjudgment but a glaring deviation from the truth. This is because they had equated others with the Lord of all worlds, giving created beings the devotion, obedience, or reverence owed to Him alone. Their confession is a testimony against themselves, showing that misguidance becomes unmistakable when its consequences are faced, and it stands as a warning before the same end is reached.

translation: When we equated you with the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This is a confession by the people of Hell, addressed to the false deities and powers they had worshipped. They acknowledge that they had made those created, powerless beings equal to Allah—the Lord and Sustainer of all creation—by directing to them the worship, obedience, and reverence that belong to Allah alone. It exposes the enormity of shirk: equating anything with the Lord of the worlds is manifest misguidance, and their admission comes only after it is too late, serving as a warning to the living not to commit the same error.

translation: And none led us astray except the criminals.
interpretation: This is the confession of the people of the Fire: they admit that the main cause of their ruin was the criminal leaders and seducers who invited them to shirk and sin, yet their confession is a regretful acknowledgment of having followed them, not a valid excuse, since they chose that path willingly.

translation: So we have no intercessors.
interpretation: This is a confession of utter helplessness on the Day of Judgment: those who denied the truth realize too late that no one can plead their case before God or avert the punishment they have earned, and every imagined support has vanished.

translation: nor a devoted friend
interpretation: This phrase declares that on the Day of Judgment, those who denied the truth and wronged themselves will find no loyal, intimate companion to help them, intercede for them, or lessen their punishment. It emphasizes that human closeness and friendship cannot avail in the Hereafter unless rooted in faith and God-consciousness; ultimate support and relief come only from God.

translation: If only we had a return [to the world], then we would be among the believers.
interpretation: This expresses the disbelievers’ futile regret in the Hereafter and shows that the time for choosing faith is limited to worldly life; once it ends, the wish to return and believe cannot alter one’s fate.

translation: Indeed, in that is surely a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the events and punishments of past nations are clear proofs of Allah’s power, wisdom, and truthfulness of His messengers. Despite these signs, the majority of those addressed did not respond with faith, showing that acceptance of truth is not determined by numbers or visible evidence alone but by hearts willing to submit. It also consoles the messenger and believers: the rejection of the many does not diminish the truth, and Allah’s sign remains a decisive warning and guidance for those who reflect.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is truly the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God’s lordship over you is characterized by absolute might and all-encompassing mercy. His being al-‘Aziz means He is invincible, wise, and able to accomplish whatever He wills, while His being al-Rahim means His mercy is vast, constant, and reaches His creation through guidance, forgiveness, provision, and protection. His might never makes Him unjust, and His mercy never makes Him weak; rather, He is powerful to save and merciful to forgive those who turn to Him.

translation: The people of Noah denied the messengers.
interpretation: Their denial of Noah was, in effect, a denial of all the messengers, because every prophet came with the same essential message: to call people to the worship of God alone and to obey His guidance. By rejecting Noah, they rejected the prophetic message itself and thus stood condemned as deniers of the messengers as a whole.

translation: When their brother Noah said to them, “Will you not fear Allah?”
interpretation: Noah is described as their brother to show that he was one of them and known to them, not a stranger or enemy. His question is a compassionate warning: he calls them to have taqwa—to be mindful of Allah, avoid His anger, and protect themselves from punishment by turning away from idol worship and giving up their defiance.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: The speaker, a prophet addressing his people, declares that he is a faithful envoy from God: his mission is not self-serving or invented, but a trust he conveys exactly as revealed. His trustworthiness is the basis for accepting his call, since he neither adds to nor withholds from the divine message.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This is an address from a messenger of Allah to his people, calling them to make God-consciousness the basis of their conduct—by upholding His commands and avoiding His prohibitions—and to follow the messenger’s guidance, since he conveys only what Allah has revealed. Obedience to the messenger in matters of divine guidance is therefore an expression of obedience and reverence toward Allah.

translation: And I do not ask you for it any reward. My reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The speaker, a prophet delivering God’s message, declares that he seeks no payment, favor, or worldly gain from the people for conveying the revelation and calling them to truth. His sole recompense and reward are with God alone, the Lord of all creation, who sustains and governs everything. This establishes the purity and sincerity of his mission: he does not preach for personal benefit, status, or material return, but only out of obedience to God and concern for the people’s guidance. His trust and hope are placed entirely in the Lord of the worlds, not in any human response or reward.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This is a prophetic call to make awareness of Allah the foundation of life—guarding one’s heart and conduct against disobedience and seeking His pleasure—and then to follow the messenger’s guidance as the concrete way that awareness is lived out. Obedience to the messenger is not obedience to a human whim; it is acceptance of the revelation he carries, and therefore it is inseparable from obeying Allah. The verse teaches that true faith unites inward reverence with outward compliance to divinely guided instruction.

translation: They said, "Should we believe you while the lowest [of people] follow you?"
interpretation: This verse exposes the disbelievers’ arrogant refusal to accept the truth because its followers were mainly from the poor, weak, and socially lowly, not the influential elite. They judged the message by the worldly status of its adherents rather than by its truth, revealing their pride, prejudice, and false standard of worth. It warns against dismissing divine guidance because it is first embraced by the humble, and shows that arrogance and obsession with status can blind people to the truth.

translation: He said, "And what knowledge do I have of what they used to do?"
interpretation: In context, Prophet Noah is rejecting his people's contempt for the poor and lowly believers who followed him. He declares that he has no knowledge of their former deeds or hidden intentions, nor is it his task to judge them by outward status or past reputation. His duty is only to convey the message, while their true account and recompense belong to God alone, who knows all that they did. Thus, social rank or prior conduct cannot justify rejecting a sincere believer.

translation: Their account is only upon my Lord, if you but perceive.
interpretation: Final judgment and reckoning belong exclusively to God, not to any prophet or person. Human beings must not scorn or dismiss others based on outward status, because only God knows the hidden reality of hearts and will judge all deeds with perfect justice; if people truly understood this, they would not set themselves up as judges over believers.

translation: And I am not one to drive away the believers.
interpretation: This is Prophet Noah’s declaration that he will not expel or reject those who have believed in him, even if they are poor, weak, or of low social standing. Faith is not measured by worldly rank, and the inner reality of people is for God to judge; Noah’s duty is to convey the warning, not to act as a gatekeeper who drives believers away.

translation: I am only a clear warner.
interpretation: This verse clarifies that the messenger’s role is strictly to deliver God’s warning plainly and openly. He has no authority to compel belief, judge hidden motives, or turn away sincere believers; his task is to convey the message with clarity, while the final reckoning and judgment belong to God alone.

translation: They said, “If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those who are stoned.”
interpretation: This verse reports the threat made by Noah’s people against him: they demanded that he stop calling them to God and warning them of the consequences of their disbelief, and they warned that if he continued, they would stone him to death. It expresses their violent rejection of the truth, their arrogance toward God’s prophet, and their attempt to silence the call to faith through intimidation and punishment.

translation: He said, “My Lord, indeed my people have denied me.”
interpretation: This is Noah turning to his Lord after long preaching, complaining not from doubt but from grief that his people persistently rejected him and called him a liar; he therefore seeks God’s help and judgment, acknowledging that guidance and response belong to God alone.

translation: So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment, and save me and those believers who are with me.
interpretation: This is Noah’s supplication to God after his people persistently rejected his call. He asks God to “open” a decisive separation between him and them—meaning to judge, decree, and distinguish truth from falsehood—and to deliver him and the believers along with him from the coming punishment. It teaches that when a people stubbornly reject divine guidance, the final judgment belongs to God alone, and that His faithful servants are saved by His mercy and protection.

translation: So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship.
interpretation: This verse declares that Allah rescued Nuh and the believers who accompanied him from the flood by placing them in the ark, which was fully loaded with them and the creatures Allah had commanded him to carry. It shows that Allah’s promise of deliverance for the faithful is certain, that He uses created means to accomplish His will, and that those who follow His messenger are saved while the rejecting people are left to their deserved destruction.

translation: Then afterwards We drowned the rest.
interpretation: This is a declaration of Allah's just punishment: after He had saved Nuh and those who believed with him in the Ark, He caused the remaining disbelievers—who had rejected Nuh's call and persisted in their denial—to be drowned. It shows that deliverance is for those who respond in faith, while ruin overtakes those who remain entrenched in rejection.

translation: Indeed, in that is surely a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the preceding event is a decisive divine sign pointing to God's power, wisdom, and faithfulness to His messengers. It also exposes the disbelievers' willful resistance: their failure to believe was not due to a lack of evidence, but to a hardened rejection of the truth. The verse thus teaches that miracles and clear signs do not by themselves produce faith; faith requires a heart willing to submit. It also establishes a recurring principle: the majority's disbelief does not invalidate the sign, nor does it excuse them from accountability, and it consoles the messenger that rejection is not a failure of the message but a condition of the rejecters.

translation: And indeed, your Lord—He is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: God affirms that His lordship is characterized by two perfect attributes: absolute might and all-encompassing mercy. His might means He is invincible, sovereign, and able to execute justice, while His mercy means He forgives, guides, and shows compassion to those who turn to Him. Together they teach that His authority is not harsh tyranny but sovereign power joined with mercy, so the believer responds with reverent fear and hopeful trust.

translation: Aad denied the messengers.
interpretation: This means the people of Aad rejected their prophet Hud, and by rejecting him they rejected the prophetic message itself. God describes their denial as a denial of all messengers because every messenger came with the same essential call: to worship God alone, obey Him, and follow His guidance.

translation: When their brother Hud said to them, "Will you not fear Allah?"
interpretation: Hud, though one of their own people and a brother to them in lineage and community, calls them to taqwa—God-consciousness and reverent fear of Allah. His question is a gentle but serious rebuke: they had turned away from the worship of the One God and persisted in heedlessness, so he appeals to their reason and conscience, urging them to fear Allah’s punishment and to return to obedience before it is too late.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: This is a prophet’s declaration to his people that he has been sent by God and is faithful in delivering God’s message. His trustworthiness means he neither invents nor alters the revelation, nor seeks any personal gain through it; therefore, his call deserves to be heard, believed, and obeyed as a call to God.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: It is a command to the people to guard themselves against Allah’s punishment by fulfilling His rights and avoiding His prohibitions, and to obey the Messenger in what he conveys from Allah, for obedience to him is obedience to Allah.

translation: And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse declares that the messenger conveys the message with complete sincerity, seeking no payment, favor, or worldly return from the people. His sole recompense and reward come from God alone, the Lord of all creation, who is the only one worthy of being served and the only one who truly rewards.

translation: Do you build on every high place a sign, amusing yourselves?
interpretation: This verse rebukes the people of ‘Ad through Prophet Hud for erecting grand monuments and lofty structures on every elevated site or roadway merely for vanity, display, and frivolous amusement. It condemns the misuse of God-given power and resources for boastful, purposeless construction instead of worship, justice, and the good of creation. The rhetorical question implies that such extravagance is a symptom of arrogance, heedlessness of the Hereafter, and ingratitude toward God.

translation: And you take for yourselves strongholds, hoping that you may remain forever?
interpretation: This is a rebuke to the people of 'Ad: they poured their strength into building immense fortresses, palaces, and monuments, deludedly thinking that such worldly structures could guarantee permanence or stave off death. The verse exposes the folly of seeking immortality through material power and architecture, warning that only God is everlasting and that no human construction can secure eternal abode in this life.

translation: And when you strike, you strike as tyrants.
interpretation: This verse condemns the misuse of power: it rebukes those who, whenever they use force, authority, or strength, do so with arrogance, cruelty, and oppression, treating others as subjects to be crushed rather than with justice and restraint. It exposes tyranny as a moral corruption and a sign of a people who have forgotten accountability before God.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This is the call of a Prophet to his people: let your reverence for God and your concern for His judgment move you to accept His Messenger and follow the guidance he brings. Obeying the Messenger here is not obeying a mere human being for his own sake; it is obeying the one sent by God, who seeks no reward or status from you, so that obedience becomes an act of faithfulness to God.

translation: And fear the One Who has provided you with what you know.
interpretation: This is a command to be mindful of God and to avoid His displeasure by recognizing that every known blessing you possess—life, sustenance, faculties, wealth, family, and all means—comes from Him alone; therefore, obedience and gratitude belong to Him, not to anyone or anything else.

translation: He has provided you with livestock and sons.
interpretation: Allah is reminding them that their prosperity and continuance come from His continual favor: livestock as sustenance and wealth, and children as strength and legacy. These blessings should move them to gratitude, humility, and obedience to the One who granted them, rather than to heedlessness or arrogance.

translation: And gardens and springs.
interpretation: God recounts these as blessings He had granted the people of ‘Ād: cultivated gardens and flowing springs, which sustain life and prosperity. Their mention is a call to recognize the Giver, not to be deceived by comfort, and to use such favors in gratitude and obedience before the same God who gave them can withdraw them.

translation: Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a great Day.
interpretation: This is a compassionate warning from a prophet to his people: he does not desire their destruction, but fears that their continued disbelief and defiance will bring upon them the punishment of a momentous Day—the Day of Resurrection and Reckoning. The greatness of that Day lies in its severity, its absolute justice, and the inescapable accountability before God. The verse therefore stresses the urgency of responding to prophetic guidance and the grave consequence of rejecting it.

translation: They said, "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers."
interpretation: This is the response of a people whose hearts have become hardened by arrogance and heedlessness. They openly declare that divine warning has no effect upon them: whether the messenger counsels them or remains silent, they will not change their ways. Their words are not a reasoned rejection of the truth but a defiant dismissal of prophetic guidance. It shows that admonition benefits only those willing to listen; for the obstinately proud, the same warning that could reform them instead becomes a witness against them.

translation: This is nothing but the custom of the former peoples.
interpretation: The disbelievers among ʿĀd rejected Hud’s warning by claiming that his message was merely an inherited way or customary belief of earlier generations, not a divine truth. They treated the call to faith and the warning of punishment as old traditions, denying that they would be held accountable or punished by God.

translation: And we will not be punished.
interpretation: It expresses the disbelievers' arrogant denial of accountability after death: they claim that no punishment will ever befall them, thereby rejecting the messenger's warning and the reality of divine judgment.

translation: So they denied him, and We destroyed them. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse teaches that rejecting God’s messenger and treating him as a liar leads to ruin, and the destruction of such deniers stands as a clear proof of God’s justice and power; yet most people still refuse to believe.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse establishes that God’s lordship over His creation is characterized by two inseparable attributes: absolute might and boundless mercy. His power is never overcome, yet He does not deal with His servants merely by force; He is able to exact justice, and He is also ready to forgive, show compassion, and respond to those who turn to Him. Thus, no oppressor should feel secure from His power, and no repentant sinner should despair of His mercy.

translation: Thamud denied the messengers.
interpretation: The people of Thamud rejected their prophet Salih and the message he brought from God. Since every messenger conveyed the same essential truth of God's oneness and accountability, their denial of him is counted as a denial of the messengers as a whole.

translation: When their brother Salih said to them, 'Will you not fear Allah?'
interpretation: This is a rhetorical call to God-consciousness: Salih, though one of their own and a brother to them in lineage, confronts their heedlessness and asks why they do not fear Allah—why they do not let awareness of His majesty and accountability restrain them from idolatry and corruption. The question is meant to awaken them: if they truly feared Allah, they would abandon their false gods and heed His messenger.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: The speaker, a prophet sent by God, declares that his mission is divinely commissioned and that he faithfully conveys the revelation entrusted to him without alteration, concealment, or personal motive. His trustworthiness is the proof of his truthfulness and a call for the people to accept the divine message he brings, since rejecting him is rejecting the One who sent him.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This is a directive from a messenger to his people: revere God by fulfilling His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, and accept the messenger’s guidance as the concrete expression of that reverence. Obedience to the messenger in what he conveys from God is not separate from fear of God; it is the practical proof of it, and rejecting his call while claiming to fear God is contradictory. Thus the verse binds inward God-consciousness to outward compliance with divine instruction through the appointed messenger.

translation: And I do not ask of you for it any payment. My payment is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The messenger declares that he seeks no wage, material benefit, or personal favor from the people for delivering the divine message; his sole reward and recompense rests with Allah, the Lord and Sustainer of all creation. This establishes his complete sincerity, freeing his call from selfish motives and placing his dependence entirely upon God.

translation: Will you be left secure in what is here?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical question of rebuke and warning: the people addressed are being told not to presume that their present worldly comforts, dwellings, and blessings will remain with them forever, or that their security means they are safe from God’s judgment. Their ease is a test, not proof of divine favor, and it can be taken away if they persist in denial and wrongdoing. True security belongs only to those who live in faith and obedience.

translation: in gardens and springs
interpretation: This is a promise of Paradise for the God-conscious: they will dwell amid lush, eternal gardens and flowing springs, signifying unending refreshment, delight, purity, and divine favor as the reward for faith and righteous deeds.

translation: And crops and palm trees whose spathes are tender.
interpretation: This verse points to the delicate, ripe, and fresh fruit clusters of the date palms alongside cultivated fields as evidence of God’s abundant provision. The word “هضيم” conveys softness, readiness, and lushness, showing that the sustenance granted was easy to obtain and rich in benefit. It serves as a reminder that such blessings come from God alone and should inspire gratitude, not the arrogance and denial that the people of Thamud displayed.

translation: And you carve out of the mountains houses, exulting in arrogance.
interpretation: The verse exposes a spiritual misuse of blessing: the outward act of building secure and impressive homes becomes a symbol of arrogant self-reliance. Their ability to carve dwellings from the mountains was not condemned for craftsmanship itself, but for the inner state it fostered—insolence, a false sense of permanence, and forgetfulness of God. It warns that no fortification or worldly prosperity can protect a people who rebel against their Creator.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This is a call to protect oneself from Allah’s punishment by fulfilling His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, and to submit to the messenger’s guidance. Obedience to the messenger is not separate from obedience to Allah; it is the practical expression of God-consciousness, because the messenger conveys only what Allah has revealed and commands only what aligns with His will.

translation: And do not obey the command of the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse prohibits believers from following the instructions of those who exceed Allah’s limits through disbelief, oppression, and corruption. Such people misuse Allah’s blessings, lead others away from truth, and spread disorder; obeying them leads to ruin. Therefore, obedience belongs to Allah and His messengers alone.

translation: Those who spread corruption in the earth and do not reform.
interpretation: This describes people whose defining conduct is destructive wrongdoing: they ruin life, justice, and moral order on earth, and they refuse to set things right. They are not portrayed as merely falling into sin, but as committed to corruption, resisting correction, and never working to repair what they have broken or to establish righteousness.

translation: They said, 'You are only one of those bewitched.'
interpretation: The disbelievers accuse the prophet of being under a magic spell, meaning his mind is deranged and his message is therefore unworthy of serious consideration. This accusation reveals their arrogance and their inability to refute the prophet's call with rational argument, so they resort to slander and character assassination. It also shows a recurring pattern among those who reject God's messengers: they dismiss the truth by attacking the messenger rather than reflecting on the message itself.

translation: You are only a human being like us, so bring a sign if you are among the truthful.
interpretation: The people of Thamud reject Prophet Salih's message by arguing that he is merely a man like themselves and therefore cannot be a messenger from God. They demand a miraculous sign as proof, revealing their stubborn insistence on sensory miracles rather than reflecting on the truth of his call. The verse highlights the recurring Qur'anic theme that prophethood is not negated by the messenger's humanity, and that demands for signs often stem from arrogance and a refusal to submit.

translation: He said, "This is a she-camel; she has a share of water, and you have a share of water on a known day."
interpretation: This verse conveys Salih’s announcement to his people that the she-camel is a clear sign from God and that the water is to be shared by a fixed, alternating arrangement: one day it belongs to the she-camel, and on another appointed day it belongs to the people. It functions as a divine test of obedience, gratitude, and faithfulness to the covenant: they must honor the ordained schedule and not harm the she-camel. It also teaches that God alone apportions provision and that His signs carry binding moral obligations.

translation: And do not touch her with harm, lest a punishment of a great Day seize you.
interpretation: This is a divine warning: the she-camel is a sign from God, so harming her would be an act of defiance against God and His messenger. The punishment threatened is not a light consequence but a severe chastisement on an immense Day—either the day of their destruction in this world or the Day of Judgment—showing that aggression toward God’s signs brings grave accountability.

translation: So they hamstrung her, and then they became regretful.
interpretation: Their regret came only after they had committed the crime, when it was too late to undo the harm or avert the consequence. It shows that wrongdoing may bring a temporary sense of defiance, but it ultimately leaves the soul remorseful; however, remorse that comes after the appointed punishment is not accepted as a means of escape, because true repentance must precede the consequence and produce faith and reform.

translation: So the punishment overtook them. Indeed, in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: The punishment is depicted as the direct and inevitable consequence of their persistent denial and transgression after God had given them a clear sign. Their destruction serves as a lesson about God's justice and power over those who reject His messengers, while the observation that most of them did not believe shows that the problem was not lack of evidence but a willful refusal to submit, so the sign remains a warning for later generations.

translation: And indeed, your Lord—He is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: God affirms that His lordship over you combines absolute might with boundless mercy: He has power to overcome every opposition and to hold all things under His command, yet He responds to His creation with compassion, forgiveness, and loving-kindness toward those who turn to Him. His majesty does not make Him distant, and His mercy does not make Him weak; rather, His power and mercy together call the believer to awe, trust, and hope.

translation: The people of Lot denied the messengers.
interpretation: Their denial of Lot was, in reality, a denial of the prophetic message itself and therefore of all messengers, since every messenger came with the same fundamental call to worship God alone and heed His guidance. By rejecting Lot and persisting in their corrupt conduct, they rejected God's authority and invited just judgment.

translation: When their brother Lot said to them, 'Will you not fear Allah?'
interpretation: Lot is called their brother to remind them of his kinship and sincere concern for them, not because he was a stranger or enemy. His question is a reproach: why do they not practice taqwa—why do they not guard themselves against Allah’s anger and punishment? It implies that their shameful conduct should have made them fear God and stop, and that heedlessness of God is the root of their persistence in sin. The rhetorical question is meant to awaken their consciences and warn them of the consequences if they refuse to fear Allah.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: This is a prophet’s declaration that his message comes from God and that he conveys it with complete honesty and fidelity, neither adding to it nor withholding from it. His trustworthiness is the basis for the people to accept his call, obey God, and heed the warning he brings.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
