translation: And indeed, your Lord is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of them do not give thanks.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God’s favor and generosity toward humanity are vast and continuous: He provides sustenance, grants faculties, sends guidance, delays punishment, and offers forgiveness. Yet despite this abundance of blessings, most people fail to recognize them as coming from God, fail to respond with gratitude, worship, and obedience, and instead attribute His gifts to other causes or use them in ways that displease Him.

translation: And indeed, your Lord surely knows what their breasts conceal and what they declare.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah’s knowledge is all-encompassing: He knows the hidden thoughts, intentions, and secrets within people’s hearts just as He knows their open words and deeds. It establishes divine omniscience as the foundation of perfect justice and accountability, warning those who conceal hostility or hypocrisy that nothing is hidden from their Lord, while reassuring the Prophet that God is fully aware of the plots and denials of his opponents and will deal with them accordingly.

translation: And there is nothing hidden in the heaven and the earth except that it is in a clear Book.
interpretation: This means that Allah’s knowledge encompasses every concealed and unseen thing in the heavens and the earth. Nothing, however hidden or absent from human perception, is outside His knowledge. All of it is recorded in a clear Book—the Preserved Tablet—so nothing is lost or forgotten, and every matter is established with perfect knowledge and justice. It calls the servant to reverence Allah in secret and in public, and assures that all deeds and realities will be brought to account.

translation: Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that concerning which they differ.
interpretation: The Qur'an is the decisive, divinely revealed criterion that clarifies for the Children of Israel the major matters of creed, law, and sacred history about which they fell into dispute—such as the true status and mission of Jesus, the binding and altered parts of the Torah, and prophetic succession. It confirms the truth they concealed or distorted, corrects their conflicting interpretations, and settles their disagreements by God's authoritative word. This is itself a sign of its divine origin, because an unlettered prophet could not have accurately disclosed their internal disputes except through revelation from the All-Knowing.

translation: And indeed, it is guidance and mercy for the believers.
interpretation: The Qur'an guides believers to the truth and brings them mercy by correcting their beliefs and actions, directing them to what benefits them, and leading them to eternal success; this guidance and mercy are received by those who believe in it and follow it.

translation: Indeed, your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Almighty, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: Allah will settle the disputes and differences among people by His perfect decree, for His judgment is just and final; nothing can escape or overturn it, because He is the Almighty Who cannot be resisted and the All-Knowing Who knows all that is hidden and revealed.

translation: So rely upon Allah; indeed, you are upon the clear truth.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet, and through him every believer, to place complete reliance and trust in Allah alone. Such reliance is not a sign of weakness but a firm confidence in God’s power and wisdom. The reason given is that the Prophet is established upon the manifest truth—the clear, unmistakable divine message. Because his path is true and his cause is from God, he is assured that God will support, protect, and guide him. Reliance on God is therefore the proper response of one who possesses certainty in the truth and who knows that all matters ultimately rest in God’s hands.

translation: Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet and defines the limits of his mission: he is a warner and conveyer of the message, not one who can compel hearts to believe. Those who persist in denial are likened to the dead, whose senses no longer benefit them, and to the deaf who cannot hear the invitation, especially when they deliberately turn their backs in aversion. The obstacle is not a lack of prophetic clarity but the spiritual deadness and willful rejection of the disbelievers. Guidance belongs to Allah alone; He alone can revive hearts and open ears to the truth.

translation: And you cannot guide the blind away from their error. You can only make hear those who believe in Our verses, for they are Muslims [submissive to Allah].
interpretation: This verse teaches that prophetic guidance cannot penetrate hearts that insist on rejecting the truth; it reaches only those disposed to accept God's revelation. The 'blind' are not physically blind but spiritually unreceptive, and the 'hearing' is inward acceptance. Thus the Prophet's task is to deliver the message, while the actual turning of hearts belongs to God. Those who believe in His signs and submit to Him are the ones who truly hear and benefit.

translation: And when the word falls upon them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth speaking to them, [declaring] that the people were not certain of Our signs.
interpretation: This refers to the moment when God's decree of judgment becomes due and humanity's persistent rejection reaches its term. God then brings forth a creature from the earth as a decisive, miraculous sign of the Hour. Its speech is not mere animal noise but a divine testimony against human beings: they lived without firm conviction in God's revelations, treating His signs as uncertain or untrue. The verse thus signifies that unbelief and doubt cannot prevent the fulfillment of God's promise, and that the final signs will expose the truth of what people denied.

translation: And [mention] the Day when We will gather from every nation a troop of those who reject Our signs, and they will be set in ranks.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, Allah will assemble from every people a body of its deniers of His revealed signs; they will be marshalled and held in ordered rows, unable to escape or resist, until they are brought to account and driven toward their punishment. This shows that rejecting divine revelation will not be ignored: the deniers will be singled out, publicly gathered, and placed under Allah’s sovereign control in ranks for judgment.

translation: Until, when they come, He will say, 'Did you deny My signs while you did not encompass them in knowledge? Or what were you doing?'
interpretation: This is a scene of divine rebuke on the Day of Judgment: God confronts those who rejected His revelations, exposing that their denial was not based on any true understanding or evidence, since they never comprehended His signs. Then He asks what they were actually occupied with instead, meaning their lives were spent in falsehood, heedlessness, or deeds displeasing to Him. The verse condemns rejecting divine guidance without knowledge and holds people accountable for what they chose to do in place of faith and obedience.

translation: And the decree will fall upon them because of the wrong they committed, so they will not speak.
interpretation: The divine judgment of punishment becomes due and is carried out against them on account of their persistent injustice and rejection of the truth. At that point they are left utterly speechless, unable to offer any excuse, defense, or plea, for their guilt has been fully established and every argument has collapsed.

translation: Have they not seen that We made the night so that they may rest in it, and the day giving sight? Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: This verse is a call to reflect on the purposeful design in the alternation of night and day. The night is appointed for stillness and rest, while the day is made light-giving so that people may see, move, and work. These are not random phenomena but clear signs of Allah's wisdom, mercy, and power. Yet only those who believe truly perceive them as signs, because faith opens the heart to recognize the Creator behind creation and to accept that the One who ordered the night and day is fully able to bring about resurrection and account. Thus the verse gently rebukes heedlessness and directs the believer to gratitude, reflection, and acknowledgment of Allah's lordship.

translation: And on the Day when the Horn is blown, those in the heavens and those on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills. And all will come to Him humbled.
interpretation: The blowing of the Horn signals the onset of resurrection and judgment, and its terror will seize every being in the heavens and earth because of the overwhelming majesty of that moment and the certainty of reckoning. Allah alone exempts whom He wills, showing that security and fear are entirely under His decree and that no creature can claim immunity by its own power. Then all without exception will come before Him in humiliation and submission, stripped of authority, pride, and any capacity to resist His command. The verse thus anchors the heart in God's absolute sovereignty and in the inevitability of the final summons, when every created being is brought low before Him.

translation: And you see the mountains, thinking them solid and fixed, while they pass by like clouds. This is the handiwork of Allah, who has perfected all things. Indeed, He is Aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse exposes the difference between human perception and divine reality: the mountains seem immovable and permanent, yet they are not truly static, for they move and will pass away like clouds under Allah’s command. It points especially to the resurrection, when the apparent solidity of the world will dissolve, and it reminds man that all creation is Allah’s perfectly ordered work. Since He is fully aware of every deed, people should not be deceived by worldly stability but live with accountability before Him.

translation: Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and they will be safe from the terror of that Day.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, anyone who appears before God with a good deed—performed sincerely and grounded in faith—will receive a reward better and greater than the deed itself: divine acceptance, forgiveness, multiplied good, and ultimately Paradise. Such people will be shielded from the overwhelming fear and panic that will seize creation on that Day, enjoying perfect security and peace.

translation: And whoever comes with an evil deed — their faces will be cast down into the Fire. Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?
interpretation: This verse declares the fate of those who come on the Day of Resurrection carrying evil deeds: they will be thrown into the Fire upon their faces, a state of utter humiliation and helplessness. The question is rhetorical, affirming perfect justice: the punishment is not arbitrary but exactly corresponds to the sins they committed in life. “What you used to do” refers to their deliberate choices and actions, for which they are held responsible. Thus the verse warns that evil deeds inevitably lead to disgrace and punishment in the Hereafter, and that God’s recompense is entirely just.

translation: I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, which He has made sacred, and to Him belongs everything. And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims (those who submit to Allah).
interpretation: This verse proclaims the core of pure monotheism: the Prophet is commanded to devote worship exclusively to Allah, the Lord of Makkah, the city Allah Himself made inviolable and set apart as a sanctuary. All things in existence belong to Him, so no created place or being shares in His divinity. Being "of the Muslims" means being among those who wholly submit to Allah, aligning one's will with His command and worshiping Him alone. The sanctity of Makkah is not inherent to its stones but is granted by Allah's decree, and the Prophet's mission is to call people to that same submission, away from any worship of creation and toward the sole worship of the Creator.

translation: And to recite the Qur'an. So whoever is guided, he is only guided for himself; and whoever goes astray, then say, 'I am only among the warners.'
interpretation: This verse establishes that the Prophet's duty is to convey and recite the Qur'an, not to compel anyone to believe. It teaches that divine guidance benefits the one who accepts it, while misguidance harms only the one who chooses it. The Prophet is not accountable for people's acceptance or rejection; his role is solely to deliver the warning, leaving the outcome to God.

translation: And say, 'All praise is for Allah. He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.'
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet and the believers to announce praise and gratitude to God alone, because He will bring about clear manifestations of His power, truthfulness, and justice—both in the world and within people’s own lives—until those who are sincere come to recognize them as divine signs. It also warns that God is never heedless of human deeds; every action, hidden or open, is fully known to Him and will be met with perfect accountability.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ta-Seen-Meem.
interpretation: The basmala is the invocation of Allah’s name and mercy before reciting His revelation, and “Ta-Seen-Meem” is one of the disjointed letter openings of the Qur’an, placed at the head of Surah Ash-Shu‘ara’ as a divine sign; its precise meaning is left to Allah, while it points to the miraculous nature of the Qur’an, which is built from the same Arabic letters the people used yet remains beyond their power to match, thereby calling them to receive the revelation with attentive faith.

translation: These are the verses of the clear Book.
interpretation: They are the revealed signs of the Book whose clarity is manifest and which makes the truth clear, so it is a perspicuous scripture whose guidance and divine origin are evident.

translation: We recite to you from the news of Moses and Pharaoh in truth, for a people who believe.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Qur’an’s account of Moses and Pharaoh is not legend or hearsay but revealed truth, and that its benefit is specifically for those who have faith: it trains believers to see history as the arena of God’s justice, where tyrannical power is exposed and the oppressed are ultimately delivered, and it strengthens certainty that divine guidance and accountability are real.

translation: Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a group among them: slaughtering their sons and sparing their women. Indeed, he was of the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse exposes the essence of tyrannical rule: Pharaoh’s arrogant self-exaltation led him to fracture society into rival factions and to crush a vulnerable group through calculated violence. The killing of sons while sparing women was a policy of domination—destroying potential strength and resistance among the oppressed while keeping them subjugated and exploitable. Such corruption is not merely political but spiritual, and it sets the stage for God’s deliverance of the weak from unjust power.

translation: And We intended to confer favor upon those who were oppressed in the land, and to make them leaders, and to make them inheritors.
interpretation: This verse declares that Allah, in His wisdom and justice, willed to rescue the oppressed Children of Israel from Pharaoh's brutal subjugation, to elevate them after their humiliation, to make them guides and leaders in both worldly and religious affairs, and to grant them inheritance of the land and authority after Pharaoh and his people were destroyed. It affirms that Allah's decree ultimately favors the weak and oppressed when He chooses, overturning the power of tyrants and giving succession to those whom He wills.

translation: And We will establish them in the land and show Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers from them what they used to fear.
interpretation: God assures that the oppressed Children of Israel will be given a firm place and authority in the land, while Pharaoh, Haman, and their forces will be made to witness, through the very people they sought to subdue, the dreaded outcome they had tried to prevent: the rise of one who would bring down their power. The verse declares that divine decree will inevitably overturn tyranny by means of those it had enslaved and suppressed.

translation: And We inspired to the mother of Moses: “Suckle him; but when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed, We will return him to you and will make him one of the messengers.”
interpretation: This verse portrays God’s direct care and guidance for a mother in her most vulnerable moment. The “inspiration” given to Moses’ mother was not prophethood or a new scripture, but a steadfast inward assurance that moved her to act in obedience even when it seemed to contradict her maternal instinct. Casting her child into the river was not abandonment but trust in God’s hidden plan, paired with the command to abandon fear and grief because the outcome belonged to God. The promise contains both immediate mercy—restoring the child to her—and a far greater destiny: that this child would be raised as one of God’s messengers. Thus the verse teaches that divine protection can operate through frightening means, and that obedience joined with trust in God’s promise transforms loss into return and hardship into a mission.

translation: Then the household of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he would become for them an enemy and a cause of grief. Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners.
interpretation: This verse reveals how Allah turned the oppressive plan of Pharaoh’s house against itself: they took the infant Moses into their own palace, yet Allah decreed that he would grow to confront Pharaoh, expose his false divinity, free the Children of Israel, and bring grief and ruin upon his regime. Their crime was not an innocent mistake but a deliberate transgression—Pharaoh, his minister Haman, and their forces were guilty of arrogance, tyranny, and rejecting the truth—so their destruction through the very child they sheltered was a just recompense and a sign of Allah’s sovereign power to fulfill His will despite the schemes of the powerful.

translation: And the wife of Pharaoh said, 'A comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him; perhaps he may benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son.' And they did not perceive.
interpretation: This verse unveils the hidden hand of Allah working through the very household of tyranny. The wife of Pharaoh, Asiya, moved by a God-given compassion, unknowingly protects the infant who will later confront Pharaoh and liberate the Children of Israel. Her plea reflects a hope for personal joy and possible adoption, yet the closing phrase 'and they did not perceive' signals that Pharaoh and his court were blind to the divine irony: the child they spared would be the instrument of their downfall. Thus, the verse teaches that Allah's decree can use the mercy of a believer within an oppressive system to fulfill His promise to the oppressed, and that human plans, however powerful, cannot thwart the unfolding of divine destiny.

translation: And the heart of Moses' mother became empty [of all but Moses]. She was about to disclose him, had We not strengthened her heart, so that she would be among the believers.
interpretation: This verse portrays the depth of a mother’s anguish and the testing of her faith. After entrusting her infant to the river, Moses’ mother felt an inner void: every worldly hope and comfort was stripped away, and she nearly revealed the child’s identity out of overwhelming love and fear. But God steadied her heart with patience, trust, and reliance upon His promise. Her faith was not merely an emotion but a firm conviction that God would protect and return her son. Thus, the verse teaches that true belief sometimes means restraining natural impulses and holding fast to God’s command even when one’s heart is under severe pressure.

translation: And she said to his sister, "Follow him." So she watched him from a distance while they were unaware.
interpretation: This verse conveys that Moses’ mother, after entrusting her infant to the river, instructed his sister to trace him discreetly. The sister observed him from afar without Pharaoh’s household realizing who she was or why she was watching, which was part of God’s hidden arrangement to preserve Moses and eventually restore him to his mother.

translation: And We had prevented him from [suckling from] wet nurses before, so she said, 'Shall I direct you to a household who will nurse him for you and who will be sincere toward him?'
interpretation: This verse conveys God's providential care: He made the infant reject all other wet nurses so that the child would be returned to the very household He intended—his own mother—thus fulfilling His promise and preserving the mother-child bond. The sister's discreet suggestion becomes a means by which divine decree unfolds through ordinary causes, teaching that sincere guardianship and well-wishing toward a child entrusted to one's care are acts of faithfulness.

translation: So We returned him to his mother so that her eye might be gladdened and she would not grieve, and so that she would know that the promise of Allah is true; but most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse conveys that Allah’s delay or hidden plan never means abandonment: after the trial of Musa’s mother, He restored her child in a manner she could not have devised, turning her fear into comfort and her grief into certainty. Her restored joy was not merely personal relief; it was a sign that Allah’s promise is absolutely true and unfailing. The closing words rebuke the majority who do not recognize Allah’s wise governance, because they judge by outward appearances and cannot perceive how He fulfills His promise through events that seem, at first, to contradict it.

translation: And when he reached his full strength and was mature, We gave him wisdom and knowledge. And thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse teaches that when Moses attained complete physical, intellectual, and spiritual maturity, God granted him sound judgment, prophetic discernment, and beneficial knowledge. These gifts were not merely natural developments but divine rewards for his sincere devotion and excellence in conduct. The verse establishes a lasting principle: God bestows wisdom and knowledge upon those who perfect their worship of Him and their dealings with others, doing good with sincerity and constancy. Thus, true maturity and divine favor are linked to moral and spiritual excellence.

translation: And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness on the part of its people, and found therein two men fighting: one from his faction and one from his enemy. The one from his faction appealed to him for help against the one from his enemy, so Moses struck him and killed him. He said, 'This is from the work of Satan. Indeed, he is a clear, misleading enemy.'
interpretation: This verse shows Moses acting out of zealous support for his oppressed kinsman, but the blow he struck went beyond what he intended and caused death. His immediate recognition that this was 'from the work of Satan' means that the conflict, rage, and fatal outcome belonged to the pattern of Satan's deception and enmity toward humanity. Satan is described as a clear, misleading enemy because he beautifies retaliation and discord, leading people into harm even when they imagine they are defending a just cause. Moses' response also teaches that a believer must not attribute evil to God, but must see sinful escalation and its destructive consequences as arising from Satanic influence and human weakness, and must turn back to God in remorse and seeking forgiveness.

translation: He said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me." Then He forgave him. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that true repentance begins with admitting one's own fault before Allah, without making excuses or shifting blame. Moses, peace be upon him, despite his high station, did not claim innocence; he confessed that he had harmed his own soul and asked Allah alone for forgiveness. The immediate response of divine forgiveness shows that Allah is ever ready to forgive those who turn to Him with sincere remorse. His names al-Ghafur and al-Rahim indicate that His forgiveness is not merely a cancellation of punishment but is accompanied by mercy, care, and restoration. Thus, no believer should despair of Allah's mercy, and every sin, however serious, can be forgiven when followed by genuine repentance and reliance on Allah's boundless compassion.

translation: He said, "My Lord, because You have favored me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals."
interpretation: Moses acknowledges God's grace and favor upon him—especially the forgiveness, guidance, and protection he received—and responds with a firm resolve never to assist, defend, or align himself with those who commit crimes and spread corruption. It is a declaration of repentance and a commitment to stand on the side of justice and righteousness, refusing any partnership with wrongdoing.

translation: So he entered the city in the morning, fearful and watchful. Then the one who had sought his help the day before cried out to him for help. Moses said to him, "Indeed, you are clearly misguided."
interpretation: Moses’s words are a rebuke of the Israelite’s repeated readiness to become entangled in violent quarrels and to draw Moses into them. Calling him “clearly misguided” identifies his conduct as manifest error and rashness, not a rejection of helping the oppressed as such. The verse thus warns against habitual strife and shows Moses in a state of fear and vigilance after his earlier accidental killing, aware that his action may bring consequences.

translation: And when he was about to strike the one who was an enemy to them both, he said, 'O Moses, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not want to be of the reformers.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment when Moses, after having unintentionally killed an Egyptian the previous day, is about to intervene forcibly again against an oppressive enemy. The enemy's protest is both a warning and an accusation: he frames Moses's actions as a pattern of tyranny rather than reform, seeking to discredit him and to escape the consequences of his own wrongdoing. The verse teaches that past errors can be exploited by opponents, that the pursuit of justice must never degenerate into habitual violence or self-appointed domination, and that true reform is distinguished by restraint, justice, and the repair of wrongs—not by killing or coercing others in the name of reform. It also warns believers that even a single misdeed can become a pretext used against the truth, so their conduct must remain consistent with the justice and mercy they call others to.

translation: And there came a man from the farthest end of the city, hastening. He said, "O Moses, indeed the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you, so depart; indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisers."
interpretation: This verse is a lesson in Allah’s unseen protection of His chosen servants. The warning comes from a man of the city’s outskirts—an unexpected source—showing that divine help is not restricted to the powerful or the prominent. The ruling elite of Pharaoh had resolved to kill Moses after the matter of the slain Egyptian became known, but Allah used a sincere believer to deliver timely counsel. The man’s haste and self-exposure reveal courage and pure faith: he sought no favor, only to give faithful advice. Moses’ departure was not mere escape; it was the opening of a new decree, leading him to Midian and eventually to prophethood. Thus, when the wicked conspire, Allah’s plan prevails, and He can send relief through the most unlikely people.

translation: So he left it, fearful and watchful. He said: My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse portrays Moses fleeing Egypt after the accidental killing of an Egyptian, in a state of fear and alertness, aware that Pharaoh’s regime would seek retaliation. His immediate recourse is not to his own strength or alliances but to God, asking to be delivered from the unjust and tyrannical people. It teaches that when one is oppressed by worldly powers, true safety lies in turning to God, and that separating oneself from a system of injustice is part of faith and prudence. The supplication also affirms God as the only true protector who can rescue the believer from the grip of oppressive people.

translation: And when he turned his face toward Madyan, he said: 'Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the straight path.'
interpretation: This verse shows Moses, upon him be peace, placing his trust in God after leaving Egypt and setting out toward an unfamiliar land. Though he had chosen a direction, he acknowledged that true guidance and a safe, right course come only from God. His words express hope, humility, and dependence: he did not rely solely on his own knowledge or planning, but asked God to guide him to the most balanced and correct way—both outwardly, the road to safety, and inwardly, the path of truth, righteousness, and sound decision-making. It teaches that whenever a believer faces uncertainty or a new stage in life, he should take the available means, turn toward the good, and then sincerely ask God for guidance to the straight, moderate path.

translation: And when he arrived at the water of Madyan, he found there a group of people watering [their flocks], and he found beside them two women holding back [their flocks]. He said, “What is your situation?” They said, “We cannot water until the shepherds drive away [their flocks], and our father is an old man.”
interpretation: This scene presents Moses as a man of active moral awareness and compassion: he notices the two women standing apart and asks about their condition, not out of idle curiosity but with a readiness to help. Their answer reveals that they are constrained by social custom and by the frailty of their elderly father, who cannot perform this task himself. The verse thus commends the strength that serves the weak, protects the dignity of those in need, and honors the responsibility owed to an aging parent. It also suggests that God was guiding Moses through an ordinary act of kindness toward refuge, family, and ultimately prophethood.

translation: So he watered [their flocks] for them; then he turned back to the shade and said, “My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need.”
interpretation: This verse expresses the station of pure servanthood and humble reliance upon God: after exerting himself for others, Moses does not look to them for reward or recognition, but turns away to the shade of his own poverty before his Lord. His words teach that true supplication begins with acknowledging one’s utter neediness, not with prescribing to God what should be given. He asks for no specific blessing, only for whatever good God sends down, showing complete trust, refined manners in prayer, and the recognition that every good—material or spiritual—descends solely from God’s generous giving. The shade becomes a symbol of human weakness and dependence, and his plea becomes a model of turning one’s need into worship and one’s emptiness into openness to divine provision.

translation: Then one of the two women came to him, walking with shyness. She said, 'My father invites you so that he may reward you for having watered for us.' So when he came to him and told him his story, he said, 'Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people.'
interpretation: This is a scene of divine providence and noble character. The woman’s approach is marked by modesty and dignity, showing that her errand is not bold or improper but respectful and purposeful. Her father’s invitation is an act of gratitude and justice: he seeks to reward Moses for his kind service, not merely offer charity. When Moses recounts his past, including the fear and hardship he fled from, the righteous elder reassures him with words of safety: he need not fear, for God has already delivered him from the unjust people. The verse teaches that good deeds are not forgotten, that modesty is a virtue, that hospitality and gratitude honor the needy stranger, and that God can turn a fugitive’s fear into security through unexpected means.

translation: One of the two women said, "O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy."
interpretation: This verse sets the criterion for employment and entrusted responsibility: the best person to hire is one who combines strength—ability, competence, and capacity to do the work—with trustworthiness—honesty, integrity, and reliability with what is placed in his care. The woman’s advice reflects wisdom, discretion, and sound judgment, recognizing Musa’s character after he had helped them. It also teaches that selecting people for tasks should be based on merit, capability, and moral trustworthiness rather than favoritism, and it affirms that women may offer valuable counsel in matters of practical and family concern.

translation: He said, 'Indeed, I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, provided that you serve me for eight years; but if you complete ten, that is up to you. I do not wish to impose hardship on you. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the righteous.'
interpretation: The verse conveys a marriage proposal governed by mutual consent and a clearly defined term of service as the bridal gift: eight years obligatory by agreement, with ten as a voluntary completion, not a condition. It establishes that a father may act as guardian in his daughter's marriage, that labor or service can be stipulated as dower when both parties agree, and that the contract should avoid exploitation or undue burden. The speaker's declaration that he does not want to make it difficult and that he hopes to be among the righteous shows that dealings in marriage and employment should be marked by good faith, leniency, and reliance on Allah's will.

translation: He said, "That is between me and you. Whichever of the two terms I complete, there will be no injustice against me. And Allah is Trustee over what we say."
interpretation: This verse records Musa’s acceptance of the agreement: he acknowledges that the marriage contract and term of service are settled between him and his father-in-law. By saying “whichever of the two terms I complete,” he means that fulfilling either the shorter or the longer period is valid and discharges his obligation, and no one may then reproach him, demand more, or wrong him. He closes by invoking Allah as Trustee and Witness over their words, affirming that Allah is fully aware of the agreement and will hold both parties to what they have pledged.

translation: So when Moses had completed the term and was traveling with his family, he perceived from the side of Mount Tur a fire. He said to his family, 'Stay here; indeed, I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you from there some information or a burning ember from the fire so that you may warm yourselves.'
interpretation: This verse marks the transition from Moses's years of exile and service to the beginning of his prophetic mission. His journey with his family and his perception of the fire on the side of Mount Sinai were ordinary circumstances that God used to draw him toward a moment of divine revelation. At first, Moses thought only of practical needs—news or a brand to warm his family—showing his care and responsibility as a husband and father. Yet the fire was a sign of God's presence, and his search for a little light and comfort became the doorway to hearing God's speech. The verse teaches that God's guidance often arrives through the unnoticed and the mundane, and that a person's faithful attention to immediate duties can lead to the greatest spiritual encounters.

translation: So when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree: 'O Moses, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse marks the moment God directly addressed Moses and commissioned him as a prophet. The call came from the right side of the valley, a place made blessed by divine revelation, and from the tree—showing that God can use any created means to convey His message, while the voice and authority are His alone. The declaration 'I am Allah, Lord of the worlds' affirms His unique divinity, His absolute sovereignty over all creation, and the foundation of Moses' mission: to call people to worship the one true God.

translation: And [I commanded]: 'Throw down your staff.' But when he saw it quivering as if it were a serpent, he turned away retreating and did not look back. 'O Moses, come forward and do not fear; indeed, you are of the secure.'
interpretation: This scene shows God preparing Moses for prophethood by confronting him with a miracle that exposes his natural human fear. The staff becoming a living serpent is not a mere wonder but a sign of divine power that even Moses, who speaks with God, cannot face without alarm. God’s command to come forward and not fear is a granting of security: Moses is not told that danger is unreal, but that he is protected by God’s guarantee. “You are of the secure” means his safety and success in the mission rest on God’s protection, not on his own strength. The lesson is that nearness to God does not remove human weakness, but it supplies the reassurance needed to obey and continue.

translation: Insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without blemish. And draw your arm to yourself from fear. These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: This verse signifies that God equips Moses with clear, sensory miracles that confirm his prophethood and calm his fear. The hand emerging luminous white without disease is a sign beyond ordinary causation, demonstrating God's power over nature. Drawing the arm close to himself against fear is a gesture of reassurance and reliance on God, removing dread from his heart. The two proofs—the shining hand and the staff—are sent to Pharaoh and his nobles, yet their rejection is not due to insufficient evidence but to their entrenched fisq: willful departure from truth and obedience. Thus the verse teaches that divine signs occur by God's command, that fear is dispelled by trust in Him, and that persistent rebellion against clear proofs renders a people accountable.

translation: He said, "My Lord, indeed I killed one of them, so I fear that they will kill me."
interpretation: This verse shows Moses acknowledging before God the killing he had committed and his very human fear of retaliation. It teaches that fear of harm does not negate faith; what matters is turning to God and seeking His help rather than relying on oneself. Moses' petition also reveals that when God assigns a great mission, He does not leave the servant alone, and the request for support is part of trusting God's provision.

translation: And my brother Aaron—he is more eloquent than me in speech. So send him with me as a helper to confirm me. Indeed, I fear that they will deny me.
interpretation: This is Prophet Moses asking God to appoint his brother Aaron as a prophet and companion in his mission. He acknowledges Aaron’s greater fluency and asks that he be sent as a support who would corroborate his truthfulness, because Moses fears that Pharaoh and his people will reject him. It reflects humility, the need for sincere help in conveying God’s message, and reliance on God to strengthen His prophet through another believer.

translation: [Allah] said: “We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and We will give you both an authority, so they will not reach you. Through Our signs, you and those who follow you will be the victors.”
interpretation: This address to Moses conveys that God’s help often comes through human means—here, his brother Aaron—but the effectiveness of that support is from God, who grants them a protective authority that their enemies cannot overcome. The promise is not based on their own strength or numbers; it is tied to God’s signs. Therefore, true victory belongs to those who follow the divine message, even when they appear weak before worldly powers.

translation: So when Moses came to them with Our clear signs, they said, “This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we have not heard of this among our forefathers.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the nature of arrogant rejection: Pharaoh and his people did not meet Moses’ clear divine signs with honest reflection, but dismissed them as invented sorcery and used ancestral tradition as their criterion of truth. Their claim that they had not heard such a message among their forefathers was not a valid proof against revelation; it was merely conformity to inherited ways and a refusal to submit to God’s authority. The verse thus warns that attachment to power, custom, and the practices of ancestors can blind people to manifest truth and lead them to slander God’s signs rather than accept them.

translation: And Moses said, 'My Lord is most knowing of who has brought guidance from Him, and who will have the [good] outcome of the Home. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.'
interpretation: This is Moses' answer to Pharaoh and his court when they rejected his call and threatened him. He entrusts the final judgment to God, declaring that God alone knows whose guidance is truly from Him and who will receive the blessed end in the eternal abode. The verse establishes that true success is not measured by worldly dominance or numbers but by fidelity to divine guidance, and that those who persist in injustice and oppression will never ultimately prosper, even if they seem powerful in this life.

translation: And Pharaoh said, 'O chiefs, I have not known for you any god besides me. So kindle for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay and make for me a lofty tower, so that I may look at the God of Moses; and indeed, I think he is among the liars.'
interpretation: This verse exposes arrogant power usurping divine authority. Pharaoh does not argue from proof but from his own ignorance and dominance: because he recognizes no god but himself, he demands that reality submit to his decree. His order to Haman to bake clay and build a tower is a theatrical attempt to challenge Moses' God on Pharaoh's own material terms—reducing the unseen Creator to something he can inspect from a height. Yet his final words reveal his motive: he already brands Moses a liar, so the tower is not sincere inquiry but propaganda and self-deification. The verse warns that unchecked political and egoic power can deny God, manipulate labor and resources, and mistake material elevation for spiritual truth.

translation: And he and his soldiers were arrogant in the land unjustly, and they thought that they would not be returned to Us.
interpretation: This verse exposes the root of Pharaoh’s tyranny: he and his forces magnified themselves over the land without any right, rejecting God’s sovereignty and treating their worldly power as absolute. Their arrogance was not merely political but spiritual—they denied that they were accountable to God and persuaded themselves that no return to Him, no resurrection, and no judgment would ever occur. Thus their injustice was sustained by self-deception, as they measured reality only by their own dominance and forgot that all authority returns to God.

translation: So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea. Then look how was the end of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This is a declaration of God’s just punishment: when Pharaoh persisted in arrogance, enslavement, and rejection of the truth, Allah took him and his forces and hurled them into the sea, drowning them. The command to “look” invites reflection on the final end of those who commit oppression: their worldly might, armies, and claims of power did not save them; their outcome was total ruin, and the verse establishes that tyranny ultimately meets divine retribution.

translation: And We made them leaders inviting to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped.
interpretation: Allah caused them to become leaders in misguidance, so that their example and authority drew people toward the Fire. Their leadership was not a favor but a curse, because it called others to disbelief and punishment. On the Day of Resurrection, neither their followers, their wealth, nor any power will be able to help them; they will be utterly abandoned to Allah’s judgment and punishment.

translation: And We caused a curse to follow them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the disfigured.
interpretation: The verse means that Allah made the curse cling to them and pursue them in this worldly life, so that they are stained by disgrace and rejection, and on the Day of Judgment they will be among those made ugly and cast away from mercy, humiliated before all creation. Their punishment is thus both a present disgrace and an eternal exclusion from divine favor.

translation: And indeed We gave Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the former generations, as clear insights for mankind, and guidance and mercy, so that they may remember.
interpretation: This verse states that after earlier peoples were destroyed for rejecting their messengers, Allah granted Moses the Torah. It served as illuminating proofs for people, showing them divine laws and signs; as guidance leading to truth and right conduct; and as mercy for those who accept it. The purpose is that people may remember God's warnings, learn from the fate of past nations, and reflect on His favors so they return to Him.

translation: And you were not on the western side [of the mount] when We decreed to Moses the matter, nor were you among the witnesses.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad, establishing that he was not present at the scene where Moses received the divine command on the western side of Mount Tur, nor was he among those who witnessed it. Therefore, his precise knowledge of these past events could only have come through revelation, which confirms his prophethood and the truthfulness of the Qur'an.

translation: But We brought forth generations, and long ages passed over them. And you were not a dweller among the people of Madyan, reciting Our verses to them; but We are the Senders [of messengers].
interpretation: This verse establishes that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) did not acquire the story of Moses and Madyan by being present among those people or by personally reciting earlier revelations to them. After the earlier generations, long ages passed and memories and scriptures were altered or lost, so Allah raised new generations and then sent the Prophet as a messenger with fresh revelation. Thus his accurate narration of past events is evidence that it comes from Allah, the One who sends messengers and reveals what they convey.

translation: And you were not at the side of the Mount when We called out, but it is a mercy from your Lord, so that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, so that they may remember.
interpretation: This verse establishes that Muhammad was not present at Mount Sinai when God called Moses, so his knowledge of that event comes only through revelation. That revelation is a mercy from God, confirming his prophethood and commissioning him to warn the Arabian people, who had not previously received a messenger. The purpose is that they may reflect, remember God, and take heed, showing both God's mercy in sending guidance and human responsibility to respond to it.

translation: And were it not that a calamity would befall them for what their hands have sent forth, they would say: "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so we could follow Your signs and be among the believers?"
interpretation: This verse states one of the reasons Allah sends messengers before punishing a people: it removes any excuse they might raise when calamity strikes them because of their own sins. If no messenger had been sent, they would plead that they were not given guidance and would promise faith only when it is too late. The sending of prophets is therefore a mercy and a clear proof against humanity. It also shows that people are accountable for their deeds, that sins bring consequences, and that turning to God only under the pressure of disaster is not true faith. The verse invites people to respond to the messenger and revelation now, before the time of regret, rather than waiting for affliction to force a conditional promise of belief.

translation: So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, 'Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?' Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before? They said, 'Two sorceries supporting each other,' and they said, 'Indeed, we are disbelievers in all.'
interpretation: The verse exposes the insincerity of the disbelievers’ demand. They wanted the Prophet to bring signs exactly like Moses’ miracles, yet they had already rejected Moses’ revelation. By calling the Torah and the Qur’an “two sorceries supporting each other,” they showed that their objection was not based on evidence but on a settled refusal to accept any divine message. The verse thus means that such people will reject every messenger and scripture; their problem is not a lack of proof, but obstinate disbelief in all revealed truth.

translation: Say, 'Then bring a book from Allah that is a better guide than both of them, so that I may follow it, if you are truthful.'
interpretation: This is a divine challenge to those who rejected the Prophet and dismissed the revealed scriptures as sorcery. It means: if you truly believe there is a book from God that offers better guidance than the Torah and the Qur’an, then produce it and I will follow it. Since they cannot, the verse exposes their rejection as false and shows that the Qur’an’s guidance is superior and cannot be matched by any fabricated claim.

translation: So if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their own desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his own desire without guidance from Allah? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse exposes the true root of rejecting the call after clear proofs: it is not a lack of evidence but a preference for one’s own desires over divine guidance. The deepest misguidance is to make the self and its whims the final authority, cutting oneself off from Allah’s guidance. Such a person has no secure standard and no light beyond his own inclination. Because they choose wrongdoing and persist in it, Allah does not grant them the guidance that would turn them back; their misguidance is the fitting consequence of their injustice.

translation: And indeed We have conveyed to them the Word, so that they may remember.
interpretation: Allah has delivered His revelation to them in successive, connected reminders through His messengers and scriptures, leaving them no excuse; the purpose is that they may take heed, recall the truth, and return to Him.

translation: Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it — they believe in it.
interpretation: This refers to the sincere people of earlier revealed Books who, because they already believe in God’s previous revelations, recognize the Qur’an as consistent with that guidance and therefore accept it as truth from their Lord. Their prior faith prepares them to believe in this final revelation rather than reject it.

translation: And when it is recited to them, they say, “We have believed in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were Muslims before it.”
interpretation: This verse describes people who had received earlier scripture and who, upon hearing the Qur’an recited, immediately accept it as the truth from their Lord. They do not reject it out of pride or loyalty to their previous community; rather, they recognize it as consistent with the guidance they already followed. Their statement that they were already “Muslims” before it means they had already submitted themselves to God and His revealed will, so the Qur’an comes to them not as a strange new message but as the confirmation of the same foundational truth. Their faith is thus sincere, humble, and prepared to receive further revelation from God.

translation: Those will be given their reward twice for what they patiently endured, and they repel evil with good, and out of what We have provided them, they spend.
interpretation: This verse describes believers who combine steadfast faith with righteous action. Their reward is doubled because they patiently persevered in belief, especially those among the People of the Book who accepted the earlier revelation and then also believed in the final message. They do not respond to harm with harm; rather, they repel evil by doing good, overcoming hostility with kindness and moral excellence. And because they recognize that their provisions come from God, they give freely in charity and in His cause. Thus their double reward reflects both their patient faith and their active devotion: inward steadfastness joined with outward goodness and generosity.

translation: And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it and say, “For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that when believers encounter idle, foul, or provocative speech, they should not engage with it or answer in kind. They preserve their dignity, affirm that each person is accountable for their own deeds, offer a greeting of peace rather than conflict, and refuse to pursue the company or disputes of those who speak and act ignorantly.

translation: Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills. And He is most knowing of the guided.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true, inner guidance—the turning of the heart to faith—belongs to Allah alone. Even the Prophet, out of his deep love and concern, could not force or produce faith in someone; his role was to convey the message and call to truth. Allah alone grants guidance to whom He wills, and His choice is grounded in His perfect knowledge of who will accept guidance, who is sincere, and who will remain rightly guided.

translation: And they say, 'If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land.' Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary, to which are brought fruits of all kinds as provision from Us? But most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse addresses the excuse made by the disbelievers of Makkah for rejecting the Prophet’s message: they claimed that embracing his guidance would cost them their security and homeland. Allah refutes this by reminding them that He had already granted them a sacred, safe territory—the Haram in Makkah—where they lived in security and to which provisions and produce were brought from every direction. If Allah could provide them safety and sustenance while they persisted in disbelief, He would not deprive them of those blessings if they followed His guidance. Thus their stated fear is not the real reason; rather, most of them do not understand or acknowledge the truth about Allah’s power and grace.

translation: And how many a city have We destroyed that exulted in its means of livelihood? So those are their dwellings, not inhabited after them except a little. And We are the Inheritors.
interpretation: The verse warns that arrogance and ungratefulness amid worldly comfort invite divine destruction. A people who become intoxicated by their prosperity and turn away from God may be wiped out, leaving their homes as abandoned signs of their fate. In the end, all wealth, power, and dominion return to God alone, the eternal Owner and Inheritor of everything.

translation: And your Lord would never destroy the cities until He sent to their mother [city] a messenger reciting to them Our verses. And We would never destroy the cities unless their people were wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse establishes Allah’s justice in dealing with nations: He does not bring destruction upon a people before first sending a messenger to their central or principal city to recite His revelations and warn them. The “mother” of the cities is their main city, the center to which the surrounding towns and villages are connected, so that the warning reaches the whole population. Only after the message has been conveyed and the people persist in rejection, oppression, and wrongdoing does punishment come. Therefore, their destruction is not arbitrary or unjust; it is the consequence of their own chosen corruption and defiance.

translation: And whatever you have been given of anything is only the enjoyment of worldly life and its adornment; but what is with Allah is better and more lasting. Will you not then reason?
interpretation: This verse directs human reason to weigh the transient against the eternal. Every worldly gift—wealth, status, possessions, pleasures—is limited to this life's enjoyment and decoration, and will pass away. The reward, mercy, and pleasure of Allah in the Hereafter are qualitatively better and never end. Therefore, a rational person should not let the temporary dazzle of dunya become the goal of life, but should use what he is given in obedience to Allah and seek the everlasting good. The closing question rebukes those who fail to use their intellect to recognize this clear priority.

translation: Is the one to whom We have made a good promise, and he will surely meet it, like the one whom We have given enjoyment of the life of this world, then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forth [for punishment]?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question establishing that the two are not equal. The first person is the believer who has received Allah’s good promise of reward and will certainly encounter its fulfillment in the Hereafter. The second is the disbeliever who is granted only temporary enjoyment in this worldly life, but on the Day of Resurrection he will be summoned and brought to account, ultimately among those delivered to punishment. Thus, worldly ease is not a sign of divine favor, and the lasting promise of good for the righteous is far greater than the fleeting pleasures of this life.

translation: And [mention] the Day when He will call out to them and say, 'Where are My partners whom you used to claim?'
interpretation: This is a divine rebuke on the Day of Judgment: Allah will address those who associated others with Him, not because He has partners, but to expose their false claim. Their alleged partners will be utterly absent and powerless to answer, help, or intercede. The question declares the bankruptcy of shirk and affirms that all worship and allegiance belong to Allah alone, while those who invented such claims will face the consequence of their denial and accountability.

translation: Those upon whom the decree has become due will say, “Our Lord, these are the ones we led astray. We led them astray just as we ourselves were astray. We disavow them before You; they did not worship us.”
interpretation: This verse exposes the illusion of misplaced obedience on the Day of Judgment: the leaders who misled others confess their role, yet they disown any claim to divinity or true worship, because the followers’ devotion was never really directed to them. It shows that moral responsibility cannot be transferred; temptation and bad example may come from others, but each soul’s choice to prefer created guidance over God’s guidance is its own. Their disavowal before God affirms that all lordship and worship belong to Him alone, and that obeying anyone in defiance of Him is ultimately a self-chosen idolatry for which the follower, not merely the misleader, is accountable.

translation: And it will be said, “Call upon your partners.” So they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and they will see the punishment. If only they had been guided!
interpretation: This verse depicts the utter helplessness of those who associated false deities with Allah. On the Day of Judgment they are told to call upon their so-called partners, but those beings cannot answer or aid them at all. At that moment they witness the punishment and recognize too late that had they accepted true guidance in the world, they would not have fallen into this ruin. It exposes the worthlessness of false objects of worship and the irreversible regret of those who rejected divine guidance until it was too late.

translation: And [mention] the Day when He will call them and say: What did you answer the messengers?
interpretation: This is a scene of the Day of Judgment: Allah, the Exalted, will address those who rejected His revelation and ask them what response they gave to the messengers He sent to them. The question is not for information but for exposure, rebuke, and accountability. It establishes that divine guidance had reached them through chosen messengers, so on that Day they cannot claim ignorance or excuse themselves; their answer will reveal whether they accepted and followed the message or turned away, and it will seal the case against those who denied it.

translation: So the reports will be obscured from them on that Day, and they will not ask one another.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection, when those who denied the messengers are called to account, every answer, argument, and piece of knowledge that might help them explain themselves vanishes from their perception. They are left utterly unable to respond, and they do not turn to one another asking questions or seeking explanations, because the terror and certainty of that moment have silenced them and exposed the futility of all their former disputes.

translation: But as for the one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds, perhaps he will be among the successful.
interpretation: This verse means that no matter how far a person has strayed, the door of return remains open: sincere repentance from sin and disbelief, faith in God and His messengers, and righteous action together place one under divine hope and promise, so that such a person may attain falāḥ—success, deliverance, and eternal felicity in the Hereafter. The expression “perhaps” (ʿasā) from God conveys a firm hope and an assured promise of acceptance, not uncertainty on His part; it invites the sinner not to despair and urges the believer to combine inward faith with outward good deeds.

translation: Your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses. They have no choice. Glory be to Allah, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: This verse establishes that absolute creative power and the sole right of selection belong to Allah alone—whether in creating, appointing Prophets, granting revelation, guiding whom He wills, or decreeing honor and favor. Creatures have no authority to dictate to Him, object to His choices, or claim a share in His prerogative. His choosing is based on perfect wisdom and mercy, not on human preference, status, or desire; therefore He is glorified and far above the partners and rivals they falsely associate with Him.

translation: And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they reveal.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God’s knowledge encompasses both the inward secrets of people—their hidden thoughts, intentions, desires, and beliefs—and their outward words and actions. Nothing is concealed from Him, whether kept in the heart or expressed openly. Therefore, people should live with sincerity and God-consciousness, knowing that He will hold them accountable for both their inner states and their external deeds.

translation: And He is Allah; there is no deity except Him. To Him belongs all praise in the first [life] and the Hereafter, and to Him belongs judgment, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse affirms that absolute divinity, praise, authority, and final return all belong exclusively to Allah. Since no one shares His divinity, no one else is ultimately worthy of worship or unconditional praise. All blessings in this world and all outcomes in the Hereafter originate from Him, and every decree and judgment rests with Him alone. Therefore, human beings are not autonomous ends; they are moving toward Him and will be brought back for reckoning. The verse calls the heart to sincere monotheism, gratitude, submission to His rule, and accountability before Him.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered: if Allah should make the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, who is a god other than Allah that could bring you light? Will you not then hear?'
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical proof of Allah's exclusive divinity and power. It confronts those who associate partners with Him by pointing to a mercy they constantly depend on: the coming of light after darkness. If Allah were to withhold daylight and make night unending until the Resurrection, no claimed deity besides Him could restore light or bring day. Thus the verse establishes that only Allah controls the alternation of night and day, and that any false god is utterly powerless. The closing question, 'Will you not then hear?', is not merely about physical hearing but about listening with an accepting, understanding heart—recognizing Allah's oneness and responding to His signs with faith and gratitude.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered: if Allah should make the day over you perpetual until the Day of Resurrection, who is a god other than Allah who could bring you night in which you rest? Then will you not see?'
interpretation: The verse uses the hypothetical permanence of daylight to awaken insight: if the sun never set, human life would be impossible to endure; no idol, force, or claimed deity could restore the night's rest. So it establishes that only Allah, who orders the alternation of day and night, deserves worship and gratitude, and it rebukes those who do not perceive the signs of His oneness and mercy in the created order.

translation: And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, so that you may rest therein and seek from His bounty, and so that you may give thanks.
interpretation: The alternation of night and day is a deliberate expression of God's mercy. Night provides stillness, rest, and recovery, while day provides movement, work, and the opportunity to seek provision. These are not merely natural cycles but gifts meant to meet human needs and draw people toward gratitude. The aim is that people recognize God's kindness in the ordinary rhythms of life and respond with thankfulness, using both rest and work as occasions for obedience and remembrance of Him.

translation: And [mention] the Day when He will call out to them and say, 'Where are My partners whom you used to claim?'
interpretation: This is a rhetorical question on the Day of Judgment, confronting the polytheists who associated partners with Allah. Allah, exalted be He, asks where those alleged partners are—those beings they claimed shared in divinity or deserved worship alongside Him. It declares their false claims utterly baseless and powerless: the idols, intercessors, or imagined deities cannot answer, help, or avert punishment. It establishes Allah's exclusive lordship and exposes shirk, warning that every claim of partnership with God will collapse when His call goes out and no partner can be found or summoned.

translation: And We will draw out from every nation a witness, then We will say, 'Bring your proof.' Then they will know that the truth belongs to Allah, and lost from them will be what they used to fabricate.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, God will bring forth from each community its prophet as a witness who testifies that he delivered the divine message and that the people either accepted or rejected it. The deniers will then be commanded to produce their evidence for worshipping others besides God. At that point they will recognize with certainty that all truth, sovereignty, and the exclusive right to be worshipped belong to Allah alone, and the false claims, invented deities, and baseless intercessors they relied upon will vanish and prove utterly futile, leaving them without excuse or support.

translation: Indeed, Qarun was from the people of Moses, but he wronged them. And We had given him such treasures that their keys would indeed burden a company of strong men. When his people said to him, 'Do not exult; indeed, Allah does not like those who exult.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that wealth and status, even when granted by God, are a test and not proof of superiority. Qarun's greatness became a cause of oppression against his own people, showing how attachment to riches can corrupt justice and brotherhood. The enormous keys symbolize that his resources were vast, yet they could not justify arrogance or injustice. The warning 'Do not exult' means do not rejoice in worldly abundance with pride, heedlessness, and disdain for others, because God does not love those whose joy is rooted in self-importance and forgetfulness of Him. True favor lies in gratitude, humility, and using what God gives for good, not in hoarding wealth or lording it over people.

translation: And seek, through what Allah has given you, the Home of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of this world. And do good as Allah has done good to you, and do not seek corruption in the earth. Indeed, Allah does not like corrupters.
interpretation: It directs a person to use the blessings, wealth, and abilities God has granted as means to attain the eternal Home, by spending and acting in obedience, charity, and justice, while not neglecting the legitimate worldly share of needs, lawful enjoyment, work, and provision. Goodness should mirror God’s goodness: be generous, just, forgiving, and beneficial to others. Corruption is any pursuit of harm—moral, social, economic, or environmental—and God’s declaration that He does not love corrupters means such conduct removes one from His love and approval.

translation: He said, “I have only been given it because of knowledge I have.” Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him of generations those who were greater than him in strength and greater in accumulation? And the criminals will not be asked about their sins.
interpretation: This verse exposes the self-deception of Qarun, who credits his wealth to his own knowledge and merit rather than to God’s favor. The rhetorical question reminds him that earlier nations surpassed him in power and wealth, yet God destroyed them when they persisted in arrogance. Therefore, worldly strength and abundance are neither proof of divine approval nor protection from judgment. The final clause means the guilty will not be questioned in a way that lets them deny, excuse, or escape; their crimes are known, and God’s justice proceeds without need for their defense.

translation: So he went out before his people in his adornment. Those who desired the worldly life said, “Would that we had the like of what Qarun was given! Indeed, he is a man of great fortune.”
interpretation: The verse exposes the spiritual danger of measuring success by material display and of letting love of this world shape one’s judgments. The observers’ longing for Qarun’s wealth is not neutral admiration but a symptom of a heart oriented only to the worldly life; it mistakes temporary grandeur for divine favor and ignores the moral accountability behind wealth. Qarun’s public parade of his adornment is an act of arrogance and self-glorification, and the verse warns that such admiration from worldly people can become a trap: it normalizes oppression, blinds one to the poor and to the Hereafter, and makes wealth itself an object of ultimate concern. True honor is not what is paraded before people, but what is accepted with God through faith, gratitude, justice, and detachment from worldly excess.

translation: And those who were given knowledge said, 'Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for one who believes and does righteous deeds; and none will receive it except the patient.'
interpretation: The verse contrasts the misguided awe of worldly wealth with the insight of true knowledge: those granted knowledge recognize that God's reward, earned through faith and righteous action, is superior to any material gain. The pronoun 'it' refers to that reward—or to the virtuous state that leads to it—which is not attained by wishful thinking or by admiring the rich, but only by those who remain steadfast: patient in obedience, in avoiding sin, and in enduring hardship for God's sake. Thus the ultimate criterion of success is not abundance of wealth but faith, good deeds, and perseverance.

translation: So We caused the earth to swallow him and his dwelling, and he had no party to help him other than Allah, nor was he able to defend himself.
interpretation: This verse declares that when God’s punishment comes, all worldly support collapses. Qarun’s wealth, followers, and influence could not protect him from the divine decree; no group could rescue him besides God, and he could not rescue himself. Its meaning is a warning against arrogant reliance on riches, status, or human alliances, and a reminder that true security lies only with God. The one who exalts himself through God-given blessings, using them for oppression or self-glorification, will find that his apparent power is utterly powerless before God’s judgment.

translation: And those who had wished for his position yesterday began to say, “How Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it! Had Allah not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us. How the disbelievers do not succeed!”
interpretation: This verse exposes the folly of envying worldly wealth and status. When the arrogant wealthy man is destroyed, those who had coveted his position suddenly realize that provision is entirely in Allah’s hand: He expands it or narrows it according to His wisdom, not according to a person’s worth or power. Their own safety is a mercy from Allah, not a result of their merit; had He willed, they too could have been swallowed by the earth. True success is therefore never attained through disbelief, oppression, or the accumulation of riches, but only through submission to Allah and righteousness.

translation: That home of the Hereafter We assign to those who do not desire exaltedness in the earth or corruption. And the outcome is for the righteous.
interpretation: God reserves the eternal abode of the Hereafter for those who purify their inner will from arrogance, self-exaltation, and the desire to dominate or oppress others, and who likewise reject spreading corruption, injustice, and disorder in the world. True honor in His sight belongs not to the proud or the corrupters but to the God-conscious, whose reverent obedience and avoidance of sin lead to the final, praiseworthy end.

translation: Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it; and whoever comes with an evil deed — those who committed evil deeds will not be recompensed except for what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse establishes God's generosity and perfect justice: a good deed is rewarded with something greater and more lasting than the deed itself, while an evil deed is recompensed only according to its own measure, without any increase or injustice. Thus every person's final outcome corresponds exactly to what they chose to bring before God.

translation: Indeed, He who has ordained the Qur'an upon you will surely bring you back to the place of return. Say, 'My Lord is most knowing of who has brought guidance and who is in clear misguidance.'
interpretation: This verse is a divine assurance that the One who made the Qur'an a binding trust upon the Prophet is fully able to fulfill His promise: He will return him to the destined place of return—whether understood as Mecca after emigration, or ultimately the return to God in the Hereafter. The command to declare that God knows best teaches that final judgment between the guided and the misguided belongs to God alone, for He knows hidden motives, sincerity, and outcomes. It consoles the believer facing opposition: the same divine power that established the revelation will also establish its bearer's end, and no human verdict can override God's knowledge and decree.

translation: And you did not expect that the Book would be delivered to you, except as a mercy from your Lord. So never be a supporter of the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse teaches that divine revelation and guidance are not earned by human expectation, effort, or merit; they are granted purely as a mercy from God. The Prophet is reminded that receiving the Book was an unanticipated gift, and therefore the proper response is gratitude, humility, and unwavering loyalty to the One who sent it. Consequently, he must never lend aid, comfort, or support to those who reject God’s message or oppose it, because doing so would contradict the purpose of that mercy. The verse establishes that closeness to revelation requires alignment with God, not with disbelief, and that divine guidance should produce firm commitment rather than compromise with falsehood.

translation: And let them not turn you away from the verses of Allah after they have been sent down to you. And invite to your Lord, and do not be of the polytheists.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet, and by extension every believer, not to allow the opposition, pressure, or schemes of others to divert him from the revelations and guidance of Allah once they have been received. He must remain steadfast in calling people to the worship and obedience of his Lord alone, and must never adopt the way of those who associate partners with Allah.

translation: And do not invoke with Allah another deity. There is no deity except Him. Everything is perishable except His Face. To Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse establishes pure monotheism and the absolute exclusivity of God in worship, invocation, and ultimate authority. It forbids directing any act of worship or supplication to anyone besides Allah, because there is no true deity but Him. It then declares that every created thing is subject to perishing and annihilation; only Allah’s eternal Essence—expressed here as “His Face”—remains forever. Therefore, all judgment, decree, and sovereignty belong solely to Him, and all creation must ultimately return to Him for resurrection and reckoning.
