The messengers’ clear signs should have produced humility and acceptance, but instead the people took pride in their own limited understanding, as though their intellectual or worldly attainments made them independent of God and His prophets. Their rejoicing was not true joy in truth but a delusion of self-sufficiency, and it led them to mock the warnings. The punishment they mocked then became the very reality that closed in upon them, showing that divine truths rejected in arrogance eventually overtake the rejecter. It warns that knowledge without submission to God can become a veil rather than a light, and that no human learning can protect anyone from the consequences of denying the truth.

translation: So when they saw Our punishment, they said: “We believe in Allah alone, and we disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him.”
interpretation: This is the belated confession of the polytheists when Allah’s punishment comes upon them: they renounce their idols and proclaim faith in Allah alone. But their declaration is not accepted, because it is born of overwhelming terror and compelled certainty, not of willing faith in the unseen. The verse teaches that faith and repentance must come before punishment and before the veil of the unseen is lifted; once divine chastisement is witnessed, such a confession cannot ward it off or benefit the one who makes it. It also establishes that all worship belongs to Allah alone and that every object of shirk is false and to be rejected.

translation: But their faith did not benefit them once they saw Our punishment. Such is the way of Allah that has already passed among His servants, and the disbelievers were then the losers.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fixed divine law that faith or repentance offered only at the moment of witnessing the punishment is not accepted, because it is compelled by terror rather than sincere choice. The earlier nations did not benefit from their last-moment belief, and the same rule applies to all later peoples. Allah's established way with His servants is that those who persist in disbelief until the punishment becomes visible are abandoned to loss, and at that point the disbelievers lose deliverance in this world and every good in the Hereafter.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ha, Meem.
interpretation: The letters Ha-Meem are among the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'at) that open several surahs; their precise meaning is known only to Allah, and they serve as a divine sign of the Qur'an's inimitability and an invitation to reflect on its revelation.

translation: A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the Qur’an is not a human invention or merely inherited wisdom; it is sent down by God Himself, whose essential nature is mercy. The names al-Rahman and al-Rahim together show that His mercy is both all-encompassing in creation and providence and specially guiding and forgiving toward those who turn to Him. Therefore, the Qur’an itself is a direct expression of divine mercy: it invites people from darkness to light, warns out of compassion, and heals and guides hearts that receive it. To accept it is to accept the mercy of the Most Merciful; to turn away from it is to cut oneself off from that offered mercy.

translation: A Book whose verses have been expounded in detail, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know.
interpretation: God describes the Qur'an as a Book whose verses are clearly set forth and distinguished, revealed in the Arabic tongue so that its meanings, proofs, and guidance may be understood by those who possess knowledge and apply their minds to it.

translation: As a bringer of good tidings and a warner; but most of them turn away, so they do not hear.
interpretation: The Qur’an is sent with a twofold purpose: to give glad tidings to those who accept it and to warn those who reject it. Yet most of the people addressed turned away from it, and so they do not hear it in the sense of receiving its message with acceptance. Their failure is not merely physical deafness but a spiritual deafness caused by wilful aversion: because they refused to listen with an open heart, the guidance of the revelation could not penetrate them.

translation: And they say, 'Our hearts are within coverings from that to which you call us, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier. So work; indeed, we are working.'
interpretation: This verse exposes a willful, self-justifying rejection of divine guidance. The disbelievers describe their hearts as veiled, their ears as deaf, and a partition as standing between them and the Messenger—not because the truth is unclear, but because they have chosen spiritual closure. Their words “So work; indeed, we are working” are a declaration of disengagement: each side will persist in its own course. The meaning is that when people erect barriers against revelation and refuse to hear or understand, they bear responsibility for that choice, and the final outcome will reveal who truly follows the right path.

translation: Say, "I am only a human being like you. It has been revealed to me that your god is one God; so take the straight path to Him and seek His forgiveness. And woe to the polytheists."
interpretation: The verse establishes that the Messenger is a human being, not a divine figure; his authority comes solely from revelation. Its central message is pure monotheism: there is only one God, so people should direct their worship, obedience, repentance, and lives sincerely toward Him alone. Seeking His forgiveness means turning back from sin and relying on His mercy. The warning of woe to the polytheists is because associating partners with God corrupts this pure relationship and leads away from the straight path to Him.

translation: Those who do not give the zakah, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse exposes the root of the polytheists’ corruption: their denial of the Hereafter produces a life unmoved by final accountability, so they withhold the obligatory purification of wealth and the rights of the needy. Their refusal to pay zakah is therefore not merely a legal lapse but evidence of a deeper rejection of God’s authority and the coming judgment. Because they disbelieve in the meeting with their Lord and in recompense, they feel free to keep what God has commanded them to give, and this confirms them as kuffar—those who cover and reject the truth.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have an uninterrupted reward.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true faith must be paired with righteous action, and for those who unite the two, God guarantees a reward that is neither cut off nor diminished, but perpetual and given without any grudging or reproach.

translation: Say, 'Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days and set up equals to Him? That is the Lord of all worlds.'
interpretation: This verse confronts the contradiction of those who reject God while living upon an earth He created and ordered. Making rivals or equals to Him is exposed as false and unjust, because the act of creating the earth in measured stages belongs to Him alone. The 'two days' point to His sovereign decree and wisdom, not to any limitation like human time. Thus the verse establishes pure monotheism: the Creator and Sustainer of all existence is the only true Lord, and no created thing can share His lordship.

translation: And He placed therein firm mountains above it, and blessed it, and measured therein its sustenance in four days, equally for those who ask.
interpretation: The verse declares that Allah alone is the Creator and Provider: He stabilized the earth with firm mountains, placed blessing in it, and decreed its provisions in precise measure over four days, so that His creation and sustenance are ordered, sufficient, and plainly answerable for anyone who inquires about His power and wisdom.

translation: Then He directed Himself to the heaven while it was smoke and said to it and to the earth, “Come, both of you, willingly or unwillingly.” They both said, “We have come willingly.”
interpretation: This verse establishes God’s absolute sovereignty over all creation. The heaven and the earth, though inanimate, are addressed as beings capable of responding to His command, showing that the entire universe is subject to His will and cannot resist it. The phrase “willingly or unwillingly” means that submission to God is inevitable; no created thing can escape His decree. Their reply, “We have come willingly,” expresses perfect, immediate obedience and readiness to fulfill His purpose. It signifies that the natural order of creation is aligned with God’s command, and it serves as a contrast to human beings who often resist divine guidance. The verse thus calls the listener to reflect on the harmony of the cosmos and to adopt willing submission to God.

translation: Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days and revealed to each heaven its command. And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps, and as a guard. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse presents the ordering of the cosmos as an act of divine decree: God finishes the heavens as seven distinct realms, each given its own command and function, so that the whole creation is subject to His governance. The stars in the nearest heaven are both an adornment and a protection, indicating that the physical order has purpose and serves God's wise arrangement. The final attributes affirm that this measured, purposeful creation proceeds from absolute power joined with all-encompassing knowledge, not from chance or disorder.

translation: So if they turn away, then say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Aad and Thamud.
interpretation: This verse delivers a severe warning to those who reject the prophet's message after it has been made clear: their turning away exposes them to a divine punishment that comes as a sudden, overwhelming blast, just as it destroyed the ancient peoples of 'Aad and Thamud. Their ruin shows that no strength, wealth, or civilization can protect a people who knowingly deny God's messengers and persist in arrogance. The messenger's role is only to warn; the choice to turn away brings consequences according to God's unchanging law.

translation: When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them, [saying], 'Worship none but Allah,' they said, 'If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels. So indeed we are disbelievers in what you have been sent with.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the false pretext of those who reject divine guidance. The messengers came with a consistent call to pure monotheism—that no one be worshipped except Allah—and they warned from every direction, both of coming punishment and of the need to return to God. The people’s objection that God could have sent angels instead of human messengers was not a sincere search for truth but an evasive demand aimed at avoiding submission. God’s will is not a license for disbelief; His choice to send human messengers is wise, suited to human guidance, and binding upon those who hear it. Therefore, rejecting the messengers He sent is itself a rejection of Him, making them disbelievers in the very message they were entrusted to convey.

translation: As for 'Aad, they became arrogant in the land without right and said, 'Who is stronger than us in might?' Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is stronger than them in might? And they used to deny Our signs.
interpretation: This verse exposes arrogance as the root of 'Aad's rebellion: they measured truth by worldly power and assumed that superior strength justified self-exaltation. Their question, 'Who is stronger than us?', was not a sincere search for truth but a boast that blinded them to the obvious reality that the One who created them must be greater than His creation. The verse therefore teaches that human strength is borrowed, limited, and dependent, while God's power is absolute. Denying His signs follows naturally from this arrogance, because a heart intoxicated by its own might refuses to submit to a higher authority. The warning is that no civilization, however powerful, can stand against the Creator whose signs it knowingly rejects.

translation: So We sent upon them a roaring, violent wind in days of misfortune, so that We might make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world; but the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgracing, and they will not be helped.
interpretation: This is a warning that rejection and arrogance bring a humiliating punishment even in this world, but that is only a partial and temporary disgrace; the punishment of the Hereafter is far greater in shame and severity. The statement that they will not be helped declares that neither their strength, wealth, false deities, nor any created power can rescue them once God's judgment comes.

translation: And as for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of humiliating punishment seized them because of what they used to earn.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Thamud, whom God guided by sending them His prophet Salih and clear signs, showing them the path of truth. Yet they deliberately chose disbelief and misguidance over faith and obedience. Because of their arrogance and persistent evil deeds, a devastating punishment — described as a thunderbolt or blast of humiliating torment — overtook them. The verse teaches that God does not compel belief; He offers guidance, but people remain responsible for their choice, and punishment is the just consequence of their own actions.

translation: And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah.
interpretation: This means that Allah delivered the believers from the destructive punishment that came upon the deniers, because they had faith in Him and practiced taqwa—guarding themselves against His displeasure by obedience, avoiding disbelief and sin. It teaches that sincere faith joined with God-consciousness is the cause of divine protection and salvation, while arrogance and rejection bring ruin.

translation: And on the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire, they will be driven in ranks.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when those who rejected Allah and opposed His messengers are forcibly gathered and herded toward Hell in an orderly, humiliating procession. The word yūzaʿūn indicates that they are marshaled and held back so that the first of them wait for the last, none escaping or arriving out of turn, until all are assembled before the Fire for judgment and punishment.

translation: Until, when they arrive at it, their hearing, their eyes, and their skins will testify against them concerning what they used to do.
interpretation: This is a scene of absolute accountability: the faculties and even the body itself become witnesses, exposing every deed the person committed and stripping away any possibility of denial. It signifies that God’s justice is so complete that a person’s own senses and limbs will speak the truth against them, confirming that nothing was hidden from divine record and that the punishment is deserved. The testimony of hearing, sight, and skin also shows that the whole person is implicated in what they chose to do, so no part of the self can claim innocence or ignorance.

translation: And they will say to their skins, 'Why have you testified against us?' They will say, 'Allah has made us speak, He who gives speech to all things; and He created you the first time, and to Him you are returned.'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the disbelievers will be confronted by the testimony of their own skins and body parts, and they will be astonished that their own selves bear witness against them. Their skins will reply that Allah, the One who grants speech to all things, enabled them to speak. This demonstrates that Allah’s power over creation is absolute and that no deed can remain hidden from Him. He originated humankind in the first place, and every soul must ultimately return to Him for accountability and recompense. The verse affirms divine justice, the inevitability of resurrection, and the complete subservience of all creation to Allah’s command.

translation: And you did not conceal yourselves from [the testimony of] your hearing, nor your eyes, nor your skins against you; but you thought that Allah did not know much of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse condemns sinners who committed deeds without fearing that their own hearing, eyes, and skins would testify against them on the Day of Judgment. Their deeper fault was a false assumption about Allah: they thought He did not know much of what they did. It teaches that Allah is fully aware of every action, hidden or open, and that a person’s own faculties and body will serve as witnesses, so no one can escape accountability.

translation: And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has ruined you, so you have become among the losers.
interpretation: This verse exposes how a corrupted conception of God can itself become the cause of perdition. The people addressed presumed something false about their Lord—such as that He would not resurrect them, would not hold them accountable, or was indifferent to their deeds—and that presumption shaped their lives and led them to ruin. Their loss is not arbitrary; it is the fruit of a wrong inner orientation toward God. The verse teaches that what a person believes about God profoundly determines their conduct and final destiny, and that entertaining belittling or false thoughts about the Lord ultimately brings about one’s own downfall in the Hereafter.

translation: So if they endure patiently, the Fire is still their dwelling; and if they seek to be favored, they will not be among those who are favored.
interpretation: This verse describes the final and irreversible state of those condemned for rejecting faith. Whether they bear the punishment patiently or not, Hell remains their settled abode. Likewise, if they try to excuse themselves, seek reprieve, or plead for God's favor after judgment, their plea will not be accepted. The verse emphasizes that the time for repentance and acceptable appeal has passed, and divine judgment in the Hereafter cannot be reversed by patience, regret, or requests for leniency.

translation: And We have appointed for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them, and the Word became justified against them, along with nations that had passed away before them of jinn and mankind. Indeed, they were losers.
interpretation: This means that when people persist in rejecting guidance, God may leave them with intimate companions—devils from among jinn or humans—who beautify falsehood, sin, and worldly desires, making them seem good both in the present and in retrospect, while blinding them to the Hereafter and to the lessons of the past. Thus the decree of punishment becomes binding upon them together with earlier jinn and human communities that likewise rejected truth. Their loss is ultimate: they lose faith, guidance, and eternal success, having exchanged the Hereafter for deception and fleeting illusion.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, 'Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, so that you may overcome.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the tactic of the obstinate disbelievers: rather than listening to the Qur'an and pondering its proofs, they urged people to ignore it and to disrupt its recitation with clamor, idle talk, or distractions, hoping thereby to overpower the truth and silence the Prophet. Their command reveals that they feared the Qur'an's influence and could not meet it with reasoned argument, so they resorted to suppression and noise. It stands as a warning that falsehood may try to drown out divine guidance, but such schemes cannot ultimately defeat the truth.

translation: So We will surely make those who disbelieve taste a severe punishment, and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do.
interpretation: This is a solemn divine warning: those who reject faith and persist in denying God will inevitably suffer a painful punishment in the Hereafter, and their recompense will be measured by the most evil of their deeds. It emphasizes God's perfect justice—unbelief and deliberate wrongdoing bring severe consequences—and it warns that rejecting the truth leads to ruin, while the punishment corresponds to the gravity of their crimes.

translation: That is the recompense of Allah’s enemies: the Fire. In it they will have the abode of eternity — a recompense for what they used to deny Our signs.
interpretation: This verse declares the final end of those who make themselves enemies of Allah by rejecting His revelation. Their recompense is the Fire, and it is described as an eternal home, not a passing punishment. The reason for this recompense is their persistent denial of Allah’s signs/verses: they knowingly rejected the proofs and guidance sent to them, and that rejection became their settled way. Thus the verse connects the permanence of the punishment to the deliberate and ongoing nature of their denial of the truth.

translation: And those who disbelieved will say, “Our Lord, show us those who led us astray from among the jinn and humankind, so we may trample them beneath our feet, so that they may be among the lowest.”
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the disbelievers will ask God to expose the two kinds of misleaders—the jinn and human beings—who caused them to go astray. Their request is not for justice but for revenge and humiliation: they want to place those misleaders beneath their feet, lowering them to the deepest rank of disgrace. This shows that both seducers from among jinn and humans bear responsibility for leading others into disbelief, and that the followers’ regret on that Day will not excuse their own willing obedience to them.

translation: Indeed, those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' and then remain steadfast — the angels descend upon them, [saying], 'Do not fear, nor grieve, and receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised.'
interpretation: This verse sets forth the essence of true faith: to acknowledge Allah alone as Lord and Sustainer, and then to persevere upon that acknowledgment with sincerity, obedience, patience, and steadfastness until the end. Such people are met by angels who descend to reassure them, especially at the moment of death and in the life of the grave, removing fear of what lies ahead and grief over what is past or left behind, and giving them the glad tidings of the Paradise that Allah had promised to the steadfast. Their constancy is not merely a one-time confession but a lifelong orientation: they remain firm upon divine guidance through ease and hardship, trusting Allah's promise, and so they receive security, comfort, and hope in place of anxiety and sorrow. The verse indicates that steadfastness carries the reward of angelic support, inner peace, and the ultimate good news of eternal success.

translation: We are your guardians in the life of this world and in the Hereafter, and therein you will have whatever your souls desire, and therein you will have whatever you ask for.
interpretation: The angels—by God’s command—address the steadfast believers, declaring that they are their guardians and close allies in this worldly life and in the Hereafter: in this world they protect, strengthen, and guide them, and in the next they remain with them, bringing glad tidings and removing fear and grief. Then they announce that Paradise will grant believers the full realization of every inward desire and every request they make, so that no longing is left unfulfilled and no supplication is left unanswered.

translation: A welcome provision from a Forgiving, Merciful Lord.
interpretation: This describes the reward of the believers in Paradise as a banquet of honor prepared for them by God, flowing from His forgiveness of their sins and His mercy toward them. It teaches that final bliss is received as generous hospitality from the Forgiving, Merciful One, not as a right owed to the servant, and that His mercy combines pardon with abundant bounty.

translation: And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, 'Indeed, I am of the Muslims'?
interpretation: This verse teaches that the most excellent and honorable speech is not merely eloquent words, but speech joined to calling others to Allah, to righteous action, and to humble submission. The one who invites to God must first be sincere in obedience and good works, so that his invitation is supported by his conduct rather than contradicted by it. His declaration that he is among the Muslims is an expression of humility and identity: he does not claim purity or superiority for himself, but simply acknowledges his submission to God and his belonging to those who surrender to Him. Thus true excellence of speech is measured by faith, sincerity, righteous deeds, and humble devotion, not by reputation or rhetorical skill.

translation: And the good deed and the evil deed are not equal. Repel [evil] with that which is better; then the one between whom and you there was enmity will become as if he were a devoted friend.
interpretation: This verse teaches that good and evil are not equal in worth or outcome, and that the believer should not answer hostility with hostility. Rather, evil should be actively repelled by what is better: patience, forgiveness, kindness, and excellent conduct. The promised result is that even a bitter enemy may be transformed, by God’s grace, into a close and sincere friend. The verse therefore establishes a moral standard of overcoming harm with goodness, softening hearts, and breaking cycles of enmity through superior character.

translation: And none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except the possessor of a great share.
interpretation: The pronoun “it” refers to the noble conduct of repelling evil with what is better and overcoming enmity through patience and kindness. This verse teaches that such a high moral station is granted only to people of sabr—those who restrain anger, endure harm, and persevere in doing good—and that attaining this disposition is itself a great portion of good, honor, and reward in this life and the Hereafter.

translation: And if an evil incitement from Satan stirs you, then seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse teaches that when Satan tries to provoke a person through whispering, anger, doubt, or desire, the remedy is not to yield to it but to turn immediately to God for protection. Seeking refuge with Allah means entrusting oneself to His safeguard, acknowledging one's weakness before the enemy, and relying on His power. The closing names assure the believer that Allah hears the seeker's plea and knows the hidden temptation and intention, so no whispered harm is beyond His knowledge or care.

translation: And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allah, who created them, if it is Him you worship.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the night, day, sun, and moon are all created signs pointing to God’s power and lordship, not objects worthy of worship. Prostration belongs exclusively to God, the Creator of all these things, because worship must be directed to the One who originates and controls creation. If a person truly intends to worship God alone, then the proper response is to submit to Him alone and not to any created thing, however magnificent or luminous it may appear.

translation: But if they are arrogant, then those who are near your Lord glorify Him by night and day, and they never tire.
interpretation: This verse means that if the disbelievers persist in arrogance and refuse to worship God, their refusal does not diminish Him in any way. The angels who are near their Lord continuously glorify and praise Him throughout the night and day, never growing weary or bored. It is a rebuke to human pride: while some turn away from worship out of haughtiness, the closest servants of God remain constant in His praise, showing that worship is not a need God has, but a duty and honor for the servant.

translation: And among His signs is that you see the earth barren and lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells. Indeed, He who gives it life is the Giver of life to the dead. Indeed, He is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse offers the revival of dead, barren earth by rain as clear evidence of Allah's power to resurrect the dead. The earth's dryness, stillness, and lowliness represent death and inability; when Allah sends water, it moves, expands, and brings forth life. The One who can thus give life to lifeless soil is certainly able to give life to dead bodies and raise them for judgment. It affirms that resurrection is not difficult for Allah, because His power encompasses all things without exception.

translation: Indeed, those who distort or deviate concerning Our signs are not hidden from Us. Is one who is cast into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection? Do what you will; indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse is a stern warning to those who corrupt, deny, or twist the meaning of God's revelations. It states that such people cannot escape God's knowledge or judgment. The rhetorical question contrasts the disastrous end of the one thrown into Hellfire with the safety and security of the one who arrives on the Day of Judgment saved from punishment. The command “Do what you will” is not a permission but a threat: it exposes human freedom and responsibility, warning that whatever path people choose, God sees all their deeds and will hold them accountable.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it has come to them [will be held accountable], and indeed it is a mighty, precious Book.
interpretation: This verse declares that rejecting the Qur’an after it has reached a person is not a rejection of something weak or negligible, but of a Book whose honor, truth, and authority are divinely guarded. Its being “precious” means it is protected from being discredited, corrupted, or overcome; disbelief does not diminish its rank or cancel its binding claim upon humanity, but only exposes the rejecter to loss.

translation: Falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it: it is a revelation sent down from One Who is All-Wise, Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse asserts the absolute integrity and inaccessibility of the Qur'an to falsehood from any direction: no lie, distortion, contradiction, addition, omission, or invalidating doubt can approach it, whether regarding what it reports of the past or what it foretells, nor from any angle of its meanings and rulings. It is a revelation sent down by Allah, whose wisdom is perfect in His speech and decree, and who is praiseworthy in all His acts.

translation: Nothing is said to you except what was already said to the messengers before you. Indeed, your Lord is certainly the Possessor of forgiveness and the Possessor of painful punishment.
interpretation: This addresses the Prophet Muhammad, consoling him that the mockery, denial, and accusations he encounters are not unique but have been directed at every messenger before him; thus he should remain steadfast, knowing this is the established pattern of God's dealing with those who call to truth. The verse then declares that God's forgiveness is vast for those who turn to Him, while His punishment is painful for those who persist in rejecting Him, so the same divine attributes that offer hope also warn against arrogance and denial.

translation: And if We had made it a Qur'an in a foreign tongue, they would have said: 'Why have its verses not been made clear? What, a foreign tongue and an Arab?' Say: 'It is guidance and healing for those who believe. And as for those who do not believe, there is a deafness in their ears, and it is blindness for them. Those are being called from a far place.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the disbelievers’ bad faith and evasive objections. Had the Qur’an been revealed in a non-Arabic language, they would still have rejected it, complaining that its verses were not made clear and objecting to a foreign scripture brought by an Arab prophet. The real issue is not the language of the Qur’an but the state of the heart. For those who accept faith, the Qur’an is guidance from error and healing for spiritual sickness. For those who persist in denial, their rejection has caused a deafness in their ears and blindness in their insight, so they are like people being called from a very distant place—unable to hear or respond to the truth.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, but they differed about it. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been decided between them. And indeed they are in disquieting doubt about it.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by reminding him that Moses was given the Torah, yet his people disputed over it—accepting, rejecting, or distorting it. Such opposition to divine revelation is not new. The 'word that preceded from your Lord' is God's decree to delay judgment until the appointed Day of Resurrection. Were it not for that decree, He would have already settled the matter between them in this world, punishing the rejecters. The final clause means that those who dispute the truth remain in a state of unsettling, suspicious doubt about the revelation—whether the Torah they corruptly argue over or the Qur'an they reject. Their doubt does not harm the truth, and God will ultimately judge all disputes.

translation: Whoever does righteous work, it is for his own soul; and whoever does evil, it is against it. And your Lord is not unjust to His servants.
interpretation: This verse establishes that every deed returns to the one who performs it: righteousness benefits the doer himself, and evil harms only the one who commits it. God is absolutely just and does not wrong any of His servants in the least; He does not punish anyone for another’s sin, nor does He diminish the reward of any good deed.

translation: To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour. No fruit emerges from its sheath, and no female conceives or gives birth except by His knowledge. And on the Day when He will call to them, “Where are My partners?” they will say, “We declare to You: there is no witness among us.”
interpretation: This verse establishes that knowledge of the Hour and all hidden matters of creation belong exclusively to Allah. The emerging of every fruit, every conception, and every birth occurs under His knowledge and power, so no created being shares in His divine knowledge or authority. Then it depicts the polytheists on the Day of Judgment, when Allah asks where the partners they ascribed to Him are. Their former claims collapse, and they confess that none among them can witness to any partner besides Him. Thus the verse affirms Allah’s sole lordship and knowledge, and exposes the helplessness and falsehood of every claimed partner besides Him.

translation: And whatever they used to invoke before will fail them, and they will be certain that there is no escape for them.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, every false object of worship, mediator, or supposed helper that people called upon besides Allah will vanish and abandon them. At that moment they will no longer entertain any hope of deliverance; they will be certain that there is no refuge, no turning away, and no escape from Allah’s judgment. The verse exposes the futility of relying on anything other than Allah and shows that such attachments betray their followers precisely when help is most desperately needed.

translation: Man does not tire of praying for good, but if evil touches him, he is despairing and despondent.
interpretation: This verse exposes a human weakness: when life is good, a person keeps asking for more and never wearies of seeking benefit, but when hardship or harm comes, he quickly loses hope and becomes utterly despondent. It criticizes a faith and character that are stable only in ease and collapse in adversity, and it implicitly calls for patience, trust in God, and steadfastness in both blessing and trial.

translation: And if We make him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him, he will surely say, 'This is mine; and I do not think the Hour will be established. And if I were returned to my Lord, indeed I would have with Him the best.' So We will surely inform those who disbelieved about what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment.
interpretation: This verse exposes the mindset of the ungrateful disbeliever: when relief comes after hardship, he claims the blessing as his own right and due to his own worth, rather than receiving it with gratitude as a gift from God. That self-centered attitude breeds denial of the Hereafter and accountability. Even if he admits the possibility of returning to God, he presumptuously assumes he will be given the best with Him, as though divine favor were owed to him. The verse then declares God's justice: He will expose the reality of the disbelievers' deeds and make them taste a harsh, severe punishment. Prosperity and ease are therefore a test of gratitude and humility, not proof of entitlement or salvation.

translation: And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and draws aside; but when evil touches him, he is given to extensive supplication.
interpretation: This verse exposes a deep inconsistency in human nature: ease and blessing often make a person arrogant, forgetful, and distant from God, whereas hardship suddenly makes him fervent in prayer. It is a rebuke of turning to God only in need while neglecting Him in comfort, and it calls for steadfast gratitude, humility, and remembrance of God in both prosperity and adversity.

translation: Say, "Have you considered: if it is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, who is more astray than one who is in extreme dissension?"
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet to present the rejecters with a decisive challenge: if the Qur’an is truly from God, as its truth and signs indicate, then rejecting it does not diminish God in any way; it only exposes the rejecter’s own ruin. Such a person is in the utmost misguidance because he has turned away from the clear guidance after it has become evident, and he persists in a stance of deep, hostile opposition—far removed from truth, from sound reasoning, and from the path of salvation.

translation: We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth. But is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is, over all things, a Witness?
interpretation: Allah promises that He will manifest evidences of His power, wisdom, and truthfulness both in the vast external world—its horizons, phenomena, and created order—and within the human self—its origin, faculties, conscience, and spiritual condition—so that the reality of the Qur’an and the prophetic message becomes undeniably clear. These outward and inward signs are meant to lead to certainty that the revelation is true. Then the verse directs attention to a greater and sufficient testimony: Allah Himself is Witness over all things, knowing and recording every reality, so His testimony alone is enough to establish the truth and to hold people accountable for recognizing it.

translation: Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord. Unquestionably, He is encompassing all things.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner state of those who deny the Hereafter: they are not merely unaware but are caught in a persistent doubt about standing before their Lord. This doubt is culpable because Allah, who encompasses all things, has full knowledge of them and complete power over them. His encompassing means no deed, intention, or denial is outside His awareness or control, and He will inevitably bring about the meeting they question, for resurrection and judgment are entirely within His grasp. Thus the verse both rebukes their uncertainty and affirms that Allah's sovereignty leaves no room for escape.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ha-Mim.
interpretation: The Basmala is an invocation of Allah's name and mercy at the outset, while 'Ha-Mim' is one of the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'at) that open several surahs; its precise meaning is known only to Allah, and it serves as a divine sign pointing to the Qur'an's miraculous nature and calling for attentive reflection.

translation: Ayn, Seen, Qaf.
interpretation: These are among the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta‘at) with which Allah begins several surahs; their exact meaning is known only to Allah, and they serve as a sign of the Qur’an’s miraculous and divine origin.

translation: Thus Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise, reveals to you and to those before you.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the revelation sent to Muhammad is not a new or isolated phenomenon, but proceeds from the same divine source and method by which earlier prophets were inspired. It identifies Allah as al-Aziz, whose might is absolute and none can overpower, meaning He is fully able to send, preserve, and establish His revelation; and as al-Hakim, whose wisdom is perfect in ordaining revelation, choosing messengers, and guiding humanity according to what is best. The address consoles the Prophet and instructs believers that the message he receives is continuous with previous prophetic guidance, so its origin is one, its authority is divine, and its purpose is governed by power and wisdom, not by human invention or caprice.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse establishes that absolute ownership and dominion over all creation belong exclusively to God. Everything in the heavens and earth is His possession, under His authority, and subject to His will. Therefore, He alone deserves worship, obedience, reliance, and ultimate loyalty. His names al-‘Ali and al-‘Azim mean He is infinitely exalted above any deficiency, equal, or limitation, and He is immense in His essence, attributes, and majesty. No created being shares in His sovereignty, greatness, or right to be exalted.

translation: The heavens are almost rent asunder from above them, and the angels glorify and praise their Lord and ask forgiveness for those on the earth. Unquestionably, indeed Allah — He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse conveys that even the immense heavens tremble before Allah’s majesty and near rupture out of awe of His greatness, while the angels are constantly engaged in His praise and seek forgiveness for the inhabitants of the earth. It teaches that Allah alone is the true source of forgiveness and mercy, and that His mercy is so vast that heavenly beings implore it for earthly people. Therefore, no one should despair of Allah’s pardon; rather, one should turn to Him in repentance, since He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.

translation: And those who take besides Him protectors, Allah is Guardian over them, and you are not a disposer of their affairs.
interpretation: This verse affirms that although people may wrongly take others besides Allah as guardians, Allah remains fully watchful over them and is the ultimate authority over their deeds. The Prophet is not a guarantor or controller of their choices; his duty is only to convey the message, while judgment and reckoning belong to Allah alone.

translation: And thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an, that you may warn the Mother of Cities [Mecca] and those around it, and warn of the Day of Assembly, about which there is no doubt. A party will be in Paradise and a party in the Blaze.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Qur'an was revealed in clear Arabic so that the Prophet Muhammad may warn the people of Mecca—the foremost city of revelation and the center of the sacred precinct—as well as all peoples surrounding it and, by extension, all humanity. It commands warning of the Day of Resurrection, the Day when all creation will be gathered for judgment, a reality about which there is no uncertainty. On that Day, humanity will be divided into two groups: one destined for Paradise through God's mercy and faith, and another destined for the blazing Fire because of disbelief and rejection of the truth.

translation: And if Allah had willed, He would have made them one community, but He admits whom He wills into His mercy. And the wrongdoers will have neither protector nor helper.
interpretation: This verse establishes that unifying all people under one creed is entirely within God’s power; He does not do so because His wisdom requires distinction through freely chosen faith and His grace. Guidance and entrance into divine mercy are bestowed by God’s will upon those He knows will accept it, not by human merit or compulsion. The wrongdoers—those who persist in rejecting Him and His messengers—will find no guardian to protect them or helper to save them from His judgment.

translation: Or have they taken besides Him protectors? But Allah is the Protector; He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse repudiates any claim that beings other than Allah can truly guard, aid, or manage human affairs. Allah alone is the Walī—the Guardian whose authority, protection, and help are absolute and independent. The raising of the dead is singled out as proof that this guardianship belongs exclusively to Him, because no created being can give life after death. Since He has power over all things, no partner, idol, or intercessor can share His rule or act apart from His will. Therefore, the only sound response is to turn to Him alone as one’s Protector and to trust that He is able to resurrect, reckon, and dispose of every matter according to His wisdom.

translation: And whatever you differ about, its judgment is with Allah. That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn.
interpretation: This establishes that no human opinion, custom, consensus, or authority has the final say in matters of disagreement; ultimate judgment belongs to Allah alone, and His revealed law is the criterion. The Prophet’s acknowledgment, 'That is Allah, my Lord,' joins submission to His judgment with pure worship of Him, so accepting His ruling is part of tawhid. 'Upon Him I rely' means entrusting every affair to His wisdom, justice, and power, while 'to Him I turn' means returning to Him in repentance, obedience, and seeking His decision. Therefore, differences should be referred back to Allah rather than becoming a source of ego, partisanship, or defiance, and the believer’s path is trust in Allah and turning to Him alone.

translation: Originator of the heavens and the earth. He has made for you spouses from among yourselves, and pairs among the cattle; by this He multiplies you. There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.
interpretation: This verse establishes that Allah alone originates and creates all things without any prior model. His creating mates from among human beings and pairs among livestock is a manifestation of His mercy, making companionship, reproduction, and provision continue among creation. Then the verse declares His absolute transcendence: nothing in creation resembles Him in His essence, names, attributes, or actions. At the same time, it affirms that He is All-Hearing and All-Seeing, meaning His hearing and sight are perfect, unlimited, and uniquely His, utterly unlike the hearing and sight of creatures.

translation: To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: This means that God alone possesses the keys to all that is in the heavens and the earth—the means, stores, and authority over every affair. He alone decides how much provision each creature receives, granting abundance to some and limiting it for others according to His wisdom and will. Because He knows all things—past, present, future, hidden and apparent—His distribution of sustenance is never arbitrary but is perfectly measured, wise, and just.

translation: He has ordained for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah and what We revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: that you establish the religion and do not become divided therein. Heavy upon the polytheists is that to which you call them. Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back [to Him].
interpretation: This verse declares that the essential religion God legislated for Muhammad’s community is the same core message entrusted to Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: sincere worship of God alone, obedience to Him, and firm adherence to the religion without splitting into opposing sects over it. The prophets were sent with one fundamental demand—establish true religion—though their detailed laws could differ according to God’s wisdom. The call to pure monotheism and unity is difficult for the polytheists because it dismantles their false gods and partisan divisions. God alone selects whom He wills for His guidance and favor, and He guides to Himself those who turn to Him in repentance and humble return.

translation: And they did not become divided except after knowledge had come to them, out of mutual envy among themselves. And were it not for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord until an appointed term, it would have been decided between them. And indeed those who were made inheritors of the Book after them are in disquieting doubt about it.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the splitting of communities into conflicting factions over revealed truth is not caused by a lack of evidence, but by selfish rivalry and envy after the truth has become clear. It warns that such division is a moral and spiritual disease, not an intellectual necessity. It also shows that Allah, in His wisdom, delays final judgment until a fixed time, allowing people to be tested by what they inherited and how they handle it. Those who receive the Book after earlier generations are especially cautioned: if they fall into doubt and dispute, their doubt is not a valid excuse, because the problem lies in their own disordered relationship with the revelation they were entrusted to preserve.

translation: So to that, then, invite; and stand firm as you have been commanded; and do not follow their desires. And say, “I believe in whatever Scripture Allah has sent down, and I have been commanded to act justly among you. Allah is our Lord and your Lord. We have our deeds, and you have your deeds. There is no argument between us and you. Allah will bring us together, and to Him is the final return.”
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet—and by extension the believers—to persist in calling to the divinely revealed way after the truth has become clear. Steadfastness here is not passive endurance but unwavering adherence to God’s command, refusing to bend toward the desires and pressures of opponents. The confession of faith in all that God has sent down of Scripture defines the Muslim stance as one of continuity with divine revelation, not sectarian rejection. The command to act justly among all people shows that justice is a core prophetic obligation, even toward those who disagree. Since God is Lord of all, no group can claim Him exclusively; each person or community is responsible for its own deeds. The absence of a remaining argument means the truth has been conveyed, and coercive contention is set aside in favor of God’s final judgment. All will be gathered to Him, and the ultimate return is to His judgment and recompense.

translation: And those who dispute concerning Allah after He has been responded to—their dispute is invalid before their Lord, and upon them is wrath, and for them is a severe punishment.
interpretation: This verse means that once God’s truth and call have been accepted and people have responded in faith, those who continue to argue against it are not seeking the truth but resisting it out of stubbornness. Their arguments carry no weight or validity before their Lord; because of their willful opposition, they deserve divine anger and a painful punishment.

translation: Allah is the One who sent down the Book in truth and the Balance. And what can make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.
interpretation: Allah affirms that He alone revealed the Scripture with truth and established the standard of justice and moral equilibrium by which truth is weighed. The exact timing of the Hour is concealed from all creation, and no one can know it; yet it may be extremely close, so people should live in mindful readiness for it rather than presume they have time.

translation: Those who disbelieve in it seek to hasten it, while those who believe are fearful of it and know that it is the truth. Unquestionably, those who dispute concerning the Hour are in far-reaching error.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Hour as an inescapable reality that faith makes a person take seriously. Deniers mock it and demand it come quickly out of arrogance and unbelief, but believers are deeply apprehensive of it and certain that it is true. To argue about or deny the Hour is therefore not mere doubt but a profound misguidance, because it turns a person away from accountability before God and from the ultimate justice of the Hereafter.

translation: Allah is Subtle and Kind to His servants; He provides for whom He wills; and He is the Strong, the Almighty.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah’s care for His servants is subtle, all-encompassing, and wise: He knows their inner states and hidden needs, and He manages their provision with gentleness and mercy. His giving is not compelled by anyone; He grants material and spiritual sustenance to whom He wills according to His wisdom, and His withholding is also part of that wisdom. The verse then joins this tenderness with “the Strong, the Almighty” to show that His kindness is never weakness: He is fully capable, invincible, and none can resist or overturn His decree, so His servants should rely on Him alone.

translation: Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, We will increase for him in his harvest; and whoever desires the harvest of this world, We will give him thereof, but he will have no share in the Hereafter.
interpretation: This verse teaches that a person’s ultimate aim shapes their outcome: one whose striving is directed toward the Hereafter will receive God’s multiplied reward and success, while one whose effort is fixed solely on worldly gain may obtain some of it, yet by choosing the temporary over the eternal, he forfeits any portion in the Hereafter.

translation: Or do they have partners who have ordained for them a religion which Allah has not permitted? Were it not for the decisive word, it would have been judged between them. And indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: This is a rebuke to those who take other than God as lawgivers, following invented religious rules, prohibitions, and rites that God never authorized. It establishes that the sole right to legislate religion belongs to God; any religious law attributed to idols, false deities, or human authorities is invalid and is a form of associating partners with Him. The delay in punishment is not acceptance: God's prior decree—the decisive word—postpones the final judgment until the appointed time. On that Day He will settle all disputes, expose the false claims, and the unjust—those who legislated or followed religion without God's permission—will suffer a painful chastisement.

translation: You will see the wrongdoers apprehensive because of what they have earned, and it will inevitably befall them. But those who believe and do righteous deeds will be in the gardens of Paradise; they will have whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the great bounty.
interpretation: The verse portrays the inner state of the unjust: their own misdeeds produce dread, because the punishment they fear is not merely a threat but a reality closing in upon them. In contrast, faith joined with righteous action places a person in the flowering gardens of Paradise, where desire is not denied but fulfilled in the presence of the Lord. The ultimate blessedness is not only escape from punishment or attainment of pleasure, but the honor of nearness to God and His generous favor—a favor too great to be earned by works alone, and therefore called the great bounty.

translation: That is the good news with which Allah gives glad tidings to His servants who believe and do righteous deeds. Say, 'I do not ask you for it any reward, except affection for the near of kin.' And whoever earns a good deed, We increase for him good therein. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Appreciative.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the promise of divine good news belongs to those who combine sincere faith with righteous action. The Prophet is told to make clear that he seeks no personal payment for delivering the message; the only request he makes of the people is their love and affection toward his near kin. This is not a material wage but a means of drawing hearts toward the Prophet, his family, and the truth he brought. The verse then assures that whoever performs a good deed will have that good multiplied by God, and it closes by affirming that God is most forgiving of shortcomings and most appreciative of even the smallest acts of goodness.

translation: Or do they say, “He has fabricated a lie about Allah”? If Allah willed, He could seal up your heart. And Allah wipes out falsehood and establishes the truth by His words. Indeed, He knows well what is in the breasts.
interpretation: This verse confronts the slander that the Prophet fabricated revelation. It declares that God alone controls revelation and the human heart: if He willed, He could seal the Prophet’s heart, so the Prophet has no independent power to invent or conceal anything in God’s name. At the same time, God’s established way is to erase falsehood and confirm the truth through His revealed words. Because He knows the innermost secrets of every heart, He knows both the Prophet’s truthfulness and the accusers’ hidden motives. The verse therefore reassures the Messenger and warns the slanderers that falsehood cannot ultimately prevail against God’s truth.

translation: And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons misdeeds, and He knows what you do.
interpretation: The verse establishes that accepting repentance belongs exclusively to Allah: when a servant sincerely turns back to Him, He accepts that return and erases the sins that came before it. His pardon is not granted out of unawareness, for He fully knows every deed people perform, whether hidden or open; therefore repentance is a real return to the One whose mercy is coupled with complete knowledge, and sincerity in that return is what matters before Him.

translation: And He responds to those who believe and do righteous deeds, and increases them from His bounty. But the disbelievers—for them is a severe punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes that God’s response, acceptance, and generous increase are tied to faith joined with righteous action. “Responds” means He answers His believing servants, accepts their supplications and deeds, and draws them nearer to Himself. “Increases them from His bounty” means He does not reward them only according to strict measure; rather, He multiplies His favor beyond what their deeds deserve, out of pure grace. In contrast, disbelief cuts a person off from this divine response and increase, so the disbelievers face a severe punishment. Thus the verse teaches that faith and good works open the door to God’s overflowing generosity, while rejection of faith brings loss and painful consequence.

translation: And if Allah were to enlarge the provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth, but He sends down by measure as He wills. Indeed, He is, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing.
interpretation: This verse explains that God’s wisdom in distributing sustenance is a mercy, not a limitation. If everyone were given unlimited wealth and ease, many people would exceed their bounds, become arrogant, oppressive, and forgetful of God, using abundance as a means of corruption. Therefore God apportions provision according to His perfect knowledge of what each person needs, what they can bear, and what will serve their ultimate good. His being Acquainted and Seeing means He knows both the hidden motives and outward circumstances of His servants, so His giving and withholding are never arbitrary; they are precisely suited to His wisdom and justice, even when people do not understand the reasons behind differing shares of worldly provision.

translation: And He is the One who sends down the rain after they have despaired, and spreads His mercy. And He is the Guardian, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse teaches that relief and provision are entirely in Allah’s hand: He alone brings rain after drought and hopelessness, showing that human despair cannot limit divine mercy. His sending rain is a sign of His wider mercy, which He spreads to revive lands, hearts, and lives. As al-Wali, He carefully manages and protects the affairs of His servants; as al-Hamid, He is praiseworthy in every act, even when His wisdom is hidden before the relief arrives.

translation: And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and whatever living creatures He has spread throughout them. And He is capable of gathering them whenever He wills.
interpretation: This verse presents the creation of the heavens and the earth, along with the countless moving creatures dispersed throughout them, as clear signs of God's limitless power, wisdom, and sustaining care. The One who brought such vast and diverse life into existence and spread it across the universe is certainly not incapable of gathering all of it together again. The phrase “whenever He wills” affirms that resurrection and the final assembly are entirely under His decree and power; no creature can escape or resist it. Thus the verse links the evidence of creation to the certainty of the hereafter, reminding humanity that the same divine ability seen in originating and sustaining life will bring about the final gathering for judgment.

translation: And whatever misfortune befalls you, it is because of what your hands have earned; and He pardons much.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the trials and calamities that strike people are often the consequence of their own sins and misdeeds, while God, in His mercy, forgives and overlooks many of their faults rather than punishing them for every wrong. It calls the believer to self-accountability, repentance, and gratitude, and it reassures them that God’s pardon is vast, so no one should despair of His mercy even when facing the results of their actions.

translation: And you cannot escape on the earth, and you have no protector or helper besides Allah.
interpretation: This means that no human being can elude God's decree or escape His reach anywhere in the earth; nothing one relies on—power, wealth, or false deities—can shield one from His judgment, and apart from God there is neither a guardian to protect nor a helper to deliver. It affirms that all authority belongs solely to God, that every soul is subject to His will and accountability, and that seeking protection or aid from any other source is ultimately futile.

translation: And among His signs are the ships in the sea, like mountains.
interpretation: This verse directs attention to Allah’s power and favor in subjugating the sea and enabling great vessels to float and travel upon it. Though these ships are enormous, resembling towering mountains, they remain under His command, serving as a clear sign that calls people to reflect on His might, wisdom, and blessings, and to turn to Him in gratitude and worship.

translation: If He wills, He stills the wind, so they remain motionless on its surface. Indeed, in that are signs for every patient and grateful one.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the wind and the seas are entirely under Allah’s command. If He withholds or calms the wind, even great ships become fixed and unable to move, showing that human strength and technology depend completely on His permission. The sign is not merely in the calm itself but in what it reveals: Allah alone controls the causes and means by which people travel, trade, and survive. For the person who is deeply patient and deeply grateful, such moments are lessons. Patience is exercised when circumstances are difficult or delayed, and gratitude is shown when blessings come easily. Both attitudes recognize that every state—motion or stillness, ease or hardship—comes from Allah and carries a reason to turn to Him, trust Him, and thank Him.

translation: Or He could destroy them for what they have earned, but He pardons much.
interpretation: This verse means that if Allah willed, He could sink the ships and drown those aboard because of the sins they have committed, but out of His mercy He pardons many of their sins and does not punish them immediately. It teaches that human wrongdoing deserves consequences, yet Allah often overlooks and delays punishment, giving people opportunity to repent and showing His forbearance and forgiveness.

translation: And let those who dispute Our signs know that they have no escape.
interpretation: This verse warns that those who argue against God's revelations to undermine or deny them will come to know—when God's decree and judgment become inescapable—that there is no refuge, no fleeing place, and no way to avert the consequences of their denial. Their disputation cannot harm God or defeat His purpose; it only exposes their own misplaced confidence, for all avenues of escape are closed before His power.

translation: Whatever you have been given is only the enjoyment of the life of this world; but what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe and upon their Lord rely.
interpretation: This verse teaches that all worldly gifts, possessions, status, and pleasures are merely temporary provisions of this fleeting life. They are not the true measure of success or honor, nor should they become the ultimate goal of the heart. What Allah has prepared for the believers is superior in quality and everlasting in duration. This promise belongs specifically to those who combine sincere faith with trust in their Lord—meaning they depend upon Allah alone, accept His decree, seek His pleasure, and do not let the pursuit or loss of worldly things distract them from the eternal reward. Thus the verse calls the believer to weigh everything by its enduring value with Allah, and to place reliance on God rather than on the transient gifts of this world.

translation: And those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, and when they are angry, they forgive.
interpretation: This verse describes the conduct of the faithful: they restrain themselves from grave sins and shameful acts, and they do not let anger drive them to vengeance. When provoked or wronged, they choose to pardon and overlook, showing that true strength lies in self-control and magnanimity, and that forgiveness is an act of devotion and moral excellence.

translation: And those who respond to their Lord and establish prayer, and whose affair is [conducted by] consultation among themselves, and from what We have provided them they spend.
interpretation: This verse describes essential traits of the believing community: they answer their Lord’s call with sincere obedience, uphold the prayer as a constant act of worship and God-consciousness, conduct their shared affairs through mutual consultation rather than domination or unilateral decision, and freely spend from the provisions God has given them. It presents faith as both vertical devotion to God and horizontal responsibility toward others—worship, consultative justice, and generosity are inseparable marks of true submission.

translation: And those who, when oppression befalls them, defend themselves.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the believers are not passive in the face of injustice: when transgression or oppression is inflicted upon them, they are permitted to defend themselves and seek to restore their rights. It affirms the legitimacy of self-defense against aggression, while the broader Qur'anic context directs that forgiveness and reconciliation remain virtuous where possible, so retaliation is a right, not an obligation to vengeance.

translation: And the recompense of an evil deed is an evil deed the like of it; but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation—his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not like the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse establishes proportionate justice: a wrong may be requited only with its equivalent, without transgression or excess. Yet it directs the wronged person to a nobler path—voluntary pardon accompanied by reconciliation and reform. When someone gives up a rightful retaliation for the sake of peace and correction, Allah Himself guarantees the reward, for no human being can truly compensate that sacrifice. The closing statement warns that Allah does not love the unjust: neither those who commit wrongdoing nor those who exceed the limits in responding to it.

translation: And whoever defends himself after being wronged — those have no blame against them.
interpretation: This verse affirms that a person who stands up for himself and seeks redress after suffering injustice is not to be blamed or held liable; the fault and accountability belong to the aggressor. It establishes the legitimacy of resisting oppression and reclaiming one’s rights, provided the response remains within the bounds of justice and does not itself become an unjust transgression.

translation: The blame is only against those who oppress people and transgress in the land without right. Those will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes that blame and punishment fall upon those who wrong others and seek to dominate or corrupt the earth unjustly; their deliberate oppression and unjust aggression merit a painful torment in the Hereafter.

translation: And whoever is patient and forgives — indeed, that is among the matters of true resolve.
interpretation: This verse teaches that patient endurance and forgiveness are not signs of weakness, but acts of strong moral resolve. When a person has the ability to retaliate or hold a grudge yet chooses restraint and pardon, that is one of the highest and most difficult forms of self-mastery and virtue. Such forgiveness is praised as a matter requiring firm determination, because it conquers the ego’s desire for revenge and reflects trust in God and concern for peace.

translation: And whoever Allah sends astray, he has no protector after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, 'Is there any way to return?'
interpretation: This verse establishes that guidance and misguidance ultimately belong to Allah's decree and wisdom: when a person turns away from His guidance, Allah may leave him astray as a just consequence, and then no one—neither prophet, angel, nor any false object of reliance—can take His place as a protector or guide. On the Day of Judgment the wrongdoers will witness the torment and, in their desperation, ask whether there is any route back to the world. Their question is not a sincere promise of reform but an expression of utter regret; it comes too late, and there is no return. The verse thus warns people to seek Allah's guidance and act righteously while there is still time, for after death no intercessor or ally can reverse His decree.

translation: And you will see them being exposed to it, humbled by disgrace, looking with a faint, furtive glance. And those who believed will say, “Indeed, the losers are those who lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in an enduring punishment.”
interpretation: This verse describes the humiliation and regret of the wrongdoers on the Day of Resurrection as they are brought before Hellfire. Their disgrace is so intense that they cannot look directly; they only steal hidden, fearful glances. The believers then recognize the true nature of loss: it is not merely losing wealth or status, but losing one’s own soul and one’s family in the Hereafter through rejection of faith and persistence in wrongdoing. The verse concludes that the wrongdoers are not facing a temporary affliction but a punishment that remains fixed and ongoing, because their transgression was rooted in a settled denial of divine truth and accountability.

translation: And they will have no protectors to help them besides Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no way for him.
interpretation: This verse declares that on the Day when the wrongdoers face judgment, every presumed support besides God will collapse. The false deities, human patrons, wealth, power, or intercessors they relied on will neither rescue them nor shield them from God's decree. It teaches that true help and protection belong solely to God, and any hope placed in others is ultimately powerless. Then it states the terrifying consequence of divine abandonment: the one whom God leaves astray because of his own persistent rebellion, rejection of truth, and preference for misguidance has no route back to guidance and no escape from the punishment. God's leaving someone astray is not arbitrary injustice; it is the just outcome of a heart that has repeatedly turned away, so no path, plea, or helper remains.

translation: Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day that cannot be averted from Allah. On that Day you will have no refuge, and you will have no [means of] denial.
interpretation: This is a call to hasten toward Allah with faith, repentance, and obedience before the fixed Day of Judgment, which He has decreed and which no created being can delay or turn back. On that Day, no shelter, helper, or escape can shield anyone from Allah’s reckoning, and no denial, excuse, or rejection of the truth will benefit the soul; every person will meet the consequences of their deeds.

translation: So if they turn away, then We have not sent you as a keeper over them; upon you is only the conveyance. And indeed, when We cause man to taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if a misfortune befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, then indeed man is ungrateful.
interpretation: This verse defines the Prophet’s role as a deliverer of the divine message, not as one who can compel hearts or guard people against their own choices. It then exposes a flaw in human disposition: when ease and mercy come from God, a person often rejoices in a way that overlooks the Giver, but when hardship follows from his own deeds, he tends to complain and becomes ungrateful. The verse teaches that both blessing and adversity are tests, and that ingratitude is not caused by God’s injustice but by man’s forgetfulness, self-centeredness, and failure to recognize that mercy is from God and that consequences often come from one’s own actions.

translation: To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He grants to whom He wills females, and He grants to whom He wills males.
interpretation: This verse affirms that absolute sovereignty over all creation belongs to Allah alone. His creative will is unrestricted: He fashions and bestows offspring according to His wisdom, not according to human plans or desires. He may give daughters to some, sons to others, both to others, or none, as He wills. The mention of females first underscores that such a gift is entirely from His decree and refutes any notion that one gender is inherently a sign of divine favor or disfavor. It calls for contentment with Allah's decree and recognition that His knowledge and wisdom encompass what is best for His servants.

translation: Or He grants them both males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the giving of children—whether daughters, sons, both together, or none at all—is entirely subject to Allah’s decree, wisdom, and unrestricted will. Fertility and barrenness are not ultimate measures of a person’s worth or divine favor; they are part of Allah’s knowledge of what is best for each soul and His power to carry out whatever He wills. Thus a person should neither pride himself on offspring nor despair in childlessness, but should turn to Allah in supplication and trust, recognizing that His knowledge is perfect and His power is absolute.

translation: And it is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger to reveal, by His permission, what He wills. Indeed, He is Most High, Most Wise.
interpretation: This verse clarifies that Allah’s communication with prophets is not ordinary human speech. He may reveal directly to the heart, speak from behind a barrier as He spoke to Musa, or send an angelic messenger who conveys His command by His permission. Revelation is therefore entirely initiated by Allah’s will, and His exaltedness and wisdom govern how He guides whom He chooses.

translation: And thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will among Our servants. And indeed, you guide to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse means that the Qur’an is a spirit from God’s command: it revives hearts and minds with true life, just as a spirit gives life to the body. It was sent down by God’s decree, not by human acquisition. Before revelation, the Prophet Muhammad did not know the details of the Book or the reality of faith; this shows that prophetic knowledge is a pure divine gift. God then made this revelation a light that He uses to guide whichever of His servants He wills, meaning that true guidance belongs to God alone, who grants it through the light of the Qur’an. The Prophet’s mission is to call and lead people to the straight path—the path of Islam and pure monotheism—while God is the One who actually places guidance in hearts.

translation: The path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to Allah do all matters return.
interpretation: This verse identifies the straight path as belonging to Allah alone, the sole Owner and Sovereign of all creation. It teaches that the path pleasing to Him is not defined by human opinion or worldly authority, but by the Lord to whom everything in existence belongs.
